THE PATIENCE OF THE DARK
Book One of The Shattered Empire

By
Zachary King






Prologue
The clatter of dice and the soft scrape of cards on wood echoed faintly atop the wall. Three guards hunched over a battered little table, uniforms loose, helms pushed back, laughter kept low like children sneaking sweets. The pass yawned behind them, black and cold and entirely unobserved.
The voice cut through their mirth and left nothing. “What in the blue hells are you three doing?”
The cards froze in mid-play. All three guards looked up sharply, their faces draining when they saw who stood before them. Sergeant of the Guard Corren Vey loomed in the torchlight, broad-shouldered, scar-lined, his expression carrying the particular stillness of a man who has decided what he is going to do before he says a word.
They scrambled to their feet, snapping to attention. The Sergeant’s steps boomed as he stalked closer, towering over the little table as though it were an altar of shame.
“I asked a question,” Vey barked, the kind of voice men learned to move their feet at before thinking.
“Sir,” stammered Alix Sentel, the youngest of the three, his hand trembling at his side. “We were just… playing cards to pass the time. These shifts get long, and we…”
“Just killing time,” Vey repeated, his voice suddenly calm, almost soft. That softness was worse than a shout.
The woman across from Alix, Ashlyh Shaed, swallowed hard and found her courage. “Yes, sir. Only that. No gambling, no harm. Nothing ever happens up here. Not in years. Some say there’s nothing even left out there.”
Vey’s head turned slowly until his eyes locked on her. “Shaed, is it?”
“Ashlyh Shaed, sir.”
“Well, Ashlyh,” he said, and without warning, he seized the flimsy table with one hand and hurled it over the battlements. It clattered down the stone face, vanishing into the black maw of the pass below. His voice roared after it. “It is not your job to think. It is not your place to listen to rumors. You are the watch on this wall, the eyes that keep the rest of us breathing! Do you understand?”
The three snapped in unison, “Yes, sir!”
Corren Vey strode to the edge of the wall, looking out across the frontier. The wind tugged at his cloak, carrying the scents of pine and frost and something else, faint, bitter, like ash. He had smelled that on the wind before. The last time, three men had died before morning.
“You think it’s quiet because the nightmares are gone?” His voice dropped to a low growl. “No. They’re patient. They wait. We used to know that. We used to take recruits out beyond the walls, make them see what we fought. Some never came back. But those who did… they were soldiers, forged by fire.”
He tugged off his helm, and the torchlight caught the long scar running from the corner of his left eye down to his jaw.
“You three will have wall duty for a week. Midday to midnight. Dinner and washroom breaks only. If I hear one whisper of idleness, I’ll throw you over myself. If I catch you again, I’ll hang you for dereliction of duty.”
“Yes, sir!”
Vey’s glare softened, only slightly. “You’re lucky it was me. The new lord arrives today, and from what I hear, he’s stricter still.”
That brought their heads up. Ashlyh blinked. “New lord, sir?”
Vey nodded. “Aye. The king cycles them every three years. Sir Jorah is returning to his keep. His replacement is on the road even now. Sir Evens Garkins of Woford.”
All three guards froze. Alix breathed the name like a prayer. “The Evens Garkins? The one who led the coastal defense, who crushed the eastern rebellion?”
“And some say,” Ashlyh added, her voice hushed, “that he’s a Ringbearer. That he’s to rebuild and take command of a new Brotherhood, to march against the great evils when they return.”
The third guard, silent until now, leaned forward. “Is it true, Sergeant? Will he lead us to reclaim the frontier? To rebuild the Shared Empire?”
Vey snorted. “Children’s tales. I don’t know if the rings are real, nor do you. He comes to hold this pass, to keep the lands of men safe. That is all.”
The third guard straightened. There was a strange light in his eyes. “The rings are real.” He said it without heat, without investment, the way you say a thing you know and have known a long time. “No man chooses them. They choose their bearer.”
Vey’s brow furrowed. Something about the man’s tone scraped across his instincts like a whetstone. He stepped closer, squinting. “Who are you again? I thought I knew every man on this wall.”
Something in the space between his question and the answer told him more than the answer would. His body knew it first. His hand was already moving to his hilt when the guard finally smiled. It was wrong, too slow, too deliberate. With each step, he seemed to grow, his shadow stretching, the torchlight bending oddly around him.
The other two turned. Alix's hand went to his sword without touching it. Ashlyh said nothing. Her face said everything.
The false guard’s helm hit the stones with a hollow clang. His face melted pale, features smoothing into something inhuman. The nose was gone, the flesh too perfect, his eyes black and flat and lit from somewhere that wasn't light.
“You were right, Sergeant,” the thing said, its voice warped, too calm. “We are the nightmares. And tonight we become yours again.”
Alix staggered back, breath broken. “What are you?”
The creature smiled. “You can call me Dar. It was a good game, Alix. You too, Ashlyh. But all games end.” He drew a dagger, its blade catching no light. “We will find the rings. And Lucent bids me tell you something first.”
Vey’s sword rasped free. “Lucent?”
Dar’s grin widened. “Very good. His message is simple.”
An arrow hissed from the dark and buried itself in Alix’s throat. He collapsed, choking, blood pooling fast. A second shaft slammed into Ashlyh’s eye. She fell straight, the way bodies do.
Vey roared. His sword was in his hand. His feet found the stance before he told them to. “Come then!”
Dar blurred forward, faster than a striking viper. His dagger punched into Vey’s gut, the force lifting the Sergeant off his feet before he was slammed down beside the corpses of his guards.
Pinned, gasping, Vey spat blood and clutched weakly at the blade.
Dar bent low, his voice intimate, his breath cold. “The time of man is over.”
He wrenched the dagger sideways, then yanked it free, leaving Vey writhing. From the shadows, two green-skinned creatures scuttled forward, Goblins twisted by some darker hand, their eyes gleaming sickly yellow.
“Take positions,” Dar ordered. “Loose arrows until their screams drown the bells. I’ll open the gate.”
As Vey tried to drag himself upright, the screaming had already started below. He knew the voices. Some of them, he knew. Dar crouched beside him once more. “No, no. Stay alive, old soldier. Bleed, but not too much. You’ll live long enough to watch us gut your keep from within. You’ll hear your men die and know it was your failure that let it happen.”
Corren Vey lay on the stones, breath ragged, hot blood pooling under him. He reached for his sword, but his fingers were too slick to grip it.
Dar crouched low, pale face inches from his. The creature’s voice dropped to a whisper, each word cold as river ice.
“You’ll live, Sergeant. That’s your curse. You’ll wake with this wound, with the memory of your men’s screams, with their blood on your boots. And you will carry my master’s words to every corner of your kingdom.”
Vey snarled, but it came out wet, a bubbling growl.
Dar smiled wider, dagger still slick with his blood. “Lucent says the time of man is over. Remember that. Speak it. Spread it. Let them know their walls are dust and their lords are shadows clinging to dying light.”
He twisted the dagger once more, not to kill, but to sear the memory into nerve and bone, then ripped it free. Vey arched in agony, teeth gritted against the scream that tore from him anyway.
The Goblins cackled from the parapet as they loosed their first volley, arrows raining down into the courtyard. Shouts erupted, the clang of steel, the crack of alarm bells.
Dar stood and looked down at him one last time. “Bleed. Crawl. Live. That is your task tonight, Sergeant. A witness is worth more than a corpse.”
Then, like smoke, he slipped away toward the gatehouse, his shadow melting into the night.
Corren Vey clutched his side, the world swimming. Every breath was agony, but his eyes stayed open, fixed on the bodies of Alix and Ashlyh, on their faces slack in death. He forced the sight into his mind, knowing he would never escape it.
He wanted to close his eyes. To surrender. But the thought of Dar’s grin, of Lucent’s name, kept him awake. If his men’s lives were the price, then his duty now was to bear witness. He got his elbow under him. An inch. Then another. To crawl, to live, and to tell the tale of the night the nightmares returned.







Chapter One
Weslin pounded down the stone corridors of the palace, his short legs and rounded frame protesting with every stride. The air was cool and smelled faintly of lamp oil and old dust, stirred by the echo of his hurried steps. His lungs burned, each breath louder than the slap of his boots on the polished floor. Shadows swayed with each flicker of torchlight, stretching long across carved columns and banners that lined the hall. Once, he nearly clipped the edge of a marble pedestal, his shoulder grazing the cold stone before he pushed harder.
This was no ordinary sprint. The King himself had sent him. These were the King’s halls, solemn and echoing, and his duty weighed heavier with every step. Pages did not run in the royal palace. They walked with quiet dignity, heads bowed, every movement rehearsed. But when the King sent you to fetch a knight, you did not go at your own pace.
The corridor curved sharply, its vaulted ceiling drawing his eye up for just a heartbeat to where painted heraldry looked down on him: golden crowns, silver blades, crimson dragons that seemed to stir in the torchlight. He rounded the bend too fast, boots skidding on the smooth floor, nearly pitching him into a wall. He caught himself, chest heaving, heart pounding in his ears.

Ahead, framed in the glow of a sconce, stood a broad-shouldered man adjusting the clasp of a dark, tailored cloak. He moved with the unhurried care of one preparing to depart, as though the palace and its duties no longer bound him.
“Sir Harmon… Please! Hold!” Weslin wheezed, the last word scraping out of him. He tried to wave, stumbled, and collided headlong into a suit of decorative armor.
The crash was thunderous. Steel plates clattered across the polished floor, a spear rolled into the shadows, and a bowl of glass beads, left on a nearby stand as decoration, upended, scattering across the hall like marbles. The echoes reached clear to the kitchens.
Flat on his back amid the wreckage, Weslin shut his eyes tight. His chest heaved. Every breath was fire in his throat. Glass beads pressed into his back through the tunic. Somewhere nearby, a piece of armor was still rocking, its clatter ticking down to silence like a rebuke. The first time Gus trusts me with page duty, and I've ruined it. A feast day of all days, and I've ruined everything.
A shadow fell over him. “You know,” came a voice, unhurried, faintly amused, “I’ve a bear rug that lands the same way. Quieter, though.” A faint pause. “Less red in the face. And hairier.”
Weslin cracked one eye open. Sir Harmon Diem loomed above him, one eyebrow cocked, the hint of a grin pulling at his mouth.
With a grunt, Harmon lowered himself onto one knee beside the boy. His joints cracked, and he winced. “Gods, these knees,” he muttered. “Too many miles. Word of advice, lad, never get old. You may look wiser, but your joints will betray you for it.”
He leaned closer, brushing aside beads and resting a firm hand on Weslin’s shoulder. “No cuts. No broken bones?” His gaze moved once, assessing, already knowing the answer. Weslin shook his head quickly, still too winded to speak.
“Good lad.” Harmon slid an arm under his back and another beneath his arm, then lifted him in one smooth motion. Even from one knee, the knight’s strength was undeniable. He set Weslin carefully on his feet and steadied him until the boy found his balance.
Only then did Harmon push himself upright. He rose with another grunt, the effort clear in his movements. Straightening his cloak, he gave a crooked smile. “Sadists made stone floors,” he muttered.
Weslin’s face burned hotter as Harmon brushed a few stray beads from his tunic. Weslin wobbled, caught himself, and looked over the disaster: scattered beads, crooked armor plates, and one lonely spear rolling slowly into the shadowed edge of the hall. “Steady, lad,” Harmon said with a small smile. “Which of you came off worse?”
Weslin gulped for air, words broken by his ragged breathing. “The King… sent me. He needs you… before you leave.”
“Ah,” Harmon said, the grin widening. “So that noise wasn’t wasted. Well struck, page. You’ve carried out your duty, whether by feet or by falling.” He clapped Weslin on the shoulder hard enough to jostle him.
Weslin wobbled, caught himself, and looked over the disaster: scattered beads, crooked armor plates, and one lonely spear rolling slowly into the shadowed edge of the hall. Weslin swayed, then steadied. “Not the Grand Hall, sir,” he added quickly. “His Majesty said… his private study.”
That drew Harmon’s brows up. For a moment, the humor left his face, replaced by something sharper, thoughtful, edged with concern. Then it was gone, replaced by the genial mask again.
He tugged his cloak more securely across his shoulders and motioned down the corridor. “Now then, His Majesty waits. Let’s keep him from waiting longer. And mind the beads. I’d rather not end up on the floor beside you.”
Harmon had just steadied Weslin on his feet when the corridor filled with the swish of silks and the hard stamp of boots. A tall man in a fur-lined coat of the royal colors strode in, chambermaids trailing like frightened birds. His eyes swept the wreckage, toppled armor, scattered beads, boy and knight, and his face curled with disdain.
“What disgrace is this?” he snapped. His voice cracked like a whip. His gaze landed on Weslin. “Of course. You. I should have known. Trouble has a habit of finding you. Though I imagine it saves time when it needn’t look far,” Cotter said coldly in his nasally voice. “Look, ladies, is he even wearing a page’s tunic now? On a feast night?” He shook his head slowly, savoring the venom. “Gus must have taken leave of his senses. He and I shall have words later.”
Weslin opened his mouth, but Cotter cut him down with a hiss. “Silence. You’ll clean this wreck, now, and tomorrow you’ll take ten lashes for the shame of it. Perhaps pain will teach what instruction has not.”
The words struck harder than a hand, and Weslin wilted. Harmon’s voice entered, calm, deep, carrying iron under velvet. “Enough.”
The steward startled, as though seeing him for the first time. He gave a stiff bow, the edge of arrogance still in his spine. “Sir… forgive me. I’m Nicholas Cotter, head steward of Fowther Palace. A busy day, you understand. Pages must be kept in line, especially on a feast night. One careless boy can shame an entire household before the first bell is rung. I assure you, this staff strives for perfection.” Nicholas’s glare shot daggers at Weslin, “We try to limit the incompetence, yet some seep through. What is one to do?” 
“Incompetence,” Harmon repeated, his tone dropping like a hammer. He took a step forward, boots grinding on glass beads. “Yes. I see it plainly.” Harmon pauses for a heartbeat. “Yours.”
The chambermaids froze. Cotter’s face drained of color. “This boy,” Harmon pressed on, laying a hand firmly on Weslin’s shoulder, “just saved you from explaining to the King why I nearly missed His Majesty’s summons. An audience that your staff told me not ten minutes ago I didn’t have. He ran himself near to collapse. Fell, bloodied, humiliated himself, all to do his duty.” Harmon’s eyes, sharp as drawn steel, locked on Cotter. “That is loyalty. That is courage. And you would reward it with lashes?”
Cotter swallowed. His lips parted, but Harmon snapped a hand up sharply. “Silence. You’ve said enough.” Harmon didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t need to. “If this is the measure of your judgment, then this palace is far less well run than its gilded walls pretend. Fine stone and polished floors don’t excuse poor stewardship,” he said flatly.
Cotter flinched as though struck. The chambermaids exchanged glances, their silence louder than whispers. Harmon’s voice softened only when he turned back to Weslin. “Your name is Weslin, isn’t it?”
“Yes, sir,” he answered.
“Weslin. I require a companion this evening. Walk with me.”The boy blinked, wide-eyed, then nodded with such force his hair flopped into his face.
“Then you’ll walk with me to His Majesty’s Chambers.” Harmon gave him a reassuring squeeze on the shoulder. “No lashes. No punishment. You are with me now.”
At last, he turned back to Cotter, his tone once more edged with that polished steel. “See this mess cleared before His Majesty hears of it. He expects order in his halls, not shrill voices and toppled armor.” He paused, as though reconsidering, then added almost kindly: “Still, for all its flaws, this palace is one of the finer ones I’ve seen. You should be proud… provided you learn to keep it worthy of its walls.”
Cotter’s mouth opened, closed, and he gave a jerky bow. “Yes, Sir Harmon. At once.”
With that, Harmon and Weslin moved on together down the corridor. Weslin matched his stride to the knight’s, chest swelling, the sting of Cotter’s venom fading beneath the weight of Harmon’s words. For the first time, he felt neither chastised nor chosen.
As they reached the end of the hall, Cotter’s voice carried after them, sharp and flustered: “Let’s get this cleaned up, but you heard the man!”
Both Harmon and Weslin glanced at each other, and the same small smile tugged at their lips before they walked on.
As the steward’s voice faded behind them, Harmon and Weslin walked in silence. The boy’s stride was straighter now, chest lifted as though the knight’s hand still rested on his shoulder.
“Thank you, sir,” Weslin said, his voice quieter than he intended. “For what you did back there.”
Harmon glanced at him, a hint of humor in his steel-gray eyes. “Nothing to thank me for. You had a mission, and you carried it out. Running half the palace, crashing through armor, nearly killing yourself to do it… That’s more than some grown men would dare. I could hardly stand by and let your devotion be mistaken for mischief.”
Weslin flushed, unsure if it was from pride or embarrassment. “Still, sir. I’ll remember it.”
“Do that.” He let the silence take a breath before continuing. “But remember this. Remember it as well, loyalty earns enemies first. Friends come later.” 
They turned into another corridor, where two towering carved-oak doors loomed ahead. Weslin slowed, glanced to either side, then stepped toward a seemingly plain stretch of wall. From his pocket, he drew a small iron key. He slid it into an almost invisible hole and turned it. With a soft click, a hidden panel eased open, revealing a narrow passage beyond.
“This way, sir.” He produced a small iron key from his pocket that Gus had pressed into his hand for this errand, along with strict instructions on where to use it. 
Harmon’s grin spread as the wall shifted. “Ah. One of my favorite things about this palace. The secrets are tucked away where no one expects. King Wymark had a gift for such things. I mean Wymark the First, not Edric, the current King’s grandsire.”
They stepped inside. Torchlight guttered in iron brackets, their flames low and flickering. The air was cool and damp, carrying the faint scent of dust and stone. The stairwell curled upward, its steps worn smooth by centuries of secret use. Narrow alcoves yawned on either side, some empty, others filled with half-rotted crates or forgotten banners sagging in cobwebs.
The ceiling pressed low, the walls closed, and every sound seemed to echo, Harmon’s boots striking stone, Weslin’s quicker steps, even the rasp of their breathing. Strange markings etched into the stone walls hinted at old masons’ hands, wards, or signatures, perhaps, long faded by time. Weslin almost touched one, then thought better of it. Some things looked like they didn’t want to be touched. “This place feels… different,” Weslin whispered. “Like no one should be here.”
“That’s the point,” Harmon replied. His hand brushed the wall as he climbed, fingers tracing grooves in the stone. “A king’s strength isn’t only in what is seen, but what is hidden.”
Weslin hesitated, then ventured: “You knew the Mad…” He stopped himself too late.
Harmon’s head turned sharply, eyes narrowing. “Know your place, boy,” Harmon said sharply yet showing some restraint in his tone. “King Liam Wymark was a great man. My friend. Do not dishonor his memory with tavern-born names.”
Weslin swallowed hard, his earlier confidence faltering. “Yes, sir. Sorry, sir. It won’t happen again.”
The knight’s gaze softened with the weight of years. He let his palm rest flat on the cold stone, eyes distant. “It is a shame what befell him near the end. But he had his reasons. Another word of advice, son, never speak ill of the dead. It is bad form.”
“Yes, sir,” Weslin whispered. He glanced back, for the first time seeing the true age in Harmon’s face, not hidden by humor.
“Good lad.” Harmon let the silence settle. Together they climbed, their torchlit shadows stretching and swaying along the narrow walls, until another disguised panel swung open at Weslin’s touch. The hidden way delivered them into the warm light of the King’s private study.
Though the midday sun still shone beyond the palace walls, the King’s windowless study glowed with lamplight and fire, a room that felt like night no matter the hour.
“Sir, he told me once I got you here, to invite you to sit. He’ll be alone shortly. Do you need anything else of me?”
“I am good. But don’t go far, I might need you soon.”
“Of course. I’ll be just outside,” Weslin said as he made his way to exit the study.
“Very good, son.”
Weslin bowed and slipped through the main door. As it closed, Harmon turned toward the far wall. A single painting dominated the chamber, a sweeping battle scene, lances lowered, banners snapping, soldiers triumphant. He froze before it. At first glance, it was reverence, but then his jaw clenched, his breath shortened. His hand trembled until he forced it flat against his thigh. Sweat prickled at his hairline.
The painting dissolved in his mind. He heard the clang of steel and the screams of dying men. The copper tang of blood rose thick in his throat, and the sour stink of smoke and charred flesh seemed to fill the chamber. Sweat beaded across his brow and ran down his temples. His hands clamped into fists, knuckles white, as his body locked against the onslaught of memory.
Faces surged forward, more vivid than oil on canvas: comrades cut down, friends’ eyes glazing, mouths open in screams that still echoed across his nights. He could smell their sweat, the iron of blood splashing on stone. It was as if the chamber itself had become the battlefield.
The painter had captured victory. Harmon saw only the dying. His knuckles had gone white. He didn’t remember making a fist. His chest tightened, breath coming shallow, until a voice broke through like a blade drawn behind him….
“Father commissioned that before his death. He said if he were to lead our people, he had to be reminded of the price paid for their freedom. We placed it here, where he always liked to sit.”
Harmon blinked. The battle, the screams, the blood receded like smoke in a sudden wind. He turned.
A man stood behind him, not yet thirty, clad simply in black and blue with gold piping, the crest of his house on his chest.
Edric’s smile carried warmth, but his eyes studied the older man carefully. Harmon dragged a hand across his forehead, wiping the sheen of sweat away, though his fingers still trembled faintly. The King’s gaze lingered on the gesture, but he said nothing. Harmon dropped to one knee. “Your Highness.”
“As you were, Sir Harmon,” King Edric said gently. “I invited you here to talk, not for a ceremony.”
Slowly, the knight rose, his body still taut. “Of course, Your Majesty,” Harmon said, giving the title just enough weight to remind Edric he would not be nudged out of it.
“Harmon… you’re family,” Edric said warmly. “Like an uncle. When we’re in private, how many times have I asked you to call me Edric? You have stood with my family since the very beginning.”
“At least once more, Your Highness,” Harmon replied, with the faintest ghost of a smile.
“Stubborn as ever.” Edric chuckled, then sobered, his gaze flicking toward the painting again. “You and my father were close. Brothers in all but name. You’ve given me that same warmth. For that, I’m grateful.” He gestured toward a couch in the chamber’s center. “Please, sit. Wine? Anything?”
“No, sire. Not right now.” Harmon lowered himself onto the couch.
Edric turned a chair to face him. “Then let’s speak plainly. Governor Drake is expected shortly, but until then, what was it you wished to tell me?”
Harmon straightened. “Your Grace, I’ll not waste time with preamble. My days as your sword are drawing to a close. I cannot fight as I once did. The realm deserves a commander still in his prime. A commander who’s one with the men.”
The King leaned forward, voice low. “You’ve carried this realm longer than most men carry their own lives. If you say your time has come, I’ll hear it. But why now?”
Harmon’s jaw tightened, just for a moment. “Because I can feel it,” he said quietly. “I’m not the man I was, and I won’t pretend to be.”
The King studied him, the warmth in his expression cooling into something more measured. “If this is to be done, it will not be done in haste. A transition like this demands ceremony. The court will expect it. The people will as well.” He leaned back slightly. “We announce it at the feast. Let it be known properly.”
Harmon shook his head once, firmly. “With respect, sire, the realm won’t wait for ceremony. Nor will our enemies.” His voice sharpened, not in defiance, but in urgency. “If I’m to step down, it must be done with purpose, not pageantry.”
He held the King’s gaze a moment longer, then pressed forward. “We mustn’t linger long,” Harmon said firmly. “We have enemies all around. Just as age does not wait, neither does war. We need a replacement in place soon.”
The King was silent, though his mind began to move as swiftly as a general counting soldiers on a battlefield. Names rose unbidden in his head. Each of them had their merits, yet one was too cautious, another too volatile, and the last too untested. None carried the weight of the man before him.
The King leaned back, studying Harmon as though measuring the weight of the words. “You, stepping away,” Edric said slowly. “I never thought I would see the day. Yet time comes for all of us, even for the Sword of the Realm. Tell me, then, what lies ahead for the great Harmon Diem, once this burden is set down?”
Harmon let the silence stretch before he answered. His gaze was steady, though weariness edged his voice. At last, he drew a long breath. “There is one more service I would render, sire. I would not fade into idleness. To the northwest of Kensington lies an island, scarcely charted. Some say it is rich. I would lead men there, raise a township, and serve as its Mayor, its lord and keeper. Not to guard what already stands, but to expand.”
Edric’s expression hardened. “Expansion is rarely seen as charity. It is seen as an ambition. And ambition starts wars.”
“I have weighed it,” Harmon said quickly. “That is why it must not be the Crown’s hand, but mine. Let it be my venture, with your sponsorship. Grant me ships, supplies, and a small force. With your blessing, the guilds will shoulder the cost. Without it…” He shook his head. “Without it, the dream dies on the tide. And, sire, in all my years, I have never asked for myself. Only for you. Only for Opindale.”
The King did not answer at once. He rose slowly, crossing to the great map table. One hand rested on the parchment, but his gaze was far beyond it.
“I must consider,” he said at last, voice quiet. “Too many moves at once. For the kingdom. For you. For all of us.” His words cut further discussion to its end. The silence stretched, heavy and unresolved.
Harmon sat back, the weight of years and memory pressing on him. The painting loomed behind, its painted banners forever bright, while in his mind the screams of the fallen refused to fade.
Edric turned back around toward Harmon as the chamber doors opened. A short balding man in a plain brown robe entered first, followed by Governor Meridian Drake of Aldoria in a sky-blue tunic edged with sea-green piping. Weslin trailed close behind.
Weslin snapped to attention. “Your Highness. The Governor of Aldoria, Lord Meridian Drake, and Chancellor Ayhmeri.”
Chancellor Ayhmeri bowed. The King gave a curt nod. Ayhmeri gestured to Weslin. “Close the doors and see that we are not disturbed.”
“Yes, Chancellor.” With a moment’s hesitation, Weslin obeyed and slipped out.
“Your Highness,” Drake began, “thank you for this invitation. It is an honor.”
“I am honored as well,” Edric replied, his tone cordial but heavy. “Aldoria is a true ally, and you are a true friend. I only wish this were a simple courtesy before tonight’s feast. But there is a second purpose. Please, sit.”
The Chancellor remained standing while Drake lowered himself to the couch. “I believe privacy is best,” the King said, “for what you are about to hear.”
At the words, Harmon’s attention sharpened, his earlier thoughts dissolving. He reclaimed his seat near the King. Drake leaned forward, brows drawn tight. “Your Highness, clarify the matter.”
The King gestured toward the knight. “First, meet Sir Harmon Diem. My sword, and commander of my armies. He is here as my counsel, and now yours.” A flicker of unease crossed Drake’s face as the King continued.
“Stormhaven has fallen victim to a Veydrassil attack. Reports are scarce, as most of our embassy staff are here for the feast, but what has reached me speaks of devastation.”

The Governor’s color drained. “My wife… my children. They stayed behind.” His voice cracked, panic breaking through. “Are they alive? Tell me!” His hands clawed at his tunic.
The King’s voice was steady, though grave. “I have no word on them yet. Our people inside the embassy walls are trapped, sending what they can. I will press them harder, but news will come slowly.”
Drake surged to his feet, trembling. “I depart at once. Grant me leave, Your Grace.”
“Meridian,” the King snapped, shedding all ceremony, “you cannot.”
Drake’s face twisted, anger and terror blending. “And why not?”
“Because you will walk into a trap. If the Veydrassil still occupy Stormhaven, this is no raid. They remain for a reason. If you go, they will cut you down before you take ten steps inside your city,” answered Harmon, speaking up for the King.
“They are my people,” Drake shot back, voice raw. “My countrymen. They need their leader.”
“With what force do you intend to stand?” Edric’s tone cut like steel. “You came with thirty men at most. Do you think their deaths alongside yours would aid Aldoria? What would it do to those still resisting, to see their Governor slain by an oppressor’s hand?”
Drake faltered, breath shaking. “Then you would have me sit here and call it wisdom.”
“No,” the King said firmly. “You will not ride to your death. Sit. We will send aid, but it will take time. Forces must be prepared, supply lines drawn, allies secured.”
Drake’s fists clenched, but he sank back down. The King turned to Harmon. “Sir Harmon, your counsel?”
The chamber was heavy with silence, the weight of unspoken fear pressing in. Drake’s eyes burned, his family’s faces vivid in his mind, and no answer came to soothe them. The thought of them trapped in Stormhaven hung between them all, unresolved, suffocating.
Harmon sat back slowly, his eyes narrowing as if he were staring past the walls of the chamber into the city itself. His breath came long and measured, though the furrows on his brow deepened with each passing moment.
His hand lifted almost absently to his chest. The silver chain there caught the lamplight, and his fingers closed around the plain ring that hung from it. He pressed it to his palm, knuckles whitening, as though he were praying with it or drawing some strength through its familiar weight.
The silence stretched. Edric’s gaze flicked toward the old knight, but he said nothing, waiting. Drake’s breathing remained ragged, the governor teetering between anger and despair.
Harmon kept his eyes down, thumb running across the curve of the ring as though tracing a memory in the metal. His jaw tightened. When he finally raised his head, his gaze was steady, but the room could feel the heaviness of the thoughts behind it.
“For starters—” 
“They are in a private meeting!” Weslin’s voice cracked with effort as he tried to hold back a man in armor.
“Get off me, boy, I have news for my governor,” the intruder snapped, shoving past him.
“Weslin, it is all right,” the King ordered, raising a hand. “Thank you. Back to your post.” Weslin released his grip, bowed quickly, and slipped out, closing the doors behind him.
The man in armor strode forward, saluting. “Your Highness. Governor. I bring urgent news.”
The King frowned. “Master of Arms Terance, what is this sudden intrusion?”
Drake stiffened. “I already know, unless you have something else to add.”
Terance blinked. “How, sire? The runner has just arrived.”
The Governor’s head snapped toward him. “This is not about Stormhaven?”
Confusion spread across Terance’s face. “Stormhaven? No, my lord. This is from the north. The pass has been attacked. An army of beasts from the Abandoned Plains. The Northern Garrison is believed to have fallen.”
The chamber fell silent. The King’s voice broke first, low and grim. “God above…”
Drake muttered, “Creator help us all.”
Chancellor Ayhmeri said nothing, his lips pressed thin.
Harmon stepped closer, voice steady. “Casualties? Any confirmation?”
“None, sir,” Terance admitted. “The runner and five others made it here. One was gravely wounded. They saw flames consuming the garrison as they fled.”
The weight of the words hung in the air. Then Terance asked softly, “What happened in Stormhaven?”
The King’s reply was flat. “An attack by the Veydrassil.” Terance cursed under his breath, then fell silent.
All eyes turned to Harmon. He stood with his head bowed, fingers tightening around the ring that hung at his chest as if in prayer. Then, in a single breath, he lifted his chin, his posture shifting, energy surging back into him.
“That alters the field,” Harmon said with command returning to his tone, straightening as if pulled by a line. “Too many questions, too little certainty. We lack knowledge, and that is the greatest danger of all.” He turned first to Terance. “Ready, every man. The palace goes to full alert, garrisons are armed, and walls are watched. Assume siege until proven otherwise. You have my blessing to take charge of securing here.”
Then to the King: “Sire, coordinate with Governor Drake and Chancellor Ayhmeri. Aid to Aldoria must be planned now, but without leaving us blind at home.”
His tone sharpened, leaving no space for debate. “We cannot chase shadows. Not anymore. If Stormhaven burns and the pass is lost, the enemy is already moving faster than we are. We must take control before this spiral completely beyond us.”
The chamber pulsed with his words, urgency hanging thick. Harmon paused, eyes narrowing in thought. No one in that room would be followed to a tavern. No one except a boy who looked like he was running an errand for the kitchens. “Weslin. Back in here.”
The doors opened again, and the boy hurried inside. “Over here, lad.”
Weslin came at a trot. “Yes, sir?”
“I have a task for you. Do you accept it?” Asked Harmon.
Weslin’s grin was instant. “Yes… I mean, yes, sir,” he said.
“Good. Do you know the Broken Bolt?” Harmon asked.
“Yes, sir,” Weslin said, nodding his head. “It’s down the road from my da’s bakery.”
“Then go there. Ask for Luca. Tell him…” Harmon leaned closer, his voice dropping, “The pawn has moved to King’s five. Order food. Sit and wait for me. Understood?”
“Yes, sir. Pawn to King’s five.” His voice carried a thrill at the secret.
“Exactly. And Weslin, tell no one where you are going or what you carry. I chose you because no one will suspect you, and because I trust you. From this moment on, you are my squire.”
The boy’s eyes went wide, his face lighting as if the whole world had opened. He nodded so hard his hair flopped into his face, then sprinted out through the doors, leaving them swinging wide as his footsteps faded down the corridor.
Harmon watched him go. The doors swung back once, twice, and settled. In the lamplight, his expression had changed, not the quiet amusement he wore in corridors, but something closer to a general who has just put his best piece on the board. 
He turned back to the King. “Sire, I would have it made formal. Weslin is now my squire, effective immediately.”
Edric studied him for a moment, then gave a slow nod. “Granted. I think the boy will rise to it.”
“Good,” Harmon said, adjusting his cloak. He turned toward the door.
“Where are you going?” Governor Drake asked, his voice tight.
Harmon’s reply was sharp, final. “To put a torch in that fog. I’ll return in five hours, and we’ll see what it burns away.” And with that, he stepped out, leaving silence in his wake.






Chapter Two
The Broken Bolt sang with life. Even with the sun high over Opindale, the Broken Bolt roared like midnight, a perfect place to disappear. The festival crowds crammed the benches. Fiddles shrieked, boots stamped in time, mugs slammed down hard enough to froth ale over the rims. Dice clicked across a back table while half the room bellowed a song the other half didn’t know. Smoke from the hearth curled up into the beams and clung to the rafters, giving the lamplight a low golden haze.
Harmon stepped in, his cloak wrapped around his shoulders and a walking stick in hand, his gait measured and slow. To the eye, he was just another weary old traveler. To those who truly watched, his steel-gray eyes were anything but tired. He let the door fall shut behind him and gave the room a sweep that seemed casual, but marked every angle.
Serving girls threaded the crowd with the precision of a drill line, skirts flashing candlelight as they spun between tables. At the bar, a heavyset man bent over his plate like a starving wolf, elbows high and greedy. Lovers laughed too loudly in a corner booth. Two soldiers rattled dice, both cheating with the kind of clumsy confidence that only grows after six mugs of ale. Harmon watched it all pass, not for the charm of it but for the cracks beneath.
The knife was strapped to a boot under a table. The quick nod two men exchanged across the room before pretending not to see each other. The tavern was a chorus of laughter and clatter, but Harmon’s skin prickled. “Merriment this loud rarely comes without purpose,” he said to himself in a low tone.
Near the far wall, a boy sat perched on the edge of his chair. Weslin. His chin was lifted high, trying for manly, but his feet didn’t quite touch the floor. Two mugs waited untouched before him, beads of condensation sliding down the sides, and he guarded them with all the fierce loyalty of a page on his first errand.
Harmon almost smiled at the sight. Almost.
He moved deeper into the room, cloak brushing chair legs. It didn't take him long to make his way to the bar. Harmon slid into an empty seat at the bar, leaning his walking stick against the counter. He tried to catch the attention of a passing serving girl, but she was gone before he could raise a hand. Another slipped past with three mugs balanced on a tray, never looking his way. He gave a faint grunt and settled in, foot tapping despite himself to the fiddle’s quick tune.
From the corner of his eye, he noticed a man in a plain tunic rise from the table behind him. The man gave an irritated sigh and ducked behind the bar, vanishing into a small cove, cleverly set where the press of bodies and poor angles would have hidden it even from a careful eye. Harmon turned slightly in his seat, studying the angles he’d missed, then faced forward again just as the man returned and came to stand before him.
“What can I get you, sir?”
Harmon blinked. The man towered over most of the room, shoulders broad. Not a barkeep. The thought arrived before Harmon could stop it. He filed it and said nothing.” Then keep the full second description intact. 
“I’ll take your best ale,” Harmon said.
“Short or full?”
“It is my night off,” Harmon replied dryly. “Make it a full.”
“That will be a copper.”
Harmon arched a brow. “That is all?”
The man shrugged once. “Yes! Should stop any complaints.” He turned to draw the drink, leaving Harmon to study the crowd again.
By the time Harmon looked back, another figure had taken the barkeep’s place. Short and stocky, he was not built for intimidation, but the way he carried himself demanded respect all the same. His face was weathered, the kind of face that seemed older than its years, each line etched by a lifetime of hard choices and harder living. He reached for a glass behind the bar, poured, and raised it to his lips in an easy motion, drinking while Harmon studied him in silence.
“What is one of the King’s polished gems doing in a pit like this?” the man asked, his Orin accent rough and heavy.
Harmon reached for his mug of ale. “Looking for you.” Harmon took the ale, drank, and set it down with care. “Men like you don't stray far from what they know. Where else was I going to find a piece of dung like Adin?” 
They locked eyes across the bar, silence pressing tight between them. Adin’s grin split into a laugh that shook his shoulders, one hand slapping the counter, causing Harmon’s ale to jump in its glass. “By the gods! Time spared you nothing.”
“And you,” Harmon said, “still as ugly as the day I met you.”
Adin’s grin softened, though his eyes stayed sharp. “Your patrols picked up some of my lads. Are you here to drag me in?”
“If I meant to arrest you,” Harmon said flatly, “we wouldn’t be talking.”
The answer hung, sharp and final, until Adin laughed again, lower this time. “Fair. You have never softened.”
Harmon leaned back, gaze sweeping the bar, his meaning clear. “Not here. Let us talk where no one can overhear.”
Adin gave a small nod and signaled to the tall barkeep. “Luca,” he called, “bring us a table.”
As the man approached, Harmon’s eyes lingered on him longer this time, noting the quiet strength in his frame, the constant sweep of his gaze. 
Luca was already moving by the time Adin pushed off from the bar. The man did not weave through the crowd like a common server. He cut through it. Every step measured. His plain tunic did little to hide the muscle in his arms or the calluses of a man who had gripped more than mugs in his time. His eyes, dark and restless, never stayed still, sweeping the room, catching every glance, every twitch of a hand toward a pocket or a knife.
Harmon watched him approach and felt the hairs rise on the back of his neck. This was no barkeep. This was a man used to scanning battlefields. “Gentlemen,” Luca said, voice low and even, already turning. “This way.”
He led them across the tavern floor, threading them through laughter, music, and shouted wagers until the noise thinned. At the far end, he stopped at a booth half-swallowed in shadow. The candle there burned low, its small flame casting just enough light to see each other’s faces, but not enough for prying eyes.
Adin slid in with the easy confidence of a man who trusted the ground beneath him. Harmon took the seat opposite, cloak settling around him as he leaned his walking stick against the wall. Luca placed a fresh pitcher and two cups on the table, then stepped back without a word. He did not return to the bar. Instead, he stationed himself near a support beam, arms folded across his chest, eyes sweeping the room again, always watching.
Harmon’s gaze followed him, lingering. Soldier, his instincts whispered. Or something near enough. Harmon had seen men like that before, men who smiled with their hands full of mugs but always kept one eye on the door. The kind you wanted on your side, but never fully trusted.
Adin caught the look and smirked. “Now you see why I keep him.”
The two old friends sat across from each other, the noise of the tavern fading to a dull roar beyond the shadowed booth. Adin leaned back, his smirk shifting into something sharper. “Very well. We speak in earnest.”
For a moment, neither man spoke. They raised their mugs, knocked them together with the ease of long habit, and drank deep. The sound of the mugs clashing was sharp and familiar, an old joke between them that had outlived battles, oaths, and betrayals.
The moment their cups thudded back to the table, both men broke into laughter, the kind that came from memory as much as humor. For a heartbeat, they were not commander and outlaw, but younger men again, remembering simpler times. “It is so good to see you, old friend,” said Harmon. Something crossed Adin's face that wasn't quite a smirk, there and gone. “Yes,” he said simply. Then: “Harmon, still?” He tipped his cup once in acknowledgment. “It was always the truest one.” 
“Yes, it's been too long. What is your name now, Harmon? Good to see you as well,” said Adin.
The laughter faded, leaving the candlelight and the weight of the years between them. Adin leaned forward, lowering his voice. “What’s with the boy? What’s his story?”
Harmon didn’t hesitate. “Weslin? He’s a page from the palace. A good lad. There is weight in him.” He gave Adin a knowing look.
Adin’s eyes narrowed. “Not another project, Harmon. Not like Arthur’s son. We both remember how that ended.”
Harmon’s jaw tightened. “That was another matter entirely. Arthur’s boy had promise, and I would make the same choice again. What happened to him was not due to a lack of talent. The world had other plans, he had other plans after—” He stopped himself, the words trailing off.
For a moment, Adin said nothing, his scar pulling tight as he studied Harmon’s face.
Harmon’s eyes drifted back toward the bar, where the tall barkeep was already wiping down mugs, his gaze never still. “So that is Luca,” he murmured, the words less discovery than confirmation of what his instincts had already marked. “Tell me about him.”
Adin followed his glance, lips twitching into the faintest smirk. “Let me put it this way. Every man who has come through that door, meaning harm, has left without finishing what he started. Some didn't leave at all.” 
“Not a common tavern hand,” Harmon said, evenly. “If I’m to trust him, I’ll need more than that.”
Adin leaned forward, lowering his voice so only Harmon could hear. “Luca is no hand. He is a special case. I am his steward, in a way. His skill set… it is not one you can measure by coin or by training. It’s a gift,” Adin said quietly. “And a curse. One given from higher hands than ours.” If you ever see it, you will not see it again. Understand?”
The words carried weight beyond boasting, and Harmon felt it. His gaze flicked once more to the man behind the bar, then back to Adin. He gave a slow, deliberate nod. “I understand.”
Adin leaned back, letting the matter close. “Good. Then let's leave it there.” 
Adin refilled their cups, his voice dropping low. “All right, Harmon. You didn’t come to trade old memories. What’s gnawing at you?”
He drank deep, but when the mug came back down, his expression had shifted. The humor drained, replaced by something heavier that settled in the lines of his face. Adin saw it at once, and whatever jest he had ready died on his tongue. He leaned in, knowing the next words would matter.
Harmon leaned in, the candlelight sharpening his features. “Stormhaven has been struck. Aldoria reels, and the word is that the Veydrassil are behind it. Reports are scarce, but the damage was heavy.”
Adin’s hand stilled on the pitcher. “Aldoria?” He gave a bitter laugh. “Our closest ally burns, and the first I hear of it is from you?”
“It isn’t only them,” Harmon said. “The northern pass was attacked as well. Whether the garrison still holds or not, no one can say. And yet Opindale is already preparing to march in support. They may be walking straight into ruin, blind.” His eyes locked on Adin’s. “What do your people know?”
Adin’s smirk was gone. He set the pitcher down and spread his hands. “Nothing. Not a whisper. My eyes and ears, from the docks to the frontier, have given me nothing. That should not be possible. For something this large… silence is not natural. It’s enforced.”
Across the room, two men laughed so hard that one of them spilled his ale and didn't notice. The fiddle climbed high and bright. None of it touched the shadow where these two men sat. 
Silence stretched, broken only by the din of the tavern beyond their shadowed booth. Harmon sat with it, his fingers resting on the rim of his cup, weighing the void of answers.
At last, Harmon spoke. “I was hoping you had something. Now the urgency just grew.” Harmon's eyes went narrow.
Adin knew that look. He leaned forward. “The armies, Harmon. When do they march?”
“They don't. Not yet.” The cup turned once in his hand. “We know nothing. And I will not march men into a grave for it.”
“If I know you, there is a plan in that head of yours. So, let's hear it? There is never just one Plan,” said Adin. 
“I do indeed. You remember the idea. The one I would never let die.” He paused, looking for recognition in his friend's eyes. “A team that can go where armies cannot. Slip in, slip out, being the eyes a commander needs, before the banners march.” His voice cut through the gloom. “That is what we need, now. Not a host to draw eyes. That even the dullest eye would catch. Not a council to slow them down with debate. A handful to answer to me and me alone, who can work outside official means and take action when called.”
Adin huffed a short laugh, though there was no humor in it. “You are still chasing that idea? I thought it was tavern-talk, something we dreamed up over too much ale. Too long ago.” His eyes narrowed. “And now you mean to build it?”
Harmon’s reply was steady. “Now I mean to use it.”
The booth seemed smaller for the words, the shadows pressing close as though the tavern itself held its breath.
Adin leaned back, rubbing a thumb along the rim of his cup. “So that’s your answer, then. A handful of specialists instead of banners and drums.”
Harmon nodded once. “Armies march too slowly, and they draw too much attention. We need a group small enough to slip through cracks, sharp enough to survive what they find, and loyal enough to bring word back.”
Adin smirked faintly. “Loyalty’s a tall order. You know the kind I run with. They’ll come for coin, not crowns.”
“Then they’ll have it,” Harmon said. “If loyalty can be bought at all,” he said, his hand settling flat on the table.
Adin leaned back, considering. “You’ll need blades, quick hands, eyes sharp enough to read the dark, and someone who can patch a man back together after the rest goes wrong. That much I know. But who fills those roles?” He shook his head. “I will look into it. But I will not promise you results.”
Harmon glanced toward the bar, then back at Adin. “Can I have Luca?” Harmon said, eyes still on the man, the decision already settled behind them.
Adin’s scar twitched as he studied his old friend. After a pause, he gave a slow nod. “For you, my friend, I will consider it. That is what I can give you… for now.”
Harmon inclined his head. “That will be enough.”
Adin’s brow furrowed as he studied his old friend. “When?”
“Fourth bell. Tonight. Brackenstall Stables,” said Harmon.
Adin gave a low chuckle, though there was no mirth in it. “Tonight, then. I’ll bring what I already have within reach. No time to be choosy.”
The words hung in the candlelit dark, an agreement cut from silence and necessity.
Harmon watched Adin over the rim of his cup and allowed himself a small smile. “You will come through. You always do.”
Adin snorted, but his eyes warmed. “Do not start flattering me. It makes me nervous.”
The laughter between them faded, leaving only the flicker of the candle and the low murmur of the tavern beyond their booth. For a heartbeat, it almost felt like old times, but the silence that followed was heavier, as though both men knew the moment for jests had passed. Adin’s eyes lingered on Harmon, searching his face the way only an old friend could, and he let out a slow breath.
Adin broke the silence first. His voice was low, almost rough. “I cannot ride with you,” Adin said, eyes dropping to the table. “You know why.”
Harmon’s hand rested on the table, the faint glint of the ring catching the candlelight. Adin’s eyes flicked to it, then back up. They didn’t need words to understand.
“I know,” Harmon said quietly. “I know the price it would cost you. I know what you’ve gone through. That is why I will not ask it of you, old friend.”
Neither spoke. Somewhere past the edge of their booth, a fiddle hit a sour note, and the laughter spiked. Neither man looked up. Some silences don't need protecting from noise. They survive it. “God knows I would like to,” Adin leaned back, a heaviness in his tone. 
For a moment, the weight hung between them. Harmon broke it with a thin smile. “Besides, I could use your hands here while I’m gone. I will need you to get your spiders and birds moving,” Harmon said with a hint of authority behind it. “Whispers, Adin. Everything your people can find before we move. Send it the moment you have it.” 
Adin gave the smallest of nods, the shadow of pain in his eyes replaced by grim acceptance. The glance they shared was brief but deep, a wordless bond forged from years of battles neither man could count.
For a heartbeat, Adin held his stare, then he gave a rough laugh that carried more sadness than humor. “Still know how to twist a man’s arm without touching him.”
“Truth does not bend,” Harmon said.
They sat in it a moment, the candle guttering, the tavern’s roar soft beyond the shadowed booth. Then Adin raised his cup. “To the work,” he said.
“To the work,” Harmon answered. They knocked cups, drank deep, and let the old ritual settle their nerves.
Harmon stood. “Weslin.”
The boy didn’t stir. Across the room, his eyes were fixed on the dance floor where the fiddlers played and serving girls spun in quick circles. He looked spellbound. The world beyond the music had vanished.
“Weslin,” Harmon called again, louder this time. A few heads turned, but the boy remained rooted, lost in the sight.
“Weslin!” The third call cut sharply through the tavern. Weslin jerked as though struck, his face flushing crimson as he realized half the room had seen him standing slack-jawed. He stumbled an apology to no one in particular and hurried toward Harmon’s booth, weaving past patrons and tables until he arrived, head bowed.
“Sorry, sir,” he said quickly, his face turning red. 
Adin’s brow arched, the scar above his eye catching the candlelight. “Easily distracted, this one.”
“He’s young,” Harmon said, though there was no real bite in his tone. “And he ran farther tonight than most grown men would dare.”
Adin gave Weslin a slow, appraising look. “Palace page, eh? You’ll have your hands full if you stick to his side. But maybe you’ve got the legs for it.”
Weslin straightened, the shame receding enough to speak. “I'll do my best, sir.” He wasn't sure why, but the man's appraisal had felt like being weighed on something older and heavier than a palace steward's scale. 
Adin let out a rough chuckle. “It will have to suffice.” Adin leaned back, a smirk tugging at the scar on his face. “Where are you off to now?”
“I have to convince the boy’s father to let him come with me.”
Adin raised his voice in a mock-grand tone, drawing a glance or two. “That should not be so hard. You’re the Sword of the Realm. The man should be honored.”
“Well, he is the baker’s son,” Harmon answered dryly, giving Adin a knowing look.
Adin blinked, then laughed. “Not that baker’s son?”
“The same.”
“Ah, now I see.” Adin shook his head with a grin. “Well, good luck with that. Harmon, that is what you are going by now, yes?”
“Yes,” Harmon said, lifting his cup. “And thank you. Here’s to us, and the hell we raised when we were young… and again when we were not so young.”
Both men raised their cups. “Hear, hear.” They drained them in one pull, slamming the mugs down together in the old rhythm. Neither noticed Luca slip by to refill them mid-conversation, but the mugs were still heavy in their hands. Harmon fared the better, though Adin set his mug down with a wince that earned a grin from his friend.
Harmon rose, steady as ever, the ritual complete. “Fourth bell,” he said. “Tonight.” He left as fast as his words were spoken. 
Adin gave a slow nod. His eyes followed Harmon through the crowd, through the laughter and the dice and the stamping boots, until the door opened and the street took him. The tavern closed around the space he'd left, loud and indifferent. Adin reached for his cup. Set it down without drinking. Sat with the candle a moment longer.






Chapter Three
Adin sat and watched his friend gather the boy and leave the tavern. After he was gone, he took a long pull from his tankard, with his mind racing. Luca appeared beside him, standing next to his chair. “Is that him?” Luca's voice was low. 
Adin watched Harmon go a moment longer before answering. “Not how you remember him?” He smiled. “That is him. I would know him anywhere.”  A brief smile appeared on his face before he continued. “We had some good times back in the day.”
“And why have you decided to help him? You are not on the same side of the king’s law anymore.”
“There is something you do not know,” Adin said quietly as if the memory was on his tongue. “Who we were.” He paused and stood a little taller. We answered to no king. Only to God himself. Because of that, and that alone.” He paused, the memory surfacing and being pressed back down. “I know he will have my back. He knows I will have his. That has not changed in all the years between. There is a kind of trust that does not come from law or blood. It comes from what you have seen together, what you have done.” He almost said brothers. He let it sit. “Brothers,” he said finally, then shook his head once. “No. There is no word for it.” A muscle near his temple shifted, as if it were painful to leave. 

Luca did not push. He had learned which silences Adin came back from quickly and which ones he did not, and this was the second kind. Whatever he had been to Harmon, whatever Harmon had been to him, it lived somewhere below any word either of them could reach for.
The two of them made their way to the kitchen area of the pub. Adin was moving with a purpose. He hadn’t made haste like this in a while, and it showed in his gait. The kitchen roared, fires burning in three hearths, staff moving with the practiced indifference of people paid not to notice things. The smell of smoke and rendered fat was thick enough to wear. Adin moved through it without slowing, and Luca followed close enough to catch the words when they came. The stairs at the back left corner dropped them into the cellar's cold, barrels stacked man-high, the air sharp with oak and spirits, the noise of the kitchen overhead becoming a murmur.
Luca asked, “There’s a question that still isn't sitting right. Why the different paths?”
Adin paused at the top of the stairs, one hand braced on the railing as he caught his breath, then said, “The world did not change. We did. This led us down different paths. We both still have a lot of mutual respect. This idea of his is something we thought of years ago, but it resulted in nothing. But if he is coming to me now to help build it, then yes, I am in, and who I am now will help more than who I was then. And as for what he shared with me, it all lines up with some of the stories I have been hearing on my web. Meaning I can profit a bit from it as well.”
“So,” Luca asked carefully, “then you lied.”
“Not a lie,” Adin said, justifying himself. He had not told Harmon about the fragments because fragments meant nothing yet, and because a man like Harmon, told half a thing, would charge toward the rest of it. Adin had learned long ago that information given too soon was as dangerous as none at all. “I withheld, it's different, he said as he started down the stairs. It was a short trip down to a room about half the size of the kitchen. Large bags of flour were stacked on top of each other in the far corner. A rack of meat that was bought earlier that day. There were barrels stacked from the ground to the ceiling against the wall across from the stairs. This room had a pulley system attached to a rig on the ceiling to help move and stack the barrels or bags of flour. They made their way down the wall with the casks of ale and other spirits to the end, when Adin then paused as he started to look for something on his body.
Luca looked around the room, then turned fully towards Adin. “So, you’re going to need me,” Luca said. He held Adin’s gaze deliberately. “You know the cost.”
Adin did the same. “I am well aware of the cost. Yes, I want you with him because I know you can get out of any trouble. I also want one of my own with him,” Adin said. “Someone I trust.”
“I understand. As long as you are willing, you know I will serve.”
“That is all I ask.” Adin said.  He found what he was looking for deep in a pouch inside his cloak. He pulled out a small rod-like item about the length of his pinky and narrow, one end flat, while the other was bent into a circle. He quickly inserted it into a tiny hole next to the last barrel, so small that if you didn’t look closely, you would have missed it. He fished around with the rod until it looked as if it locked into place, then he turned it counter-clockwise a good turn and a half until the circular part was flat. He pressed down on it, and a sound of air releasing came as part of the wall swung open. Inside appeared to be a small room with a desk, a chair, and a few shelves filled with books and numerous other things.
Luca entered first, followed by Adin. When Luca looked around the new L-shaped space, he realized it was deeper than it appeared from the doorway. The other hallway of this hidden room was lined with crates, chests, and other storage containers. Adin closed the door behind them as Luca made his way over to a wall directly across from the door and fiddled with something on a shelf. Light filled the room from what looked like an oil lamp on the wall, yet no oil was present. The light was clean and steady, nothing like the flicker of oil or tallow. Luca had grown used to it the way you grow used to anything in this life, by deciding not to question it.
Luca had activated a dozen of these over the years and still did not entirely understand them. He did not ask. Some of Adin's resources were better accepted than examined.
Adin made his way over to his desk on the far side of the room. On his way, he activated a few more of the same type of lamps. He walked around his desk so that it faced the door; some habits die hard, Adin thought, and how silly that is in a secure room like this. He sat quickly and began searching through the drawers and the papers on his desk.
Luca examined a painting that was on the floor, leaning up against the wall. “When are you going to hang this?” He paused as he took it in. “Wait, isn’t this a Selvian...”
 His voice dropped. He crouched to look at it properly, hands on his knees, the way you look at something you are not sure is real. “I stood in front of this once. Thirty years ago, perhaps more. Ropes were keeping the crowd back.” He straightened slowly. “There were ropes.”
“Yes, it is, and yes, there were,” Adin said.
“Shouldn’t this be hanging in a gallery or something? I mean, this is the….” Luca trailed off in disbelief.
“The Last Light of Aether, considered one of his greatest works,” Adin finished. “It may have been on display before, but I didn’t like my painting being there. So, I freed it and brought it home.”
“Most men would have had a copy made,” Luca said.
“Most men would have,” Adin agreed. He had already moved back to his search. “Not me. Regarding your question about when I’ll hang it, I’m not planning to set up a permanent shop here yet. When I decide on where that will be, I’ll hang it.”
“Not sure you want this to be your permanent setup? Why not here? We have worked out of here for ten years now. You like it here. I like it here. Are your nomadic ways popping back up again? You need to talk?”
“What are you now, my confessor?” Adin said.
“No. I mean, you do have me playing bartender. Hearing people's sad stories is part of the job. A job you do not pay me enough for.”
“Not enough?” questioned Adin raised his eyes.
“Yeah, a good crier makes more than I do, and comes with less listening,” Luca added.
Adin was not laughing. Looking up from his search, he said, “I don’t hear anyone else complain about their pay. You could always find work elsewhere? I am sure there are plenty of others,” he said the word a bit heavier and paused before continuing, “who are looking for you.”
“Easy. It was a jest.” Luca set the painting back where he found it. “You have always carried the gravity. I only balance it.”
Adin continued his search. Luca made his way behind Adin’s desk to the shelf, eyeing a ring that sat on display where it always did, untouched. The ring of black stone bound in iron, its surface gleaming coldly, beautiful, but with a weight that made the air itself feel wary. Luca always liked going through Adin’s treasures.
“Are you going with him?” Luca asked, looking at the ring.
“What? No.”
“If the stories are true. I thought with this here, you have the strength of twenty men and the endurance of a much younger man. In your case, a much, much younger man.”
Adin did not even look up this time. “You are full of jokes today. I should make you tomorrow’s entertainment.”
“Well, you could. But I don’t think you want my kind of jokes getting out,” replied Luca.
“True.” Adin paused, reaching for something that had fallen behind a drawer. He pulled out what looked like a book. “Found it.”
“What?” Luca asked.
“It is a ledger, one that I keep of names of people who can get stuff done, like you.”
“No one is like me; I am the last.”
Adin looked up from the ledger. He held Luca's gaze for a moment, long enough that the statement had somewhere to land. Then he looked back down. “Yes, I know. If anyone would understand it is me. Yet, they do all have skills.”. People who have been overlooked or wrongly labeled. People who will be perfect for Harmon’s mission.”
Luca picked up one of the statues on the shelf and looked it over as he asked, “Who do you have in mind? Also, don’t think I didn’t notice that you didn’t answer my question about why you don’t use that ring. I can see he is.”
Adin completely ignored the second part of the statement and said, “Get over here, and I will show you.”
Luca set down the trinket he had been fiddling with and looked at the ring again. “Well, if you're not going to use it, I could.”
The speed at which Adin moved from his desk to shove Luca and stand between him and the ring gave Luca pause and put a flash of fear in his eyes. Luca stumbled back a few steps. “Easy! It was just a question.”
“We are not here to play around,” Adin growled, stepping squarely between Luca and the ring. “You know that you can’t. You’d grow sick,” Adin said coldly. “Go mad. Die within moments.” He steadied himself and waited for his pulse to level. “I have entrusted you with my secret, and if you were as smart as you claim, you would know why I am hiding and not using the ring.”
Luca raised both hands in surrender. “Fine, fine,” Luca said, palms raised. “I’ll stop jesting with you. I would love to see that man again.”
Adin slowly calmed down. “I wish I could. With great power comes even greater drawbacks,” Adin said quietly with a slight quiver to his words.
Luca lowered his hands slowly. The room was quiet, save for the faint sound of the tavern above them, boots on floorboards, a distant laugh. Neither man looked at the ring. Some things are loud enough without being touched.
Both men let the matter drop there. Adin signaled for them to return to his desk.
“You’re going,” Adin said. “In case you were wondering,” his head was already in the ledger.
Luca shrugged off the confirmation. He moved slowly back to the desk, asking, “May I go through the crates and find some extraordinary daggers for this venture?”
Adin turned to a large case and said, “Very well. You might find one in the chest better than the crates. There is a belt of four that will suit you. Take the belt, not the blades alone. When you throw one, whether it strikes or misses, it will return to its sheath. That should be sufficient. Now, the names.”
Luca held the belt without moving for a moment. In his line of work, the returning blade was not a luxury. It was the difference between a clean job and a loose end. He understood exactly what he was holding. “Yes. That will serve,” he murmured.
Adin opened the book to its back pages, then turned back three pages to a list of names. The two pages of this old ledger were filled with names accompanied by strange markings that Luca could not decipher. Adin picked up a pair of spectacles from around his neck, set them on his nose, then looked down at the page and began running his hand down the column of strange markings.
He read in silence, his finger tracking the column with the patience of a man used to waiting for the right answer. Then it stopped. “He doesn't want banners,” Adin said, half to himself. “He wants a key.” He looked up from the page. “I find myself wondering what door he hasn't told me about.”
“You believe he kept something from you?” Luca asked.
“Possibly. It doesn’t matter now, but I do like to know a few moves ahead if I can.” Adin sat back up and returned to his ledger.
“Now, let’s see,” Adin said as he continued scanning. “Gusterson?”
“Absolutely not. He is not fun to work with. He’s also a hammer, and you need someone with more finesse.”
“The brothers. Aymir and Taerel.” Adin made the note without asking Luca's opinion. “They docked last night. I call that providence.”
“You do know they are not really brothers, right?” Luca said.
“Of course. It is my job to know. But they are.” Adin said.
“I would agree. They will fit right in.”
“That makes three. We need about seven more or so.” A pause before asking, “Who else can you think of?” Adin asked.
“I would want a big hitter. Renic was in the common room today. We could use his strength. He is a skilled sword-hand, not a bad thief either.”
“Isn’t he a part of the Oloho tribe? You think he will play well with others?”
“If the coin is right,” Luca said with a shrug.
Adin grunted in agreement and made a note. “Then he may serve well enough. But men like that do not come cheap, and we have no time to haggle.” He tapped the ledger with two fingers, his expression turning harder. “We cannot afford delays. What do you think of Senna? She ran the Copperveil district two years back.”
“Retired,” Luca said. “Or claims to. She will come out for the right ask.”
Adin made a mark. “Orist. He owes me three favors. Put him down.” His finger moved. “Fell. River routes. Knows every lock between here and the eastern crossing. Not cheap. But reliable, which is rarer.” Another mark. “And a man called Cael. Former crew captain. Can move twelve people through a checkpoint with no paperwork and no bribes.”
“He is not a fighter.”
“I did not ask for another fighter. I asked for someone who can move.” Adin circled the name. “And here. Pelkin. Not clever. But steady.”
Luca leaned over. “Pelkin will not like Renic.”

“Then Pelkin will manage his feelings. Both names go down.” He sat back. “That is close to enough. Three more, perhaps four.”
Luca glanced at the growing stack of names, brow furrowing. “How are you going to notify everyone? What if they say no?”
Adin gave a short, humorless laugh. “I am not asking. When someone like me sends you a note, you do not decline, not if you intend to keep your place in this city. We will also cast a wide net, more names than we need, and see who answers.” He pushed the ledger toward Luca. “Start writing the summons. I will use my network to deliver them.”
Luca dipped a quill, already scribbling as Adin dictated names. The scratch of ink filled the room as the list grew. Some names were argued, others struck out. Finally, a small stack of sealed notes sat ready on the desk beside Luca’s new dagger belt.
Adin leaned back, rubbing at his eyes. “He wants to ride at the fourth bell. Before dawn.” The words hung between them, heavy as stone.
“That’s tight.” Luca glanced at the shaft of light slanting through a narrow vent. “Just under half a day.”
Adin gathered his notes, stacking them with deliberate care, then pressed them into Luca’s hands. “Get these delivered. Use every alley rat, every cutpurse, and every errand boy you know. I will send runners to cover the rest. By the time the fourth bell sounds, they must be here, armed and ready.”
Luca slipped the satchel across his shoulder, the weight of parchment and steel settling against his side. He buckled the dagger belt tight and gave a nod.
“Once these summons go out,” Adin said, holding Luca’s gaze, “there is no turning back.”
Luca’s answering smile was thin, but steady. “Then we’d best not falter.”
They sealed the hidden door behind them and moved through the tavern’s bustle, one toward the city and its shadows, the other toward his network.
He thought about Harmon's face when they had spoken. The weight sitting in it, the years behind the eyes. He wondered if he wore the same weight and simply could not see it on himself. He decided it did not matter.
Outside, Opindale carried on as it always did, festival noise, vendors, the smell of food and horses in the heat. The sun was still high. The fourth bell did not care.






Chapter Four
Market Street had been swallowed alive. Harmon and Weslin stepped into it together, and for a moment neither spoke, the noise and color pressing in from all sides. This was not the usual feast day energy, the king’s birthday crowds, the tournament week revelry, the high-born wedding processions that spilled out of the cathedral and into the market for a day. Those Weslin knew. This was something else. The city had been preparing for this for months, and it showed in ways that the regular feast days never quite managed.
The buildings had not just been cl”aned’ They had been transformed. Fresh paint on every storefront, not the quick coat of a landlord trying to impress for a week, but real work, careful work, the kind that said Opindale knew it was being looked at by people whose opinions carried weight across six kingdoms. Banners of deep blue and black with gold tassels stretched between every post, the city’s colors flying with a precision that someone with authority had personally overseen. The cobblestones had been swept twice. Weslin had never seen the cobblestones swept twice.
The crowd Itself was different. The regulars were there, the locals who knew how to work a feast crowd for extra coin, the merchants who doubled their prices and smiled while doing it, the children darting between legs. But woven through all of it were faces that did not belong to Opindale. Diplomats in foreign cuts of cloth, moving with the careful awareness of people in a city that is not their own. Delegates with small entourages, speaking in languages Weslin could not name. Merchants from the island cities with their elaborate hats and their habit of standing still in moving crowds, watching everything. Sailors from ports so distant their ships were a curiosity at the docks, drawing crowds of their own.
At the far end of the square, a fire-breather sent a plume of blue flame skyward, and the crowd roared. Weslin watched it the way you watch something you have seen a hundred times, with mild appreciation and no real surprise. He had grown up in this district. Every alley, every vendor, every loose stone in this road. The fire-breather had been doing the same trick since Weslin was nine years old. He moved through the crowd the way water moves through stone, not because he was in a hurry, but because he knew where everything was before it was there.
Harmon watched him and felt the ring heavy on his finger.
Near the heart of the district, a wide clearing had been made in front of the old stone courtyard, and the King’s charity feast was taking shape. Long tables were being set, iron cauldrons already in position, and the first of the beggars had gathered at the edges with the patience of people who had learned exactly how long things took. The King’s own kitchen staff would bring the food. Fresh bread, barrels of stew, fruit, and cheese were carried out in full view of every foreign dignitary who happened to pass. It was a good city. A city that remembered its poor even on its grandest day. Harmon had always thought so. He also knew it was deliberate. Edric understood what it meant to be watched.
The pact re-signing only came around once a decade, and it rotated between the kingdoms with a stake in it. Ten years ago, it had been held in Aldoria, in the great hall at Stormhold. Ten years before that, somewhere else. Today it was Opindale’s turn, and the city was performing accordingly, every stone and banner and scrubbed storefront a statement to the delegations who had come from across the world to see whether this kingdom was worth the ink on the treaty.
Most of the crowd was here for the celebration. Weslin was here for the wonder of it. Harmon was here because somewhere in this press of foreign faces and loose coin and diplomatic goodwill, there were people who were not here for the pact at all, and he had spent enough years in rooms like this one to know how to spot them.
But that was not today’s work.
Today’s work was at the end of this road, in a bakery that smelled of warm bread and everything Harmon was about to disturb.
He fell into step beside the boy. “Do you think your father will welcome the news?”
“I am not sure. He has always been so protective of my mother and me. It took both of us to convince him to let me take the position in the palace.” 
“This is understandable. Are you his only child?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Then that is the sign of a good protective father. If this is something you want, wholeheartedly, then I will speak with him. So I will ask you plainly now, do you want this? Know there is no reprisal if you say no. This will be your choice.”
“Sir, can I be honest?”
“Always.”
“I do not understand why you chose me,” Weslin admitted. “I was only there today because someone fell ill.” His breath caught, then steadied. “I was only there today because Gus gave me a shot. I’m usually just an extra hand to help with the bed maids or the kitchen staff. So I don’t completely understand.”
Harmon’s expression turned serious. “I won’t lie to you. What I’m asking is a heavy responsibility,” he said, voice gentle but firm. His words land slowly, tested. “I chose you because you did not quit. I know knocking over that suit of armor was an accident, I’m not such an old fool as to think otherwise. But I watched you push yourself, out of breath yet determined to finish your task.
