That’s why you’re special,” Harmon said, resting a steady hand on the boy’s shoulder. “I believe it comes from how your father raised you. I know him, and I know he’s a good man.” Harmon paused to let his words sink in, meeting the boy’s eyes. “But none of this matters unless it’s what you truly want. So I’ll ask you again. Do you want this?”
“I know this will sound childish, but I have always wanted to go on adventures. See more than this one city. Be more than the baker’s son.”
“This is no storybook, son. It is work. Hard work. You will be my squire, but you will be more than that as well. You will be more of an aide-de-camp. I will teach you the skills you will need to complete your duties before I get into any wild dreams of weapons play. Understood? If your head is filled with stories, this is not for you.”
“I do understand. That is why I believe that is something I want to do. I want to be more, someone my father can be proud of.”
Harmon stopped him and bent over to look him in the eyes. “You are someone,” Harmon said. “I know it as surely as I know my own name that your father is already proud of you. Never doubt that. He may be hard, but he is proud of you.”
Both of them smiled at each other and then continued their march to the bakery. The crowd did not get any smaller, and they worked hard not to run into anyone. 
Just beyond the main area of the market was the road to the docks. From their higher position, it was a clear view of the entire Westside dock. It stretched toward the clear waters of the river. Trade ships and fishing boats rocked gently in their moorings. The great stone piers, built generations ago, jutted into the waves, lined with cranes and warehouses that smelled of damp wood and brine. It was here that goods flowed into the city, and with them, whispers of foreign lands, rumors of war, and the quiet dealings of those who thrived in the shadows. The closer they got to the docks, the more chaotic the revelry was. Sailors who had just made landfall mingled with locals and tourists alike, their coin flowing as freely as the ale. Taverns overflowed, their doors propped open to let out bursts of laughter, the scent of spiced rum, and the occasional stumbling patron. The stone piers, usually a place of work and barter, had transformed into an impromptu promenade, lined with vendors selling skewers of roasted fish, glazed nuts, and sugared fruits.
At the heart of this whirlwind sat The Silver Spoon Bakery, nestled between a cobbler’s shop and a spice merchant. Unlike its neighbors, it wasn’t adorned with bright banners or excessive decorations. It didn’t need to be. The smell of warm bread and sweet cakes poured from its doors like an unspoken invitation, cutting through the heavier scents of the street. A line had formed outside, a mix of regular patrons and curious foreigners drawn by the promise of something fresh from the oven.
“Dada should be in the back with Mom. Elaine will be up front. Sometimes she brings her granddaughter, Mira. I can’t wait to tell them.” Weslin broke into a full run, heading to the back door to avoid the crowd. 
Harmon slowed to a halt, taking in the sight of the Silver Spoon Bakery as Weslin dashed off. The unassuming shop of stone and timber glowed warmly against the bustle of the street, its open door like an inviting hearth. But to Harmon, that friendly glow felt more like the glare of judgment. The bakery loomed before him like a wall, an immovable obstacle between the life this family knew and the duty that would soon shatter it.
He had stood fearless before warlords in a gilded hall and faced sorcerers who could unravel a man’s mind with a whisper. Yet this simple building, with its shuttered windows and the comforting scent of fresh bread, held his next steps in a pause. Behind it was a man who had once spilled more blood than most armies. Now a humble baker, a father. A man who had buried his past, and Harmon had come to disturb that grave. 
He stood rooted to the cobblestone”, fi’t clenched at his side, weighed down by the knowledge of what he was about to do. He was about to take this man’s only son into a war that had not yet declared itself, for reasons that had seemed clear in a king’s chamber and felt considerably less so in front of a bakery.  
He exhaled through his nose, forcing himself forward. By the time Harmon rounded the corner to the back entrance, the boy was already standing before the man who would decide his fate.
Mjakazi stood in the doorway, framed by the flickering glow of the kitchen’s hearth. He was dressed in a simple tunic, dusted with flour, his sleeves rolled up to reveal forearms still thick with the strength of his past life. His hands were wrapped in fresh bandages. Harmon knew those hands had once wielded a sword that could carve through men like paper.
The years had softened him, but not erased him.
Mjakazi’s white eyes, those haunting, unnatural orbs, settled on Harmon. There was no anger, no immediate threat, but there was something worse. Recognition. The knowing look of a man who understood exactly why an old ghost had come knocking.
Harmon straightened, shoving down the weight in his chest, and stepped forward. 
Weslin was already tugging at his father’s sleeve, proudly pointing out the formal page’s tunic he wore for the feast day. As Harmon stepped up beside him, the boy beamed with excitement. “Dada, look!” Weslin exclaimed. “This is the knight I told you about. He says he’s going to make me his squire! Isn’t that great news?”
Mjakazi’s eyes shifted from his son to the knightly figure of Harmon. His gaze was wary and unyielding. “Is that so?” he asked quietly, a hard edge underlying the words.
Harmon inclined his head respectfully. “Yes, sir. I’ve come to ask for your permission to have Weslin serve as my squire.”
For a moment, nothing stirred. Mjakazi’s voice cut through the heavy air of late afternoon, sharp as a hammer on iron, the sun dipping west but not yet gone. “No.”
Weslin flinched as if struck. “What? Why?” he burst out, staring up at his father in disbelief.
Mjakazi’s broad form filled the doorway. “I am not going to send my only son off to die at this man’s side,” he growled, his tone final.
“Please, Dada,” Weslin pleaded, desperation breaking into his voice. “I-I can do this. It could be good for me!”
“You don’t understand, son,” Mjakazi said, tempering his voice, though resolve still hardened it. “You’re not ready for the world beyond these streets. I know what’s out there.” His white eyes narrowed. “And I won’t throw you to those wolves.”
Weslin’s fists balled at his sides. “I am nearly fourteen,” he argued, his voice cracking, then he forced it steady. “No guild has called my name. This might be my only chance to be more than,” looking down, he said, “Than a baker’s son.”
Mjakazi drew a sharp breath, battling his own emotions. “What is wrong with being the baker’s son? No, don’t answer. My answer is final, Weslin,” he said sternly. “You will respect my decision, do you hear me?”
Tears of frustration brimmed in the boy’s eyes. In a last burst of defiance, Weslin turned toward Harmon.”Sir Harmon, please!” Weslin begged, his hands shaking. “Sir Harmon.” His voice cracked clean through. “Please. You can fix this. Just tell him you need me. That is all. Just say the words. Please.”
Harmon raised his hands in a calming gesture. “Weslin,” he said softly, “I gave my word. That holds. I will not force his hand, nor will I allow you to disrespect his authority. If he says no, then that is the end of it.”
Weslin stood trembling, his dreams crashing down around him. “No… Dada, you can’t—!” he started, voice choked with anguish.
“Enough.” Mjakazi’s command came out quiet but firm. He jutted his chin toward the door. “Inside. Now.”
The boy looked as if he might protest again, his face flushed, tears spilling over, but the resolve in his father’s gaze brokered no argument. Weslin swallowed hard, his eyes darting between Harmon and Mjakazi in hurt disbelief. Then, with a strangled cry, he spun on his heel and fled into the bakery. The door swung shut behind him with a slam, cutting off the sound of his sobs.
Mjakazi’s rigid stance eased slightly once the boy was gone. He lifted his pale eyes to Harmon. “It’s been a long time,” he said gruffly. “You look older.”
Harmon managed a faint smile. “The years have a way of catching up with me, I am afraid.”
Mjakazi crossed his arms over his flour-dusted tunic. “If this was about me,” Mjakazi said quietly, which was worse than if he had raised his voice, “you do not come through him.” He looked at Harmon the way a man looks at something he thought he knew. “You’ve hurt the boy. So why are you here, after all this time? It’s not like you cared what became of me. You left me,” Mjakazi said. “After everything.”
Harmon’s jaw tightened. “After everything…” he echoed quietly. “Mjakazi, I risked my life to get you out. I brought you here to give you a chance at a new life.”
“And then you vanished,” Mjakazi shot back, his voice low and accusing. “Yes, you saved me, only to abandon me. For all you knew, I could’ve picked up my sword the day after and gone right back to being the monster I was.” His white eyes flashed. “And you wouldn’t have been there to stop it.”
Harmon stepped closer, meeting the other man’s glare. “I had faith you wouldn’t,” he said. “Just because I wasn’t by your side doesn’t mean I wasn’t looking out for you.”
Mjakazi let out a hard, barking laugh. “Looking out? I was alone, Harmon. You were the only person I knew in this land, and then you were gone. You didn’t see the darkness I went through. The nightmares, the guilt, the rage, I faced all of that without the brother-in-arms who promised me a new start.”
“Do you truly think the fortunes that found you here were mere coincidence?” Harmon replied, his voice gentle. “Who do you think arranged for Adien to take you in at his tavern, all those years ago? Who paid your keep until you found your feet? And the dockyard job that led you to meet Thim Hather, the baker.” He paused for emphasis, “Did you think it happened by luck?” He held Mjakazi’s stunned gaze. “I set those things in motion, my friend. I paid him to take you on as an apprentice. I wasn’t equipped to guide you through your nightmares and grief, I’ll admit that. I did the only thing I could think to do. I made sure you had opportunities for honest work and people around who cared. I never left you to suffer. I was there in the only ways I knew how.”
Mjakazi’s mouth had fallen open. The memories came slowly, the way they do when you have to relearn what you thought you already knew. The baker who gave him work without question. The room was waiting when he needed it. The dockyard foreman who seemed to expect him. His hands curled in his lap, the bandages creasing at the knuckles. He cleared his throat, but nothing useful came out. He tried again.  “All this time,” he says, and the words come rough. “You were helping me from the shadows?”
Harmon offered a tentative smile. “I did what I could. And when I saw you with Zeriah, happy, building a family, I knew you would be fine. You had finally found peace.”
A faint, crooked grin tugged at Mjakazi’s lips at the mention of his wife. “Zeriah,” he repeated, softening. “Did you know she’s Nyahani’s daughter?”
Harmon blinked. “Nyahani… the healer from back then? I didn’t know.”
Mjakazi nodded. “The very same. After your ‘shadow work’ and Nyahani’s kindness got me through those first few years, I kept tabs on them, on her and her little girl. Then one day in the market, I recognized that little girl, all grown up.” A light entered his voice as he continued. “When I realized who Zeriah was, it felt like fate. We talked for hours… and, well, you can guess the rest.” He spread his bandaged hands in a gesture of wonder. “Somehow, that sweet girl I remembered became my wife. She saved me in her own way.”
“No wonder,” Harmon said quietly. “A man can endure almost anything if someone is waiting for him on the other side of it.” He hesitated, then asked, “Does Zeriah know… about your past?”
“Every dark detail,” Mjakazi replied. “And she still loves me. She saw the good in me when I couldn’t see it myself. Through every nightmare, every fit of anger, she stayed. I thank God every day for her.” His voice caught, and he drew a steadying breath. “I’ve spent thirty years trying to become the man she believes I am.”
Harmon felt a sincere smile cross his face. “You’ve done well for yourself, Mjakazi. Better than many men with far fewer scars.” For a moment, the two stood in amicable silence, the weight of old ghosts finally lifting between them. Then Harmon squared his shoulders, recalling the true purpose of his visit. “Now,” he said quietly, “I think you know I didn’t come all this way just to dredge up old memories. There’s something else.”
Mjakazi fixed his visitor with a steady, knowing look. “Aye. There is.” He straightened, bracing himself. “So, why are you here, Sir Harmon?”
Harmon drew a breath. “I’m truly here to ask for your permission to take Weslin as my squire,” he said plainly.
Mjakazi’s eyes widened in disbelief, then narrowed. “Really.” He pauses to take in the information before continuing. “So that’s it,” he said, voice rough. “After all these years, you come back to my door, not for me, but for my son? No. My answer is still no.”
“I’m not here to collect a debt,” Harmon replied firmly. “If anything, I owe you. I learned he was your son just before I made the trip here.” 
“Then why him? Of all children, why Weslin?”
Harmon held his gaze. “Because I felt it the moment I met him. A spark,” Harmon gave Mjakazi a knowing look. “He is not just any boy, is he, Mjakazi? Tell me. Have you had him tested?”
For the first time, Mjakazi lowered his head and shook it.
“Why not?” asked Harmon.
A stiffness overtook Mjakazi, “Because I was afraid. Because I knew what it would say.”
“You know how dangerous that is? Especially for him,” said Harmon. 
“Yes, I know,” snapped Mjakazi, his tone lessened when he continued, “ God, I know.”
Harmon exhales once, controlled. “I understand.” 
His voice came low. “Tell me he is not like me.”
Harmon stepped forward. “Has he ever shown signs of it?” Harmon asked with a hint of worry in his tone. “Of being like you?”
Mjakazi’s answer came quickly, honest, and almost desperate. “No. And thank the Creator for that. He is a happy boy. A good boy. Light where I was in shadow.”
“Then let me help keep him that way,” Harmon urged. “You’ve done your part in raising him in peace. But peace doesn’t last,” Harmon said quietly, eyes never leaving Mjakazi’s. “You know it as well as I do. Some would twist him, use him as their weapon. That would double if they ever learned who his father was. They would shape him into something you’ve fought to protect him from.”
Mjakazi’s large hands curled into fists, his breath coming heavier. He turned toward the bakery door as though he could shield it with his body alone. “I will not let them take him. I will not see him ruined.”
“You won’t,” Harmon said quietly. “Not while I live. But, Mjakazi, war is stirring. I know you can feel it. Enemies, we both know, are gathering. Just like in your time before, the events that changed you. Weslin doesn’t need to become a soldier, but he does need the chance to grow into the man he’s meant to be. With training. With protection. He will be better prepared to face it, rather than let it sweep him up in the current.”
Mjakazi shut his eyes and let out a long, ragged breath. When he opened them, pain lingered there. “He’s not made for war, Harmon. I tried so hard to keep him gentle.”
“And you succeeded,” Harmon said softly. “But you can’t keep him untouched forever. Nor keep what he is from him any longer, either. Better he walks forward under your blessing, with my shield between him and the world, than to stumble into it alone when it comes for him anyway.”
Silence stretched, heavy as the stones of the street. Finally, Mjakazi spoke, voice rough as gravel. “This will break Zeriah’s heart. And mine. But if what you say is true, I cannot keep him blind to it. I wanted to be a better father to him than mine to me. Maybe if he were, I would be what I am.”
“I know, and you are,” Harmon whispered. “But I give you my word, I will guard him as if he were my own blood. And when the time comes, I will bring him home.”
Mjakazi’s shoulders sagged. The fight drained out of him, leaving only the ache of a father who loved his son too much to let go, and too much to keep holding on. His eyes shifted to the door, to the laughter and life within. “So,” he rasped after a long pause, “You’re leaving before dawn?”
Harmon nodded. “Before first light.”
Mjakazi closed his eyes, summoning strength. “Give me a moment,” he murmured. “Please.”
Harmon bowed his head. “Of course.”
Harmon stepped back and gave him the silence. Mjakazi looked at his feet, then at the sky, where the sun was burning low and orange over the rooftops. He turned to face the bakery as though memorizing it. His shoulders rose and fell three times. When he looked back, Harmon only nodded. There was nothing to say that the nod did not already carry.  
Mjakazi stood in the doorway of the bakery, his shadow stretching long across the cobblestones. “Weslin. Zeriah. Come out here.”
Footsteps pattered within, then the boy emerged first, cheeks flushed, eyes red. Zeriah followed, drying her hands on her apron, her eyes searching her husband’s face, knowing at first look what was about to happen. Her eyes were already starting to fill with tears.
Mjakazi’s voice faltered before he found his strength. “Your path is changing, Weslin. Sir Harmon has made a reasonable argument for you to be his squire.”
Weslin’s mouth dropped open, his eyes shining as though the world had suddenly cracked wide and poured its light on him. “Truly?” he whispered, then looked from his father to Harmon. 
“Yes, my son. Truly,” Mjakazi answered, struggling to hold back his emotions.
Zeriah froze. Her gaze darted from the knight’s steady stance to the boy’s eager face, then back to her husband. “Mjakazi…” she breathed.
He lifted a hand, silencing her gently, though his own throat worked against the words. “I tried to keep him here, safe at the hearth, away from all that I once was. But the world is changing again. We can no longer pretend it won’t reach our door. So I have given my word.”
Zeriah pressed a hand to her mouth, a muffled sob escaping.
Weslin, trembling, stepped forward. “Dada, does this mean…?”
Mjakazi pulled him into his arms, crushing the boy against his chest. His voice shook as he spoke into Weslin’s hair. “It means I am proud of you. More than I can ever say. You are my joy, Weslin. Remember that. Always.”
The boy clung to him, tears streaming, though his smile trembled through them. “Thank you, Dada. I’ll make the most of this. I swear it.”
When at last Mjakazi released him, Zeriah was there. She cupped her son’s face in both hands, her thumbs brushing away the tears. Her eyes shone with her own. “Be a good lad. You are my treasure.” She whispered. “Be brave, but never stop being kind. That is what will keep you whole.” She kissed his brow and pulled him into her arms, holding him as though to etch the memory of him into her bones.
Finally, she let go, her hands slipping away reluctantly. Weslin stepped back toward Harmon, wiping his face but standing taller now, as if the weight of his parents’ love gave him strength.
“You’ve given me more than trust tonight,” Harmon said. His hand gripped Mjakazi’s forearm with old familiarity. “I know what this costs you, brother. I will not waste the gift of your son’s life.”
Harmon bowed his head to Mjakazi and Zeriah both. “He will be guarded with my life,” he said quietly.
Mjakazi managed a stiff nod, his voice hoarse. “Then bring him home. Whole.”
Harmon laid a hand on Weslin’s shoulder. “Come, lad. It’s time.”
As they turned toward the road, the family’s tears glistened in the fading light. Behind them, Mjakazi drew Zeriah into his arms, holding her as though she were the only thing keeping him from breaking apart completely.
They walked into the crowd together, and the feast closed around them like water over a stone. The noise returned, the fire-breather, the merchants, the sailors with their loose coin and looser laughter. None of them knew what had just happened in that doorway. Weslin walked with his chin up and his eyes forward, and Harmon did not speak because there was nothing useful, he could say. Some things needed to be carried for a while before they could be put down.






Chapter Five
Harmon Diem stepped through the great carved oak doors of the Grand Hall, and sound struck him first. By the time he entered the Grand Hall, night had fallen over Opindale. The torches blazed, as a tide of voices rolled across the vast chamber, laughter colliding with the ring of goblets, the scrape of chairs, the low murmur of a hundred side conversations. The vaulted ceiling soared above, beams of blackened oak rising into shadow. From them hung the banners of the three great realms: Opindale’s blue and black edged in gold, Aldoria’s crimson and silver, Moradaer’s dark green and onyx. Firelight from iron sconces made the colors shimmer across the stone, turning fabric into flame.
The air itself seemed alive. Spiced wine steamed from golden flagons, roasted boar glistened with a honey glaze, and the scent of fresh-baked bread wafted from the servers weaving between the long trestle tables. Harmon breathed it in as he walked, though the feast meant little to him. He measured people, not platters.
The envoys from Aldoria sat with a practiced, brittle stiffness, their whispers shielded by silver goblets while their gazes flickered toward every speaker like cornered prey. Opposite them, the Moradaer delegation maintained a veneer of unshakable composure, a calculated display of power that stood in silent defiance of the hall's cacophony. Between these factions sat the High Families of Opindale, a sea of rustling silks and jewels that flashed like signal fires in the torchlight. Here, elegance and steel were inseparable. Every gentle smile was sharpened by a hidden intent. Harmon read it the way he read a battlefield. Every position chosen. Every alliance is visible in who leaned toward whom. The feast was real enough. The warmth was not. 
At the far end, the King’s table dominated the dais, raised high above the floor. King Edric Wymark sat with practiced ease, every gesture carefully measured to strike a balance between warmth and authority. At his side, Queen Mirelle shone like a jewel set against the court’s splendor. Her gown of deep violet was threaded with silver that caught the firelight, and though her smile was gentle, her eyes missed nothing. Harmon noted how she leaned in when Edric spoke, the two moving as one, their presence steadying the dais as if the whole realm drew strength from their bond. Nobles closest to them shifted, eager to bask in the couple’s notice.
Harmon’s gaze shifted beyond them, and there his breath caught. High Seer Rhanis Tal-Kor sat swathed in layered robes heavy enough for a winter storm. The hall was warm with fire and bodies, yet the Seer’s garb seemed to swallow him whole. A prickling sensation crept up Harmon’s neck, the same instinct that had stirred before battlefield ambushes. He kept his expression still, but unease lingered. He had learned long ago not to dismiss such feelings too quickly.
He pressed forward, each step drawing him nearer the dais. Courtiers bowed as he passed, his presence too commanding to ignore even when he wished it otherwise. He inclined his head only slightly, eyes never straying long from the King.
At last, he reached the dais and bent in a formal bow. Edric rose, smiling as he raised his goblet, and the hall echoed with cheer at the King’s casual toast to “old friends and loyal hearts.” All eyes turned to Harmon, waiting for the famed knight to raise a cup in return. But Harmon’s hands stayed empty. He did not reach for the wine a servant pressed toward him, nor join the wave of lifted goblets. Instead, he touched a finger lightly to his nose, the smallest of signals, but one that carried more weight between him and Edric than a dozen shouted toasts. The King caught it at once, his smile never faltering, though the lines at the corner of his eyes tightened.
The cheer rolled on, but for Harmon it seemed dull, as if stone walls had muffled the sound. He saw only the King, and the King saw him. When Edric leaned close, his voice slipped beneath the noise of the hall.
“What have you learned, Harmon?” he whispered.
“Not enough. This requires privacy,” Harmon said, elevating his register without ornament.
He gave the smallest nod. The joy of the feast no longer touched him. Whatever lightness lingered in the hall, the weight in the King’s whisper told him this night would not end in merriment. Behind the pageantry, something dangerous was already moving, and he would soon be at its center.
The King placed both hands on Harmon’s shoulders, his grip firm beneath the guise of greeting, his voice carrying easily to those nearby, but his eyes spoke of urgency. When he returned to his seat, his gaze slid across the dais to the Governor’s chair.
It was empty. 
For a moment, the sight of the vacant chair seemed to swallow the hall. Murmurs stirred among the tables, rippling outward like a restless tide. Delegates from Aldoria stiffened visibly, their governor’s absence a shadow over their honor. The Moradaer envoys leaned together in hushed calculation, while the High Families of Opindale whispered behind jeweled hands. Even the musicians faltered before resuming their tune, the false brightness only sharpening the unease.
Harmon caught the shift instantly. A noble missing might pass unnoticed. But the Governor of Aldoria was gone. He kept his face composed, but inwardly he felt the weight settle.
The King's hand moved and a page appeared, bowing close at his shoulder. Harmon could not hear what passed between them. He did not need to. He watched Edric's face the way a man watches weather on an open plain, looking for the signs before the storm arrives. The page spoke three words. Edric's jaw tightened once, barely, the kind of movement that only meant something if you already knew what to look for. Then the mask was back, seamless, and the page withdrew. 
The boy withdrew only a step, then moved toward Harmon, bending close. “My lord,” he murmured, “the King requests you join him at once.” His eyes flicked nervously to the empty chair before lowering again.
Harmon gave a single, sharp nod. He rose smoothly. With a bow, the boy escorted Harmon through the side passage toward the smaller council chamber.
Inside the council chamber, the air was quieter, heavy with the scent of wax and cedar. The chamber lay just off the Grand Hall, a place reserved for councils too delicate for the ears of courtiers. Shelves of leather-bound volumes lined the walls, beside tall windows that overlooked the torchlit courtyards. A broad oak table dominated the center, its surface scattered with rolled maps, sealed letters, and the gleam of an astrolabe half-buried in parchment. A pair of iron braziers cast steady light across the room, lending warmth against the chill that seemed to seep from the stone.
Governor Drake was already there, seated stiffly at the table, his face pale from worry. Chancellor Ayhmeri stood nearby, his thin hands clasped before him, gaze fixed on the maps as though he had been studying them while waiting. Both men looked up as the side door opened and King Edric entered with Harmon at his side.
The door shut softly behind them, sealing away the noise of the Grand Hall. For a moment, no one spoke, the crackle of the braziers filling the silence. Then Edric moved to the head of the table, his expression carved with the weight of fresh reports.
“You’ve heard what I have,” Edric said, his voice low yet authoritative. “Stormhaven struck. The pass is aflame. Beyond that… rumor and smoke.” His gaze shifted to Harmon, yet his words were steady, grave. Edric folded his hands. “Do you have a plan?”
“Yes, I do,” Harmon replied, his voice steady. “And it’s not an army.”
The King’s eyes narrowed, studying him with new intrigue. “Go on, then.”
“A strike team. No more than thirteen,” Harmon said, resting both hands on the table. “Fast. Unseen. In, learn, out before they know.” 
Edric leaned back, considering. When he spoke again, he came with the weight of the crown, “Very well,” Edric said. “Take whom you deem fit from the garrison.”
Harmon shook his head. “Not this time. Soldiers win battles. This requires something else. It would take too long to train anyone the skills this would require. I will use alternative means to acquire the talents needed. Men and women often looked past.”
“You would trust hired loyalties with this?” “Harmon.” The King said it with the weight of a man who had heard many requests. “You ask more than most men would dare. From anyone else, this conversation would already be finished.” 
“Because an army goes in blind. It makes noise. It draws attention. It commits before it knows what it is committing to. And then it dies.” He looked at the King. “I have written enough of those letters. This will leave us with a bigger force when the fighting begins.” Harmon looked over the room, “It will limit those who will die.”
“I sense another request,” Edric said, steepling his fingers. “Go on.” 
“Yes, my grace,” Harmon said. “If this succeeds, I will step down. The team becomes mine.” The words came out steadier than he felt. He had carried them long enough that they should have been easy by now. They were not. He paused, clearing his throat. “For those who stay, I will need full pardons.”
The King considered him. “You know, Harmon, you do ask a lot. If anyone else asked, the answer would be no.”
Harmon did not move. He had heard kings consider things before. It was rarely the same as doing them. Ayhmeri's voice broke his reverie. “That is something to consider, Your Sire, it could prove to be a significant asset.”
“My King,” Harmon said. “The pardons must be granted. Gold alone will not hold these people.”
Edric was quiet for a moment. His eyes moved to the maps, then back. “Pardons are not a small thing, Harmon.”
“No,” Harmon agreed. “They are not.”
The braziers crackled. Drake was watching the door. Ayhmeri had gone still in the way that chancellors go still when they are listening to everything.
“What you are asking,” Edric said carefully, “is for the crown to extend its grace to people it has never seen, for a mission it cannot acknowledge, led by a man who will no longer carry its name when this is finished.”
There it was. Said plainly enough for the room to follow. Harmon met his eyes.
“That is what I am asking.”
Edric looked at him for a long moment. Something moved behind his eyes that had nothing to do with strategy.
“If I release you from the title,” Edric said, his voice measured, his words chosen for the room, “what does the crown receive in return?”
“The mission completed,” Harmon said. “Stormhaven answered. The northern threat assessed.” He paused. “And something the crown does not currently have. A capability that carries no name and leaves no record. One that will still be there when you need it.”
Ayhmeri's hands unclasped and reclasped slowly. He understood the shape of it.
Drake understood nothing except that no one had said no yet.
Edric turned his goblet once on the table. It was a small gesture. Harmon had seen it before. He had seen it when Edric was seven years old, sitting in a chair too large for him, turning a cup he was not supposed to have, working through something he did not yet have the words for.
“And if I need to call on that capability,” Edric said quietly. “In a moment that truly requires it.”
“Then you call,” Harmon said. “And I will answer.” Not because you command it were the words not spoken. They did not need to be.
“As a friend,” Edric said.
“As a friend,” Harmon said.
The room was still. Ayhmeri looked at the maps. Drake pressed both hands flat on the table and breathed.
Then Edric looked away. Just for a moment. Just long enough. His jaw worked once, the way a man’s jaw works when he is deciding whether to say something he will not be able to unsay. He looked back.
The mask was nearly all the way back when he spoke. “The pardons are granted.” His voice was the king’s voice. Steady. Final. “The title passes when the mission is complete.” He straightened his robes. “See that it is.”
Harmon inclined his head. “It will be.”
Edric nodded once. Then he looked at Harmon the way you look at someone you have known your entire life and are not ready to stop knowing, and said nothing, because there was nothing left that the room could hear.
Harmon held his gaze for one breath longer than necessary.
That was enough.
Governor Drake took this moment to speak up. “Stormhaven?” Drake asked. His voice cracked. “My family?” 
Harmon’s attention shifted to the Governor, “I will find them,” Harmon said. “That is my oath.”
The governor’s shoulders shook, and for a moment, he pressed both hands to his eyes. When he lowered them, his face was wet. “Then… then you will have my gold. Every coin I can muster. Only bring them back to me.”
The King exchanged a long look with Harmon, then with his Chancellor. Ayhmeri gave a single grave nod.
Edric exhaled and rose from his chair. He crossed to Harmon without hurry. “Assemble your team. You have my blessing. May God, the Creator, bless it as well.” 
Harmon clasped back, feeling the weight of the moment. “I will have a package delivered early tomorrow. It will be from my head steward, our means of communication while I am gone. We plan to ride before dawn.”
“Very well,” said the King. He released Harmon and crossed to Governor Drake, gripping the man’s arm with quiet strength. “We will do what we can. I promise.”
Drake’s throat closed with emotion. “Thank you, sire,” he managed, voice trembling.
Harmon stepped forward, took the governor’s hand in his own, and held his gaze. Drake nodded at him, lips shaping the words: thank you.
For a moment, the chamber was still, the weight of war, of family, of loyalty binding them together. Then Edric cleared his throat, straightening his robes. “Come. The feast will not wait forever.”
“ Edric said quietly, speaking as the King, not his friend. “No one learns who stands behind this.” His voice was quiet in the way that kings’ voices are quiet when they mean to be obeyed. “No one. Not even those you trust.” He is looking him in the eyes now. “Understand?”
Harmon gave a single nod. They moved back toward the Grand Hall, not as individuals, but as men bound to a single course.
As the side doors opened, the hum of conversation faltered. Dozens of eyes turned toward them, nobles weighing gestures, envoys calculating meaning, servants pretending not to stare. Harmon felt the weight of those stares, each one searching for weakness or advantage. He kept his expression even, shoulders square, as though nothing more had passed in that chamber than a polite word of welcome.
King Edric strode ahead with the ease of a man long accustomed to scrutiny. He mounted the dais, raised his goblet once more, and the hall quieted. A warm smile spread across his face, practiced yet genuine enough to settle the room. “Friends,” he began, his voice carrying easily across the hall.
Harmon followed and took his seat at the King’s side, his movements deliberate, calm, as though all that remained was to dine. The weight of their secret lingered like a stone in his chest, but outwardly he was every inch the loyal Sword of the Realm, ready to share bread and meat as if nothing had changed.
The feast had begun.






Chapter Six
Weslin sat stirring his stew, his grip tight on the spoon, the broth gone lukewarm. From his place on the Grand Balcony, he had a clear view of the long tables stretching down the hall. Banners of Aldoria, Opindale, and Moradaer draped high from the rafters, their silks gleaming in torchlight, the weight of nations on full display. Yesterday he would have pressed his face to the railing to see it better. Tonight the whole display felt like it was happening to someone else.
He shifted in his seat, the wooden chair creaking under him. His stomach was a knot, food forgotten. Harmon had given him one task. Watch. Listen. Come back with something useful. It had seemed simple enough in the corridor when Harmon’s hand was on his shoulder and the instruction was clear. Up here, surrounded by pages and body servants taking their breaks between duties, it felt considerably less simple.
He had tried to join a conversation near the railing. Two older pages had looked at him the way people look at someone they do not recognize and gone back to talking. A kitchen girl had moved away when he sat near her. He did not know any of them. He was Weslin from the west docks, the baker’s son who had been a page for less than a day, wearing a new cloak and a pin he did not fully understand. He might as well have been invisible.
Which was exactly the problem. The balcony was supposed to be the advantage. Pages and body servants heard everything, not the speeches and toasts the nobles performed for each other, but the real things, the whispered things, the things said in corridors and behind hands. Harmon had to have known that. That had to be why he sent Weslin up here instead of keeping him on the floor. But knowing it and actually hearing it were two very different things when no one on the balcony wanted to talk to him.
He wiped his palms on his tunic. He had heard nothing useful. Nothing at all. Just the noise of the hall below and the low murmur of conversations he was not part of.
He set his spoon down. Closed his eyes.
He was not sure why. It was not a plan. It was the thing you do when you are trying harder than trying seems to be working, when you press your hands over your ears to hear better, when you hold your breath to see further. He told himself he was focusing. He told himself that if he could just shut out the noise of the hall for one moment, he might catch something.
He caught something.
Not a sound. Not exactly. More like the edge of a sound, the feeling of words pressed through a wall. Close. Closer than the hall below. He opened his eyes.
The servants near him had not moved. Their mouths were still. The kitchen girl was refilling a goblet three seats down, her eyes on the work, her face showing nothing. Two pages were watching the musicians below. No one was speaking.
But something was.
She smiled at me when I brought the second platter. She has never done that before.
It arrived so clearly that Weslin turned to find who had spoken. The page nearest him was staring straight at the hall below, his jaw set, his lips perfectly still. His face was the face of someone performing indifference very carefully. He had not said a word.
Weslin looked back at the kitchen girl. She was still pouring wine, completely unaware.
He pressed back against his chair. His heart was going faster than it should. He looked away, looked at the banners, looked at the floor, looked at anything that was not the people sitting near him.
Another one came through.
If Aldric folds before the third hand, I will have his boots by midnight.
Weslin blinked. Across the balcony, three pages were gathered near the back wall, not talking, all of them watching the hall below with the studied innocence of boys waiting for something. One of them was turning a playing card over and over in his fingers, slow and absent, like a man who does not know his hands are moving.
Now is the time.
That one was different. Heavier. It did not feel like a page thinking about cards or a boy thinking about a girl. It felt like something with a purpose behind it, a thought attached to a decision already made. Weslin looked down at the hall below, scanning the tables, but he could not tell where it had come from or who had sent it.
More came, and they did not wait for him to be ready.
The grey cloak. Do not look at the grey cloak.
She knows. She has always known. I will deal with it after.
My feet are killing me. Four more hours of this.
He asked me to prepare the east wing guest room. Third door. Told me to tell no one, not even the head steward. Gave me a coin to keep my mouth shut. I kept it.
I should have eaten before the shift.
If the envoy leaves early, it means the letter did not reach him. If he stays, it means it did.
They came faster now, none of them waiting, none of them announcing themselves, a page worrying about his aching back arriving in the same breath as something that felt like treason and something that felt like a boy deciding whether to apologize to his sister. Weslin could not sort them. He could not slow them. He could not tell which ones mattered and which ones were just the noise inside someone’s head at the end of a long night, because they all felt equally loud and equally real, and none of them were his.
He gripped the edge of the table. His spoon rattled in the bowl.
The thoughts tightened around him, not painful yet, but pressing, the way a crowd presses when it gets too close, when there is no longer enough air. Someone’s guilt. Someone’s hunger. Someone’s cold, specific dread belonged to a face he could not find in the hall below. A flash of something that might have been grief or might have been fury and was gone before he could tell the difference.
He turned his head, slow and deliberate, and looked at the servants again. Still silent. Still moving. Not one of them was looking at him. Not one of them was aware that anything had changed.
His palms were soaking through his tunic.
Whatever this is, he thought, stop.
It did not stop. It pulled back slightly, the way a tide pulls back before it decides what to do next. He sat very still and breathed and told himself he had imagined it. He had been trying so hard to hear something useful that he had started inventing voices. That was what had happened. That was the only thing that made sense.
He almost had himself convinced when a familiar voice broke through everything.
“You look like you swallowed a loaf and regretted it,” Allison said.
Weslin turned to see Allison sliding onto the bench beside him, quick as a sparrow. She snatched a roll from his plate, tearing into it with a grin.
“That’s the face you’re making,” she added between bites. “Somewhere between terrified and trapped.”
Weslin groaned. “I’m fine… aren’t you supposed to be in bed?” 
“Of course. And I’m the Queen of Opindale,” she said, nudging his arm. “Snuck out. So? How does it feel, Sir Squire?”
He nearly choked. “How… how did that get to you?”
Allison’s grin widened. “Pages see everything. Even from the shadows.”
For a moment, her smile faltered, a quick flicker that Weslin almost missed. There was something beneath it, envy, maybe sadness—but she buried it fast behind another teasing smirk.
“You idiot,” her voice softened, yanking him into a hug. “Look at you, I’m glad it was you who got it.”
The words eased something in his chest. Weslin hugged her back, relief softening his nerves. “Thanks,” he whispered.
She pulled away, ruffling his hair. “Still an idiot. And now you’re Harmon’s idiot. That’s worse.”
Weslin chuckled, shaking his head. “Don’t worry. I’m not about to forget where I came from.”
“Good,” she said with mock sternness, giving him a playful shove. “Then eat your stew before you pass out in those fancy boots.”
Weslin smiled, the weight of his task easing for a moment. Some of the pressure on his chest lifted.
A shadow blotted out the torchlight. Weslin did not need to turn around. His body knew before he did, the shoulders tightening, the jaw setting, the particular cold that had nothing to do with the hall’s temperature. 
“Well, look who crawled up into the balcony,” Braden Marloch drawled with a mocking tone, his smirk returned, deeper. “The little sparrow himself. Thought you could flap your way above us?”
Weslin’s stomach knotted hard. Years of sneers, shoves, and whispered humiliations pressed down all at once. He had prayed Braden wouldn’t notice him here, a foolish hope.
“You always find me, don’t you?” Weslin muttered, his voice sharper than he intended.
Braden leaned close, the swagger of a guildmaster’s son dripping from him. Joran and Malric, his ever-present shadows, chuckled behind. “Someone is bold tonight, and look at his new cloak and pin. A baker’s brat dressed up in borrowed feathers. Do you really think anyone here believes you belong?”
The words cut sharply, just as they always had. But this time Weslin forced himself to look up, to meet Braden’s eyes. Fear in his heart, but courage in his voice, he said, “Better a baker’s son than a parasite clinging to his father’s name.”
Joran’s laugh cut off. Braden’s grin twitched.
“Careful,” Braden said softly, then shoved him back against the bench, hard enough to rattle the spoon in his bowl. “You think Harmon will keep you long? You’re a page, nothing more. He’ll toss you aside like the scraps from your father’s oven.”
The venom hit deep. Weslin’s throat burned, but he spat back, “At least scraps have worth. They feed people. What do you feed, Braden, besides your own pride?”
For a heartbeat, the sneer faltered. Then Braden’s hand clamped Weslin’s shoulder, grinding down. “You’ll regret this,” Braden said. “I should’ve broken you when I had the chance. Maybe then you’d know your place.”
The pressure wasn’t just on Weslin’s shoulder. It pressed into his head, heavy and invasive. Thoughts not his own clawed at his mind. ‘I should be the squire. Not him. He doesn’t deserve it. He never deserved anything. I’ll break him.’
Weslin gasped, clutching the table’s edge. Allison stood abruptly, eyes sharp. “Enough, Braden,” Allison said, stepping between them. “You’ve already proven what you are.”
He shot her a look, cruel and mocking. “Stay out of this, stable-warmer. Or maybe I will remind you too where you belong.” He made a rude gesture with his other hand. Joran shoved her down. The three bullies laughed. Braden continued, “Stay down there, everyone knows you’re used to it.” 
Something in Weslin snapped. The years of dread, the years of humiliation, the heat building in his chest, he could not cage it anymore.
Burn! The word wasn’t spoken. It exploded out of him.
Braden looked down at his hands and screamed. That scream came out of him like something tearing loose. He stumbled back, clawing at his own arms, his chest, ripping at his collar. “I’m burning,” he screamed. “I’m burning, I’m on fire, get it off, get it off.” He spun, slapping at flames that no one standing near him could see. His skin was unmarked. His clothes were whole. Nothing in the room had changed.
Only Braden, on his knees now, is still trying to put out a fire that was not there
Weslin felt it, the raw connection, Braden’s pain searing through his own skull. For a moment, he thought it would tear him apart, then it vanished, leaving silence.
Braden collapsed in a heap, gasping, trembling. He choked out in a weak voice, “It’s inside me, I’m burning, make it stop.” 
Weslin didn’t wait. He bolted, boots hammering stone, heart slamming in his chest. Don’t stop. Don’t look back. Find Harmon. Allison hurried back to her feet and ran after him. 
Weslin ran for the stairs, turning right into the Grand Hall. He had barely taken two steps when pain struck like a hammer to the skull. His knees buckled. He crashed to the marble floor, clutching his head as the world spun. It was not just pain. It was a flood. A thousand voices poured into him at once, shouting, whispering, snarling secrets they thought no one else could hear.
He Is too young for her.
The Governor will be moved soon. He is too weak.
Can’t trust Ayhmeri, not after the last war.
If the Moradaer envoy knew what I sold, I’d be dead by morning.
My debts will ruin me before winter comes.
Weslin gasped, his breath ragged. The thoughts tore through him like shards of glass, overlapping until he could not tell one from another. He squeezed his eyes shut, palms grinding against his temples as if he could press the noise out.
“Weslin!” Allison was suddenly at his side, dropping to her knees, hands gripping his shoulders. Wes.” Her voice dropped to something tight and quiet, the teasing completely gone. “Talk to me. Right now. What is it?” 
“I… I don’t know,” he choked. “There are too many.”
Allison glanced around. Nobles at nearby tables began to turn, their conversations faltering as eyes drifted toward the disturbance. A murmur rippled outward. No one rose. No one called for aid. A few leaned closer to their companions, voices lowered behind lifted goblets, watching without appearing to watch. A few exchanged passing glances, more irritated than concerned, as if the moment were an inconvenience rather than an interruption. Servants continued their routes with practiced precision, though their steps slowed just enough to betray their awareness.
Allison, knowing the wrong eyes were on them, tried to get him off the floor. “Come on, get up,” she urged, hooking an arm under his and hauling him up with surprising strength. “We need to go,” Allison said urgently. “Before anyone starts asking questions.”
Across the hall, Harmon had been deep in talk with Lord Alric Valmere when he saw Weslin collapse. His jaw tightened. He had known. He had known, and he had moved too fast again. He bowed his head briefly to Valmere. “If you would excuse me, my lord, there is something urgent I must see to.” Valmere started to protest, then followed Harmon’s gaze and fell silent, giving a stiff nod.
By the time Harmon reached them, Allison had Weslin half-stumbling toward the side corridor. Harmon caught the boy’s arm, steadying him. Harmon’s grip tightened slightly. “Breathe, lad. Just breathe.” His voice was firm, grounding Weslin against the storm.
They found a bench in the corridor where Weslin collapsed, shaking. The voices were already fading, but they left him drained, his breathing ragged. He clung to Allison and Harmon both, wide-eyed.
Harmon knelt in front of him. “I moved too fast.” He said it quietly, the way he said things he meant completely. “That is mine to carry, not yours.” 
Weslin slumped on the bench, chest heaving, hands still trembling. He tried to speak when Harmon asked what happened, but his throat caught, words spilling out in gasps.
Allison leaned forward quickly, her voice firm though her eyes were wide with worry. “He collapsed in the hall,” Allison said quickly, “Came down from the balcony. Braden had been cornering him up there. Then one second, he was moving, the next, he was on the floor, clutching his head like something was tearing him apart. Everyone saw it.” Her fear showed in the pace at which she was talking. 
Weslin forced out a ragged whisper. “Voices… too many. Everywhere. They won’t stop.”
Allison squeezed his hand tighter, looking to Harmon with frightened confusion. “You know something. What is happening to him? What can I do?”
Harmon’s gaze lingered on the pin at Weslin’s collar, the faint gleam of the yellow shard catching the light. He drew a slow breath. “That confirms it.”
Allison straightened. “What? Tell me.”
Harmon met her stare, then turned back to Weslin. “You are an Adept, Weslin.” He let the words settle. “A Yellow. I had my suspicion when we first met. I ran a test. That,” he pointed to the pin Weslin was wearing. “The pin. I placed a slice of a yellow shard. If I were right, it could have helped you tonight. I misjudged the timing. You were not ready. I thought the feast would work in our favor. Enough noise, enough minds, enough to blunt the first opening. I did not account for how strong the first opening would be.”
Weslin blinked, his eyes wide and wet. “An… Adept?”
“Yes,” Harmon said gently. “You are my squire now, and as part of your training, you will learn to master this gift as surely as you will learn to wield a blade. Don’t worry about it now.”
Allison pulled Weslin against her side, holding him close as though she could shield him. “So all of that… it was real?”
“Yes,” Harmon admitted. 
Weslin pressed both hands to his face, his body shaking with relief and fear mingled. He whispered through his palms. “I didn’t want to hurt him, I don’t want to hurt anyone.”
Weslin drew a few more uneven breaths, then lowered his hands. Harmon gave him a nod. “Now, tell me what happened. As much as you can remember.”
Welsin haltingly recounted Braden’s taunts, the shoves. He tells these boys about his past encounters with him. Then the shove Allison, causing a sudden rush of anger that flared into something more. His words shook, but the truth spilled out. “I thought it. I wanted him to burn. And he did. I felt it in my head, like the thought left me and struck him. I never wanted… I never meant…” His voice broke, shame choking the last words.
“I know,” he said. “That is why I am going to teach you.” Harmon was still for a moment. He looked at Weslin with an expression that had no name for it exactly, not pity, not pride, something older than both. Then he exhaled once, slow and quiet, the way a man exhales when he has heard a true thing and is deciding how to carry it. He nodded once. Harmon leaned in, eyes intent. “That was projection, Weslin. “You did it in the grip of raw emotion. That is why it was so dangerous. I will teach you to control it and not hurt anyone,” Harmon said, steady as iron. “My promise.” His words softened the blow. 
Allison gave his hand one last squeeze, then stood reluctantly. “I should go. If I do not, my mother will send the guard to drag me back home. She thinks I am still sick.” She bent down and hugged him tightly. “Be careful, Wes. Please.”
“I will,” he whispered.
She offered Harmon a small bow. “Thank you for helping him.” She stood. Looked at Harmon for a moment with eyes that were doing several things at once. “Keep him in one piece,” she said. “He is the only friend I have who does not bore me.” Then she pulled her cloak straight and walked back toward the noise like someone who had never been anywhere else. 
Harmon gave her a small smile, “He is in good hands, I promise.”
Allison gave them both one last glance, then hurried down the corridor and disappeared into the hall. The silence she left behind seemed heavier. Harmon rose to his feet. “We cannot linger. The King has given us leave. We ride before dawn. Tonight, we make ready.”
Weslin, still unsteady but determined, pushed himself upright. His legs wobbled. His breath hitched, then leveled. “Where do we go first…?”
Harmon placed a steadying hand on his shoulder. “First, we will go get changed. There is a meeting we must attend.”
Weslin met his eyes, fear and resolve mingling in equal measure. Harmon gave him a firm nod, then turned toward the corridor’s shadows.
“Come, lad. It is time.”
And together, they walked into the night.






Chapter Seven
Harmon and Weslin approached the Brackenstall Stables, their boots kicking up the damp scent of hay and earth as they crossed the uneven cobblestone path leading to the entrance. The structure loomed ahead, weathered by time but still sturdy. Thick beams of dark oak reinforced with iron brackets, the kind of craftsmanship meant to endure generations. The scent of aged leather, fresh straw, and the faint musk of horses lingered in the cooling evening air.
“I follow. But why now?” Weslin asked. “Hearing thoughts, I mean. That’s the passive ability? “
“Yes. Passive ability. No will. No focus. You have not been exposed to yellow shards before. “
An old wooden sign, cracked and softened with time, hung slightly askew above the entrance, etched with the name Brackenstall in curling script. Lanterns had been lit along the outer posts, their glow flickering against the stone walls, casting long shadows that danced across the courtyard.
“I thought this place was abandoned when the Brackenstalls left for Merchant Island.”
“When they went to Orrvale, on Veldris,” Harmon said. “Map-names, Weslin. Not tavern talk.
“Yes, sir. But the question remains, if this place is abandoned, why are there horses here?”
“Mr. Holt, my steward, saw to that while we were at the feast,” Harmon answered, already pushing open the doors.
Weslin didn’t get the chance to ask another question when Harmon got to the doors of the stable and heaved them open. Dust rolled like fog, the main hall stretching long beneath ribbed rafters. The smell of oats and oil clung to the dark, a row of empty stalls catching the lantern glow at the far end. Beyond the lofted feed bags, a heavy door waited, the kind meant to keep voices from wandering. 
Harmon pointed out, “That's where we're going,” Harmon said, nodding toward the door. “Now we meet them.” Weslin followed as they moved down the row of stables towards the door, their footsteps muted by the straw.
As they reached the door, the faint murmur of voices on the other side confirmed they were not the first to arrive. The voices grew in volume as they got closer. Weslin was still reeling from the feast, from the balcony, from the floor of the Grand Hall, from his father's arms two hours ago. He had not had a moment to set any of it down. And now he was standing at a heavy door in an abandoned stable in the dark, listening to the voices of strangers on the other side, and something in him understood, without anyone telling him, that the life he had lived up until this exact moment was about to stop being the only life he knew. 
“We check the room. Then we enter,” Harmon said. Weslin just nodded, not paying that much attention to Harmon, as he pondered his thoughts a little more about all that had happened. Harmon cracked the door and took a look.
The back room was built for discretion, low-beamed and close, a scarred table under a single lantern. Shadows pooled at the edges, smoke and leather hanging in the air. Figures ringed the table, half in light, half in dark.
From the narrow crack in the door, a lone eye peered in, and Harmon kept pressed to the wood. He recognized a few of the gathered figures. Adin, Luca, Garran Thornebrook, and Lysana Vaelor. Still, most of the others remained unknown, their faces half-obscured by shadow, their voices beginning to sharpen.
Adin stood near the table’s head, a picture of controlled elegance even in travel gear. He wore dark, well-tailored leathers beneath a deep green cloak, a dagger at his hip that was more than just for show. His usual air of effortless charm was tempered by something keener, sharper, amusement, calculation, or quiet exasperation.
Across from him, Garran Thornebrook sat like an iron statue, his arms crossed over his broad chest, the steel at his side catching the low light. His blue eyes swept the room, unreadable but ever-watchful, as if waiting for the inevitable.
Lysana Vaelor leaned against the wall, her arms folded tight, fingers tapping against the reinforced leather of her bracers. Her golden hair caught the lantern’s glow, but her expression was anything but warm. Tension coiled in her stance, as though she were ready for the moment things turned ugly.
And Luca, or who he believed was Luca, was almost unseen, a shadow within the shadows, his dark leathers melding into the room’s dimness. His daggers were strapped tight across his chest, his hood drawn low, his presence quiet but unmistakable.
Against the far wall, a woman in reinforced armor lounged with one boot propped, smirking as she watched two men trade barbs across the table. One wore a blue traveling coat cut like a duelist, the other, younger, leaner, with the stance of a brawler.
“A brawler’s fists have no place in proper battle,” the man in the blue traveling coat sneered.
The younger man leaned forward, grin sharp. “Try me in one.”
A pale woman in travel leathers pressed her fingers to her temple and exhaled once. “If you are done posturing, we proceed. The rest of us would like to speak.”
Lysana pushed herself off the wall and dropped into a seat beside the pale woman, rolling her eyes. “Men,” she said. “Give them a table, and they will start a war.”
“This was predictable.” The words came from the same pale woman, much louder this time.
“You sound surprised,” she said dryly from her spot on the wall. “Were you expecting clasped hands and harmony?”
The man in the blue coat scoffed. “I expected at least the appearance of professionalism.”
“Professionalism?” The younger man laughed once. “You?” A voice from the left added, dry as dust, “That temper cost you contracts and so much more.”
“You lost a kingdom’s favor because you picked the wrong side,” Kerswell shot back.
The younger man smirked. “Fair. But it was fun.”
A mountain man leaned in, voice heavy. “Well, now, if this is the tone, we are wasting time.”
“You assume I wish to work with any of you,” the pale woman murmured.

“Funny,” Lysana said, cool as glass, “I had the same thought.” A chair scraped. Someone stood.
In the back, two men passed coins, betting on whether the room would break before the lantern died. Garran Thornebrook watched, relaxed, calculating, while a hooded figure dozed with his head on the table, pretending not to hear.
Also in the room was a man who stood with his arms crossed in bulky robes, a little too big for him normally, his expression unreadable as he observed the scene. 
Another beast of a man in well-worn armor and a woman in standard everyday wear, with a bow on her back, sat together, speaking in low tones, likely discussing strategy. Her fingers tapped an idle rhythm against the table, her brow furrowed in thought.
Harmon had seen and heard enough. He whispered over to Weslin, “Ready?” Weslin nodded once, eyes fixed on the door.
Harmon eased the door shut, a breath held between them, the room on the other side one spark from flame.
The door swung open, and Harmon and Weslin stepped inside. The conversation lulled as all eyes turned toward them. He made his way to the far wall so he could get a good view of everyone.
Before Harmon could speak, the door opened once more. A woman in dark robes with a staff and a pack on her back strode in, fashionably late, her expression unreadable as she took in the room. She didn’t apologize; she never did.
Harmon cleared his throat and stepped forward, beginning to address the group. “I had Adin here reach out to you on my beha….”
But before he could finish his second sentence, the woman who was sitting with the beastly man pushed back her chair, sounding sharp in the silence. Now that Harmon could make out her face, he knew her as Lioea Thornethe.
“No,” she said, blade-cold. “Not with him. You said nothing of him.” She stood, met Harmon’s eyes, and turned for the door. Weslin jumped back at the sudden interruption. All eyes turned to her and tracked her as she left. 
“Go,” Harmon said evenly, eyes locked on Adin, “No one follows.”
Harmon exhaled sharply, glancing at Adin, who merely raised a brow. Adin started to move to get her, but Harmon just said, “Let her go.” Harmon was not surprised by the reaction. They all knew who he was and what he did.
He had not always been the man standing in this room. There was a version of him that people in certain trades would always remember first, no matter how many years had passed. He did not blame her for walking out. He had been trying to walk away from that version of himself for longer than most people in this room had been alive. The difference was that he could not leave it behind completely. It had a way of following him through doors. As if it were their cue, the room erupted in talking.
“I will not work with that man,” the blue coat man snapped, jerking a thumb toward the younger man he was having words with.
The woman by the wall pushed off it slowly. “You refuse to work with anyone who won’t bow. Bit of a reach, noble boy.” 
The blue coat man shot back. “I have standards. You may find the practice unfamiliar.”
“I’d choose the next words carefully, noble boy,” She muttered, pushing off the wall, hand moving towards her dagger.

“Considering you could get inside our heads whenever you want. Just make us give you our pay,” Garran said flatly and coolly.
“I don’t,” the pale woman yelled, emotion running high. An argument she had too many times.
Across the room, Luca remained silent, his gaze flicking between the bickering figures. A small smile on his face, enjoying the spectacle of these so-called professionals.
Adin, meanwhile, leaned back against the table, watching it all unfold with amusement as well.
Harmon inhaled through his nose, slowly, and turned to Adin. The two men exchanged a look, one of mutual disbelief.
Behind them, Weslin stood a step back, watching the chaos unfold. He said nothing, but his expression made it clear he was questioning the wisdom of this entire gathering and his being there. He stood very still and pressed his thumb against the yellow stone in his pin and tried to think about nothing, which was harder than it sounded with this many people all feeling things at once. Someone's anger was bleeding through, sharp and close. Someone else's contempt sat in the back of his throat like something swallowed wrong. He kept his eyes on the floor and breathed and told himself he was getting better at this. He was not entirely sure that was true. But it was the only useful thing he had to tell himself right now, so he kept telling it. 
The voices grew louder, overlapping until no one could hear the other. Arguments spilled over, old grudges rising to the surface. It was building into complete chaos. 
Harmon rubbed his hands once, then stilled them. He had not done this in years. The room climbed toward chaos. He took one more deep breath. Then a booming voice came from him, “Quiet!” The word cracked through the room. Steel struck stone. 
Not because anyone decided to stop. Because the word hit the room like a hammer, and the room had no answer for it. And then the sword was there, white and vast, its point driven through the stone of the floor with a crack that ran outward in three jagged lines. The lantern above the table swung in the disturbance and sent shadows lurching across every face.
Where Harmon's face had been, there was nothing. A veil of shifting energy, smooth and featureless, that caught the light and returned none of it. No eyes. No expression. Nothing that could be read or reasoned with or appealed to.
The man who had been reaching for his dagger did not finish reaching. The woman halfway to the door did not finish walking. In the back, a coin that had been in the air came down and was not caught.
Weslin had pressed his back flat against the wall without knowing he had moved. His thumb was jammed against the yellow stone in his pin so hard it left a mark. The feelings in the room had changed completely. A moment ago, they had been anger, contempt, calculation. Now there was only one feeling, and it was old and cold and the same in everyone.
Adin had not moved at all. His arms were still folded. His face was still composed. But his eyes had gone somewhere very private, and what was behind them was not wonder.
Then the sword was gone. The veil was gone. Harmon stood where he had stood, adjusting the collar of his coat, expression unchanged.
“Now,” he said. “We begin.” He did not raise his voice. He did not need to. He walked to the center of the room, unhurried, and looked at each face in turn. “You are here because someone believed you had something this mission needed. Not all of you do. I will find out which of you that is before we are done tonight.” He let that sit a moment. “The work is dangerous. The time is short. You will know what you need to know when we are moving.” He set one hand briefly on Weslin's shoulder. “This is my squire. Remember his face.” Then he turned to Adin. “Take me around.” 
“You will learn more when we are on the move. For now, know that it will be dangerous, and we must make haste. But first, you all know who I am, and you know Adin here. This young man beside me is Weslin, my squire. I do know a few of you. The others by reputation alone. The rest I don’t know. Adin, my friend, take me around.”
Adin stood straight up and moved closer to his friend. “Where would you like to start?” Adin asked while looking over the crowd. Harmon moved right in front of the man in the blue coat, who was still staring at the hole and cracks left by the sword. 
Adin moved to introduce him, but Harmon began. “ Kerswell, the high family?”
“That is correct.” He replied, still not lifting his eyes from the cracked stone.
Harmon studied him. “Why are you here?” Dain gave Adin a puzzled look. 
He lifts his head to meet Harmon’s eyes, “I erred. They disowned me. Not much to tell. It's Dain Kerswell.”

“Yes, the blade remains my trade, among other necessary skills.”

He smiles back, “I believe I am good. I also have heard of you, and I know you are good. And a decent thief, as well.” He then moves to the next person, the younger man. She smiled and let out a giggle at his jest.

Before he could answer, a voice called from the corner near the door. “Are we being hired or measured?”

“Yes, sir.” The man leaned back slightly, easy as old timber. “Figured you’d wonder that. Ain’t here for logs or elk, if that is what you’re thinkin.” He gestured to his shoulder, “See, a Breach took my crew. Left me with this little piece here.” A bird appears before anyone saw it arrive. Dark-feathered, small, utterly still on his shoulder, its head turned at an angle that felt less like watching and more like listening. Its eyes caught the lantern light and did not release it. Harmon did not move. Several others did, chairs scraping, hands going to weapons before their owners caught themselves and pretended they had not.

Adin believes my skills would be useful.” He gave Harmon a steady look. “Name’s Neavin,” Harmon looks over to Adin. Adin just returns a smile before he replies. Harmon just nods his head, then turns his head back to Neavin and puts his hands on his empty shoulder and says, “True. Anything I need to know? Be honest.”
“No, we cause no fuss and are ready to work,” replied Neavin.

The smoke and leather smell of the room had thickened since they entered, warm from too many bodies in a low-ceilinged space. Next was the pale woman. He paused for a moment and just looked at her before saying. “I take it you are my yellow?”
“Yes,” she said. “Aurelia.”

Baldwin’s boots scraped harshly against the stone floor as he stepped back. His nostrils flared, eyes locked onto Harmon like a predator sizing up game. “You will pay,” he growled, the words forced through his teeth. In one fluid motion, he grabbed the haft of his weapon that was sitting next to the chair where he was sitting and swung it in a brutal arc, meant not to intimidate, but to end him. The hammer split the air with a roar, but Harmon wasn’t there. He’d moved before it even reached its apex. 
No blade, no counter. Just motion. Harmon’s body swayed with effortless grace, a pivot here, a sidestep there, ducking beneath a two-handed swing that cracked a beam above him. Dust rained down. His cloak whispered against the air, but his face was calm, unreadable, calculating. The ring on his finger pulsed once, a breath of something borrowed from deeper than muscle and bone, there and gone before he could mark it. No one noticed. Not even Harmon, until afterward, when he felt the space where the warmth had been. 
Baldwin’s strikes grew faster, sloppier, desperation mounting with each clean miss. He snarled through gritted teeth, sweat beading beneath his brow. “Stand and fight, damn you!” 
Then Harmon stepped back, just once. Planted his feet. A whisper of energy coiled through him, strength borrowed from something deeper than sinew and bone. He met Baldwin’s charge with a single open-handed strike, palm against breastplate, and released the gathered force. The impact rang like thunder trapped in a jar. Baldwin’s body flew back, hammer spinning from his grip, crashing through a set of crates before slamming against the wall. The stone cracked behind him. He slid to the ground, wheezing, eyes wide and stunned, not in pain, but in disbelief. He looked at Harmon as if the man had changed shape in front of him. Harmon simply adjusted his coat, expression unchanged.
Luca had not moved during any of it. He stood where he had been standing, exactly as still as before, but the smile was gone. He was watching Harmon the way you watch something you have known a long time and thought you understood. The ring. The veil. The force of the strike. He had suspected. He had not been certain. He was certain now, and certainty in this case meant that everything he had agreed to tonight carried more weight than he had assigned it when he walked through the door. 
Harmon slowly made his way over to the fallen man and squatted down in front of him. Speaking just over a whisper, “You did not stay because you wanted the work,” Harmon said. He was looking at the man the way you look at something you respect, even when you do not need it. “You stayed because she asked you to. That tells me something about both of you.” He stood. “Tell her I said the door is still open. If she reconsiders, she knows where I will be.” 
Baldwin took a few more moments to get to his feet, collected his hammer, and left without saying another word, slamming the door behind him.
Harmon stumbled. One step, the weight going somewhere unexpected, caught on the table's edge before it became a fall. It lasted less than a breath. No one in the room was looking at him yet. No one except Adin, who had positioned himself exactly where he was standing for exactly that reason, and who said nothing, and whose face showed nothing, because that was the arrangement. Harmon leaned on the table, taking slow, methodical breaths. Adin’s look of concern only grew as he neared. “Don’t give me that look, old friend.” He said it in that soft tone he had used earlier, so only the two of them could hear.
“You may tell yourself that. But you chose a lesson, instead of just ending it,” said Adin. 
“I believe I did. They needed to know who held command. Quickly.”
“I understand, I do. You and I have not been those men for a long time. And the people in that room have never been soldiers. They chose their own path, which means they will not be held by the same things that held a garrison.” A pause, quiet and even. “A gilding hand, not a closed fist.” 
 Harmon took a moment to understand what his friend was telling him, “Thank you for your concern, old friend.” He took a breath, “Now that the lesson is over, where were we, Adin?” Harmon moved to what looked like he was leaning up on the table, half-sitting on it. Then asked, “Who are those two over there, more interested in their conversation?” Pointing to the two exchanging money from what just transpired. Adin tapped Harmon on the shoulder and motioned for him to come closer to whisper in his ear.
“They’re mine,” Adin said quietly. “The Brothers. Altisflumen. Aymir. Taerel.”
“Altisflumen?” Harmon said. “They are a long way from home.” 
“Yes. They wanted distance, from what I understand. They are good, and I trust them completely.”
“Wait, you said brothers, were they adopted?”
“No. Same father, different mothers. Dad raised them both. Their bond is unbreakable. Earn their trust, and you will not stand alone. “
“I will take your word for it,” said Harmon.
“I thought they would be good to go with Luca,” Adin added. 
“Right. Almost forgot about him. Alright, Adin, who is left?” asked Harmon. 
The man who is now leaning up against the wall nearest to where they are standing he was the one with the bulky robes Harmon had earlier taken note of. He spoke on, “Me, sir.”
“And who might you be?” asked Harmon
“I am Brother Aldrek of the Fourth Order,” he answered. 
“Fourth Order, you must be a white.”
“I am. A former knight, I was a breaker of men. I was called to be more than a hammer of war. I was gifted the power to mend and was sent by his will to provide his mercy to the sick and wounded. So I left Sir Thorne behind and became Brother Aldrek Thorne.”
Harmon had no words, just looked at the man who stood before him in reverence. “Thank you, you will do fine.”
Outside, a horse shifted in its stall, the sound muffled through the heavy door. The rest of the stable was quiet. The city beyond it was not. 
Sitting next to Aldrek was the man with his head down; it looked like he hadn’t moved at all since Harmon got into the room. Harmon leaned down next to his ear and said, “Are you asleep, or hiding?”
The man raises his head to see everyone, his eyes are completely open, “I was not sleeping, it's something I do when rooms get crowded. Sorry if it was rude.”
Harmon rose, then said, “Not rude really, just concerned. So, who are you, and why are you here?”
“My name is Ceadric Valen, but just call me Ash, everyone else does. Nothing is going on worth mentioning. Adin said there might be work.” Another shrug, easy as breathing. “I said fine. Here I am.” 
“Ash? Why?”
“Long story. I am a Red is the short version. And tend to burn stuff down.”
“Makes sense, ok. Are you feeling alright?”
“Crowds make me nervous, hence the head down.”
“Understood. Then we move on.”
Harmon moved through the remaining three without slowing. The first was a tracker, capable enough by his own account, but his eyes moved wrong, checking exits more than faces. Harmon had seen that look before. It meant a man whose loyalty went to whoever paid last. He shook his head once and moved on. The second was a woman who claimed to be a forger of documents and passage seals, which was useful, but she named three cities she had worked in, and the details did not hold together under a single follow-up question. He thanked her and kept moving. The third said almost nothing, which Harmon respected, but offered even less when pressed, which he did not. He gave each of them a coin, and one by one they left. 
Harmon took a second to take in the whole room before he turned towards the younger woman who came in after him. He looked right at her, “I am sorry, but the team has been filled. Thank you for coming.”
She lowered her head, “I understand,” was her reply. A tear appeared at the corner of her eye. Harmon looked at her and said nothing for a moment.
“Are you ok?” Harmon asked. 
“Yes, sir, I was just hoping for the work, is all. It's been a while, I need the coin.”
Harmon grimaced a bit, “You will be paid for your time tonight, you were here.” Harmon as he made his way to her. “You did nothing wrong. It was just not meant to be.” He slid two coins into her hand.
Her eyes lit up when she saw the silver. Two coins were more than a week's honest work. She knew it and did not pretend otherwise. “Thank you, my lord. Thank you.” She said, then left quickly.
Harmon turned on his heel and looked over everyone else in the room. “Dain?”
Dain looks around and then stands up, “Yes.”
“Are you still a demon with that blade at your hip?” asked Harmon
“I am Uzhiel himself, Sir Knight,” he replied. 
“Good. You stay because I have seen you duel. From here on out, it is Sir. Pay attention, your life may depend on it.”
“Yes… Sir.”
Harmon shook his head, but then continued, “Faelan?”
“Yes, Sir,” he followed suit and stood.
“You’re out. Pack up. Thank you for your time.”
“What? This is…”
Before he could finish, Harmon cut him off, “This is what?” as he raised one hand.
Seeing this gesture, Faelan rethinks what he was going to say. “Nothing.” He grabbed his stuff and made his way to the door. As he passes Harmon, Harmon grabs his arm and holds out two coins. Faelan looked at the coins. His jaw tightened. “Keep it,” he said. “I don't take charity.” He walked.
