“Fine,” replied Harmon as he let him go. He then made his way to all of those who were not on the mission. He handed out the coin to each of them, and one by one, they left.
As the door shut, Harmon made his way to the front of the room again, standing where he started, “For the rest of you, welcome. Know this: they are the lucky ones. We have a lot to do and little time to get it done. Listen closely.” All eyes were locked on him, and he then continued. “There are horses out back. Choose one. Tack is in the shed. Mr. Holt waits by the cart. You will treat him with respect.” He let that sit. “He has your packs. As well as some other things you might want to bring.”
Nyssa looked as if she was going to ask a question. Harmon raised a hand to stop her. “Hold your questions until we are underway. I will brief you then. Make haste for the west docks. A boat is waiting. Go.”
Without another word, the remaining people gathered up their stuff and made their way out to the horse paddock out back, each with questions unspoken. Harmon turned to Weslin, who was just sitting on the floor by this point, “You go as well. Get a horse. Mr Holt has the one I chose for you, your pack, and a special bag. Questions?”
“Do I need to ready your horse as well?” Weslin asked.
“No, mine is ready,” replied Harmon
A look of relief washed over Weslin's face. “Good sir. I don’t know how to do that.”
Harmon smiled, “I will teach you. Many things, in time. This I promise. Now run off.”
“Yes, sir.” Weslin ran off when Harmon looked up. There is only one person left in the room, and it is Dain. Dain brought his hands together briefly, bowed once, and mouthed, ‘Thank you.’ Harmon just nods his head.
“Motley crew,” Harmon said, standing next to Adin. Adin laughed softly.






Chapter Eight
The echoes of the Feast still lingered in the streets behind them, half-eaten garlands tangled in gutters, spilled wine dried in crimson streaks beneath streetlamps, and the faint, sour smoke of last night’s fire dancers curling up from alley hearths. Somewhere deep in the city’s belly, a flute played its final song, off-key and alone. 
The fog had swallowed the echoes, replaced revelry with silence, and turned the wharf into something sacred and somber, like a cathedral built of water, stone, and breath. A place for departures, not parades.
Yet on the Western Docks of Opindale, Harmon stood watching the world move, slow, deliberate, and heavy with purpose, as this band prepared to head upriver.
Harmon stood at the edge of the dock, taking stock of the team in silence, noting habits, spacing, and the small tells that never lied on a first task.
The riverfront stretched long and low along the curve of the Andralis River, stone docks slick with night moisture and the faint sheen of fish oil and algae. Wooden pylons jutted into the dark water like the ribs of a half-drowned god. Moss crept up from beneath the boards, and a pair of barn owls sat silently atop a broken lantern post, eyes pale and unblinking. Somewhere downriver, a bullfrog croaked once and went quiet.
The air was damp, smelling of rope mold, cold iron, and river brine. The kind of smell that clung to your boots long after you left it behind.
A few lamps still burned along the loading quay, but their light was low and golden, barely strong enough to fight the creeping silver mist that rolled in off the water. The fog moved in slow coils across the cobbled wharf, swallowing the occasional crate, piling, or stray rope with lazy hunger.
Further off, in the deeper dark, loomed the silhouettes of trading ships and barge-haulers tied along the upper docks, massive, broad-decked creatures meant for cargo runs out to the bay and the sea beyond. But just beyond it, in the southernmost berth, the vessel was preparing to depart. It was smaller. Sleeker. Built for speed and maneuverability, not bulk.
The Wyrm’s Wake, river-runner class. A two-deck, curved hull built of black alder and reinforced with riversteel plating along the keel and sides. The entire bow was shaped in a long serpentine curve, ending in a carved river-drake head, fangs bared and polished with old blood-red lacquer. 
Runes, etched deep into the alder at its birth, flickered faintly with the pulse of the river. A wide, braided line stretched out from the mount, vanishing upriver. It was already connected to the first segment of the tetherline rail, a buried system of interlocked stone pylons threaded with enchantments and embedded gear-drives that pulled boats against the current using pre-loaded anchor charges and momentum slings. It was part magic, part engineering, part madness, but it worked. What mattered to Harmon was not the system, but how the crew handled it.
The sounds of final preparations echoed up through the fog. A plank creaked. A hammer rang softly against a rail. Hooves clattered against cobbles as a nervous horse was led toward the ramp, breath misting in the cold. A canvas sail flapped loose and was quickly caught by two crewmen, hands rough and practiced, moving like they’d done this a hundred times. They had.
Around the dock, the workers moved in silence, muffled voices trading instructions, straps tightened, crates shifted, saddlebags passed from hand to hand. The clank of tack and harness. The low groan of a wooden beam accepting another burden.
At the head of the ramp, Harmon stood, with hands clasped behind his back, his long dark cloak rippling gently in the river’s breeze. The silver trim at his shoulders caught the lanternlight in cold flashes. The ring on his left hand was plain iron, the kind a man might keep for sentiment or habit. Nothing about it invited a second look. That was the point.
He did not speak. He watched the people around him. He took notes on who lent their arms to help with what was not theirs, who hung back until pressed, who calmed an animal with a touch rather than a shout. These were the things he counted.
A commander in stillness, Harmon’s presence was a kind of gravity, quiet but undeniable. He watched as horses were coaxed up the ramp, tack still damp with dew, and as bundles of gear were fastened down with rough canvas rope. Crates thudded onto the deck in rhythm, and the crew moved with the practiced speed of urgency, not panic.
Most of these faces were new to him. Not all strangers in name, but strangers in action. This wasn't a regular squad. This wasn’t a polished unit trained in proving grounds. It was something else entirely. The start to his vision of what he had planned for years and for the first time, he was seeing it. Harmon still wasn’t sure whether it would work. If these people could work together, it was worth the risk.
“Last horse is up,” Harmon called over his shoulder in a command voice. “That gate closes in three minutes.”
He took a long pull from a brass thermos at his side, steam rising from it. Spiced tea, by the smell of it. Something strong and rooty.
From the stone steps behind him, Adin approached, hands in his coat pockets, strolling. He looked out of place, not because of his clothes, which were clean and elegant, but because of the stillness in his eyes.
Adin stopped beside Harmon, watching the activity below.
“Still can’t believe you are doing it,” he said quietly. “Are you sure about this?”
Harmon grunted. “It is late for second thoughts. These are the people you placed in my hands.”
“Yes, but they weren’t…” Adin trailed off, gesturing vaguely toward the boat without naming names. “They’re different.”
“They are something. Uncertainties aside,” Harmon muttered, “It begins here.”
Adin sensed something different about his friend this time. It had been years since they’d last stood side by side, but he knew this man better than anyone. The one before him felt harder. Sharper. He wondered if it was the ring’s influence.
The two stood in silence for a moment, the river lapping at the pilings below.
A gust of wind rolled through, bringing with it the faint sound of bells from across the river, the Temple of the First Order, just beginning their dawn chime.
On the far bank, the city of Opindale began to stir. Smoke drifted up from the baker's chimneys. A small fishing skiff pushed off into the fog, one lone figure rowing. Lanterns along the bridges flickered as city wardens did their final sweep before shift change. The world was waking up—but not this part of it. Here, in the riverborn edge, it always felt like time held its breath before letting go.
Back on the deck, a crewmember called out: “Towline charge set. Anchor relays ready.”
Harmon raised a hand. “Hold until full board.”
He turned to Adin again, voice lower now.
“You didn’t come just to watch,” Harmon said. “But I’m glad you did. There’s something else I need to ask.”
“More?” Adin asked, arching a brow. “You’re starting to run out of favors.”
“Let me know when we are even.” They both gave a low chuckle. Adin looked at him again, and in that moment, the man he knew was standing before him. He was still in there, and that eased a little of Adin’s worry. 
“So, what is it?”
Harmon reached into his pack and retrieved a map case. He unfolded it, showed Adin, then pointed to a spot, “Can you get me a ship there? Have it waiting on us. In, let's say, fourteen days.”
“This will not be cheap; word of the danger will be widespread in a day or so. It will be hard to find a crew who will risk it.”
“Give them this, I’m sure someone will take it for that,” said Harmon as he passed over a coin purse. Adin took a quick look inside. Platinum caught the lanternlight.
“I am sure it will. Is that all?”
“You know me so well. One more thing. I was unable to return to the palace tonight. Could you get this to the king?” As he passed over a satchel this time.
Adin couldn’t help but take a peek. It was just a mirror and another smaller sack.
“The smaller one is for you,” Harmon chimed in. 
Adin looked up at Harmon with a puzzled look on his face, then removed the small sack while placing the satchel on the ground and opened it. “A stone? Wait, is it a sending stone?”
“Yes, it is; it is the one we used back in our adventures.”
“I didn’t know you still had them. Am I your backup messenger plan?” Adin asked. “I can do that.” His face lit up with a grin, and his eyes drifted toward old memories.
Harmon examined the man. He knew that look on his face. “That, among other things. Now, don’t go getting that nostalgic look on your face. No matter how much I would like for us to ride again, I need you here. I put a note in the sack for you, but I will tell you now. Something bigger is moving, “ Harmon said quietly. “I need someone here I trust. Someone who can act if things turn.” He paused. “They know help is already in the city. They do not know it is you,” another breath. “Mr. Holt has all their pay if something should befall me, they’re covered.”
“Something befall you? This is meant to be a simple peek and report,” Adin said, but his voice lacked conviction. Harmon only gave the faintest smile in reply, one that didn’t reach his eyes. They clasped wrists, firm and quick. “Fourteen days,” Adin murmured. “Be careful.” Then he turned, his figure swallowed by the fog.
Down at the dockside, someone whistled, short and sharp. The final ramp was lifting. Horses were tied, gear stowed, and the last of the figures filed on board. The dock quieted for a moment. Then Wyrm’s Wake let out a low groan as it began to move. They were on their way.
The deck swayed underfoot, a slow rocking rhythm as the riverboat cut its way northward through the dark, silken waters of the Andralis. The city of Opindale faded behind them like a memory, its lantern-lit docks dwindling to pinpricks against the predawn mist. Only the occasional glimmer of tower braziers marked the city’s sleeping sprawl, while the sky above grew a deeper shade of bruised blue, whispering of a coming dawn not yet ready to bloom.
The boat was wide and flat-bottomed, built to haul cargo, livestock, and soldiers upriver, but now refitted for a quieter purpose. Ten war-trained horses stood secured in pairs toward the rear. Canvas tarps stretched over the midsection, covering supplies and rough sleeping space, while crates of rations and spare equipment had been lashed down with sailors’ knots. The scent of riverweed clung to the damp boards, mingling with horseflesh and the faint tang of lantern oil. 
Near the stern, a small elevated pilot house overlooked the vessel, its window shutters propped open to catch the air. The crew was minimal, just two hired hands and a grizzled steersman who guided the vessel with a long tiller, eyes half-closed but instinctively aware of every twist and pull in the water.
Harmon stood near the horses, one hand braced on the rail, watching the murky current glide beneath them. He had been silent for most of the launch, his gaze drifting from the vanishing city to the team that had just embarked on something far more delicate than a patrol.
The slap of boots echoed across the deck as Weslin returned, stopping beside him with a sharp nod. “They’re gathered.” He had dark circles under his eyes, and his jaw was set in the careful way of someone who had not slept and was not going to admit it. Behind them, Opindale was already gone, swallowed by the river bend and the pre-dawn dark. Weslin had not looked back. Harmon had watched to see if he would. He had not. That told him something. 
Harmon glanced at the others, now assembling near the aft quarter by the horses. Some leaned against the railings, others squatted beside their packs, rolling shoulders and shaking off the early chill. Luca, Garr, Dain, and Nyssa were among them, their faces half-cut by lanternlight and river shadow. The only sounds were the soft clop of hooves on the deck and the murmuring shuffle of riverwater against the hull. 
Lysana stood at the rail on the north side of the deck, one hand resting on the wood, looking upriver into the dark. Not anxious. Just oriented. The way a tracker faces the direction they are about to move before they commit to the step. When Luca came to stand near her, she did not turn, but her posture changed slightly, the kind of change that is not quite relaxing but is something adjacent to it. Neither of them spoke. 
Harmon stepped forward, the slow sway of the deck beneath him unacknowledged. His voice was low but carried, measured, and certain.
“I won’t waste your time with ceremony. Most of you I haven’t worked with. That’s not an obstacle, it’s an asset. This mission doesn’t require familiarity. It requires precision, adaptability, and discretion.”
He paused a beat, gaze drifting across the shadowed faces watching him.
“We have received word that there was an attack at the northern pass. We don’t know by whom. Refugees came through, fewer than two dozen, but their stories are inconsistent. Scattered. Some say there was a fire. Others say the sky turned black. All we know is that whatever hit the pass, it wasn’t a simple raid.”
A silence followed, deep and uneasy. Even the horses shifted restlessly behind them.
“Almost at the same time, Stormhaven was hit. A similar story, a small group of refugees with hollow-eyed, ash in their hair. All they brought was fear. They are saying the gates were still open when they fled. Since then, no word. No riders. No more refugees.”
The tone shifted, darker, colder. “They may already be graves.” Harmon crossed his arms, “We do not know. We will shed some light on the matter before we add to those graves.” 
He turned slightly, eyes sweeping from stern to aft, voice low and even.”Our assessment points to the Veydrassil,” Harmon said. A subtle shift ran through the group at the name.
“If that’s true, then the former Brotherhood won’t be far behind. Where the Red Cloaks go, the old hounds follow, and they don’t ask questions first. Capabilities? Mostly Adepts, if the pattern holds. Well-armed. Disciplined. Fanatical. The kind who believe death is a message. If the stories about the Pass are even half right, we might not be chasing ghosts. We might be walking into a trap. Either way, we need to know what we are up against.” 
He leaned forward slightly, voice firm. “We are here to scout, assess, and pull truth out of smoke. Soldiers would not work for this. That is why I asked Adin for people with a particular set of skills. He gave me the lot of you. I don’t know why each of you came. Honor, debt, a clean slate, coin. It doesn’t matter. What matters is that you’re here, with eyes open and steel ready. Perfection isn’t required. Presence is.”
He paused. “But here’s the thing.” He stepped toward the rail, fingers resting loosely on the polished wood, voice tightening with purpose.
“I want a small team. Fast, quiet, surgical. You’re not here to march in rows or light fires. You’re here to disappear into places no one else can reach, to pull answers out of silence. Sometimes,” Harmon said evenly, “you need hardened hands to do necessary things.”
He let the weight of his last words settle.
“But you should also know, if this goes wrong, there’s no wall to fall back to. No horn call to bring reinforcements. This isn’t a battlefield. It’s a fracture line. If it breaks, we break with it.”
Ash’s voice, dry from thrust, called out, “You trying to talk us out of going?”
If that speech changed your mind,” Harmon said, “you were never going to be much use anyway.” He looked at the voice’s direction. “I don’t see anyone leaving.” 
A ripple of laughter moved through the group, which broke up the tension that was building. Harmon holds up his hands to bring back. 
“Yet some may want to leave. That is fine, just do it at the first transit station. No hard feelings, and a pocket full of gold. All I ask is that you keep your mouth shut until we return.  The real test is if you stay. Because no one will ever know what you did, and they never will.  You might, no, you will save lives and give the kingdom a much-needed asset. Information.”
A low murmur erupted in the group as conversation and prayer started. Harmon saw some doubt on a few faces. But no one moved. 
He stepped back into the center of them, voice calm and iron-flat.
“We have a chance to be a part of something that has not been tried before. You may never tell the story over a pint, but you will know. Also, three hundred gold. Each. When you return. Does that answer your compensation question, Dain?” He didn’t wait for an answer before continuing. “Adin already has the payment in full.”
He paused and looked each one in the eye, searching for reservation. Not a one.
“Okay then. Here is the start of the plan. We’re going to split into two teams. One team of four is headed to the pass to assess damage, gather intelligence, and track survivors. The other team, five strong, is bound for Stormhaven to do the same, but there might be more waiting there. The Pass team will be headed up by Luca. The Stormhaven team will be led by Garr. My command cell will operate alongside the Stormhaven team. We will provide support, track movement, and get reports.”
He glanced toward the dark river, then back to them.
“You’re not riding into glory. You’re riding into smoke. I expect clarity. I expect control. If there’s something to report, report it back to me. If you have a question if it should be reported, report it. We will get the word back to the King. This team is the only eyes and ears we’ve got. We could stop senseless bloodshed. I know I ask a lot, but this is what I am asking, and what is required.”
A pause. A few glances were exchanged between the team, but no one spoke. Only the river, whispering past.
“That is all.” He let the silence settle for a moment, the way he always did after something that needed to land. “Get some rest. The next few days will not be kind.” He glanced at the dark water moving alongside them. “Tomorrow morning. Well. This morning.” The correction was acknowledged without apology. “Sleep. The river carries us for now.” 
He turned, leaving them to murmur among themselves. The wind picked up slightly, brushing through the deck with a scent of river moss and the wild tang of dew-drenched trees rising along the banks. 
Luca had not moved during any of it. He stood where he had been when the briefing began, at the edge of the group, close enough to hear everything and far enough to watch everyone. When Harmon finished, he did not murmur with the others. He was quiet in the particular way of a man who has already decided what he thinks and sees no use in announcing it. He pulled his hood slightly lower and looked north, upriver, toward the dark where the pass would be waiting. 
Owls called distantly, and frogs sang in lazy rhythm somewhere beneath the reeds. The boat moved on, and the wilderness swallowed it. As the others began to slip into a quiet routine, unrolling bedrolls, tending to gear, or simply slumping down where they were, Nyssa didn’t. She lingered at the edge of the group, arms crossed, face half-hidden beneath the shadow of her hood.
She materialized beside Harmon the way she always did, with the ease of someone who had never been told no in a way that stuck. 
“You know most men find night watches more enjoyable with company,” she said.
“I am not most men.”
“No.” She considered him with something that was partly assessment and partly amusement. “That has been established.”
She let the silence run a moment, which was not her instinct, which meant she was deciding something. “There is something I need to tell you. I would have told you sooner, but there was never a quiet moment.”
“There is one now.”
“There is.” She looked out at the water. “There is a man named Riven. He knows Stormhaven the way I know people. From the inside, through the back, via routes that do not officially exist.” The performance in her voice was present, but doing less work than usual. “He would open that city for us in ways I cannot do alone.”
“Where is he?”
“Forgehallow. Locked up.” A pause. “Before you say it, yes, I know. But Riven in a cell is worth more than most people walking free.”
“That is the professional case,” Harmon said. “What is the other one?”
She looked at him then. Measuring. “You are very good at that.”
“I have been doing it a long time.”
Another silence. When she broke it, the flirtation was simply gone, like a coat she had taken off. “He is family. Not blood. The kind that means more than blood because you chose it.” She said it to the water, not to him. “I was heading to Forgehallow before this job came along. I thought I could do both. Get him out. Do the work. Come out the other side with everyone I care about still breathing.”
“And you need me to make that possible.”
“I need you to make a small detour that also happens to get us a very good thief.” The lightness tried to come back. It only made it halfway. “I am not above asking. Or begging, if it came to that. Though I would prefer not to beg. It ruins the mystique.”
Harmon looked at her for a long moment. “Get some rest.”
“Is that…”
“It means get some rest, Nyssa.”
She studied his face, found whatever she was looking for, and pushed off the rail. “Thank you,” she said. Not lightly. Not with anything on top of it. Just the words.
He turned back to the river. “Goodnight.”
She went. He stayed. He thought, there is still more to that story. He filed it and watched the water.
He turned and looked back at the water crashing up against the side of the boat, aware that this mission carried more than it showed. Either this was the beginning of something bold or the final chapter. He slid down to sit there, leaning against the railing, listening to the water.






Chapter Nine
The boat cut through the still waters of the Andralis River in the late morning, like a slow arrow, its hull creaking as oars dipped rhythmically on either side, nudging the vessel into the wide bay near the western docks of Rellisford. They had traveled about six hours upriver from Opindale. The sun sat warm and high above, casting a golden glow across the river's surface that shimmered like hammered bronze. The air smelled of water and weathered rope, mingled with the dry musk of cargo crates and the sharp tang of pickled fish baking under dockside tarps.
Weslin stood at the bow of the boat, boots planted wide on the damp, sun-warmed planks, the river wind tugging gently at the ends of his coat. The spray along the bow had gone brackish as they neared land, and the current slowed to a lazy pull, the kind that seemed to tug at thought as well as hull. His hands rested on the railing, calloused fingers curling around the wood while his eyes stayed fixed ahead, Rellisford. It wasn’t grand. It wasn’t regal. But it lived. This was the first place Weslin had been other than Opindale, so he studied it like a schoolboy. 
The town unfolded along the southern bend of the river like a patchwork cloak stitched from timber, stone, and sweat. It was layered and working, less a monument and more a machine. The docks came first, jutting out from the muddy bank like thick, gnarled fingers reaching to catch them. Heavy ropes swayed from tall pulleys, creaking where they connected to a towering iron winch mid-haul on a barge stacked with barrels of plum wine and bolts of sun-dyed fabric. Dockhands swarmed like ants, muscled and shirtless, shouting in coarse harmony as they hefted crates and barked orders. One man shoved a cart forward with his shoulder while another cursed the stubborn anchor chain they were trying to reset. The air was thick with brine, river mud, and the sharper tang of iron and tar. 
Above it all, gulls wheeled and screamed, and black river crows perched on the tops of mooring posts, heads twitching for any sign of spillage. One dove down and wrestled a half-eaten fig from a pile of straw, only to be chased off by a younger boy swinging a wet rope like a whip. 
Behind the chaos of the waterfront, stone-and-timber warehouses rose in rows, stacked two or even three stories high in places. The old sigils painted on their exteriors had faded with age: a red door, a coil of rope, a bundle of crowned wheat. Each one whispered of merchant families, of distant cities, of lineage and silent deals made in smoke-filled chambers. One warehouse sagged near its foundation. Weslin guessed that was Rustside, the name he'd heard muttered by some of the crew, a crumbling, neglected structure with mold licking up from its base and a visible lean to its frame. Even from here, he could catch the scent wafting out of its shaded maw: mildew, aged grain, and the ghosts of long-forgotten shipments.
But it was the town beyond the warehouses that truly caught him. His eyes followed the slope of the cobbled main road, where shops pressed close, their trade clear without signs: herbs drying in bundles, a forge glowing with copper pans, bright cloth rippling like prayer flags. A butcher argued with a woman in a headwrap, cleaver resting on a stump, while cages rattled nearby with restless poultry. Four inns stood along the bend like weary guardians, one spilling laughter from open windows, another gleaming with white pillars and polished glass.
Between it all, life churned. Though this place paled beside Opindale in size, the life here resonated with Weslin in a way the city rarely did.
Children raced through alleys with chalk-dusted hands and bare feet. A fox darted from the reeds along the riverside, startled by the slow grind of their boat’s hull scraping against the shallow bank. Dragonflies skimmed the water, luminous in the sunlight. A woman paused to sweep the bakery's stoop, her sleeves rolled and her cheeks flushed, while beside her a man adjusted a painted sign outside his narrow storefront, arguing with himself about whether it should face east or west.
The closer they got, the deeper the rhythm settled into Weslin’s chest. Rellisford breathed, not in the frantic pulse of a city but in the long, steady inhale of a town that knew its place in the world. It had its feet in the mud and its hands in the coin-pouch. Every shout, every clang of metal, every flutter of bird or banner felt like a note in some old song that only Rellisford remembered how to hum.
It was the scent that hit him next, bitter ale and smoke, sweet bread and tannins from the dyehouse he hadn’t even seen yet, layered over the wet rot of the dock edge and the coppery tang of freshly caught riverfish.
Weslin lingered a moment longer at the bow. Then, all at once, he turned and jogged toward the stern, weaving between crew, crates, and coiled rope.
At the stern of the boat, Harmon sat hunched over his journal, his writing hand steady despite the gentle roll of the current beneath him. His fingers were ink-stained, his brow furrowed in concentration. The page before him was nearly filled, thoughts, numbers, and half-finished plans all tangled together in his looping script. 
He paused as the dock came into clear view, the crunch and clang of the riverfront swelling in his ears. The journey had been long, six hours of drifting, rowing, planning, and silence, but as he capped his inkwell and closed the journal, a quiet satisfaction settled over him. The boat shifted slightly beneath him, the groan of wood on water marking the end of the ride. He slid the journal into his satchel and looked up.
Around him, the crew stirred with purpose. Someone was adjusting saddle gear, checking each buckle with methodical precision. Boots thudded lightly on the deck. Quiet banter flowed between a few who leaned lazily over the rail, watching the dockhands below work like ants in a hive.
The first ropes were thrown out. With practiced ease, the sailors moved into place, shouting terse commands and tying off the vessel to the thick, moss-covered posts of the dock.
Harmon stood, brushing off the front of his tunic. “All right,” he said, voice clear but not raised. “Let’s get the teams up. I want a word before we unload.”
“Yes, my Lord,” Weslin replied, already hurrying off.
He walked toward the center of the deck, gathering his thoughts as boots and orders echoed around him. Horses neighed from the rear cargo hold, eager for the river rocking to end. The scent of hay and sweat wafted up from below, mixing with the sun-warmed wood and distant aroma of roasted nuts drifting in from the market square.
It didn’t take long for Weslin to get everyone together, as most were close to stern, where Harmon wanted to meet. As they gathered around, Harmon took in everyone. In the light, they all looked a bit different from how they had on the water. He noted it. Or perhaps it is my eyes. 
“We are docked.” He let that settle. “Time to split up. Listen.” Harmon’s gaze moved like a tally. “Aurelia. Neavin. Weslin. You are with me.” Then, without pause, “Ash. Aldrek. Dain. Nyssa. Garr. Stormhaven. You get off here, Saddles first. No wandering.” He turned his chin toward Luca. “Lysana. Aymir. Taeral. Luca. The pass.” He called out. “Garr.” 
Garr turned to look at Harmon. “Here’s coin,” Harmon said, flicking the purse toward him. “Food, tack. Other needs. Be quick, we leave before the next bell.”
For a beat, nobody moved. Too many eyes, too many new streets, the dock noise pressing in. Harmon let the hesitation live just long enough to sour. Then his tone cut clean.
“Weslin.”
“Sir. Harmon pointed once, not looking away from the group. “Your pack. Here. Now.” Weslin was already moving.
“While he is gone, you four gather around.” The group drew a little tighter around Harmon. Harmon hands a purse to Luca now. “Here is the same thing for you. This is for you to get what you need when you stop at Barrowmead. Your mission is to head to the pass and report back to me on what you see and what is happening. If at all possible, try not to get discovered. But if you see something you can help with, you have full autonomy to take action. Please keep me updated so I can relay it back to the crown. Any questions?”
Aymir speaks up first, “So what are our rules of engagement?” Aymir asked. “Shadow work, yes. But if a patrol gets too close? Can we take them down?”
“If you cannot give me a clean report, you use judgment.” He let his eyes settle on each of them, one by one. “Remember this. A missing patrol becomes a story. Stories grow legs. Protect the mission. Protect each other.” A smaller pause. Less comfort in it. “You are not fools. Let's not start acting like you are. Questions?”
There was a long silence until Luca spoke up, “How are we to report back to you? We will be hundreds of miles away.”
Harmon just nodded and looked around the group to see if Weslin was on his way back or not. Hurrying up the way was Weslin with his whole pack on his back. Harmon gave a little smile at the effort this young man was giving. 
“Back, Sir Harmon,” Weslin said, breathless.
“As I see, hand me the pack, please.”
Weslin did so with no hesitation. “What are you looking for? I might be able to help you find it.”
Harmon didn’t answer Weslin. He just rummaged around in the pack until he found a small black bag. He handed Weslin his pack back. “Thank you. Just wait there.” He said, not looking at Weslin at all, opening the bag and retrieving the contents took up his complete attention. He removed a shiny silver bracelet and handed it to Luca, “This is how we communicate.” Turning and handing the second one to Weslin. “Put it out, both of you.”
Both Luca and Weslin did as they were ordered and placed the bracelet on their left wrist. Harmon waited until each bracelet was secured. He did not rush them. “Listen carefully,” he said, raising his wrist slightly. “This allows direct thought communication. It is not magic shouting. It is a focused transmission.”
His eyes settled on Luca. “Choose Weslin in your mind. Form the message. Send it. Do not speak.” Luca concentrated.
Weslin stiffened, eyes widening. “He says I need new clothes.” A flicker of restrained amusement crossed a few faces. Harmon did not indulge it. “Good. That confirms the connection.” His tone shifted into doctrine. “You do not broadcast. You select the mind. You send once. Weslin relays. That is the chain.”
His gaze hardened slightly. “Misuse it, and you create confusion. Use it correctly, and you remove distance. Understood?”
Luca just nodded his head. “Good, now go with honor,” Harmon said, stepping back from the group. “Weslin, go unload your horse from the boat and prepare to ride.”
“Yes, Sir” was the simple reply from Weslin. The docked boat groaned of old wood and iron as they made their way off, ropes slapping against waterlogged posts. Harmon and Weslin were the last to disembark, each leading a saddled horse down the narrow ramp as the rest of the team disappeared into the bustling streets ahead. By the time Weslin mounted his horse, Luca's team was already at the road's fork. Weslin caught a last glimpse of them turning north, Luca at the front of the boat, Lysana just behind him, and then the bend took them, and they were gone. Harmon was already riding east. 
 The air in Rellisford was thick with the scent of river silt, charcoal smoke, cured meat, and spiced bread. Merchants shouted over each other in the upper rows while children darted barefoot between barrels and crates. Harmon gave a short whistle to signal their exit, but no one looked back.
The two of them paused just long enough to adjust saddle bags and check the contents of a wrapped package Harmon had taken from the ship’s captain. “Weslin, put this somewhere safe. It is delicate.” Weslin grabbed the bundle and put it in a saddle bag. Being extra careful, he put his blanket around it to give it some more padding. 
As they mounted, Weslin glanced toward the stone archway that led deeper into the city. “This place smells like a forge, and a bakery had a brawl,” he muttered. Harmon smirked but said nothing, guiding his horse toward the stables just off the main square where they were supposed to meet the others. 
They moved through the press of carts and crates, the scent of brine giving way to horses and frying fish. Aurelia was not hard to find. She had positioned herself at the stable entrance where the lane opened onto the square, her horse quiet beside her, her pale violet eyes moving across the market in small, deliberate arcs. She had likely been aware of Harmon for the last two minutes. When Weslin spotted her, his face brightened. She gave him one calm look that took his measure without making a performance of it. She rode with graceful flow, her earthy-toned robes draped over her mount. He took notice of a Mindstone pendant that rested just below her throat. The Yellow light from it was dancing in the early morning sun.
“Aurelia,” Harmon greeted. “Glad I caught up with you before we headed out.”
“Really? What do you need, sir?”
He dismounted and walked closer to her. “I want you with me,” Harmon said. “Not just as a Yellow Adept. I need you handling communications.” 
Her eyes narrowed slightly. “How wide a range are we talking?”
“What can you manage?”
“Five miles is my clean range, direct link, surface thoughts, soft sends. I can push further... astral projection, if I’ve linked with the mind before. But that drains me, and it will drain a shard as well.”
“We'll try to keep it under five then. But if we split teams, I’ll need you to bridge the distance.”
She nodded slowly. “I can do that.”
He motioned to Weslin, who was sitting in the saddle quietly behind him, eyes scanning the square. “This is Weslin. He’ll be your support. Whatever you need, shard prep, notes, meditation blocking, he’s yours to command.”
He paused, voice lowering just a bit. “And there’s something you need to know about him...”
Aurelia leaned in to hear.
“He’s a Yellow.”
Aurelia blinked, caught off guard. Her eyes flicked over him, then softened. “You’re sure?”
“He was never tested,” Harmon said. “Not a late bloomer. His dad let him slip through. I suspected something when we met, but it was confirmed at the feast.” 
Weslin sat straighter now, hands clutching the reins. Harmon continued, voice low but steady.
“He held a shard, and the voices flooded in, dozens at once. Then his rival cornered him, a bully who wouldn’t let him pass. Weslin panicked, wanted him to burn, and the boy thought his skin was on fire. Screamed like it was real.”
Aurelia inhaled, visibly shaken. “That’s an instinctual projection. Raw talent. Dangerous without guidance.”
“Exactly. I want you to train him. On the road, while we work. I know it’s not proper, but he can’t wait.”
She looked to Weslin, who met her gaze with hope and just a trace of fear. He nodded earnestly.
“I won’t let you down,” he said, almost whispering.
Aurelia gave a small smile, placing her hand gently over her pendant. “Then I won’t let you go untrained.”
“Thank you, I will owe you for this.” 
With that, she turned and led her mount toward the outer gate. Weslin watched her go. “She said yes.” He said it once to confirm it was real, then immediately: “What if I cannot learn fast enough? What if I do something wrong and hurt someone again?” He looked at Harmon. “What happens then?” 
Harmon looked at him the way he looked at things. He was still assessing. “Then we deal with it.” No softening in it, but no edge either. “You are not the first person to carry something dangerous they did not ask for. You will not be the last.” He moved his horse forward. “You will not be doing this without guidance. That is why she said yes.” A beat. “What happens next is yours to earn.” He did not wait for an answer. 
They turned back toward the heart of town, where raised voices and a tightening crowd had begun to draw attention.
At the corner of a cart vendor’s stall, Nyssa stood stiffly, arms folded, face casual, but Weslin could see the tension behind her eyes. Across from her, a squat man with a nose like a hawk and bright, accusing eyes was jabbing a finger at her.
“That’s her!” The man’s voice cracked like a whip. “I never forget a face.” He jabbed two fingers at his own temple. “Steel trap.” He started to move around his booth, “You lifted two gold bars. Rings, off my cart.”
Nyssa did not step back. She blinked once, slow, offended on purpose. “Sir, you are mistaken. I have not set foot in Emberfast. You must have me confused with another customer you tried to cheat. I’ve got one of those faces,” she said with a thin smile.
“Liar.” Spit flashed in his beard when he said it. “Same hair. Same eyes. Same smug mouth.”
Nyssa’s smile stayed thin. Her eyes did not. “Then you should call a guard, not a crowd.”
The nearest onlookers leaned in anyway. The merchant tasted that attention and swelled with it.
“As you wish,” he snapped, his voice carrying. He took a moment to draw in a breath, making a show of it for his new onlookers. Then he let out a bellow, “GUARDS!” 
Harmon cursed under his breath. He was already moving, stepping between them, palms open in a calming gesture. “Let’s not make this a scene,” Harmon said. He did not raise his voice. He did not need to. “Maybe we can sort this out like neighbors.”
“She’s a thief! And now you’re harboring her. I want justice!” The man blew a whistle, sharp and loud. The man blew a whistle, sharp and loud. This time, Harmon did not curse. He simply moved, faster than the situation technically required. 
“Nyssa, go. Now!” She didn’t argue. She melted into the crowd like smoke, disappearing down the side street.
Harmon turned, scanning the crowd. Already, he could see heads turning, whispers starting. He moved quickly, rounding up the others. 
Dain came out with bags in his hands. “Why is someone blowing that damned whistle?” He looked around, dumbfounded.
Harmon spotted Dain and rode towards him, “We have worn out our welcome here. Go. Tell everyone you see, we meet outside of town.”
Dain just nods his head, quickly handing off the bags to Harmon and Weslin.
Within minutes, they were all back on horseback, riding hard down the trade road out of Rellisford.
When they’d finally slowed to a trot outside the town’s edge, all of them grouped back up, getting into two columns. Everyone but Harmon was checking behind them. They were not followed. 
The dirt road curved gently into the open countryside, the sounds of Rellisford fading behind them into birdsong and the distant hiss of wind brushing across wheat fields. The team rode in staggered pairs, some in conversation, others quiet. Nyssa trailed just slightly behind the main cluster, her shoulders hunched and lips moving in a low mutter.
Pathetic.” She said it like a verdict. “One day.” The words came out clipped and sharp. “I could not last one day without ruining it.”
She didn’t notice when Harmon pulled up beside her. He didn’t get her attention until his shadow fell across her saddle.
Harmon didn’t look at her. His gaze stayed fixed ahead, scanning the horizon. He said nothing.
Nyssa’s jaw worked once. “I know. I ruined it.” Her voice tried to be careless and failed. “You do not have to say it. I know.”
Harmon just rode beside her and let the road speak first. Nyssa could not stand the quiet. “There is too much I cannot explain. I do not even know what else can come back on us.”
Harmon gave a small nod, eyes forward. When he spoke, it was flat, professional. Worse than anger. “All right. This changes the plan.”
Nyssa flinched like he had touched a bruise. “No. Harmon, do not.” The words came too fast. “Do not toss me aside. Do not cut me loose.”
“Enough.” One word. Clean. He kept his gaze on the horizon. “I am not cutting you loose.” He swallowed before delivering the blade of it without heat. “I cannot use you as I intended. Your face is known here now. I need someone who already works in the dark.”
Nyssa managed a small, wounded exhale. “Oh.” She stared at the road until her breathing returned, and so did her poise. 
“Now,” Harmon said. “Tell me more about this Riven. Will he help?”
She nodded, still quiet.
“We are going after him. With your face soon to be plastered everywhere. I need someone who already works in the dark around here.”
He spurred his horse forward, the plan shifting with each mile. Behind him, Weslin glanced back at Rellisford one last time. The town was already going small in the haze, the docks and the warehouses and the bakery woman and the fox in the reeds all folding together into distance. He had been there less than two hours. It already felt like something he would remember.
He faced forward and rode.






Chapter Ten
The wind rolled down the high cliffs of Forgehallow like a hammering breath, hot and dry even in the dying hours of the day. The city was built into the bones of the mountain, its foundations older than any kingdom’s claim. Long before the Empire had sent banners and laws into the highlands, the wildcat smiths of Forgehallow had carved out their halls with blood, fire, and invention. One of the few places where old laws bent under the weight of innovation. And in its deepest hold, a prison unlike any other clutched Riven Duskwind in silence and steel.
The main road curved along a shelf of blackstone, wide enough for a caravan, and watched by sentries in plated leather, their helms fitted with breathing filters for the slag-heavy lower tiers. Sparks and smoke rose from open forges built right into the cliff walls, giving the streets a hellish orange glow. Massive iron fans turned high above, circulating air through ducts like a city-sized bellows system.
They had been riding east of Rellisford for a day and a half when the road began to climb, and the air began to change. The green of the lowlands gave way to black rock and red stone, and the faint smell of something burned that never quite cleared.
The scent of scorched iron hit them before they saw the walls of Forgehallow. Ash rode ahead of the others, eyes narrowed against the rising heat that shimmered across the path like a mirage. Smoke belched from chimney stacks that jutted from the cliffside heart of the city, black mouths pumping soot that hung over Forgehallow like a storm that never broke.
“Smells like home,” Ash said with a quick, offhand delivery, a crooked half-smile tugging at his mouth. His memory flickered to his father’s forge.
Neavin replied in his short, grounded cadence, “Aye. Sweet mountain home. Fresh air, if you’re used to stone.”
Harmon and the others rode in quietly behind him, cloaks drawn tight. They all emerged from the mountain road leading into Forgehallow’s lower tier just as the sun dipped below the high ridge. The road dipped sharply, curling into a narrow pass between jagged redstone outcroppings until finally revealing the spiked gates of the Ember Gate, tall, reinforced steel with twin sigils of the Miner's Guild and Forgemaster’s Guard burned into the iron.
Dain pulled ahead, brushing dust from his dark doublet, the one with the silver trim he reserved for noble illusions. Nyssa rode beside him, eyes constantly scanning, the only one with any real memory of the town. Harmon rode rear guard, with Aurelia and Weslin between.
Wiping his nose, Garr muttered, “Feels like the mountain’s… alive. Listen.”
“It’s breathing,” Weslin said, pointing before he realized he was doing it. “The fans, the ducts. I mean, it’s made to, on purpose.
A guard in piecemeal metal armor, each plate clearly forged by a different smith, stepped forward, “State your business.”
Dain flicked his reins and rode forward, wearing the face of smug nobility like a second skin. “We are here on contract,” Dain replied, polite as a blade. “Mining interests. We will not be staying long.”
The guard squinted, then nodded and waved them through. In Forgehallow, coin opened more doors than blood. As they were passing through, Harmon stopped at the guards and asked, “Do you know a good place to stable our horses?”
“Just around the corner. You’ve got the coin, they’ll take care of them. Coin has to be right.” He gave Harmon a wink. “Now, carry on. Clear the gate.”
Harmon nodded a thanks, then rode on. The streets inside were narrow and slick with soot. Sparks danced in the air like fireflies. From every other doorway came the sound of hammering, shouting, grinding, work that never stopped, day or night.
It didn’t take them long to find the stable. The Mercenary-Run stable sat like a broken tooth on the edge of Forgehallow’s outer district, half-swallowed by the stone cliffs surrounding the city’s eastern blast gate. Once part of the city’s original defensive wall, the blast gate had been built during an age when Forgehallow feared invasion more than collapse, thick steel doors twenty feet tall that now hung permanently open and rusted, bolted into disuse. Around the gate's gaping mouth, opportunists had erected a series of stone-and-metal lean-tos, scaffolds, and bolt-on structures until the whole thing resembled some monstrous, makeshift barn fused into the city's bones.
 The stable itself was a tangled marvel of industrial decay and rugged utility. Heavy iron beams, salvaged from collapsed mine shafts, formed the skeletal frame, bolted directly into the cliff’s face. The roof was patchworked from copper sheets and fire-treated oak, scarred with old burns from stray sparks. Heavy chains hung between beams, swaying in the draft like grim ornaments.
A large chalkboard mounted above the entry arch read “DUNFEATHER STABLES - PRIVATE MOUNT STORAGE - NO REFUNDS - NO LOITERING - NO QUESTIONS”, the last rule underlined twice.
Harmon led the group in, jaw set, eyes scanning. Inside, the stable smelled of sweat, soot, ash, leather, and horse piss. The floors were layered with gravel, straw, and broken rock, nothing fancy, just durable enough to keep hoof and boot from slipping. Instead of stalls, there were partitioned alcoves, some of stone, some of thick corrugated steel, where animals and odd mounts were kept. A mechanical hoist system ran along the back wall, clearly intended for heavier creatures or supplies. The place was lit by sputtering lanterns strung on wire, and the constant din of industry echoed in from the city beyond: hammers, steam valves, shouting.
As they stepped in, the stablemaster, a hulking, bald man wearing a leather apron stained with alchemical oil, looked up from repairing a bridle with a set of comically tiny pliers.
“Something I can keep alive for you?” the stablemaster grunted, not looking impressed.
“We’ve got nine horses. Good ones. We’ll need them stabled, fed, and untouched until we return,” Harmon said evenly, stepping forward and dropping a small leather pouch onto the nearby anvil with a heavy clink.
The Stablemaster opened the pouch with a practiced pinky claw, sniffed, then grunted. “That buys you four days. After that, I eat the loudest one.” His smile was a big, toothy grin.
“Deal,” Harmon replied without missing a beat. 
Nyssa chuckled under her breath. “He’s charming in the way danger is,” Nyssa said. “Careful, Harmon. You collect that sort.”
Ash smirked. “He’d drink us under the table,” Ash said, already moving on, “Then sell the table.”
As the stablemaster barked at two stablehands, one with a mechanical leg, to start leading the horses away, Aurelia laid a calming hand on her mount’s neck. “Do we trust them?” she asked softly.
“No.” Harmon didn’t hesitate. “They don’t trust us either. That makes it fair. Gold buys trust as much as anything.”
 Dain leaned near one of the stalls, eyeing a strange beast, part mule, part something reptilian, snorting softly in the corner. “Aggressively rustic,” Dain observed. He glanced at Nyssa. “You dealt with these people?”
 Nyssa shook her head. “Closest I came was getting chased out once,” she said, eyes flicking away. “Different reason. Different day.” 
The group took a last look at their mounts as they were guided away into the deeper recesses of the old gate-turned-stable. The shadows swallowed them slowly, clinking with chains and the scrape of hooves on stone. Harmon took the claim ticket from the half-ogre and slid it into a hidden pocket in his vest.
The group made its way out into the streets and left the cave that was the stable. The first full glimpse of Forgehallow opened before them like the lid of a ticking clockwork device. The air was warm, kissed with the bite of soot and the lingering sting of metal cooled too quickly. Tall smokestacks rose like jagged fingers from the earth. Stone and steel clashed in the architecture, buildings hunched together in a jagged sprawl, half-built or constantly rebuilt, stitched with brass piping and odd mechanisms that whirred. It wasn’t a beautiful city. It was raw, alive, and unapologetic.
Nyssa stepped forward, boots crunching slag as she watched a pulley groan overhead, lifting a crate of ore. “Forgehallow,” she muttered, half-caution, half familiarity. “Still loud, hot, and half-mad.”
Aurelia squinted up at the skyline, her brows knit. “It smells like burnt lightning.”
Ash grinned, inhaling deeply through his nose. “No... this is the scent of invention. Chaos. Unchecked genius.”
Brother Aldrek gave a quiet grunt, not quite disapproving, but not far from it either. “I’ve seen cleaner battlefields.”
Dain turned his head, eyeing a group of soot-blackened smiths arguing over the calibration of a steam-powered hammer the size of a cart. “And I suppose they’d call that culture,” he said, lips curling in distaste.
Weslin stared at the steam hammer long after Dain looked away. He had grown up on the docks. He knew what it meant when men built something that could break other things. But this felt different. This felt like a city that had forgotten to ask whether it should. 
They walked the slanted streets. “Nyssa, you know this place better than the rest of us. Where should we go?” asked Dain.
“I have only been here once before.”
“That is one more time than I believe the rest of us.”
“'I have only been here once before. I do not know much. I stayed at a place called The Iron Flask once. It was decent enough.”
Harmon chimed in, “Then that is where we will go. Do they have rooms, or is it just a tavern?”
“No, they have rooms. Good ones.”
“Well, lead the way then, Nyssa,” replied Harmon.
The group made their way to the tavern Nyssa recommended, The Iron Flask. A cozy place built into a repurposed smelting hall. 
Stepping inside was like inhaling a breath of comfort amid the forge-born chaos of the city.
The air smelled of cinnamon smoke, aged wood, and the faint trace of clean oil, not the sour kind that clung to forgehands. Soft citrine-glass lanterns hung from the rafters, casting warm pools of light onto the mismatched but purposefully chosen furniture below, and the old crucibles had been turned into makeshift fireplaces. 
 Each table told a story: one carved with dragons by a local sculptor, another made from the tailgate of a decommissioned mine cart, polished to a deep sheen. A long stone hearth ran along the back wall, its fire always crackling and kept by a rotating charm that turned the logs with a soft mechanical click every few minutes. 
The floors were darkwood, kept remarkably clean despite the muddy boots that passed through, and the walls bore banners from a dozen mercenary companies, some retired, some fallen, some still active. Between the cloth hung portraits of adventuring parties, blurred from age but framed with care.
 The bar counter itself was an old cannon chassis, plated flat and burnished to a smooth finish. It curved like a crescent moon around a raised serving pit, where bottles sat in soft light, and brass pipes vented off the gentle hiss of cold storage runes. 
Nyssa spoke so only her team could hear, “See that man who is standing behind the bar? He’s the owner of the place. Old Cerran, as the locals called him. He was once a caravan captain, now a tavern-keeper with a knack for keeping trouble outside and trust inside. 
Cerran was a tall, weathered man with salt-and-ash hair slicked back, a beard that curled neatly around a strong jaw, and deep-set eyes that somehow saw everything without judgment. He moved with the calm efficiency of someone who’d dodged sabers and sweet-talked anything. His sleeves were rolled, his apron spotless, and his voice had the gravel of age but the tone of a father who knew when to be firm and when to laugh. Regulars greeted him by name. Outsiders got a nod and a warm drink before they even asked.
The clientele was diverse, but not dangerous. Some off-duty forgehands, inventors with ink-stained sleeves, a few mercenaries with scarred faces but polite manners, and a small band of staring tinkerers arguing over blueprints at the corner table. Laughter rolled through the air, softened by the warm acoustics of the arched stone ceiling and dulled timber beams. An old playerless piano in the corner had a note pinned to it: “Plays itself when she's in the mood.”
Music flowed in gentle notes from a subtle enchantment, a soothing melody with an old miner's rhythm, not quite bardic, but familiar like something heard once in childhood and never forgotten.
She drew their attention to the upper balcony, which featured private booths, shaded by velvet drapes and used mostly by negotiators, thinkers, or lovers who wanted privacy but not distance. On the ground floor, the tables were full but never crowded. “They told me this is a safe place. Even the roughest laughter stays polite because of Old Cerran. No blade’s been drawn here in a long while, not since he set a man’s own sword in front of him on the bar, asking him if he wanted a second chance or a third grave.”
The performance dropped out of her voice for just a moment. “This place gives me the feeling of a well-worn coat, patches and all, but it was stitched with craftsmanship and dignity. This is the kind of place that didn’t try to impress... it just made you feel…. Welcome.”
The team from Opindale took a booth in the corner, beneath a carving of a massive warhammer with runes etched into the handle.
“All right,” Harmon said, setting his pack beside him. “We’ve got a prisoner in a fortified hold, in a city run by inventors and weapon smugglers. We need him out, clean, and without violence.”
“That’s like saying you want to rob a dragon and not wake it,” Nyssa replied. “Forgehallow doesn’t do subtle.”
“Which is why we’re starting with Dain.” Harmon leaned forward. “Charm your way in. You are a noble from Reldwyn. Riven is a political prisoner or a diplomatic asset, your choice. Coin is not the obstacle. Get him out clean.” 
“The easy job.” He said it with the tone of a man who knew perfectly well it was not easy and appreciated the framing anyway. 
“I’m giving you the one I need you at. Everyone else? Recon. Get to know the streets. Find where they’re holding him, guard shifts, escape routes. Nyssa, you’re on the recon team, and for the creator’s sake, keep your head down. Aurelia, Weslin, you’re with me. “Keep it tight. I’ll secure rooms and a place to plan. Stay put.”
“Understood,” Aurelia said, her tone cool and focused.
“Dain, go get what you need to get ready,” ordered Harmon.
Dain got up and made his way to Garr, “Going to need some coin, good lad, I need to get a few things to get this right.” Garr looked up at him and didn’t know if he just smirked or if that was a permanent look on his face. He shook his head as he fished out the coin purse. He handed over two coins. 
“Just two coins? Come on, I need finery, not homespun scraps.” He glanced around with mock offense. “No insult meant.”
“Look again,” Garr muttered as he put the purse away. “Then speak.” 
Dain opened his hand to see not silver, not gold, but platinum. “Never mind, this will do nicely.”
Harmon spoke up, “I will need change, and have them give you a receipt for it as well, now off with you.”
Dain rose, tucked the platinum away with the care it deserved, and walked out with his shoulders back and his chin at exactly the angle a lord's son learns before he learns anything else. 
Harmon looked over the group. “I’ll get us rooms, three to start. Stay put.” He rose and headed for the bar.
After Harmon left, the rest of the team just sat looking at each other, with this awkward silence. Garr made a coughing noise. When Ash spoke up, “So how long do you think it’ll take Dain to insult the entire garrison? I’m betting... what, ten minutes?”
Nyssa grinned. “Ten? He probably insulted half the garrison before he got through the door. That jaw’s sharper than his blade.”
Brother Aldrek said, “If he gets himself thrown in,” Aldrek said, folding his arms, “I’m not paying for two bail-outs.”
Neavin, without looking at the group as he took in the whole room, “Let’s pray the guards don’t mind speeches. Or nobles. Or his face.”
They all give a little chuckle at that. Aurelia said, “He means well, even if he speaks like someone who’s never heard the word tact.”

Weslin shied away from the conversation as he tries to think of something to say.
His thoughts were broken by the heartmaid who showed up with a round of drinks for the crew. She placed each one in front of each person, as fast as she could, she went to her next table. 
Weslin had been listening to all of it without finding a place to land. When the second round of quiet confessions came around the table, he held his cup and tried to think of what his reason was. Not the official one. The real one. After a moment, he said, without looking up, “I don't want to go back to being the boy who knocked over the armor.” He said it to the table more than to anyone at it. “I want to be someone different when this is done.” He glanced up, realized everyone had heard him, and looked back down. “Sorry. That probably sounds stupid.”
Ash looked at him. “Nah,” he said. “Sounds about right.”
Brother Aldrek had not touched his cup. He looked at it the way a man looks at something that does not concern him. “I do not drink,” he said. He did not make a virtue of it.
“Did he just get us all the same thing?” Nyssa asked.
Garr laughed, “Drink it first, and you will see.” Each person kind of shrugs and takes a drink.
With a new smile on her face, she said, “This is wine and a good wine at that.”
“Mine is an Ale,” Neavin said.
Brother Aldrek looked inside his cup, and seeing what those two had just said, he took a drink, and to his delight, it was just water. He grunts in enjoyment, and he takes another drink.
In a better mood, Nyssa takes another drink, “Well,” she said, swirling her drink lazily, “if the mission goes half as smoothly as getting here, we’ll be legends... or very colorful smears on someone's wanted poster.”
Ash leaned back in his chair, boots kicked up on an empty one beside him, “So,” he said lazily, “guess it’s sink or swim now.”
Brother Aldrek gave a dry grunt, the weight of too many battlefields in his voice.
 “Funny thing about battles, iron sharpens iron, or it breaks. Guess we’ll see which we are.”
Nyssa drummed her fingers on the table’s scarred wood. “Sink, swim... or drown each other trying.”
Garr rumbled low, crossing his massive arms over his chest. “Harmon doesn't pick fools. If he thinks this will work, I trust him. Even if it feels like madness right now.”
Aurelia smiled faintly over her cup. “Not the point, I think.”
Neavin, quiet until now, set down his mug with a soft thunk. “We keep acting like loners. We won't last the week.”
That pulled a small, sharp laugh out of Ash.
 “Touch of optimism in you, Neavin. Thought you moody types were all about doom and gloom.”
Neavin shrugged, the movement slow and deliberate. “Doom and gloom, sure. But survival, too. And right now? We need each other.”
There was a silence at that, the kind that wasn't uncomfortable so much as heavy, like a weight settling across all their shoulders.
Ash rolled his mug once between his palms, watching the surface of the drink ripple before he spoke.
“Let’s not get sentimental,” he said lightly, but there was an edge under it. “We’re here because Harmon brought us, and Harmon pays on time.”
A few nods answered him. Nothing dramatic. Just an agreement.
Garr shifted in his seat, massive shoulders settling. “And because the man he answers to doesn’t tolerate messes,” he added. “Adin’s name carries weight. You don’t start fights under that shadow unless you’re trying to get remembered for the wrong reasons.”
Aurelia glanced around the table, measuring the room the way she measured people. “That’s not trust,” she said calmly. “It’s alignment. Temporary. Functional.”
Neavin snorted quietly into his cup. “Means we don’t need to like each other. Just need to not get in each other’s way.”
Nyssa leaned back, letting the moment breathe. “Fine by me,” she said. “I’ve done worse jobs with people I trusted less.”
Brother Aldrek folded his arms, the motion deliberate. “Coin buys cooperation,” he said. “Discipline keeps it from becoming something uglier.”
Ash raised his mug the rest of the way. “There it is,” he said. “We play nice. We get paid. We leave with the same number of holes we came in with.”
A pause settled over the table. Not warm. Not cold. Solid.
Then Neavin nodded once. “For the job,” he said. “That’s all it needs to be.”
Nyssa leaned in, voice soft but insistent. “Fine. Some are here for a second shot at something, aren’t we?” She looked down at her cup and leaned in, voice low. “Or a third.” She looked deeper into her cup, “At something worth the trip.” 
Ash raised his mug in a mock salute. “Third shot, or more if we're being honest.”
Aldrek gave a low, humorless chuckle. “For me, it's penance.”
Garr snorted. “For me, it's the fight. Always the fight. Plus, I owe Harmon.”
Aurelia looked down into her drink, voice barely above the tavern’s low rumble. “I’m here to prove it wasn’t all for nothing.” This gave everyone pause before they all took a drink.
Neavin glanced around the table, his pale eyes sharp. “Then maybe that's enough. For now.”
They sat with that for a few heartbeats, different, broken, and stubborn, and for the first time, a thin thread pulled between them, unseen but real.
Ash broke the moment, slapping his boots down with a thud. “Well. If we’re stuck with each other, might as well learn to aim past each other’s heads, eh?”
Nyssa grinned wickedly. “Speak for yourself. I aim exactly where I mean to.”
More laughter this time, a little lighter, a little easier.
And just as the tension started to finally bleed off, Harmon’s boots clunked back across the floor, a keyring swinging from his fingers.
“Rooms sorted,” he said, voice low but satisfied. “I hope you lot didn't burn the place down while I was gone.”
Ash tossed him a lazy salute. “Not for lack of trying, boss.”
They all gathered themselves, the air between them just a little different now. Still strangers. But not entirely alone.






Chapter Eleven
Harmon had paid generously, and it showed. Three suites, spacious by any measure, each held a heavy four-poster bed and thick woolen rugs that softened both step and sound, their intricate swirling knots and geometric patterns speaking of distant weavers long forgotten beneath countless passing feet.
The beds themselves were quite a surprise for a town this small. Coarse but clean linen sheets, thick woolen blankets, and a fur throw folded neatly at the foot promised warmth against the cold. Above them, heavy canopies of dark carved wood bore vines and gryphons worn smooth by age. A faint trace of lavender clung to the bedding, subtle but unmistakable, a small luxury amid an inn that would otherwise have smelled of ale and smoke.
Each suite opened into a private sitting area gathered around a modest hearth. The stone walls were thick enough to mute all but the loudest sounds below, and brass lanterns cast a steady golden light that played across old tapestries stitched with heroic hunts and legendary duels, their colors dim but their stories intact.
Harmon had claimed the central suite, its wide windows giving him a view of both alley and avenue, and set up a crude command post on the main table, maps unrolled, reports from contacts in the city pinned with brass daggers. Aurelia and Weslin occupied the adjoining suite, which was quieter and more isolated, the perfect place for what they needed. 
Aurelia sat cross-legged near the hearth in her and Weslin’s room, a small leather pouch open before her, its contents carefully arranged on a low stool: a sprig of dried holly, a shallow bowl of water, a simple brass mirror no bigger than her palm. None of it was necessary for her magic, not truly, but it helped beginners to focus.
Across from her, Weslin sat stiffly in a chair facing her. In his hands, he clutched the smooth, palm-sized shard Harmon had given him earlier, the faintest golden shimmer coiled inside it like smoke. His blue-gray tunic was freshly laundered but wrinkled from travel, and his boots still carried a stubborn dust from the road. His hair, dark and shaggy, fell into his eyes as he listened intently.
Neavin and his bonded spirit, shimmer barely visible, appeared like a distortion in the air, a ripple of presence, were in the same room with them. Not a separate thing. Not a summoned creature. It was Neavin, and Neavin was it, a perfect, indivisible union. The spirit hummed faintly at the edges of perception, like a low, comforting chord that filled the room without ever needing to be heard aloud. He was here to listen and see what he could learn as well.
“You need to understand something before we begin, Weslin,” Aurelia said, her voice even but firm. “This isn't a game. This isn't a story you heard growing up. Every mistake you make could hurt someone, or worse, yourself.” She paused to take a drink of water.
“You’re behind where most students start,” Aurelia said evenly. “That doesn’t mean you can’t catch up. It does mean you’ll be pushed harder than you’re ready for. You will not be rushed. We go as fast as you progress. Understood?”
Weslin’s fingers fumbled the shard, nearly dropping it before he caught it with a muffled curse. His ears flushed red, but he puffed up his chest. “I get it, ma’am,” Weslin said quickly. “I won’t waste the chance. I’ll work harder. You’ll see.”
Aurelia paused, studying him. The eagerness in his face was almost disarming, bright, open, unscarred by failure or fear. She let a small, reluctant smile touch her lips. “It's not about the amount of energy, Weslin.” Her voice stays even. “Control is. Discipline. Focus mental strength.” She paused. “You'll need to be sharper with your mind than Harmon will make you with a sword.” 
Weslin straightened his back, nodding fiercely. “Yes, Ma'am. I’ll... I'll be sharp. Like a blade. Like a real Adept.” His boots tapped an erratic rhythm against the table leg.
Aurelia reached out, gently but firmly pressing a hand to his bouncing knee, stilling it. “First lesson,” she said softly. “Stillness is your first weapon. Still mind, still body. You can't catch a river in a closed fist. You have to be the bank that guides it.”
He nodded again, more carefully this time. Around them, the fire popped once, and beyond the thick stone walls, the low murmur of their companions moving about their rooms filtered in like the pulse of a heartbeat. He closed his eyes and focused on staying still, listening to the rhythms of the world around him. 
Neavin followed suit. He closed his eyes and stilled his breathing. He could feel his bond with Veyrith, like a cord connected to him, not knowing where, but also everywhere. He went deeper on the cord, feeling a slow, patient thrum of trust, then another cord, this one of loyalty, and it was tied firm around his soul. Hearing thoughts traveling through the cords, Veyrith's thoughts were not like a man’s; they were filled with scents and instincts, flashes of memory that brushed against his mind like a passing mist. 
“Cold Floor, Too Still. Humans chitter like mice. No threat. Safe here. Need to run soon. Hunt soon.”
Then the following thoughts changed, “Neavin is pack. Bound, not caged. Chose this. Chose him. I am free.” 
The spirits’ memories rippled once more to the past, Blurred images of running wild in his mind. A calm filled Neavin. Beneath the whirl of animal thoughts and the steady thrum of loyalty, Neavin’s mind sharpened with a quiet sense of gratitude. He was glad he had stayed. He had come into the room to listen and observe, and somewhere in Aurelia's quiet instruction to Weslin, he had found something that applied equally to him. The stillness was not emptiness. It was space. 
If mastering the art of mental discipline could strengthen the bridge between him and his bondmate, this could make their bond not just a tether, but a true unity. Then every word she spoke was a weapon he would gladly learn to wield. 
Aurelia raised a hand, graceful and slow, and spoke in her warm, patient tone.
“Now, to move to the training lesson, today is about resonance,” she said, her voice like a balm. “Before you call power, before you direct it... You must first listen to it.”
She placed the mirror flat on the stool and gestured. “Focus not on yourself, Weslin. Focus on the world around you. Let the mirror catch it. Let the water reflect it. Let the spirit between you and the world hum with it. Feel that pulse.”
Neavin shifted slightly, a wave of warmth rolling through the room, not overpowering, but undeniably there.
Aurelia let the quiet work, the mirror catching candlelight, the water holding it. After a time, she asked, gentle but direct, “What do you think I asked you to do, and why?”
Weslin looked up, “To teach me how to focus?”
“No, what else do you think it could be?”
Weslin’s knee started to bounce, heat rising in his cheeks. “I, I do not know.” Aurelia stilled his leg with a hand. “You do. Try again. What did you take from both exercises, and how does it help you learn?”
He swallowed, then found the words. “To let the noise pass without taking me with it. To notice what is there, even when no one speaks.” His leg began to bounce faster.
Aurelia walked by, putting her hand on his knee to stop it from bouncing, “Calm yourself, remember lesson one. Deep breath. Think. What happened to you at the feast was this,” Aurelia said calmly. “You felt the world too close…” Another pause. “This teaches you to be still while it moves.”
Weslin closed his eyes and tried to clear his head like before. When he opened them again, he was in a new state of mind. He was still nervous, yet different. “I was overwhelmed by everything going on.”
“Good, so now take that and ask why I would ask you to do these simple exercises?”
Again, he took another deep breath, and instead of panic, he didn’t know the answer; he took his time and let his mind come to a thought. “Because there will always be a world around me, so I must be able to focus on the world out there? As well as hearing the connections beyond sound.”
“Very good. Yes, we are different from most other adepts because when we are surrounded by the very thing, we can manipulate it. Yes, it can and mostly is overwhelming. So we need a way to focus, keep doing this exercise until the next time we can meet. Understood?”
“Yes, ma’am.”
“Good, I will try to meet with you every other day, that way it gives you time to work on the exercise. Mission will dictate the rest.”
Weslin got to his feet, “Yes, Ma’am.”
Garr filled the doorframe without knocking. “Harmon needs you in the other room,” he said. He did not wait for an answer. 
Aurelia inclined her head, and Garr vanished. Weslin glanced up. “You knew he would come,” Weslin didn’t ask. He knew.
“I keep a thread open, I heard the thoughts before he moved,” she said.
Neavin rose, Veyrith a weight of feathers on his shoulder. “If you do not mind, I would like to attend these lessons when I can. The stillness steadies the bond. It keeps me from slipping too far into her and losing my own edge.”
She smiled, “No, I do not mind, just know I am not doing this for you, but you are welcome to keep coming.”
He bows his head, “Thank you.” She just nods back, still with a smile on her face.
Weslin and Neavin stepped out together, and Aurelia gathered her things. “He is going to be good indeed,” she thought, then a quieter truth, “and good may not be enough tonight.” She turned toward Harmon’s suite.
When she arrived, she noticed the air inside Harmon’s suite was dense with the smell of wax and parchment. The lavender scent from the bedding was a strange counterpoint to the grim business at hand. Nyssa, Ash, Garr, and Brother Aldrek were already in there, sitting around the wide oak table. The brass lanterns above cast long, shifting shadows across their faces. Maps and loose reports lay spread out between mugs of untouched ale and a half-finished loaf of travel bread. Beyond the windows, the sky had been pressing lower all afternoon, the kind of grey that meant weather before morning. Harmon stood at the head of the table, one hand resting firmly on the maps, the other tucked behind his back, his jaw set in a hard, thoughtful line.
He swept his gaze across them, not hurried, but deliberate, as if weighing each of them on invisible scales before he spoke.
“All right,” Harmon said, he looked across them all once more. “We move at dusk. Scout first. Final preparations after. Then Dain makes his attempt.”
He tapped a dagger against the map, pointing to several rough circles he had drawn. Exits, alleys, and other points of interest. “First, Nyssa, Ash,” he said, locking eyes with each of them in turn, “your job is simple, but critical. We need eyes on this city. I want a proper map in my hand before nightfall, not the butchered sketches we bought off the caravan we passed. Find the true entrances, the choke points, and patrol routes if you can. I want streets, guard posts, sewer accesses if they exist.”
Ash gave a quick, sharp nod, already shifting on his boots like he was ready to run through the wall. Nyssa just grinned, twirling a dagger once between her fingers before letting it vanish into a hidden sheath on her belt.
“And the prison itself,” Harmon said, voice low. “Shift changes, watch posts, guard count. In and out, fast. No heroics. If this turns loud, I want exits, not excuses.” 
Nyssa’s grin flashed, Ash’s jaw set, and for a heartbeat, they shared a look that said neither would be the one to blink first.
“Try not to burn half the quarter just to make a point,” Nyssa muttered, rolling her shoulder. “I know about you.”
Ash’s smile was all teeth. “Try not to pick the wrong pocket and get us all killed. Know about you as well.”
The sharp edge lingered, and Harmon let it hang a moment before moving on. They would have to learn from each other the hard way.
Nyssa chuckled softly, but both of them straightened a little, ready.
Satisfied, Harmon turned his gaze to Brother Aldrek, whose bulk leaned against the far wall with arms folded over his tabard. His mace hung at his hip, quiet but heavy.
“Brother Aldrek,” Harmon said, his voice softer but no less firm, “your task is shadow work. When Dain leaves, I want you trailing him. Blend with the crowd; your robes will help. Keep back far enough not to draw the guards' attention, but close enough that if something turns foul, you can reach him in time. Understood?”
Brother Aldrek gave a shallow bow of his head, a slow, deliberate thing that spoke of certainty rather than submission.
“Good.”
Harmon moved around the table now, slowly, hands behind his back, his boots silent against the thick rugs. His next words were directed at Aurelia, who sat with Weslin beside her, the boy perched eagerly on a chair far too big for him, legs swinging just a little above the floor.
“Aurelia,” Harmon said, “link those on the prison recon and hold it as long as you can.”
“Understood,” she said, calm but steady.
“Weslin, you stay with her. Learn, keep her safe while her mind is elsewhere. Observation is your mission tonight.” 
Weslin sat up straighter, practically vibrating with the need to prove himself. “Yes, sir!” he said, a little too loudly, then flushed red when a few smiles flickered around the room. Harmon didn’t chide him, just moved on, already calculating.
