Weslin kept his expression steady and his hands in his lap and told himself that observation was a real job. It was. Harmon had said so. He had not said it like it was a consolation, but Weslin had heard it that way and was doing his best not to keep hearing it that way. He looked at the table and breathed. 
“Neavin,” he said finally, meeting the man's sharp eyes, “I’ll need your eyes airborne once we move. Give me the city from above, not just the prison, but the approaches. Watch for followers. Look for anything out of place. If Ash and Nyssa are followed, I want to know before they do.”
Neavin gave a small, almost imperceptible nod, but there was a gleam of eager pride behind it, the pride of being trusted.
“Weslin, you are responsible for him, too,” Harmon added, almost as an afterthought. This time, Weslin just nodded his head. 
Neavin touched two fingers to his brow toward Weslin. A promise. Harmon looked across them all. “Tonight decides whether we get him back at all.” 
Aurelia's hand moved to her shard. “I cannot set the link without Dain,” she said. Not a request. A constraint. “Where is he?” 
Harmon answered, “Suite across the hall.”
Aurelia drew a slow breath and closed her eyes, centering herself in the familiar pattern of her craft. Weslin, seated nearby, leaned forward unconsciously, his small hands clenched in the folds of his tunic as he watched her every movement.
Aurelia’s right hand lifted and hovered above the center of the table, palm down, fingers slightly spread. A faint golden shimmer began to gather around her wrist, subtle at first, like heat distortion over stone. Then it thickened, threads of luminous energy weaving outward in gentle spirals. The Shard at her throat began to glow as she drew power to fuel this connection.
Mind to mind, heart to heart, thread to thread, she murmured inwardly, invoking the discipline of connection the way she had been taught long ago. These words have no meaning to the magic itself. 
The first strand shot outward, unseen by mortal eyes but humming in Neavin’s mind like a faint pluck of a harp string. He blinked once, sharply aware, feeling the moment her consciousness brushed against his. It wasn't intrusive; more like a whisper beside his ear, offering him the chance to answer.
Neavin opened himself carefully, and the thread anchored, a warm presence sitting just at the edge of his mind.
Aurelia moved on without pausing, drawing another line of gold, this one seeking Ash and Nyssa as they lingered by the door. Nyssa flinched for just a heartbeat, her thief’s instincts rebelling against anything slipping past her guard, but Ash placed a reassuring hand on her shoulder, and together they allowed the tether to latch.
Brother Aldrek was next. His acceptance came heavier and grounded, the link settling without resistance. Aurelia’s brow furrowed slightly. Sweat beaded at her temple. This many threads took focus. Now comes... the more delicate part.
Without opening her eyes, she reached across the hallway, through the faint soul-echo she could sense from Dain. It took longer. The walls blurred in her mind’s eye like mist, but she pressed through it carefully, searching for the spark of his mind in the next suite.
“There,” she whispered.
Dain’s presence was sharp-edged, alert even while dressing, like a blade half-drawn from its sheath. She sent the thread, careful not to startle him, a brush of intent more than force. After a moment’s hesitation and a suspicious pause on Dain’s end, he accepted the link with a mental grunt of acknowledgment. It wasn't perfect, slightly thinner than the others, but it would hold for now. Aurelia exhaled shakily.
The final connection was Harmon himself. She found him easily, his mind like the center of a wheel, firm and unyielding. It was as if he opened it just for her. When she tethered him, the whole web tightened, drawing taut until it hummed softly across their collective thoughts. 
One by one, the team would feel it settle, a faint sensation of awareness of each other, not true thoughts yet, but presences, emotional impressions, a readiness to speak or listen mentally when needed.
Aurelia opened her eyes. They glowed faintly gold for a heartbeat before dimming back to warm brown. “It is done,” she said softly, her voice a little hoarse.
Weslin, wide-eyed, leaned closer. “How do you hold it all at once?”
Aurelia offered him a faint, tired smile. “You do not hold it. You weave it. Like a tapestry. Each mind strengthens the others.”
Harmon nodded approvingly. He rolled his shoulders slightly, already feeling the link’s potential stir across the bond.
“Good work,” Harmon said. His thought carried across the new web, steady as a drumbeat.
Aurelia sank into a chair, her shoulders bowed, a tremor running through her fingers as she brushed the shard at her throat. A sheen of sweat caught in the firelight, and her words came measured, deliberate. “It is simple in use,” she said quietly. “Think of the person you mean,” she said quietly. “Shape the words. They will hear you.”
Nyssa sent a dry flicker of a thought, Ash answered with a crisp “heard,” Aldrek’s presence settled like stone, and for a heartbeat the web quivered before holding firm.
“Feels like shackles,” Dain’s voice slipped across the tether, dry and sharp.
“No,” Aldrek countered, his thought like a hammer-strike, “discipline. Unity.”
“Chains dressed in finer words,” Dain shot back, earning a roll of Nyssa’s eyes. Aurelia’s hand tightened on her shard, sweat beading at her brow.
“Thank you, Aurelia. How long do we have?”
“With my current shard, I would say about three hours.”
“Good. Everyone, let's get a move on.”
Nyssa gave a lazy mock salute and nudged Ash with her elbow, and the two of them slipped out the door like smoke.
Brother Aldrek moved back into the shadows of the room, melting into a watcher’s stance. Across the hall, they could hear faint movement, the sounds of Dain preparing, leather buckles clicking, and the heavy thud of boots being drawn on.
Dain stepped into the room with his usual swagger, road dust scrubbed away and beard trimmed to a courtly shadow. His coat was cut in deep navy velvet, lapels neat and fitted close at the ribs, flaring just slightly at the hips. Silver thread marked the cuffs and high collar, subtle flourishes that hinted at coin. A cream silk cravat, pinned with a modest sapphire brooch, lent a merchant’s polish, while pressed trousers and polished boots grounded the look. At his side, a sword belt with its ornate hilt finished the image, wealth dressed as purpose, arrogance tempered into poise.
“You clean up well,” Harmon said, folding his arms and motioning for Dain to come closer to the command table. “But remember, you’re not here to impress. You’re here to buy.”
Dain raised a brow. “Right. Lord Alric Rendsdale of House Emberlight, cousin to the Wraithmoors,” Dain recited. “Enough coin to move a clerk,” Dain said. “Enough temper to make him hesitate.”
“Cold, but invested,” Harmon said. “A cousin you once trained with is locked up. Your House would rather the records stay clean. You want the problem to go away, not a sermon about forms.”
Aldrek’s hood tipped, a rasp of disapproval that was half prayer, half warning. Dain only smiled.
“Riven’s your old friend. You don’t care what he did. You just want it handled quietly. Bribe first. Pressure second. Bluff last. Don’t make threats unless you’re prepared to make them stick.”
Dain nodded once. “Got it. And backup?”
Harmon gestured to Brother Aldrek, already in his robes and shadowed hood, leaning quietly by the wall. “He will follow once you are on the move. Stay a full block behind. He will blend in with the beggars and street priests. If things go sideways, he will step in. 
“What about the others?” Dain asked. 
“They are in motion,” Harmon said. “Routes, patrols, choke points. You felt the tether, use it.” Dain nodded. 
Garr snorted. “The way you preen in that getup, I half expect you to trip over your own boots. One slip, and the rest of us pay the price.”
Dain’s smirk sharpened, his hand brushing the cuff of his coat. “Jealous, Garr?” Dain said lightly. “Some of us were made to stand in halls and talk to lords,” Dain said lightly. “Others were meant to be seen, not heard.”
The air bristled. Garr’s jaw worked, muscles tight as stone, and his hand twitched near the hilt at his belt.
“Enough,” Harmon cut in, voice iron. “Save it for the enemy. Pride won’t matter if you’re both dead before dawn.”
The room eased, but Garr’s glare lingered, promising this wasn’t over.
Harmon stepped toward the window and turned to the last man in the room. “Neavin. I need you airborne,” Harmon said. “Stay sharp and keep them safe.”
Neavin closed his eyes. “Understood.”
Veyrith, his bonded spirit, still a falcon on his shoulder, folded her wings and stretched in anticipation. The falcon was one of her favorite shapes. When Neavin released her fully, her form solidified, her talons clicking softly against the stone floor.
Neavin whispered a word in the Old Tongue, and Veyrith leapt soundlessly to the open window, wings flaring wide.
Then Neavin's breath slowed. His hands lowered to his knees. His vision shifted. Snapped.
The room around him faded, and the world opened through Veyrith’s eyes, a sharp, crystalline burst of color and clarity. Wind streamed across feathers. The rooftops below sprawled like a broken puzzle of slate and chimney smoke. His heartbeat stilled, matching hers. Every flick of movement, every flutter of cloth or glint of armor, pulled at his attention. He could feel the currents, the heights, the breath of air over his wings. He was flying.
“Eyes are open,” Neavin whispered, voice half his own. “I’ll track him from the skies.”
“Good,” Harmon said, eyes sharp. “Then it begins.”
Dain turned and strode for the door with his sword bouncing gently at his hip.
Harmon watched him go, the quiet weight of planning coiling tight around his shoulders.
“Keep him safe,” he murmured to no one in particular.
Then, to the room at large, “We move on his signal.”
And the command center fell into measured silence, broken only by the hum of thought, the press of wind beyond the windows, and the gathering storm outside.






Chapter Twelve
The streets of Forgehallow buzzed with a constant hum, not from crowds, but from industry, the rhythmic pounding of forge hammers and the low thunder of ore carts over cobbled stone. The city wore soot like a second skin, its buildings scarred with smoke and pitted stone. Black chimneys loomed overhead, exhaling constant streams of gray into the ever-hazy sky.
Dain Kerswell cut a distinct figure amid the grime and sweat of the Forge Quarter. He looked exactly as Harmon had intended. Nothing screamed excess. Everything marked him as coin and calculation. He carried the cane for show, kept his shoulders square, and let the costume do what costumes were built to do.” He paused at the edge of the Forge Quarter. “Behind the calm was something sharper. Honed by loss.” Behind his calm exterior was calculation, honed by loss.
As Dain stepped out into the smoke-drenched late-afternoon, Neavin’s voice sounded soft in his head. “Here is where you are going. Take the main road south, pass the ash market. Turn left at the blacksmith’s yard with the shattered anvil sign. You’ll see a narrow stone stair beside a rusted water wheel. Take it. The Magistrate’s Tower is short, square, black-bricked with iron-banded windows. Hard to miss. Two guards were posted out front. They don’t like questions. Do you have any?”
“Understood,” replied Dain, already moving. His travel did not take long. He worked through the soot-covered streets and trash-ridden throughways without difficulty. 
After a few minutes walking, he stopped outside a squat, imposing building, the Magistrate’s Tower. Unlike the rest of Forgehallow’s architecture, it loomed tall and rigid, its blackstone façade polished and reinforced with iron. The symbol of the Forgehallow Crest, a hammer over a flame, was etched into the arch above the double doors. Windows, few and narrow, offered no warmth or welcome.
Dain glanced to the sky. A falcon circled high above, wings outstretched, drifting like a silent guardian. Through that creature’s eyes, Neavin Torrick watched—his spirit-bound companion acting as overwatch.
“Eyes sharp?” Dain murmured under his breath, hands coming together in a semblance of prayer. To a passerby, he was just another noble offering thanks before entering a government office. In truth, he was listening, waiting.
The falcon completed a wide arc. “All clear,” Neavin’s thought carried steady through the link.
Across the square, Brother Aldrek stood cloaked in the garb of a wandering preacher. His robes hung loose, bulky and patched, designed to obscure the armor he wore beneath. He moved with the slow rhythm of a man used to being ignored, humming a wordless tune as he leaned on a wooden staff.
It is time he thought, lifting his hands briefly before folding them in prayer. He looked up with a smile and moved to the entrance like a new man. 
Dain Kerswell swept up the short steps to the tower entrance, boots clicking against the soot-stained stone with noble purpose. The streets behind him were alive with clangs and hisses from distant forges, and the scent of ash and molten metal was even stronger here. He kept a silk kerchief near his nose, though the gesture was as much for appearance as comfort. His cloak, a lush, deep green lined in silver trim, billowed slightly as he approached the iron-barred doors of the city’s grim Magistrate’s Tower.
Two guards stood at attention, though loosely so, outside the main door. Both wore dull gray cloaks over piecemeal chainmail, one smoking a thin roll of something foul, the other half-slouched with his spear angled casually across his shoulder. Dain went right past them as if they were not there, entering the tower. 
The doors of the Magistrate’s Tower swung wide, creaking slightly on hinges thick with soot and ash. Inside, the air was stale, warmed by coal-fed braziers, the scent of scorched metal clinging to everything. Stone walls bore black streaks from the fires of a forge long ago shut down and converted into civil offices. Thick iron girders supported the ceiling, and the floor beneath Dain’s polished boots was scuffed slate, worn smooth by generations of heavy boots and chained feet.
Inside, two guards sat behind a tall ironwood desk, their blackened breastplates dulled by soot and long hours. Their armor bore the mark of Forgehallow’s civic garrison, an anvil flanked by twin hammers, but no pride shone in the eyes above their stained collars.
Dain’s entrance echoed through the room. He walked with shoulders squared, the fur-trimmed lapels of his newly acquired nobleman’s coat swaying slightly with each step. He tapped his cane once, a small silver-tipped thing, more for flourish than use.
The first guard, a square-jawed man with oil-slicked hair and a scar along his jawline, lifted an unimpressed brow. “Can we help you?” he asked flatly, glancing up from under his helm.
Dain gave a slow, deliberate look over the pair, as though judging whether they were stable enough to pour his wine. He adjusted his gloves with pointed irritation.
“I am here,” he said, as if the sentence alone should have been sufficient, “to secure the release of one of your prisoners,” voice clipped and clean like polished glass.
The second guard, younger and a little too eager to be part of something amusing, smirked. “Which little lordling got in trouble this time, then? Came to spring the stable boy who pissed himself in the tavern?”
Dain gave a soft, almost offended exhale, as if their very breath wasted his time. “It is not a ‘lordling.’ He is a man of... particular importance to the family I represent. A common-born man, yes, but not common in value. His name is Riven Duskwind.”
At the name, both guards shifted subtly. A flicker of something, recognition, discomfort, passed between their eyes. But the younger one was quicker to mask it, clearing his throat and replying with a practiced shrug.
“I’m sorry, my lord. No one by that name’s in our records.”
Dain tilted his head, lips pressing into a tight smile. “Let us not insult each other with this,” he said. “I have coin. You have a prisoner. The arithmetic is simple.” Keeping eye contact with the guard at the desk, “I have it on good authority that he is here. And I’m willing to pay a sum to secure his immediate release that would make both of your lives... substantially more comfortable.”
The older guard scratched his neck, his voice gruffer now. “Again, we don’t know who you mean, my lord. Maybe you were misinformed. Lotta folks come through here. Not all of them stay long.”
Dain’s nostrils flared. “This town,” he hissed, voice low at first, “is a smudge on the map, a blackened thumbprint on Aldoria’s ledger.” His tone sharpened with each word. “Your kind choke on soot and call it breath. You guard a tower as if it were a throne, yet you can’t even name the prisoner you’re paid to keep.” His last step forward brought venom. “Now fetch me someone who commands more than a broom and a half-rusted spear.”
The younger guard blinked, visibly annoyed but unwilling to argue directly with someone dressed better than the mayor. “Wait here,” he muttered, and turned toward the heavy inner gate with an irritated sigh.
As he moved, Dain muttered to no one in particular, adjusting his collar, “Honestly. You’d think a city responsible for manufacturing half the Alliances’ pikes could forge a working brain or two.”
The older guard didn’t respond, only kept his hand on his spear and eyes on Dain, who made a point of not looking back.
The younger guard paused, turning just as he was about to disappear through the gate. He eyed Dain’s fine coat, his polished boots too clean for the city’s ash-caked streets, and couldn’t help himself.
“With a tongue like that, my lord, be careful you don’t end up as one of our guests.”
Dain slowly turned his head. The look he gave could’ve frozen molten iron. He took a step forward, gloved hands folded behind his back, voice as smooth and deadly as a drawn rapier. Harmon’s voice slid into the link. “Drop the name Saewyn Olgrave. You’re steady.”
“Oh? And with a face like yours, I imagine you’d enjoy scrubbing floors in the house of Lord Saewyn Olgrave. That’s assuming you’re not consigned to the mines for impersonating a thinking man.”
The name hit like a hammer.
Both guards stiffened.
Lord Saewyn Olgrave, second cousin to the royal line, master of eastern trade routes, and recently elevated to head of the Governors’ Inquisition’s regional oversight council. A man with the power to make accusations disappear, or men, if it suited him. And Dain had just invoked his name like someone who knew him.
Dain tilted his head, a mock-apologetic smirk curling across his lips. “Now then. Shall I ask Lord Olgrave whether this is how you treat emissaries? Or shall we pretend, for both your sakes, that this moment never happened, and you let me speak to someone who wears more than recycled rust for a uniform?”
The older guard was already motioning toward the gate, his voice low and tight. “Right... of course, my lord. We’ll take you to the Warden.”
The younger one opened the heavy door, suddenly paler, his smirk long gone.
Dain gave a satisfied nod, brushing a speck of ash from his cloak as he stepped forward. “How very reasonable. Lead on, gentlemen.”
The iron-banded gate groaned open, the reek of damp stone and metal drifting out to meet him. He followed them inside, head high, the corridors of this backwater dungeon already beneath him.
The narrow hallway gave way to a large, dimly lit office built into the base of the tower. Iron sconces flickered along the curved walls, casting long shadows over thick stone and faded banners bearing the mark of the local magistrate, three rust-red keys crossed beneath a broken crown. The air was cooler here, cleaner, like the filth of the prison above hadn’t yet corrupted it.
Behind a wide oak desk sat a woman with sharp features and colder eyes. She was in her early forties, lean and angular, wearing a dark leather coat with the emblem of the city watch pressed into the shoulder. A ledger lay open before her, but she wasn’t reading it. She was watching Dain the moment he stepped in.
“You must be the storm my men warned me about,” she said, rising slowly. “Warden Caldra Hesk. I assume you’re here for a reason.”
Dain offered the barest nod, his hand grazing the lapel of his deep navy coat as if wiping off the air of the room. “Lord Alric Rendsdale of House Emberlight from Estmere. I am here to secure the release of a man wrongly imprisoned under your authority. His name is Riven Duskwind.”
She arched an eyebrow, settling back into her chair like a woman preparing for a game of strategy. “Duskwind, is it? You’re not the first to come sniffing around for that one.”
That caught Dain off guard, but only briefly. He smiled thinly. “Then I trust his release is imminent. Whatever offense he’s caused, I’m prepared to pay restitution. House Emberlight values its debts and its allies.”
Caldra tapped a quill against the desk. “A noble offering coin. How refreshingly blunt.” Her tone was dry, skeptical. “And yet, I don’t recall receiving a writ from your House. Nor any notice from the embassy. Odd, wouldn’t you say? For such an urgent matter?”
Dain narrowed his eyes. “You know very well how slow diplomacy moves. I chose not to wait while letters shuffled hands. The boy’s important to us. And I don’t like delays. “We also prefer discretion.”
“Important?” she repeated, leaning forward. “To you? Or to someone higher up the ladder?”
“I’m acting on behalf of my family,” Dain said carefully.
Caldra’s gaze didn’t flinch. “So you said. And what interest does your family have in a man with no lands, no title, and a dangerous list of friends?”
“You mistake nobility for blindness. Connections come in many forms,” Dain replied coolly. “Riven is... more useful free than he is buried in a hole under your keep.”
Her smile was humorless. “That’s where we disagree. Here in Forgehallow, we measure usefulness in stability. Not in favors owed or coin offered.” She rose again, slowly circling her desk like a hawk eyeing a restless fox. “You think this is about him? Some stray your house claims as property?”
Dain stiffened. But she didn’t stop there. She leaned back in her chair, one brow arched, studying him now with a cold curiosity. Like she was dissecting something pinned to a board.
“Tell me something, my Lord…” she said, rolling the title in her mouth like it was spoiled fruit. “Did they send you down here hoping your name might do what your reputation clearly hasn’t?”
Dain’s lips twitched. “I wasn’t aware I had a reputation in Forgehollow.”
“Oh, you do now.” Caldra stood, walking slowly around the desk like a wolf circling. “The boy who walked in playing dress-up. All polish, no leverage. You came in here expecting a bow, maybe a ‘yes, m’lord’ or two, and a quick transaction like this was a damn stablehouse negotiation. But this isn’t your family’s estate. This is the Tower. And I don’t give a single copper who you think you are.”
She stepped in close now, her voice lowering, sharp as a knife dragged across silk.
“You wear that coat like it was earned,” she said while looking him up and down, “I can smell the starch on it. “You walked in here carrying a name and a coin purse and the assumption that in every city, someone will bend. That works in courts. This is not a court.” 
That one landed hard.
Dain’s jaw tightened, the twitch of his fingers drifting toward his saber. One more word and he’d draw—
“Stay cool, kid.” Harmon’s voice slid into the link, firm as iron.
“Nyssa’s thought came through like smoke through a keyhole, barely there, carrying everything. “Breathe, Lord Fancy. Be the noble. Leave Dain locked away with his pride. Keep the mask on.”
Dain closed his eyes. A breath in. A slower breath out. And then she added, a little too smug:
“You nobles all think you can come crawling into the Tower, flashing names and coin like it still means something, especially when it’s for one half-dead mercenary who’s spent the last three days rotting below.”
And for a moment, she realized it. The way Dain’s expression sharpened, the flash of focus in his eyes. She’d said too much.
He smoothed his coat. Adjusted his cuffs. Drew his spine tall.
When he looked up, the storm behind his eyes had settled, but the cold remained.
“An enlightening observation,” he said, voice sharpened to a needle. Then, with a small, aristocratic tilt of the head. “But I find those who speak of importance so often lack it themselves.”
He paused for effect, “After all, power whispered rarely needs to raise its voice.”
That landed.
Caldra blinked, just once, and her mouth curled into something half-smile, half-snarl.
But her voice was all steel.
“Still doesn’t change a thing,” she said. “No one by that name in our records. Enjoy the walk back to your manor, my Lord. Try not to trip over your pedigree on the way out.”
She motioned to the guards.
Caldra offered one last sardonic smile. “Show our guest the way out. With all the warmth and courtesy our city is famous for.”
One of the guards gave a faint grunt. “Aye, Warden.”
Dain raised his chin as they stepped forward. “Don’t touch me,” he warned, adjusting his gloves with dramatic flair. “I remember the way.” He used the link to pass on, “Looks like it’s going to be the hard way.”
Harmon’s voice came through the link, “Get as much detail as you can.”
“Already am,” Dain murmured. Quietly through the link, almost to himself, he added two more words. “Old man.” He had not planned to say it. It had just come out. He decided he did not regret it. 
They didn’t lay hands on him, but the walk back through the corridors was slow and shadowed with deliberate tension. The younger guard bumped his shoulder into Dain’s as they passed the gate back to the entry area. Not hard enough to start a fight. Just enough to remind him he was leaving empty-handed.
One gave him a sharp shove as they passed through the threshold, and Dain stumbled down the tower’s worn steps, his cane clattering momentarily against the stone. He landed hard on one knee, the impact jolting through his leg. A smear of dirt marked the side of his coat.
A figure across the street stirred, the bulky silhouette of Brother Aldrek, mid-sermon. He took a half step forward, hand twitching near his belt, but a subtle shake of the head from across the street stilled him.
“Don’t blow the cover.” He heard in his head.
 Dain rose, dusting himself off with slow dignity. He turned back toward the tower, expression unreadable, and with a smirk of disdain, lifted his hand, not in a noble wave, but in a common gesture of dismissal aimed at the iron-clad tower itself. With noble arrogance, he sauntered off as if the event that just transpired didn’t even happen. 
 Behind him, Brother Aldrek received a notification through the link, “Stay at the door. Eyes open.”
 He did just that. The payoff was just a few moments later, the door to the tower opened, and two men left the building. The first to step out of the tower, he moved like a shadow peeled from the wall, tall, rangy, with the lean build of a man used to traveling light and fast. His face was narrow, sun-starved, with deep lines at the corners of his mouth that hadn’t come from laughter. A patchy beard traced his jawline, unkempt enough to seem forgettable. He wore a soot-stained duster common among the city’s low-tier merchants, but it was too clean in the wrong places, too new at the cuffs, too straight at the collar. Boots were polished but scuffed at the toes. His eyes scanned like a man mapping escape routes with every blink, and though he moved with civilian casualness, Brother Aldrek recognized the gait of someone trained, someone ready to run or kill. 
The other one was shorter and broader. He lit a pipe with fingers that bore faint Ink stains, maybe a clerk or scribbler by trade, or someone posing as one. His belly was soft, but not enough to slow him. His cloak hung low, brushing the dirty stone, and the way he wore it, angled to cover one side of his chest, suggested he might be hiding something beneath. Unlike the first, his face bore a smile, the kind meant to deflect suspicion. But his eyes were wrong: alert, dry, too aware of the street around him. When a child passed too close, his hand reflexively dropped to his side. Not a thug, not a soldier. Something else. Watching. Measuring.
Both of the men pulled up their cloak hoods and stepped off. Brother Aldrek sent the message to the group, “Two just left the building. “
 He watched the alley opposite the tower. “One’s heading down toward the Noble District, a navy blue cloak pulled, walking quickly, but not in a rush. The other is tailing Dain, not even subtle about it. He has a charcoal-gray duster on, with working boots and soot-stained trousers.”
“I have the one heading toward the Noble district,” Neavin said. “I will hand them off to the recon team. Are you moving to the noble district, Nyssa?”
“We are here and ready to go, just tell us when and where,” replied Nyssa.
The link was working, though barely. Thoughts arrived with the rough edges of people still learning to speak in a new language. Above them all, the falcon wheeled in a slow arc, the only one of them entirely comfortable with the altitude. 
The noble district was another world. Whitewashed walls gleamed, cobbles swept clean beneath flowering hedgerows, fountains spilling in quiet courtyards. Even the air was different, lilac and fresh bread instead of ash and rot.
Ash exhaled slowly. “Feels like another damn country.”
Nyssa walked beside him, hood up, but unbothered by the stares of passing servants or the occasional guard.
From the rooftops, Neavin’s voice came through the link, calm and clipped. “Heading in on North Street. Are you ready to intercept?”
Nyssa pulled her hood tighter and slipped ahead, eyes sharp. Ash followed beside her, one hand resting near the pouch at his belt. They moved fast, quieter than most would expect given Ash’s broad-shouldered frame. Their new target had made no effort to evade detection, and the man was in no rush.
“Got him,” Neavin’s voice said over the link. His falcon circled high above, wings catching the updrafts of forge heat. “He’s heading east, toward the Ironcrest Quarter.”
Nyssa motioned for Ash to follow as they cut through a tight alley between two clothing shops.
“We’ve got eyes,” Neavin confirmed.
They kept a good eye on him, close enough to keep him in sight, but far enough back so as not to draw attention. He walked for a bit longer until he reached a tall, green-and-gold estate wall and disappeared through a side gate.
Ash muttered, “That looked like a noble’s private entrance.”
The two of them kept walking to get a better view of where he went. The manor was made of old stone, had iron vines across the gates, and a sigil carved deep into the face of the structure: the twin-tailed fox. Her breath hitched.
“No,” she whispered. Then bitter laughter cut through. “Of course it is. Who else would it be?”
Ash gave her a side glance. “Friend of yours?”
Her voice hardened as her gaze locked on the sigil. “That is Lord Iven Merrick’s estate,” she said, her voice hardening as her gaze locked on the sigil. “Patron, protector, collector… of rare and dangerous things. If our man walked into Merrick’s gates, then our trouble just doubled.”
“Meaning?” asked Ash.
“He doesn’t take kindly to those who poke around his interests.” She turned abruptly. “We need to get back to Harmon. Now.”
Down the street in the other direction, Dain walked with calm purpose, cutting through the dusk-lit industrial blocks alone, though every sense warned he wasn’t truly alone. The clicks of boots behind him were spaced too perfectly to be chance. He said nothing, just let the rhythm of the street guide him until he reached a side passage near a collapsed forge. He paused there, pretending to inspect an old steam valve.
“I have a tail,” he murmured through the link.
“I see him,” Brother Aldrek’s voice replied through the mental link. “Can’t tell who he is, but I know he came from the tower.”
“Then we tighten the net and find out,” Dain muttered.
They looped once more through Forgehallow’s cracked veins, leading the man into a dead-end loading alley. Dain leaned casually against a steel girder as the man stepped forward, and Aldrek dropped behind him, mace half-drawn.
“Turn around,” Aldrek said. Calm, even. Dangerous.
The man froze, then did as told. No weapon in hand, just sweat on his brow and nerves behind his eyes. “Easy. I’m not here to start a fight.”
Dain said. “You’ve been on me since I left the prison.”
The man hesitated, hands up. “I’m not here to hurt you. Well… I was. But I’m not now.”
Aldrek’s tone was ice. “Explain.”
“They told me to rattle the noble, teach you a lesson. I volunteered,” the man said quickly. His hands twitched. “At first, because it was safer to be close than refuse. Then, because I knew if I got near, I could talk. Not right what’s happening in that tower, not right at all. And this,” his voice cracked, desperate now, “might be my only chance to fix it.”
Dain arched a brow. “Why?”
“Because I knew if I got close, I could talk. I’ve been trying to find someone who might help. Someone who has not bought with the coin of those who run this city.”
The man licked his lips. “Fix what’s wrong. There are three of them in the prison. Riven’s one of them. The others… don’t know their names, but I’ve seen them. They’re kept off-books, moved at night. Some of the guards are on someone’s payroll, and a standing order that no word of them leaves the walls.”
Aldrek’s eyes narrowed. “And you just happened to grow a conscience?”
The man shook his head. “I’ve had one. But there’s no oversight. I thought this might be my only chance.”
“Whose payroll?” asked Aldrek.
He swallowed. “Someone important. The kind of important you don’t survive knowing. Then, today, I added another.”
Aldrek studied the man, then took a step back. “We believe you.”
The man exhaled in relief. He stood very still for a moment. His hands, which had been raised in surrender, came slowly down to his sides. He looked at Aldrek, then at Dain, as if checking that this had been real, that someone had heard, that the telling of it had actually happened. Whatever he found in their faces seemed to satisfy him. “Then I’m gone. I was never here.”
He disappeared Into the smoggy veil of Forgehallow’s twisting alleys.
Moments later, Harmon’s voice came through the link, “Get back to the inn.”
Dain looked at Aldrek. “Roundabout route. We double back.”
“And split,” Aldrek agreed. “Make sure we’re not followed.”
The two shook once, then moved in opposite directions, fading into the night of this mountain city, toward the Iron Flask tavern, and the next step in whatever this was becoming.






Chapter Thriteen
Snow crunched beneath iron-shod hooves as Luca and his team rode north, the frozen trail winding away from the last fragile breath of civilization, Riverrun’s End.
Luca rode at the front, his dark cloak trailing behind him like the wing of a raven. Though he said little, the others followed his lead without question. Behind him, Lysana rode with reins held loose in one gloved hand, casting a lingering glance back at the town disappearing into the swirling gray. Taerel kept his rifle slung tight across his back, the faint scrape of metal on leather marking each steady trot. Aymer, wrapped in wool and waxed canvas, tugged his scarf higher against the rising wind.
Riverrun’s End had served its purpose, nothing more than a cold waypoint on the road north. Built where the Andralis River spilled from the frozen heights of Blackfrost Lake, the gray-stone port town clung to life like a barnacle on a dying whale. It was neutral ground by decree, a trading post and political buffer between three wary kingdoms that still bore the scars of war while diplomats toasted peace far away in Opindale.
The town rose in weathered tiers, sloping upward from the docks that could berth six merchant ships and two river barges. Timber-and-stone buildings leaned against one another like old soldiers, battered by snow and wind. At the north end of the wharf, a drydock scaffold stood like a ribcage over a disassembled two-mast cog, where the hammering of tools and the creaking of timbers never ceased.
Four squat stone barracks overlooked the harbor, their yards churned to slush by boots and training drills. A detachment of thirty Aldorian soldiers occupied them, sent as liaison to the new garrison forming near the Pass.
Beyond the barracks, narrow lanes wound between rows of cramped houses, their chimneys coughing gray smoke into the frozen air. Traps and drying racks hung from porches, heavy with hare, elk hide, and river fish. Further inland, a cluster of shops surrounded a small cobbled square where merchants sold smoked meat and rough spirits beneath sagging awnings.
By the time their packs were loaded and Riverrun’s End had vanished behind the veil of snow, the silence broke.
“Still think we should’ve stayed the night,” Taerel said, his voice carrying through the cold. “That inn had beds. Real beds. The kind where you wake up sore in the hips instead of the spine.”
“You saying you need softness, Ty? I thought your people slept on stone and bathed in ice water,” Lysana said, grinning.
Taerel replied, “We do. But that doesn’t mean we don’t appreciate the occasional mattress that doesn’t squeal like it’s being murdered.”
Aymer chimed in, “You were just mad because the innkeeper wanted to braid your hair.”
Taerel spoke through gritted teeth, sounding a bit frustrated. “He tried to oil it. Called me a ‘Western lion’. I am not… No. I am absolutely not built for that kind of attention.”
Lysana laughed, short, bright, and warm. Even Luca cracked a grin that didn’t quite reach his eyes. It was a strange dynamic, four people from different lives, strangers no more than fifty hours ago, each carrying old scars, riding toward either new ones or maybe something else.
But Luca said nothing more, already watching the road ahead. When Lysana fell behind in adjusting her saddle straps, Luca slowed his mount until they were side by side.
Luca said quietly, “You good?”
She looked up, surprised. “Fine. Just a strap.”
 He nodded. “Call out if you need anything, or if you fall too far behind.”
This small exchange lifted Lysana’s eyebrows, just a little.
They rode for a bit longer, and it was late morning when the snowfall intensified. The clouds dropped low, iron-heavy and choking the sun, casting the world in shades of blue and steel. Trees became silhouettes. The wind bit harder now, stinging exposed skin. It wasn’t just snow anymore. It was sleet mixed in, sharp as ground glass.
 They rounded a bend and reined in abruptly.
 A wooden cart stood sideways in the road, wheels half-buried in ice. Its driver, a lean figure in patchwork leather armor, stepped out slowly from behind it. He held a chipped longsword in one hand and in the other, a short club. No insignia, no colors. But every inch of him screamed desperate and dangerous.
“Well, well,” the bandit leader said. “Look what the storm dragged in.” He grinned widely, teeth yellow in the gray light. “You’ve wandered too far from your warm little town, rich ones. Those cloaks alone could buy me a new cart. The weapons…” His eyes lingered on Luca’s dagger, “Maybe we’ll take those as well, drop them slowly.”
“I don't think you know who you're dealing with,” Taerel said. 
From the tree line, three more figures emerged, one of them leveling a repeating crossbow. Another man shouldered a rusted hatchet, and the third was a woman with two long knives, licking her lips like she was already counting coin.
“I don't think it matters now,” the bandit said, snapping his fingers. 
The crossbowman called out. “Dibs on the rifles! Especially the long one with the iron-banded barrel!”
Lysana whispered to Luca, “They’re too relaxed,” her eyes now locked on the tree line. “They never planned to let us walk.”
So here's how this goes,” the bandit leader said. “Leave the weapons, the coats, the packs. Maybe we'll let you walk.” 
“That's not a deal, that's begging for an arrow,” Lysana said. 
“No,” Luca said low and flat. 
“What was that?” the bandit squinted. 
“Here's the only deal you're getting,” Luca said. 
He stepped forward. His cloak blew back in the wind, revealing the dark obsidian-threaded armor beneath, dull and jagged like cooled volcanic glass.
“Leave everything and walk south. Do not look back.” He took a long, slow breath through his nose, “Or you can stay, and never see the light of day again.” Luca said with no emotion in his voice.
There was a beat of silence. In one instance, the bandit leader laughed a deep, hearty laugh. “That’s the stupidest threat I’ve—”
Luca did not smile. He did not speak. He simply looked at the bandit leader with the particular patience of someone for whom the outcome had already been settled, and waited for the man to make the last decision of his life. 
 A ripple passed through the ground.
The bandit leader’s expression turned to a snarl in a flash, and he snapped his fingers 
The crossbowman lifted his weapon. A jet of blackness exploded from behind him, wrapping around his arms and yanking him violently into the trees. There was a dull crack of bone. He didn’t scream.
One of the knife-wielders spun toward the noise. A dagger flashed from Luca’s hand, obsidian-edged and whisper-quick. It hit the woman in the throat with surgical precision. She fell to her knees, coughing blood, and collapsed without a sound.
The dagger was gone from her throat, back in Luca’s belt. Lysana saw the dagger leave his hand and return to his belt in the space of a single breath. She blinked once. Made note of it, asked nothing. There would be time for questions later, assuming the later arrived. 
The last two rushed forward, howling.
But Luca was already moving. He stepped sideways into the shadow of his horse and disappeared.
He reappeared behind the axe-wielder, grabbing him by the jaw and yanking him backward into the dark. There was a muffled groan, then nothing.
The bandit leader was the last one. He turned and ran.
But his shadows caught him before he made it ten steps. A lance-like object jetted out of the darkness of his own shadow and pierced his heart. He crumpled to the frozen ground.
 And then… silence.
Taerel stared at the empty road for a long moment. When he spoke, the aristocratic polish was still there, but it had been shaken loose from its setting. “I will need some time,” he said carefully, “to decide how I feel about traveling with you.” 
Aymer said with eyes never leaving the tree line, “I’m not sure whether to thank you… or decide I’ll be sleeping lightly from now on.”
Lysana smiled faintly, “Both.”
Luca said nothing. He stood in the center of the snow-slick road, breathing evenly, eyes scanning for more threats. Then he turned back to his horse.
“We move,” Luca said. 
They rode in silence. The storm howled louder.
Snow piled in thick drifts as the storm closed its fists around the road. The bandits had long since vanished into the whiteness. Their corpses were left for the cold to claim. Luca rode in silence at the front, his broad shoulders hunched, cloak rimmed in ice. His face was calm, distant, unreadable, his hands steady on the reins despite the storm.
The wind howled through the trees with an ancient, bitter voice. Snow fell in slanted waves, not flakes but claws, wet and heavy, biting into skin even through layers of wool and leather. Visibility narrowed to a hand’s span in front of their faces.
“Storm’s turning,” Taerel muttered, pulling his scarf higher over his mouth. “We need shelter, or we’ll freeze upright in the saddle.”
“No argument here,” Lysana said beside him, brushing snow from her brow. Her voice was clipped, focused. She scanned the tree line. “There’s a cliff bend not far from here. If it’s still the same as I remember, it should have a hollow just past the rise.”
It was Luca who nodded first, his gaze piercing through the snow as if he could see the shape of it already. A few minutes later, they reached it—tucked beneath the curve of a rocky overhang, half-buried by snow and ringed by sparse fir trees, the hollow loomed like a mouth left open in warning.
“Dismount, head for the cove,” Luca said, already swinging down. “Get those horses inside.”
They moved fast. Taerel and Aymer tethered the horses near the back, while Lysana led them under the shelter. Aymer, tall and powerfully built, pulled his rifle from the saddle scabbard with gloved fingers. Snow melted along its edges. As he moved, his shoulder brushed Taerel, shorter but no less capable, with tawny skin, piercing eyes, and a jagged braid that trailed from his temple like a whipcord.
“What are we going to do for a fire?” Lysana asked. “It is still freezing in here.” 
“I don’t know, all I can find is wood that is all wet.” Replied Luca
“You want firewood,” Aymer said, tossing a glance toward his brother, “you’re the one with the hatchet.”
Taerel rolled his eyes but grinned. “At least I know how to use it.”
Taerel crouched by a half-rotted log at the edge of the hollow, outer bark soaked and useless. With practiced hands, he split it, peeling back to the dry heart. Aymer hovered too close, offering advice he didn’t need.
“You’re angling it wrong,” Aymer said.
“I’ve lit more fires than you’ve had meals,” Taerel shot back, not looking up.
“Aye and half of them smoked us out,” Aymer grinned.
“At least mine burns,” Taerel snapped. 
The spark caught then, flaring to life just to prove him right.
Lysana knelt, unpacking two small wax-wrapped tinder bundles from her satchel, southern kindling bought cheap in Tenlane, good for starting fires in damp weather. “Use these first,” she said, tossing them over.
Taerel caught one, tucked it under the dry splinters, and struck steel to flint. Sparks leapt like insects. Smoke hissed. Then, slowly, the fire caught. The golden glow spread. Shadows flickered across the hollow walls, jagged stone, and hanging icicles like frozen teeth. Their breath misted, drawn into the warmth like moths to flame. They laid out bedrolls in a rough crescent, kept the horses close, and built a small windbreak from stones and a weather-beaten tarp to shield the fire’s glow. 
Aymer went to find more wood to bring to Taerel to ensure they had enough for the night, quickly returning with a good armful. Taerel went to work. He stacked extra wood near the fire. “Don’t want to be stumbling around trying to find fuel in this storm, at night.”
Dinner was simple but warm. Dried meat soaked in broth, boiled roots, and crumbling dark bread. Aymer passed around a battered flask of honey-wine, sharp and sweet, and they drank in grateful silence.
“I’ve missed real food,” Taerel said, tearing off a piece of bread and dunking it into the pot. “Food in Riverrun’s End tastes like it was chewed once already.” He grimaced, recalling the taste.
“Dried feet with ambition,” Aymer added.
“Don’t knock ambition,” Lysana said, her mouth twitching at the corner. “Keeps you warm longer than soup.”
“You've been up here before, right?” Taerel asked, adjusting a boot near the fire. “You know these lands?”
Lysana nodded. “I trained under Harmon. Did a sweep through these hills for a patrol mission years back. This hollow was a shelter marker then as well. Used by long-range scouts and supply runners.”
“Ever see anything strange?” Aymer asked, raising a brow beneath his mask.
Lysana hesitated, her eyes glinting in the firelight. “Not see. But we heard things. Old wind stories. Hushed echoes through the trees, voices that didn’t match anyone in the patrol. Woke to claw marks in the snow once, deep ones, far too wide for any wolf.”
Taerel leaned in. “What kind of beast?”
“Didn’t stick around to ask,” Lysana said. “But the locals, few that there are, call them frost-haunts. Say the spirits out here never sleep. Say this land remembers blood.”
Silence fell for a beat, the fire cracking.
Taerel exhaled sharply. “Great. Just great.”
“Better than Luca’s ghost stories,” Aymer muttered.
At that, Luca chuckled, low and smooth, like rolling coals. He had been sitting quietly near the edge, head down, watching the flame curl against the stone. When he looked up, his eyes gleamed with the knowledge of too many winters.
“You want a real tale?” he asked. “I’ll give you one.”
“Creator help us,” Taerel said.
But Luca’s voice came quietly, steadily.
“Not far from here, past the frozen ridgelines, they speak of something older than the mountains. Something that hunts by warmth. Doesn’t need to see. Just... feels you.”
“What is it?” Aymer asked, tone more serious now.
“No name,” Luca said. “Not one it ever gave. The tale is. It mimics the voice of its prey.” He paused, letting his eyes move around the group. “Hides in the storm.” Lower, he said, “Screams like a dying child.”
No one laughed this time.
Aymer was first to speak, “So what really can we expect?” Hoping the story Luca just told was a campfire story and not true.
Lysana gave him a look of despair, as if to say, “You poor boy, you have no idea of the horrors up here.” “Wolves. Elk. The usual.” She said it without flinching and looked back at the fire, and if there was more to say, she had already decided this was not the night for it. 
Taerel looked at Lysana. “Are there really folk up here? Settlers? Homesteads?”
She nodded. “A few. Some hunters, off-grid types. People who wanted to disappear, build their own corners of the world where no one bothers them.”
“Or where no one finds them,” Aymer said quietly.
The fire popped. For a long moment, nothing moved but the smoke curling toward the icicle ceiling. The group finished up their meals and cleaned up a bit, and then repacked their stuff. Their bedrolls were laid out in a rough circle around the fire. Luca spoke up, clearing his throat. “We should stand watch,” Luca suggested, shifting position to a good vantage point. “I will take the first shift.”
Lysana said, “No need, I will take second then.”
Aymer said, “Since I know Taerel needs his beauty sleep, I will take third.”
“Fine. I will take the last one.” Taerel glanced at Aymir. “Thank you, brother.” 
They all gave a little chuckle and went to make their provisions for the rest of the evening. 
Aymir had been watching her since the hollow. Not in the way Luca watched her, which was its own thing entirely, but the way a soldier watches someone they are deciding whether to trust with their flank. When the others were busy with their packs, he said quietly, “You've done cold missions before. Properly cold.” It was not flattery. It was reconnaissance. Lysana looked at him. “A few.” He gave a short nod. “Good to know,” he said, and went back to his kit. 
The fire burned low, crackling softly beneath the growing hush of the night. Shadows danced against the rocky walls of their makeshift camp, licking across bedrolls and gear in slow, flickering patterns. One by one, the others settled into their blankets, the silence broken only by the occasional shuffle of boots or the sigh of cold breath. Luca remained seated by the fire, shoulders squared as he took first watch, the hood of his cloak drawn up against the biting air.
Luca leaned forward, something that might have been a grin tugging at the edge of his mouth. “All right,” he said. “Might as well pass the time. Have you all ever heard about the frost-wasps up here?”
Taerel groaned. “Don’t start.”
“No, no,” Aymer said, grinning. “Let the man tell it.”
Luca’s voice lowered. The firelight cast shadows over his face, giving his eyes a glint that could have been amusement or warning.
“Way up north, closer to the Forgotten Lands, there are creatures that don’t belong on this side of the mountains. One of them’s the frost-wasp. Big thing, body like a bloated beetle, wings like torn silk. It flies low in the storm winds, seeps into your camp like smoke. You don’t hear it until it’s already too close.”
Lysana snorted. “That’s not real.”
“Ah, but here’s the thing,” Luca said, holding up a finger. “They don’t sting. Not like bees. No, they... burrow. Into warm flesh. Lay their eggs. You feel a tickle in your neck, and next thing you know, you’re the hive.”
Taerel made a show of pulling his scarf up over his neck. “Now I know you’re full of it.”
“Oh, maybe,” Luca said. “But some of the settlers up here swear by it. Had a trader in Greyharbor say he saw a man burst open right at his campfire, full of squirming larvae.”
Lysana rolled her eyes but pulled her cloak tighter around herself. “Stop playing shadow boy.”
They laughed, even as the fire popped. The conversation drifted from there, hunting stories, old friends, and strange foods from far-off lands. Luca remained still at the edge, his eyes reflecting firelight like twin coals, half-listening but not joining. It was long before the conversation died out and gave way to sleep. 
The wind, once relentless and needling, had faded not long after sunset, leaving behind only a gentle, steady fall of snow. It drifted in through the broken trees and scattered crags like fine silver ash, catching in the moonlight until the whole mountaintop looked like a world carved from pearl. The silence that came with it was almost holy. But Luca couldn’t feel its peace. His eyes scanned the pale horizon, but his thoughts were turned inward, chewing on doubt. He'd always worked alone, in the shadows, solving problems with clean exits. Now, he was responsible for three others. 
He shook his head clear and went to check on the horses. He removed their feeding bags. checking on their general well-being, making sure today’s long ride hadn’t injured them. Stay busy, and you won’t think about it, his inner dialogue told him. But no matter how busy he made himself, cleaning up the camp and watching the opening, his insecurities kept creeping back in. 
A while later, Lysana took his place. She offered him a brief nod, nothing more, and settled in at the edge of the camp, sword across her lap. While the others slept, she worked silently, pulling a cloth along the length of her blade with calm precision. Oil glistened along the steel, catching bits of moonlight in her careful movements. She wasn’t worrying about leadership, or the road ahead, or whatever strange things might be lurking beyond the veil of white. She was simply present, letting the night exist around her. The snowfall softened even more now, slow and rhythmic, like the sky had grown tired of fighting. It was the kind of quiet that made you forget the world was ever cruel. Just white air, silver light, and the slow ritual of steel being tended. Lysana didn’t need to say a word. The stillness was enough.
Then came Aymer’s watch. He sat with his back to a frost-slick boulder, cloak drawn tight, eyes tracing the dark horizon. His fingers absently rolled a carved wooden token between his hands, a small charm Taerel had given him long ago. He wasn’t looking for trouble, not exactly. Just listening and watching.
Then it came. A scream ripped through the night, human, ragged, and gone too quickly for wind. It left behind a silence that felt wrong.
Aymer was already on his feet. “That was no wind,” he snapped, rifle in hand. “Up. All of you.”
 Taerel blinked groggily. “What?”
 “Something’s out there. I heard a scream.”
 Lysana sat up, reaching for her weapon. Luca was already throwing on his cloak.
 Snow fell softly now, whispering against the earth. The night was still, but that scream had cut through it like a blade.
 “What direction?” Luca asked.
 “Northwest, I think,” Aymer said.
 Lysana looked to Luca. “Could be travelers. Or settlers.”
Luca frowned. Damn it. Cannot ignore it, filled his head, but it was not spoken. 
 “You said some folks live up this way,” Taerel added. “Hunting lodges, off-grid homesteads. People looking to get away from everything.”
 “Or run from something,” Aymer muttered.
 Luca moved quickly, “We leave the camp set up. Bring only what we need. Weapons. Cloaks. No torches, we don’t want to give our position away too soon. But grab that hooded lantern, that should work.”
 “Let’s move,” Luca said, stepping out into the snow.
 The night stretched wide before them, cold and silent again.
They moved with purpose, firelight falling behind them as they stepped into the snow. Cold whispered across the hollow.
The night ahead waited. Wide. White. Watching.






Chapter Fourteen
The sound of breath was louder than their steps now. Every exhale misted out in a long plume, swallowed by the dense winter air as quickly as it formed. Their boots plunged into the thick snowpack, each step sinking nearly to the knee with a soft crunch and a sucking sound that clung like a whisper. The trail ahead was barely visible, just a faint ribbon between white-laden trees and windblown drifts. Where the storm had blown hard the day before, the snow had formed uneven ridges that forced the team to navigate more like mountaineers than soldiers.
Taerel cursed as his boot snagged on a buried root, forcing him to throw a hand out to balance. “Ghosts don't plant roots under the snow,” he muttered. “Right. That’s… right.” He nodded and continued talking to himself. “I mean, just checking.”
Aymer snorted, adjusting the rifle slung across his shoulder. “Maybe it's a snow wraith. Turns your guts to ice before you see it.”
Lysana gave a dry chuckle as she hauled her legs through another drift. “And here I thought it was the frost-fanged elk we had to worry about. The ones that wait in silence and charge when you're taking a piss.”
Taerel glanced at her with a grin. “Those? N. They only go for the handsome ones. You’re safe.”
Aymer rolled his eyes, breath pluming from his nose. “You remember that mountain guide from the tavern last night? The one rambling over stew like it was his last meal? “He swore he saw flesh-pale things crawling under the trees. Long arms. No legs. Dragging themselves forward like centipedes the size of dogs.”
Taerel scoffed. “Said they smelled like moldy bread and screamed like babies when they hunted.”
Lysana shook her head, amused. “And here I thought the wine was the worst part of dinner.”
Aymer chuckled. “He called them 'Gravepullers,' remember that? Claimed they’d dig their way up through snowbanks and tug animals down from underneath. Scraping first, then silence.”
Taerel made a mock shiver. “Sounds like a bard’s tale cooked up to keep drunks inside the tavern.”
Lysana’s smirk faded slightly. “Maybe. But the way he described the carcass he found… bones cracked clean, marrow sucked out... wasn’t the kind of detail you make up over a bowl of stew.”
Aymer shrugged. “Still better than thinking it's what we’re trained to expect, Worgs, raider hounds, or those wolf-bred trackers the Orcs breed.”
Just ahead, a faint ridge in the snow caught Luca’s eye. He gestured subtly, and the team shifted pace, instincts kicking in.
A few yards later, Lysana crouched low, brushing snow away from a patch of churned ice. Her hand paused as more details revealed themselves. She outlined deep claw marks, a wide-set, and they must be heavy. Not canine. Something broader. Almost... plated, she thought.
Taerel looked up from another spot just off the trail. “Got something else over here, too. Smaller tracks… narrow, but deep. Padded feet. Moving in a scattered line, like scouts circling something bigger.”
Lysana joined him and examined the prints. Her expression darkened. “Not the same creature. Different stride. Quieter.”
“More than one predator,” Luca said. “Different species.” He looked to the trees, the brush beyond, then back to the trail ahead. He looked at his team, “Eyes up. We’re not alone.”
Luca said nothing. He moved ahead, each step deliberate, his blade resting across his shoulder. The others followed without discussion. Behind the silence, his mind ran the same question it had been running since Rellisford, whether the trust trailing behind him was something he had earned, or simply something people defaulted to when they did not know what else to do with their eyes in the dark.
Lysana’s gaze lingered on his back for a moment, reading every shift of his shoulders like a language she hadn’t yet learned. There was steadiness there, and something colder beneath it.
The deeper they moved off the main path, the more the forest thickened, the trees gnarled and heavy with snow, their black limbs bowed and creaking. The moon filtered through a high veil of cloud, just enough to throw silver highlights across the untouched snow. Now and then, the wind stirred the canopy and sent a fresh flurry down like sifted ash, coating shoulders and hoods in silence.
Then Luca’s hand snapped up, a quick, cutting gesture, and the line stopped instantly.
Lysana moved to his side, crouching as her eyes scanned ahead. About fifty yards out, the moonlight caught something dark in the snow, not part of the natural terrain. Her lips pressed into a line as she stepped forward carefully, boots sinking, eyes flicking from patch to patch of broken whiteness.
Taerel and Aymer immediately fanned out. The brothers moved with practiced fluidity. Aymer veered left, rifle raised, scanning the tree line, while Taerel took the right, boots light despite the weight of snow. Neither said a word now.
At the center of the road, the shapes resolved into two mounds, black and twisted. As Lysana knelt beside the nearest one, her hand brushed through the snow to reveal part of a saddle, torn leather crusted with frozen blood. A horse's body, ribs exposed where something had feasted, its side ripped open with savage intent. Steam no longer rose from it. Whatever happened was hours ago.
Lysana sucked in a sharp breath and gestured for Luca to come closer. “Multiple tracks. Some human,” she whispered. “Most not.” 
She pointed toward the wilderness flanking the road. The snow there was trampled and torn, dragged through by creatures that didn't care to hide their trail.
Luca gave a short whistle, three sharp notes, and the brothers returned immediately. No words were needed. They read the scene in silence, their expressions shifting from curious to grim.
Lysana stepped closer, brushing snow from a clean print near the center. The claw marks were deep, wide, and clean through the ice.
“Wolves?” Aymer asked, voice low.
She looked up. “No. Worse,” she paused, taking a closer look. “Worgs.”
Taerel frowned. “And what are those? Pretend I’ve never been this far north.”
“They’re bred hunting beasts,” Lysana said, steady but grim. “Orc stock. Twisted through ritual.” She brushed more snow aside. “Not born, made that way.” 
Aymer leaned in, squinting. “So, wolf-like?”
“Not just wolves,” she corrected, tracing the splayed pad and talon grooves with a gloved finger. “Think bigger. Smarter. A worg’s built for war. Broad as a horse through the chest, jaws that crack bone like kindling. Their eyes shine like wet coals, aware, calculating.”
She brushed aside more snow. “They do not howl or circle. They stalk, drive prey where they want it. They don’t kill out of hunger, but because someone commanded them. And if a pack’s loose here without a handler…”
Her gaze lifted toward the black tree line. “Someone has let them off their chain.”
Luca’s voice came cold and certain. “How many?”
“At least four,” she answered. “Maybe more.”
He nodded once. “Spread out, and let’s keep going.”
The four slipped back into formation, vanishing into the white wilderness, the wind closing behind them like a breath withheld.
The snow clawed at their knees now, a heavy drag with every step. The drifts had thickened along this stretch of the forest road, pushed up in uneven mounds by wind and time. Saplings leaned low beneath the weight of white, their branches creaking with slow complaint. No one spoke for a while, their breaths fogging in the air, the only sounds the wet crunch of boots and the occasional snap of a distant branch.
Taerel broke the silence. “How far do you think they’ve gotten?”
Lysana bent low with a gloved hand just above the crust of snow. She did not answer, she didn’t move. Her eyes followed the twin gouges in the frost, signs of dragging, heavy, deliberate. When she finally spoke, her voice was quiet, but sharp as a blade through cloth.
“That depends on whether their quarry’s alive or dead.”
She looked back, her breath curling like smoke.
“If it’s alive, they’ll move slower,” Lysana said. “They keep the meat fresh that way. Not for eating. For control. If the order was delivery, not slaughter, they won’t rush it.”
Aymer’s face twisted. “Control?”
Lysana brushed snow aside, exposing a blood-soaked tuft of fabric snagged on a root. “They don’t always eat right away. Worgs like to break things first. Legs. Arms. Ribs.” Her voice stayed flat. “They drag it out. Keep it breathing. That’s how they make it behave.”
She paused, then added, “Sometimes they’re told to wait. Keep it alive so their masters can decide what to do with it. Or so they can all feed together.”
She straightened. “But if the order was kill… then they’re already gone. Whatever’s left would be scattered through the trees by now.”
They walked on now with dark images running in their minds, as the tracks guided them deeper into the brush line where the road had long since vanished under snow. It was colder here, the trees thick enough to block the wind and trap the chill like a held breath.
A few minutes later, Lysana raised a hand and crouched again. “They stopped here.”
The team clustered around. The snow was trampled flat in a wide crescent. Bits of leather and snapped belt straps were buried in the slush. One dark patch looked like bile. Another frozen blood.
“Feeding?” Taerel asked.
Lysana shook her head. “No bones. No deep blood pools. Looks like a pause. Maybe a break. Could’ve been checking wounds. Could’ve been resting.”
“Still dragging,” Luca said quietly from behind them, his voice a low growl that almost blended into the wind. Lysana looked at the space where he had been. Then she went back to the tracks. Some questions were kept for later, when there was time to sit with them. He was standing off the trail, crouched behind a tree. “Two bodies. Weight shift is consistent. The small one struggled more.”
He vanished back into the shadows before anyone could respond, already ten paces ahead by the time they registered he’d spoken.
Aymer nudged Taerel with his elbow and smirked. “Ten crowns,” Aymer murmured. “I take down one before you.”
Taerel snorted, adjusting his rifle as he kept walking. “You’ve the aim of a drunk ox in the dark. I’ll take that bet. Just don’t cry when I do, before you get your powder dry.”
“Please,” Aymer grinned. “You’ll be busy figuring out which end of the gun’s the dangerous one.”
Their laughter was soft, but real. A needed flame in the bitter cold.
Behind the laughter, Luca slipped between birch trunks like a shadow given flesh, his coat dissolving into the snow-splattered trees. The cold did not seem to touch him. Neither did the warmth behind him. His world had already narrowed to sign, scent, and what came next. 
As they pushed deeper into the woods, the wilderness grew heavier like a tightening fist. The trees clustered close, twisted in places where the wind had battered them for decades. Ancient trunks groaned under the weight of old snow, and new flakes drifted lazily through the air, settling in quiet piles. Their boots crunched softly in the otherwise undisturbed snow, leaving a narrow line of motion behind them, four figures threading through a land that hadn't seen company in months.
“Do they not have sled dogs for this sort of thing? Why didn’t we get some of those?” Aymer muttered, adjusting the rifle on his back. “Maybe a fur-lined throne while we're at it.”
“Could have stayed home,” Taerel replied dryly, stamping his feet as he walked. “Heard it’s warm next to the fire. Real cozy. Comes with soup.”
Aymer smirked. “And miss all this?” He gestured broadly at the endless woods. “These towering sticks and glorified dandruff?”
Taerel gave a short laugh and nudged his brother with an elbow. “Shut up and keep walking. You are scaring the snow.”
Lysana didn’t laugh. She was too focused, eyes locked forward as she dropped to a knee again, brushing aside the top layer of snow. The lantern’s dim, hooded light glinted off her brow as she studied the nearly invisible signs ahead. She didn't speak for a moment. Her gloved hand hovered over something unseen.
Luca slowed beside her, one hand on his sword hilt, scanning the dark between the trees. “Still have them?” Luca asked. 
She shook her head. “No. That's just it. They've faded. Completely. One moment, I could see where the Worgs had run; their stride was long, chaotic, staggered. And now…”
She stood slowly, eyes narrowing into the black beyond. “It is like they vanished. No break in the pattern. No blood. Just… gone.”
A gust of wind carried through the pines, low and cold, stirring the lantern flame. Shadows danced across their faces.
Taerel scanned the dark woods around them, the trees clawing upward like black fingers against the night sky. He turned a slow circle and grunted. “Do… any of you actually remember how we are supposed to get back?”
Aymer raised an eyebrow. “Back where?”
Taerel gestured vaguely toward the way they'd come. “Back to the cove. Y’know. Our camp. The place with food. Heat. Not trees.”
“Oh, you mean civilization? No idea,” Aymer said cheerfully. “I assumed we were just going to keep walking until we found a dragon.”
“Great,” Taerel said, deadpan. “Glad we brought the smart one.”
“I thought you were the smart one,” Aymer replied with a grin. “Luca’s the serious one, I’m the charming one, and you’re, what? The decorative one?”
“Decorative?” Taerel scoffed. “I’m the one who kept us from falling through that frozen creek two hours ago.”
“And I’m the one who told you it was thin ice,” Aymer countered.
“You told me after I stepped on it!” Taerel said. 
Lysana let out a long breath through her nose, glaring over her shoulder. “Both of you shut it, or I will leave you here. The Worgs wouldn’t even bother eating you, too much gristle.”
That quieted them. Aymer stepped forward, raising the lantern a bit higher. Lysana reached for the lantern without looking. “Give me that.”
“By all means, Lightbearer.” He handed it over with a slight bow.
She did not dignify it with a response. Instead, she held the lantern low and stepped ahead. “Stay here. I’ll scout it.”
Taerel frowned. “Alone?”
Lysana glanced once at the churned snow behind them, then at the untouched ground ahead. “Yes, alone,” she said. “One set of prints. Less noise. Less scent. If they’re watching, they will see a group. If I move, they’ll miss it. Plus, I am trained to do this.”
She didn’t wait for an answer. “Stay here. Watch the trees. Quiet.”
Without waiting for protest, she moved forward, boots silent on the snow. The others exchanged glances but did as told, crouching low among the thick roots of an ancient birch.
Lysana moved ahead, each step deliberate, her eyes on the ground, sorting through what she knew and what did not fit. Something did not fit. 
“Tracks don’t just disappear,” she whispered. “Not even in snow this deep…”
She swung the dim, hooded lantern in a slow arc, casting amber light across the forest floor. The snow glittered, untouched, pristine. Too pristine.
Then, the ground dropped.
She stopped at the edge of a great, shallow slope, wide as a river bend, stretching out in a long depression like something had scooped the earth out centuries ago and left the wound to fester. Snow coated its rim and clung to the thick branches that hung low over the edge, casting the entire area in dense shadow. But in the middle… her breath caught.
She stared.
Mouth slightly agape.
What she saw in that sunken hollow turned her blood to ice.
It took her a second to recover, then she dropped the lantern light low, shielding it with one hand, and turned back toward the others. She raised her arm high, made a sharp wave toward herself, then dropped low and extended her hand flat toward the snow.
‘Come. Quiet.’
They obeyed immediately.
One by one, the team crawled up beside her on their stomachs, pressing through pine needles and ice. Aymer flopped into place next to her, chin up like a lazy cat, and murmured, “So… what’s got you looking like you saw a ghost get eaten by another ghost?”
She didn’t answer. Not yet. Luca arrived last, easing into position beside her, his hand gripping the frozen ground close to hers, and then they all saw it together.






Chapter Fifteen
“Luca’s found an orc raider camp.” The room went still. Weslin’s voice carried the weight of it, low and unshaken, the faint glow of his bracelet reflecting against the shuttered window.
Aurelia sat watchful near the wall, Neavin leaned back in a chair still recovering from overlinking with his bonded, and Ash stood at the doorframe, winded but alert. Nyssa paced while chewing the inside of her cheek.
Harmon did not look up right away. Bent over the battered travel map spread across the small desk they’d dragged in from the hall, his eyes followed the ridgelines and river forks marked in ink. Behind him, the others leaned into the silence, the kind that came when soldiers heard what they already feared.
“Is he certain?” Harmon asked.
Weslin nodded once. “He is watching them now. Mobile camp. Not… big. Maybe four near the pen. Another enclosure, makeshift. Holding… humans.” 
Harmon’s head lifted. “Alive?”
Weslin’s voice thinned. “He believes some are.”
Nyssa’s tone broke the silence, dry and forced. “Please tell me someone didn’t devour all the bread. I scraped my skin raw on thorns and brush. I deserve one bite of something that does not taste like bark.”
“Bread is dry enough to be bark,” Ash replied. “Take it. Call it thanks for not making me run alone.”
“Do not either of you talk about moving again,” Neavin groaned, rubbing at his temple. “I just spent half a day riding a bird’s mind, keeping it from smashing into a cliff. My bonded did the flying, I just collected the headache.”
Aurelia smiled faintly, yet calmly said, “Impressive effort, Neavin. But unless your flight brought back something useful, I will not name it scouting.”
“Useful?” he muttered. “I learned birds are smarter than half this team.”
Ash barked a laugh. “That explains your attitude. You left part of your brain in the nest.”
“At least mine’s still working,” Neavin shot back. “Last I checked, lighting things up ain’t a trade.” 
Nyssa leaned on the table with a sharp smile, eyes locked on him. “Careful, Ash. He’s got a point. You spark at every argument you lose.”
“Better than stealing the cutlery every time someone blinks,” Ash said.
“It was one spoon,” Nyssa countered. 
The laughter faded, replaced by the low hiss of wind against the shutters. For a heartbeat, the weight of Weslin’s report hung there again, cold and heavy.
“Why does it even matter?” Neavin asked quietly. “They’re hundreds of miles away. We can’t help them from here.”
The silence that followed tightened.
Ash spoke first, voice lower. “It matters because someone’s out there bleeding for the same side. Even if we can’t reach them.”
“Or it matters because it could be us next,” Nyssa said. “We still don’t know what we’re walking into.”
“That’s comforting,” Ash muttered.
“It’s called honesty,” she shot back.
“The intelligence is clear,” Aurelia said, her tone cutting through evenly. “Five orcs, a mobile camp, prisoners alive. That is what requires our attention.” 
Nyssa folded her arms. “Organized orcs. That’s what worries me.”
“Orcs aren’t careful,” Neavin said, rubbing his temple again. “These were. Too quiet. Too deliberate.”
“And Luca’s charging in without a healer,” Ash added. “Brilliant.”
“Three days with this crew,” Nyssa muttered, “and I already don’t want any of them dead.”
“Sentimental,” Neavin said. “I’ll alert the historians.”
“You do that,” she replied. “I’ll make sure they spell your name wrong.”
Weslin’s voice again, steady. “He can confirm two corpses. Six more tied to trees. Hard to tell their state.”
“Bastards,” Nyssa said. “That camp’s not for raiding, it’s for silencing.”
Garr’s jaw tightened. “A choke point. Anyone fleeing the pass dies there.”
“Five orcs visible,” Weslin added. “Red cloth on their arms. Raid-mark, I think. Someone wants them recognized. Luca thinks there are more in the trees.”
“Tribal marking,” Harmon said quietly. “Raiders.”
Neavin gave a low whistle. “They’re sweeping west, forward trail, fallback route. That is not orc cunning, that’s command.”
“What’s Luca intend?” Harmon asked.
“Strike,” Weslin replied.
Harmon’s eyes narrowed.
“Three in high cover, rifles trained on the pens, too far out for them to spot us.” Weslin continued. “A bow on the far side. Luca drops from the slope to free the prisoners. Lysana moves to join, and others hold overwatch. If the orcs scatter, they’ll pick them off.”
“Timing?” Garr asked.	
“As soon as shadows cover the approach.”
Ash leaned forward. “Quick. Precise.”
“Too precise,” Harmon said, tone like a blade’s flat edge. “Tell him to take no unnecessary risks. Move with a steady footing. I leave my trust with you. “
Weslin tapped his bracelet, the glow sharpening briefly. “Telling him now.”
“Make certain he obeys.” Harmon finally looked up, command radiating from his stillness. “This isn’t about glory. It’s about silence. That camp’s strangling to scream. If Luca can cut its throat, good, but no more than that.”
Weslin inclined his head and relayed the order through the shimmering link.
The door creaked open with the ease of someone entirely too confident, and Dain stepped through first, brushing ash from his shoulders as if it had personally offended him.
“Well, good news,” Dain announced, his voice just loud enough to cut through the murmur. “We’re not dead, the streets still reek of horse filth, and Brother Aldrek somehow refrained from killing a single city guard for breathing too loudly. I call that a win.”
Aldrek followed, silent and heavy as always, the steel cap of his mace glinting under his cloak.
“Only because the last one outran you,” Nyssa said from her chair, smirking.
Aldrek gave a sound somewhere between a grunt and a laugh.
“Tell that to his boot,” Dain shot back. “It’s still in the alley.”
He paused long enough to let the line land, cloak settling as the grin faded.
Harmon didn’t return the smile. “Report.”
Dain adjusted his gloves, drawing out the moment just enough to look deliberate, not stalling. “The Magistrate’s Tower is exactly the festering pit I was warned about. Two guards at the gate, half drunk, half stupid. Walked past them like fog. The inner hall smelled of rust and arrogance.”
“They denied Riven’s name,” he continued. “So I tried diplomacy. A bribe, an insult, and finally Lord Saewyn Olgrave’s name.”
Harmon blinked once. “You used that?”
“With all the grace it deserves,” Dain said. “Worked, too. They hauled me straight to the Warden. Polite bunch, if you overlook the smell and the fact that one of them had his helmet on backwards.”
Harmon gave him a look that killed the grin halfway.
“Right,” Dain said, tone shifting. “The front chamber’s large, arched ceiling, torch sconces every ten paces. Single entry, double exit. The one on the left leads deeper into the main corridor. Counted four side doors off it before I reached the office. I saw no guards posted inside that stretch. They trust the turns and the locks, no need for patrols.”
