He started pacing, letting the rhythm of the memory guide him. “Each door’s numbered and iron-banded. Two stood ajar, two sealed. One had stains under it, old, dark. Probably an interrogation room. You can smell oil and lye from the cracks.”
“The Warden’s office sits near the rear of the same hall. Standard lockplate, heavier hinges, no external bar. Weapons case behind her desk, crossbow, short blades, a cudgel, and she’s close enough to the armory that you can hear hammer strikes through the wall. If a fight starts, she’ll have company in seconds.”
His tone slipped toward humor again. “Quite the decor. The desk, carved from ship timber, still smells like salt and arrogance. Keys hanging behind her like trophies. She sits high enough to make sure you’re looking up when she calls you insignificant.”
Harmon raised a brow.
Dain sighed, catching himself. “Apologies. Still shaking the noble out of my voice.”
“She denied everything. Said no Riven in custody, no record, no concern. Called me refreshingly blunt, which is noble-speak for stupid. I pushed, she didn’t blink. I mentioned my House, she called it property.”
The humor was gone now. “That’s when it turned. She stood, circled, looking for a crack. Told me I wore the coat like it was earned. I almost gave her a reason to test that theory.”
He drew a slow breath, jaw tightening. “Then she slipped by saying three days, then immediately tightened her jaw as she’d said too much. That’s the truth she didn’t mean to give.”
Dain straightened his gloves, voice steady again. “So, tactically: one main entrance, four side rooms, two choke points, and the Warden within shouting distance of an armory. If we go in, it’ll have to be fast and loud.”
He looked up, a flicker of wryness returning. “And for what it’s worth, she’ll remember me. It's hard to forget someone you wanted to strangle.”
Brother Aldrek then spoke up, “He must have done something to spook her because of what happened next.”
“Were you at the door the whole time?” Harmon asked at last, his voice low but firm.
 Aldrek gave a single nod. “As ordered. Watched the street. Waited.”
 Harmon gestured subtly with the cup in his hand. “Keep going.”
“Two came out,” Aldrek said. “Quiet as a breath. The first one stepped into the light like a shadow peeling from the wall, tall, lean, built like a man who lives on the road. His face… narrow. Tired. Lines at the corners of his mouth, but not the kind made by laughter.”
He spoke plainly, but his words painted the memory in sharp detail.
“Had a patchy beard. Just enough to forget. Clothes were wrong, looked like soot-stained merchant garb, but the wear was off. Too clean at the cuffs, too new at the collar for the road. That one’s seen training. Moved like he was always mapping exits.”
Harmon’s expression didn’t change, but his knuckles whitened just slightly around the stem of his cup.
“The second one was broader. Shorter,” Aldrek went on. “Lit a pipe like he didn’t have a care in the world. Fingers stained with ink, maybe a scribe, or someone posing as one. Carried a bit of weight, but not enough to slow him. His cloak dragged low, hung strangely over one side like he was hiding steel. He smiled too easily, but his eyes weren’t with the grin. Alert. Dry. Measured every child that passed. Had a hand that dropped too naturally to his belt.”
 “They split?” Harmon asked.
“Aye,” Aldrek said. “Sent word through the link. One headed toward the Noble District, blue cloak, trying not to look like he was rushing. The other took after Dain, wasn’t subtle about it. Gray duster, working boots. The kind that says ‘I’m no one’ just a little too loudly.”
 He paused, eyes narrowing faintly at the firelight.
“Dain led him a ways. Down through Forgehallow’s broken veins. Into an alley behind a dead forge. I followed in from the rear.”
 Harmon looked up from the fire. “Confrontation?”
“Not quite. Dain called him out. Calm. Professional. I stepped in behind. Drew halfway, told him to turn.”
“And he did?” Harmon asked, skeptical.
“Hands up. Sweat on his brow signaled he didn’t want a fight. He claimed, he was told to follow me. To spook me into not seeking any further action. He volunteered, apparently.”
Harmon frowned. “Why would anyone volunteer for that?”
“He wanted to talk. We let him. Truth leaks even from liars.” Dain said.
“He said he wanted to speak,” Aldrek replied with a steady, even voice, giving Dain the side eye. “Knew this might be his only chance. He overheard Dain’s conversation with the warden. Thought a noble could help the others. He told us there are at least three others inside the prison, these off-book prisoners. He odd movements of the Prisoners. He also said he overheard guards bragging about the coin. Orders from somewhere higher.”
 Harmon let out a long, steady breath, eyes fixed on the embers. “And you believed him.”
Aldrek didn’t answer immediately. Then: “I did. Man was shaking, but not with fear. With relief. He thought he’d believed he made it to someone who might do something.”
“So we learn nothing other than the one we are searching for is in prison, but for some reason, as a special prisoner, but why?” asked Harmon, a bit frustrated.
Nyssa’s voice came low from where she sat, still pulling the last of the soot from her gloves. “I can answer that.”
The others turned, and for a beat, she didn’t meet their eyes, just stared into the fire, jaw tight.
“We tailed our mark through the merchant district into the Ironcrest Quarter. High walls, manor gates, guards with polished greaves who haven’t seen a real fight in years.” She finally looked up. “He wasn’t hiding. He wanted to be seen. Like bait on a hook.”
Ash gave a subtle nod beside her, letting her speak.
“We followed at a distance. Through the alleys, past bakeries with gold-leaf windows. Neavin had the skies. His falcon tracked from above. Then we saw where the man went. A side gate. Private entrance.” Her lips pulled into something between a grimace and a grin. “And of course, it was that estate.”
She looked directly at Harmon now. “Lord Iven Merrick. Twin-headed hammer wrapped in ivy. He always did have a flair for presentation.”
There was a pause. Nyssa leaned back slightly, crossing one leg over the other.
“You know him,” Harmon said. “Tell us how.” 
“ Merrick’s not just a noble. He’s a patron of the arts. A funder of museums. A sponsor of trade expeditions. He smiles at marble busts and speaks in soft diplomatic tones. But what is he really?” Her tone darkened. “A collector. Of rare things. Dangerous ones. Anything powerful, ancient, or forbidden enough to come with a curse and a blood toll, he wants it under glass. Or in a vault beneath his house. That is what I take he wants, but there is something about him saying he is even hungrier for more.”
She looked around the room again, quieter now. “He hired us, Riven and I, once. Years back. Told us it was a simple lift. Get in, steal a box from a rival’s archive, get out. He paid well. Too well. Why would I care back then?” Her hands tensed in her lap.
“But what we really stole? It wasn’t just some trinket. It was powerful, yet something felt wrong. Riven knew it. I knew it. We didn’t stick around to find out what it did.”
She glanced at the others. “That’s why we fled the city. Why we went dark. I told him not to come back. But he did.” Her voice caught for just a breath. “And I think that’s why he ended up in that prison. That bastard wants us for more jobs, and now he has his thief. He never forgets a debt. We were paid in advance for the contract.”
She turned to Harmon now, eyes sharp. “If that man we followed today is dealing with Merrick, then this isn’t random.  Merrick doesn’t forget debts. And he doesn't let go of something once he decides it’s his.”
A beat of silence followed
“If Merrick’s involved,” she said slowly, “then this isn't just about one man and a failed job. That man would raze a city and salt the ashes if it meant gaining a single ounce of power. And anyone in his way, anyone who knows too much, vanishes. Quietly. Permanently.”
She met Harmon’s gaze, voice dropping to a whisper.
“He cannot know we’re involved. If he finds out… we won’t just be hunted. We’ll be looking over our shoulders for the rest of our lives. Trust me. I’ve seen what he does to loose ends.”
Her eyes lingered on the edge of the map, as if something dark crawled just beyond the borders.
“This isn’t just Merrick playing lord in Forgehallow. Whatever he’s part of… It’s older than this city, older than the crown. And whatever it is… it’s waking up.”
Nyssa’s words hung in the air like the lingering scent of burnt copper, unmistakable and hard to forget. The others had listened closely, eyes low or half-lidded from exhaustion, but all alert in the way people were when truths felt sharper than weapons.
 After a beat of silence, Harmon pushed himself off the table he’d been leaning on. His shoulders rolled, joints giving a quiet protest. He looked over the group with the same practiced calm he wore in the field, though now there was something more fatherly in it, a measure of earned command softened by concern.
 “All right,” Harmon said, voice carrying across the stone and wood of the old room. “That’s more than enough for tonight. We will move fast in the morning, and I need you all sharp, not half-dead from hunger and worn to threads.”
He glanced toward the door. “There’s a tab under my name downstairs in the common room. Use it. Eat something that didn’t come from a dried pack or out of a ration box. You’ve earned it. Yet stay vigilant, and mouths closed.”
A low, grateful groan came from Weslin, who was already halfway out of his chair. “That’s the best thing anyone’s said to me in three days.”
Ash gave a dry chuckle. “I second that. If I see another steamed root or prison biscuit, I might burn the table out of spite.”
“You’ll eat, then change,” Harmon said, leveling a look across the table. “And rest. I mean real rest. No pacing half the night, no tinkering with gear, and no brooding in dark corners pretending you’re writing poetry.”
Nyssa raised her eyebrows at that. “Was that last one aimed at me or Dain?”
“Both,” Harmon replied without missing a beat.
There was scattered laughter, worn down, yes, but real, and it loosened something tight in the room.
Harmon turned toward Aurelia next, giving her a small nod. “Cut the link, Lia. Let everyone breathe their own air for a bit.”
Aurelia was already gently pulling her shard pendant from where it nestled against her collarbone. She held it between her palms, closing her eyes. A faint shimmer passed over her features like moonlight on water, and then the link unraveled, thread by invisible thread, until the soft mental hum that bound them all quieted into silence.
“Done,” she murmured, slipping the shard back into the folds of her robes. “Though I’ll miss the chorus of your thoughts. So... poetic.”
 “Mine are mostly complaints and mental swearing,” Ash said, rising. “You’re not missing much.”
 As the others began to shuffle out, boots scuffing tiredly across the floor, Dain lingered. He hadn’t moved to follow yet. His hand came out gently, catching Nyssa’s forearm just before she passed.
“Hey,” he said, voice low, touched with something rare in it—honesty stripped of defense. “Back there... what you said. In my head. Thank you.”
Nyssa blinked, caught off guard for the barest second before that familiar crooked smirk tugged at her lips. “You’re welcome, your lordship,” she said, dragging out the title like a teasing whip. “Don’t get used to me being nice, though. I’ve got a reputation.”
Dain gave a small, surprised laugh, the kind that came unguarded, like breath stolen from a storm. “Wouldn’t dream of it.”
She studied him for a second, that tilt of the head she used when deciding if she liked someone or wanted to rob them blind. “You look better in silk, by the way,” she said. “Almost makes you look important. Until you talk.”
And with that, she vanished toward the stairs, steps light despite the exhaustion dragging at them all.
Dain stood there for a beat, watching her go, then looked down at the clothes he wore, dark, elegant travel gear more suited for a nobleman than a prisoner. His fingers traced the edge of the fabric, slowly. The weight of it sat heavily in his palm. Tailored lines. Gold-threaded buttons. The kind of thing he used to wear before things broke apart.
 “It feels good,” he admitted quietly to Harmon, who stood nearby, pretending not to eavesdrop. “Playing the noble again. For a minute, it almost feels like I haven’t lost everything.”
Harmon nodded, his gaze distant. “Clothes don’t lie, Dain. But they don’t tell the whole truth, either.”
“No,” Dain said, softer now. “They don’t.”
Harmon’s voice shifted, this time raised so the last stragglers could hear. “Let’s go. Food, then gear. If it squeaks or smells like rust, fix it or clean it. We move at full speed tomorrow. No dragging behind.”
A tired “Aye, sir,” came from Ash.
“By the Light, I’ll sleep through breakfast,” Weslin muttered.
“You always sleep through breakfast,” Aurelia added, not looking up.
“I regret nothing,” Weslin said, walking backwards toward the door.
Harmon chuckled and turned his head toward the corner where Weslin was just about to leave. “Weslin, hold up a moment.”
The young man paused, brows lifting.
Harmon motioned him over with a quiet seriousness. “A couple of things I want to go over with you. We will just be a second.”
Weslin gave a small nod, stepping closer, and the door to the quiet war-room finally swung wide, letting the smell of roasting meat and warm ale drift in from downstairs.
One by one, they left. The heavy wooden door eased shut behind the last of them with a muted clunk, and silence settled again across the war room. Only the flickering hearthlight remained, casting long shadows across the table.
Harmon stood there for a moment, arms crossed, jaw working slightly as he looked at the table’s spread of maps and notes. Harmon turned his gaze toward Weslin, who had hovered by the edge of the doorway like he wasn’t quite sure if he was dismissed or still needed.
“Walk with me a second?” Harmon asked, voice quieter now, gentler.
Weslin perked up, adjusting the strap of his satchel. “Of course, sir.” 
But Harmon didn’t move toward the door. Instead, he stepped back toward the room, gesturing for Weslin to follow. “Just needed a word before we head out.”
Weslin’s boots thudded lightly on the stone as he stepped closer, standing a pace away like a squire might before a knight’s review.
“Any word from Luca?” Harmon asked, the question coming out low, laced with something soft and tight beneath it.
Weslin’s face shifted, just a flicker, but he shook his head. “Not yet, sir. No final report. But it’s only been about an hour. I’m sure it’s coming.”
Harmon nodded slowly. “I know. Just… hard not to worry.”
“You know his name,” Weslin said, steadier now. “He is the Shadow Walker. There’s no cleaner blade in the dark. If there was trouble, he handled it. And if he couldn’t—”
“Then none of us could’ve,” Harmon finished, the ghost of a wry smile tugging at his mouth. “I’ve only ever heard the stories. The order he came from, half the tales sound like myths, but every one of them ends with someone dead and a crown scrambling for answers.”
“They say he once walked into a sealed court and walked out with the Duke’s thumb,” Weslin said quietly. 
“That one, I have heard.” Harmon looked away, a crease forming between his brow. “But stories or not, he’s with us now. He is part of this. He is in my charge. Do you understand?”
Weslin offered a faint grin and nodded his head. “He’ll send word. He’s fine. We will all be fine.” He said it not only to reassure Harmon, but to convince himself as well. He could see it on him, the particular stillness of someone managing something they would not name out loud. He said nothing. Some things did not need naming. 
Harmon looked at him for a moment, really looked, and nodded. Harmon took a slow breath, “This is why I made you my squire,” he said, voice settling into something firm but kind. “You’ve got heart. More than most men I’ve fought beside.”
Weslin’s cheeks colored, and he looked down, one boot toe scuffing slightly at the stone floor. “Thank you, sir. I’ll keep earning that.”
“I know you will,” Harmon said. There was a pause then, long enough for the quiet of the room to press back in. The fire crackled softly behind them.
“So,” Harmon said, easing into the next line like he already knew the answer. “What did you pick up today, working around the command center?”
Weslin brightened, happy for the subject shift. “Lots of messenger traffic. I helped move supplies as well.”
Harmon gave a low nod, “And Aurelia?” he asked, a little quieter now, leaning on the edge of the table as he turned toward him fully. “How’s the training with her going?”
Weslin stood a little taller. “It’s… different. Hard in a different way. She had me practice two things today. First was a stillness drill. You sit, not moving, not thinking, just letting your mind go quiet. Not easy.”
Harmon smiled faintly. “No, it isn’t.”
“And the second was a focus exercise. She gave me this pendant to hang in front of a candle flame and told me to hold every detail of it in my mind. Every crack, every reflection, without blinking. Felt like it was peeling my brain apart by the end.”
“That’s the point,” Harmon said. “Stillness to clear the mind. Focus to sharpen it. Do both tonight before bed. Half an hour each.”
Weslin nodded seriously. “Yes, sir.”
“And again, first thing in the morning. Once we’re back on the road, you’ll start proper training with me. Weapons, field discipline. You’ll keep studying under Aurelia, too. So don’t expect much free time.”
Weslin gave a tired grin. “Not exactly what I’d call relaxing, but I didn’t sign up to be a noble’s cupbearer.”
“No,” Harmon said, clapping a hand on his shoulder. “You didn’t. You signed up to serve something better. Now, run along. Eat while the food’s still warm. I don’t want to see you again tonight unless Luca messages.”
Weslin gave a sharp nod, almost a salute, and turned for the door. “Yes, sir.”
The door creaked open and shut behind him, his steps already fading down the hall.
For a while, Harmon stayed where he was.
The warmth of the room seemed dimmer without the voices in it. The maps on the table flickered in firelight, edges curled and ink smudged by use. He reached out, drawing one of them toward him with a calloused hand—the one from the northern border, where the Veydrassil had last moved in shadow.
 He stared at it for a long time.
 The faces of his team passed in his thoughts like ghosts. Dain, carrying grief beneath silk and bravado. Nyssa, sharp as a dagger and twice as fast. Aurelia, always watching, always calculating what she could and couldn’t heal. Ceadric, burning from the inside out. And Weslin, young, yes, but solid. A spark of something that might one day be a flame.
He exhaled through his nose and pressed a palm flat to the map. The report would come. He could wait. For now, there was only the quiet. The fire. The weight of the map under his hand. And somewhere in the back of his mind, still warm, the thought of a boy who believed in dangerous men and was working hard not to become one.






Chapter Sixteen
The wind whispered like a warning across the ridge, dry and cold, carrying with it the acrid scent of ash from the half-dead fires burning below. From their perch atop the broken lip of the crater, the world dropped steeply into a jagged basin where the orc raiders had made camp. Crude fencing of scavenged wood and rusted spikes marked a rough perimeter, and beyond it, chaos had made a home.
Caged wagons sat at odd angles in the mud, doors hanging open, splintered and bent. Makeshift tents leaned against uneven rock. Worgs paced the outer ring, chains clinking with every restless prowl. Even from this distance, their breath steamed in the cold.
Luca crouched low, cloak dragging softly against dust-blown stone. His eyes tracked the camp in slow, methodical sweeps. Every movement below was logged, measured, and weighed. He exhaled once, deliberately.
“All right,” he murmured, voice barely louder than the wind. “We got the go-ahead.”
Aymir let out a soft huff of breath beside him, half grin, half anticipation. He nudged Taerel with the barrel of his rifle.
“You showed us your magic earlier,” Aymir said quietly. “Now we return the favor.”
They settled in behind a boulder, movements practiced and economical. Taerel popped the chamber and began loading cartridges, fingers steady despite the cold.
“Six beasts,” he said. “Four of us. No, five.”
“Five,” Aymir replied, peering down his scope. “I do not miss.”
“Neither do I,” Taerel said. “Or should we recall the winter fair four years ago?”
Luca lifted a hand. The brothers stilled instantly.
“Save it,” Luca said, not looking back. “Sound carries.”
No argument. No delay. “I go in first. If the prisoners can be cut loose before we raise an alarm, good. If we start firing before that, they die screaming. We do this right, or we do not do it at all.” Luca said with command in his voice. 
Taerel muttered, “Your funeral,” but there was no mockery in it, just understanding.
Lysana shifted beside them, already crouched low, bow strung and resting across her lap. Her eyes traced the basin, angles, and routes mapping themselves behind her gaze. “Where do you want me?” She adjusted her grip on the bowstring, already shifting her weight.
Luca pointed toward a jagged rise across the crater’s far edge. “There. You’ll see everything coming in or out. Anything that moves toward me, Orc, Worg, or worse, you put it down before it makes a sound.”
She nodded once.
“When the prisoners are free,” Luca said, eyes narrowing on the distant shapes clustered near the tree, “stealth is no longer an issue.”
He turned slightly toward her. “Once that happens, leave your post and join me. Close and fast.”
Lysana moved to her post.
He looked back at the brothers. “You two stay up here. No matter what. Cover us. Don’t waste a shot. If it moves, you put it down. With this wind, it will be hard to relay information. Do the best you can.” The wind gusted again, tugging cloaks and stirring grit into the air. Taerel gave Aymir a knowing look as Luca walked away from them. Below, an orc barked something guttural and shoved a captive forward with the butt of a spear. The prisoner fell and did not rise.
Luca’s face hardened. He stood just enough to free his shoulders and reached beneath his collar. From a hidden recess, he drew free a small amulet, a black shard of polished onyx bound in silver wire. It pulsed faintly, slow and steady, like a second heart.
He closed his fist around it and breathed out. Shadows gathered close, clinging beneath the skin. “On my mark,” he said. “We end this fast.”
He was gone without another word.
Luca slipped forward like breath through smoke, dissolving into the shifting dark. His Shadow Walker gift did not make him invisible. It bent him, blurred him, turned him into a distortion where certainty failed. The moon ducked behind the clouds, and he took advantage, sliding low along the ridge until stone gave way beneath his palms.
He paused. Listened. A low murmur, rhythmic and wrong, barely audible beneath the crackle of fire and the hiss of wind through pine. Voices. Soft. Syncopated. Chanting in unison. The words dragged through the air like bone across stone, old and deliberate. The sound was coming from the tree.
Luca eased forward, heart slowing despite the chill crawling up his spine. As the firelight sharpened, so did the shapes beneath it. There are Nine. Not five, he thought.
His breath caught. He slid over the ridge lip and dropped into a crouch, moving beneath the cover of a shattered cart wheel and a burned-out barrel. The chanting grew clearer now. Male and female voices, humming in broken synchrony. Not fervent. Not pleading.
Mechanical. Looping. It wasn’t prayer. It was binding.
The tree loomed ahead, its roots clawing up through churned mud and ash. Nine prisoners were lashed to them with chains, wire, and blood-soaked hemp. Bodies slumped forward, heads ticking in time with the chant. At the edges, the dead had been fed to the roots. Ribs cracked and left like cages. Limbs taken. Flesh fused to bark.
Worgs’ tracks ringed the mud. Claw marks. Viscera. A gnawed thigh bone lay near a bucket of old entrails.
These were not trophies. They were rations. Luca’s stomach hardened.
The living was barely that. Eyes wide but distant. Mouths agape, lips split and dry from heat and endless sound. One woman’s head twitched every few seconds, her voice slipping off the chant before snapping back in line. Another man convulsed every seventh beat, a reflex wired deep into his body.
This wasn’t devotion. This was possession.
Luca crouched behind a half-buried cauldron and drew his dagger. Its black edge caught no light. He brushed the chain at his throat once, feeling the shard’s pulse beneath his shirt.
Above, Aymir lay prone along a narrow granite outcrop, rifle settled perfectly into stone. He had checked it four times already. There was a rhythm to readiness.
He breathed out one word, barely sounding at all.
“Zaa’hil.”
The eye opens.
Beside him, Taerel shifted behind a notch of rock, careful not to silhouette. He flicked a tarnished copper coin across his knuckles, caught it without looking. The bite in his palm told him luck still held.
“Company,” he muttered.
A second patrol emerged from the trees. Five more orcs, larger than the first. One wore an iron pauldron shaped like a wolf’s head. Another dragged a length of chain fitted with hooks, letting it scrape for effect. Two more Worgs paced beside them, leashed but barely restrained.
They were carrying another prisoner.
Lysana watched from her high perch, bow drawn, arrow nocked. She adjusted her stance without shifting weight. Hood up. Braid tucked. One slow breath through her nose. A flick of fingers across the fletching. Make it count.
Taerel’s boot slipped. Not a fall, but close. He jammed his foot between two stones as pain flashed up his calf. He stilled, forced his breath slowly, then raised a hand.
Palm to chest. Circle. Two points. I’m stuck. Still have a shot. Aymir answered with a single nod.
Below, one of the returning orcs barked orders, gesturing toward the firepit, then the tree. The new prisoner was dropped near the flames, unconscious. The two original guards turned and started toward the roots.
Luca flattened to the dirt. His hand slid to the first lock, fingers testing tension, silent. The chanting stopped. All nine prisoners went still at once, as if a wire had been cut. The woman’s head snapped up. Blind eyes blinked twice. Her lips moved again, but now they trembled. She wasn’t chanting, she was whispering. Her head turned. Her gaze locked directly onto Luca. No eyes. No light. Just focus. The gag slipped loose around her neck. Nothing. The woman did nothing. No cry. No gasp. Not even a moan.
Two Orcs dragged her from the tree and hauled her toward the firepit, her feet leaving shallow lines in the snow. Her head lolled against the pull of the chain, mouth slack, eyes unfocused. Luca watched, frozen. As they passed through the firelight, her face changed.
Not a flicker. Not a shift of skin. Something else pressed through, superimposed, wrong. In his next breath, he saw another face layered over hers, a face he remembered. Pale. Clean. Deep blue eyes. Hair the color of summer wheat, not the black matting her skull now wore. The woman’s lips did not move. The other face smiled.
Luca shook his head hard, once, as if he could dislodge the vision. His breath caught, sharp and painful. He had lived long enough to know the difference between a trick of light and something reaching. This had been reaching. He did not know from where. He did not know why that face. He folded it away with the precision of a man who has learned that some things only make sense after the blood has dried. One of the Orcs leaned in, jaws opening, teeth bared as he reached for her throat.
Luca sprang into action. He crossed the firepit in three strides, blade whispering through the air. The first orc sagged forward, throat opened cleanly. The second barely had time to turn before Luca cut behind the knee, rose with the motion, and drove steel up through the palate. The body twitched once, then folded into the mud.
A rifle cracked from the ridge. The runner at the tent mouth pinwheeled backward into the coals, fur smoking as it burned.
Aymir held his breath and his line. Ten orcs. Two Worgs. Four still penned and slamming iron. He fired once, breaking a charge at the perimeter, then shifted without thought, tracking the next angle. Snow sheared across his scope.
Lysana loosed. The arrow hissed through falling flakes and vanished behind an orc’s ear. The body dropped as if the ground had given way beneath it.
Below her, the Worgs broke.
Chains snapped against iron rings as the beasts surged free, splitting instinctively. One tore downslope toward the ridge. The other bounded uphill, straight for Lysana, fur matted with blood and foam.
Aymir already had the first in his sights. He fired. The round caught the beast’s shoulder and twisted it sideways, spraying snow and blood. It kept coming.
Taerel slid half a step behind cover, worked the bolt smooth and sure. He waited for the blur to clear the pine trunk and fired. The bullet took the Worg through the eye. It tumbled end over end, stopping a stride from Aymir’s boots.
The second beast hit the ridge top with a roar that shook branches loose. Lysana barely saw it through the curtain of snow. She dropped from the rock, landed hard, rolled, dagger flashing free.
The Worg skidded where she had stood, claws shrieking on stone, then turned and lunged. She cut sideways, shallow but true, drawing a red line along its flank. It whirled, jaws wide. She slid beneath the leap and drove her blade deep into its gut.
Hot blood sprayed across her arm, steaming. The beast shrieked and twisted for one last strike…
A rifle cracked. The Worg collapsed mid-turn and slammed into the snow at her feet. Silence fell thick as the storm. None of them paused for confirmation. There was no time for it. In the heart of the camp, the remaining Orcs were fully roused now.
Four broke toward Luca near the firepit, axes raised, screaming. The rest peeled back toward the pens, hands on chains and crude locking mechanisms, working fast but carefully, opening just enough to prepare for release.
Inside the cages, the remaining Worgs battered the bars, snarling and foaming. One smashed its skull into a beam hard enough to crack bone. Another chewed at the slats, spitting blood and splinters. The cages held. Barely.
Luca moved first. A flick of his hand sent a silver dagger spinning end over end. It struck an orc clean through the eye socket. As the body fell, the blade shimmered and vanished, reappearing against Luca’s belt with a soft metallic click.
Another orc swung low. Luca danced aside, ducked a wide follow-up, and whispered something lost in the wind.
The shadows answered. They surged from beneath his feet, oily and cold, coiling like living smoke. One orc screamed as the darkness seized its leg and dragged it down. Luca pivoted and plunged his blade through the exposed throat. Blood steamed against the snow.
Aymir fired again, dropping an orc mid-run. Taerel’s follow-up severed a knee, sending the last attacker crashing face-first into the churned slush.
Only bodies remained near the firepit. Luca swept his gaze wide, breath heavy but steady. Too steady.
On the ridge, Aymir reloaded fast. Taerel mirrored him. Four rounds each. The pens were still chaotic.
The remaining caged Worgs slammed themselves against the bars again and again, eyes wild, teeth snapping. Cracks spidered through the timber braces.
Taerel raised his rifle.
CRACK.
The largest beast took the round square in the chest. It flailed, smashed the bars once more, then collapsed in a heap of blood-slick straw.
CRACK.
Aymir dropped another mid-lunge, ribs and spine breaking under the impact. The third fell to Taerel’s shot through the jaw. The fourth to Aymir’s, cracking bone and ending the thrashing.
The pens went still. Snow fell harder now, muting sound, swallowing heat. Lysana was already moving, sliding down the incline, bow slung, second dagger drawn. She landed behind Luca, breath coming tight, eyes sharp. Her look asked the question he was already thinking. “Is that all of them?”
Luca didn’t answer. He moved forward slowly, daggers ready, eyes sweeping the camp, counting bodies, counting shadows. His shadow stretched wide behind him like a hound straining at the leash.
Around them, embers popped. Tents flapped. The storm pressed close. At the tree, Aymir and Taerel approached the prisoners cautiously. “No, no… stay still,” Aymir said sharply as one man thrashed against his bonds. “Do not move.”
“We cannot cut them free yet,” Taerel said, planting himself between the tree and the clearing. “If there’s another wave…”
A groan cut him off. Two Orcs stirred near the overturned crates. Not dead. Just dying. They dragged themselves upright, blades scraping the snow, eyes locked on the prisoners. Taerel turned first. “Aymir!”
“I see them.” Aymir met the first charge head-on. Steel rang. Sparks sprayed. He twisted, cut deep across the thigh, ducked a hammer swing by inches, then slashed the throat clean and stepped past the falling body.
Taerel moved more slowly, his injured foot dragging. Pain flared, but he raised his scimitar in time to catch a vertical chop. The impact nearly drove him to one knee.
The prisoners screamed behind him. “We are orc-taken! We are orc-taken!” The chant broke into ragged panic.
Taerel twisted, used the slope, shoved the orc off balance, and drove steel into its side. Not a killing blow, but enough. The orc stumbled, overextended, and Taerel finished it with a hard cut to the neck. Two down. The clearing went still again.
Too still. Across the camp, beyond the firelight, something moved in the trees. Not retreating. Waiting. No one spoke.
The storm pressed close, swallowing sound and distance alike. Snow fell thicker now, muting the crackle of dying fires and the wet hiss of blood on heat.
Luca moved first, slow and deliberate. Not advancing so much as confirming. His eyes swept the camp in methodical arcs, tracking bodies, tracking gaps. Every corpse mattered. Every shadow mattered more.
Aymir circled the perimeter with rifle lowered but ready, boots crunching softly through churned slush. Taerel stayed nearer the prisoners, blade still out, body angled protectively despite the tremor in his injured leg. Lysana shadowed Luca, steps light, breathing controlled, her attention flicking between the tree line and the pens.
They were alive. That was the problem. The prisoners remained lashed to the black-rooted tree, unmoving. No struggle. No relief. Just slack faces and distant eyes, some still murmuring under their breath. Taerel frowned. “They should be breaking down. Crying. Running.”
“They’re not even looking at us,” Aymir said, lowering his voice. “Just past us. Like they’re waiting.”
Luca didn’t answer. He crouched near the firepit, the pressure in his ears deepening as he drew closer. The air felt wrong here. Not hot. Not cold. Focused. “Something is still holding,” he said. He brushed ash aside with his gloved hand. 
The pattern underneath wasn’t random. Not scattered. The coals had been laid deliberately, curved lines spiraling inward, bone fragments placed at regular intervals like punctuation marks. A ritual.
Luca cleared more ash. Something pale glimmered beneath the soot. “Hold,” he murmured.
Aymir froze mid-step. Taerel shifted his stance. Lysana’s head snapped toward the tree line. Luca’s fingers closed around a length of gnarled wood half-buried in cinder and snow. Carved. Runes bit deep into the shaft, lines etched with silver that caught the firelight in dull pulses. Eye marks. Spirals. Binding chains worked so tightly into the grain they looked grown, not cut.
A staff. The pressure intensified, buzzing faintly against teeth and bone.
“That’s it,” Taerel said, fingers tightening on his scimitar hilt. “That is the anchor.”
Luca didn’t respond. His gaze lifted slowly, scanning the camp again. Too quiet. Snow shifted beyond the firelight. Not falling. Moving.
Aymir’s rifle rose a fraction. “Mugs are still warm in that tent.”
Lysana dropped to a knee. “So, someone stayed behind.”
Luca released the staff and straightened. “Or someone never left.” The sound came again. Snap. Crack. Snap.
Branches parting under deliberate weight. From beyond the outer ring, the tree line opened. He stepped into the firelight.
The war chief was immense, taller by a head than the others, grey-green skin stretched taut over scar-laced muscle. One eye was clouded white, the other black as coal. Jagged armor hung from him like pieces torn from corpses. Across his chest were trophies of bone and tooth, fingers and ears woven into cord and sinew.
In his hand, he carried a cleaver that looked more like a butcher’s tool than a blade, its edge nicked and dark with old blood. He didn’t roar. He didn’t rush. He smiled.
Luca’s shadow rose behind him, stretching long and wrong across the snow. Lysana stepped forward, daggers reversed in her grip.
Behind them, Aymir and Taerel didn’t hesitate. Taerel tore his injured foot free and slung his rifle. Aymir did the same. Steel flashed as scimitar and saber came free, both men charging downslope without a word.
The war chief lifted his cleaver and pointed it at Luca. A challenge. Luca stepped to meet it. No words. Only movement.
The chief came forward in a sudden rush, cleaver sweeping low. Luca slid off the line, blades catching sparks as steel kissed steel. The impact drove through his arms and into his shoulder, nearly rocking him back a step. He rolled with it.
Lysana cut in from the side, blades flashing for the gap beneath the arm. The chief crashed his elbow back, catching her hard enough to stagger her, then brought the cleaver down in a brutal arc meant to split Luca in half.
Luca folded under it, felt the wind of it skim his scalp, and answered with a cut across the chief’s forearm. Not deep. Deep enough to draw blood. The war chief laughed. A deep, wet sound.
He pressed forward, forcing Luca back step by step. Each swing carved furrows into the snow where Luca had been a heartbeat before. Luca let him overcommit, reading rhythm, waiting for the moment the weight carried too far.
Aymir hit the chief’s shoulder from the flank, saber biting shallow and skidding off armor. Taerel followed, scimitar flashing for the knee. The chief twisted, absorbed the blows, and backhanded Aymir hard enough to send him skidding through the snow.
Taerel met the cleaver head-on. The impact drove him to one knee. Pain flared white-hot through his injured leg. He gritted his teeth and held.
Luca moved. He stepped inside the arc, caught the cleaver wrist with his right hand, and drove both blades up under the ribs. The armor held. The breath did not.
The chief roared and wrenched free, staggering half a step.
Lysana struck again, both daggers punching beneath the collar plate. Luca surged with her, steel sliding home at the neck.
The war chief dropped to one knee, breath hissing, that terrible smile still fixed on his face. Then he fell forward into the snow and did not rise. Silence snapped tight again. Only the wind remained, and the hiss of dying fire.
Luca remained still for a long breath, blades loose in his hands, eyes locked on the fallen war chief. Snow settled across the corpse in thin sheets, softening edges, dulling color. He waited for movement. None came.
Beside him, Lysana held still for the same three seconds he did, reading the same silence. She did not speak. Neither did he. Two people who had been trained to distrust quiet, checking it anyway, together, before they let themselves believe it. She straightened slowly, one hand pressed to her ribs where the chief’s elbow had caught her. She tested the breath, nodded once to herself, then turned toward the prisoners.
They were weeping now. Not loudly. Not all at once. Just small, broken sounds, like something long held finally cracking. A man slumped forward against his chains, shoulders shaking. One of the women sobbed openly, fingers digging into the bark behind her as if she needed to feel something solid to stay upright.
Taerel lowered his scimitar but didn’t sheath it. Not yet. “It’s done,” he said, voice rough. “The orcs are dead.” The words didn’t land the way they should have.
None of the prisoners ran. None rushed forward. They stayed where they were, eyes glassy, expressions slack, as if the fight had happened somewhere far away.
“They don’t look…” Lysana hesitated, searching for the word. “Present.”
Luca turned from the corpse and approached the tree slowly. The pressure in the air had eased since the chief fell, but it hadn’t vanished. It lingered, like the echo of a sound too loud to forget.
One of the prisoners looked up as he neared. A young man, hollow-eyed, grime caked into the lines of his face. For a moment, something sharp flashed behind his gaze.
Then he moved. He shoved past Taerel with a sudden burst of strength and lunged for a fallen orc’s axe half-buried in the snow. “You killed him!” the man screamed, voice tearing apart. “You murdered the blood-chief!” He swung wildly.
Luca stepped aside, calm and precise. As the axe cut empty air, Luca was already behind him. The hilt of his dagger cracked sharply against the base of the man’s skull.
The prisoner collapsed unconscious before he hit the ground. Silence snapped tight again.
Taerel swore under his breath. “What in the hells was that?”
“Influence,” Luca said. “Still there.” He turned back toward the firepit.
The staff lay where he had left it, half-buried in ash and snow, its runes pulsing faintly, stubbornly. The glow had dimmed since the chief’s death, but it was still there. Still reaching. “That the staff caused all of this,” Aymir asked, knowing the answer. 
Luca crouched and studied the staff again. The pressure buzzed against his teeth, weaker now but persistent, like a headache that refused to fade.
Taerel struck it with his scimitar. The blade rang and skidded off clean, leaving no mark. Aymir packed snow around it until only the top showed, smothering the glow. The snow melted in seconds, not from heat but from something else entirely. Luca tried water from his pack. It beaded on the runes and ran off like oil from stone. Each attempt left the staff exactly as it had been, pulsing faintly, patient, as if it had been waiting for them to run out of ideas. 
Lysana paced, frustration on her face. “So, what, then?” Taerel asked. “Spell for a spell, or something simpler.”
“Sometimes,” Luca said slowly, “it is the simple answer that works.”
He shrugged his pack off and rummaged through it, fingers closing around a thick burlap sack meant for travel rations. He hesitated for a heartbeat, then pulled it down over the staff, fully covering the runes. 
The glow dimmed. Not extinguished. Muted. The pressure eased enough to breathe again, but it didn’t vanish. They waited.
At first, nothing happened. Then one of the women gasped, sharp and sudden. Another prisoner blinked hard, confusion flooding his face. A third sagged forward, retching into the snow as if waking from a nightmare that had lasted far too long. A fourth didn’t wake at all.
He slumped sideways, eyes rolling back, breath hitching once before stopping altogether. Moments later, one of the older men stiffened, a thin sound tearing from his throat as his body seized and went still, snow already dusting his face before anyone could reach him.
Another followed moments later. One collapsed silently. The other clawed weakly at his chest, mouth working soundlessly, then sagged into the mud as whatever had been holding him together finally let go.
The spell wasn’t breaking. It was peeling. Slowly, unevenly. “Where am I?” someone whispered. “What happened?” another asked.
Luca stood, sack-wrapped staff in hand. “It’s weakening. Not done. But weakening.”
They moved carefully then. Lysana and Aymir cut chains one by one, slow and deliberate, watching for sudden turns. Most of the prisoners barely noticed their bonds falling away. Some collapsed outright. Others backed away, trembling, staring at their hands as if they didn’t recognize them.
When the last chain fell, Taerel lowered himself to one knee among them, keeping his voice low, steady. “Tell us what you remember. Just the last clear thing.”
A woman spoke first. Her voice was cracked, distant. “We were near Fort Dran. Heading west to trade. There was talk of unrest, but nothing certain.” She swallowed hard. “The sky changed. Fire came from the cliffs. They hit both sides of the pass. Too fast.” Aymir stiffened.
Another man nodded weakly. “We ran south through the canyon. Thought we’d made it. They caught us anyway.” His fingers brushed his throat. “Not with blades. With fear. With something else. We stopped thinking straight.”
“That’s enough,” Luca said gently, but firmly. He knelt so his eyes were level with theirs. “You’re safe for now. But we need to move. Scavenge what you can. Food, blankets, anything useful. And take something small from the fallen. A ring. A token. Something to bring home.”
He rose and looked back across the ruined camp, the buried tracks, the snow already working to erase what had happened here.
“Grab what you can,” he said. “We need to put some distance from here now.”
Snow fell heavier now, soundless and steady, burying blood, bodies, and answers alike.






Chapter Seventeen
Maps were strewn like fallen leaves across the broad oak desk, creases forming crooked valleys, inked roads glistening faintly in the low golden light of early morning. At the center of it all, bent over with a tension that had become part of his shape, was Harmon. Sleeplessness clung to him like an old coat. The dark smudges beneath his eyes told of hours spent in silent calculation, and his jaw sat clenched in the low light like a man trying to hold an army back with his teeth.
He hadn't slept. The hollowness in his face wasn't weariness alone. It was the particular strain of a man who knew exactly what was at risk and could do nothing about it until morning brought word.
The knowledge that more than three hundred miles away, Luca and the others were risking their lives. Every hour without word added weight to his chest, and by now, he wore a mountain.
He pushed himself up from the desk, hands bracing on the edge of the wood as if the act itself required negotiation. His limbs moved slowly, almost reluctantly, as he stood and stepped over maps, parchment rolls, a compass, and a half-drunk cup of cold tea. The air in the room was heavy with ink, sweat, and worry.
He walked the room slowly, boots whispering over the worn rug beneath his feet. With each step, the stiffness in his body protested. He hadn't noticed the ache in his knees until now, nor the knot just under his shoulder blade that had taken root there sometime around midnight. But it was the pull of the light, thin as a thread of salvation, that drew him.
The window, until now ignored in favor of the ever-turning gears in his mind, bled with the early fire of dawn. And as he reached it, drawing the curtain aside with the edge of a tired hand, the light poured across his face, painting him in gold and shadow. It was the first time he had truly looked out since they’d arrived.
Forgehallow stretched beyond the glass like a living machine. Chimneys coughed out morning smoke, rooftops glinted with soot-frosted dew, and the low hum of waking industry murmured through the cobbled veins of the city. Far beyond, the sharp hills of the north cut against the sky like broken teeth, and somewhere past them, hidden by time and terrain, Luca’s team was either resting in success or bleeding in silence.
A quiet breath left him. Not a sigh, more like the kind of exhale a man gives when he's remembering how to breathe again.
He stared at the rising sun, the first he’d truly watched in decades. 
“This is falling apart,” he murmured to himself, voice low and raw, like a confession to the morning. “I built this too wide. Too ambitious. Now it’s slipping.”
His gaze dropped, voice barely above a breath now. “I believed I could hold together too many threads. Fool’s work.”
He looked down at his hand, the right one, and thumbed the ring on his finger. The metal pulsed faintly against his skin, not with light but with weight. Magic pulsed from it, subtle and disciplined, like the low drumbeat of a heart, keeping him sharp. Keeping him standing. Without it, he knew, he would have collapsed hours ago. The cost of that ring’s power was something he had stopped counting.
A knock, too sharp to be polite, too familiar to be alarming, rattled the frame of the door before it creaked open. Boots on wood. Urgency in motion.
Weslin. He was halfway to Harmon before he could even turn from the window, breath tight and eyes lit with something unreadable. “Sir,” Weslin said, slightly out of breath.
Harmon turned fully now, drawing himself upright even as fatigue clung like iron weights to his limbs. He studied Weslin’s expression, the kind that only came when something had broken the silence across miles.
“We’ve got a message,” Weslin said, voice steady but edged. “Came through the twin bracelet.”
Harmon’s eyes sharpened like drawn steel. “From who?”
“Luca!” A long pause, not of confusion but of gathering. Then Harmon nodded, already moving past the scout, hand grazing the map-littered desk as he went, brushing a curled edge back into place out of unconscious habit.
“Come with me,” he said. “We’ll talk while we eat.”
Together, they descended the narrow tavern staircase, footsteps muffled on the worn steps, the scent of smoke and early fare rising to greet them like an old friend.
As Harmon reached the lower floor, the voices of his team drifted to him first. Ash’s low laugh, cracked through the room like fire through dry wood. Aldrek murmured something into his cup that sounded like a prayer. Nyssa was already poking at Neavin with some sharp remark while Aurelia rolled her eyes. Dain leaned back in his chair, half a grin tugging his lip, and Garr, silent as always, watched them all like a sentinel of stone.
They were already gathered around a long oak table near the fire, the kind of table that held secrets, plans, and stories in equal measure.
He paused for a heartbeat at the foot of the stairs, letting the sight root him. They were still together. Still breathing. Still his. And now, Luca had reported.
They claimed a small, square table near the far corner of the inn’s common room, slightly away from the larger cluster of morning patrons but close enough to feel the warmth of the central hearth. A wide sunbeam slanted in through the high windows, catching the motes of dust swirling in the air like lazy dancers. The low din of the tavern ebbed and flowed, wooden plates clinking, a pipe player near the fireplace strumming a slow, almost mournful tune, and the occasional laughter of two traders discussing the price of good flax.
Weslin eased himself down across from Harmon. His brow was still furrowed, though now it bore more fatigue than tension.
Harmon kept his voice low, forcing the words to stay close to the table. The fire cracked loudly enough to swallow anything that slipped past his teeth. He leaned forward, resting his forearms on the table, fingers loosely interlaced. “All right, boy,” he said, voice gruff but even. “Out with it.”
Weslin nodded and quietly relayed the message from the bracelet. Luca’s voice still echoed faintly in the back of his memory. “They’re… back at their camp,” Weslin said, then pushed on. “Ten survivors pulled out. Rough shape. But alive.”
Harmon nodded slowly but said nothing, his face unreadable.
“There’s more,” Weslin continued. “Luca said… something strange happened at the site. He’s got an item. He wants someone here to look it over. Something about mind control.” The last words came with a subtle shift in his voice, uncertain, as though he didn’t quite believe them himself.
Before Harmon could respond, a voice slurred into their bubble of conversation like a lazy wave lapping at the shore. “What’ll it be, gents?”
The waitress slouched at their table. Apron streaked with flour and grease. “Break-fust, aye.”
“Two house plates,” Harmon said.
“Drunks?” asked the waitress.
“Apple juice,” Weslin said.
“Two,” Harmon added. She nodded and shuffled back toward the kitchen, the floor creaking beneath her shoes.
Still staring at the table, Harmon exhaled through his nose. “They’re alive and saved civilians,” Harmon said, fingers tightening briefly on the bracelet. “That's all that counts. Tell them job well done, and to send a report in full when able.”
Weslin nodded and pulled his sleeve back slightly to reveal the twin bracelet, already glowing faintly in response. He tapped the bracelet as it had become a habit for him now, and whispered the words Harmon had given him.
Harmon leaned back in his chair then, and it was like watching a massive bellows release. The tension dropped from his shoulders; he closed his eyes and took in a long breath, his chest finally moving freely.
“Well,” he muttered. “That’s one thing. One out of ninety-nine.” A slow, dry smile tugged at the edge of his mouth. “Let’s enjoy breakfast before the next fire starts.”
The common room was beginning to buzz a little louder now. A merchant in a fur-collared coat was loudly complaining about the roads to a poor farmhand who clearly didn’t care. A pair of local hunters was playing a dice game near the window, their laughter peppered with crude jokes about a girl in the stables. The hearth crackled softly, and somewhere above them, boots thudded across the ceiling beams, likely Aurelia pacing again.
It didn’t take long for their food to arrive. The house breakfast was simple but hearty. Thick-sliced fried ham with crisped edges, two golden eggs over toast, a scoop of skillet-fried potatoes tossed with onions and herbs, and a sweet-buttered biscuit on the side. A pint of apple juice in a frosted clay mug accompanied each plate, chilled from the root cellar.
Weslin wasted no time digging in, clearly famished.
Harmon, meanwhile, took a bite and grunted in approval. “Not bad,” he said through a mouthful of ham. “Could use some heat, but I’ll take flavor over spice this early.”
They were halfway through their plates when Garr approached the table, walking with that wide-legged confidence born of too many years on rough ground. He was still shrugging into his long-coat, his sword belt hanging loosely at his side.
“Mornin’, old man,” he said, voice dry as kindling. “Mornin’, kid.” He nodded at Weslin. “Food smells better than the room upstairs, I’ll give it that.”
He stood beside the table, arms folded, waiting for either of them to acknowledge his presence beyond a look.
Harmon swallowed, then dabbed at the corner of his mouth with a napkin. “We’re just finishing. Sit down if you’re here to talk. Otherwise, get your own plate.”
Garr smiled but didn’t move. “Just wanted to check in before the whole crew assembles. Place has a feel to it this mornin',” Garr said. “Guesson you already know.” 
Harmon gave him a knowing look. “They always are.”
The last of the eggs and bread disappeared from Harmon’s plate as he set his fork down with a sigh and leaned back in the creaky wooden chair. Weslin, cheeks stuffed with the last bite of ham, gave a small grunt of satisfaction. Around them, the common room of the tavern was still buzzing with the quiet hum of morning. Harmon stood, wiping his hands on a linen cloth, and motioned for Weslin to follow. Together, they crossed the worn planks toward the table where the others waited, Nyssa lounging with one boot on a bench, Neavin still eating, Aldrek watching the room like a sentry.
Dain leaned back with his arms stretched across the top of the bench, idly sharpening a slim dagger while muttering something that made Aurelia raise a disapproving brow. Ash was nursing a chipped mug of black tea, steam curling up beneath his chin. He looked up first as Harmon approached.
“How’s everyone doing?” Harmon asked, his voice steady but with a slight smile tucked into the edge of his tone.
Dain was first to reply, flipping his dagger in his palm. “I have been in considerably worse positions,” Dain said, flipping the dagger again. “Upside down in bandit camps, for instance. Or explaining myself to angry husbands. This ranks somewhere in the middle.” 
Nyssa smirked. “I’d say I’m peachy, but there’s not a peach within a hundred miles of this place.”
Neavin didn’t look up. “Still breathin',” he said, not looking up. “Reckon that's fine enough.” Brother Aldrek simply nodded, his heavy brow knit in mild concern. “Fed. Focused.” Aurelia gave Harmon a serene glance, her voice low and measured. “Prepared, as ever.”
Ash took a slow sip from his mug, then spoke in his usual gravelly voice. “Still alive. That’s my standard lately. Doesn’t take much to impress me.”
Weslin chuckled softly behind Harmon, still wiping grease from his chin.
Harmon pulled up a stool and leaned in, his tone shifting to something more clipped, urgent. “Luca’s team made it back to their camp. The raid was a success.”
The team let that settle in before Harmon continued. “For us, we need to have this done tonight. At dusk, we will breach the prison. One last look around this morning. Split into teams to cover more ground.” He paused, letting the words settle over the group.
“Garr. Ash. You’re heading to the local records office. Maybe the library as well, if needed. I want those building drawings. You’re inspectors,” Harmon said. “Structural safety. Aging foundations. Say the city’s had complaints. You don’t ask for answers. You ask what’s already on the shelf. Sound official, look bored, and make them think it’s nothing.
Ash gave a low grunt. “So, lie like it’s just another Jovis. Got it.”
Harmon shot back, “Today it's only Martis.”
Garr smirked. “I’ll handle the charm. You handle looking like you’re about to punch someone if they breathe wrong.”
Ash raised both hands, feigning offense. “Intimidating? Please. I’m adorable.” A few smirks and giggles flickered around the table.
Harmon moved on. “Nyssa, Neavin, you’re covering the exterior. I want every inch of that prison mapped. Number of guards, pacing, and vantage points. Neavin, I want your little friend in there. If he can shift small enough to slip through the bars, do it. We need an inside layout, even if it’s rough.”
Neavin gave a small grin. “He’s eager,” he said, wiping his fingers on his trousers. “I’ll let him loose.”
Nyssa twirled a lock of her hair around one finger. “We’ll play nice with the guards. Or not. Depends how rude they decide to be.”
“Aurelia,” Harmon said, his tone softening slightly. “You’re going to do what you do best. Slip through the minds of the guards, patrols, and even the staff. Find out what they’re thinking, what they know. Names, routines, anything that feels off.”
She gave a graceful nod. “Understood.”
“Careful with it,” Harmon added. “Shallow touches only. We don’t need them noticing.”
“You’ll take Weslin with you. Show him and talk to him about what you are doing. He’s due for his second lesson anyway. Make sure he completes it before you head out.”
Weslin blinked. “Wait, lesson first? And then mind-reading patrol?”
Aurelia gave him a gentle, knowing smile. “Yes. Lesson first. Then the fun begins.”
Harmon’s eyes shifted to the last pair. “Aldrek. Dain. You’re our pressure team. Find a place with loose lips. Use the noble getup if you have to, drop a name or two. Anyone talking about the prison? The prisoners? Anything they’ve heard, any rumors they’re holding back. Also… keep your ear to the wind on Lord Merrick. I don’t trust that man based on the stories I have heard, and I want to know what he’s planning, and who he’s working with, if he’s positioning himself for something bigger.”
Dain leaned back and stretched. “So, drink, flirt, and pretend I care about local gossip? Sounds exhausting.”
Aldrek gave him a sidelong look. “Try not to flirt with anyone dangerous this time.”

“Where’s the fun in that?” Dain winked.
Harmon stood up straight, voice firm. “Alright. Any questions?”
Nyssa raised her hand lazily. “And what exactly will you be doing while we’re running around dodging guards and charming bureaucrats?”
Harmon didn’t miss a beat. “I’ll be here. Suffering. Doing commander stuff, like reading reports, drinking bad coffee, and pretending I don’t want to strangle half the people in this city.”
Dain grinned. “Just like your study, then?”
“Exactly,” Harmon replied dryly. 
A round of chuckles rippled through the table. Garr stood first, nodding toward Ash. Aurelia rose in one fluid movement, turning toward Weslin with that gentle but expectant teacher’s presence. Nyssa was already halfway to the door, with Neavin tucking food into his cloak and following silently. Dain groaned theatrically as he stood, and Aldrek simply followed, calm and steady.
The group broke apart like clockwork, each team sliding Into motion, the air thick with purpose. Boots found cobblestone. Outside the tavern, the sky was beginning to brighten into the pale gold of a new day, one that they were already asking a lot from, and more before it was done.






Chapter Eighteen
After breakfast, Aurelia and Weslin returned to their rooms, a small chamber tucked beside Harmon’s command space. The morning had a hush, the kind that settled in just before the weight of the day truly began. Aurelia moved with quiet purpose. Weslin, by contrast, seemed energized, his steps quicker, eyes alert, as if ready for another lesson before the first flame cooled.
The chamber was dim, touched by the soft spill of morning light slipping through slatted shutters. Aurelia sat cross-legged across from Weslin, her long sleeves rolled back to her elbows, a yellow shard resting gently in her palm like a piece of captured sunlight. Her eyes were closed, calm and composed. A single candle burned between them on the floor, its small flame flickering in tune with breath, alive in its own way.
Weslin sat. The candle between them leaned slightly toward him and then thought better of it.  Weslin mirrored her posture, shoulders square, back straight, though a thin line of tension traced his brow.
She opened one eye, then the other. Something in her expression shifted as she looked at him, not quite settling, like a woman checking a face against a memory she wasn't sure was hers. “Did you practice what I showed you yesterday?” she asked, voice soft, the kind that invited honesty.
Weslin gave a small nod. “Yeah. Twice.” He almost smiled. “Before bed, I kept losing count. But this morning it stayed.”
Aurelia's expression warmed, something close to pride. “Good,” she said quietly. “That is the work. Most want the power and refuse the patience it takes to hold it.” She leaned forward slightly. “And while you were in your meditative state… what did you hear?”
Weslin blinked, uncertain. “I… didn’t know I was supposed to be listening for anything,” he admitted, the words tripping over each other slightly.
A soft smile curved her lips. “Ah. That’s the trouble, then.” She closed her hand around the shard and tapped it once with her fingertip. “There is a difference between a door opening and a door being opened. One is weather. The other is will.”
She sat back, spine straight as a drawn bow, her voice turning lyrical, almost like reciting an old mantra.
“Hearing is passive. It slips in through cracks. Wind at your window. Footsteps behind you. The hush before a lie.” Weslin’s eyes dropped, absorbing her words.
She continued,”Listening… listening is a choice.” She said the word again, and for just a moment her voice went somewhere else, somewhere older. Then she pulled it back. “You lean into it. Your skin. Your bones. The silence between sounds. It is intentional. It is an invitation.”
“You can hear anything,” she continued, tapping her temple. “But are you listening? To truly hear, you have to stop speaking over what you want to believe and start listening. That’s what the shard teaches, too.”
She opened her hand. The shard glowed faintly in her palm, golden and pulsing like a heartbeat caught in crystal.
“This,” she said, “is older than any book, any tower, any old law. Once, magic flowed like underground rivers, fluid, wild, nourishing,” she said quietly, as if reminding herself as much as him. “The world drank from it like a spring. It wasn’t studied or summoned; it was simply felt. The ethereal plane wasn't some distant concept; it was stitched into the air itself.” She passed the shard to him gently. It pulsed warm in his hand.
“But then the breach was sealed. And the ether, cut off from its source, began to harden. Not like ice. Not like clay. Like stone. A deep, cosmic stillness took hold, and it flowed no more. And when the pressure became too much…” She tapped the shard. “It shattered. Fractured into the shards we now hold.”
Weslin stared at it, brows drawn. “But that happened a long time ago. So… how do we still have shards? Where are they all coming from?”
Aurelia gave a knowing smile, the kind that suggested a deeper truth had just been nudged into view.
“Good question. Most don’t think to ask it. The answer is… mine. The ether still leaks through, here and there, or so we believe.” Her fingers curled slightly, the certainty thinning at the edges. “Without it, the world would wither. But it doesn’t stay soft. As soon as it hits our plane, it begins to solidify again. Crystallize. Become what you hold in your hand.”
Her tone shifted, growing heavier and more political. “These places become rich veins,” she said. “Most of the time they are unstable and never where you want them. Few last long. Fewer are worth the blood it takes to hold them. Still, even one can elevate a nation.” She looked at him with a quiet intensity.

“Once, adepts didn’t need to be gifted; they were simply in tune. They knew the songs, the feel of current beneath skin. But now? The bloodline is thinning. The knowledge is fading. Fewer are born who can touch the current. And we call this the Debt now, like they owe the world an apology for being empty.”
She shook her head slightly, voice a little sad. “But the shards… they still remember. They still radiate.” She went quiet. Not for him. For something else, behind her eyes, something that had no business being in this room. Then she blinked, and it was gone, and she was simply Aurelia again, sitting across from a boy with a glowing stone in his hand.
Weslin looked down at the crystal in his hand. It glowed faintly, the light licking at his palm.
She tilted her head. “Do you remember the feast at Opindale? The night of your first touch?”
He nodded slowly. “Yeah… Harmon gave me a mission and a gift.”
Her brow lifted slightly, inviting more.
“It was a pen,” Weslin said. “He handed it to me before I went off to the servants’ quarters. Told me to carry it, keep it close. He went as far as putting on my tunic. Said it might help me… hear things clearer. I didn’t know what he meant at first, but I was there to gather whispers, gossip, nothing official. He must’ve suspected I was adept… wanted to see if I could pick up anything passively.”
Aurelia nodded thoughtfully. “A test. That makes sense. He did tell me that.”
“I didn’t even realize there was a shard in it until later. I just… started hearing things. Voices that weren’t spoken. Thoughts, maybe. Like feelings turned into echoes. I thought I was imagining it. But then...” His hands curled slightly around the crystal.

“Then Braden came at me, and everything just lit up. Not like fire, more like fury. Like lightning behind my eyes. I didn’t even know what I was doing, but he screamed. Said he felt like he was burning.”
Aurelia nodded slowly, as if this confirmed something she already suspected. “That’s because you invoked the shard. There are two ways to use it. The first is passive, its presence alone fuels your gifts, strengthens your senses, sharpens what you already have.” She raised one finger.
“But the second is to call it in. To pull its essence through you. That’s what you did when you were afraid. Or angry. Or both. It wasn’t training, it was instinct. We will go over the differences later and what it all means.”
She let the moment settle. “But that path, while powerful, is dangerous if untamed. You can burn through your spirit faster than your body can follow.” She reached out and gently pressed the shard in his hand back toward him. “Today, we’re only learning the first path. Not invocation. Just… feeling.” Weslin nodded, brow furrowed in focus.
“The shard radiates,” she continued, rising smoothly to her feet. “Like a sun under water. Its energy reaches, even if you’re not ready to reach back. I want you to sit. Breathe. And when you feel it, not think you feel it, but truly, raise your hand. Then, still with your eyes closed, point in the direction of the shard.” He nodded again, slower this time.
She moved a few feet back, setting the shard in a small stone bowl, letting its light spill faintly against the walls.
“Now breathe. We’ll do this several times. Each time, I’ll place the shard further away. You’ll learn to feel its call from a distance. It’s like learning to see heat in winter, or smell rain before it falls.”
She stood, quiet and composed, and began to walk the circle around him. “You’re going to learn the language of the shard, Weslin.”
The morning had broken pale and cold over Forgehollow, the rising sun weak behind a swathe of silver clouds. A fine dusting of snow clung to the cobbled streets and iron-shod roofs, crunching lightly beneath boot and wheel. Smoke coiled from the chimneys in long, lazy trails, and the scent of coalfires and molten metal hung in the crisp air like a cloak.
Dain adjusted the silver clasp at his collar and gave his reflection a final glance in the warped mirror by the Iron Flask’s hearth. He wore a tailored charcoal tunic with blue satin lining and an embroidered half-cloak clasped with his family crest, subtle but unmistakably noble. Beside him, Brother Aldrek had exchanged his road-worn robes for ceremonial vestments: layered ivory and gray with a modest chain of prayer stones resting across his chest.
“Shall we?” Dain asked, sweeping back the curtain at the door as a gust of cold air kissed their faces.
The two departed the Iron Flask and made their way through Forgehollow’s bustling mid-morning traffic, their boots brushing snow from iron-grated steps and flagstones. They followed the direction of a name passed quietly by a merchant the evening prior: The Gilded Chamber.
“It’s where the quiet hands and loud purses meet,” the man had said over a mug of hot ale. “If you want whispers with weight, that's the place.”
Dain had heard the name again that morning from the blacksmith tending the horses. “Some call it a dining hall, others a council by candlelight. Either way, you’ll find the city's decision-makers elbow-deep in spiced wine and deals.”
They arrived at mid-bell, the Gilded Chamber nestled within the second level of the central tower's south arm, above the city's ancient forge archive. Its carved archway doors were flanked by wrought-iron sconces shaped like hammerheads, flickering with amber light. 
Two attendants in dark green livery opened the doors.
Warmth embraced them at once. The scent of cinnamon-spiced cider and roasting meats filled the air. Heavy velvet curtains framed a long hall whose black-steel columns were veined with gold and copper. Firelight flickered from chandelier bowls hung on chains, casting moving armor-shapes across the vaulted ceiling.
A steward approached, a wiry man with gray-streaked hair and eyes like frosted glass.
“Welcome to the Chamber,” he said with a shallow bow. “May I assist you, my lords?”
“You may. I’ve only just arrived in Forgehollow,” Dain said smoothly. “I am Lord Alric Rendsdale of House Emberlight. A minor line. I was sent by my father to explore new routes, particularly ones in Aldoria, now that the new treaty has been signed in Opindale between Opindale, Aldoria, and Moradaer. Naturally, we seek a favorable passage and exchange.”
He glanced subtly toward the gathering crowd. “House Emberlight is prepared to offer generous terms to those aligned with our interests.” He pressed a gold coin into the steward’s palm; the man’s demeanor brightened instantly.
“But of course,” the steward said, slipping the coin away and gesturing toward the room. “First, beneath the tapestry of the Old Forge, that’s Lord Veyric Bram, overseer of the mountain routes and riverways. If it flows, he taxes it. Rumor says he drinks more than he earns, yet his coffers never dry.”
“To your left,” the steward continued, “is Lady Elsin Corveira. Fortunes in horse breeding, half the northern stables are hers. She once gifted the Emperor a mare, believed to be faster than the wind. She’s… selective with company.”
He pointed again. “Count Hollus Fenwright there, carriages, freight lines, and those new iron wagons from the west. He’s pouring coin into something he calls an engine, a wheeled forge that moves on rails and never tires. Financed half the prototypes running the mountain routes.” Beside him, Lord Trellik Houn, a forge baron with a worker’s build and scarred hands, examined a crescent-bladed weapon with his apprentices.
“If you’ll excuse me,” the steward said as a noblewoman in violet beckoned.
“Thank you,” Dain replied, letting the polite smile fade once the man turned. The mask of Lord Rendsdale slipped; the hunter beneath watched the room instead.
“Circle the room,” he told Aldrek quietly. “See what words they offer a man of faith.”
Aldrek bowed and moved among the crowd.
While Dain traded easy conversation and gathered fragments, Bram’s debts, Corveira’s tourney plans, Fenwright’s rail contracts, Aldrek walked softly through the gathering, offering blessings and brief prayers. A mother of two asked for protection for a son sent to the front; an aging knight for strength to endure winter. One woman confessed guilt for poisoning her husband’s mistress; Aldrek answered only with a grave silence and a quiet prayer.
Dain eventually reached the long oak bar at the hall’s edge. The air thickened with spiced wine and the murmur of discreet deals. He rested one hand on the polished wood, then a voice cut cleanly through the noise behind him.

“Lord Rendsdale,” came a voice from behind, smooth, clipped, and pretending to be polite.
Dain turned slightly. Lord Iven Merrick stood there, dressed like old money, the kind that arrives in the right room and hopes no one checks the date on the coin. His ring was too big, his robe too new, his smile too practiced.
“My lord,” Dain said with a small bow. “Forgive me. I don’t believe we’ve been introduced. But then, introductions are so rarely honest in places like this, aren’t they?”
“Indeed,” Merrick smiled. “Masks are more useful,” he said lightly, “when you already know the face beneath them.”
“A charming philosophy,” Dain replied smoothly. “I prefer to let the mask do the work. It’s usually better dressed.”
A brief chuckle passed between them, polite and sharp. The music from the quartet faded to a single violin line as the space between them tightened.
“You caused quite the ripple,” Merrick murmured. “Poking about the Bastion. Asking after ghosts.”
“Did I?” Dain sipped his whiskey. “I have a fondness for forgotten things, old swords, lost names, the occasional man the world misplaces.”
“A romantic, then?”
“A collector.”
Merrick leaned in, quiet now, like a man who has stopped needing volume. “Tell me, Lord Rendsdale, what is it you're really looking for in Forgehollow? Or shall we keep dancing with riddles and pretty metaphors until one of us steps on the other's toes?”

Dain turned fully now, facing him square. “My toes are rather resilient. But if we’re dancing, I’d like to lead.”
“Brave,” Merrick studied him a moment longer than courtesy allowed. “Curious,” he said at last. “Your name never crossed my desk.”
Dain chuckled. “Titles are like wine labels. Lovely to look at, but ultimately meaningless unless what’s inside holds weight.”
“I find bloodlines hold weight.”
“Yours or someone else’s?”
Merrick’s smile faltered, just a hair. Dain pressed, gently, like testing the edge of a blade. I admire the work, actually,” Dain said, and he almost meant it. “Most men born to titles never had to decide if they deserved one. You did.”
“Easier to forge than inherit, wouldn’t you say?” said Merrick.
“Easier, yes. But rarely done without the smell of soot,” replied Dain.
A breath of silence. Their smiles had not changed. That was the problem. The laughter around them dulled, sensing pressure neither man acknowledged. 
The noise around them swelled, voices rising just enough that neither man needed to lower his own. They fenced in words, each smile fixed, neither man blinking.
At last, Dain said quietly, “Some of us carry our scars in the open. Others hide them in prisons.”
Merrick stilled. “You wound me, my lord.”

Dain gave a soft laugh. “Was that too plainspoken for polite company?” He paused to really take in Merrick, and how his attention had not left Dain for a second since this had begun, finding it almost enjoyable, he realized, before continuing, “Then let’s call it what it is, a conversation between two liars, pretending we still believe in truth.”
Merrick studied him for a moment, the humor never quite leaving his face, but something colder behind his eyes now.
“You’re looking for him,” he said, not a question, his grip tightening imperceptibly on the stem of his goblet. “And you think he’ll tell you something I won’t.”
“I think ghosts talk more freely than kings.”
“Do you believe in ghosts, Lord Rendsdale?”
“I believe in men who become myths because someone powerful needed them forgotten.”
Merrick’s voice lowered. “You come into my city wearing a borrowed name, sniffing after relics locked away before your crest ever existed. And all I see is a man afraid he’s already too late.”
Dain didn’t flinch. “And you,” he said, raising his glass, “are a man who thinks owning the key makes him the keeper of the vault.”
Merrick laughed. “Oh, gods, you think you’re the only one looking for the lock. Is that all this is?”
“No,” Dain said, smiling now. “This is just foreplay. The fun is still to come.”
He turned and left the words hanging like a drawn blade.
“Tell me one thing,” Merrick called softly after him. “Why him? Why Riven Duskwind?”
Without turning, Dain’s reply came low and razor-edged. “Because sometimes the most broken blade still remembers how to cut.”
Merrick turned on his heel with a flourish of his dark emerald cloak, clearly intending to make a show of retreat. His boots clicked smartly across the marble, once, twice, thrice, but then he paused.
Stillness, except the quartet in the far corner, easing into something older than either man would admit knowing. Merrick turned. Not slowly, not dramatically, but like a man snapping shut a well-oiled dagger.
He strolled back toward Dain, not a trace of hurry in him, only that dangerous kind of ease worn by men who have survived rooms that wanted them dead.
“Forgive me,” he said. “It’s unlike me to walk away from an unfinished riddle. Especially when the answer’s standing right in front of me, wearing Estmere silk and smugness like a tailored sin.”
Dain grinned around the rim of his glass and took a small, thoughtful sip. “You flatter me. Though I suspect your compliments come with a receipt.”
