“I don’t give receipts,” Merrick said. “I write ledgers. And I never forget a debt.”
From across the hall, a man-servant in crimson livery hurried toward them, sweating beneath his silver tray. Merrick extended a hand without even glancing. The goblet arrived too late for his liking. He took the drink, tasted it, and scowled. “Warm,” he muttered, then turned a sideways look at the man. “You had one task, Albin.”
Albin mumbled an apology and disappeared faster than he’d arrived. Merrick watched him go, then turned back to Dain. “Forgive the staff. Good help is rarer than truth these days.”
Dain’s grin sharpened. “You might try treating them like people. I hear it’s all the rage in civilized circles.”
Merrick chuckled, but there was no warmth in it. “I didn’t claw my way to a title by chasing fads.”
“No,” Dain said. “You bought it. I imagine it came wrapped in velvet and tied with the blood of better men.”
Merrick stepped closer, close enough that the flickering candlelight danced in both their eyes. “Wealth may not birth rights,” he said, “but it buries them just fine.”
“You speak like a man who’s buried a few himself.”
“I speak like a man who knows where they’re buried.” Merrick’s voice dropped. “And where is the next plot waiting?”
That drew a genuine smile from Dain, not the smirk of the moment before, but something darker. “Careful,” he said. “That almost sounded like poetry.”
Merrick looked mock-wounded. “My apologies. I forgot myself.”
“You always remember yourself,” Dain said, circling him now, slow, unhurried. “You remember your name, your holdings, your forged title, your silver tongue. But what I wonder, Lord Merrick, is whether you remember what it was like to be small.”
A flicker of something in Merrick’s gaze, pride, maybe, or shame poorly buried. “I remember enough,” Merrick replied. “Enough to know that small men don’t get to ask big questions.”
Dain's reply came low and silk-slick. “Ah, but small men, they ask the best ones. Because they know the cost of not knowing.” He stepped closer now, and the air between them sharpened. “You want to know why I’m here.” 
Merrick didn’t answer.
“I am here because someone is meddling with things he does not understand. I want our shadow back, and I want to know what you want with him,” Dain continued. “Not the ghost. Not the myth. The man you’ve shackled somewhere below your Iron Halls.”
Merrick’s brow arched. “Careful, Lord Rendsdale. You’re bleeding through your lie.”
“So are you. It is one thing to build a lie for your life, it's all something else when you try to make others play along.”
Silence. The kind that draws curious eyes from across the room. Merrick sipped his wine again, thoughtfully this time, and turned slightly as if admiring the golden chandelier above them. “Yet I see a man so desperate to be relevant again, you have to swing for the bottom.”
Dain didn’t flinch. He smiled and gave a half-bow, courteous and mocking all at once. Speaking so only Merrick could hear, “At least you are willing to see you are the bottom, just another beggar at the feast.” Their eyes met. “Good evening, Lord Merrick.”
He turned, this time for real, letting the weight of their final words hang like a guillotine. Just as fast as it started, he was gone, leaving only the taste of smoke and secrets behind.
The crowd filled the silence. Soon after he left, laughter rushed back like air into lungs when a heavier presence joined Dain at the bar.
Brother Aldrek. Taller than most, robed in deep burgundy trimmed with silver, the sigil of the Creator’s Flame etched at the collar. His mace hung peace-bound at his side, though his gaze never needed binding.
He lifted a hand to his brow, then chest, a gesture of faith and signal both. “Hold a breath, Brother. Eyes are on us. Let them think we pray, not plot.” They spoke in fragments after that. Names without detail. Conclusions without paths.
Aldrek stepped beside him, placing his right hand palm down on the table. Dain mirrored the gesture. Heads bowed, they formed the posture of a ritual blessing used before meals or decisions. The murmur around them softened automatically.
“I talked to the miners’ guild,” Aldrek said, tracing a slow circle over his heart before laying his hand atop the first. Dain followed suit.
“Lord Tannith owns the lease north of Forgehollow’s old silver mine. Long abandoned. But Merrick bought it six months ago.”
“Merrick owns Tannith’s old mine, but why?”
“Looks that way. The miners haven’t worked since,” Aldrek said, then paused. “They were pushed off. Quietly. Yet with pay, my guess is to stay silent.”
“Paying a crew to do nothing on land no one’s allowed near…” Dain murmured.
“Vault site,” Aldrek said flatly. “Has to be.”
He touched two fingers to his brow and lips, a silent invocation, then took a swig from his tin flask. Dain mirrored the motion with his wineglass; to onlookers, it seemed like a prayer.
“Two dockhands told me they saw a group leaving past midnight three nights ago,” Aldrek continued. “No lights. Cart tracks deep as trenches. Thought smugglers, until they heard chains.”
“Chains?”
“Not on cargo. On people.”
The silence that followed was heavy.
“Maybe he brought in free labor to move something. I don’t want to think about what else it could be. The stories about these so-called vaults, and what it takes to open them.” 
Brother Aldrek paused to clean his mind of the images of that before picking back up, “One off Ironrun’s men, a guard, heard Merrick drunk-bragging that he was hiring a lockbreaker. Needed someone to open ‘etched warding’ on a private vault.”
Dain’s hand tightened on his glass before he lifted it and held the cup aloft, three seconds, then down again. A sign of restraint.
“Put it all together,” Aldrek muttered. “Doesn’t sing a song, but it hums the tune.”
They sat quietly for a moment. Then Aldrek’s eyes swept the room once more. “Figured you’d want to know.”
He rose, closing the benediction. Dain stood with him. Just as he reached for his glass, a small messenger boy, no older than eleven, came right up to him. Dain glanced at Aldrek. Aldrek gave the smallest shake of his head. Neither of them knew the boy. 
The boy didn’t look at him at all, only slipped the note into Dain’s palm as if following practiced instructions. The boy just vanished. Dain read it once. He folded it with the same care a man uses when he does not want to look like something has shaken him. He passed it to Aldrek. He took it, read it, and handed it back without speaking. Neither of them looked at the other. 
The two men turned back to the counter in silence, lifting their drinks once more. Beyond them, the laughter of Forgehollow rolled on, unaware of the storm it had just birthed.






Chapter Nineteen
Harmon returned to his makeshift command hub, which was dimly lit by amber-glow crystals humming inside wire-caged housings overhead. They cast a sickly light across a broad steel-plated table where maps, parchment scraps, half-burnt candles, and grease-marked mugs formed a chaotic landscape of their own. The stone walls wept condensation, and the forge heat below made the air humid and claustrophobic.
Harmon stood at the table’s head, arms folded tight across his chest, jaw locked.
The others returned not as a team, but as fragments. Shattered pieces of a plan, strained by time and pressure, and the first real cracks of something that had not had time to set. No one spoke at first, but the sound of bootsteps hammering up the stairs, fast and angry, warned Harmon before the first bodies even emerged.
Ash stormed in, jaw tight, eyes flaring. Behind him, Garr, face like a thunderhead, followed close. They were mid-argument and not bothering to lower their voices.
“I told you not to use your full flame in a paper-flooded archive,” Garr snapped. “But sure. Scare the clerk half to death.”
Ash spun on him. “And I told you if I didn't light up the back hall, we were walking into an ambush. Turns out I was right.”
“You scorched half a map! I needed that corridor survey!”
“Then next time move faster and stop breathin' down my neck like a bookkeeper with a grudge.” They pushed into the room, still snapping. Harmon didn't speak. Not yet. Ash threw down the folded blueprint hard enough to rattle a cup off the edge of the table.
“We got 'em. The library was slow, but Garr talked fast. I just glowered. Worked wonders.”
“That's one way to put it,” Garr muttered. “Glaring at a clerk like you was sizing him for a coffin.”
Ash shot him a sideways look. “He didn't ask for a bribe. You're welcome.”
“You elbowed the blueprint drawer off its hinge.”
“Boys.” Harmon's voice didn't rise. It didn't have to. “Do I look like I care about the drawer?”
Garr and Ash fell quiet. Not peacefully. The tension hung between them like steam off forge steel. More footfalls. Louder. Faster. More than two sets.
Nyssa and Neavin came up the opposite stairwell at speed, boots striking stone too fast for anything but anger. The door burst open behind them hard enough to rattle the lamps in their cages.
“You don't do that in a city.” Nyssa crossed the threshold with her hand cutting once through the air, sharp as a blade. “You don't freeze in the open without warning.”
“I told you.” Neavin turned on her before she'd finished. “I said the connection was slipping. I warned you. If I stop, it shows.”
“You didn't stop,” she said. “That's the whole problem. You kept walking. Straight into a watched lane like nothing in the world could touch you.”
“Because something was there. I felt it.”
Nyssa laughed. One short, hard sound with no humor in it at all. “You felt it. Right. While you were chasing ghosts through Veyrith's eyes, I was counting uniforms and doing the math on how fast we'd end up in a room we don't come out of.”
“Wasn't your call to make.”
“It became my call,” she said, stepping closer, “the second your eyes went gray, and you stopped being a person and started being a body I had to keep upright in a crowd.” Her voice was tight, controlled, but the edges were starting to fray. “Do you have any idea what that looked like? You were muttering. Your eyes were bleeding light. A child noticed you, Neavin. A child.”
“Veyrith had eyes on the prison wall,” he said, his voice going flat and low. “Every rooftop approach. Every guard rotation. What I was doin' was worth it.”
“Worth it.” She said the words slowly, like she was turning them over to find what was wrong with them. “I had to walk a patrol away from you with a smile on my face and a story about my brother who gets spells sometimes, God bless him, he doesn't mean nothin' by it.” She shook her head. “Worth it. Sure.”
“You covered it.”
“I always cover it!” The control cracked. Just for a second. Something raw came through beneath, and she yanked it back hard, her jaw tightening. “That is the problem. I always cover it, and nobody ever once thinks to ask if I am all right after.”
The room went very still.
Even Ash didn't move.
Neavin looked at her. Something shifted in his face, something that was not quite regret but was at least adjacent to it. Then it hardened back over.
“Next time I'll let you know,” he said. “Before.”
“Next time,” Nyssa said, quiet now, which was somehow worse, “you tell me what you need and what to expect. Because if I don't know, I can't help you. And if I can't help you, we are both in a cell before sundown, wonderin' where it went wrong.”
“Alright, that's enough.” Garr stepped forward, broad shoulders filling the space between them, one hand angled toward each. “Y'all are burning rope we don't have.”
Ash looked at the ceiling. “Nobody's wrong in here. That's genuinely the worst part.”
That cracked something. Voices overlapped. Accusations bled into each other, each one feeding the next instead of burning out. Below, the forge hammers picked up their rhythm again, steady and low, pressing up through the floor like a heartbeat that had never once stopped for anyone. 
Harmon brought his fist down on the table. The sound was brutal. Final. Everything stopped.
“I don't care who was right,” he said. His voice wasn't loud. It didn't need to be. “Answer me one thing. Did you see a deal breaker?”
Neavin swallowed. “No.”
“Good.” Harmon didn't look at him anymore. “Then the mission stands. Sit down. If you brought something useful, put it on the table.” Neavin crossed the room and laid out his sketch. No defense. No commentary.
Garr sat first, slow and deliberate. Ash dropped into his chair. Nyssa took hers last, arms folded tight, jaw set, eyes still burning like something had been lit in them that wasn't going to go out on its own.
Neavin stayed standing. Breathing hard. Hands clenched at his sides like he didn't trust them not to shake.
Aurelia entered quietly. She moved the way she always moved in rooms like this, like she was passing through rather than joining. Weslin followed just behind her, hesitating in the doorway, pressing back against the frame. The air in the room had weight to it. He could feel it from the threshold.
Aurelia didn't go to the table. She moved to the far wall and turned slightly away, arms folded in against herself. Her fingers flexed once against her sleeve and then stilled, too deliberate to be calm. “Report,” Harmon said.
“Surface guards only.” Aurelia did not turn. “Routine thoughts. No external pressure. Nothing sharp enough to linger.”
“The Warden?”
“Didn't sense her.”
“And the boy?”
“He observed.”
Weslin took a step forward. “That was my instruction.”
Harmon's gaze cut to him. “That was the plan.”
Nyssa seized it. “So while the rest of us are bleeding through patrols and getting our cover stories straight, the two of you stood back and watched.”
Aurelia turned then. Slowly. The way a person turns when they have decided to stop pretending something is not happening.
“Why,” she said, her voice flat and precise as a ruled line, “are you talking to me?”
Not a question. Something colder than a question.
Nyssa blinked. “Excuse me?”
“I am not asking you to excuse anything.” Aurelia's eyes moved across the room, taking in each face with an expression that contained nothing at all. “I am observing that you are all still here, breathing, intact, and apparently furious about it. Which is remarkable, given what could have gone wrong today.” A pause. “You want credit for surviving your own morning. That is what this is.”
The silence was the kind that happens right before something breaks.
“You want to talk to me about credit.” Nyssa's voice had gone quiet. Precise. That was the danger sign. “You walked through a crowd reading minds and came home and you want to stand there and tell me what this is.”
“I walked through a crowd doing my job,” Aurelia said. “As did you. As did everyone in this room. And yet here we all are, performing our grievances for each other like it changes anything.”
“Performing,” Garr said the word carefully, like he was checking its weight.
“She ain't wrong,” Ash said, not looking up. He sounded tired in a way that went deeper than the morning. “We're all right about everything, and we're all making it worse. That is a real accomplishment for one day.”
“I don't need a eulogy, Ash,” Nyssa said.
“Wasn't offering one.” He finally looked up. “Just saying what everybody already knows.”
Neavin's voice came in low and flat from the corner. “Better quiet than reckless. Half-formed visions in a tight street get people pulled in for questioning.”
“And a man going blind in the open gets the rest of us flagged.” Nyssa did not look at him. “So, we're even.”
“Are we.”
“No.” She looked at him then, direct and level. “We're not. But we're out of time to settle it, so it'll keep.”
Aurelia had watched the exchange without moving. When the room went quiet again, she said, still in that flat even tone, “If the argument is finished, there is work to be done.”
Weslin, still in the doorway, had not made a sound. He was watching Aurelia the way you watch someone you thought you knew do something you don't recognize. Without meaning to, he had taken a half step back into the hall. Not retreating. Just making room for something he didn't have a name for yet. 
Harmon stood. The scrape of his chair was the only sound.
“I am paying for results,” he said, each word placed with the deliberate care of a man who does not intend to repeat himself. “This is not a result.”
He looked at each of them. Long enough to mean it.
“You don't have to like each other. You don't have to agree. You don't have to trust the reasons behind every call that gets made in this room.”
A pause.
“But you will respect that everyone here is good at what they do. Everyone of you. That includes the boy.”
Another step forward.
“If you cannot stand next to someone long enough to finish the job,” Harmon said, “Then just leave.”
Silence. No one moved. No one spoke.
The silence that followed wasn't peace. It was the kind of quiet that happens when people are holding something back hard enough that the effort shows. Glances stayed sharp. Nothing was forgiven. Old grievances sat exactly where they had been dropped.
But the job was still on the table.
And in this room, that was the only thing that mattered.
Aurelia stood near the door through all of it. Hood up, arms folded, watching them with eyes that had gone somewhere else a long time ago and not fully come back. Thousands of thoughts pressing behind her face, all trying to come forward at once. She shook her head once, a small private motion, and when Weslin caught it and stepped toward her, hope already moving across his face, she turned and walked out without a word.
“Aurelia?”
She didn't stop.
He followed her into the outer hall, his voice quieter now, unsure of itself. “We were supposed to train again. Second lesson. You said after.”
She stopped just before the stairs. Her back was to him.
“Go meditate,” she said.
“What?”
She turned then. Slowly. And the face she turned with was not the one he knew from the morning session. There was nothing warm in it. Nothing patient. Nothing of the woman who had sat across from him with a candle between them and told him that listening was a choice.
“Close your eyes,” she said. “Breathe. Maybe you'll become less of a burden while you're at it.”
No heat in it. That was the thing that made it land the way it did. She said it the way you say something obvious. The way you say the floor is stone or the sky is gray. It was simply true, and she was tired of being the only one who knew it.
Then she descended the stairs. Footsteps silent. Gone.
Weslin stood in the hall and did not move.
Harmon had watched from the doorway. He waited one full minute. Then he turned and went after her.
He caught her in the corridor. His hand closed around her upper arm, not gently. “What the hell was that?”
She didn't pull away. Didn't tense. Just stood there the way something stands when it has stopped caring whether it is held or released.
“I told him what he needed,” she said.
“You told a fourteen-year-old boy to be less of a burden.”
“Yes.”
Harmon stared at her. “Aurelia.”
“He is not fragile,” she said. “Treating him like he is does him no favors.”
“That's not what that was, and you know it.”
Something moved through her face. Fast. Gone before it finished arriving.
“I owe him nothing beyond what keeps him useful,” she said.
“I'm not paying you to carve pieces off him,” Harmon said. His voice had gone cold in a way that had nothing to do with anger and everything to do with someone drawing a line. “I'm paying you to train him. That is the job. If you have something going on inside your head right now that makes that impossible, you tell me, and we figure it out. But you do not take it out on the boy.”
“I'm fine.”
“You're not.”
Her jaw tightened.
“I'm not paying you to fall apart either,” Harmon said. “Get it together. Do your job. If you can't, walk away now and save us both the time.” He stepped closer, voice dropping. “You think Forgehollow is rough? Wait until you see what the wastes do to people who run out of people willing to stand next to them.”
A long silence.
Then Aurelia nodded. Once. The motion precise and small and empty of everything except compliance.
“Understood,” she said.
Her breath hitched. Just once. Something sharp caught beneath her ribs and then was gone, pressed back behind a stillness so practiced it had become indistinguishable from calm.
Harmon let go of her arm.
“Good,” he said.
She disappeared into the shadows. He stood a moment in the corridor, the forge's heartbeat pressing up through the floor beneath him, slow and indifferent, and thought about what a woman who had lived that long and worn that many faces looked like when one of them finally started to slip. Then he turned and went back toward the tavern floor.
The main room had settled into the particular quiet that comes after the lunch crowd thins and before the evening crowd finds its courage. A few men at corner tables. A barmaid moving between them without hurry. The fire in the hearth had burned down to coals, and nobody had bothered to feed it.
Dain was at the bar. A glass in front of him that he hadn't touched, one elbow on the wood, watching the room the way men like him always watch rooms, cataloguing without appearing to. He glanced at Harmon when he approached, but said nothing. Just waited.
They stood together in the kind of silence that happens between people who have been in enough difficult rooms that they no longer need to fill the space before the information arrives.
Aldrek came through the door two minutes later. He didn't slow at the threshold. He crossed directly to them, reached into his coat without preamble, and set the folded parchment on the bar in front of Harmon the way a man sets down something he would rather not be carrying any longer.
The black wax seal had already been broken. The twin-tailed fox was still faintly visible where it had split.
Dain looked at it. Then at Aldrek. Said nothing.
Harmon unfolded the note. The words were short. Casual. Precise in the way only cruelty ever manages to be.
Would you be a good chap and let Nyssa know I never forget a debt. —M.
The parchment bent slightly under his fingers. A controlled motion. The kind of man makes when he is deciding how much of what he is feeling he can afford to show.
“He didn't guess,” Harmon said quietly. “He has eyes on us. On her. Probably on all of us.”
Dain's jaw tightened. He looked at the note without touching it, the way you look at something that has already decided what it is going to cost you. “How long do you think he's had them?”
“Long enough to connect her name to yours,” Harmon said. “That's all that matters right now.”
Aldrek had not moved from where he stood. His hands were flat on the bar, his eyes on the middle distance. “Merrick is not a man who sends a message like this and waits to see if it lands,” he said. “He already knows it will. This is not a warning. It is a demonstration.”
“He's telling us he can reach us,” Dain said.
“He's telling us he already has,” Aldrek said. The fire in the hearth popped once. Nobody looked at it.
Harmon folded the note. Set it down flat. “We still have to get Riven tonight. That doesn't change.”
Dain was quiet for a moment. When he spoke, his voice was careful, the voice of a man raising something he already suspects will not land well. “We don't even know if he'll agree to come with us. Why risk everything for a man who might refuse?”
Harmon didn't answer right away. Not because he couldn't. Because the true answer sat in a place that was more personal than strategic, and saying it out loud in a tavern with a foreman's note on the bar between them would make it sound like sentiment rather than calculation, and he could not afford for it to sound like either. “His choice isn't the mission,” he said finally. “Removing him from Merrick is.”
Dain looked at him. Read the rest of it in his face. The part Harmon wasn't saying. He exhaled through his nose. “Then we get him,” he said. “I'll take your word on it.”
Aldrek bowed his head slightly. His eyes closed. He drew one slow breath, the kind a man draws when he is reaching for something from a depth he does not visit lightly. When he opened his eyes again, what had been doubt had settled into something quieter and harder and more durable.
“Right,” he said. “Up we go.”
Harmon handed the note back to Aldrek. The three of them moved toward the stairs without discussion. The decision made the way decisions get made between people who have each independently arrived at the same place and are simply acknowledging it.
The stairwell was narrow and damp, old condensation slicking the stone walls, a single sconce stuttering at the first landing. Harmon adjusted his collar. Dain cracked his knuckles without realizing he'd done it. Aldrek climbed with his hands loose at his sides and his eyes forward, the practiced ease of a man who has walked toward worse than a room full of arguing professionals.
Before they reached the top, the argument came down to meet them.
Raised voices. The sharp, particular edge of people who have been holding things in and run out of reasons to keep doing it. Ash's voice unmistakable. Garr answered with the rigid restraint of a man who has decided that if he raises his voice, something worse would follow.
Dain tilted his head slightly. “Sounds like we're late.”
“Then we end it,” Aldrek said and pushed the door open.
The room fell silent the way rooms do when the people in them realize someone has been watching.
Ash stood near the table, blueprint half-unrolled and forgotten at his elbow, soot still smudged across the back of his hand. Garr was by the hearth, arms crossed, the tension in his shoulders the kind that doesn't leave just because the shouting stopped. Weslin had pressed himself against the far wall, eyes narrow, taking everything in and giving nothing back. Nyssa stood rigid, arms folded tight across her chest, jaw set hard. Neavin sat at the corner of the table, fingers tapping an uneven rhythm against the wood, not looking at anyone.
Every head turned. Dain stepped in first. Measured. The slight lift at the corner of his mouth that was not quite a smile and not quite anything else. “Did we interrupt something important?” he said. “Or is this the rehearsal before someone says something unforgivable?”
No one laughed. Aldrek followed, drawing off his gloves. “We need to speak.”
Ash snorted. “Perfect. That's exactly what this needs. A sermon.”
Harmon stepped forward. He didn't raise his voice. He looked around the room once, long enough that each person in it understood they had been seen and accounted for, and then he unfolded the parchment and turned it so the broken seal caught the firelight.
“You're right,” Aldrek said. “We're not steady. Trust is thin. Tempers are close to the edge.” A pause. “But this changes the situation.” Aldrek held the note up so the broken seal caught the light.  
Nyssa's eyes found the fox sigil and stayed there. The color left her face before she could stop it. The smirk she wore like a second skin, the one that had been there through every argument and every sharp word and every moment this morning she'd had to swallow something she didn't want, slipped. Just for a second. Just enough to show what was underneath it. Her hands had gone flat against the table's edge. Not gripping. Just resting there, like she needed to know something solid was under them. Nobody mentioned it.
“It means someone is close enough to connect names,” Aldrek said, his voice even and deliberate. “And willing to use them.”
Dain moved a half step forward, eyes still on the seal. “I don't know Merrick well,” he said. “But I know men like him. Men who send messages like this don't bluff.” His jaw tightened slightly. “He's telling us to walk away from Riven. And if we don't, he intends to act.”
The room took that in. Nobody moved. Nobody spoke.
Harmon let the silence settle just long enough to mean something. Then he cut through it. “If anyone wants out,” he said, “that moment has passed.” Nothing.
“Good,” he said. “Then we stop burning time.”
He looked around the room one more time. The same faces. The same bruises underneath them. “Whatever eyes are on the street right now will only sharpen if we hesitate. That means we move tonight.” The tension didn't disappear. It aligned. The difference was small, and it mattered more than anything else in the room.
Neavin leaned forward first. His fingers stopped their rhythm against the wood. “Outer patrols thin just after the second bell,” he said. “Not on paper. The guards rotate inward for meal breaks. It's by habit, not orders. Which means it'll hold.”
Nyssa's eyes moved to him. Not warm. Not hostile. The look of someone listening to information they need from a source they are not finished being angry at. “West alley watch goes lax when the food carts come through,” she said. “I saw it twice. Everyone's eyes follow the bread.”
They did not look at each other when she finished confirming his count. They didn't need to. The information fit together, and they both knew it, and neither one of them was going to say so out loud. A few of the others almost smiled. Almost.
Aldrek spoke next. “I walked the perimeter at dusk. There's a stretch on the north face where the guards are running on instinct more than attention. They've done the same route long enough that they've stopped seeing it. That's where they'll be softest.”
Weslin had been quiet through all of it, back against the wall, watching. He swallowed once. Then he straightened slightly, the way someone does when they have decided to say a thing and are committing to it before the nerve runs out.
“The bakery deliveries don't just pull the guards,” he said. “They pull everyone. Vendors, porters, message runners. The whole street thickens.” He glanced up, more confident now. “If we move inside that, we're not two people walking toward a prison. We're just part of the crowd.”
No one told him he was wrong.
Harmon leaned over the blueprint. The access corridor ran behind the loading bay on the west side, wide enough that two men carrying something heavy between them wouldn't draw a second look from anyone who wasn't specifically looking for it. Twelve minutes between the rotation and the next watch. Thirteen if the bread cart ran late, which, in Harmon's experience, it usually did.
The door from the stairwell creaked. Aurelia stepped back into the room. She didn't announce herself. Didn't look at anyone directly. Just moved to stand near the door the way she had stood near it before, and the room absorbed her the way it absorbs a drop of cold water, a small shift in temperature that everyone notices and nobody names.
The silence stretched one beat longer than it should have. “Crowds make minds noisy,” she said quietly. “That works in our favor.”
Weslin was looking at her. She didn't look back. Whatever had happened in the hall was still sitting between them, not resolved, not addressed, just present the way certain things are present in rooms when the people who share them have run out of time to deal with them properly.
Garr straightened from the hearth. “If it breaks,” he said, simple and flat, “I'll hold the corridor.”
Harmon watched the last piece settle. No posturing. No performance. Just people who were very good at staying alive in bad situations doing the work of staying alive in one more bad situation, and carrying everything that had happened this morning inside them like stones in a coat pocket, heavy and unspoken and not going anywhere.
“Alright,” Harmon said. “That's enough to work with.” He stepped to the table and rolled the blueprint fully open. The paper was worn at the folds, the corridors marked in two different hands from two different sources, and the west loading bay was circled twice.
“We go in fast,” he said. “Clean if we can manage it. Loud if we can't. Either way, we don't linger. We get Riven out, and we're gone before anyone thinks to ask the right questions.” He looked around the room. At each of them. “We came here for him. We're not leaving without him.”
No one answered with words. They leaned in over the blueprint, shoulders almost touching, the amber crystals buzzing overhead, and below them, the forge hammers kept their rhythm, steady and indifferent, the way the work always is, not caring who picks it up, only that it gets done.






Chapter Twenty
A thin veil of morning mist clung to the road as Luca’s team rode east-northeast, toward the mountains that loomed like sleeping giants beyond the tree line. The sun, still low in the sky, scattered pale gold through skeletal branches and left long shadows across the frost-hardened dirt path. Birds were silent. Only the sound of hooves crunching the frosted earth and the soft creak of saddle leather accompanied them.
Behind them lay the cave where they'd sheltered the night before with the rescued refugees. Luca had insisted they rest, even at the cost of time, and given up most of their remaining rations to the battered travelers. Taerel had seen to their wounds. Lysana, despite her quiet nature, helped as well. When dawn came, they pointed the refugees south, toward the port city, giving them directions, warnings, and hope, and then watched them vanish into the trees.
Now, riding with half-empty stomachs and tight supplies, the weight of duty pressed heavier than their gear.
Taerel rode in the rear, beside Aymer, their horses trailing just behind Lysana and Luca. The brothers spoke in silence, hands moving in fluid, precise gestures just above their saddles.
Taerel's fingers moved again, pausing just long enough for Aymer to catch him signing a message. ‘We could’ve moved quickly last night if we had a way to speak.’
Aymer nodded subtly, signing back, ‘We weren’t ready, too many unknowns. I know what you are getting at, we held that back, deliberately, remember?” Aymer added. “The cost we chose not to pay.’
Another flick of Taerel’s hand. ‘I could make something. Something simple. A pair of bands, maybe. Enchanted to carry sound or sight.’
Aymer’s jaw tensed. He glanced toward Lysana, who was riding a few lengths quietly behind them. ‘You want to show them?’ he signed.
‘We need to talk about telling them,’ Taerel sighed, eyes flicking ahead to make sure Lysana wasn’t watching. ‘About what I am.’
Aymer kept his expression neutral, only the smallest twitch of his brow betraying his thoughts. ‘Not yet. We don’t know them well enough to drop something that heavy.’
Taerel grimaced. He wanted to share. He wanted to help. It felt wrong hiding who he was, hiding the truth about the magic bound into his blood, a lineage that could script enchantments with just the right tools and time. His mask, a masterwork of his own design, projected the image of warm brown eyes and black hair, concealing his true self. It hides his ivory white hair, eyes like bleached stone. He could barely remember what he actually looked like.
“I could make something for us,” he signed. “A way to communicate. Better than hand signs or yelling. A talisman, maybe. Or etched stones.”
“Maybe later,” Aymer countered. “If this ride goes well, if we see something in them worth trusting. But don’t rush it. This team... it could work, it may not. Don’t ruin it by springing your soul on them too early.”
“But you trust them, don’t you?” Taerel asked.
“I want to. That’s the…” He paused, speaking not softer, but heavier, “difference.”
A shadow flicked beside them. Lysana had drifted back. “You two playing some kind of game back here?” Her reins tightened once in her fist as she asked, arching a brow. Her long braid of golden-blonde hair swayed as her horse pulled alongside. She wore a faint smile, but there was sharpness in her gaze. She’d been watching.
Taerel straightened, flashing an easy grin. Aymer, the older and more composed, answered first. “Just passing the time. Counting pines. Ty’s ahead by five.”
“Six,” Taerel added, lifting a brow.
Lysana looked between them, unconvinced. “Counting trees, huh? Sounded more like code.”
“Game's got rules,” Aymer said, deadpan. “Can't share.”
Lysana snorted. “Fine. Just don’t be plotting to ditch us. I’d have to hunt you down.”
Taerel held up his hands. “Perish the thought entirely.”
As she rode ahead again, Taerel leaned toward Aymer, “She suspects,” he murmured, too quickly, like he wished it weren’t true.
From up ahead, Luca caught the sound of her laugh, low, quick, real. It shouldn’t have mattered, but something in it cut through the cold that had lived behind his ribs since the orc camp. For the first time, he wondered if distance was just another kind of cowardice. “Of course she does,” Aymer said. “She's smarter than both of us.” 
Up ahead, Luca rode alone, silent and upright in the saddle. His cloak billowed in the breeze, eyes fixed ahead but distant. Ever since the fight at the orc camp, he'd said little. He moved like someone shouldering too much weight but refusing to shift it to others. Aymer watched him with a thoughtful frown.
“You think he knows we know?” Taerel asked quietly.
Aymer hesitated. “About him being a Shadow Walker? Yeah. No one takes out four orcs that fast unless they’re trained for something darker than war.”
“Should we ask?” Aymer was about to answer when Luca abruptly raised his closed fist, then gave a short circular gesture, his signal for the others to close in. 
One by one, the horses picked up pace, crunching through the snow until the group gathered around him.  
Aymer was the first to speak. “What do you need?”
Luca glanced at them all, eyes steady. “We got a late start today, helping the refugees and resting up from last night. It was the right call, but we’re behind. We need to make up ground.”
A brief pause. “For the next few hours, we’re pushing.”
He shifted in the saddle, the wind tugging strands of hair loose from beneath his hood. “I want to stop before sunset. Still need time to hunt and resupply. “If we’re lucky,” Luca added. “If not, we make do. We gave up more than we could afford. I wanted some light to improve our chances. I don’t want us out alone in the dark.”
There were nods around the circle, Aymer gave a small thumbs-up, Lysana tapped her reins, and Taerel gave a lazy salute.
But then Taerel leaned forward, his horse stepping slightly ahead. He cocked his head toward Luca, his grin both playful and curious. “One question,” Taerel said lightly, too lightly. “Forgive the bluntness, but are you a Shadow Walker?”  Lysana looked dumbfounded by the question, and Aymer just slapped his head.
Luca’s head snapped toward him. For a long time, he said nothing. His stare, sharp as a drawn blade, held Taerel in place.
Luca turned back without answering, his face fixed. “Let’s move.” He spurred his horse, and the others followed, hooves tearing through frost-covered earth.
Above them, hawks circled. The crunch of ice under hooves mixed with the creak of leather and the breath of beasts working hard. Despite the cold, sweat gathered under furs and armor. Fingers tingled, muscles ached, but no one complained. There was purpose in their movement, urgency beneath the cold.
As they crested a small ridge, Taerel leaned toward Aymer and muttered, “You think he heard?”
Aymer chuckled. “I think he heard you,” Aymer said dryly, “and he’s likely deciding how to make you disappear into those woods.”
“I should think I'd haunt rather well,” Taerel replied, then sat straighter.”  “Hey, Lysana, if I vanish, make sure someone tells a dramatic tale. Preferably involving fire.”
Lysana rode up alongside, smirking. “Oh, I’ll tell them you screamed like a goat before you went.”  She looked ahead to where Luca rode, the distance between them measured not in strides but in the silence he carried. Whatever he was, she realized, she wanted to understand it.
The laughter broke the tension as they pressed on, snow falling lightly now from the cloud-thick sky.
Ahead, the trail bent through a shadowed forest, and beyond that, the rising spine of the mountains loomed.
The gallop carried them far. Hooves thundered over snow-slick foothills, the horses’ breath steaming in the sharp mountain air, time bleeding away with every mile. Frosted trees blurred past in streaks of white and brown as the narrow trail turned east-northeast, the sun dragging long shadows across the terrain. Wind stung their cheeks, threading under collars and stifling cloaks. Packs bounced at their sides, and the cold clung to their fingers despite riding gloves.
Snow hissed under hooves where it had drifted, the rhythm of their ride a pulsing, driven tempo, each beat an answer to Luca’s push for time.
But after a stretch of hard riding, Luca lifted his hand and eased back on the reins. His stallion let out a soft, damp snort as it slowed to a walk. The others mirrored the motion, reining in until the column bunched close again, horses stamping lightly, breath heavy in the air.
Luca angled his mount off the road and nodded toward a shallow depression nestled just beyond the tree line.
“Right there,” he said, his voice lower now, laced with calm command. “Little dip just off the trail. Trees thicken just enough for cover, and it looks dry underfoot. Let’s make camp. Still enough light left, so we’ll hunt, eat, and sleep properly for once.”
Taerel twisted in his saddle to glance back at the sky. “Didn’t realize we were stopping this early,” he said, already loosening his reins.
Luca gave a small shake of his head. “Rather stop now and eat warm than keep pushing into cold silence. We’ve got ground to make tomorrow. Better to rest right. As well as rest the horses.” No one argued.
They pulled off the road together, winding between bark-dark pines and snow-laced branches. Frost crackled beneath hooves, and the occasional branch creaked overhead. The clearing, though modest, offered shelter, a few downed logs, and a windbreak from the trees.
As soon as they dismounted, the silence shifted from trail noise to purposeful motion. Taerel immediately led his gelding to a low-hanging branch, tying the reins with practiced ease as the camp took shape around them.
Nearby, Lysana loosened her saddle’s straps and whispered gently to her mare, brushing down the coat with swift, efficient strokes. Her fingers were red from the cold, but she moved with the grace of someone used to rough country nights. She clicked her tongue, adjusting the feed bag around the horse’s muzzle. “There you go, eat up. You did well today.”
Aymer dragged a gloved hand down the neck of his mount, then checked the sight on the long rifle slung at his back. He thumbed open the chamber, sliding in a smaller cartridge with quiet precision.
“I’ll see if I can bring back something with legs,” he said, shouldering the rifle.
“You mean like a deer?” Taerel called over, grinning as he wiped down his saddle.
“No, like a cursed elk with antlers made of knives,” Aymer fired back, deadpan. “Yes, a deer.”
Lysana chuckled as she pulled her bow free from the pack strapped to her mare. “I’ll go forage. I’ve been in this forest before, might even find us something weird and glowing.” She winked and added, with a theatrical bow, “Time to put my super-awesome ranger skills to the test.”
Taerel raised his arms. “Finally! I’ve been waiting to see what a real ranger looks like.”
Luca stepped forward before the banter could spiral. The last threads of sunlight caught in his hood as he looked at each of them in turn, his voice even but edged with finality.
“Don’t be long,” he said. “There’s something we need to talk about tonight. Something that can’t wait any longer.”
The words settled heavily.
Aymer paused mid-check of his rifle. Lysana’s smile faded just a breath. Even Taerel, still crouched by the fire pit, glanced up with narrowed eyes.
“Got it,” Aymer said.
“Be back soon,” Lysana added, tightening the bowstring.
They stepped off into the trees, the snow crunching softly underfoot, the evening chill chasing behind them. A raven called somewhere deeper in the woods. The scent of pine and smoke slowly rose as Taerel sparked flint to kindling.
The camp slowly took shape, humble, temporary, but alive.
And in the stillness that followed, the unsaid began to build, like frost gathering along the edge of a blade.
They were gone for only a few hours. Long enough to feel the cost of it. Lysana was the first to return, hood drawn back and cheeks pink from the cold. Her boots were damp from snowmelt, and in one hand she carried a bundled satchel of greens and roots, the other holding a limp rabbit by the hind legs. Her bow was slung behind her shoulder, the string freshly waxed.
“I bring gifts,” she said with a grin, shaking the satchel toward Taerel, who had just coaxed the fire to life.
She knelt beside him and unwrapped her haul. “Wild onions, burdock root, a handful of dried nettle leaves I found under a fallen log, and one unfortunate rabbit who wasn’t fast enough.”
Taerel leaned over the roots and gave a low whistle. “That’ll do just fine.”
Not long after, Aymer emerged from between the trees, his coat dusted with frost and a small blood trail marking his return. Over his shoulders, he hauled a young musk deer, its legs bound tight with cord. It wasn’t huge, but it was enough.
“Wasn’t far,” he muttered, easing the carcass down onto a flat stone near the fire. “Took a clean shot just below the ridge. Lungs. Didn’t run far.”
As the sun began to dip below the treetops, the group got to work.
Lysana and Taerel handled the rabbit, swiftly skinning it with practiced cuts. The hide peeled back in one fluid motion, and Lysana set it aside on a flat rock to cure later. Taerel broke the rabbit down into sections, legs, backstrap, and organ meat, then began simmering a pot of water drawn from a melted snow boil.
Luca and Aymer handled the deer. Aymer worked with quiet efficiency, skinning the animal with long, steady slices of his belt knife. Steam lifted from the exposed muscle as the cold air met fresh warmth. Luca cut the usable meat free, haunches, ribs, tenderloin, and passed each piece back to Taerel to rinse and add to the stew pot. Blood mixed with snow in red streaks across the ground.
Bones were cracked to expose marrow, dropped into the simmering pot for added richness. Lysana ground the burdock root into coarse shavings and added it alongside the chopped onions and nettle. The scent that rose was earthy and deep, tinged with woodsmoke and wild herbs.
By the time stars started to blink into the sky, a thick stew bubbled over the fire. Each of them sat close, steam rising into their faces as they sipped from carved wooden bowls. No one spoke much, just the quiet rhythm of spoons and firewood crackling, a shared warmth that pressed back against the mountain’s chill.
When they’d eaten their fill, they turned to preserving the rest. Taerel pulled out a packet of coarse rock salt wrapped in waxed cloth, handing portions around. Aymer sectioned the remaining venison into thin strips, laying them on a flat stone to be rubbed thoroughly with salt and a pinch of crushed juniper from Lysana’s pouch, antiseptic and flavorful. These strips were then wrapped in thin sheets of oiled cloth, bound in twine, and tucked into their waxed leather satchels, meant to be hung away from camp overnight.
Lysana took the liver and heart, slicing and lightly salting them to cook in the morning. The rabbit hide was stretched and pinned between two forked branches to dry, its fur still intact.
The camp settled into a rhythm. Bellies full, packs heavier with preserved meat, and the fire burning low, just enough to keep the wolves guessing.
They moved with quiet efficiency, scraping out the pot, rinsing their bowls with boiled water, wiping them dry, tossing bones into the dark beyond camp. Taerel took the time to bury the offal near the base of a frost-slicked pine, patting the disturbed snow flat again with the heel of his boot.
Luca watched them move, efficient, wordless, together. A month ago, he would’ve eaten alone, half-awake with his back to a wall. Now, their quiet chatter felt like armor of a different kind.
As the last of the tasks wound down, Taerel gave a crooked grin and reached into his pack. “Figured tonight deserved a little something extra,” he said, pulling out a tightly-wrapped bundle of oiled cloth. Inside were thick slices of sweet bread, dense and golden, speckled with crushed nuts and dried berries. He hadn’t meant to keep it this long.
He passed them around, and for a few quiet moments, they sat in a loose ring around the fire, savoring the unexpected treat, warmth on their tongues, sugar on their breath, and silence settling like a blanket.
That’s when Luca leaned forward, his gaze flicking from one face to the next, and said, “All right. It’s time we talked.” He paused, taking in all of them before he went on, “I owe you all an explanation,” he began, eyes fixed on the fire.  “About who I am and why I do what I do.” 
The group fell silent, the crackling fire the only sound.  They listened, the weight of unspoken truths hanging heavy in the air. 
Finally, his voice broke through the hush. Low. Rough. The kind of voice that had carried secrets too long.
“Before I tell you this story…there are a few things you need to understand.”
He lifted his gaze then, and for the first time, they caught the eyes, crystal blue, not just bright, but unnatural. Cold fire behind ice. No one else in the world had eyes like that. Not anymore. They were the mark of something old. Something broke open. The kind of eyes that saw through lies and straight into the heart of a man.
“First,” he said, “no one knows the real story. Not the ballads. Not the Brotherhood. Not even the bastards who were there. You’re gonna hear it now. Once. Second…” His mouth pulled into something between a smirk and a wince. “I’m not a Shadow Walker. I’m the Shadow Walker. The first. The one the stories got wrong.” 
He leaned forward, elbows on knees, fingers curling into each other like he might wring the truth out of his bones. “I’m not proud of the things I’ve done. I’ve carried a lot of blood in silence. The only reason I’m telling you now is… I guess I’m tired. And maybe, just maybe, I trust you fools more than I should.”
He exhaled long through his nose. The flames danced in his eyes, turning them into something sharp and ancient.
“So if I go quiet, or I make a call you don't understand, let it stand. I'm not asking for pity. I'm asking for trust.” 
Then he sat back, spine straightening like a man about to carry a weight he’d dropped too long ago.
“This story ain’t small. And it doesn’t have a happy ending. But it’s mine.” He let the last word hang for a moment, just long enough to taste the fire again. “Here it goes.”
He looked into the fire for a long moment. When he spoke again, his voice had dropped to something quieter and more careful, the voice of a man picking up something he had put down a long time ago. “My name is Luca now. It was not always so. I was born Luk’on, a child of war, not the Second Magic War you’ve heard whispered about, but the First, when the skies cracked, and the Pearl shattered, spilling power and madness into the world.
“My mother and father were both killed in that war. I do not remember their faces, only the smell of smoke and the weight of silence that fell after their deaths. My sister, Eryel, and I were taken in by our uncle, his name was Velion, and his wife, Saela. Our grandmother lived with us as well, a quiet seer with cloudy eyes who often spoke to things we could not see. We lived in a hidden village called Tafeld, long forgotten now. It existed before the sealing of the ethereal plane, before the walls between realms were nailed shut with divine fury.
“Back then, I was taught there were four planes: the Material, the Heavenly, the Infernal, and the Ethereal. Between them lingered the Fae, not a realm, but a veil, a wild space where the forgotten and formless drifted. After the First Magic War, the gods feared what might still crawl between those worlds, so they sealed the Ethereal Plane, using it as a prison for the beast from the Material Plane. Due to this, it left the Infernal unbarred... and from that darkness came Uzhiel, a demon-lord who wrapped himself in silence and shadow.  He was not the only one; a few escaped with him.
“When the Ethereal was sealed, the Creator intended to seal the Heavenly as well, to keep even angels from tampering with mortal fate. But one exception was made: a Watcher, one who would serve as both judge and ferryman. His name was Ariel.
“Ariel was unlike the other angels. He walked among men, not with pride, but wonder. He was drawn not to their temples, but to their flaws, to their pain, and most of all… to beauty.
And he found that beauty in my sister, Eryel.
“She was the only light I ever truly knew. After a head injury in childhood, I was not… whole. I drifted, lived in fragments. She was my anchor. She called me “Luk’on” and I called her ‘Sissy’, always, until the day it changed.
“Ariel came often to our village in disguise, but not to deceive, to dwell. He watched Eryel in the fields, in the rain, in prayer. He came to love her.
“And she loved him.
“To impress her, he did something no angel should: he reached into me and healed my broken mind. I remember the moment, like waking from a dream I’d lived my whole life. My first words to her as my full self weren’t ‘Sissy’… but ‘Eryel.’ Her name. My first true word.
It was then that Ariel revealed himself. No wings, just presence. We saw the truth of him, and I loved him like a brother.
“But love between angel and mortal was forbidden.
“And the demons were watching.
“Uzhiel, hungry for passage between realms, saw a crack in the Creator’s plans. If an angel could fall for a mortal… then perhaps heaven could be breached, just as the infernal already had.
“They set a trap.  
“They came in human skin, demons possessing villagers, and manipulated others, hiding in flesh and soul. To lure Ariel in,  the group, made of mortals and demons alike,  killed Eryel in front of him.” 
Luca stopped. The word sat there in the firelight, plain and final, the way true things are plain and final when they have finally been said out loud after years of living only in the dark. He did not look at any of them. He was looking somewhere else entirely. He was enraged and took his sorrow out on them.  Ariel suspected one, a man he believed corrupted. In battle, he struck him down… but the man was not fully possessed, or so the Creator claimed; Ariel had broken the balance. He was cast down.  
“His wings torn from him, he became something in between, no longer angel, not quite mortal. He retained fragments of his grace: he could still see the divine judgments etched into the air around souls, and could send champions to fulfill them. But his form darkened. His hair paled like ash, yet his eyes turned to crystal blue, because he saw good as well as evil. He called himself the Shadow Watcher.
“He buried Eryel with his own hands after the attack. The demons had murdered her and burned Tafeld to cinders. I returned too late; the smoke was still rising.
“I found my uncle Velion’s body beside the well. I found Saela… what was left of her. And I found Ariel, kneeling at Eryel’s side, weeping smoke, his fingers still glowing with failing grace.
“He looked at me and said, ‘You are not ready for this path. Do not walk it. There is no mercy in shadows.”
“I looked into the eyes of my sister, gone. My anchor. My light.
“I said, ‘Then teach me to walk without mercy.’” He stopped again. Longer this time. The kind of pause that is not about finding words but about deciding whether the next ones are still survivable. The fire burned. Nobody filled the silence. 
“He drew a short sword from his side and cast it into the dirt. ‘Then let the shadows claim you,’ Ariel proclaimed.”
“I stepped forward. As my hand closed around the hilt, a cloak of darkness wrapped around me. An onyx medallion appeared at my throat, etched with runes I did not know but could feel pulsing inside me. My eyes changed like Ariel’s. In that moment, Luk’on died. I became Luca, the Shadow Walker.
“We hunted. Ariel could no longer interfere directly. But he could still see the contracts, glimpses of fate’s judgment upon the wicked. He became a silent god of vengeance, receiving tribute from those who begged for his justice or revenge. He never accepted gold. Only intent. He judged their words, and I carried out the sentence.
“It was just Ariel and me for decades, quiet work,” Luca said. “Never long enough to leave a mark. We found that names don’t last when no one stays to speak them. Over all that time, somehow, their number never lessened. They were always more, so the number of contracts grew.
“We created an order. A small circle of assassins chosen by Ariel and trained by me, each one capable of bearing a shard of the onyx and resisting its hunger. We called ourselves:
‘Usiku Wavuli,’ The Night Veil.
“Drawn from an old tongue, the name meant more than just shadow. It meant concealment with purpose, darkness wielded for light.
“We were assassins of evil. We struck down demon lords, cult leaders, and corrupted kings. We carved justice into stone.
“We fought in the Second Magic War, tracking and eliminating Lucent’s lieutenants, beasts made from their magic and madness. I fought beside Jasper, a ring bearing you might know. Though he does not always admit it.
“But Ariel… he was changing.
“Angels are not meant to stay in the material plane. Even as a fallen one, he was bound by a higher law. Over time, his body began to turn to stone, his soul fossilizing beneath the weight of divine punishment. Before he became fully inert, he crafted a Stone, the Judgment Stone. It holds a sliver of his will, enough for a bearer to send me on contracts when Ariel no longer can.
“But the Stone is dangerous. It cannot be held longer than thirty judgments at most before the bearer begins to fracture, drawn into Ariel’s crumbling consciousness.
“Adin has the Stone now. He does not know the cost. Or maybe he does.”
The silence that followed was tight, not calm.
“I serve because I must. Choice left me a long time ago. I’m still going because justice does not rest, and vengeance is still owed.
“So when you ask who I am… I am the weapon born of a fallen angel’s love. I am the promise made beside a sister’s grave. I am Luca, last of the Night Veil, bound to the Stone, haunted by the name “Sissy” I will never say again.
“And I have not yet judged my last soul.”
When Luca finished speaking, the silence returned, this time heavy, not hollow. The fire crackled softly, trying to fill the space he’d left behind, but even the flames seemed to burn lower, as if they, too, understood the depth of what had been shared. No one rushed to speak. No one dared.
Aymer stared into the coals, his jaw clenched just slightly. He didn’t look at Luca, not out of disrespect, but because some pain deserves its own space. Taerel shifted where he sat, arms wrapped around his knees, face drawn tight in thought. There was no joke, no sarcastic jab from him this time. Just a quiet nod, respect, earned and unspoken. Lysana did not speak. She reached forward, almost without meaning to, and her hand brushed the edge of his glove. Stopped there. The contact was nothing, barely a touch, but she felt the warmth of it even through the leather, and something in her chest tightened with a recognition she couldn't name. She had survived her own fire. She knew what it looked like in someone else. The firelight caught the sheen in her eyes, which she refused to let fall. She drew her hand back slowly. The cold moved in between them, quiet and immediate. He looked away first, and she let him. 
Snow drifted down from the branches overhead, soft flakes catching in their hair and on their shoulders. The forest around them had gone still, like the trees themselves were listening. Luca let out a slow breath, then pushed himself to his feet. He glanced at the others, then at the darkness beyond the circle of firelight.
“I’ll take first watch,” he said it the way he said most things, like the decision had already been made some time ago and he was only now letting it be heard. None of them argued.
One by one, they rose and moved to their bedrolls, the soft crunch of snow underfoot the only reply. No goodnights. Just the rustle of cloaks, the settling of bodies, the quiet creak of leather and armor. Sleep would come eventually, fitful, maybe, but enough to carry them forward.
Luca stood with his back to the fire, eyes scanning the trees, shadow and snow melting together. He caught the faintest sound behind him, a soft exhale, maybe her turning in her bedroll. The sound shouldn’t have meant anything, but it eased the silence more than the fire ever could. For the first time in years, he didn’t feel entirely alone in the dark. The story was out now, no longer gnawing at his ribs. And though the cold still bit, it didn’t feel quite as sharp.
Not tonight, but it would.






Chapter Twenty-One
The last golden streaks of sunlight filtered through the warped, grime-slicked glass of Harmon’s room in the Ironflask Tavern, casting fractured ribbons of amber across the scuffed floorboards. Outside, Forgehollow stirred with the restless energy of early evening, the rhythmic clanging of a distant forge, laughter rough and raw from miners freed of their toil, and the drifting song of a hawker peddling roasted almonds. Smoke, soot, and song braided into the dusk air, and from some unseen alleyway came the half-hearted strumming of a lute, the tune slurred by ale and apathy.
Inside the cramped upper chamber, the air felt close, burdened with tension that clung to skin and breath alike. Maps, sketches, and ink-smeared diagrams littered the table, pinned and layered with empty mugs and the low, twitching light of a lantern that guttered with every draft. Seven figures crowded the space, shoulders brushing, voices hushed. The room was too small to hold the decision it demanded.
Harmon stood at the head of the table. His palms braced against the scarred oak. Beneath the edge of his hood, lines carved by years of command and compromise cut deep across his face. His beard, streaked with ash-gray, caught the failing light like old silver. There was weariness in him, but something harder beneath it. Resolve.
“That’s the plan,” he said, voice low and carved from stone. “You all know your assignments. If there are questions, speak now.”
A ripple moved through the room: shifting boots, a creak of leather, a glance exchanged here, a frown there. 
Then Aurelia stepped forward. She stood straight, arms crossed over the gleaming surface of her light tactical armor, jaw set. Her voice, usually velvet and controlled, was edged now with steel. “I’m having second thoughts.”
Harmon raised an eyebrow. “What are you not sure about?”
Aurelia hesitated, then gestured subtly toward Weslin. “Him. I know I can do my part, but Weslin’s still learning. Still finding the edges of what he can do. Are you certain he’s ready for this?”
The room turned, all eyes falling on the boy near the window. Weslin stood in silhouette, framed by the fire-hued sky beyond. His back was straight, his hands laced behind him, but the stiffness in his shoulders betrayed the weight of her words.
Harmon's voice remained calm. “Do you believe he’s not?”
Aurelia exhaled, slow and shallow. “I just don’t want to be the one who puts him in harm’s way.” The words stayed between them longer than she meant them to.
Harmon’s voice hardened, not unkind but immovable. “And if you go in instead, we lose the link. Your gifts don’t work past those runes. The mental tether is essential, and you’re the only one who can keep it stable. You knew that when we began.”
He turned his gaze to Weslin, steady. “The boy says he can do it. Then he can.” A brief pause. “Trust what you taught him. Trust his courage.”
Aurelia's lips pressed tight, but she nodded, stepping back.
Nyssa, lounging with one boot on the bench, stood and approached Weslin. She offered him a crooked grin. “You’ve got a whole pack of troublemakers at your back, kid. And me? I’m the one who makes sure people like you come out alive. Stick close. If something explodes, I’ll try to make sure it’s behind us.”
Weslin tried to smile. It came out lopsided, but honest.
Harmon looked around. “Any other questions?”
Nyssa raised a hand. “Yeah. Where can a girl find a decent stash of bluefire powder in this town?”
Harmon smirked. “That’s on you. We’ve got a few hours after this to gather what we need. Use them wisely.”
He turned then, gesturing to Dain. “You’re dismissed. Prep what you need. We move tonight.”
Dain gave a curt nod and disappeared through the door, silent as a shadow.
Harmon straightened. “Neavin, Dain, and I step back now. Once boots hit the street, Garr takes point. Field command is yours.”
Garr, steady and unreadable, simply nodded. Garr let the silence sit a beat, then said, “Anybody not clear on their part, speak up now. Once we're out that door, there's no going back for second guesses. 
“Aurelia,” Harmon continued, “link them.”
She was already moving. Fingers brushed her temple. A pulse of golden energy shimmered through the room, threading into each of them. Familiar. Comforting. A mind-bridge built of trust and trained will.

“Gather the remainder of your belongings. We leave no traces. Nothing left behind.”
He rolled up the maps, stuffing them into a weathered satchel, his hands quick, efficient. But his jaw tightened with every fold. This wasn’t just a strategy. This was something deeper.
Outside, the tavern roared with life, but in this room, it felt far away. “Ash,” Nyssa called as she cinched her belt, “Try not to incinerate anything important until we’re out the door.”
The pyrokinetic flashed a grin. “Can’t make promises. Chaos helps.”
Weslin shook his head, smiling faintly. “You’re all mad.”
Garr clapped him on the shoulder. Solid. Reassuring. “And you’re one of us now. Get used to it.”
Aldrek murmured something no one could make out, under his breath, then met Weslin's gaze with a tired but sincere smile. “We do this clean. We do it fast. And we bring him home.”
A quiet settled over them. Not peace, but purpose. Outside, night unfurled its shadowed cloak across Forgehollow. And the mission began, with no turning back on anyone's minds.
The night air outside the Ironflask had cooled, laced with the faint bite of coal smoke and the sour tang of the tannery downriver. Most of Forgehollow was winding down, but the pocket of alley just east of the tavern still pulsed with life, dim lanterns swinging on rusted hooks, distant shouts from gamblers and drunks, the heavy clatter of boots on stone.
Nyssa adjusted the fit of her gear in the shadow of a boarded-up bakery, her lean frame crouched in the dark. She worked quickly, fingers tightening the clasps of her reinforced leather, checking hidden pouches, blade sheaths, and the twin coils of tripwire looped across her waist like a bandolier. A soft jingle of glass followed as she lifted a small satchel and gave it a light shake, vials and charges, everything she needed for entry.
Weslin stood a few paces away, adjusting the collar of his cloak. His fingers trembled slightly as he fumbled with a clasp. Nyssa watched him out of the corner of her eye.
“You’re doing that thing again,” she said, voice low.
“What thing?”
“That thing where your hands pretend you’re not nervous, but they’re lying.”
Weslin blew out a breath and dropped his hands. “I keep running through it in my head.”
Nyssa slipped a throwing knife into her boot and stood. “Good. Keep running it. Repetition keeps the screaming quiet. “
He looked at her, uncertain. “That's supposed to be comforting?”
“Nope. Just true.”
She gave him a small smirk, then reached over and fixed the clasp he’d been struggling with. “Breathe slower. Shoulders back. Let the cloak do the work.”
Weslin nodded. “Thanks.”
From around the far side of the bakery, soft footsteps padded in from the street. Ash emerged from the gloom, his coat half-unbuttoned, his gloves cinched tight. 
“You two look cozy,” he drawled.
“We were bonding,” Nyssa said, straightening. “You’re late.”
He gave a crooked grin, then glanced upward at the cracked clock face just barely visible above the smog-stained rooftops. The 10th Bell hand sat one notch shy.
“About ten minutes left,” Ash said. 
 “I had to find more burn paste. You people keep asking me to control myself, so I figured I’d better prep for when I don’t.”
 “Garr’s in position. Dain’s outside the walls with the horses, staging our exit. Aurelia’s with him, but she’s already tethered to Weslin; that link’s steady. She’ll ride his thoughts once he’s inside.”
Nyssa pulled the hood over her hair, flattening the auburn strands. “Then we stick to the rhythm. I’ll get us through the first lock. Weslin’s eyes are on the wards. He could feel Aurelia in his mind again, not words this time, just presence. She’s stronger at reading magical weave and hearing them. They double up, they might be able to hear the hum.”
She paused, fingers brushing her hip idly, eyes distant for just a moment. “Wish Dain was on this side of the wall.”
Ash snorted. “Of course you do. Maybe if he were here, we could solve everything with smirks and sweat.”
Nyssa gave him a look. “It’s not like that. He just knows how to work with his hands. I mean, with a blade.”
Ash grinned but didn’t push it.
“Right,” she said, clearing her throat. “Let’s move.”
They started toward the bend in the street, where the path forked toward the prison’s rear wall and the lower delivery gate. Their route was narrow, boxed in by slumping brickwork and the occasional shuttered stall.
Then Nyssa froze, one hand raised.
Footsteps. Heavy. Unhurried. Not drunk. Not rushed. Three sets, approaching from the mouth of the side street.
Weslin ducked behind a broken barrel, heart hammering. Nyssa eased herself into the shadows near a stooped doorway, her hand brushing the hilt at her side. Ash didn’t hide. He just stepped back into the deeper dark, the faint heat around him fading until even the rune-light died down to nothing.
Around the corner came three guards in polished black-and-brass, faces bored but wary. Between them, shackled at the wrists and dragged forward by a heavy collar chain, walked a hunched, familiar figure.
Brother Aldrek Thorne.
His robes were torn and streaked with dried blood, one eye swollen shut. But he was upright, moving, and silent. Even in chains, there was weight to him.
Nyssa narrowed her eyes, then gave the smallest nod. “We’re on schedule. No matter what it looks like.” No one argued. That didn’t mean no one noticed.
Ash's voice barely stirred the air while shaking his head. “Well. That’s a wrinkle.”
Once the guards and Aldrek were out of sight, the team moved.
Nyssa led them around the rear of the building, where the stone foundation dropped into a lower service crawl flanked by rusting metal grates. She crouched low, pried one loose with a soft grunt, and slipped inside. Ash followed next, then Weslin, careful to mute the clink of his gear as he slid in behind them.
The tunnel smelled of mildew and oil, a service duct long forgotten except by rats and rainwater. Aurelia’s voice fluttered in Weslin’s thoughts, calm and focused.
The crawlspace narrowed, then widened into a dark corridor of old storage rooms and barrel vaults, some flooded, others choked with debris. Here, the wards began, they believed.
Weslin paused at the first one, a circular marking etched into the stone, pulsing faintly beneath layers of grime. It vibrated like a distant horn, low and resonant in his chest. He swallowed, touched the small wooden case he carried, the jeweler's kit they’d bought earlier that day,  delicate metal picks, silver needles, and other small, finely crafted tools, nestled in velvet.
“There,” he whispered. “It’s… alive.”
Nyssa crouched beside him, eyes darting. Her usual grin was absent. She watched the rune warily, the way a fox might eye a trap. Ash stood behind them like a statue, gaze flicking down the tunnel toward the open iron sewer gate beyond.
Outside, through grates and cracks, the faint sound of the city still bled in, horses on cobbles, a hawker calling about sweetbuns, the wet clang of smiths closing for the night. But down here, beneath the feet of a city that never really slept, the weight of stone and silence bore down on them.
Weslin could feel Aurelia in his mind again, not words this time, just presence. Steady, rooting him in place. Her heartbeat was calm. She trusted him.
Even though he didn’t trust himself.
He heard Harmon’s well-known, steady voice, drawn from years of experience, ‘Find the base rune. I know you can. Follow it. We’re with you in the link.’
He nodded to himself, unwrapped the kit, and began.
Ash broke off from the others near the third left corridor, shoulders hunched low as he slipped into the shadows of the offshoot tunnel. Every footstep sloshed through ankle-deep runoff that churned up flecks of grease and sodden paper, the kind that stuck to your boots no matter how hard you scraped.
This corridor, narrower than the rest, had long since been forgotten. Rusted maintenance doors lined the walls, most hanging on busted hinges or sealed shut with decades of grime and neglect. The floor sloped slightly downward, a natural funnel for whatever the town didn’t want to deal with. He passed through a shattered bulkhead, ducking beneath exposed pipework that dripped brown water onto his hood.
His coat, already soaked from the waist down, dragged at his legs like wet canvas. Ash gritted his teeth, pushing forward.
Get in. Get it done. Get out.
That was the rhythm in his head. A mantra. He needed to keep himself centered. Every sound was too much. Even breathing. 
His boots squelched in silence now, his breath soft and steady as he moved past an old utility junction, the brick walls giving way to concrete and riveted iron supports. The silence was complete, no echoes, no rats, not even the groan of old water through the pipes. It made every breath sound louder, his heartbeat too present to ignore.
Stay calm, he told himself. It’s just another job. You’ve burned half a dozen fort doors and walked out smiling.
But this was different.
They were inside the belly of something older, something meant to never be seen again. It was the kind of place that only existed on building documents, to be discovered again. The last marker he passed was nothing but faded black ink. With a place that has been visited for so long, it is hard to tell what you might encounter. 
The air was warmer now. Not hot, but warmed, as the skin of a dead fire still holding onto the memory of flame. That was the coal room, close.
He reached the rusting ladder just beyond a bent steel valve, its base stained dark from a long-forgotten spill. The ladder creaked under his weight as he climbed slowly, every rung a protest. At the top, a narrow iron hatch. This was his point.
Above him, if the blueprints hadn’t lied, sat the western wall of the prison and the lower storeroom used for dry goods, rice, root vegetables, and coal for the kitchen braziers. He’d seen guards hauling sacks in for the vendor carts.
The coal chute ran into the back corner, a rusted track system fed by pulley bags. It wasn’t part of the main prison, just an ancillary room, but it connected to the hallway near the mess, and more importantly, sat close to the internal barracks stairwell. With the right push, it would burn just enough to force a response.
Ash dropped to one knee in the filth and unshouldered his satchel. Inside, wrapped in a treated cloth, were the components.
First device, a thick glass flask, filled with fast-burning oil and resin chips. At its base, a rune-etched spark coil timed with a slow fuse glyph. Aurelia had said, “It will ignite clean. No magical burst, no flare signature. A kitchen fire got out of control.”
He paused, holding the flask in his hand. It felt warm, even though it shouldn’t. His pulse, maybe. Or nerves. He set it carefully near the chute, tucked behind a broken crate of spoiled grain. He adjusted the glyph, a quarter-turn on the rune to match the delay.
Then he stopped.
His eyes narrowed, scanning the dim light cast by a single flickering Glowshard, which he’d cracked earlier and wedged near the wall. His breath fogged faintly in the cold, not quite fear, but tension. A sense that the lines hadn’t all been drawn yet.
Ash ducked under the rusted ladder and pressed his back to the slime-slick stone, letting the weight of the moment settle on his shoulders.
One fire. Enough to draw attention. But then what? He thought.
His jaw clenched. Water dripped in steady plinks somewhere deeper in the tunnel, the sound as sharp as nails in his skull. The stink of rot clung to his tongue like it had fingers. He could taste rust in the air, copper and filth and something acrid he couldn’t name.
What if they weren’t moving fast enough? What if something went wrong?
And then it hit him. Not like one of his visions. No divine whisper. Just gut instinct, an old itch between the ribs. Like the wind before a storm.
They’re not just here for Riven. That changed everything. Every bad job he’d survived started with that same feeling.
One fire wouldn’t cut it. Not with the prison guards still clustered close to the stairs, and time tightening everywhere else. Not with alarms ready to sound at the first whiff of magic. If they were going to drag three out, they needed more.
He reached into his satchel. His fingers curled around the second flask, cold iron rim, glass belly, the little glyph on the base. A backup. Meant to buy them time. Or save someone’s life.
Ash exhaled slowly. He knelt, moving like a shadow along the slick tunnel wall, back toward the far side of the storage room. Just beyond this point, under the mess hall, was the old grease trap chamber, unused for years, according to the blueprints. Dry, neglected, but still slick with buildup. One good spark, and it would go up as a torch dropped in a grain silo.
He tucked the flask behind an overturned barrel crusted with rust and cobwebs, nudging it until it disappeared into shadow. A flick of his thumb activated the delay rune. Four minutes? Maybe seven if the damp slowed it.
That was the plan. That should’ve been enough.
But something tugged at him, a tension behind his eyes, like heat trapped behind his skull.  You could call it divine intuition.
He glanced up the ladder again. The first hatch, the storeroom he’d scouted. And then, just beyond it, his eyes caught something else.  Another hatch. Lower set. Partially rusted. Not on the blueprints. If it hadn’t been forgotten, it would have been locked tighter.
Ash swore under his breath, already weighing whether this was a gift or a trap. Curiosity flared, quick and dangerous.
He climbed. Slowly. Boots slid against the iron rungs. He eased the second hatch open with both hands and peeked through.
Another storage room, smaller, windowless, and darker than the first. The air here was thick with the smell of oil. Yet that was not it. Ash took another sniff.  This time, he got the hint of something bitter and a heavy scent of tallow. Fat? No, something else, pine resin? He finally came to that conclusion as he worked through his senses.  
His brows lifted as he took in his surroundings.
Barrels. Dozens. Crates marked in faded red paint with the old sigil of the garrison. Practice rounds. Cannon powder. Fat-soaked rope for fire drills.
Explosives.
Ash grinned, eyes glowing faint amber in the gloom.
“Well,” he whispered, “aren’t you just asking to be set on fire?”
He dropped back down, landing with a splash in the ankle-deep water. His coat dragged like kelp, but his stride picked up. A pulse in his chest, adrenaline, excitement. A half-mad idea took shape.
