He scrambled back to the grease trap and found the trail, the runoff ditch that cut between the rooms. He fished into the side pocket of his coat, pulled a cracked vial filled with thick black liquid, tar oil, mixed for torches, waterproof, smoky as sin. He popped the cork and poured a winding stream from the edge of the second device’s hiding spot, through the runoff, curving toward the back wall of the explosive storage hatch.
Slow burn. Enough to slither. And when it hits that stash?
Ash snorted under his breath.
“Boom.”
He tucked the empty vial away, grabbed a broken crate splinter, and dipped the tip into the oil trail. A backup fuse, just in case the delay rune misfired. He wedged the splinter upright in a crack between two stones.
Standing, he looked at the dark path he’d made. Oil fire. Oil to boom. Boom to panic. Panic to…Opportunity! “Hell of a plan,” he muttered with a crooked smirk. “You clever bastard.”
His stomach tightened, but it wasn’t nerves. It was pride. Real, quiet pride. No visions had fed him this one. No mentor whispering tricks. Just him, thinking fast, pulling from the dirt and ash of his past. Then Ash turned and ran.
Weslin was already bent low, eyes scanning the ward etched into the stone just beyond the threshold. It wasn’t one glyph. It never was. A full spread of runes lay out in a precise weave, curling from the center like a spider’s web.
He had the jeweler’s kit open beside him, fingers hovering just above the delicate tools. His brow was furrowed. Breath was shallow. He didn’t need to rush. He needed to be right.
This wasn’t about cutting a wire or snapping a hinge. These wards were self-fed, drawn from a shard’s charge, anchored by a single glyph. One rune out of the dozen was the keystone. Not because it was weaker, but because everything else depended on it. Distort that, and the magic would fold in on itself, fast.
But finding it was like trying to pick a single voice out of a crowded room. Every mark shimmered faintly, still holding charge. Still live.
He leaned closer, trying to trace the pattern with his eyes.  And then Aurelia's voice slipped into his head, clear and cool as rain. There. See the bend? Just left of center. The break in the symmetry. That’s your anchor.
His gaze narrowed. The rune wasn’t larger or brighter. But now that he knew what to look for, he saw it,  the way the flow of the circle fed inward, not out. A quiet center. A sinkhole.
Weslin nodded once. Didn’t speak. Just reached for the crystal-tipped stylus.
He steadied his grip, held his breath. And began to distort.
Not a line through, not a slash or a smear. He altered it, carefully warping the edge of the rune, bending the curve until it no longer held meaning.
The glow flickered, another hair’s breadth adjustment. The entire glyph pulse shivered, then collapsed like a lung deflating. Gone.
The magic died without a sound. Weslin sat back on his heels, exhaling slowly. “Clear.”
Nyssa gave a small nod, already turning toward the door.
He allowed himself the ghost of a smile as he packed up the kit. “Thanks,” he murmured to the room, to the silence, to whoever was listening.
But the path ahead was open. And for now, the silence held, as if drawing breath.






Chapter Twenty-Two
Brother Aldrek sat in a stone-walled chamber, dimly lit by a swaying lantern overhead. The desk between him and the officer was battered, stained with ink, and worn with age. An iron mace, his, lay beside a folded report.
The officer leaned forward, eyes bloodshot from lack of sleep. His voice was already thin with irritation.
Aldrek remained still, his chains quiet. “Not all truth comes from canon.” A pause. “Some was written by those too afraid to admit what they saw. I speak only what I’ve seen. What the Creator has guided me to speak.”
“You were preaching at the Stonewalk Promenade,” he said. “Talking about fire from the skies, stars turning to ash, the death of the world. Armed. In public.”
Aldrek inclined his head. “The people needed to hear it. Even in silence, the truth burns.”
The officer’s fist slammed the desk. “You were inciting a riot and preaching heresy! That filth you spout isn’t in the Book of the Creator. It’s outlawed—”
Then it happened.
A tremor ran through the floor like a held breath, followed by a dull boom that echoed through the walls. Dust trickled from a ceiling joint.
The officer stiffened, hand flying to his sword hilt. “Flames, what now?”
He glared back at Aldrek. “Stay here. Don’t move a muscle. You’re locked down well enough.” He stormed out, muttering curses and orders as his boots vanished down the corridor. The silence afterward was sacred.
Aldrek sat still a moment longer. He bowed his head, whispered something only he and the Creator would understand. Then the shimmer of light beneath his skin, White magic, came alive at his wrists.
He closed his eyes, focused on the tension in his shoulders. He exhaled as pain flared, bones snapping before the shackles finally gave way, leaving his wrists burning and numb. The chains clinked softly against the stone.
He took a moment and let the light from his shard wash over his hands, relieving the pain, before he reclaimed his mace with quiet reverence and stepped into the hall.
He passed through cells, empty and shadowed, while others were full of murmuring voices and rattling chains. He gave them no attention. He turned a corner and reached a wall that hadn’t seen attention in decades, a sealed stone arch with a rusted iron door half-sunken in the frame. Dust and cobwebs clung to the corners like old memories.
The hinges were fused. The bolts rusted through. And an old supply cart, splintered and overturned, had been shoved in front of it as if to forget it ever existed. Crates of spoiled grain slumped nearby, molded over with the stink of rot.
Aldrek exhaled through his nose. He planted his mace into the ground and rolled his shoulder once. Then he grabbed the edge of the cart, muscles coiling, and hauled it aside with a growl. The old wood groaned but shifted. Crates toppled, and grain spilled in dry, stinking waves. A rat hissed and darted away into the gloom.
He knelt at the edge of the door, placed the hooked head of his mace into the rusted seam, and pushed. Metal groaned. Anther loud snap. A bolt cracked in half, ancient metal giving way.
He braced his foot against the wall, shifted his grip, and slammed the mace into the side once more, another pop. The door stuttered inward an inch.
Light spilled from the other side. Then the door gave, the gap no wider than it needed to be before voices echoed down the hall. And there stood Nyssa Quill, brows lifted in amused surprise, twin daggers in hand, and her silhouette outlined by torchlight behind her.
“Well, well,” she said, stepping lightly through the gap, “if it isn’t the heretic himself, tearing down prison doors like some holy hammer.”
Weslin followed, tall and composed, a sword resting across his shoulder. His smile was faint but genuine. “It’s… it’s good to see you, Brother.”
Aldrek stepped back, brushing rust from his hands. “You are late.”
Nyssa smirked. “You were early.”
Weslin turned his eyes toward the corridor. “We don’t have long. They’re distracted for now, but we’ll only get one shot at this. We need to find the keys.”
“First floor,” Aldrek nodded. “Office block. The records should be there, if they’ve kept any.”
“I saw it,” Nyssa said, already moving. “Main offices, off the east wing. We passed it during the fire run.”
Together, the three of them slipped back into the corridors of the first floor, shadows sliding through firelit halls, toward the offices where the hunt for Riven Duskwind would begin in earnest.
The Warden’s office sat at the far end of the east wing, wide double doors slightly ajar, brass handles tarnished and scraped. The hallway outside had been abandoned in the panic. Ash’s fire had driven most of the guards topside.
Aldrek shoved the door open with his shoulder, scanning the room with quick precision. The walls were lined with old maps, prison schematics, a row of ledgers on one shelf, and a desk piled with disorganized parchments. The Warden had fled in a hurry.
Nyssa was already moving, instantly starting to flip through scrolls and drawers. Weslin checked the armoire methodically, while Aldrek tried to force open a smaller lockbox behind the desk.
“Hey,” came a gravel-thick voice behind them. “You guys redecorating or just trashing the place for fun?”
Ash leaned in the doorway, breathing hard but still managing that crooked grin. His coat had burn holes in it, one shoulder scorched, and soot streaked across his cheek. A few sparks still danced off his fingertips like nervous ticks.
“We’re looking for a ledger,” Nyssa said, not looking up. “We need to find Riven.”
Ash raised an eyebrow. “Ledger, huh?”
“Keys,” Weslin muttered from across the room, searching a bookcase. “We’ll need keys to the lower levels.”
“Also, keys,” Aldrek added, holding up a drawer and tossing it aside when it came up empty.
Ash snorted, running a hand through his damp hair. “Right. Because someone not on the books is in the book.” Ash pushed off the doorframe. “Keys are usually on a hook by the desk. Just saying.” 
“Help,” Weslin said, calm but firm. “Find the keys. In and out, remember?”
Aldrek pried open a lower drawer near the back, the one untouched in the Warden’s rush to flee. He rummaged around and pulled out a ring of keys. Twenty thick iron ones, some labeled, most not. “I’ve got them,” he said as he shook them once. 
“Good,” Weslin said, already moving. “Let’s not waste the chaos.”
Nyssa smirked. “Bout time you embraced the chaos, pup.”
Ash laughed. “Took you long enough.”
They left the office behind and slid down the hall, keeping close to the walls. The stairwell leading down into the second level, where the real cells were, the ones carved into stone and shadow, waited like a mouth.
Nyssa glanced at the others as they reached the landing. “Alright, we hit level two. We don’t know which wing he’s in, but it’s probably isolation. Someone like Riven wouldn’t be tossed in with the general rats.”
“Agreed,” Aldrek said. “Too dangerous. They’d keep him away from voices.”
Ash’s face turned a little more serious, heat fading from his eyes. “Then we split. Weslin and I can clear the west wing,” Ash said it anyway, knowing none of them liked it.
“I’ll take east with Nyssa,” Aldrek nodded. “We move fast, quietly. First one to find him signals the others.”
“What about guards?” Weslin asked.
Ash cracked his knuckles. “Most of them are screaming upstairs. The rest? I’ve got a few tricks left.”
The stairwell was steep, narrow, and smelled of old stone, damp air, and fear. The four of them descended together, soldiers of a moment, shadows with a purpose.
Riven Duskwind was waiting below, untouched by the chaos above. Now the hunt had begun.
The corridor sloped downward, pressing in like a throat swallowing them into the dark. Weslin’s boots made barely a sound, but each step landed with too much weight, not from the stone beneath, but from the knot forming in his chest.
Ash moved beside him, casual as ever, fire-kissed eyes scanning shadows like this was just another walk in the woods. But Weslin? Weslin was trying not to breathe too loudly.
They’d split at the hallway fork, Nyssa and Brother Aldrek veering right, Weslin and Ash left. The second subterranean floor was lined with narrow cells, most sealed tightly. The air tasted like rust and stone dust. Old magic, faded fear. The prison stank.
Weslin stopped. His breath caught as his eyes snagged on the edge of the ceiling above.
There, half-obscured by soot and mineral drips, lay a delicate series of runes. They were meant to blend into the architecture. Defensive. Passive until provoked.
He swore under his breath, a whisper only the stones would hear.
“You see something?” Ash asked, pausing with a hand resting casually on the hilt at his hip.
Weslin hesitated. “Yeah. It’s a ward. I… I missed it.”
Ash looked up, frowning. “You sure?”
“That wasn’t there a moment ago,” Weslin said as he pointed, his voice tight. “It was active now, tripped,” Weslin said bitterly. “It was lit, see that faint shimmer?”
Ash squinted. “Yep. Damn. Can you untrip it?”
“No,” Weslin said quickly. “If I tried to unravel it now, I’d destabilize the layer underneath. Wards like this are stacked; if you break one out of order, the feedback could collapse the whole floor. Or worse.”
Ash gave a low whistle. “Lovely. Then let’s not trip anymore.”
“I should’ve caught it,” Weslin muttered, eyes still on the rune. “I’ve been training with Aurelia on this. She’s been helping me learn how to focus past the noise. Most Adepts don’t listen for the sound of the power itself anymore,” Weslin said, then blinked as he'd just heard himself. “Sorry. That's not, I'm doing the thing where I talk when I'm scared.” But I’m still… still learning how to hear it. So it's fresh. Loud in my head.”
Ash tilted his head, listening now, not just with his ears. “You were listening too hard, maybe.”
“I was focused on her voice,” Weslin admitted. “We’ve been linking; she helps filter everything. I thought I had it.” His face tightened. “And now the link’s severed. That ward didn’t just maybe alert someone, but it muffled our net as well.”
Ash didn’t tease. Instead, he gave a short nod and reached up to pat Weslin on the shoulder. “You caught it late. You still caught it. And we’re still walking. You’re doing fine.”
They resumed their sweep, checking cells. Each held remnants of shattered lives. Bent bedframes, dried blood on old straw, scratches worn deep into the walls like tally marks from ghosts. Most cells were empty now, but the silence they left behind was a heavier kind of noise. Weslin tried not to look too long at the claw marks near one iron door, or the dried flowers someone had left near another.
“Nothing,” Ash muttered after a while. “Not even a whisper of Duskwind.”
“Nyssa and Aldrek will have had better luck,” Weslin replied, though he didn’t believe it.
Ash gave a half smile. “Well, at least we're getting more exercise than I expected.”
Weslin frowned but let it go. The fire-mage’s humor was always two steps off serious. Ash wasn’t cocky. He just refused to show when he was nervous.
Weslin envied that. They met the others at the stairwell. Nyssa shook her head. “Clean,” she said. “One junkie, two crazies, no con men.”
 Brother Aldrek crossed his arms. “Onward, then.” They descended.
The third level opened into silence. But not the kind that comforted. This was the hush of absence. The corridor stretched long and wide, arched high above with old stone ribbing like the inside of a cathedral. Iron sconces lined the walls, but no flames burned. Instead, small crystals pulsed from above, dull blue and rhythmic, like the slow heartbeat of the prison itself.
Aldrek and Nyssa took the left wing, branching off through the central corridor. Weslin and Ash swept the right.
These cells here were larger, maybe meant for long-term containment or dangerous prisoners. Each door was constructed from heavy black steel plated with ward-etched star iron, the kind of door that dared you to try. The viewing slits were narrow, fitted with a lock neither could figure out at a glance, and the hinges didn’t squeak. This floor was kept.
But most of the cells. Empty, but not all.
Aldrek paused at one, eyeing the scrapings across the walls in what might’ve once been blood. A small figure sat curled in the corner, head twitching to a rhythm only it could hear. Then it spoke.
“No air, no air, no air... but that’s all right. They said I didn’t need it where I’m going.”
He moved on.
Nyssa stepped past another, where a pair of eyes gleamed out from under a ragged blanket. Then the blanket shifted, and three Joblins hissed as they scurried backward into the dark. Small, hook-nosed eyes glowing like lantern ticks.
One gave a cheerful wave.
Nyssa blinked. “That’s a new one.”
Further down, one cell held something massive, a hulking beast covered in plated bone and scars, chained at four points. It breathed heavily, as if even sleep took effort. She couldn't tell if it was snoring or growling.
Aldrek glanced inside. “Orth.”
Nyssa looked over. “You’ve seen one before?”
“Fought one once. Preferred not to again.” But none of the cells held what they were looking for. Not yet. 
The team regrouped near the center of the third floor, silent confirmation passing between them. Empty. Ash looked toward the stairwell leading down again. “Well,” he said with a small smirk, “time for the good stuff.” They began to descend the stairwell to the fourth level, and halfway down.
BOOM. 
A pressure in the air followed, heavy and deliberate. The second explosion sounded overhead, deeper, throatier, more intentional. Dust rained from above, and the walls trembled slightly beneath their boots.
Weslin jumped. “That wasn’t a collapse, right?”
Ash casually dusted his coat. “That one was mine.” They stared. He shrugged. “I figured we might need a little more breathing room on the way out, so I rigged up a few more gifts for our friends above. Just enough to make‘em sweat.”
Nyssa arched a brow. “That wasn’t exactly a candle pop.”
Ash smiled. “I like big distractions. And I’ve still got one more surprise on the timer. Should go off any moment.”
A slow, heavy footstep echoed behind them. They turned. A man stepped from the corridor shadows, huge, wrapped in dark leather reinforced with polished bone plating. His arms were exposed and crisscrossed with glowing veins of red magic that pulsed just beneath the skin like lava in stone. His presence filled the corridor like heat.
“I was told someone would come,” he said calmly, voice like crackling coals. “You’re later than I thought.”
Ash’s smile vanished.
The brute continued. “Lord Merrick was clear. Riven Duskwind doesn’t leave this place. And neither do those who try to take him.” He raised a hand to the small glowing gem embedded in his ear. “They’re here.”
A low crack echoed from somewhere above. 
BOOM.
The walls rumbled. A second passed. Then came a roaring gust of heat, distant, but violent. The brute flinched slightly.
Screams echoed throughout the area. They all heard, “—we’re—cut off—fire’s spread—second floor is…”
Another voice screamed through a wall horn, “We can’t make it to the stairs! There’s fire everywhere…. we’re sealed in.”
Then... nothing. Silence.
He growled, smacking the gem. “Damn it.”
Ash stepped forward, flames licking across his knuckles. “Sounds like your backup’s going to be late.”
“You did this?” the brute asked.
Ash didn’t flinch. “Third surprise. I might’ve set fire to your artillery shed.”
“Clever,” the brute said with a cold grin. “Let’s see if your fire holds.”
He lifted both arms, and blue flame erupted from his palms.
Ash let out a little laugh. “Now this is interesting.” He stepped between his team and the threat, flexing his hands until both were wrapped in fire, his natural, crimson-orange blaze crackling around him like a living aura.
“You three, finish the mission,” Ash said, not looking back.
“Alone?” Weslin said.
Ash smiled faintly. “I need the practice. No more words. Go!”
The two men lunged, fire to fire, the air itself twisting between them as the hallway lit with violent color. Flames went everywhere.
The fourth floor felt like descending into a vault buried beneath time. Everything here was tight. Precision-forged. These vault doors were seamless slabs of star-forged iron, reinforced with runes. There were no torches here either, only soft white glow-stones set into the ceiling, casting sterile light.
They moved slowly now. One wrong door could trigger a dozen alarms. But as they passed, cell after cell revealed men and women too broken to speak, too dangerous to be allowed light. Down here, even the glow-stones seemed reluctant, their light thin and flat, as if they had learned not to show too much of what they were illuminating. 
Then Aldrek stopped. “Here,” he said. 
Nyssa moved to the cell he pointed to, gaze narrowing. Three prisoners inside. One was tall and broad, arms like quarried stone, with the stillness of a man who had learned that moving first was usually a mistake. The second, delicate, smooth-faced, with an arched brow and a gaze that missed nothing. Possibly female. Possibly not. Definitely dangerous. And the third…
A smirk, even before he finished looking up. Dark hair. Clever eyes. Lean frame with the look of a man who hasn’t had a full meal in a while. “Well,” Riven Duskwind said. “Took you long enough.”
Nyssa smiled despite herself. “Had to make an entrance.”
Weslin blinked. “This is him?”
“That’s him,” she said, still smiling. 
Behind them, a noise of creaking boots. Weslin looked up.”Uh… is that guard supposed to be there?”
At the far end of the hall stood a man in a prison guard’s uniform, turned away from them, shoulders hunched like he hadn’t heard. Aldrek stepped forward and charged, swift, silent.
He tackled the man in one swift motion, sending both to the ground in a clash of armor and curses. The guard rolled with it, groaning. “Bloody hell, get off me, you ogre.”
The hood slipped back. Nyssa sucked in a breath. “Dain?!”






Chapter Twenty-Three
Aldrek’s knee kept him pinned to the floor. Dain felt discomfort in his ribs. He groaned, low and annoyed. “Off me, brother,” Dain said evenly.
His lip was split, a bruise already purpling under his eye, but his eyes were alert, and that familiar half-smirk tugged at the corner of his mouth. “Good hit, brother,” he said, coughing.
Aldrek grunted and rose, yanking him upright with one firm pull.
“You disguised yourself as a prison guard?” the priest said, unimpressed.
“Improvisation,” Dain replied, brushing soot from his borrowed uniform. “Your tackle was appreciated. Brought the role together.”
Nyssa crossed her arms. “What are you doing here?”
Dain tapped the insignia stitched above his chest, the rank sigil of a senior escort officer. “I’m here to get you out.”
From inside the sealed cell behind them, Riven’s voice drifted through the slit in the door, dry as old parchment. “Charming plan so far. Do I get to be rescued before or after the punchlines?”
“We’re working on it,” Nyssa called back.
“What happened to the drainage tunnel?” Aldrek asked, ignoring the sarcasm.
“Scrapped,” Dain said. “Blocked by twelve guards standing watch over the vault corridor. They're not forged, but they’re elite. Professional. Won’t move. Won’t blink. We never would’ve made it through.”
Weslin stepped up, brows knitting. “But... the plan…”
Dain fixed Weslin with a look. “Rule one, my young man, expect the plan to break.”
“You already told me rule one was keeping my eyes open,” Weslin shot back.
Dain shook his head, “They are all rule one,” He tried a smile. The pain in his ribs killed it before it finished. He breathed out carefully and continued.
“Harmon knew it might fall apart,” Dain said. “Once we saw the link was dead, we sealed it. No runners. No signals. If that spread, the whole descent burned.”
Nyssa’s eyes narrowed. “So he didn’t trust us to let us know about the backup?”
Dain shook his head. “It wasn’t about trust. It was about containment.”
From behind the door, Riven muttered, “Sounds like your boss is paranoid. I like him already.”
A moment later, another boom shook the walls, causing dust to trickle from the stone ceiling. Followed by another crash, steel on stone, or maybe stone melting. The faint roar of fire echoed through the vents. Dain gave the group a questioning look. “Ash,” Nyssa said under her breath.
Aldrek murmured a prayer, fingers brushing the symbol carved into the haft of his mace. “Let the fire purify what must burn.”
Dain glanced upward, unfazed. “He’s doing his part. Time for us to do ours.”
Nyssa reached for the locking mechanism, fingers brushing the cold steel.
“Wait,” Weslin hissed, stepping forward. Everyone froze.
Weslin leaned in close, eyes scanning the frame. “There’s a ward concealed under the locking. Let me look.” He examined for a few moments. “Definitely a ward,” Weslin said. “Once it’s tripped, it runs to completion. There’s no cutting it short.”
Nyssa’s hand hovered, now still. “How do you know?” she asked.
“I heard it, and when I went to look away, I saw the smallest flicker.” He didn’t look up. “Aurelia taught me to listen to the magic’s hum, not the way it feels. This one’s tight, like pulled thread. Looking at it, this one is delicate; it could go off if done wrong.”
“Good catch, pup,” said Nyssa
“You can disarm it?” Dain asked.
“I’ve never done one alone,” Weslin admitted, voice quiet. “But I’ve practiced enough to try.”
Nyssa crouched beside him. “Do what you were trained to do, pup. I’m right here.” She gave a reassuring squeeze to the soldier, and he blushed a bit.
Weslin nodded. He pulled the same silver chisels and an etching needle and got to work. He switched the smallest blade, barely longer than a fingernail, and pressed it gently to the first rune. The ward buzzed.
He inhaled, then began to move, not fast, but with a steadiness that came from knowing the room had no margin for error. One rune at a time. He was missing the connection with Aurelia, yet he went on. He nicked and scraped, deforming curves and slicing along precise axis lines, turning active glyphs into inert scars.
When the final rune bent under his chisel, the magic dispersed with a soft hiss, like breath escaping from a glass lung. The lock gave a quiet click. No fire.

The cell inside was cold by design. The walls were bare blackstone, sealed smooth, with embedded ward lines dimmed from lack of light. The glow-stones overhead were dulled and crusted with age, casting the cell in a bluish haze that left most of it in shadow.
All three men were chained in place, seated on low stone benches, iron cuffs bolted to the floor. The chains gave each of them just enough room to sleep on the floor. 
The first was tall, lean in the shoulders, but broad at the chest. His skin was sun-worn, olive-toned, with dark hair and the sharp eyes of someone who measured every person in the room within seconds. His boots were still polished. That was the first giveaway, soldier.
Riven stood the moment the door opened, chains clinking at his ankles, a slow grin spreading across his face.
“Nyssa Quill,” he said, voice low and warm. “I was starting to think you’d left me here on purpose.” She stepped into the cell without hesitation. He moved to her, and they embraced, tight, fierce, and wordless. For a moment, the prison fell away. Her arms wrapped around him with an urgency that betrayed more than friendship, and he buried his face in the crook of her neck like someone breathing freely for the first time in days.
From the threshold, Weslin caught Dain’s expression shift as the moment passed, just a flash. Something in it that Weslin could not name. He looked away first. Some things were not his to hold onto.
“So…” Dain said, clearing his throat. “Are you going to introduce us, Nyssa? Or should we just assume this is the charming one?”
Nyssa stepped back, her hand still on Riven’s chest, steady and familiar. “This is my brother,” she said smoothly. “Riven.”
“Guilty.” Riven’s smile was easy, confident. He laughed and turned, gesturing casually to the other two. “And these two fine gents are Haldrin, the never-stopping lecturer. And Torrek doesn’t talk unless the walls start caving in.”
The second man, Haldrin, gave a stiff nod. He had graying brown hair tied back with a scrap of parchment, spectacles resting on his nose despite a bruised cheek. His robe, though singed at the hem, still bore the crest of the Althrun Collegium. Books had shaped his posture, back straight and chin elevated.
The third, Torrek Mull, didn’t bother standing. He was massive, arms corded with muscle and old scars. His clothes were thick canvas, tailored for movement, dirt still crusted into the folds. A wide iron collar ringed his throat, runes flickering faintly along its edge. He lifted his gaze slowly, like stone grinding against stone.
“Don’t talk much,” Riven said. “But when he does, it’s usually to say something like, Move, or Duck.”
A distant boom shuddered through the floor. Dust sprinkled from the stone ceiling. Somewhere far above, Ash was still fighting, and the outcome was still unknown.
Nyssa started to work on each of their chains, popping them one by one. 
Aldrek stepped forward, eyes scanning each of them. “Any injuries?” he asked, voice low but firm. “Tell me now.” His hand hovered near the symbol on his mace, a faint glow building at his fingertips.
Riven shook his head. “Bruised pride, maybe. But we’re good.”
Haldrin winced and touched his side. “A cracked rib, I think. Nothing serious.”
Aldrek stepped to him, placed a steady hand over the injury. Soft white light pulsed from his palm, and Haldrin exhaled slowly as the pain dulled.
“Better?”
“Yes,” the scholar replied, surprised. “Much.”
Torrek didn’t speak but nodded once. Aldrek didn’t press him.
Dain stepped forward and tossed down a wrapped bundle. “Time to change. We’re walking you out like you belong here.”
Aldrek caught one of the sets midair. The robes were stiff, formal, the kind worn by court scholars or traveling magistrates. Deep chestnut brown with embroidered crimson edging, the fabric was clean, if plain, and unmistakably official. Matching sigil pins gleamed from the inside fold, forged insignias from a sanctioned research guild.
“Get dressed,” Dain said. “We’ve got a window, and it’s not going to stay open forever.” A knock rang out from another cell.
Riven turned. “That must be the new guy. He was meant to be with us when we went on his lordship's little job.”
They moved to the door, footsteps cautious. Another weak knock, then silence. The cell was darker than the rest, its glow-stones nearly dead. Only the faint gleam of iron reflected through the slit.
Two men stood within. One was pressed close to the door, beard wiry and unkempt, his eyes sunken but alert. The other hung back, his frame larger, shoulders broad despite the grime clinging to his skin. Both looked like they hadn’t eaten a proper meal in weeks, their clothes ragged, cheeks hollow, skin pale under a layer of prison dust.
“We’re getting you out,” Nyssa said softly, already examining the lock. Nyssa’s eyes flicked to the corridor, then back to the lock. “We move now,” she said. “You keep pace, or you don’t come.”
Weslin stepped up and froze. His brow creased. “Wait.” He swallowed. “Water ward.”
Dain looked sharply at him. “Serious?”
Weslin nodded. “Water-bound,” he murmured. “Different weave, I can handle it.” His words were more confident than his body language as he got to work.
Nyssa leaned close. “You’ve got this, pup. Focus.”
Weslin dove right to work, moving with efficiency. When he finished the final stroke, a hiss released from the wall, joining him, letting out a breath he didn’t know he was holding. The ward faded. The lock clicked. The door opened.
The two men stepped forward slowly, blinking against the light.
Nyssa scanned them both. “Names?”
The taller one coughed and said, “Calen.” He rubbed his wrists as the chains fell away.
The other hesitated. Then, with a dry smile that didn’t reach his eyes, he muttered, “Tarn.” His gaze lingered on Dain a moment too long before he looked away. 
Dain raised an eyebrow but said nothing. He tossed each of them a folded magistrates’ robe.
“Put these on. You’re the inspection detail now. Try to look like you belong. You two are good to go, right?”
They obeyed without comment and nodded their heads in confirmation. As they pulled the clothes on, Dain added, “We’re leaving as the delegation Harmon and Neavin used on their way in. They left under the first distraction. You’re filling the numbers.”
“Harmon’s waiting?” Calen asked.
“Yes,” Dain said quickly, stepping away.
Tarn’s face darkened. He muttered nothing, just clenched his jaw as if trying to grind the name from his memory. His hands trembled slightly as he fastened the robe’s front clasp.
A dull boom shook the floor again. The group pressed upward. “That didn’t sound good,” said Aldrek.
They arrived back on the third level, and what they saw shocked them. Ash sat propped against a scorched wall, his coat burned at the sleeve. The body of the Forged brute lay face down beside him, arms sprawled out, steam curling from his tunic.
Weslin gasped, wide-eyed. “Is he dead?”
Ash cracked one eye open. “Not last time I checked. He’s just taking a long nap.” He winced as Aldrek knelt beside him and pressed a hand to his chest. Light spilled through the contact, warm and quiet. Ash hissed again and rolled his shoulder.
“Little tougher than I thought,” he muttered, sounding out of breath a bit. “But hey... I did say I needed the practice.”
Dain tossed him a robe. “Put this on. You’re part of the escort team now.”
Ash blinked in surprise. “Dain?”
“Surprise,” Dain said with a smirk. “Let’s get moving.” They climbed up the next stairwell, the scent of smoke thickening as they rose.
Walls blackened, guard towers half gone, smoke veined the pre-dawn sky. Rubble and fire blurred the yard into a battlefield still breathing. Ash peered around the smoke. “That... could’ve gone worse.”
Nyssa coughed into her sleeve. “Next time, maybe 50% less.”
Dain straightened his posture, and the group followed suit. They moved as a column, formal, organized. Nyssa led with authority, Aldrek beside her, his eyes downcast and his expression passive. Weslin clutched a thick ledger stolen from one of the desk drawers. The two new prisoners walked stiffly behind, robed and silent.
“We are the inspection,” Dain said, each word flat and final. “The fire will give us our cover. Eyes forward. Nobody speaks unless I do.” The group made its way fully into the courtyard. The guard’s attention slid past them, split between smoke, flame, and three competing commands.
Dain pointed to a litter and barked in a clipped accent, “Need more help near the breach!”
One of the guards waved them on without even glancing. “Go, go! South wall’s still hot!”
They slipped around a broken siege cart, ducked under a cracked arch, and passed through the side gate into a narrow alley.
Neavin popped up from behind a scorched stone fountain. He brushed dust from his shoulders, eyes gleaming. “Was wonderin' if I'd have to come in after you,” he muttered.
Nyssa raised an eyebrow. “Some of us had to pick up stragglers.”
Ash nodded toward the wreckage. “You’re welcome for the distraction.”
Neavin snorted. “I give it a 7.5. You lost points for symmetry.”
The drain hole yawned behind the old fountain, a narrow passage bored into stone, barely wide enough to crouch-walk. They dropped into it one by one. Neavin slid down last, sealing the entrance behind him with a muted pulse of earth magic.
They walked in darkness for a while, the air damp and earthy. The tunnel was ancient and moss-lined, narrowing and widening like a living vein beneath the city. Eventually, they reached a crumbling stone stairwell that led up through a cracked drainage spout into what had once been a noble’s keep.
Half a tower still stood, its spine twisted toward the sky like a broken finger. Vines had overtaken the outer walls, curling through cracks in the mortar, clawing through stone with slow hunger. The crest carved into the stone archway had been worn to a ghost of itself by wind and time.
A wide road curled from the ruin, sunken with age, swallowed by grass. But it was not silence that greeted them. The clash of iron on iron echoed across the clearing, grunts, a barked curse, the unmistakable chime of a blade striking armor. They crested the last rise and stopped.
Harmon stood in the center of a torn courtyard, his silhouette framed by the rising dawn and the ruin’s shattered wall. His armor glinted in the fractured light, polished steel overlaying deeper, arcane seams of etched magic. His great sword shone with the majesty of such a sword, haft tall as a man, its edges crackling faintly with energy that shimmered like heat rising from stone.
Three figures surrounded him, Forged, Merrick’s men. Each wore the black and iron uniform of their hidden order, weapons raised, circling like wolves. But Harmon was no prey.
He moved like a storm given flesh. Fast. Relentless. He snatched the sword from the stone with one hand. The air cracked as he spun, blade cleaving in a clean arc. One man didn’t even scream, his head separated from his shoulders, body tumbling backward like a sack of grain. The second lunged.
Harmon ducked beneath the swing, twisting low and letting the man’s blade skid across his shoulder. He answered with a reverse stroke, slicing across the gut, then kicked the man backward into the ruined archway. The man staggered, blood spraying from his midsection, and Harmon slid his sword tip between the ribs. He was dead before he slid down the stones.
The last Forged tried to run. Harmon raised a hand, and the Forged’s boots locked into place. The ground trembled. With a blur of unnatural motion, Harmon was behind him. He whispered something, no louder than breath, and brought the blade down diagonally.
The last Forged collapsed, bisected, and still twitching. Harmon swayed. The great sword dropped from his hand with a low clang, and he dropped to a knee. His shoulders heaved.
Weslin broke from the group, rushing ahead. “Harmon!”
He slid down beside the armored warrior, arms out to catch him as he slumped forward.
“I’m fine,” Harmon grunted. “Just... get me on the horse.” As soon as the words left his lips, the sword and his armor were gone.
Weslin stared. The sword was gone and the armor with it, as if neither had ever existed. He filed it away in the part of his mind that had gotten very crowded in the last few weeks and kept moving.
Aldrek was already there, one hand glowing white as he steadied Harmon under the arm. “You overexerted. One day, your pride’s going to kill you.”
“Not today,” Harmon said through gritted teeth.
They guided him to his steed, already saddled and waiting in the cover of vines. Weslin helped hoist him up into the saddle, and Harmon sat heavy, reins slack in one hand. Hoofbeats thundered from the far path.
Garr arrived first, sword still drawn. His black cloak caught the wind like a banner. Aurelia followed close behind, eyes scanning, her breath misting from the cold of her internal focus.
“What happened?” Garr demanded, pulling up beside Harmon’s horse.
Harmon lifted his head, jaw tight. “They were waiting,” he said. “Not to kill me. To measure me. Seems this passage is a secret to everyone.”
Garr’s eyes swept the bodies. “You left no survivors.”
“They saw too much,” Harmon said. “Aldoria and Opindale have kept the peace for too long. I will not be the thing that ends it.”
Aurelia stepped closer, laying a hand on Harmon’s side. Her fingers brushed the cut in his armor. “He needs rest.”
“He’ll get it,” Garr said. He turned, raising his voice. “Mount up! We ride now. If they find this ruin empty, let them wonder where the wind took us.”
Ash was already swinging himself onto a borrowed gelding, his coat scorched and reeking of smoke. “I’ll take wind over shackles,” he muttered.
Nyssa helped Riven into the saddle behind her. “Just hold on,” she whispered, and he gave a grin that didn’t reach his eyes.
The two men rescued from the extra cell exchanged glances. Their borrowed robes hung awkwardly on thin frames. One of them, who had called himself “Calen” without conviction, clutched the saddle horn like it might vanish. The other, “Tarn,” stared long at Harmon with eyes full of old memories and older hatred. No one questioned it.
They rode hard into the darkness of the valley, one fire out, others waiting. Nyssa glanced back once at Harmon, seeing the weight in his shoulders that no victory could ease.






Chapter Twenty-Four
The twenty-seventh Hall of Fowther Palace shimmered beneath a thousand lanterns, their golden light dancing over silk banners and arching stone. A string quartet played from the upper balconies, their instruments laced with subtle enchantments to carry every note with perfect clarity. Outside, the bells of the fifth night of the Accord Renewal rang out across the city.
It was the fifth day of the Ten-Day Accord Festival, an ancient tradition that celebrated the enduring peace between Opindale, Aldoria, and Moradaer. Lords, emissaries, and guardsmen from across the realms mingled in laughter and rivalry, unaware how fragile the night truly was.
“I hear your mines have slowed production,” said Lord Vaugre of Moradaer, swirling his cup. “Something about unstable rock beds?”
Governor Meridian Drake smiled. “Only unstable tongues, my lord, “ he said, though the warmth didn’t quite reach his eyes. “We’ve unearthed a vein of green iron that should make next year’s trade all the more profitable. Unless Moradaer prefers pearls to swords these days?”
“Pearls make excellent bribes,” Vaugre replied. “And sharper lords than you have been undone by them.”
King Edric watched the exchange with faint amusement. He leaned toward his wife, Queen Mirelle, and whispered, “The fifth night always brings out the peacocks.”
“Let them strut,” she murmured. “You’re still the lion.”
Musicians shifted to a lilting march, and a few of the younger lords and ladies began to dance. Gowns swirled, and laughter spiraled toward the high rafters.
Edric stood. His voice carried without magic, clear, strong, and commanding.
“Friends,” he began, his voice carrying without effort. “Tonight, we celebrate not just memory, but meaning. Since I was a boy, I’ve looked forward to the Accord Renewal. This table, these banners, they remind us of what is possible when kings and governors choose peace over conquest. I pledge, before gods and grain, that Opindale will honor this Accord until my final breath. And beyond.”
A round of “hear, hear” echoed, led by the High Duke of Moradaer and the Governor of Aldoria. Applause swept through the chamber like wind over fields.
When it faded, Edric gestured to Chancellor Ayhmeri, Master of Arms Aldric Terance, Governor Drake, the High Duke of Moradaer Calven Thrymos, and Head Steward Colton. “Now, if my honored leaders and your aides would follow me, we have urgent matters to discuss.”
They moved into the Hall of the Griffin, a private chamber of dark woods, etched maps, and silver candelabras. The air inside was still, almost sacred.
Edric began, “You’ve all likely heard rumors of an attack at the Pass and another on Stormhaven. I’m here to confirm both of them. Coordinated. Deadly. And we’ve heard nothing since.”
There was a moment of shared alarm, glances traded, aides whispering. “We’ve deployed a team to sperate fact from myth,” Edric continued. “A small team, that is meant to insert and gather information. Before we do anything, we need to know what we are up against.”
“They’re scouts then?” asked the Calven Thrymos.
“A hybrid,” said Edric. “Two of Harmon’s rangers. The rest are the non-traditional type. Untrained together,” Edric said. “Which is its own risk. Yet Harmon handpicked them all.”
“Non-Traditional? We’re talking criminals?” the Moradaer aide asked with disdain.
“Harmon said talented,” Edric replied.
“And their orders?” Ayhmeri asked.
“Reconnaissance only,” Edric answered. “They’re there to gather information. Observe, report. I have no intention of violating our newly signed treaty by launching military operations inside friendly lands.”
Chancellor Ayhmeri nodded. “Unorthodox, yes. But effective.”
“Because anyone bold enough to attack the pass is an enemy we must name,” Edric said. “Before more men die for guesses.”
High Duke Calven Thrymos started to ask a question when Head Steward Colton leaned to Governor Drake. “A word, my lord.” The scrape of Governor Drake’s chair broke the conversation when he stood. Edric was grateful for the brief respite.
The two of them stepped into a stone corridor on the other side of the room. Colton’s face did not change until they were beyond the glow of the chamber doors. Even then, his voice stayed level, as if the corridor belonged to him as much as the hall did.
“We have them,” he said, voice level. “Your wife. Your children.” Drake paled.
Colton continued, “You will do what is required before the final feast. Or their end will be… methodical. Painful. Clever. Dare I say a work of art?” He handed over a velvet pouch. Drake opened it by shaking hands. Inside was a bloodied lock of hair.
Colton smiled. “Hair grows back, dear governor. Body parts don’t. Please, don’t hesitate.” Colton lingered just long enough for the words to settle, then stepped away, leaving Drake with his thoughts.
Drake took one slow breath, then another, forcing his hands to still. When he turned back, the mask was already in place, even as his stomach tried to climb his throat. He stood there a moment longer than he should have. The door was just a door. The people behind it were just people. He told himself that until his hands stopped shaking, then went back inside. 
“What do you know of Lord Merrick?” Edric asked, eyes narrowing.
Drake took a moment, then he folded his arms behind his back. “Lord Merrick? He’s a minor lord,” Drake said lightly. “More ambition than pedigree. My council finds him more amusing than anything.”
“What do you know of his relic recovery jobs?”
Drake’s eyes darkened. “He calls himself a connoisseur of the art and what is old. Let him dig up relics. We’ll let him choke on dust.”
The others murmured approval, half-laughing at the bit. Chairs scraped; robes whispered as the circle broke apart. Most returned to the great hall, while Drake veered off toward a balcony.
The cold wind dragged at his sleeves as he stepped into the night, as one of his aides waited.
“They know about Merrick,” Drake whispered. “Edric and the rest.”
“Do they know what Merrick’s truly building?”
“No. And they won’t either. Not from me.”
The aide hesitated. “If he succeeds…”
“He’ll break the Accord in a heartbeat,” Drake muttered. “As he does, we all will have to suffer for it.”
Drake looked out into the night sky, staring into the distance as a man with the world on his shoulders.
Back in the great hall, music swelled. A new tune began, string and flute twining together in an elegant waltz. The younger nobles returned to the dance floor. Wine flowed like a river through jeweled goblets, masking the unease beneath the music.
A merchant lord from Moradaer whispered to an Opindalian trade baron about new tariffs. A noblewoman from Aldoria hinted that her daughter might be betrothed to a minor cousin of the royal line. Deals danced as much as feet.
The king stood near the terrace arch, watching and listening quietly. Queen Mirelle moved beside him.
“If they get it wrong,” he said quietly, “we don’t get to call it a misunderstanding. Not in a friendly country.” He watched a young lord spin his partner across the floor below. “Harmon believes they’re the right people. Criminals, sellswords, and ghosts, the lot of them.” A pause, “I just keep asking myself what happens if he’s wrong. We are so close now.” 
“But Harmon believes in them?” she asked.
“Yes, and I believe in him,” Edric replied. “Gods help me, I do.”
She touched his arm, “Then so do I.”
They turned together toward the room. A servant moved discreetly toward Drake and handed him a folded note. Drake opened it under the cover of his sleeve. It began.
‘Before the final feast. Or the next piece will not be so small.’

Drake’s eyes teared up as he continued to read. He folded the parchment and slipped it into the inner pocket of his coat after reading the entire note, a quick wipe of the eyes. Hell, he thought, is not fire. It is a room full of people laughing while you burn. 
Ayhmeri caught Edric’s eye and gave a subtle nod. The two of them moved to a quiet corner, and Ayhmeri handed him a sealed scroll.
Edric opened it. “It’s not safe. Your life is not safe. Not as safe as you are made to believe. Signed a friend,” Edric said. “What do you make of this?” he asked, handing the note back to Ayhmeri.
“I have no clue, Sire. I will find out.” Knowing what his king was going to ask of him. 
They stood together, watching the feast glow with light and illusion. But behind the music and the laughter, war was coming. And only shadows could stop it.
The walls of Lord Merrick’s private sanctum trembled with the force of his rage.
A shattered goblet slammed against the mural of the Founding, splintering red wine across the mosaic of ancient kings. Another piece of pottery, a Syrellian ash dish, exploded against the hearthstones, its thousand-year-old glaze crumbling underfoot.
***
Merrick roared. “Gone?! Vanished?! Do they think me a fool?”
The fresh fruit platter lay overturned across a velvet chaise, seeds bleeding into the fabric. The smell of citrus clung to the air, now soured by the scent of broken glaze, old parchment, and fury.
His breath came ragged. The veins along his neck bulged as he stalked from one ruined relic to another, one trembling hand trailing along the edge of a cracked obsidian plinth that once held a statue of the Old Flame, now toppled and in shards.
“I gave them everything, and they leave me with nothing!”
Merrick was tall, imposing even without armor, with the build of a man who once knew hunger and swore never to know it again. His long black coat, thread woven with blood-red trim, fluttered as he turned. The chain across his chest bore relic tokens, false medals for wars he bought his way into.
“No one will drag me back into the gutters,” he hissed aloud to no one. “Not after I’ve climbed so far.”
A knock came at the side door, soft, rhythmic, and respectful.
Merrick didn’t answer. He simply stared, seething.
The door opened slowly, revealing a man in a dark marshal’s cloak. He stepped in, boots perfectly polished, hair tied back in strict Forgehallow regulation. He wore the sigil of the Forged, a serrated black star over a silver flame, emblazoned at his shoulder.
“Lord Merrick,” the man said, bowing low, fist to heart. “Commandant Jerric, reporting.”
Merrick turned sharply. “Speak.”
“They’re gone. No trace. The entire party vanished from the lower vaults and escaped into the outer wilds. Our men tried to block them but were cut off by fire from within.”
Merrick’s eyes twitched. “I know they escaped. What I want to know is how. Who helped them?”
Jerric stayed still, voice clipped and measured. “We’re investigating. From what we’ve gathered, they were seen frequenting the Iron Flask tavern the days prior. Our teams are currently interrogating the innkeeper and combing through every possession they left behind.”
“Do you think they left clues?” Merrick scoffed. “These are professionals,” Merrick snarled. “Thieves. Killers. I was one of them once. There will be nothing to find.”
Jerric inclined his head. “They were precise. They were clean. They took their wounded with them. There’s evidence of a rigged explosion to disrupt our second-level reinforcements. Fire damage on three floors. The Forged suffered five losses. We estimate a dozen, give or take,” Jerric said. “Too many sets of prints. Too many hands at the breaches.”
He turned back to the central table, now cleared save for a detailed map of the surrounding lands. His fingers hovered over the inked outline of the northern ridges.
“I know where they’re headed,” Merrick murmured. “They’re going after my vault… my treasure… the legacy I dug from beneath your precious crowns.”
He slammed his palm on the table, eyes wide. “They’ve stolen my thief, my hammer, my scholar. A year of work. Gone.”
Jerric took a slow breath. “Shall we dispatch the contingency?”
“Yes,” Merrick growled. “Send them into the eastern climb. Through the old survey route. I want them caught. Alive!”
He looked up slowly, voice now cold and exact. “I want to make them scream.”
“Yes, my Lord.”
“And let it be known,” Merrick continued, turning with fire in his eyes, “Five hundred gold for verified information. A thousand gold for one delivered alive. Seven-fifty for a corpse, provided the head’s intact.”
He moved to a nearby shelf of scrolls, still trembling with rage. One he picked up, read, and tore down the center.
“I did not crawl from filth to be humiliated,” he whispered. “Not by… Not by…” He paused, voice low, thoughtful. “What was his name? Yes… an Emberlight lord from Estmere,” Merrick said slowly. “And Nyssa is tied to him as well.”
He crushed the parchment in his fist. “They will pay. All of them. I will get my pound.” He flung the scroll into the fire. “I will salt the sky before I let them take what is mine.”
Jerric bowed again. “We ride within the hour.”
Merrick did not answer. He simply stood before the burning scroll, eyes reflecting the flames.
***
The chamber crackled with firelight and broken glass. But beneath it all, something deeper stirred, the scent of power reclaimed, or perhaps the hunger that would never be filled.
The quiet of Queen Mirelle’s bedchamber was a far cry from the warmth and revelry of the Grand Hall. The soft crackle of the fire in the hearth battled gently against the muffled echoes of distant laughter and clinking glasses, now dulled by thick drapery and stone.
Mirelle stood near the mirror, her long braid half-loosened as her closest handmaid, Melianne, helped undo the delicate fastenings of her ceremonial gown. The queen’s back was bare now, pale under the firelight, the fabric slipping away with practiced care.
“You were radiant tonight, Your Grace,” Melianne said with a smile. “His Majesty couldn’t take his eyes off you. None of them could, really.”
Mirelle offered a small smile in return. “Let’s not flatter me too much, Mel. I may start believing it.”
The maid chuckled, folding the gown into a cedar-lined chest. “It’s true, though. It’s been years since I’ve seen a gathering like this. So many carriages today, we had to reroute them through the south lane. You should’ve seen it, felt like half the kingdom poured in. And even with all that, the guards barely checked the carts. Not the way they should have. Too many arrivals at once, and the captains were trying to keep the lanes clear so the gates did not choke with people.”
Mirelle turned toward her, now dressed in a flowing ivory nightrobe, the lace tracing her collarbone. “That doesn’t seem wise.”
“Oh, no,” Melianne said, quickly realizing the slip. “I mean, it’s the fifth day. Spirits are high, the gates are overworked… I’m sure it’s nothing. Just… so many people. It makes the kingdom feel proud. Whole.”
 Mirelle walked to the window, parting the curtains. The city glowed beyond the hill, the castle’s highest towers shimmering like crown points under the moon. But the moment struck her oddly. Like breath held too long. “Is your husband still on wall detail?” she asked without turning.
Melianne nodded. “Westgate. Long shifts, but he says the view’s worth it.”
The Queen said nothing for a long moment. Just watched. Then the dread crept in, not sudden, but in a slow, curling tide. She placed her palm flat against the glass.
From the shadows of a rooftop opposite the Royal Wing, a figure crouched low beneath the overhang of a tiled chimney. Dressed in dull leathers and soot-slicked cloth, the watcher kept perfectly still, a silhouette only to the stars. He had been there since dusk. Listening. Measuring. Calculating.
A small polished lens hovered before his left eye, tethered to a silver monocle bracket by a thread-fine armature. It held steady as if pinned to the air. Through it, the Queen’s chamber was a blur of soft lamplight and golden movement, until the curtain parted.
There she was. He didn’t breathe, not for those five full seconds. He slipped the lens aside and reached into the folds of his sleeve, withdrawing a thin cylinder no longer than a dagger hilt. He unfurled a narrow scroll inside, not to write, but to read.
It was names. Two crossed out. “Soon,” he whispered, restrained, almost breathless. His hand passed over the sigil stitched inside his coat. He tucked the scroll away, slid into the shadow, and vanished.
Behind him, a single glimmer of the Queen’s window still shone. The night wrapped around the castle like a cloak, not of comfort, but of patience.






Chapter Twenty-Five
The snow had crusted hard overnight, its surface gleaming like hammered glass under the late morning sun. Pines swayed in the wind above Luca’s team as they picked their way through the narrowing forest trail, hooves crunching frost, every breath steaming. The path curled like a blade toward the looming mountain pass, an ancient road barely visible beneath the press of winter’s slow reclaiming.
Luca led, his silhouette stark against the pale glow of the day, cloak trailing behind like the shadow of a noose. He said nothing. He rarely did. Behind him, Lysana adjusted her reins with unconscious precision, the tips of her fingers red but steady, her posture alert. Aymir and Taerel followed last, their horses moving in sync, silent but for the low squeaks of saddle leather and the wind’s thin whistle through trees stripped bare.
Taerel shifted in the saddle. Not restless. Just counting something the rest of them couldn't see. But today, his body twitched with the tension of something brewing under his skin. The chill of the mountain air stole the last warmth from their bones.
“I’ve been thinking,” he said aloud, tone conversational. “About something I can make.”
Aymir, riding just to his left, cocked a brow. “The enchanted band?”
Taerel nodded. “That bracelet Luca uses to talk to the others. I think I can replicate its function. Maybe not perfectly, but enough to keep us connected.”
“You’re going to have to tell them,” Aymir said, eyes forward. “About what you are.”
Taerel hesitated, then sat up straighter. “Luca opened up last night. Told us who he really was. Where he came from. That… means something. I think it’s time I do the same.”
Aymir gave a small nod. “Then do it right. I’ve got your back.”
Without another word, Taerel urged his horse up to Luca’s side. The wind tugged at his cloak, and his pale gloves twitched as he steeled himself.
Luca didn’t glance over. “Something wrong?”
“I need to examine your bracelet,” Taerel said.
Luca hesitated, then unfastened the band and passed it over. “Don’t lose it.”
“I’m not Lysana,” Taerel said with a smile.
“Careful with that,” Lysana called from behind, the amusement clear in her voice. “You'd notice the quiet before long.”
“Touché,” Taerel said with a grin.
“I need to understand its enchantments. Structure. Runes. Everything, so that I can copy them,” said Taerel.
Luca’s eyes flicked sideways. “You can read runes?”
“Better than most.” Taerel exhaled. “Just… let me show you something.”
Taerel scanned the ridge and the road below, listening. Only when nothing stirred did he pull his horse to a stop. The others reined theirs in. He reached up and unclasped something near his temple. His fingers hesitated just a moment, then he removed the mask. It didn’t slide off with ceremony. No glow, no ripple. One moment, Taerel wore the calm brown-eyed face they knew. The next, it was gone.
His skin darkened, shifting to a deep midnight black, the color of sky before a storm. His eyes turned bone-white, pupil-less, lit softly from somewhere that had nothing to do with the sun. His hair unfurled, long and ashen, tied back into a tight warrior’s tail that hung over one shoulder like spun silver rope.
Lysana drew a breath. “By the stars…”
“I’m Zhar’ai,” Taerel said quietly.
For a heartbeat, no one spoke, nobody moved. The wind hissed through the trees, tugging at cloaks and reins.
Lysana blinked once, eyes wide. “You could have warned a girl before you turned into a walking night sky,” she muttered, half under her breath.
Aymir’s jaw clenched, then eased. “Told you he was dramatic,” he said quietly, though his gaze never left his brother’s face.
Luca did not flinch. He studied Taerel as if weighing a tactical report, not a confession. “I didn’t raise it sooner,” Taerel said, not looking away. “I am cautious. Caution keeps people alive. Trust comes later. In our line of work, information is currency. Secrets are capital.”
Taerel paused, then gave a half-bow from the saddle. “One of the last. My tribe could read and write runes in ways no one else could, feel their meanings like music. But the Brotherhood hunted us for decades. Most of my people are dead. I didn’t know if I ever could show you… or anyone. I’ve spent most of my life running, not just from them. From being seen at all. You get hunted long enough. You stop knowing what trust even feels like.”
He glanced toward Luca, his mask now tucked away, his true face open beneath the sky.
“Trust isn't something I was taught to give.” He let out a slow breath through his nose. “Not when everyone I’ve known paid in blood for what we are. I don’t know if this is the right time, or even if it’s safe… but I’m tired of hiding. And I think you two deserve the truth.”
“Then how are you guys brothers?” asked Lysana.
Aymir answered, “What gave it away?” He gave a short chuckle. “Short version.” He kept his eyes ahead. “When our father helped hide a few of his tribe, his mother was among them. We were being hunted, as well. When our father fell for his mother, it was double the pain. Things grew tense for our family. Yet, we all escaped. Taerel was raised in hiding, behind stories and shadow.”
“I show you all this because we need this,” Taerel replied. “You heard what happened to the other team. Our communications could fail at the most inopportune time. This isn’t just about trust anymore. It’s survival.”
“I thought you called each other brother because you have been together so long, but you are really brothers,” Lysana said.
Taerel smiled faintly. “Aymir got the looks. I got the ancient abilities and an unfortunate habit of second-guessing every room I walk into.” He looked down to examine the bracelet. He turned it over with reverence. “Arcanite core. Aether-harmonic bindings. Clean work,” Taerel said. “Whoever made this understood resonance.”
He tapped a sigil near the base. “This here is the nexus rune. It links with the partner band, one-way mental projection. This is some good work.”
He handed it back. “I am going to need some material, but I think I could recreate it for us.”
Luca accepted it silently, slipping it back on. “I will keep my eye out.”
They rode on. Taerel checked the seal on his gauntlet again, though it had not shifted. The sun rose higher, snow blindingly bright on the slope ahead. Around midday, the trees began to thin into wind-scarred pines twisted by years of storms. The ridge beckoned just ahead, its rocky crown giving way to a distant haze of smoke curling faintly into the sky.
Taerel and Aymir rode side by side, the muffled clop of hooves subdued beneath the soft hush of wind-swept snow. Lysana dropped back to their pace, twisting slightly in her saddle to glance at Taerel with an amused look.
“Were you planning on keeping your little secret to yourself the whole time?” she said casually, glancing ahead toward the thinning trees.
Taerel blinked. “You mean the whole… terrifying midnight-black, rune-carved soul-wielder look?”
She smirked. “Yeah, that one.”
Aymir chuckled. “He used to keep the mask on in his sleep. We thought he was shy. Turns out he’s just worried about making people nervous.”
“It’s more than that,” Taerel said, his tone sobering. “The Brotherhood hunted me, my entire life. You can see that sharing is not in my best interest. My people, the Zhar’ai, were hunted to the brink of extinction. All because they wanted to control our ability.”
“Have you always looked like a spirit from a midnight storybook?” Lysana asked.
“All my life,” Taerel replied with a smirk. The expression did not quite reach his eyes.
Ahead of them, Luca’s voice carried back through the cold. “Keep talking if you have to,” he said, not looking over, “but keep your ears open. We are close to the pass.”
Aymir snorted softly. “See? That is Luca’s way of saying he is glad you took the mask off.”
“And your mask?” asked Lysana.
“A gift, from one of the families we helped,” answered Aymir.
She gave him a playful shove with her shoulder. “You’re weird, Ty. I like weird. Just don’t go glowing in the dark without warning.”
Taerel gave a small shrug. “Because fear spreads fast. And people who get nervous make mistakes. I’ve been safer behind a lie. Plus, I just met you guys. When you're hunted all your life, you're a little hesitant to share your secrets.”
Lysana leaned forward in the saddle, her expression thoughtful. That’s when the smell hit them.
“Tar,” Aymir muttered. “Smoke. Not just a cook fire either, it's big.”
Taerel sniffed once. “Forge smoke as well. Heavy.”
They crested the final ridge as the smoke became more visible. Luca raised a hand and slowed. They crept to a low ridge, careful to keep their silhouettes below the rise. From there, the trees fell away into a snow-covered basin. From this height, they could see far across the wide valley basin. In the basin, nestled in smoke and frost, was another war camp.
A sea of movement lay below, crude orcish tents, timber palisades reinforced with scavenged iron, siege gear lashed to beasts of burden. Goblins darted between structures like rats, carrying bundles of scrap and weapons. Larger orcs, musclebound, brutal, stood watch on makeshift towers or hunched near bonfires, sharpening axes. Worgs, massive wolf-like beasts with curling fangs and intelligent eyes, paced in tight circles inside their pens.
At the camp’s center stood a totem, tall, made from a twisted spire of bone and rusted blades, bound together with sinew and marked with fresh blood. Lysana’s hand tightened on her reins at the sight. “It smelled wrong, a tang of unnatural stillness as well,” Aymir said.
Before it sat a hunched shaman in robes of stretched skin, muttering to himself as his staff pulsed with an eerie violet glow. Next to that totem, protruding from the earth like a black thorn, was a staff nearly identical to the one Luca’s other team had found in the previous orc encampment. This one was larger. Sharper. Meaner.
A chill slipped down Taerel’s spine. “That’s the same design.” Taerel's hand had gone still on his reins without him choosing to stop it. One had been bad. Two meant something had changed, or was changing, and nobody had told them yet.
Luca went still. “They’re connected, maybe.”
Below, smoke wafted from the battered walls of the pass’s fortification. Black scorch marks marred the stone, and several towers were partially collapsed. Signal fires burned on the upper parapets. Not many. But enough to show someone was still alive inside.
Luca’s voice dropped. “We need to fall back before they spot us.” They backed down quickly, following a ledge that dipped into thick pine cover. Once they were safely back from the ridge, Luca pulled the bracelet back onto his wrist and pressed two fingers against its inner side, eyes closing.
“Harmon,” he said in a low voice, “this is Luca. Confirm the visual of a major orc encampment outside the pass’s gates. Fort appears damaged but manned. Orcs number fifty-plus, with goblins, Joblins, and at least one worg pack. Central totem matches a known hostile artifact. Will provide full report shortly.” He removed his fingers from the band, exhaled slowly, and turned to the group.
“Alright,” Luca said. “Now we get every detail. Spread out. Count them. Watch their patrols. Map the damn place if you have to.”
Lysana gave a nod, already unpacking her spyglass. “I’ll check elevation, vantage, and watch lines. Maybe find a flank route.”
Aymir pulled his long scope from the saddle. “I’ll follow the supply flow. See how they’re managing rations and movement.”
Taerel pulled out a small writing board, glancing up at Luca. “I’ll look for weak points. Hidden paths. Open perimeters. And how their units move together.” He observed that their patrols held wide, unbroken arcs, as if nothing above them was worth fearing.
They held to the tree line, using each snowbank to mask their silhouettes, moving in short, deliberate surges between cover. Lysana lay prone in the frost, elbow dug into a flat stone, taking in the camp. “North wall’s loose,” she whispered, talking to herself. “Gap near the cooking pits. Could run a team through there if they’re quick and quiet.”
Aymir’s voice came low, from the brush nearby. “From what I can tell, I see they have gotten three main patrol units rotating in an hourglass pattern. They’re trained. Not tribal chaos. And... I’m seeing at least two dozen Joblins doing repairs.”
Taerel murmured, “There’s a break in their southern perimeter. Weak slope, covered in scree. Would take a climber with some guts to exploit it, but it’s there.”
Luca crouched beside a rock outcropping, watching a pair of orc sentries switch shifts. Their pattern was exact, military even. That chilled him more than their numbers.
“They’re too organized,” he muttered. “Orcs don’t do siege warfare. They don’t build palisades and wait. They charge. They break. They don’t starve people out.”
Lysana’s voice came back, flat and certain. “They’ve changed. Or someone’s changed them.”
Luca’s eyes narrowed at the swirling campfires below. The siege lines moved like a slow tide around the battered fort. He traced the formation with a gloved finger, lips tightening.
“We could break this,” he muttered, barely audible. “Slip down under the cover of the dark. Kill their leader. Scatter the Worgs. If I get to the shaman, cut the head from the snake, it might be enough.”
“No.” Came from behind him, Lysana didn’t raise her voice. Luca turned, brows raised.
She crouched beside him, chin forward, jaw tight. “That’s not our directive. We’re here to gather information, not start a war. If we engage now, without knowing what else is waiting in those hills, we risk everything, including the people inside that fort and the city.”
He studied her. Her tone wasn’t challenging; it was reminding. Grounding.
She added, “Give us time. A day. Maybe two. We’ll learn their routines. Their weaknesses. Then, when the order comes, we won’t be guessing.”
Luca stared back out at the torch-lit ring of tents. Then he nodded once, a sharp dip of his chin.
“You’re right,” he said quietly. “We don’t strike blind.”
“You aren’t alone on this one. You have a team. Let's work as one, okay.” Lysana said with a smile, and a true smile in his direction.
Luca nodded once. He looked away first.
By nightfall, the group pulled back again, setting up a low-profile camp a short ride from the ridge, hidden among fallen logs and a dense copse of trees. Snow fell in slow flakes, catching in their lashes and furred cloaks.
They gathered close around a small ember fire, just enough to warm their hands.
“Here’s what we know,” Luca said, voice low. “Orcs, goblins, Joblins, and trained Worgs. One shaman. Siege tactics. More than we first counted. Seventy to eighty total.”
Taerel’s fingers brushed the runes along his rifle once, then fell still. Somewhere out in the dark, an orc barked a short command. The sound carried thin on the wind, then faded.
Luca waited until the silence settled again before continuing. “Multiple tents for storage, crates, tar, and ironworks. No spellcasters beyond the shaman, but I can’t confirm his capability.”
Taerel added, “Totem in the center. Another of those staves. Larger. Probably more powerful.”
Aymir chimed in, “Fort looks like hell, but it’s holding. Fires on the ramparts mean survivors. Probably trying to wait this out.”
Lysana blew warm breath into her cupped palms. “That means they’re not pushing until something changes. Until reinforcements arrive. Or until their food runs out. Either way, we have time. But not much.”
Luca nodded grimly. “We’ll stay the night. Two-person rotations. One is keeping an eye on the ridge. One is watching our camp. Rotate every two hours. That way, we get rest without losing our edge.” Taerel stretched out the shift schedule, and they divvied up in silence.
I’ll send the full report to Harmon,” Luca said. “Then we wait. See what he says.” He stood, walked back to the edge of their campsite, and activated the bracelet.
“This is Luca. Full recon complete. Hostiles number seventy to eighty, more than our first count. The fort is under siege but holding. The city is largely in ruins. Orcs are unusually organized. Camp includes orcs, goblins, Joblins, Worgs, and a central shaman with a matching staff. An estimated three weak points for infiltration. Will hold position until further instruction. Expect a detailed map and cycles in follow-up.”
Luca sat quietly, one boot planted in the snow, fingers toying with the edge of his scarf. When the voice of young Weslin appeared in his head, Weslin relayed the message from Harmon. The message was sharp and to the point. ‘What can you tell me about the fort? Are the defenders alive? Anyone left in the city? Can you get word to them?’ The connection was narrow, strained, thin, and distant. Enough for words. Not enough for distinctness.
The message burned with urgency. It wasn’t a command. It was a plea wrapped in the voice of a man trying to keep a war from boiling over. Luca tensed. He turned and gathered the team without hesitation.
“Harmon wants a clearer picture of the fort,” he said once they were together. “Survivors. Defensive status. The city just outside, what’s left of it, if anyone is left in it. He wants us to send them a message, let them know we're out here. We need to find a way to do that, or create one.”
“Right, and if we blunder in announcing ourselves, we get them killed before they even know there's help coming,” Aymir said, arms folded. “We have to get it right. We have one shot at this.”
Lysana’s gaze flicked toward the ridge. “We will not blunder,” she said. “We find the right way in, or we do not go at all.”
Luca’s jaw tightened, the lines at the corners of his eyes deepening. “Which is why we do this carefully,” he said. “No chances we do not have to take.”
“Smoke patterns, maybe,” Lysana said, her eyes moving toward the ridge. “Light signals. Or we get a runner close enough to throw something over the wall without getting seen.”
“We’re not getting that close,” Luca said. “Not until we know every damn rock and ledge around that place.”
Lysana nodded. “We’ll scout for access routes. Learn the area around us, but we should wait for light to do this, making it a bit easier to find them.”
“Good,” Luca said, his voice low and focused. “We will maintain surveillance on the camp overnight still. Reporting any change, any shift, anything. While we still look for alternate entry points to the city and the fort. We need to know everything.”
Taerel adjusted his pack. “And if we find a way in?”
“Don’t go in,” Luca said sharply. “Not yet. Mark it. Sketch it. Bring it back. We get that intel to Harmon, and he’ll decide. Also, be mindful. We don’t know how deep their patrols run.”
“Got it,” Aymir said. 
Luca watched them break into motion, their boots scraping the snow, their cloaks drawing tight, their eyes already scanning the tree lines and ridge contours.
He lingered for a moment as the wind howled across the rise, pulling at his cloak like a ghost’s hand, and then began to follow. It did take them a long time to return to the ridge. The four of them pressed low against the rocks just beneath the ridgeline, watching the siege camp through narrow slits in the frost-bitten trees. Below, the sprawling orc encampment still moved like a living beast, fires flickering, shadows trudging between tents, Worgs pacing alongside iron-banded cages, and the guttural sounds of low, savage speech echoing off the mountainside.
“Do any of you see a good vantage point to get a better view?” Luca asked.
Taerel’s eyes narrowed as he scanned the ridgeline beyond their current perch. A fallen pine angled against a split boulder about thirty yards upslope caught his attention, not much, but just enough to conceal movement if they kept low.
“There,” he whispered, pointing with two fingers. “That ridge curves south. If we loop behind it, we might catch a sharper angle above the city, while still having an eye on the enemy’s camp.”
Luca gave a tight nod. “Let’s move.”
Lysana was already moving, hunched low, her boots crunching softly. “It’s steep, but doable,” she muttered. “We’ll have to belly-crawl the last stretch. Anything more upright, we’ll silhouette ourselves.”
The snow was knee-deep in places, crusted and noisy. Each step had to be deliberate, each movement measured.
Twice, Taerel reached out, steadying a branch before it could dump a sheet of snow across their backs. Lysana stayed ahead, eyes flitting between ridgeline breaks and where the smoke from the fort curled faintly upward.
As they climbed, the wind shifted. A distant orc horn called from the camp below, long, low, and guttural. Everyone froze.
No movement came in response. No footfalls, no shouting. Just the wind again, and the distant crackle of frozen wood in some unseen fire. A warning call, maybe. Or just an echo of routine.
Aymir gave a low whistle once they were closer. “This spot’s tighter,” he said, crouching behind a jut of rock. “We’ll see what we need from here.”
They settled behind the new ridge, breath tight, eyes locked to the devastation ahead.
From this new angle, they could see farther than before, past the broken outer wall, down into the remnants of the city that hugged the base of the pass. Smoke still curled up from blackened structures, most of them gutted or collapsed from the initial attack. At a glance, Taerel guessed that at least seventy percent of the buildings were reduced to charred skeletons.
Luca felt something in his chest loosen and twist all at once. Through his looking glass, Luca could make out survivors huddled within the stone arches of the city’s old chapel, its roof miraculously untouched. Inside, flickering lantern light betrayed movement, small, slow, deliberate. He thought it had to be civilians who were injured and afraid. “They’re holed up in the chapel,” he murmured. “Still people alive down there.”
“I count about thirty people, for what I can make out,” Aymir said to Lysana, who was standing beside him. Her fingers were white-knuckling a small slate where she’d scratched notes with charcoal.
Taerel, crouched nearby, added, “Saw a few inside the city wall, ten maybe. Forward observers, probably. Helping civilians. I saw a pair dragging someone into cover.”
“And the fort?” Luca asked.
“They’ve got some kind of auxiliary archer group on top of the wall,” Aymir said. “They might be able to hit targets in the kill zone if they had to, but they’re spread thin.”
Lysana gave a low grunt. “That city should’ve been wiped clean. But it wasn’t. And the orcs haven’t breached. Why? This doesn’t make any sense.”
“They’re being contained,” Taerel said. “Someone wants them alive, or they just don’t care. Look, you can see they shifted targets.”
“There has to be something else at play here,” Luca muttered.
Then his eyes fell back to the center of the orc camp. Looking for any kind of answer, but all their eyes were on the twisted black totem crowned with scavenged bones. “And that staff,” Luca said.
“A better version,” Taerel said. “No doubt. And it’s active.”
“We need to report,” Luca said. 
They backed away from the ridge, boots crunching softly in snow, breath steaming. Once they reached a safe distance, Luca lifted the bracelet to his lips and whispered the report, concise, tactical, and thorough.
Again, Luca pictured Weslin in his head, then he gave his report. “There are civilian survivors within the city. We have confirmed movement within the chapel. Defensive perimeter remains intact, fort not yet breached. Archer detachments observed on the wall and auxiliary units inside the perimeter. Damage to the city is estimated at 70% or more gone.
