A staff similar to the previous artifact is located in the center of the enemy camp, under shaman control.
Will begin phased surveillance now. Requesting guidance on potential communication with survivors and whether reinforcements are being prepared. Will report again soon.”
“Do any of you see a way to get them a message of some kind?” Luca asked.
“Maybe a note on an arrow from here, then we move?” Lysana asked.
“The orc might see that, don’t you think?” Luca replied.
“Not sure, but best I got, boss,” Lysana said.
“All right, let's see if we can think of something else before we go with that,” Luca said. “Time to start the two-man teams’ rotation. One on overwatch at the ridge, one on camp guard. Two rest, two hours each rotation.”
“Who pairs with whom?” Lysana asked.
“You tell me,” Luca said. “I trust you.” He was already turning away.
“I’ll take Taerel with me for first watch,” she said without hesitation.
Aymir nodded. “Luca and me then.”
“Sounds good,” Luca replied. “Be sharp. I want eyes on everything,” Luca said. Aymir and Luca started to make their trip back to their camp, while Taerel and Lysana started setting up a more permanent observation position.
Above them, the mountains stood still. Below them, the siege dragged on. And in the space between shadow and silence, a cold wind howled like prophecy through the trees.






Chapter Twenty-Six
The acrid stench hit first, thick, burnt oil and scorched pitch. It clawed in Aymir’s nose, dragged through his lungs, and jolted him upright before he fully understood why. He blinked hard, his heart punching against his ribs. The canvas above his head shuddered from the wind, but it wasn’t that; it was the smell. A smell he hadn’t known in years. A memory that had seared itself into his past like a brand: battlefield smoke, burning cities, and screams buried under mortar fire.
Aymir jerked his cloak aside and sat up, sweat already breaking across his brow despite the morning cold.
“Do you smell that?” he asked as Luca emerged from the frost-creased lean-to beside him, already slipping on his bracers and pulling his cloak over his shoulders.
Luca gave one slow nod as he buckled his sword belt. “Burning oil. Tar and pitch. They’ve started something.”
Without another word, the two jogged through the snow toward the ridge above their camp, boots crunched over the hard-crusted drifts. Wind screamed low across the valley, carrying the scent of smoke, fresh, foul, and purposeful.
Taerel was already prone at the edge of the ridge, scope braced against a rock. He didn’t look up.
“They’re hammering the fort. Not just arrows. Fire pots. Burning oil. Catapult loads soaked in pitch. They’re trying to cook the defenders alive.”
Lysana crouched nearby, her hand shading her eyes as she scanned the horizon. Her jaw tightened as a fresh burst of flame licked up from the city below, lighting the low clouds a sickly orange.
Luca crouched beside her, eyes locked on the distant chaos. The scent of war crept up the slope, mingling with screams and the low rumble of impact.
He didn’t hesitate. “Today’s priority changes. We find a way into that city. Now. Lysana, you’re with me.”
He turned, and this time he didn't wait to see if they were ready. “Aymir. Taerel. Eyes on the camp. Take down what you see. Movements, shifts, anything that doesn’t fit.” Aymir gave a grim nod, already wiping the lens of his looking glass.
As Luca and Lysana melted into the tree line toward the alternate ridge, Taerel sat down beside his brother. “We’ve seen a dozen battle drills,” Taerel said. “Why do I feel like this one’s different?”
Aymir didn’t answer right away. His gaze was distant. Fixed. Not on the orc camp, but on something far older. His voice, when it came, was hollow. “Because it is.” A fresh burst of flame rolled up from the city below, a low roar that crawled through the wind and rattled the frozen branches overhead.
Taerel watched him a moment longer. “You went back there again, didn’t you?”
Aymir’s eyes didn’t move. “When the oil hit, I was back in the trenches. Smoke everywhere. Fire climbing bodies.” His eyes watered. “I don’t even remember how I got out.”

Taerel didn’t push. Instead, he reached over and lightly knocked his knuckles against Aymir’s arm, grounding him as another wave of smoke tore across the ridge. “Hey. We’re not there anymore. We’re here. I’ve got your back, always.”
It took a moment, but Aymir blinked. Shook his head once. The haze began to lift. His gaze dropped back to the camp. Worgs circled something below, snarling over the kill. Aymir watched them for a moment. “Five coppers on the mangy one with the half-tail gets it first.”
Taerel chuckled. “You’re on.”
Luca and Lysana’s first attempt came on the lower ridge. A narrow rock shelf wound behind a frost-cracked boulder, offering a potential path closer to the city’s eastern flank. But halfway down, the trail gave out, collapsing beneath a recent rockfall; jagged stone and icy debris choked the ledge.
“No good,” Lysana muttered, eyes scanning the drop. “We’d break our necks before we ever reached the bottom.”
They circled wide. The second route looped through an old hunting trail, its narrow cut choked by avalanche debris and stone, sealing it as thoroughly as the first. Near the bottom, they found the remains of a collapse. “Looks like an avalanche a while back,” Luca said, looking at ten feet of compacted snow and boulders.
“Again?” Luca hissed. “How is every path sealed?”
Lysana looked at the chokepoints, then at him. Her cheeks were wind-raw, her breath coming in sharp white puffs. “It's a fort,” she said. “Keeping people out is its purpose.” No complaint in it. Just a fact. She let it sit for a moment. “Either winter did this, or someone worked these ridges before we got here.”
Luca went still. A distant scream rolled down the mountain and faded into the wind. His hands stayed where they were. So did he.
Lysana didn't move either. She stood at his shoulder, watching the same stretch of ruined wall, the same wall that kept giving them nothing. The wind cut between them, and neither of them said anything about it.
Below, the orcs loosed another volley. She watched the arrows climb and fall, black lines against the pale sky, swallowed by the noise and ruin below.
Her eyes moved to her own quiver.
“Charcoal marker,” she said. “Do you have one?”
He pulled it from his kit without asking why. She was already moving, spreading a strip of oiled map-cloth flat against her knee, the waxed kind Rangers used for field notes. She wrote four short lines, her hand steady despite the cold, rolled the cloth tight, and tied it to a shaft with a cord stripped from her bootlace.
“We can't reach them on foot. We can't call out. We can't light a signal.” She checked the weight of the arrow and balanced it once in her palm. “But they're already watching the sky. One more shaft won't stand out.”
She nocked it and waited for the next orc volley. She fired it. Her arrow flew true and struck the church’s doorframe. “Now we wait,” she said, exhaling.
They didn’t move. Didn’t speak. Snow drifted down like ash.
Lysana crouched low beneath the skeletal shadow of a pine, her breath curling in the air like smoke. Above her, the wind had picked up, biting, constant, whispering across the ridge and through the mountain trees with the chill of old bones. She and Luca had taken shelter in their second vantage point, a narrow cut of rock and pine above the battered city, waiting for a reply to the arrow she’d loosed earlier.
Snow crept into the folds of their armor and boots, numbing fingers and stiffening joints. They hadn’t moved much since launching the arrow into the church’s doorframe. Every motion risked detection. Luca shifted now, flexing his cramping legs and rotating his shoulder.
The smell of ash and oil still clung to the air, sharper now, carried by the wind. And below, the three massive bonfires in the orc siege camp lit the entire valley with flickering orange and red, casting leaping shadows along the half-ruined walls of the city. From this angle, the light made it look as if the very earth were burning.
They had been waiting for hours. Long enough for the light to thin and the cold to settle deep.
A shadow passed across one of the far parapets before vanishing again. “They’re moving more tonight,” Lysana muttered, eyes narrowed.
Luca didn’t respond immediately. He had that stillness about him again—his breath quiet, his jaw set. She knew that look. He was thinking, calculating, trying to find the thread in the chaos.
“You think they got it?” he murmured.
Lysana nodded slightly, her hood tugged low against the wind. “They got it. They just don’t know how to answer yet.”
A long moment passed before she added, “We’re not exactly a normal cavalry rescue.”
Then the movement caught her eye. Then she froze. “Look,” she whispered.
Out of the church’s doors two figures stepped into view, wrapped in what looked like dyed bedding tied to old poles. The makeshift signal flags waved slowly, deliberately—right to left, then a short diagonal, then up, pause, then down. The flags were mismatched and frayed, but the message was unmistakable.
Lysana read the signal, breath catching in her throat. “They’re short on everything—medicine, food, clean water. The wounded can’t be moved. They need help fast.”
Luca exhaled hard. “All right. That’s our open line.”
They scrambled back down the slope toward the ridge line, and the two brothers were posted up. Their boots crunched through crusted snow. At the bottom, the brothers were already sitting against a log back from the ledge, Aymir sipping from a battered waterskin, Taerel hunched over the maps and noteboards by the dying glow of a covered lantern.
Aymir adjusted the charcoal slate he'd laid across a canvas-covered plank. “Orcs rotated guard lines,” he said, more to himself. “North flank just took in replacements. Standard pattern, no surprises.”
Taerel peered through the scope again. “Check the northwest pen. That worg pup from earlier is gone.”
Aymir marked it. “Might be out hunting.”
“Or scouting,” Taerel muttered. He adjusted the scope a fraction. “Movement feels tighter today.”
Taerel gestured toward the camp. “At this rate, I’m tempted to wager on which orc spills the stew next.”
“Left-handed tusker. Guaranteed,” Aymir said. “He’s been fumbling that ladle all morning.”
Both Luca and Lysana made their way to the brothers and their position. Aymir noticed them first as they returned. “How’d it go?” Aymir asked, brushing a light sheen of frost from his eyebrows.
Luca crouched near the boards. “We made contact. They have a high wounded count. They are held up in the church. We were also right about their supplies almost being gone, and we still don’t have a way in.”
“Seems the gods are unkind today,” Taerel muttered, glancing toward the orange sky as another fire pot burst in the distance.
Luca glanced at the brothers. “We’re stretched thin. No reliable means to pass messages to each other. Limited eyes. Low supplies.” His eyes stayed on the siege camp a moment longer, as if giving himself exactly enough time to let the weight of it settle. “Taerel, I need you to ride and find a village or anything at all. Get supplies and bring them back. Anything, anything useful that you can find, and medical supplies for those inside. They are going to need that, I think. Get what you need to start those bracelets, as well. We need better ways to pass messages.”
Taerel’s gaze went to the dark timberline. “If the roads aren’t choked and the patrols don’t turn, I can be back within, let’s say, two days.” He swung into the saddle. “If they do, I'll come back when I can. Better late with provisions than swift and dead.”
“Take the eastern slope,” Luca added. “They’re more likely to have more patrols westward.”
Taerel gave a short nod and turned toward the camp.
Luca turned to Aymir. “Break down camp. We’re moving tonight. Lysana, take point and pick a new location. Somewhere east of the ridge. We’ve been there too long already.”
She nodded. “If we’re going to be ghosts, we can’t sleep in the same bed twice.”
Aymir gave a dry chuckle. “Truth in that.”
As Aymir stalked off toward the canvas shelters, Luca and Lysana lingered, glancing over the notched records the brothers had carved into the wood. Patrol rotations, forge output, and the number of orcs moving between tents. The system was crude but effective.
Each record was timestamped using the sun’s position and measured in fingers from the horizon, a technique old Rangers called the Fennar method.
They took turns scanning the camp again, confirming tallies, adding new ones. The siege didn’t sleep. Worgs prowled. Orcs rotated in disciplined patterns. Goblins argued around fires. And in the far corner near the totem, a group of humans still knelt in chains. Lysana had gone very still when she spotted them. She didn't say anything. She didn't have to. 
At the edge of camp, Taerel and Aymir stood by their mounts. “If it flips to tails,” Taerel whispered, holding up his worn coin, “tell Dad I tried.”
Aymir grunted. “Don’t be stupid. You’re too annoying to die.”
Taerel flipped the coin once more, caught it, and pocketed it without looking. “I've played worse hands.” They grinned the way men do when the next breath isn't guaranteed, and they've stopped pretending otherwise.
“Blood before thunder,” Aymir said.
“Thunder before silence,” Taerel replied.
Taerel embraced him briefly but fiercely. They tapped foreheads.
“What do we always say?” Taerel asked.
“Not goodbye. Just later.” A cold gust swept through the trees and rattled the saddle straps, as if urging him on. Taerel mounted and turned east, vanishing between the trees. The camp faded behind him. And behind him, the old fires still burned, and The Pass burned with them.
At the new campsite, in a shallow depression between two clustered firs, half-hidden by drifted snow, Luca and Lysana laid out their gear again. No fire. No noise. Just lean-tos and silent breath, and the distant sound of the siege carrying up the mountain like something that didn't know they were there. 
Aymir was cleaning his rifle by lamplight, his hands steady despite the tension in his jaw.
Lysana finally asked, “Could you explain how that thing works? I would like to know.”
He glanced up, eyes tired but focused. “Science and gears. Not magic. Chambered rounds with chemical triggers in this revolving chamber, copper bands, and etched spirals to guide the propulsion. I know how to keep it breathing, and it speaks when I ask.”
She watched him polish the barrel, her gaze flicking toward the distant fires. The wind carried a rising edge, a warning that something was shifting.
Luca stood near the edge of the ridge, cloak fluttering in the wind. “I’ll take first watch. You two get some sleep. We rotate every four hours. Tomorrow... we start again.”
They nodded, settling into their blankets, pulling hoods low. Just as the forest began to settle, Lysana jerked upright.
“Flags,” she whispered. “They’re signaling again.”
Luca was at her side instantly. The movements were slower now, more hesitant. The color of the bedding flags had changed, but the pattern was unmistakable.
“They found something,” Lysana said, brow furrowed. “A tunnel. Its condition’s unclear. If it’s good, it should run behind the town, through the undercroft. They’re marking coordinates for us to find it.”
She turned to Luca. “Give me the map.” He handed it over, and she traced a gloved finger along the edge of the valley. “Here,” she said softly. “We start here tomorrow.”
Luca exhaled slowly. “Let’s hope.”
Aymir closed his eyes for a moment. “Thank you, God the Creator.” 
The wind howled once more. Behind them, the camp sat in darkness. Ahead, the siege lit the world in flame. And somewhere out there, Taerel rode into the unknown.






Chapter Twenty-Seven
The air was cold but not biting, just enough to carry the memory of last night’s frost in the lungs. A thin cover of cloud stretched across the sky, muting the sun to a dull, pale disk that barely colored the afternoon. After nearly fourteen hours of hard riding, the camp had finally taken shape in the crook of a narrow, wooded valley, nestled beneath a scrim of trees that did little to break the northern wind.
Inside Harmon’s tent, the air was thick with quiet dread. Weslin sat beside the cot, his small frame curled slightly forward, fingertips resting on the back of Harmon’s hand. The older man lay still, chest rising shallowly beneath his blanket, a glisten of sweat dampening his brow despite the cool. Aurelia sat nearby, quietly sorting fresh linens and tonic supplies, her eyes shifting between Harmon and the boy with a faint crease of worry marring her brow.
“He’s breathing steady,” Weslin muttered, almost to himself. “But it’s too steady, like he’s stuck. Like nothing’s moving forward.”
“Still no change?” Garr’s voice broke the hush, gravel-thick and low.
Weslin shook his head, lips pale. “No fever, no convulsions. But nothing else either. He hasn’t flinched, or stirred, or blinked. It’s like he’s... not here.”
Garr hovered near the flap of the tent, his arms crossed in a pose he hoped looked like calm leadership. In truth, he felt like a man treading water in armor, every decision heavier than the last. He was trying not to let it show, but it was eating at him.
“We don’t know what kind of toll that magic took,” Garr said, aiming for reassurance and missing by a hair. “But you kept him breathing. You watched the numbers. That matters. Don’t let your head tell you otherwise.”
Weslin’s voice cracked. “I’m not even sure I’m doing that right. I’m not a real medic, I’m not even really a squire! Harmon just picked me because I knocked over a suit of armor or something, and now he’s like this, and I don’t know what I’m supposed to do.”
“He picked you,” Garr went on, quieter now, firmer. “Not anyone else. You. From what I’ve seen, you’re doing exactly what you’re meant to do. You’re watching your knight. You’re holding the line where it counts.”
He paused, just long enough to let it land.
“No training ever prepares you for what the field takes from you. But you’re here, without any of that, and your instincts haven’t failed you yet.”

Aurelia looked up, her tone soft but firm. “You’re doing better than you think, Weslin. But you can’t hold your breath every second waiting for him to wake up. That won’t help him, and it won’t help you.”
Weslin looked down at his hands. “I just… I keep thinking, what if we did something wrong? What if he’s like this because I missed something?”
“You didn’t,” Garr said, a little too quickly. He shifted, exhaling slowly. “We’re all shaken. No one’s untouched by that break. We got out, but not without cost.”
Weslin’s eyes flicked toward a folded parchment beside him, one of several. “Luca’s team hasn’t heard back from us in nearly a day. They’ve sent three messages. They’re asking for guidance, orders... anything. What should I tell them?”
Garr hesitated. That hesitation was a crack in the armor, and he felt it immediately, felt how closely it was being watched. He swallowed it down and straightened.
Weslin had been watching him and spoke again. “The messages from Luca’s team,” he said carefully. 
Garr didn’t answer right away. He moved to the small folding table near the tent wall and turned the stack of folded parchments face down without reading them.
“What do you want me to tell them?” Weslin pressed.
“Nothing,” Garr said. “Not yet.”
“But what if—”
“I said ignore them,” Garr replied without looking back. “Right now, if they don’t think they’re on their own already, they’re lying to themselves. We’ve got five fresh bodies out there with no shelter, Harmon’s down, and if we were followed…” He trailed off, the unspoken consequence heavy in the air. “We need to lock this down first.”
Weslin opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again as a stiff gust slapped the tent wall and made the poles tremble. “But what if they are in danger? What if they are waiting on something that could save their lives?”
Garr turned slowly to face him. “Then they’ll do what we’ve all done. Improvise. Adapt. Survive.”
Weslin looked like he might argue again, his eyes glassy with the threat of something rising, but Aurelia put a calming hand on his arm.
Garr exhaled through his nose. A muffled shout echoed from somewhere outside, sharp enough to make his brow tighten. He pushed out through the tent flap into the daylight, the weight of command sitting heavier than ever on his shoulders.
Weslin went back and sat beside Harmon, knees drawn in, shoulders hunched. His fingers twitched nervously on the cot’s edge, eyes locked on Harmon’s still face like the boy feared if he blinked, the man might vanish.
Aurelia sat cross-legged across the tent from him, her long robes gathered neatly beneath her. Her brow furrowed with concern, not just for Harmon, but for the boy silently unraveling in front of her.
“Weslin,” she said gently, her voice as calm as falling rain. “We need to start your next lesson.”
His head snapped up. “Now? I… Aurelia, I don’t think I can right now.”
She kept her voice soft, not pressing. “That’s why we start now. When your mind’s scattered, when fear creeps in… That’s when you need your training most.”
He shook his head. “You don’t understand. I was just picked as a squire, just a boy playing at armor and maps. I’m not ready for this. I don’t even know what all my duties are supposed to be.” His voice cracked a little, and he clenched his fists. “I’m not sure I know who I am anymore. What does my power even mean? Or what I’m supposed to do with it.”
She leaned forward, hands clasped in her lap. “That, my dear boy, is exactly why we do this.” Weslin blinked at her.
Aurelia set two fingers briefly at his wrist, steady and precise, before letting her hand fall. “You trust in the people close to you. Not just the team, but those who invest in you. You trust in the gods who shape the breath in your chest. And when it gets quiet enough… You trust in your training.”
“But that’s just it,” he whispered. “I don’t have training.”
Aurelia gave him a faint smile, warm and sad all at once. “You’ve had it since the beginning. Who do you think set up this tent? Who’s been tracking his health, organizing notes, maintaining order in a storm?” She nodded toward the folded parchments beside him. “Those are message logs you’ve been keeping. Look at the way they’re ordered, the precision. That’s not a child’s work.” He frowned slightly, looking at the stack.
“You did that,” she said. “And in the prison, you kept your head. You moved with the team. You got out. You protected others.” Her voice softened even more. “Now we need to focus on something that steadies your nerves. You need that. We need that.”
His lip trembled just a little. “I don’t know how.”
“That’s what I’m here for,” she said. “You’re not alone, Weslin. Let’s begin.”
He gave a small nod, uncertain but willing. “Close your eyes,” she said. “Picture a candle. Tall and steady. Just you and the flame.” His eyes shut. He inhaled slowly, but his shoulders were still tight.
“Now,” Aurelia continued, “imagine your fear. Your doubt. One by one, toss them into the fire. Watch them burn. Let them go.”
Silence. His brow furrowed. His fingers curled. “It’s not working,” he muttered.
“Good,” she replied. “Failure is part of it.” A faint rustle outside brushed the canvas as if something passed close, but Aurelia kept her focus on him.
He sighed, shoulders drooping. “Keep going.” She said it quietly, like it was already fact.
He took another breath. This one was deeper. Slower. Again. And again. Until something eased. “I see it,” he whispered. “The fire. It’s just me and the flame.”
Aurelia’s voice grew softer, steadier. “Good. Now reach. Listen for the hum beneath the world. That’s where the power lies. Draw it in, not forcefully. Like pulling a thread.”
A flicker of light danced in his vision. Faint. Brief. Then it sputtered. He sighed, shoulders drooping. She gave no reproach. “Again.”
This time, the light lingered. Faint as a breath, but steady. Aurelia smiled. “How do you feel?”
He opened his eyes slowly. “Safe.”
“Good,” she said, touching a hand to his shoulder. “Now let’s begin your first spell.” He sat up straighter.
“It’s not complicated, but it’s important,” she said. “It’s called True Eyes. My first spell. It allows you to see through illusion, through glamours and lies woven in magic. In this world, there will be many.”
He nodded. A small light now kindled behind his eyes. Not certainty, but something close. Hope? Weslin’s eyes went to Harmon without thinking. Aurelia followed the look, brief and measured, and then returned her attention to Weslin. “You are not casting,” she said quietly. “You are observing. Nothing here will touch him.”

The air was colder outside the tent, but not enough to chase the weight from Garr’s shoulders. He stood for a moment just beneath the flap, arms folded, letting the dull gray light catch across his worn features. Inside, he could still hear Aurelia’s calm, instructive tone weaving through the quiet tension of Harmon’s sickroom. She spoke gently but firmly, coaxing Weslin through some kind of focusing exercise, something to settle the boy’s frayed nerves.
Garr didn’t move. He just stood there, letting her words anchor him. A breath in. A breath out. Then another. He couldn’t show what he was feeling. Not now. They were all watching him. He stepped out into the open.
The camp was quiet, too quiet. No laughter, no idle banter. Just the crunch of feet on frost-bitten grass, the rustle of canvas, and the occasional soft clink of armor being adjusted. The weight of the last two days was visible in every movement, every look exchanged.
Garr turned his gaze toward the row of lean-tos near the edge of the clearing. Aldrek knelt beside a stump, wrapping a bandage around the wrist of a pale, wiry man with dark hair pulled into a tight knot, Torrek Mull, the earth-digger. Beside him sat Haldrin Vance, the aging scholar with ink still smudged on his sleeves, sipping from a tin cup with trembling hands.
He’d thought he was ready for this. He’d trained under Harmon for years, learned tactics, logistics, and leadership. But training wasn’t the same as living it. Not like this. Not with Harmon out cold and the whole weight of the company pressing down on him.
He was swimming upstream. And everyone was watching, waiting for him to slip. He crossed to the center firepit and found Dain standing near the lean-tos, arms crossed, jaw tight.
As he made his way towards Dain, he scanned the camp again. A few yards off, Calen, the younger of the two rescued swordsmen, stood near the fire, posture stiff, eyes scanning the horizon like he was still behind enemy lines. He wasn’t speaking much, but he wasn’t avoiding the others either. Just… watching.
Tarn, on the other hand, had made himself a ghost within the camp. He sat alone on the far side, cloak drawn tight, head down as if daring someone to approach. Nobody did.

“You look like someone poured a barrel of stress into a man-shaped container,” Dain said, his voice low, pitched so it wouldn’t carry.
Garr let out a hollow chuckle. It barely reached his eyes. “Feels about right.”
“Still no change?”
“No,” Garr said after a beat. “Weslin’s barely slept. Aurelia’s in there now. Trying to keep his head straight.” He hesitated, then added, quieter, “Trying to keep him from tearing himself apart.”
Dain exhaled through his nose. “I know it’s weighing on the kid. He’ll be holding it in, telling himself it’s fine. But it leaks. Always does.”
“He’s not the only one.”
A cold breeze slid between the tents, carrying the smell of ash and pine. Somewhere deeper in camp, a fire popped. They stood without speaking for a moment, the silence doing the work words couldn’t.
“I thought I’d have more time,” Garr said finally. “With Harmon. To learn the things that don’t fit in drills or plans.” His fingers flexed once at his side. “The soft parts. The parts you don’t realize you need until someone’s breaking in front of you. How he carries this weight without letting it crush him.”
Dain studied him, then reached out and clapped a hand to Garr’s shoulder. It was firm. Grounding.
“You’re doing fine,” he said. “They don’t need perfection. They need a steady hand. And you’re giving it, whether you believe that or not.”
Garr swallowed, eyes still on the tent flap.
Dain’s expression softened, though his posture stayed straight, controlled. “You’re not alone in this, Garr. But don’t mistake that for relief.” His voice lowered. “It doesn’t get lighter just because others stand beside you. It gets survivable. We carry it together. We carry it now. We’re here. And we’re alive.”
Garr nodded slowly, letting the words settle somewhere behind his ribs.
After a moment, Dain glanced toward the tent again. “I heard you earlier,” he said.
Garr stiffened slightly. “You—”
“I wasn’t listening on purpose,” Dain cut in gently. “I was walking past. But I heard enough.” He paused. “You told him to trust what he was feeling. To listen to himself. Those instincts don’t come from nowhere.”
Garr’s voice came quieter. “He thinks he’s failing. That because he’s scared, he’s doing something wrong.”
“And you told him he wasn’t,” Dain said. “You told him that fear doesn’t mean weakness. It means awareness.” A faint, rueful smile touched his mouth. “Harmon would’ve said the same thing. Just with fewer words and more judgment.”
That earned a small, real breath of a laugh from Garr.
Dain leaned back, gaze drifting across the camp. “You know… for a long time, I thought I was finished.” His tone stayed composed, but something underneath it loosened. “After what I lost, I stopped imagining a future that involved me. I told myself I was just… passing through. Coin, contracts, something to occupy the days until one finally didn’t end.”
He hesitated, then continued. “There were times I thought about disappearing. Not dramatically. Just… taking a job I wouldn’t walk away from.”
Garr turned to look at him fully now.
“But this,” Dain said, gesturing faintly at the tents, the fires, the quiet movement of people holding together, “this has a way of pulling you back. Reminding you that you still matter to someone. That you can still matter.” His jaw set, controlled again. “That old bastard in there gave me that back.”
The tightness in Garr’s chest eased, just a little. “Yeah,” he said. “He did that for all of us.”
After a moment, he added, “I was a mercenary for a while. Before Harmon found me. I told myself it was simpler that way. No attachments. No responsibility beyond the job.” He shook his head faintly. “Turns out that was a lie. I just hadn’t met people worth staying for yet.”
Dain nodded. “Seems we both took the long road to the same place.”
“I guess we’re in it now,” Garr said. “Whether we meant to be or not.”
Dain’s mouth curved slightly. “Seems so.” He paused. “And for what it’s worth… I’m here. If you need to talk again.”
The two men shared a quiet, understanding look. No ceremony. No promises. Just acknowledgment.
After a beat, Garr cleared his throat. “You seen Ash?”
“On patrol,” Dain said. His eyes moved briefly toward the trees. “He won’t be far.”
“Thank you again,” Garr said as he stepped off to find Ash.
A cold gust rolled across the clearing, stirring loose frost at Garr’s boots and carrying a faint creak from the tree line as he made his way toward the woods. Near the edge of the woods, Ash leaned against a tree, arms crossed and cloak flapping lightly in the breeze. He looked tired, more so than usual, but his amber eyes still held that flicker of irreverent fire, sharpened now by a glance toward the deeper woods.
“You’re a hard one to pin down,” Garr said, stepping up.
“I’m like smoke,” Ash replied. “Try to grab me, and I’ll just make your clothes stink.”
Garr snorted. “What? Wait, never mind, see anything?”
“Camp’s quiet,” he answered, glancing past Garr towards the other side. “No weird sounds, no creeping figures, and no exploding magical rocks. I’d call that a win.”
Ash looked off into the distance and stood up, posture tightening as a faint crunch echoed from the ridge. His expression shifted. “Company,” he muttered, low enough for Garr to hear. “But the good kind, I think.” Garr followed his gaze.
Two riders crested the ridge, Nyssa and Neavin, cloaks flaring in the wind, their pace brisk and purposeful, their mounts kicking up loose frost as they descended.
“Finally,” Garr muttered. Ash started jogging forward with Garr a step behind.
Neavin was pale but alert, eyes scanning the perimeter even as his falcon, a shimmer of pale bronze in the fading sky, swooped low overhead before vanishing into the trees. Nyssa’s hair was wind-whipped, cheeks flushed from cold and effort, but her posture was relaxed as she dismounted, though her fingers lingered a moment on the hilt at her hip.
“Tie your horses up by the others,” Garr said, motioning toward the picket line. “How are you both holding up?”
“Alive,” Nyssa said. “Mostly numb, but I’ll take it.”
Neavin gave a tired nod. “We’ve had worse.”
“That’s the mood around here.” Garr’s voice dropped into a tired rasp. “See anything we need to worry about?”
Neavin exhaled, rubbing the bridge of his nose. “Sent the falcon up from one of the higher ridges, and he caught something. Forged, a small group. Four or five at most. They were hours behind us. Looked like they were veering west, toward the mountains. Not toward us.”
Dain stepped in, his tone dry. “Merrick’s bloodhounds. Probably checking on his ‘investments.’” He jerked his chin subtly toward the cluster near Brother Aldrek’s tent, Calen, Haldrin, Torrek, and Riven. He let his gaze move briefly to Nyssa. It stayed there a beat longer than it needed to, something quiet and unconcealed moving behind his eyes before he pulled it back. “Wouldn’t be surprised if he wants them back. All five.”
Garr’s brow furrowed. “Anything else? Foot patrols? Uniforms?”
Nyssa shook her head. “Nothing visible. No standards, no banners. Just shadows in the trees and dust in their wake.”
“That’s something,” Garr said, rubbing a palm over the back of his neck as his gaze swept the perimeter once more. “We’ll make preparations for nightfall. No fires past dusk. We’ll do rotations and keep our eyes wide. And get some food down, half this camp looks ready to drop.”
As Garr turned to issue orders, Dain lingered. Nyssa was already walking his way. He caught her sleeve lightly as she passed. “Walk with me?”
She nodded, falling into step beside him as they moved toward the far edge of camp where the trees thickened just enough to muffle the world behind them. The momentary quiet felt like a relief.
“You’re still standing?” he asked, a faint smirk on his lips.
“Just barely,” she replied, cracking a smile.

They walked in silence for a moment before Dain broke it, his tone softer. “Hey… what’s the story with Riven?”
She glanced sideways, catching the careful neutrality in his question. “We grew up together. Same orphanage. Not blood, but close as it gets. He’s been in my life longer than anyone.”
Dain gave a slow nod, his smirk turning rueful. “Good to know. Just… trying to figure out the field I’m playing on.”
She laughed, genuinely, if a little wearily. “There’s no field. Just a lot of bad timing and worse luck.”
He stopped, crouched, and picked up a flat stone, rubbing the grit between his fingers. “For what it’s worth, if this all works out or not, maybe we could…”
Nyssa tilted her head. “That’s an offer?”
“A hope,” he said, standing again. “Not everything has to stay broken.”
Back in camp, Garr handed out assignments with the clipped precision of a man holding everything together by sheer will. Brother Aldrek moved through the new arrivals, checking bandages and handing out boiled root tea. Calen stood apart, but observant, arms crossed, expression unreadable. Tarn lingered farther away, face a stone wall, tension coiled tight in his shoulders.
Torrek was quiet as ever, contentedly tending a pot of stew while muttering in his strange lilting cadence, and Riven had found a boulder to lean against, eyes closed, his palm resting on the earth as though it told him secrets only he could hear. Haldrin, still pale from withdrawals, sat cross-legged near the fire, scribbling notes into a soot-streaked journal.
Ash returned from the tree line as dusk bled into deeper blue, his expression unreadable. “Perimeter’s quiet. No signs of trouble.”
“You sure?” Garr asked.
Ash nodded. “Sure as I ever am.”
Then a commotion stirred at the far end of camp.
The squeal of leather, the sudden loud clatter of hooves. Tarn, true to the distance he’d kept all day, was already on one of the horses, racing away from the camp. No explanation, no farewell.
“He’s heading southbound,” Ash muttered. “He’s not even going toward Forgehollow. He’s just… going.”
Garr didn’t move to stop him. “Let him go,” Garr said, voice flat with the decision. “If he meant to be part of us, he would have stayed.”
They just stood there and watched as the dust trailed behind him, one last breath of movement before the dark swallowed him whole.
The smell of stew wafted through the camp, simple, thin, and barely seasoned, but warm enough to stir the dull ache of hunger in every gut. The fire crackled low in its pit, the circle of orange light pushing gently against the press of cold and shadow.
They ate in silence at first, the only sounds the scrape of spoons on tin and the occasional muttered curse. A bowl clattered softly as someone shifted, the small sound cracking the quiet like a seam under strain.
Riven lifted a spoonful to his mouth, frowned, and let it drop back with a plop. “This is a heinous crime against vegetables,” he muttered, too tired to even be theatrical about it.
“Better than gruel,” Torrek rumbled from where he sat hunched beside the pot, licking his bowl clean. 
Ash raised a battered flask and gave it a shake. “To not dying,” he declared. “May we always fail upward.”
A few chuckles flickered around the fire. Even Brother Aldrek allowed a wry smirk as he leaned back against a rock, eyes scanning the flickering shadows just beyond the firelight.
The firelight danced across weary faces, faces that had seen prison walls and smoke-choked tunnels only a day before. Their eyes were red, knuckles scabbed, some still sporting the makeshift bandages Brother Aldrek had wrapped. But they were alive.
Garr sat nearby, rubbing his temples as he tried to read the room. The exhaustion was thick, too thick to cut with any speech. But no one had broken yet. That counted for something.
Calen, who had spent most of the day silent and watchful near the edge of the camp, finally stepped closer to the fire. His arms were folded tightly across his chest, but his eyes had softened.
“Thank you,” he said quietly, voice a little hoarse. “For getting us out. I didn’t think… I didn’t think I’d see free sky again.” Nobody replied, but a few heads nodded.
Brother Aldrek had finished his rounds, checking over the wounded once more. He knelt beside Torrek, who was grumbling about the bandage being too tight. “It’s tight because your ankle’s barely holding together,” Aldrek said. “You want to walk tomorrow or not?”
Torrek grumbled something inaudible. 
Aurelia emerged quietly from Harmon’s tent, pulling her shawl tighter against the evening cold. She paused beside Weslin, who stood at the tent flap, eyes distant.
“He’s stable,” she said softly to Garr, who had risen to meet her. “He’s been out most of the day. Drifting in and out. No worse, yet no better.” Her mouth tightened. “If he wakes, don’t mistake it for strength.”
Garr nodded, then looked to Weslin. “How’s our little squire holding up?”
Weslin gave a weak smile. “Still breathing. Same as Harmon.”
Aurelia placed a gentle hand on the boy’s shoulder. “He needs rest. You won’t help him by unraveling.” Weslin nodded, eyes brimming, but held steady.
Haldrin Vance stepped forward, clearing his throat. “If I may,” the scholar said, brushing the dirt from his robes as if addressing a royal court instead of a ring of war-weary fugitives. “A tale. While we eat, give us a moment of reprieve, perhaps. A tale with some truth, some fire. For those who still believe stories matter.”
Dain nodded once. “Let’s hear it.”
Haldrin smiled and stepped to the fire’s edge. He didn’t speak at first, letting the crackling logs fill the hush. Then, in a voice both melodic and fragile, he began to recite.
“Before the breaches, before the burning,
There were the Veylnar, Seven bound in flame…”
The Shattered Pearl. The story was older than most written things, part history, part myth, part warning. Haldrin wove the tale like it was stitched into his bones, his voice rising and falling in rhythm with the fire’s breath. He told of the Adept Knights who defied the heavens, the forging of the Pearl, and its catastrophic shattering.
He spoke of breaches and spirits, sparing detail but not weight. He told of a boy untouched by magic’s hue, the Reality Bender, child of no order and no god, who sang with the world and bent it to his will.
When the story ended, no one clapped. The fire hissed, a log cracked. Someone sniffed. “That’s a lot to put on a bedtime story,” Ash said, voice quieter now.
Haldrin gave a bow, more a nod of habit than showmanship. “The past always carries more weight than we think. Every scholar I’ve known learned that too late.”
As people shifted and began gathering bowls, the camp’s small noises rose again, tin on tin, boots on frost. Then the fire popped hard, and the sound cut clean through them.
A voice came from beyond the ring of light. “The story’s almost right… but not quite.”
All heads turned. Harmon stood there, as though he’d been listening longer than any of them realized. He was gaunt and pale. Sweating through his shirt. His right hand gripped a crooked branch for support, but his spine was straight, and his eyes were sharp.
The camp froze. Weslin was on his feet in an instant, bowl clattering to the ground. “Harmon?”
The old man gave a tired smile. “Someone leave a light on for me, or was that stew smoke drawing me in?”
Nobody moved for a breath. Then the whole camp rose slowly, stunned, as if seeing a ghost. And the fire crackled between them.






Chapter Twenty-Eight
The tent was dimly lit only by a low lantern that cast golden light against the canvas walls. Harmon sat propped up on a bedroll piled with folded cloaks and a wool blanket. He looked pale, the lines on his face deeper than usual, but his eyes were sharp again. A wooden bowl of stew rested in his lap, steam rising slowly from it.
Weslin hovered nearby like a shadow, his worry etched plainly in the tight lines around his mouth. He’d helped Harmon sit up, fetched his stew, and fluffed the blanket twice. He didn’t know what else to do.
Aurelia sat cross-legged in the corner near the packs, quiet, but not distant. Her gaze drifted occasionally to Harmon, but mostly she kept her attention on Weslin, reading his energy as much as his words.
Garr stood off to the side, arms crossed over his chest, eyes flicking between Harmon and the flap of the tent. He looked like a man trying to remember how to breathe normally. Next to him, Dain leaned against the support pole, his face unreadable.
“I imagine I’ve missed quite a bit,” Harmon said at last, spoon pausing halfway to his mouth. His voice was rough but steady. “Go on. Catch me up.”
Dain was the first to speak. “We made camp a little after noon today. Found a good hollow, set camp. Nyssa and Neavin scouted the perimeter; no signs of pursuit. Ash has been keeping the rotation tight. No one’s slacking.”
Garr added, “Brother Aldrek’s been tending the five we pulled from the cells. Minor injuries. Bruises, burns, and one fractured ankle. They’re stable.”
“And the five themselves?” Harmon asked, his tone even.
“Quiet,” Dain said. “Still recovering, keeping to themselves mostly. One of them, Calen, has been keeping his distance. Another, Tarn, ran off early this evening, stealing a horse. The other three seem… thankful. Or at least not hostile.”
Harmon nodded slowly, taking another bite of stew. After a moment, he glanced at the pile of folded parchments beside Weslin’s cot. “That’s all from Luca?”
Weslin shifted awkwardly. “Y-yes, sir. Reports, questions… mostly requests for guidance. They haven’t heard from us since the ride from Forgehallow.”
Harmon let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “Stack’s as tall as my thigh. Alright. I’ll get to them.”
Before the boy moved, Harmon looked between Garr and Dain. “Before anything else.” His voice dropped into something quieter than command. “Both of you. You kept it standing while I was down. I won’t forget that.”
Neither man answered. The silence did the work for them.
Weslin blinked, startled. “I’ll—uh—I’ll get you more stew.”
“Thank you, Weslin,” Harmon said gently, and the boy hurried out with the bowl.
For a moment, only the sound of the tent flaps rustling filled the silence. The lantern flickered softly, throwing a brief shadow over Harmon’s face as he adjusted his grip on the bowl.
Aurelia tilted her head. “And what about you? How long can you go on like this?”
Harmon didn’t answer right away. “Long enough.”
Aurelia held his gaze a moment past the point of comfort. She didn’t press it. But her expression made clear she had counted the days and done the math. “Long enough,” she repeated, and left it there like a stone he would carry.
He then leaned back, resting his head against the bedroll. He looked at Garr. “You did well. I know you didn’t ask for this, but you stepped up.”
Garr didn’t reply right away. He shifted his weight, then spoke quietly. “I thought I’d have more time to learn from you.”
Harmon smiled faintly. “So did I.”
Dain shifted from foot to foot. “We all did.”
Harmon was quiet for a moment. Then, almost to himself: “The things worth learning don’t fit in a drill.” He looked at Garr directly. “Staying in the room when everything in you says to leave. You did that. You don’t need me to teach you what you’ve already learned the hard way.”
Harmon looked between the two others. “It’s going to be a long road. But we’re still on it. Tomorrow, we start moving again, not far, not fast. Enough to stay ahead, enough to breathe. We’ve got the mission to finish, and maybe a new Silver Cloak to consider.”
He rubbed his temple, the weariness creeping back into his features. “I’ll speak to the others tonight. Meet the new blood. Sort what’s next.”
Then, to both of them, he added, “Tell the others to get some rest tonight. Proper rest. I’ll speak to the new blood quickly, then I’m done. We need clear minds and strong legs in the morning.”
The two men nodded and stepped toward the flap. Harmon’s eyes closed. As the moments passed, he pushed himself up slightly, waving a hand. “Go. Let the others know we’re leaving at first light. Garr, stay a moment.”
The others exited, and Harmon’s expression grew distant as he waited for the flap to close.
“Thank you, again,” he said, voice low. “For stepping up.”
Garr shifted uncomfortably. “I didn’t have a choice.”
Harmon studied him for a long moment, the lines around his eyes tightening just slightly. “That’s exactly why it mattered.”
His attention shifted down to his hand, the ring dull and cold on his finger. “The ring carried me farther in that fight than I should’ve gone. I can feel it weakening.” His throat worked once. “And I can feel what it took out of me. It does not give without leaving a mark.”
Garr stepped forward. “Then take it off.”
Harmon gave him a tired smile. “I will not take this ring off again. Not while the road is under us and eyes are hunting. If it comes off, it is because I am done.” His gaze hardened. “And you don’t tell Weslin. Understood?”
“…Understood.” Garr’s jaw worked once, quietly, the way a man swallows something he knows he’ll carry alone. Then he nodded.
Outside, the fire crackled low. The murmur of camp life was already winding down. Harmon let out a long breath and leaned back against the makeshift headrest.
“Tell them all to get sleep tonight,” he said. “They’ve earned it. Then start bringing in the new one for a quick chat, one by one.”
Garr nodded, then headed out of the tent to leave Harmon alone for a bit.
The fire burned low outside the canvas, casting long shadows that flickered like ghosts. Inside the tent, Harmon sat with his hands folded. Garr stood just outside, pulling back the flap for the first of the rescued.
A thick-set man, grime still clinging to his clothes despite the wash, Torrek had the look of a boulder chipped from the mountains, hard edges, heavy shoulders, and sharp eyes. A cut above his brow hadn’t quite healed as he ducked into the tent.
“You Torrek Mull?” Harmon asked without rising.
“That’s right,” the man said, brushing ash from his arms. “Earthbound Adept. Miner for hire. Been digging holes since I was ten. Stone, ore, old city veins. If it was buried, I found it, mostly. I was one of the best… still am.”
“You worked for Merrick?”
“Not by choice. He bought my contract out from a trade baron. Figured I could find him buried treasure under Forgehallow and in the mountains nearby.”
“What do you want now?” Harmon asked.
“To disappear,” Torrek said bluntly. “Got family on the coast. Good people. They’ve got a farm. If they’re still breathin’, I’d like to see them again.”
Harmon gave a slow nod. “You’ll be given supplies, some coin, and a map. Hear me, you need to move like you are already being followed. Back roads, cold fires, no caravans, no open inns. If anyone asks who you are, you are someone else.”
Torrek’s brow lifted in surprise. “Just like that?” He shifted his stance, as if testing whether the ground beneath him was real.
“Just like that. You walked into someone else’s property. You walk out your own man. What you do with that is yours to decide.” Harmon said.
Torrek nodded once and stepped back into the night, thoughts filled his head.
Garr brought the next in. Haldrin Vance stepped carefully, robes trailing like a half-forgotten sermon. The scholar held a journal tight to his chest, eyes sunken but alert.
“Haldrin,” Harmon said. “Royal Archive, correct?”
“Was,” Haldrin answered softly. “Until I started asking the wrong questions.”
“What sort?” asks Harmon.
Haldrin looked up at him, eyes bright. “The Pearl. Not the myths. The truth. What it was really meant for. What happened to it? What the pieces might still do.”
Harmon didn’t interrupt. “I started digging through restricted shelves and asking about its construction, the materials, the magic. As I found some answers, that’s when they came, men with coin, calling themselves investors. More like thieves. Soon after, my research vanished. And so did I.”
“You still want answers?” Harmon asked, voice calm.
“I do,” answered Haldrin.
“Then find me in Opindale in three weeks, if the road allows it. If it does not, you wait two days and you vanish,” Harmon said.
Haldrin blinked. “Truly?”
“We’ll talk. Until then,” Harmon said, “what do you need?”
Haldrin hesitated, thumb brushing the spine of his journal as if reassuring himself it was still there. “I want to go home. To the Archive. Back to my work.”
“Done. You leave at first light with Torrek.”
Haldrin clutched the journal tighter and bowed, sincere. “Thank you.” When he left, Garr stood aside for the next figure.
The tent dimmed. The next man stepped inside, slow and careful, cloak drawn tight. A short beard framed a jaw that once belonged to a younger, more idealistic version of himself. He said nothing as he stood before Harmon.
“Name?” Harmon asked, already knowing.
“Calen,” the man replied coolly.
Harmon studied him for only a moment before replying, “Calen… or should I call you Reau?” Harmon asked, his voice lowering, the name carrying more weight than the man himself.
The man’s eyes narrowed slightly. “You knew?”
“How could I not?” Harmon said, his voice softer. “I was there the day you were born, held you in my arms. Arthur brought you around from time to time. Even though about your little...” He coughs. “Experiment.” He gave a knowing glance. Reau’s expression didn’t budge, stone cold.
“You were always a sharp one,” Harmon said with a faint, sad smile. “Your father and I… we were friends. Real ones. Not the kind that just share a tent and a mission. We believed in the same things. In doing what was right.” He paused, gaze sharpening. “What happened?”
“I was hunting slavers. East riverlands,” Reau said. “Tracked them too long. Got tired. Slipped up. They caught me in my sleep. Silver-laced collar, full binding rune. Been wearing it ever since.”
He tilted his chin to show the collar’s etched gleam. Harmon’s jaw tightened, just slightly, at the sight.
“And they took my sword,” Reau said, anger filling his voice.
Harmon leaned back. “How are you holding up?”
Reau gave a small breath, not quite a laugh. “Between the new jewelry and the absence of my blade? A little hollow.”
“You know where it is?” Harmon asked.
“I do not feel it, probably the collar. I looked through the prison as we made our way out. Nothing. But I might know where it ended up.” His voice turned cold. “Merrick’s estate. Stormhaven. He kept it. Said it was art. Put it on display. For all his lies, that was one of the few truths he told.”
The way he said it was flat. Not angry. Just finished. The tone of a man who had burned through rage long ago and arrived somewhere colder on the other side.
Harmon let it sit for a long moment before saying, “We’re heading east. Toward Stormhaven.”
Reau met his eyes. “Then I’ll come with you.” His gaze flicked once, hard. “If Stormhaven holds my sword, it holds answers too. I am done being caged.”
“You are welcome to,” Harmon said.
Harmon held his gaze a moment longer. “Keeping the name back in that cell. Operating blind with that collar on. That took something most men don’t have.” He paused. “Your father would have done the same.” Reau said nothing. But something in him received it. He simply nodded his head. Harmon continued with his questioning. “Why the name change? I know you don’t hate your name,” Harmon said quietly.
“No,” Reau replied. His jaw tightened once. “Using it now would only hurt his legacy. I loved him, Harmon. Still do.”
“So, do I. I miss him every day,” Harmon said with a bit of emotion in his voice. 

He didn’t say anything else. He just pulled his collar straight, as if reminding himself it was still there, and walked out.
It was barely a moment before the tent flap opened again, his last planned meeting. Riven Duskwind strolled in like he owned the place.
“Riven,” Harmon said without looking up.
“Was wondering when it would be my turn,” Riven said with a grin. “Thought you forgot me.”
“I waiting to see if you’d run. Like Tarn.” Harmon said.
“Oh, I thought about it. But Nyssa would’ve hunted me down, and she can make the brave men break with that glare of hers. Besides…” He paused as he sat lazily, legs crossed, hands resting in his lap. “…you’re paying real coin. That’s worth staying for.”
“So you know what I’m about to ask you then?” asked Harmon.
“Do you think Nyssa could keep her mouth quiet on it for this long? I do give her credit. It took her a whole eight hours to tell me. That is some kind of record for her.”
“I bet. But I’m offering more than coin.” Riven raised a brow.
“A full pardon,” Harmon said. “Carried by the weight of the crown, of Opindale. If anyone challenges it, they can challenge me. You are free of the chains.”
That sobered him. “You’re not joking,” Riven said.
“No,” was Harmon’s reply. A long silence stretched between them. Harmon looked him in the eyes and said, “You stayed. When Tarn rode out, you didn’t. You could have. You had the horse and the dark, and nobody would have blamed you.” He tilted his head slightly. “That tells me more than anything else you could have said.” 
“A full pardon,” he said again, slower, like he was checking whether the words were real. “Not just coin. Not just a job.” He exhaled once. “Do you know how long I’ve been looking over my shoulder?”
“I have a guess,” Harmon said.
Riven nodded. Then the grin came back, but slower than before. “Yeah. I’m in. What are you going to ask of me? What is my new position going to be?”
“You’re the faceman,” Harmon said. “ A Silver Cloak. You lie, you smile, you cheat, and people believe you.”
“I open doors,” Riven said with a smirk. “You just have to tell me which ones.”
“Then here’s the first,” Harmon said, leaning in slightly. “When we reach Stormhaven, we’ll need a base of operations. Somewhere that doesn’t ask names and won’t remember faces.”
Riven’s grin spread wide. “Stormhaven’s my city,” Riven said, and some of the grin fell away. “I know places that do not ask names twice, and alleys that forget faces if you pay them right.”
“Good. Now go get some sleep, we have some long days ahead of us.”
His hand rested against the canvas, fingers stilling as he exhaled. “You know…” Riven’s grin faded. “I didn’t join because of the pardon.”
“No?”
“I joined for her,” he said softly. “But now… Now I see the man you are and am all in.”
“Welcome to the team.” Harmon said with a grin.
Riven slipped into the night, a thousand thoughts racing behind that grin.
The tent had barely settled before Harmon’s voice came again, quieter this time, meant only for one person. “Weslin.”
The boy was already there. He didn’t ask if Harmon needed rest or whether the messages could wait until morning. He just brought his ink and sat down beside the parchment stack without a word.
Harmon looked at him for a moment. “Good lad.” They worked until the fire outside burned to coals.
The morning broke cool and quiet, the sky was a soft smear of pale gray and rose above the tree line. Harmon stepped out of his tent and paused.
The camp was already in motion. Tents were half-taken down, bedrolls rolled tight. Packs were being strapped to horses, and Garr was speaking in low tones to Torrek and Haldrin beside the gelding they’d been given. The two former prisoners moved with quiet purpose, securing what little they owned to the saddle.
But it wasn’t the bustle that caught attention. It was Harmon himself out a moving around. His posture was straight, and his movements were fluid. The weight he had worn at him, grief, exhaustion, fire, seemed to have slipped from his shoulders in the night. Even without reaching into the deeper pull of the ring on his finger, something in him had settled. Returned.
He looked like his old self. He moved like it, too. The pallor still clung if you stared long enough, and the lines had not vanished. His shaking was gone. The loose edge was gone. He walked over toward the pair of Torrek and Haldrin.
Ash was nearby, cloak pulled tight, watching the old man move. He didn’t say anything. He just exhaled slowly and looked away, the way people do when something they had been quietly dreading doesn’t happen after all.
Harmon just started talking to them as he got close. “Head east to Thornhaven,” he told them, his voice firm but calm. “Remember, keep to the back roads. Thornhaven’s a port town, and ports know how to look away when coin is quiet. There’s a junction just before the bend south of the Whitecap River. Use it. It will carry you downstream to Opindale. Change your look, sooner if you can.”
Torrek gave a grunt that might have meant agreement. Haldrin adjusted the satchel on his back and nodded.
“Eyes will be hunting for you. You can count there is a bounty already out for you,” came a voice behind them. Brother Aldrek stepped into view, freshly armored, his coat drawn tight against the breeze. He handed each man a small coin pouch and a compact supply roll, tied neatly and practically.”No caravans. No open inns. Make yourselves someone else.”
“Thanks for everything,” Haldrin murmured.
“Travel with the light, we will see you in Opindale,” Aldrek said, while making the hand symbol for a blessing of God the Creator towards them.
Torrek swung up into the saddle first. Haldrin followed, less gracefully. Garr gave a parting tap to the flank of the horse, and they began to ride out.
A few of the others paused to watch them go. Weslin lifted a hand in a small, uncertain wave before letting it fall to his side. Nyssa leaned against a tree, arms crossed. Her expression was unreadable.
“They’ll make it,” Riven said, appearing beside her, sleeves pushed back to his elbows. “Torrek’s a rock. And Haldrin? He’s half-mad with purpose. That’s the dangerous kind.”
She didn’t respond. Her thumb brushed the hilt of her dagger, expression unreadable.
“You’re going to get a reputation,” he added with a sly grin. “Cold exterior. Kind heart. Team’s emotional anchor.”
Nyssa arched a brow. “If you keep talking, I’ll show you just how cold I can be.”
He held up both hands, mock-surrender. “There she is.” She gave him a small grin.
As the departing pair disappeared into the morning mist, the camp shifted back into movement. Gear was folded and packed, armor strapped, and blades checked. No one needed to be told what to do.
Harmon watched for a moment, his gaze sweeping over the team. Then he turned toward his tent. He smiled faintly to himself.
No orders given. No maps laid out. And yet the camp broke itself like clockwork, quietly, carefully, as if they had been doing this for a lifetime and not for a handful of hard miles.
A soft breeze stirred the ash at his feet, carrying the faint scent of pine and cold earth. The last embers of the fire flickered behind him, thin tendrils of smoke curling up toward the lightening sky, still burning. Still defiant.
Weslin was already moving quickly, breaking down the central supports and rolling their shared sleeping mats. Harmon began to strap his armor piece by piece, methodically, before he finished packing his pack with the clothes of the past day.
They divided the gear between their packs and placed heavier pieces in the saddlebags. Weslin’s smaller pack was nearly full when Aurelia rode up beside them.
“You’re up early,” she said, smiling down at the boy.
“I… Yes,” Weslin said, nearly tripping over himself to stand upright.
“We’ll pick up your training again on the road,” she said, her voice gentle. “Only what you can hold. Controlled. Near the edge, and no farther. Not while we are moving.” She paused and grinned a bit, “And who knows.” Her voice lifted slightly. “There may even be time to teach you an illusion or two.”
Weslin’s eyes lit up, his nerves briefly forgotten. He straightened and stood taller.
“Thank you,” he said, voice firmer than usual.
Aurelia’s smile softened. “My pleasure, little flame.”
Weslin drew in a steadying breath, shoulders squaring just slightly. They shared a nod, one of mutual understanding, teacher and student, and she turned her horse away to finish her preparations.
Soon, the last of the tents were down. The fire was ash. Tracks brushed away.
Nothing remained of the camp but footprints and silence.
Harmon looked out over the clearing one last time. What they’d built here, what had formed in the midst of prison escapes, broken orders, and impossible odds, was already gone.
But the fire still burned. He swung up onto his horse. “Let’s ride,” he said. “Quiet and tight. Eyes open.” They were off, heading northeast, toward Stormhaven, to answer the unknown.






Chapter Twenty-Nine
The frost bit deeper up here. The horse’s hooves crunched in rhythm, slow and precise, as Taerel guided it up the winding trail. No birdsong. No steady wind. Just the heavy silence of the upper ridges, where snow lay thick, and breath vanished the second it left your lungs.
A scarf was pulled high across the lower half of his face, wound tightly beneath his hood. His eyes, sharp, calculating, were the only part of him visible. The mask beneath the scarf was thin, magical, unseen to the naked eye. It filtered the cold, kept his breath from fogging the scarf, and hid the faint shimmer of power pulsing across his cheekbones. From a distance, he was just another cloaked shadow in the snow. But shadows didn’t ride like this.
He’d been on the move since before dawn. His horse, trained for silence and strength over speed, moved as if it understood urgency. They both did. The siege at the pass wasn’t breaking anytime soon. The civilian quarter, boxed in behind the fortress walls, was running out of everything: bandages, tonics, fire-starters, food. Luca’s team was working to find a back-door tunnel into the siege line, but without supplies, it would be a death sentence for the people inside.
And that meant this ride wasn’t just a scouting run. It was a lifeline. If I don’t bring something back... they bleed out. They starve. The tunnel would mean nothing.
He clenched the reins tighter. This wasn’t a mission for glory. It wasn’t for a mark on a report or some command chain recognition. Not for glory. Not for orders. For the particular people behind those particular walls, whose names he did not know but whose odds he had already run, and found wanting.
Death, he could calculate. Failure to the people waiting inside those walls was a different kind of loss entirely, one that didn't sit well with him.
The trail knifed through a natural cut in the ridge, tight, uneven stone slicked with hard-packed snow. Taerel dismounted without a sound, looping the reins around his wrist. His breath misted faintly against the inside of the scarf, but his body stayed still, honed and practiced.
The horse hesitated as the walls narrowed. Good instincts. Taerel stepped forward and tested the ground. Loose shale shifted underfoot.
Too late. His boot slid. He caught himself, slamming a gloved hand against the cliff wall, but the twist came sharp and fast, a brutal snap of tension in the same damn ankle he’d hurt a few nights ago at the other orc camp.
The ankle screamed, and for a heartbeat, the ridge tilted. He planted anyway, then eased the foot down with care, letting bone and tendon settle into a lie that would hold for a few more minutes. It would not hold long. So, he kept everything deliberate. Small steps. No leaps. No wasted turns.
He dropped low, gasping once, sharply, through clenched teeth, and crouched, already stripping the wrap from a side pouch. Snow dug into his knees as he bound the joint. Tight. Secure. Pain flickered through him with every movement.
“Bad timing,” he muttered through clenched teeth. “Not a sign.”  A faint crack echoed somewhere deeper in the ridge, sharp enough to snap him alert again.
The horse nudged his shoulder lightly, as if sensing the shift.
“Still on track,” he said softly, more to himself than the horse. And they moved again. He reached the ridge’s edge just past the sun directly above.
Crouching low, he peered over the granite rise, letting the cold seep into his thighs. Far below, half-shrouded by frost-laced evergreens, a bandit caravan crept along the lower slope. Seven riders. Two packhorses. They looked like merchant horses: saddlebags and bundled rope satchels swaying with the gait of their mounts. One man laughed, the sound echoing up the stone like it didn’t belong.
They moved without discipline, too relaxed. But not green. Not anymore. They were returning from something, not heading out. Their gear sagged underweight, not anticipation.
One of the riders glanced uphill, frowning at the empty ridge as if something in the silence bothered him.
He took in the layout like a surgeon preparing for a cut, timing the rotation, noting every gap in their awareness. Six-second coverage blind spot on their left. No rear scout on the high ridge. No vanguard watching upward. Their biggest mistake?
They thought the snowfall would protect them.
He pulled back, eyes scanning the slope ahead. If he moved fast, he could intercept at the next switchback near the creek. “Supplies are the priority,” he told himself, and still his hand did not loosen on the rifle. Seven men meant seven mouths and seven blades, and every one of them could strip the packs and vanish into the white. If he let them pass, there would be nothing left. This could be the only shot to get back quickly. The people were what drove him.  The switchback became his only choice. He reached the switchback just ahead of them.
The slope dropped in a shallow curve to the left, funneled by frozen brush and a line of broken stones. Water trickled faintly beneath a thin sheet of ice, the only sound beyond the creak of his boots in the snow. This was the place. No escape routes. No line of sight for half a mile. If he moved quickly, with enough noise, he could force them into a moment of confusion. And a moment was all he needed.
He moved down and across as a cold gust knifed across the rocks, sharp enough to raise the hairs on his neck. He had picked the exact spot to set up his trap, a rounded rock near the trail’s edge, half buried in frost. He slid a wedge beneath it, then coiled the twine. It should make enough noise for them to check out.
He dropped low again, retreating to cover with practiced speed. Less than a minute passed before he heard it, the hollow clatter of stone against ice, the quick exhale of startled breath. Someone shouted. Two of them dismounted, footsteps crunching toward the slope just below him.
One carried a short sword. The other had a handaxe and no helmet. Both looked annoyed, not alert. Good. Taerel struck from the ridge.
The rifle coughed once, and the wind stole the sound and carried it sideways along the rock face, away from the trail. Up here, the storm did strange things to noise. A shout could die at your boots, and a whisper could travel a mile. He did not wait to learn which it would be today. The first man dropped without a sound, legs twitching in the frost. The other turned too slowly.
Taerel was already on him. Steel met steel, his rapier finding the man’s side just above the hip. The bandit stumbled, grunting in pain, and brought the axe around in a wild arc. Taerel ducked low, swept behind him, and drove the hilt into the base of his skull.
The body hit the ground hard and didn’t rise. Taerel didn’t wait. He cut the reins from the nearest packhorse and yanked the heavy saddle bags free, flipping the flaps as he moved.

The first bag sat heavy and dense, nothing shifting, nothing hollow. The weight of things packed to last. He kept it.
The second was a treasure trove, jerky and tonics, bandages and sealed vials, all of it packed tight as someone had planned for misery. He slung it beside his own without stopping to count. The third was more of the same, dried fruit and field oil, bundles of cloth wrapped clean. He did not need names for it. He knew what it meant.
One more pouch, thicker, heavier, looked like firestarter bricks. He pocketed it. Voices rose above him, sharper now. No questions. Orders. Someone had found the bodies.
He grabbed the last bag, slung it onto his horse’s harness, and swung into the saddle.
It came from the ridge above, one of the bandits, faster than the rest, crouched behind a tree stump, crossbow already cocked again. The bolt missed his heart, but not by much. It tore through the side of his coat and across his upper arm, ripping a red line across his shoulder and collarbone. His vision flashed white.
He gasped, half from pain, half from shock, and kicked the horse into motion. The animal bolted forward, hooves digging deep into the slope, scattering snow behind them. Another bolt snapped past his head. A third thunked harmlessly into a tree behind. He didn’t fire back. No time. No clean shot. Just move.
Blood soaked into the inside of his coat. Warmth fled fast, leaving only the dull pull of it. He forced his breath into a narrow rhythm and kept moving. Every jolt of the saddle drove pain through his ankle, which was now nearly locked in place with swelling.
The ridgeline blurred past him in streaks of gray and white. He ducked low, one arm tight against his chest, reins pulled one-handed as they veered through the narrow pass. The trees leaned too close. He clipped one with his knee. Didn’t matter.
Behind him, he heard the bandits shouting. No pursuit. No horses on that slope, and the ground was a treacherous tilt of ice and stone that punished haste. They shouted instead, because shouting cost nothing.
He risked one glance over his shoulder. Only the wind chased him, hissing through the rocks. The ridge broke open to the west.
Taerel's horse stumbled over the rise, foam streaking its neck, steam pouring from its muzzle like smoke from a battlefield. The trail curved beneath him, half-visible through the blur of wind and blood in his eyes. His shoulder burned, hot and bright, and every heartbeat echoed in his temple like a drumbeat warning of collapse.
Just ahead, the tree line split along the overlook. A shelf of dark stone jutted out into the open air, offering a panoramic view of the valley below and the orc camp.
Fires flickered in pits dug into the snow, tucked beneath a bend in the ridge where wind and sound both broke. The camp sat low, eyes on the valley, not the heights. They did not look up. They never had. As far as they knew, the ridge was empty. Dead land. That’s what the team had counted on.
A figure stood on the edge of the overlook, cloaked and steady, his rifle leveled across the valley. The scope glinted for a half-second, catching the faintest light. Then the figure moved.
Fast. Efficient. The rifle turned, pivoting toward the sudden sound of hooves behind him, toward Taerel. Toward the shape slumped low in the saddle, blood soaking his right side, eyes barely open.
The man didn’t fire. The rifle dropped. Not lowered, dropped. The muzzle fell with a sharp jerk, the weight of realization moving faster than instinct.
“Taerel?” The name came out strained, half question, half prayer. The lookout sprinted forward, boots hammering frozen dirt, scarf pulled down as he closed the distance. Same dark hair. Same build. A mirror grown under different skies. His brother.
“Whoa, whoa, hey, hey,” he said quickly, both hands catching the reins before the horse could pitch sideways on the slope. “I’ve got you. You’re alright. I’ve got you.”
Taerel didn’t answer. Couldn’t. His lips were cracked, and his breath was shallow. He was half-folded over the horn of the saddle, one hand still gripping the closest saddlebag like it might disappear if he let go.
Aymir pulled him upright as gently as he could. Blood stained his gloves. “By God’s bread, you’re hit. What happened… No, don’t talk. Just hold on.” He turned the horse carefully and started leading it, step by agonizing step, toward the hiding spot. He took it slow, down the ridge path toward the new campsite, tucked beneath a curtain of snow-laden evergreens. Hidden. Safe. For now.
Every few paces, Aymir glanced back at his brother to make sure he was still upright. “You stubborn bastard,” he muttered. “You always do this.” A sharp breath caught in his throat as he steadied Taerel’s slipping weight.
Taerel made a sound, half a cough, half a laugh. It hurt. But it was real. Aymir looked up sharply. “Don’t. Don’t do that,” he said tightly. “Don’t be clever right now. Just stay awake. You got the supplies?”
Taerel nodded once, slow and stiff. “They’re going to lose their minds,” Aymir said quietly. “You pulled it off.”
Another glance down the slope. Just ahead now. He whistled once, a low-pitched signal. Footsteps crunched below. Someone called out. Aymir guided the horse the final stretch, then reached up and caught Taerel under the arm as he slipped from the saddle at last, more collapse than dismount. He caught him and hauled him close.
Taerel’s head hung forward, one arm around Aymir’s shoulder, his breathing ragged.
“I got what I could,” Taerel whispered, the words rough.
“I know,” Aymir said, his voice cracking. “I know.”
Behind them, the fire was already being stoked. A lean-to was cleared. Gloves thrown aside, salves and water drawn. Aymir lowered him slowly to a roll of blankets, gloves already smeared with half-frozen blood, and pressed a hand to his neck. Pulse still strong. Still there.
Taerel’s packs hit the ground. The gear was dirty, bloodstained, and half-frozen, but when Aymir opened the side flap of one of them, the first thing he saw was a bundle of wrapped cloth and tightly sealed vials. The vials were wrapped in cloth and tucked into a hard leather sleeve, packed like someone expected the world to try to break them.
Aymir looked up. “It’s good,” he said. “It’s a blessing.”
Taerel sat back, finally, eyes closed for a heartbeat. For the first time since the snow began falling, the tension in the camp broke, not fully, not loudly, but just enough for them to breathe.
Taerel, half-conscious, finally letting the weight go. He didn’t speak again. He didn’t need to. The ridge held. The fire burned.






Chapter Thirty
The ridge gave them nothing. Not a trail. Not a break in the trees. Just wind cutting through fir branches and the steady groan of the siege below, muffled but persistent, like a war drum heard through layers of stone.
Lysana pulled up on the reins and narrowed her eyes against the early light. Mist drifted over the treetops. Their breaths came in visible plumes. The terrain ahead was a mess of frost-covered rocks and tangled roots, a slope too steep for most travelers and too silent to be inhabited.
“This is it,” she said, voice flat. Not uncertain. Just grim.
Luca said nothing. He dismounted and moved forward on foot, eyes scanning the rock face like a surgeon studying a scar. The trees grew too thick here, the moss too even. Nature didn’t wrap itself this tightly around nothing.
Lysana dropped down beside him and began feeling along the base of the slope, her gloved fingers trailing over frost-hardened ferns and twisted vines. “It’s not supposed to be obvious,” she muttered.
“It’s not supposed to be anything,” Luca replied.
Then she found it. Not a cave. Not a door. Just a half-rotted wedge of wood, nearly consumed by moss, buried in a curtain of roots. The remnants of a support beam may have been angled incorrectly, having been broken decades ago. She tugged. It groaned faintly, then cracked.
Beneath it, hidden under layers of dead leaves and snowmelt, was a narrow gap in the rock, horizontal, jagged, barely visible unless you were kneeling exactly where she was. “Here.”
Luca knelt beside her. The space was no taller than a crouch and no wider than a horse’s flanks, choked with frost-laced vines and old, packed soil. The air inside was colder than the air in the forest. Older, too, stale, like something buried and forgotten.
“No one’s used this in years,” he said.
“That’s why it might still work.” She drew her long knife and began clearing the overgrowth, cutting slowly, carefully. The vines resisted like tendons, snapping back when she sliced too shallow. Luca braced the beam, shifting debris away from the entry point as she worked. Bit by bit, the mouth of the tunnel widened, not welcoming, but simply opened up. A brittle root snapped somewhere deeper in the dark, sharp enough to make them both pause. When the last of the roots gave way, they both stepped back.
The tunnel yawed open like a crooked throat, sloping downward at an angle steep enough to break an ankle if taken at speed. It was stone-cut, irregular, and built by hands that didn’t care about elegance. The opening was rough but passable, barely, and now exposed just enough for a man and a horse to squeeze through.
They didn’t hesitate. They lit their lantern and gathered up the horses, muffling the bits with strips of cloth and speaking low until the animals steadied.
Luca took the lead, guiding his horse by the halter into the dark, the beast snorting at the total darkness. Lysana followed, her free hand gripping the hilt of her blade as her boots scraped over ice-glazed stone.
