The tunnel swallowed them quickly, and within twenty paces, the light from outside vanished completely. The first twenty paces after the entrance were worse than expected.
The tunnel narrowed sharply, just wide enough for their horses to pass single file, heads bowed under the low, cracked ceiling. The path sloped downward, but the angle wasn’t the problem; it was the illusion of collapse.
Loose rock and heavy striations across the ceiling made it look unstable, as if it would cave in at any moment. Dust coated everything. At least twice, Lysana stopped and raised her hand, peering at stress cracks overhead. The third time, she didn’t halt — a thin rain of grit fell from the ceiling instead, pattering against her glove.
“Looks dangerous,” she muttered.
“It’s not,” Luca said behind her, voice even. “Look at the way the dust settles. Untouched.”
She squinted at the arch above. He was right. The detritus wasn’t freshly fallen; it had accumulated. Whatever happened here, it hadn’t moved in decades. If ever.
They kept going, moving carefully, horses trailing them with slow, hesitant steps. The path dipped lower. The air changed, colder, but less biting. Denser.
Suddenly, the tunnel opened like a jaw. No warning. No soft transition. One moment, they were shoulder to stone, and the next, they stepped into a vast, hollowed chamber, naturally formed but massive in scope. The ceiling curved high above them, too distant to catch in full by lantern light. Water dripped from ancient stalactites into quiet, frozen pools scattered across the ground like old scars. Lysana’s boot slid slightly on the damp stone, and she steadied herself with a sharp breath. Faint mineral deposits caught the lantern light, glinting with dull green and bone-white shimmer.
They led the horses forward, and the animals immediately became more at ease in the broader space. Their hooves echoed softly instead of scraping. The air, while cold, didn’t burn. It was the kind of cold you could sleep in, if you were desperate.
Which, at the moment, they were. A faint echo rippled somewhere in the vastness above them, so soft it might have been shifting stone.
“This could work,” Lysana said, brushing her glove along the stone. “Warmer than the ridge. And it echoes just enough to hear someone coming.”
“A fire wouldn’t smoke out,” Luca added. “Stone breaks upward. Chimney effect.”
She gave him a sideways glance. “Didn’t know assassins studied airflow.”
“We do. In kitchens,” Luca retorted. That earned a short huff of amusement.
They chose the northern shelf deliberately. Stone rose on three sides, the drop guarding the fourth. They doubled the tethers, ran them through old iron rings set in the rock, and left the reins short. If anything came from the tunnels, they would hear the panic before they lost the animals. Luca struck a small flint near the center of the chamber onto a firelog, and in moments, a low flame flickered to life, thin and controlled.
From where they stood, they could see five tunnels emerging from the space like veins. One was entirely collapsed, sealed with boulders, and half-swallowed by the wall. Another looked tight, narrow, and descending at an odd angle. The other three varied in height and width, but the largest was wide enough to stand side by side without ducking.
Lysana walked toward the smallest viable one first. “Scout it?” she asked.

Luca nodded. They took one lantern and moved carefully into the side tunnel, leaving their fire behind like a heartbeat fading into a dream. This route was narrower than it looked, an uneven path that twisted twice and ended in a squat, square chamber cut by hand.
Crates lined the walls, some collapsed, some intact, all crusted with decades of neglect, left behind and forgotten. Dust lay thick across the stone floor around them. Luca found and picked up a hammer, holding it sideways. He swung it, smashing in the side of one to reveal old ropes. He took a moment to take in his surroundings, then nodded to himself before saying, “This tunnel was likely used during construction. To build the fort wall. Probably served as storage.”
Lysana stepped over a crate and nudged it open with her boot. “Could’ve doubled as an emergency exit as well. Looks like no one’s been here in years. Forgotten. Never documented.”
A flicker of unease crossed Luca’s face, gone as quickly as it appeared. He paused for a moment, then said, “Speaking of forgotten, we finally heard back from Harmon. A message came through not an hour ago. Looks like I was talking to just Weslin there. Harmon was out of action.”
“Is he all right?” asked Lysana.
“Seems to be now, so he told me to do what I can and report back when something changes, or we have a plan.”
“At least that is what we are doing anyway,” she said while marking the entrance wall with an ‘X’ by scraping a stone on the wall. “No way through,” she confirmed.
They returned to the central cavern and stood in silence for a moment, gazing down the wide tunnel mouth across from them, the largest of the five, its edges smoother than the others, as if deliberately crafted and reinforced at one time. However, the support beams had long since rotted.
“This one,” Lysana said.
“Looks as if this could be the main tunnel,” Luca agreed.
He marked it with a clean double line beside the entrance. Nothing ornate. Just a way to keep track of where they had gone. They adjusted their cloaks and moved forward into the dark.
This tunnel sloped downward at a steady incline, the floor worn smooth by time, ice, and disuse. Somewhere deeper ahead, a soft tap echoed, stone shifting, or something brushing against the wall. Their boots moved quietly here, the air thickening with depth, walls pulling in closer.
After a hundred paces, the tunnel narrowed again, less a corridor now, more a crack forced open by ancient pressure. Lysana slowed instinctively, testing her footing before trusting the glossy frost beneath her boots. The stone underfoot was slick, glossy in places, where condensation had frozen in irregular sheets.
Lysana took the lead, lantern raised high, her breath controlled but shallow. “Hate this part,” she muttered.
“What part?” Luca asked back.
“Walking into nothing and pretending it's a plan. Waiting on a trap that hasn’t been sprung yet. You know the fun stuff of walking in blind.” Lysana answered. 
Luca said nothing, but his eyes were scanning ahead, watching each foot placement, just as she was.
They reached a turn where the passage curved left, steeper now, walls tighter. The footing changed. A thin dusting of frost disguised a shallow ridge in the floor, and Lysana’s boot caught it wrong. Her foot slid out. She went down hard.
The lantern struck first, cracking but not shattering, and skidded out of reach. Her shoulder hit stone. Then the slope took her. She began to slide. “Shit!”
Luca was already moving. He dropped into a controlled slide, one boot anchoring behind a stone lip, one hand outstretched. His fingers caught the back of her cloak just as her legs kicked toward open air.
There was a drop, barely visible in the dark. Five, maybe six feet. Shallow enough to survive, but narrow enough to break something doing it.
He yanked hard. Her weight slammed into him, knocking the breath from his chest, but they didn’t fall.
For a second, they stayed like that, his arm around her torso, her breathing fast and sharp, the silence crackling between them louder than a scream. A few loose pebbles rattled down the slope beside them, breaking the stillness.
“Thanks,” she said finally.
“You’re welcome,” he replied, voice flat but strained.
They climbed up the slope together, slow and controlled this time. Lysana retrieved the lantern, its glass cracked, but the light was still flickering.
She sat back on her heels, checking the cut on her hand. It was shallow, more bruised pride than injury. Luca knelt beside her, “Let me see.” He took her hands in his as he gave them the once-over. His hand felt warm, felt warm to her. He put her hands together, looked up at her, and smiled at her. It looked out of place, but still she liked it.
“I was just thinking,” Luca said suddenly, keeping his voice low as they moved, yet his voice still echoed. “You’ve heard my story. What’s yours? How did you get here in a cave with me?”
Her facial expression changed from smiling to surprised as she gasped, “What?”
“Fair’s fair. What’s your story, Lys?” he said with the short name sounding odd coming from him.
Whatever she was thinking, it crossed her face before she had a chance to decide not to show it. After staring at him for a second, thinking about everything this moment, she rolled her shoulder and leaned back against the wall.
“I guess you're right. Mine is not as rich as yours, it's simple, really. My parents were scouts,” she said. “Real ones. Mapmakers, route runners. I was born in the saddle, basically. By fifteen, I was running messages between war camps and scouting ahead. Outran wolves once. Not fun.”
“That explains your instincts,” he said.
“It explains why I don’t like standing still,” she chuckled, not looking his way. She started scanning the area for their next move.
He waited for her to continue. “Anyways, I joined the Opindale military early. Fast-tracked because of my field time. Got good. Real good. But not smart. Took a chance on a mission, flanked an enemy group, and saved the squad, good. But I somehow ended up setting half the village on fire while doing it. Not on purpose.”
“I've met men who did less and lost more,” he said. 
“Yeah. Got demoted. Not dishonorably. Just... not promoted ever again,” she said.
“Then let me guess, along came Harmon, and he picked you after that?” he asked.
“Something like that, he said something about wanting the wild ones. I said, ‘Good luck taming me. If you want to tame one, get a dog.’ He laughed. Then he told me about a new military squad he oversees. Told me my talent is too much to be wasted, or something along those lines. So yeah.”
Luca’s mouth twitched, not quite a smile. “Wild one, huh? Do you bite?”
“Maybe.” She gave him the side eye with a knowing smile on her face. They stood, brushed off dust and frost, then turned their attention to the slope.
Luca knelt by the edge, pulled a small chisel and wedge from his pouch, and began scoring footholds into the rock wall where it dropped. “Just in case we have to come back this way fast,” he said.
Lysana began marking a stable path across the slope, drawing an alternate line with a chalk line where footing was better as well. “Next time we don’t roll down a bleeding mountain,” she muttered.
“We’re improving already,” Luca said. The tunnel deepened with every step. Not just in slope, but in stillness.
The walls closed in again, narrowing to just wide enough for them to pass single file. Old beams jutted from the rock like ribs from a long-dead thing; some snapped in half, others bowed but were intact. Their light barely reached the ceiling now. The silence wasn’t comforting. It was waiting.
Lysana walked ahead, lantern up, watching for frost-slick or cracked stone. She didn’t speak until they reached a slow curve in the path, where the air changed subtly warmer, subtly drier. The signs of recent airflow were gone.
“You’ve carried more than most,” she said, eyes forward. “With everything that happened. The sister. The mission. The... Night Veil thing. Do you have any good memories?”

Luca didn’t answer at first. His boots crunched on the stone behind her, slow and even. Then he said, “Do you?”
She smirked faintly. “I asked first.”
Luca exhaled, not a sigh, just breath. Then he spoke.
“There was one contract. Years ago. Remote town, far north, near the wood line. That town is no longer standing. Man had filed a land claim, old blood inheritance, only it wasn’t his. He’d killed the family, buried them behind the chapel, and kept the daughter alive.”
Lysana’s shoulders stiffened, but she kept moving.
“She was nine. Maybe ten. I found her in a cellar, chained to a table. He had been using her. For... you know.” 
“I know,” she said.
“Gabriel heard her call for justice; he set the contract, and I went. I killed him before he touched her again. Slipped a blade into his throat while he was counting coins.”
A pause for both of them to catch their breath. “She looked at me like she didn’t believe I was real. Like the nightmare hadn’t stopped. I broke her chains, gave her a coat, and lit the fireplace. She warmed up to me and wanted to hug me.”
He slowed. “I held up a hand to stop her. Then I stepped through the shadow behind her wall and left.” Silence stretched out between them, but it wasn’t heavy. It carried something else now.
“That was a good day,” Luca said quietly.
Lysana glanced back, her face soft. “Damn,” she said. “If that was a good day, your bad days must really suck.” She smiled at him, and for once, it wasn’t guarded. “But… that’s cool. You were there for her.”
He didn’t reply, but his expression shifted, just slightly. Something uncoiled in his jaw. Lysana turned back toward the path. “Alright, my turn.”
He raised an eyebrow. “Training camp. Recon test. There’s this ridge on the west end of Opindale, cold as hell, jagged, no cover. They drop you with nothing but a flint and a half-frozen canteen and say, ‘Survive for two sun rises and return to the barracks. Oh, and do it without being seen.’ The instructors set a company-sized element to search for us, with hounds. Half of us washed out or failed during this drill. Even I thought I’d.”
She ran a hand along the wall as she passed it. “But I didn’t. I made it back, bruised, frostbitten, and limping, but I made it. Because Harmon taught me to think like the wind. Be quiet, be constant, and move when they look away.”
Luca nodded slowly. “That sounds like him.”
“He didn’t say good job,” she said. “He said, ‘Took you long enough.’ But he smiled when he thought I wasn’t looking,” she said.
Ahead, the tunnel split, a fork, each path disappearing into separate throats of stone. Neither marked. No sound. Just waiting. Lysana pointed. “Right.”
Luca echoed, “Right.” They glanced at each other. “You always fall in step with me now?” she asked, with a bit of edge.
“No, I just figured you’d take the wrong one first,” he shot back.
“Uh-huh,” was her reply.
They both smiled. Then, to her surprise, he laughed. A low, warm sound, brief, but real. It echoed off the stone like something unexpected but needed. “That’s the first time I’ve heard you laugh,” Lysana said.
“Don’t get used to it,” he said.
“I won’t,” she replied. “But… it was nice.” They headed right. Together.
The tunnel tilted again, steeper now, jagged in ways that made footing uncertain even with a good lantern. The smooth stone gave way to crumbled supports and fractured seams, as if the earth had once tried to swallow this passage and only half-finished the job.
They pressed forward carefully, navigating past broken stones and old tool racks rusted into the wall. Then the path narrowed sharply. The light from their lanterns revealed a vertical shaft ahead, ten feet across, slick and rimmed in frost, with a rotted wooden scaffold coiled around the inside like the skeleton of a staircase, or what was left of it. There were also metal rods along one wall leading to the top of the shaft. He tested one with a hard shake; it shifted in its socket. It too looked unstable, as it was missing wooden beams.
They entered the shaft, and there was a large platform, big enough for both of them to stand on with room to spare. Yet on the far end, away from where they entered and to their left was a pit. How far it dropped, they couldn’t tell as they looked into it, and the light from their lantern was swallowed by the darkness.
Luca stepped to the edge of the structure, near the pit, raising his light. “We’ll have to climb it.”
Lysana studied the scaffold. Half the rungs were missing. The rest looked like they’d break under the weight. “There’s a ledge about halfway up,” she pointed. “Could be an old repair platform.”
Luca didn’t hesitate. He moved toward the base, testing the first rung. It held. Second rung. Groaned. Third rung…
Cracked.
The wood gave way without warning, splintering under his boot, and he fell towards the pit.
Lysana lunged, one knee braced on the lip of the shaft, the other leg extended for balance. Her hand shot out on instinct, catching his wrist as his weight tipped forward. His full weight wrenched her shoulder, but she held, teeth gritted, both of them dangling in the cold dark.
His breath hissed out as he dangled, one boot scraping the wall for purchase. He looked back, seeing only shadows. “I’ve got you,” she grunted.
“I can climb—” he grunted.
“Not without both arms,” she said while heavy breathing. She hauled him up inch by inch until his free hand found a crossbeam and pulled. When they finally reached the ledge, they collapsed side by side, breathing hard, dust swirling in the lantern glow.
Luca turned his head, voice low. “Thanks.”
She looked him over. Glancing into his eyes, as his blue eyes pierced the darkness. Her face had gone somewhere else for just a moment, quick and unguarded, before she pulled it back. “Couldn’t risk losing our best climber,” she said lightly. She looked down, then back up at him with just her eyes and said, “Blue eyes are hard to replace.” Her breath still uneven, one brow lifting just slightly.
He blinked. “What?”
She leaned back, grinning. “You heard me.”
His mouth opened like he might respond, but no words came out. He looked away, suddenly very interested in the climb ahead.
Lysana raised an eyebrow. “What, no comeback?”
“I’m not used to… people saying things like that,” he said.
She softened just a little, then the ladder groaned above, and the moment passed. “You mean compliments?”
“No. Yes. I… I’m not used to that,” he clipped, tight breath.
“Ever?” she asked quickly.
He shrugged. “People don’t talk to weapons. They only use them.”
That quieted her for a breath. Then she looked up, spotting a break in the wall across from the shaft. “Hey, ladder,” she said, pointing.
A half-rotted wooden ladder led to a rounded archway above the ledge. Barely visible from below, the curve of stone above it bore an old city sigil.
Lysana tilted her head, then grinned. “You first. I’d rather someone be here if you fall again.”
Luca blinked. “What?”
“I said…” she stopped, grinning wider. “Nope. Too late. You heard me.”
He stared at her, red flickering faintly on his cheekbones from the lantern light. “That’s not… I don’t… that’s not what I—” He shut his mouth.
Lysana laughed, real, unguarded, echoing down the shaft like a breath of air that hadn’t existed here until now. “Relax. I’ll go first. You look like you need to recalibrate your brain.”
He watched her climb for a moment, then shook his head and turned back to the wall.
She called down as she reached the top. “Let’s leave the rope harness when we go. Make the return less… life-threatening.”
Luca nodded, unfastening a coil of cord from his pack and quickly rigged it up to ensure they didn’t have to climb on that old, rotten scaffold.
They were still soldiers. On mission, he thought to himself. But for just a moment, they had shared something real, between the climb, the tease, and the firelight reflected in blue eyes.
The ladder groaned beneath his weight, but he made it to the ledge, where Lysana was waiting, leaning up against the walk, next to another ladder. Higher this time.
“Your turn,” Lysana said, stepping aside.
He smiled and walked over to the ladder. This one was taller than the last. The ladder looked ancient, but climbable. Luca tested the lowest rungs with deliberate weight, then braced and pulled hard against the side rails. The wood groaned but held. Only then did he begin the ascent, slow and measured. She followed close enough to hear his breath, far enough not to crowd him.
“You’re taking this one slow,” she said, not unkindly.
“After last time?” he replied. “I’m allowed.”
“Fair,” she said. A pause. “I just didn’t expect you to be careful.”
He glanced back at her, surprised. “Is that a complaint?”
“No,” she said, climbing another rung. “Just an observation.”
He considered that, then smirked. “You observing me now?”
“Someone has to,” she said. “You look like you’d miss a step if you weren’t watched.”
“Or maybe I’d climb faster,” he said, “if I were.”
She laughed softly at that. “Don’t get ideas.”
The last few rungs ended at a circular hatch set into stone and rusted steel. “Must be the way out,” Luca said.
Luca pressed upward with one hand, the other braced against the ladder’s final rung. Nothing. It wasn’t the weight, it was the resistance. Dirt and rubble pressed down from above. Something had collapsed onto it long ago, warping the hinges and sealing it with weight.
Again. He pushed harder, breath sharp through his nose. Just sifted down from the warped hinges, peppering his knuckles. It moved this time, but only a little, before it slammed back down.
“Let me try,” Lysana offered from below.
He didn’t move. “Just... one more.” He shifted his weight, set his shoulder into the panel, and drove upward with a full-body shove. The hatch gave.
It didn’t swing open. It buckled, then popped with a metallic shriek, sending loose brick and dust pouring into the shaft. Luca staggered back, catching himself on the ladder with one arm. For a heartbeat, nothing moved above but the settling haze of grit.
Luca poked his head out to check out their situation. Two figures appeared from the rubble beyond the hatch, half-hidden by drifting ash. They too looked down at his head protruding from the ground. They were soldiers, both armored, dirt-smeared, and pale. No one spoke.
“You must be the ones we’ve been sent to look for,” the soldier said, hand still on his weapon as his gaze lingered on Luca. “We been on a patrol pattern looking for you all day. Let's get you over to the chapel.”
Luca reached up, grasped the arm, and was hauled the final stretch through the hatch. As he scrambled out into the ruin above, he turned and dropped to one knee, reaching back down.
“Your turn.” Lysana’s hand met his with a clap of skin and leather. He pulled steadily and brought her up beside him. Cold air slapped up from the broken courtyard, sharp with smoke and winter rot.
They emerged into a broken courtyard. Once part of a rear district, now a cratered skeleton of fire-scorched stone. Arrows jutted from beams like iron thorns. The air reeked of ash, oil, and smoke still lingering from the last bombardment.
The two soldiers, one young, not new to war but shaken, nodded toward a half-standing chapel at the edge of the square. Lysana slowed a half-step, jaw tight, taking in the ruin with a controlled breath. Stained glass shattered. The roof partially collapsed. But its frame stood firm.
As they approached, the smell of sweat, old blood, and burnt wood thickened. Inside, the chapel had been transformed, pews turned on their sides to form makeshift walls and bedding. Blankets were bundled in corners. Small fires flickered in repurposed sconces, providing light without exposing the room to view from outside.
Luca saw roughly forty civilians packed inside at first glance. Luca exhaled once, quietly, not relief, not disbelief, something in between. Eighteen were visibly injured. One man, pale, soaked in sweat, lay on a wooden board in the far corner, his lower half wrapped in blood-stained cloth, legs crushed and unmoving. A young girl sat beside him, holding his hand.
The room fell quiet as they entered. A soldier stepped forward, broad, jaw tight, one shoulder plate slightly dented. Luca took him for a sergeant by the presence he projected. The way the others deferred confirmed it. “You’re the ones from the arrow's message?”
“Yes. Name’s Roberts,” Luca said. The Sergeant extended his arm, and Luca met it. “Sergeant Rockwen,” he said. 

Luca then continued, “We cleared a path through the tunnels beneath you. We’ll bring supplies as soon as we can,” Luca said, looking around at what remained of their shelter. “You’ve held up well.”
Sergeant Rockwen gave a short, bitter laugh. “Not well. Just long.” He nodded toward the wounded. “Eighteen injuries. One critical. He won’t walk again. Might not wake up again.”
“I see,” Luca said, his voice following the tone of the moment.
“And the rest?” Luca asked as his eyes swept the room. Children burned. Women with torn sleeves and split lips. Men bleeding through old bandages. Everyone was tired. Too tired to speak. Too tired to hope. Even those who weren’t bleeding carried bruises around their eyes, down their arms, across their ribs. Now that he was really looking, he realized every person in the room was injured to some level.
“Forty-five civilians in total. That includes the eighteen badly wounded. The others are hurt but not seeking care. Conserving the little supplies we have left for those in need. We also have fifteen soldiers, who are still in the fight, including myself. Total of sixty survivors.”
Luca nodded his head as he took in more of the carnage. His stomach tightened at the weight of it, the quiet suffering pressing in on him harder than the cold stone walls. The Sergeant went on, “The rest of the town is either unaccounted for or…”
“Don't worry, Sergeant, you don't have to say it,” Luca said. He had already done that math the moment he walked in the door.
Sergeant Rockwen folded his arms. “How many are you?”
Luca met his eyes. “Four.”
“Four?” the man barked. “That’s all they sent?”
“No one knows. Your messages haven’t been getting through.” Luca explained calmly. A distant thump rolled through the stone overhead, faint but unmistakable, the siege breathing somewhere near them. Luca took the next few moments of quiet to fill in the Sergeant on the refugees who made it to Opindale and the other Orc camp they came across.
Silence filled the air, letting Luca’s words sink in. Sergeant Rockwen stepped back. Not dismissive, just defeated. He ran a hand through his hair and exhaled.
“Why are you not in the fort?” asked Luca.
“Before we could get it open, the mechanism failed under the pressure. The bombardment shook the housing loose. There are rumors of sabotage. They’re trying to brace it, but nothing’s holding yet.”
“How are you communicating with them inside?” Lysana asked.
“One of the lower archery holes, we talk with them there, it's mostly not in the line of sight or the line of fire at this moment,” he replied.
“Okay,” was all Luca said in response as he turned back to the room, working through his thoughts. “I swear to you, we will break this siege,” Luca said evenly. “We will get as many out as we can.” A lone ember drifted up from the guttering fire and winked out between them.
Sergeant Rockwen crossed his arms. “Four of you?” he asked, knowing the answer. Then, after a measured pause, “If you have a plan worth hearing, you have my soldiers.”
No one cheered. No one spoke. But some sat a little straighter. Some breathed deeper. A few looked up, like maybe, just maybe, this wasn’t how it ended.
He stepped aside and sat on a broken pew that had been turned against the far wall, near a guttering fire.
Lysana followed, sliding down beside him without a word. For a long moment, they said nothing, just stared at the flickering light. The wind outside moaned through a cracked window frame, brushing cold air across their boots. “This is bleak,” she murmured, low enough for only him to hear.
“Yes, it is,” he said in response, but more in reflex than giving her his attention. His eyes kept sweeping the area.
She continued to talk to him, but then noticed he was not paying attention. Then a bit louder, “What are you thinking?”
“We need to help them. Why do any of this if not to?” he said quietly, but with resolve.
“I agree,” were her only words.
“I just promised them, now we have to find a way, let's take a rest, then get back with the others and make a plan to save what is left of this village. So many others. Four of us. And Harmon sent me.” A beat. “That math doesn't sit well.”
“I won’t speak for everyone,” she said, meeting his eyes. “But I stand behind that mission. And I believe in you. Even if the others don’t… I do.” Lysana said. No waver in it. Not a word.
They looked into each other's eyes, and no lies were present. Then she said softly, without looking at him, “I meant what I said, you know.” He blinked.
“About your eyes, and you,” she added.
He exhaled through his nose. “Still not sure what to make of that.”
“You don’t have to say anything,” she said. “But… for what it’s worth, I see more in you than you let people see. What you told that sergeant, there is more to you. I am glad I am here with you.”
He turned to her slowly, expression unreadable.
She went on. “With what happened to make you like this, it didn’t take everything. You’ve still got something left. Maybe more than you know.”
There was a long silence. The fire popped once. Finally, he said, “Since my sister died… There hasn’t been anyone. Not really.” He shifted slightly, shoulders tense, as if the words had weight. He looked down at his hands, flexed them like they weren’t his. “I’ve worked with people. Killed beside them. Slept in the same camps. But not close. Not… like how I am feeling now.”
He paused again. The bombardment rolled again overhead, dull and distant beneath the stone. He waited for it to pass before meeting her eyes, looked at her, just for a second, just long enough. “You’re the first person I’ve trusted this close since Eryel. I don’t intend to lose you. Which I don't understand, we’ve just really met.”
Another pause. His mouth twitched like he regretted the honesty, but he didn’t pull it back. “Or to your eyes,” he added. Not a joke. Not quite.
Lysana’s expression softened. She didn’t speak right away. Just reached out and took his hand. Not dramatic. Not performative. Just solid. Warm. Human. Her gaze was steady. Unflinching. “We don’t have to understand. We just survive,” she said. “Then we figure out the rest.”
He nodded. “First, we survive.” He hesitated, but then curled his fingers around hers. They sat like that for a while, the fire crackling low between them. When the next distant strike trembled through the stone, Luca drew back first.
The chapel groaned faintly overhead, ancient timbers settling under the cold weight of the siege. The next bombardment hadn’t started yet, but it would. 
It always did.






Chapter Thirty-One
The sun was low by the time Luca and Lysana crested the ridge. The wind had changed. Softer now, with less smoke in the air. But the sky still burned orange over the ruined horizon, stained by two days of fire and iron.
They rode in silence, both hunched slightly in their saddles, weariness bleeding into their posture. Below them, nestled behind the bluffs and bramble-tucked ledges, their camp remained just as they’d left it. Small. Quiet. Hidden.
As they approached, a shadow stirred by the fire. Luca slowed. “Someone’s back.”
Lysana narrowed her eyes. “Two horses.”
They slid down from the saddle as they reached the perimeter, boots crunching the brittle shale underfoot. A figure stood and turned, his left arm wrapped tight in bandages from elbow to wrist, blood seeping faintly through the linen. His hair was damp with sweat, and his jaw clenched against pain.
“Taerel,” Lysana breathed.
The wounded man gave a crooked smile. “Surprise.”
Luca stepped forward, gaze flicking from the bandage to the tired slump in his shoulders. Beside Taerel knelt another man, hair darker but eyes unmistakably similar. Aymir, binding the last loop of a fresh dressing.
“He’s lucky I found him when I did,” Aymir said evenly. “He was half-slumped over the saddle, bleeding into the horse’s flank. No trail. Just a mark.”
“I told you I was well enough,” Taerel muttered, adjusting the bandage.
“Sure,” Aymir said dryly. “You looked great.”
Luca crouched down to inspect the bandage. “Crossbow?”
Taerel nodded. “Clean pass. Grazed deep. Could’ve been worse.” He flexed his fingers once, testing the numbness, and stopped before it spread.
“What happened?” Luca asked.
He didn't answer immediately. His jaw set once, then released. “I spotted a group of bandits moving through the high trail,” he said finally. “They had two packhorses loaded like a merchant train. Guessing they hit a caravan not long before I found them.”
Luca nodded once. He’d seen that kind of kill-the-wagon behavior before, strip everything of value and burn what was left.
“I shadowed them for a while. Waited until two of them wandered from the fire. Took them quietly, grabbed what I could.” Aymir’s eyes flicked over, as if checking whether Taerel was minimizing something. He exhaled through his nose, the shame finally surfacing.
“I stayed too long. Should’ve pulled out early. Got greedy. A crossbow bolt took me in the arm before I made it to the tree line. Rode hard until everything blurred. Next thing I knew, Aymir was dragging me back.”
“Came back breathing and loaded,” Lysana said. “That's not nothing.”
“Not good enough,” Taerel said. “I should’ve found a town. A route we could use. Something we could count on. This, what I brought back, won’t last.”
“You’re alive,” Luca said. “What you brought might keep them alive. That matters.”

Taerel didn’t look convinced, but he gave a nod all the same. 
The wind shifted again. Behind them, the last red strands of sunlight spilled over the ridge, cutting across their tired faces.
“We’ve got a better place,” Lysana said. “Cavern system tucked into the base of the slope, back through the old passage. Dry, quiet, shielded. We can move the camp tonight.”
Luca gave a sharp nod. “Mount up. No reason to wait.”
They rode single file, winding down the slope through the narrow cut of shale that hid their path from any wandering eyes. The sky dimmed to purple, then black. No moon tonight, only scattered stars and the glow of dying fire across the western cliffs.
The passage was tight, but they moved with practiced quiet. Horses stepped carefully across the stone, hooves hushed on the rock. When the opening came into view, dark and swallowed by roots, it looked like nothing, just another wound in the hill. But inside… 
Inside was breath. Luca lit the first lantern and stepped forward into the vast, natural chamber. The others followed, the walls blooming with flickering gold as the light spread.
A single drop of water echoed from somewhere deep inside, a reminder that the cavern lived even when the world above tried to die. Aymir let out a slow whistle. “Well. You weren’t exaggerating.”
Taerel dismounted and winced as his boots hit the stone. “This is... good.”
“Better than good,” Lysana said.
No one disagreed. They set to it quickly, hitching the horses near the dry corner, laying out their gear. Taerel moved more slowly but stubbornly refused help. Aymir let him.
Watch rotations were assigned: one at the ridge, one near the tunnel entrance. If anything came this way, they’d know. As Luca stoked a small fire in the center of the chamber, they all paused, looking around the space again. A brief silence fell.
Then they noticed it, the absence. The bombardment had stopped. No thunder. No shrieking wood. No screams carried on the smoke, just silence.
Aymir stood up slowly, looking toward the ridge. “It’s been a while since the last volley.”
A subtle tension passed through all three of them. Nobody moved. Luca nodded. Lysana opened her mouth to speak, but stopped. She looked at him for a moment, the way he moved toward the rifle without deliberating, and decided not to argue. He was already strapping his rifle across his back. “I'll be quick,” he said, already moving. The stone throat of the ridge swallowed him.
The others sat in a loose triangle around the fire, their shadows flickering on the walls. Taerel leaned back against a saddlebag. “I really hope this place doesn’t collapse on us.”
Lysana smirked. “Then try not to breathe too hard. You might finish what time has already started.”
The tension didn’t leave, but it settled. For the first time in days, they weren’t under direct threat or exposed to the elements.
The fire crackled low in the center of the stone chamber, its light dancing across the rough walls and casting long shadows. Outside the circle of warmth, the cavern stretched into darkened alcoves and narrow mouths, a web of stone veins lost in time.
Luca crouched near the packs Taerel had salvaged, pulling the leather lashings apart with the same economy he gave everything, no wasted motion. One by one, he laid out the contents, cataloging them in his head. Most of the supplies were crammed into satchels stitched from worn hide, probably looted, like the horses, from a traveling merchant or courier.
First came dried rations, hardtack, spiced jerky, and old root vegetables wrapped in burlap. Then a few medical rolls: aged linen, half-empty jars of salve, brittle herb bundles. Taerel tilted his head. “That jerky is definitely older than your sense of humor.”
Luca didn't answer. He kept going, cooking tins. Tarnished silverware. A cracked flintbox. A handful of throwing knives tucked in a belt pouch. An empty flask with an etched crest long since scratched away.
At the bottom, something more useful. Luca turned it over in his hands. A tightly bound roll of treated leather, thick and water-resistant, still supple despite its age. “This,” he murmured, “might actually be worth something.”
Taerel, resting against a nearby saddle, arched an eyebrow. “What, my random haul impressed the shadow assassin?”
Luca didn’t answer. Just gave the faintest nod of approval.
Aymir would’ve liked that moment, but he wasn’t there to see it, already halfway up the ridge by now. That silence still sat on them like a weight, every moment of it unnatural. The silence that made them uneasy was the same silence giving the people in that chapel the only rest they'd had in days.
Lysana walked over with a strip of dried meat in her hand and sat beside Luca. She studied the items as he repacked what was worth carrying. “Taerel’s got an eye for loot.”
“I have an eye for desperation,” Taerel muttered. “That’s all this is.”
“Still,” she said, elbowing him lightly, “you came back with more than most would.”
The smile came. But his eyes were somewhere else for a moment, counting something that hadn't added up yet.
Luca selected a small canvas satchel and began filling it with the essentials: dried food, clean linen, a few jars of ointment, one of the pans, and a wrapped salve stone. No frills. Just what was needed for a second trip to the chapel. His shoulders were tense, not from weight, but from thought.
He stood and secured the flap. “I’m going back as soon as I catch my breath. Yesterday would've been better. Tonight, will have to do.”
“I’ll come,” Lysana said, already standing.
Luca shook his head. “No. Two shadows draw twice the eyes. If I’m stopped, you stay hidden and hold this place. We can’t both vanish at once.”
She raised an eyebrow. “I’m fine.”
“You’re not irreplaceable,” he said. A beat passed. “But you come close,” he said quietly, something close to a smile on his face. The words sat there a moment, unclaimed by either of them.
She blinked, a flicker of something passing through her eyes. Then she grinned. “Fine. Go be a ghost.”
Taerel stretched his legs, wincing slightly. “What about me? I’m fresh and ready.”
“You’re bleeding through your bandage,” Lysana said flatly.
Taerel frowned. “That is what one calls contributing.”
“Contribute from over there,” she said, pointing to a sleeping roll.
He leaned back again with a dramatic sigh. “Tyrants. I’m surrounded.”
Luca allowed the banter to drift around him, but his mind remained sharp, chewing through variables, numbers, and distances. The supplies might last another day, two at best, even stretched thin. After that... they’d be boiling leather straps and praying for a miracle.
He stood, shouldered the satchel, and went.
Time stretched thin as the two remained in camp. A single drip, somewhere deep in the dark, tapped out its count. They listened without meaning to. Lysana had the food going before Taerel had found a comfortable way to sit with his arm. He watched her work for a moment, then pulled himself upright and started on the bedrolls with one hand. Lysana flipped the meat, stood, and looked toward the tunnel. “Where's Aymir?”
“On the ridge still,” Taerel said. “He’ll come back when he knows more. The smell of the food will make that happen faster, I bet.”
They waited, silent now. The fire crackled faintly, the only sound in the chamber. Outside, the world was still. Not calm, just… waiting. The kind of waiting that made men feel like prey. Taerel shifted where he sat, wincing as his arm tugged at the bandage. “I don’t like it. It’s been too long.”
Lysana stared toward the tunnel. “He’ll come back.”
As the dusk grew into full night, the fire had settled into a soft rhythm, glowing amber across the stone walls of the cavern. The warmth it gave off was meager but steady, and in its circle of light, Lysana and Taerel sat with plates in their laps, voices lowered to a quiet lull.
“Where are you from, exactly?” Lysana asked, breaking a piece of flatbread in half.
“South of Rindhall, in Altisflumen,” Taerel replied, chewing slowly. “A city called Varneth. Not on most maps. Built tight into the river bends. Real quiet, mostly.”
She raised a brow. “So, more farmland or stone and smoke?”
“Both,” he said. “We’ve got steam mills, waterwheels that churn all day. Plumbing in most homes. And steamships docked on the river that ran as far as the sea.” 
“Not bad,” she said.
Taerel gave a soft chuckle. “Not magic, though. That’s the key. We don’t really have Adepts out there. Or if we do, no one’s looking for them. Shards aren’t used for spells; they’re fuel or machinery, nothing more. Cracked shards power the forge motors, even a few of the street lamps in the square. But people don’t channel them. No schools. No tests.”
Lysana frowned. “So, what happens to people who could’ve been tested?”
“They get overlooked,” he said simply. “And if they adapt anyway, they go feral. Or clever. Or disappear.”
“Hunter-types,” she murmured.
“Exactly,” Taerel said. “You learn to survive quietly. Fast. If you spark a light, someone’s going to notice. And out there… people don’t like what they don’t understand.”
She was quiet for a moment, then offered him a small smile. “So, of course, you left. Makes sense now.”
He shrugged. “I like breathing places. Places that don’t feel like they were built to smother.”
Lysana chuckled. “Yeah. You’re definitely not a city boy.”
He raised his flatbread like a toast. “Rooted in tradition.”
That was when they heard the soft scuff of boots at the tunnel’s mouth.
Luca returned, half-shadowed by the stone wall as he stepped inside. The weight in his stride said more than his face, which was expressionless and pale. His satchel was lighter, emptied, but his shoulders sagged from exhaustion, not burden.
Lysana rose without a word, pulled together a warm portion of what remained, and set it beside him on the nearest flat stone. He lowered himself into place without argument, unslinging the satchel from his shoulder and letting it fall to the floor with a dull thump.
She handed him a waterskin. “You made it.”
Luca drank deeply, letting the cold water settle the tremor in his hands before he reached for the food.
“They’re holding,” he said between bites. “Barely. The wounded are stable. What we brought helped. They’ve turned the chapel into a bunker, but even the strongest walls crack when they’re that brittle.”
He glanced up. “I’ve got new numbers. Forty-four civilians inside. Eighteen wounded. One critical. Eighteen guards, tired but still standing. Doing their best.”
Then he looked at Taerel. “What’s the final count from the siege camp?”
Taerel answered with a grim sigh. “Best I could estimate, we’re looking at anywhere from eighty to a hundred total. That includes beast handlers, archers, and whatever’s pulling siege rotation. They’re running three to seven patrols a day. There are twenty-three Worgs.”
Luca gave a short nod. “All right. I need to finalize the report. Harmon’s waiting for it. I want to include more than just numbers. I want to give him a plan.”
No one spoke. Without warning, thunder. The first boom wasn’t distant. It was deep, echoing through the stone like a pulse in the spine. The second came moments later, then the third, as the siege resumed in full force. The cavern rumbled slightly from the force of the impacts. A faint cascade of dust trickled from the ceiling overhead. Luca didn’t react. He just chewed, eyes narrowed, listening.
“Guess they’re back at it,” Taerel muttered. He quickly turned when he heard footsteps pounding from the tunnel mouth. A blur of motion, Aymir, cloak flaring, boots sliding on stone as he nearly lost footing on the incline. He hit the ground sideways, skidded, then popped back up without missing a beat.
Taerel arched a brow. “There will come a day when you arrive somewhere without the accompanying spectacle. I look forward to it.”
Aymir gave him a grin. “And deny the rocks their entertainment?”
He walked to the fire like the entrance hadn’t happened and dropped down beside them, accepting the plate Lysana offered with a nod of thanks.
Luca studied him. “You were gone a while.”
“Had to be,” Aymir said, mouth full. “Wasn’t about just what I saw. It was what I didn’t see that mattered.”
Lysana leaned forward, brow furrowed. “Go on.”
Aymir set his plate down, now more serious. “It was strange. The bombardment stopped. Not staggered, not misfired, stopped. Everything froze. And for a few minutes, I thought maybe they were repositioning. But then I saw the cart come back.”
“What cart?” Luca asked.
“Hunting party,” Aymir said. “Five orcs, I had them logged leaving at first light. Came back dragging enough meat to feed a fortress. Wild drakes, boar, even a plucked carrion buzzard slung over the cart frame. They took it straight into the mess.” Lysana went still at that image, but she kept quiet. This was Aymir’s report. He’d get there.
“And then?” Taerel asked.
“Then the line broke,” Aymir said. “And not like panic. Organized. Calm. The siege crews walked off their lines. The handlers herded the beasts into their pens. Everyone moved like they had somewhere to be.”
He paused, eyes catching the firelight.
“And then they sat down. Not in shifts, all of them. Every orc, every wrangler, every crewman. Full formation. It was like a military exercise. Or a ritual.”
Lysana sat up straighter. “All at once?”
“They prepped in silence. Big pot fires, ladles, and even table setups. It was like watching a damn festival. And then they served.”
“They did all this in one go?” Luca asked, voice low.
“Every night, is what I am guessing. Last night there was a lull,” Aymir said. “Shorter. I dismissed it. Tonight, it matched the same rhythm. Same stillness before the fires rose. I don’t believe in coincidence that precise.”
“And you’re thinking…?” Taerel asked, already suspicious of the tone in his brother’s voice.
Aymir just gave a slow, casual shrug. “I’m just saying... if someone were to slip something unpleasant into that meal…”
Luca blinked once. “Poison? It’s ugly work.”
Aymir grinned. “So is a starving city. You do know poisons?”
Luca narrowed his eyes. “Yes, it is part of the trade.”
Aymir smiled and exhaled slowly. “Yes. It is.”
Lysana was already getting up. “I’ve got roots. Oils in my pack. If we start steeping it now, it’ll be ready by dawn.”
Luca turned his head. “You know poisons?”
She said it with a playful smile. “There is much you do not know about me, shadow.”
Luca smiled back, holding her gaze a heartbeat longer than necessary.
Taerel grinned. “I hate how much I like this plan.”
Aymir sat forward, firelight flickering in his eyes. “We get one shot. One big, nasty pot of something awful slipped in just before dusk. If it doesn’t kill them outright, it’ll drop them hard enough we can either strike... or get those people out.”
Taerel had been listening to the poison plan with one eye on the tunnel. “The people,” he said. “We still have to get them out.”
Luca nodded in agreement. “We do it in shifts,” he said. “Weakest first. Guards rotate as cover. We move when the patrol and bombardment pattern gives us a window. We will have to move slowly. Some of them are seriously injured, and those caverns leading here are not that simple to pass through.” He went quiet for a moment, and when he spoke again, it was almost to himself. “Good thing I held the message.” 
He pointed toward the fire. “Let’s break it all down. I want to ensure I pass on the right information.”
They quickly went over the plan: the orcs’ synchronized eating schedule, the hunting party’s return window, the central food prep area, and how they could infiltrate the mess with enough time to deliver a poison payload before dusk. They estimated travel time, best-case doses, and fallback routes.
When it was done, Luca stood and tapped the thin, rune-etched bracelet on his wrist. The silver threads glowed faintly as the connection opened.

He turned, voice low and precise. “Weslin, this is Luca. Let me tell you what’s been going on…”
As the bracelet dimmed, he looked to Lysana. “Go start your distilling. Let’s see how potent we can get.” She nodded and walked off toward her packs.
Then he turned to Aymir. “Do everything you can. Tomorrow, we go hunting for more ingredients. We’re going to need a poison so foul it’ll punch through even an orc stomach.”
Aymir gave a slow, wicked grin. “That’s a mission worth taking.”






Chapter Thirty-Two
The capital rose before them like a god made of stone. Stormhaven was no city. It was a fortress carved into the mountainside, its layered walls draped in fog of the Blackspine’s lower ridges. The outer bulwarks were wide enough to ride five horses across, ringed in silver wards that shimmered faintly beneath the overcast sky. Spires from the War Colleges jutted above the fog like the teeth of a slumbering titan. Beyond them, the burnished copper dome of the Eternal Forge exhaled its eternal smoke into the pale sky. The city didn't breathe so much as seethe, a pressure chamber barely containing its secrets.
No one spoke as they sat astride their horses in the tree line. Garr’s gauntlet creaked as he tightened his grip on the reins, the only sound anyone dared make. The smell of damp pine lingered under the ozone bite of distant wards. Even Weslin, who fidgeted at the best of times, sat rigid in the saddle, his wide eyes fixed on the behemoth of stone and magic before them.
“Hard to sneak into a mountain that doesn’t mean to let you in,” Garr muttered, his eyes still on the walls.
“We’re not going through the mountain,” Riven said, guiding his horse toward a crumbled path off the main trade road. “We’re going under it.”
They followed in single file through twisted trees and a half-collapsed stonework path that hadn't felt wagon wheels in a generation. The fog thickened as the elevation dipped, giving way to wild growth and choking vines. Eventually, they reached a weatherworn statue, half-swallowed by the forest. Moss clung to its legs, and ivy had claimed its outstretched hand.
It depicted a long-forgotten general, sword buried in the earth at his feet. No plaque. No name. Just stone eyes that gazed forever toward the city he’d died defending.
“This is it,” Riven said quietly. “This shaft was abandoned before the Guild cracked down. Too many cave-ins. Too many dead smugglers. Even the undercrawl stopped trusting it.”
Riven stepped behind the plinth, found the hilt of the buried sword by feel, and turned it once. He'd done it a hundred times and never once felt like the city deserved to keep its secrets. A click, then a grind of stone. Behind the statue, a slab of ground hissed open, revealing a metal grate veiled in rotting leaves.
“You really were a rat once, weren’t you?” Ash said, a crooked grin flashing before it faded.
“I prefer the term ‘urban opportunist,’” Riven said, smirking. “Help me with this.”
Ash and Garr moved in to help lift the grate. The hinges creaked, resisting. Beneath it: a dark stone shaft and a ladder disappearing into blackness.
“Old smuggler path,” Riven said. “Used by the fences and hawkers who didn’t want to pay stormgate tolls. Led straight to the criminal quarters undercrawl.”
Harmon dismounted, eyes sweeping the surrounding trees. “We’ll leave the horses here. Tether them under the low canopy. Garr, brush out our approach. If anyone finds them, they’ll think traders camped too close to the wall.”
They moved quickly. Weslin hesitated, one hand brushing the mane of his horse. “It’s watching us,” he whispered.

Aurelia, already beside him, placed a calming hand on his shoulder. “It’s just the weight of the place. Cities like this remember things.”
Weslin nodded but didn’t look convinced.
One by one, they descended the ladder. The metal was slick with condensation, and every rung a measured echo. Harmon went last, sealing the grate with a quiet clang above him.
Below, the air was thick and stale. The tunnel sloped forward, not down, just enough to keep the moisture flowing along a central channel carved into the floor.
They passed through a crumbling arch into a wider passage. The walls were rough-hewn stone braced with wooden support beams, some still sturdy, others gnawed by time and rot. The silence was oppressive. Even their footfalls seemed dampened.
Then they reached it. The Underlane.
What had once been a low, vaulted market tunnel now sprawled before them in eerie silence. Abandoned stalls lined the corridor like the bones of a long-dead beast. Aurelia slowed, fingertips brushing the stone as if feeling for echoes that simply weren’t there. Rusted cages. Torn awnings. Mugs tipped over mid-drink. A streak of dried blood arced across the flagstone like a final scream frozen in motion.
Ash crouched by an overturned table. “Whatever happened here, it wasn’t slow.”
Riven stood at the center of the lane, slowly turning in place. His usual swagger was gone. He'd stood here a hundred times with coin in his pocket and nowhere to be. He'd watched bards play drunk, and fences argue over gem weights, and men with bounties drink beside the men hunting them. It had been dirty and dishonest and alive. Whatever this place was now, it wasn't that.

Dain’s hand drifted to his blade, not drawing it, just grounding himself. “This place used to be full at all hours. Fences hawking cut gems. Bards, playing drunk. Hell, there’s a bar two tunnels down that only serves criminals with bounties.”
“No rats,” Garr noted, scanning the corners. “Not even vermin.”
Aurelia’s voice was soft, but cold. “It’s been emptied deliberately.”
They pressed forward, Riven now quieter, as the unease of the surrounding setting took hold, guiding them through a maze of offshoot tunnels. One led to a flooded hall. Another storage room was looted bare. At last, they reached a wider chamber with a stacked crate in the center.
Riven nodded to it. “This is the lift-up. They sealed the main shafts after clearing the undercrawl. Smaller ones like this get overlooked.”
Ash and Garr helped move the crate. Beneath, a hatch opened to reveal a short ladder and a dim shaft above.
“This’ll bring us out on the edge of the working quarter,” Riven explained. “Not our final stop. Just a shadow to hide in while I work.”
They headed up one by one. Dain went first. Garr leaned over to Harmon and said quietly, “We should check this out more. There is more here than we can see at first glance.”
“I agree, but later,” replied Harmon. Then the two of them ascended the ladder.
The team climbed up into the back room of a dusty warehouse, its windows painted shut, the air thin with the scent of old grain and oil.
As they filed out into the light of day, the city greeted them like a tomb wearing a mask of a parade.
From here, Stormhaven was unnervingly silent. The guild halls stood tall but still. Market awnings hung undisturbed. In the distance, a squad of Veydrassil marched past, uniform, mechanical, glowing brands on their skin.
Ash tensed. “Those aren’t mercs.”
“No,” Harmon said quietly. “That’s Veydrassil.”
Ash watched them go, “So that’s what they look like without their red cloaks.”
Riven lowered his hood. “Let’s move. The longer we stand still, the more this city breathes us in.” Like shadows in a city full of ghosts, they slipped into the streets. A lone bootstep echoed somewhere down the block, too distant to place, too sharp to ignore.
Stormhaven’s merchant quarter should have buzzed with vendors shouting over cracked wheels and mismatched coin. Instead, silence clung to the cobblestones. The sky was overcast, muting the light, and the chill of the mountains hung close to the skin. The only sound was the rhythmic clack of military boots, measured, exact.
They stood just inside the shadow of a boarded-over entryway, the team stacked tight behind warped beams and frost-brittle crates.
“This is wrong,” Garr murmured. “Even on a bad day, you’d hear beggars or street fights.”
“They’ve scrubbed the city,” Aurelia said, watching the distant patrols with narrowed eyes. “Not just the dirt. The noise. The color. It’s like someone washed all the people clean.”
Weslin nodded slowly beside her, lips pressed together. “The walls feel... full. Like too many thoughts echoing at once.”
“You picking anything up?” Harmon asked.
“No specific thoughts. Just... pressure.” Weslin rubbed at his temples. “It’s like trying to hear through fog.”
“Same,” agreed Aurelia. Harmon said nothing, but he noted it, just as he had done with everything else.
Across the street, a group of five Red Cloaks turned the corner. They moved with uncanny symmetry, their scarlet cloaks catching the gray light like blood spilled across snow. Each one wore reinforced leather, fitted to move, not withstand siege. At their sides hung maces, hand-crossbows, and obsidian-hilted daggers. Some bore quarterstaves etched with carved personal sigils, not true runes, just marks of allegiance or mimicry of ancient power they didn’t fully understand.
Their faces were calm, distant, and empty. Beneath their cloaks, each wore a small shard-embedded pendant or ring, the faint glow of ether drawn from the leylines barely visible to the trained eye. The magic was always there, just beneath the skin, waiting to be unleashed.
Ash watched them pass without moving. “They’re Adepts,” he muttered. “Not footmen. That one on the end? Drawing from a red shard. I can feel the fire in his aura.”
“They all carry shards,” Aurelia confirmed. “Tiny threads, but constant. They’re channeling just enough to stay ready.”
Ash tilted his head. “So they’re all tuned up. Like walking powder kegs.”
“Ain't just fanatics,” Neavin said, not looking away from the street. “Somebody's been training 'em. Feeding 'em power on a schedule. You can feel it.”
“Which makes them dangerous,” Aurelia added softly.
“They’re Veydrassil,” Harmon said matter-of-factly. “Followers of Lucent. Fanatics.”

Dain clicked his tongue. “Bold of them to wear the cloaks now. Used to be only in back alleys or cult hideouts.”
“They’re not hiding anymore,” Riven said. “They’re occupying.”
Harmon took in all the sights and lack of sounds. He muttered under his breath, eyes sweeping the unnaturally quiet streets. “Whatever was burning through this place… It’s already done its work.”
The team said nothing, but the weight of his words hung over them as they moved. Even the wind seemed to hush around the stone alleys, like the city itself held its breath.
Riven stopped at a narrow intersection and gestured to a modest two-story home pressed between a shuttered bakery and a boarded-up apothecary. The exterior was plain, with weathered paint and vines creeping up the sides, but the small iron lantern above the door still had a wick in it, unlit, but telling.
“Here,” Riven said. “Safe enough for now.”
Dain raised an eyebrow. “Charming. You sure it’s empty?”
“Used to belong to a bookmaker who got caught skimming from the Guild,” Riven said. He paused, watching the street through a crack in the curtain. “They've already checked it. Word is he fled. The Guild stripped it clean. No ledgers, no coin trail. Just dust and bad luck. So I took it.”
Nyssa gave him a look. “You really do have a place in every city, don’t you?”
He winked at her. “Comes with the job. Or whatever this job is now.”
The lock clicked open, and the team slipped inside, one by one.
The interior was dusty but intact, plain furniture, a cold hearth, a small upstairs room with a pair of narrow beds, and an attic crawlspace. Nyssa nudged a dusty chair with her boot. “At least it doesn’t smell like corpses or mold. I’ll take it.” The curtains were moth-bitten but drawn. There was no food, no signs of recent habitation, but more importantly, no sign of watchers.
“Better than I expected,” Aldrek admitted, checking the window slits from the upper room. “Limited lines of sight, good vantage if we’re pressed.”
“It’ll hold,” Harmon said. “But it’s just a stop. We’ll rest here for a moment, regroup, and move out before sundown. We still need something more permanent.”
Riven was already at the door, hood drawn. 

“Where are you going?” Harmon asked.

“Securing the place I told you about. This house, I know the owner and we can use it for short stops. Trust me, it will have a bed or two.”

“You’re not going alone,” Harmon said. He turned to the group. “Ash. Go with him.”

Ash cracked his neck. “Figured I’d get the quiet shift. Guess not.”

“Keep your hoods up,” Garr added. “And don’t look anyone in the eye.”

“Wouldn't dream of it,” Riven muttered. The pair slipped out the door a moment later. 

Once they were gone, the rest of the team began fanning out through the upper floor of the house. They kept the shutters tight, watching the city through narrow slats. Each aperture offered a slightly different view of the surrounding blocks: a cloth vendor with no wares, a tanner’s shop locked tight, and a side alley that remained perfectly clean, no footprints, no refuse, no scent.

Garr stood beside one window, arms crossed.

“Never liked cities,” he said. “You can’t see what’s coming.”

“You can feel it, though,” Aldrek replied quietly, standing nearby. “Like a prayer left unanswered.”

Dain lounged in a wooden chair near the map table, one boot up, blade across his lap. “This whole place reeks of performance. It’s a stage, and everyone’s been given a script.”

Nyssa leaned beside the other window, watching a woman slowly sweeping a spotless stoop. “Except nobody looks like they want the part.”

“You see that?” Aurelia said, pointing across the next street over. “Man in the blue tunic. He’s been standing at that corner for four minutes. Hasn’t moved.”

Weslin flinched. “He’s not thinking. I mean, I don’t feel anything from him.”

“He’s not alone,” Neavin added, leaning over her shoulder. “Two more like him by the well. Same posture. Same blank stares.”
A sudden whistle cut through the stillness. Not loud. Not panicked. Structured.
Across the square, one of the Red Cloaks lifted two fingers. The patrol at the far end of the street pivoted in perfect unison and began moving inward, tightening their sweep by half a block.
Garr shifted his weight slightly toward the door. “They’re adjusting.”
“No,” Aurelia murmured. “They’re compressing.”
“They’ve been narrowing the grid since we surfaced,” Aurelia said quietly. “Look at the intervals. It’s district-wide. They are looking for someone.”
Bootsteps multiplied. Not rushed. Not frantic. But deliberate. The patrol pattern had shifted. Where there had been two rotations per street, there were now three.
Harmon didn’t move from the window. “We’ve been mapped,” he said quietly. “Not found. Mapped.”
The woman with the broom stopped sweeping mid-stroke and stepped back inside without looking up.
The street grew smaller.
Reau finally spoke from where he stood in the corner, arms folded.

“Something hollowed this place out,” he said, gaze fixed on the street below. “And left the shell standing.”

His voice was cold. Measured. But something in it told Harmon he’d been here before, in a different city, under a different chain.

They waited, the silence pressing tighter with each passing breath. They rotated shifts, watching out the windows. A shadow slid across a nearby shutter, but it was only a torn banner fluttering loose from a hook. Nyssa noted a pair of Red Cloaks entering a house and not coming out. Dain counted two patrols per street, moving in rhythmic intervals.

Then, without warning, Neavin stiffened near the far window.

“Rooftop,” he said. “Southeast. Movement.”

Harmon moved to his side. On a tall tenement across the way, the shadow of a figure in dark robes leaned out, watching. Then, just as quickly, it was gone.

“You think it was one of theirs?” Garr asked.

“Don’t know,” Harmon said. “It's hard to tell anymore.”

Weslin swallowed. “They know we’re here?”

“Not yet,” Harmon said, turning back to the others. “But we’re not the only ones walking this city with secrets.”

They fell into silence again.

Below, the woman finished sweeping, nothing, and stepped back inside. Across the square, a Red Cloak stood beneath a hanging lantern that hadn’t been lit in days. His staff rested beside him, one gauntleted hand twitching every few seconds as if something was poking it.
Across the square, the man in the blue tunic stiffened. He had not moved in minutes. Without warning, his body jerked.
Once.
Twice.
He dropped to his knees like someone had cut a string. No scream. No cry for help. Just collapse.
The Red Cloak beneath the lantern did not rush. He simply turned his head slightly, as if listening to something only he could hear. A faint shimmer pulsed at the pendant beneath his collar.
The man on the cobblestones inhaled sharply, eyes wide, and then… stilled. He stood. Returned to his corner. Resumed the same blank stare.
Weslin went pale. “That wasn’t fainting,” he whispered. “That was… correction.” No one disagreed. No one moved for a long moment. Someone's hand had found a blade hilt and hadn't let go. 
Inside the townhouse, the team began to write down observations and patrol timings. They noted other odd movements and markings around the area, no detail too small. It was how you learned to breathe behind enemy lines, one note at a time.

Somewhere in the city, Ash and Riven were still moving. Harmon didn't let himself think about where. 

And above them all, Stormhaven loomed like a memory that refused to die.

The door creaked open just enough for Riven to slip inside, followed by Ash, hood drawn low, eyes sharp. Both men paused in the entryway, checking the windows before they spoke.

Riven shut the door quietly. “It’s weirder than you even think.”

Ash moved to the nearest wall slit and took a slow breath. “Whole city’s moving like it’s got someone else’s heartbeat.”

Harmon stood. “Talk.”

They all gathered near the crude table in the center of the townhouse loft, hands resting on blades, arms folded, waiting. The only light came from a single shuttered lantern, flickering across the old wood and maps laid out beneath it. 

Riven leaned forward. “It’s not a cell. It’s a hand, closing.”

Neavin looked at the floor, shaking his head once. 

Dain frowned. “Veydrassil? Occupying? Does it seem like them? I thought they only did hit-and-runs.”

“Not hit-and-run.” Riven set his hands flat on the table. “Full occupation. A hundred Adepts, all in their red. A thousand soldiers across the districts. They've taken the plazas, every choke point. The city has been taken.” 

“They're dug in everywhere,” Ash added. “They’re using the city's own supplies. Every stall, every cart, every warehouse is under their command, used to feed this host.”

Harmon said, “They are ensuring no one notices for as long as they can. Supply trains draw eyes.”

Riven nodded. “And they’re embedding. We’ve already seen a dozen checkpoints between districts. They’re establishing lanes of movement.”

Harmon’s jaw clenched, but he said nothing yet. His fingers drummed once on the table, the only sign he was absorbing the weight of it all.

Riven leaned back slightly. “Red Cloaks. Full uniforms, soldiers. They are not hiding. They’re setting up curfews and redistributing supplies. Ration lines are active near the plazas. We saw one force a merchant to sign over her stall to the city.”

“And she agreed?” Garr asked.

“Didn’t flinch,” Ash said. “Like she’d been waiting to.”

Aurelia’s brow creased. “That’s not compliance. That’s conditioning.”

Reau stood in the back, arms folded, silent as the mountain.

Neavin rubbed his jaw. “So we’re not looking at a rogue cult. We’re looking at organized state-backed subversion.”

“Well,” Dain said under his breath, “that escalated quickly.”

Nyssa glanced out the slit again. “How long until they find us?”

“They won’t,” Riven said. “Not where we’re going.”

He gestured to the door. “Get your gear. I found us a real place.”

Harmon eyed him. “Better than this?”

“Much,” Riven said. 

Harmon gave a slow nod. “Lead on.”

They slipped out just after dark, cutting south through a pair of back alleys and across a maintenance ditch shielded by overgrown vines. Riven led them without hesitation, weaving them through a neighborhood that had once been part of the artisan ward, now hollow and silent. 

He led them deeper into the artisan quarter, where cobbled alleys gave way to polished stone and narrow thoroughfares lined with shuttered shops. In a wealthier time, this would’ve been the heartbeat of commerce, guilds, forges, and scriveners. Now, even the lanterns seemed to burn at half strength.

They arrived at a quiet, run-down training stable, tucked behind a blacksmith’s annex. The smell of old hay and charcoal clung to the walls.

“Here?” Dain said, raising an eyebrow.

Riven only smiled. “Upstairs.”

The loft above the stables was spacious and surprisingly intact. Thick timber rafters supported a low ceiling. There were two narrow windows and four discreetly drilled peepholes in the walls, offering a view in every direction. The air was dry, warmer than expected.
A horn sounded in the distance. Low. Single note. Then another. Riven froze mid-step. “That’s not a city guard,” he said.
Bootsteps echoed below in the street outside the stable. Not patrol cadence. Heavier. Coordinated. Neavin moved to one of the peepholes and leaned in carefully. “Red Cloaks,” he said. “Eight. No, ten.”
They moved door to door across the artisan lane, knocking once. Then entering without a reply. One shopkeeper opened before they knocked. He bowed before they reached him. They still went inside. Ash’s expression hardened. “That’s a sweep.”
“Routine?” Dain asked.
“Can’t tell, normally I would say no,” Riven said quietly. “That looked like a search and confirm.”
The horn sounded again. Closer this time. Harmon did not raise his voice. “Positions. Quiet.” The stable loft that had felt like shelter a moment ago now felt like a ceiling too low. 
“This’ll do,” Garr muttered, nodding while walking into the loft area.

Dain stepped forward, inspecting the space like a merchant checking a shipment. “All this for us? I am touched,” Dain said dryly, brushing dust from his sleeve.
“You’re about to be noble again,” Riven said, though his eyes flicked once toward the street below.
Dain exhaled through his nose. “Always the lord, never the lowlife.”
“You kept that outfit because you liked how I looked at you in it,” Nyssa murmured, stepping just close enough to matter.
“Maybe,” Dain replied, though he did not look away from the peephole nearest him.
Ash shifted near the rafters. “If this turns into poetry hour, I’m taking roof watch.”
No one laughed this time. The horn sounded again. Closer. Riven’s smile faded entirely. “Keep it short,” he said quietly. “They’re sweeping.”
Nyssa’s teasing edge softened. “Then we’ll flirt when the city isn’t listening.”
Dain gave her one last glance, the levity still there, but thinner now. Below them, the patrol shifted against the stone. The moment folded back into discipline. 
Coming from outside, the first bell tolled just as the light drained from the sky. Deep. Resonant. Not the bright peal of ceremony. Not the rolling cadence of festival. This was iron striking iron.
A pause.
Then a second toll. Across the district, shutters snapped closed. A lantern was extinguished mid-street. A child’s voice cut off mid-laugh somewhere beyond the alley.
Dain looked toward the sound. “That’s not a prayer call.”
“No,” Aldrek said softly. “That’s curfew.”
A third toll rolled through the stone like a verdict.
Harmon folded the map slowly. “They own the night.”

Reau stood near the window, quiet as ever, though the corners of his mouth twitched slightly.

“Enough,” Harmon said, cutting through the levity. “Let’s get to work.”

They moved with discipline, rolling out blankets, assigning peephole coverage, and clearing a central table for operations. Nyssa brought out oil and cloth to polish the exposed hinges on the trapdoor, muttering that she'd rather not hear every mouse fart beneath them.

Harmon reached into his satchel and drew out a thick roll of parchment. “At least this time I brought the map.”

He unfurled a detailed floor plan and neighborhood schematic of the city. Old streets, storm drains, and sewer lines crisscrossed with notes in Harmon’s own tight, angular script.

“Spread out your notes. Everything we’ve observed so far. List them all here, fires, patrols, civilian reactions, and district lines. This becomes our log.”

Riven pointed to the westward alley on the map. “That’s where we saw one of the worst zones. Burned carts. Alley full of blood. They dragged someone off, and no one screamed.”

“They’re breaking people,” Aurelia said quietly. “It’s psychological warfare.”

Harmon looked around the group. “This is not a local riot. This is an occupation. Treat it like one.”

He tapped the map.

“We’re here to get intel. Not to free the city. Not yet. Our job is to determine three things: what caused this, who’s running it, and where it started. We need to see if our force is walking into a trap or if they can free this city.”

He looked each of them in the eye.

“Until then, observe. Infiltrate. Survive. And get out quietly.”

There was a moment of silence. Then nods all around. Weslin went over to the far end of the loft and nodded. He stood near them for a good ten minutes before he made his way back to Harmon's side. “Sir?” Harmon was taking in everything going on around him, lost in his thoughts. “Harmon,” Weslin tried again, voice rising. Still nothing.

Reau watched the scene for a moment. Then his eyes settled on Weslin. 

Weslin glanced over. Reau was already watching. He mouthed the words. 'Your big boy voice.' Then he gave a single nod. “Sir!” Weslin said much louder this time, breaking Harmon's concentration and pulling his attention back.

“What is it, boy?” asked Harmon.

“I received a message from Luca. He has news and a plan. He wants your input.”

For the next fifteen minutes, the two stood over the map table. Weslin spoke quickly and efficiently. “The tunnel is viable for movement and safety. Not transport. Not yet. He reinforced what he could.”
Harmon nodded once.
“The chapel won’t last long,” Weslin continued. “The bombardment is shifting west. The stone above the outer wall is starting to fracture. If that quadrant collapses, the civilians lose their last cover.”
“And the gate?” Harmon asked.
“Still jammed.”
A beat.
“The orcs aren’t pushing,” Weslin added. “They’re adjusting formation. Luca thinks they’re preparing for something coordinated.”
The words settled into the room.
“One more thing.” Weslin swallowed once. “He gave his word. Told them they would break the siege.”
No one spoke after that. “How long?” Harmon asked.
“Two days, at most,” Weslin replied. “Less if the bombardment intensifies.”
Harmon stared down at Stormhaven’s map, fingers resting against inked streets that suddenly felt too far from stone and blood.
“Tell him,” he said evenly, “reinforce the tunnel entrance. Prepare the wounded in waves.”
“Yes, sir.” Weslin stepped away to send the reply.
The loft felt tighter now. Stormhaven was closing its fist. And somewhere beyond the mountains, another clock was running. Riven walked over to him, “Harmon. The horses. We're running out of light. “
“Right,” said Harmon. He scanned the room. “Garr. Weslin. Neavin. Aldrek. Aurelia,” Harmon said, as he turned. “You five, retrieve the horses. Curfew’s already in effect. Patrols are running everywhere. If you’re spotted, you abort. No heroics. We lose the horses before we lose you.”
Aldrek stepped forward, voice steady. “Or we take them clean. Fast and decisive. A knight does not abandon his mount to the enemy.” Neavin shrugged from the doorframe. “If we can't get back, we don't. Sleep rough with the horses, bring 'em in the morning when the patrols thin. Ain't no different from the mine roads.”
He took a moment to write something and then called Dain over. “Dain, sign this as the lord. Do you know what name you’re going with this time? It should be different.”
“I was thinking along the lines of Lord Theren Vayle, a minor lord who deals in horses,” replied Dain.
Harmon then said, “Good, now create yourself a cover story. Do you need documents for that?”
Riven stepped in, “He will need a bill of sale for the horse we will put downstairs and a writ to purchase horses in the city.”
Dain pointed at Riven. “What he said.”
Harmon said, “I will get started, of course, with Nyssa's help.” He handed Garr the signed pass. “This should get you and the horse in and give you clear passage back, if we have to use the morning to do it.”
Garr grabbed the document, and within seconds, they all left. Back in the loft, Dain dropped a weather-stained satchel on the table with a dull thud. “We’re going to need a normal. Schedules. Watch rotations. Guard rotations. Contacts.”
“I’ll start mapping patrols,” Ash said.
“I’ve got eyes east,” Dain added, peering through a peephole. “Nothing but lanterns and footsteps.”
“Let’s hope it stays that way,” Aurelia murmured.
Reau, arms crossed, said, “We’ll need codewords. If they’re listening.”
“They always are,” Nyssa said softly.
Harmon's fingers traced part of the map. “We'll make this our stronghold. And if they're really bold enough to come here…” He looked at each of them once. “Then they'll learn we're not just passing through.” 
He said nothing else. He didn't need to.






Chapter Thirty-Three
 Morning was still working itself into noon when Dain adjusted the cuffs of the deep maroon doublet he wore, the fabric rich and smooth, trimmed in silver. His cloak hung from one shoulder, fastened with a polished brooch bearing a forged crest. He caught his reflection in the small polished mirror propped near one of the support beams and straightened the collar with a touch of disdain.
“You know,” Nyssa said from across the room, stretching out one leg while tightening her boot, “I liked those silks on you the first time. Good to know you're still dressing to impress.”
Dain gave a smug half-smile. “That is precisely why I kept them,” he replied, smoothing the cuff as though the answer required refinement.
She arched a brow. “A bit bold for a stable loft,” she said lightly. “Though I suppose nobles do not sweat like the rest of us.”
“You wound me, my lady,” Dain said with mock offense, placing a hand to his chest. “Would it help if I said I wore them just for you?”
Nyssa rolled her eyes. “Please. You're too proud to admit that… even if it's true.”
Nearby, Weslin stood awkwardly, fidgeting with the strap of his satchel. His eyes kept darting toward the small yellow shard tucked carefully into the inner pocket, a gift from Aurelia.
