Aurelia, seated with one leg tucked beneath her on a crate, looked up at him and gave a gentle smile. “You’re nervous.”
Weslin hesitated. “It just… feels different carrying one. Like I’m not supposed too yet.”
She stood, moving with the easy grace of someone who had spent a lifetime balancing power and restraint. “You're not alone, Weslin. You're trained. You’ve practiced. This isn’t about being ready in theory, it’s about trusting your instincts.”
She placed a hand lightly on his arm. “Use the flow, don’t tap it. Let it move through you. Control comes with rhythm, not force. Do you remember the spells we reviewed?”
Weslin nodded slowly. “True Eyes. Minor Illusion. Glamour. I think I can.”
“You can,” she cut in softly, her eyes warm and steady. “You’re not alone out there. And you’ll do just fine.”
Weslin managed a small, unsure smile. “Thanks. I’ll try not to screw it up.”
“You won’t,” Aurelia replied, her voice quiet and confident. Before Weslin could shrink back into his nerves again, Garr’s voice came from the corner. “You’ve… come too far to fall now.” He didn’t look up from the blade.
He was sharpening a blade with short, practiced strokes, counting each one. Reau sat on an overturned bucket near the map table, scribbling something into a folded leather journal. Aldrek leaned against a support beam, arms folded, occasionally glancing toward Harmon, who still hadn’t spoken.
Figuring there was time, Brother Aldrek knelt in silence for his morning prayer. He bowed his head, one hand resting lightly on the haft of his mace, the other curled in prayer. Lips moved without sound, the worn edges of his robe pooling around his armored knees. It was a habit from years past. Whenever a mission bore the weight of uncertainty, he gave his doubts to the gods before bearing steel.
Harmon stepped away from the table, his boots thudding softly on the wooden floorboards. He stood tall near the edge of the loft, one hand resting on the hilt of his sword as he took in the team.
“Eyes up,” he said, voice low but unmistakable. Heads turned. Conversations paused. Even Nyssa, halfway through another jab at Dain, went silent.
Harmon let the quiet stretch a bit before beginning. “You all know your assignment,” he said, pacing slowly, boots measured against the boards. “Stormhaven didn't fall with a scream. It fell in silence. No messenger. No flares. Just a whisper of smoke and a few half-dead refugees stumbling out of the dark.” He stopped pacing, folding his arms. His hand found the pommel of the cane without notice.
 “We're not the hammer this time. We’re the lantern. I need each of you to dig in and find out what happened, without getting killed in the process. No heroics, no theatrics. Eyes open, mouths sharper than blades. Talk to people. Everyone. Shopkeepers, drunks, guards, children, it doesn’t matter. Information is gold, and right now, we’re broke.”
He pointed toward the city with a tilt of his chin. “We need to know who is running this city. What happened to the nobles? Who are the Red Cloaks working with? Why the change to their tactics? Resistance? Bring back anything and everything. We will sort it later.”
“Also, map the occupation. Evidence of who they are and where they came from.” From the far wall, Riven gave a sharp, quiet whistle. Harmon continued as if nothing had happened, “I know I am asking a lot, yet I expect a lot. I never said this was going to be easy. We meet back here.”
Riven leaned on the window frame. “And if someone asks us what we’re doing?”
“Tell them you’re wine merchants scouting for rare bottles,” Harmon deadpanned. “Or you’re lost. I trust your creativity, Riven. Don’t get arrested.”
“Tempting,” Riven said with a grin.
Harmon swept a hand across the map. “We’ll reconvene tonight. Don’t get fancy. Don’t get dead.”
Harmon paused just long enough for the words to settle, his gaze sweeping the loft as if weighing each of them against the risks ahead. He walked back to the table and rested both hands on the edge. “I’m pairing you up based on how likely you are to get results... or survive.”
He turned to the first. “Dain, you’re on your noble cover. Nyssa, you're his escort, make it believable. Blend in but keep those eyes open. I want you both in the guild districts and the markets. If anyone’s got gossip, it’s the ones with silver tongues and gold purses.”
Nyssa gave a two-finger salute. “Always a pleasure to play Lady Ghost.”
Dain raised a brow. “Looks like we both get to wear silks. My lady.”
She winked and gave a devious smile. “Mi lord.”
He offered her a smirk. “Mi lady. This could be fun.”
“Weslin. Reau. You’re scouting the middle districts, merchant lanes, taverns, anything on the edge of the noble quarter.”
Reau gave a nod, his voice low. “Got it.”
Weslin tried to match it. “We’ll find what’s worth knowing.”
Harmon continued. “Aurelia, you’ll be with Aldrek.”
He paused for a moment, then said, “Neavin, you join them. I think that might need some more manpower.”
Aurelia gave a warm smile. “Of course.”
Aldrek, kneeling briefly beside the mast in prayer, rose smoothly. “Where there is shadow, light must follow.”
Neavin grunted, the corner of his mouth pulling up before he caught it.
“That’s the spirit,” Harmon said. “Check the temples, the silent corners, anywhere people might still gather when they’re afraid.”
Then his gaze shifted to Riven. “And you.”
Riven arched a brow, already grinning.
“You’re our key to the city,” Harmon said. “Word is, you’ve got a name that opens more doors than most keys. Time to prove it. Today’s the day to earn that pay.”
“Take Ash with you. Try not to set anything on fire.”
Riven smirked. “You had me at ‘prove it.’”
Ash rolled his shoulder, flame-etched tattoos pulsing faintly beneath his collar. “Let’s just hope they don’t recognize me from less... diplomatic days.”
“Garr, you are with me. We will check a place I noticed when we came in. After that, we lend a hand where we can. We meet back here tonight. Take the day. Find what you can. If someone is not back by the tenth bell, we search. Now go find the thread… and begin to pull.”
A stillness settled in the loft as Harmon’s final words echoed through the space. For a breath, no one moved, just the creak of the rafters above and the wind whispering against the outer walls. Then someone moved. Then everyone did.
Chairs scraped. Boots thudded against the wood floor. Cloaks were drawn tighter, weapons checked, and belts cinched. The room didn’t burst into noise, but it stirred with a quiet, focused energy. Conversations came back slowly. The blade-sharpening resumed. Boots were checked. Someone tightened a strap twice. One by one, teams drifted toward their corners of the loft.
Across the room, Nyssa had disappeared into one of the side storage areas and returned dressed in a flowing charcoal-gray dress that hugged her form without restricting movement. Her hair had been tied up elegantly, her face touched with just enough color to draw the eye without shouting for attention.
Dain nearly choked on his water. “Merciful gods.”
Nyssa offered a slow spin. “You like it, my grace?” she purred.
Dain smirked, bowing low. “My lady. You… clean up disturbingly well.”
Nyssa gave him a slow twirl, the corner of her mouth tugging into a grin. “I once had to pass as a noble’s cousin’s cousin to rob his estate. Got halfway through dinner before I stole his ledger, three rings, and the heart of his steward. Poor man still sends letters.”
Dain chuckled, eyeing her dress. “Where do you even keep that?”
She stepped closer, leaned in like she might share a secret, then whispered with a wink, “Same place I keep the knives. Want to help me find them later?” As she lifted her dress, exposing her leg, she showed off a garter with three throwing knives strapped to it.
Dain raised a brow, his smirk deepening. “Oh, I see. Deadly and well-dressed. Remind me to never argue with you in close quarters.” His eyes lingered a heartbeat before he caught himself, clearing his throat as if to shove the moment back into professional territory. “But yes… I think I could be persuaded to help with a search. For tactical purposes, of course.”
Riven passed them with an amused snort. “Don’t forget the curtsy, Nyss.”
“Jealous?” she shot back.
Riven winked. “You never dressed up like that for me.”
Nyssa threw him a mock glare while Dain's smirk faltered ever so slightly.
“Come on,” Nyssa said to Dain, linking arms. “Let’s give the city something to talk about.”
They swept from the loft, all together. Nearby, Weslin sat beside Reau, visibly trying to calm his nerves. Reau, polishing the edge of a blade with steady, practiced strokes, glanced over with that usual calm of his.
“You alright?” he asked.
Weslin hesitated, then gave a small nod. “Yeah. Just… big mission. Bigger city.”
Reau grunted softly. “You’ll get used to it. Or you won’t. Either way, you learn to keep moving.”
Weslin let out a slow breath. “That’s… comforting.”
Reau cracked a faint smile. “Didn’t say it to be comforting.”
There was a pause. The air between them felt heavy with things unsaid until Reau’s voice dropped a notch lower, quieter.
Reau set the blade down. He didn't look at Weslin when he started. “Just… be careful with Harmon. I’ve seen that look before. I had it once. Someone should have warned me.”
Weslin blinked, confused. “What? Harmon… he’s the best. He hasn’t done anything to earn that kind of warning.”
Reau nodded. “Yeah. He’s that. And more. I’ve seen him do things no one else could. Man’s a legend for a reason. But he’s also a Ringbearer.”
He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees, the blade forgotten in his hands.

“My father wore a ring. Different than Harmon’s, but the same kind of power. I grew up watching it shape him. He loved me. I never thought he didn’t. But once that ring claimed him, his love had rules. Priorities. The mission came first. Always.”
Weslin looked down, hands clasped in front of him, taking in what Reau just said. 
“I don’t know your full relationship together. I just wanted to warn you, that's all. Just know the ring comes first.”
Weslin then nodded, “I will keep that in mind.” After a moment, he fished a smooth yellow shard from his inner pocket, turning it over in his fingers.
“I keep thinking… what if I can’t do this? What if I mess something up? I’m not like the rest of you. I wasn’t trained for war, blades, or this. They gave me this shard as if it’s supposed to make me useful. But what if I’m not? What if I let him and everyone else down?”
Reau exhaled sharply through his nose, not unkindly, just enough to cut the spiral before it swallowed the boy whole. He looked at the shard for a long moment before nodding.
“Yellow’s underrated. People see fire and stone and think strength. But Yellow? That’s where the insight comes from. The instincts. It’s the only kind of power that gets stronger the more you listen instead of acting.” He held Weslin’s gaze.
“Trust the shard. Trust the power. But more than that, trust yourself. That shard doesn’t define you. It just gives you the chance to figure out who you already are.”
Weslin nodded, slowly. “Never worry about what someone else thinks. You’ll make mistakes. That’s fine. What matters is what you learn from them… and who that makes you.” Reau leaned back, a smirk returning. “Also, if you ever do lose it, just shout really loud. I’ll pretend I didn’t hear you for a minute, then come save your ass.”
That earned a small laugh from Weslin, and for the first time that morning, his grip on the shard loosened, just a little.
Reau turned slightly, finishing the careful wrapping of a silver collar at his throat. The glint of metal had caught Weslin’s eye earlier, but now, with the movement, it became impossible to ignore.
Weslin hesitated, then asked quietly, “That collar… what is it?”
Reau paused a moment, his fingers tightening the wrap as if debating whether to answer. Finally, he sighed through his nose. “It’s a binding collar. Suppresses power. Cuts me off from what I am.”
Weslin blinked. “Cuts you off? Why not just… take it off now that you’re out?”
“It’s keyed to a specific frequency lock,” Reau said, voice low. “Only the object it was bonded with can release it.” A muscle feathered in Reau’s jaw, the only crack in his usual calm. “That’s not exactly something I’ve got in my pocket.”
Weslin’s brows drew together. “That’s… brutal.”
Reau gave a small shrug. “That’s Morlin for you.”
Weslin was still unsure how to ask, yet asked anyway, but very quietly, “So, are you an Adept too?”
Something behind Reau's eyes went still. He nodded. “Different than most.” A beat passed. Then Reau added, almost absently, “I don’t like talking about my abilities and what this has taken from me.” Another pause, then, “Maybe when we know each other better.”
Weslin didn’t press. He simply nodded, respectful of the boundary, but his gaze lingered a moment longer on the collar before turning back to the others gathering their gear.
Riven sat on the floor, sharpening a throwing knife with slow, deliberate strokes, the steel whispering against the whetstone. Across the room, Ash leaned against a beam, arms crossed, watching with a half-lidded stare.
Without looking up, Riven asked, “You good with crowds?”
Ash’s lip curled. “I like ‘em best when they’re running.”
Riven chuckled. “That’ll work. You make the noise. I’ll make the memories vanish.”
Ash tilted his head. “You're always this confident, or is that just a side effect of dressing like a scandal?”
Riven finally glanced up, flashing a roguish grin. “Scandal’s easier to pull off than trust. But both look good on me.”
Ash snorted. “Guess I’ll handle the smoke. You handle the mirrors.”
“Deal,” Riven said, flicking the knife into the air and catching it without looking. “Let’s give them a show they’ll never quite remember.”
Aldrek stood near the center mast, head bowed in silent prayer. One hand rested on the hilt of his mace, the other traced a slow circle over the ancient symbol carved into the post.
Aurelia's eyes drifted to the symbol briefly. She didn't recognize the order, but the geometry was old. Older than the building. When his eyes finally opened, she said softly, “You always start with prayer.”
He looked at her, eyes calm. “I speak to what strength remains. And it listens. Sometimes.”
She offered a quiet smile. “We could use a little divine luck today.”
“Luck, no. God favors the ready,” Aldrek said, adjusting the straps on his armor. “We go into the unknown. Be steady. Be true as his guiding hand.”
From behind them, Neavin cleared his throat. “You two always this ominous in the morning? Or’s this a special occasion?” 
Aldrek gave a rare, faint smile. “Fear is not failure. Only fools walk into shadow without feeling its weight.”
Neavin let out a low groan. “Saints save me, you two are insufferable before breakfast.” He paused before he continued, “Rather have odds I can count. This city feels like walkin' into a problem someone already burned half of.”
Aurelia placed a hand gently on his shoulder. “Then solve it one piece at a time. You’re not alone in this.”
A faint clang of metal echoed from somewhere outside, distant but sharp enough to make all three glance toward the shutters. Neavin gave her a grateful, if uneasy, nod. “Right. One piece at a time.”
Aldrek grunted approvingly. “Good. Let’s be off. The day waits for no soul, nervous or otherwise.”
Aurelia froze mid-step, her eyes widening, not with fear, but clarity. “Wait,” she said, sharp enough to halt even Harmon at the door. Everyone turned.
She stepped forward, her voice low but urgent. “We’ve all felt it. The city is… off. People are acting strangely, subdued, always watching. They’re walking someone else’s path entirely. Controlled.”
There was a ripple of agreement, some nods, a few stiffened spines.
Aurelia glanced at Harmon, then to each of the others. “We don’t know who’s behind it or how far the influence goes, but until we do, we shield our minds. Everyone. Mental shielding isn’t just for Yellow Adepts. You can do this. It isn’t instinct. It takes training, intention. It’s discipline itself. Most don’t know how. They never learn it unless someone teaches them.”
Weslin looked unsure. “I’ve only practiced with you a few times. I’m not…”
“You’re ready,” she said gently, stepping closer. “It’s not about brute strength. It’s about building a wall of intention.”
She turned back to the group. “Close your eyes. Center your breath. In. Out. Ground yourself, not in this city, not in fear, but in who you are. Your memories. The things that make you. Hold to that.”
Some shifted uncomfortably. The others already followed. Ash cracked one eye open, muttering, “Feels like meditation with extra steps,” before Aurelia’s sharp look shut him up again.
“Now imagine a sphere around your mind, just above your skin, pulsing slightly with each breath. That’s your boundary. You don’t need to block thoughts. Only let nothing foreign pass that barrier. No whispers that aren’t your own. No suggestions that feel unnatural.”
She reached into her satchel and drew out a dull yellow shard, holding it aloft. “For Adepts, your shards will amplify this. Let the shard feed the shield. Don’t tap. Let it flow with your breath. The shard should move with you, not ahead of you.”
Aurelia turned, eyes briefly finding each face. “It will hold. If anything tries to push through, you’ll feel it. And if you do… don’t panic. Return to the wall. Breathe. Anchor.”
Dain cracked an eye open. “And if we start hearing voices?”
“Then you run,” Aurelia said flatly, “and you tell me. Immediately.”
Ash gave a low whistle. “City’s just getting better and better.”
Aurelia exhaled. “I’m not saying something will try to get in. But if something already has, we’ll be the first to know.”
Harmon gave a slow nod. “Good thinking, Mentalist. Consider it standard protocol for now.”
Nyssa opened one eye. “So, we’re walking into a city of secrets, half a dozen lies, and now maybe mind control? When did we start living in a fairy story?”
Aurelia didn’t argue. “Just worry about keeping your mind your own.”
One by one, the buzz of voices in the loft gave way to motion. Armor was buckled, cloaks were thrown over shoulders, and weapons found their homes beneath fabric folds or in clever sheaths. Final glances were exchanged, some serious, some teasing, others wordless but heavy with shared purpose.
The last of the city’s morning light filtered through the slats. The team split into pairs. As footsteps hit the stairs, “We move soft and wide,” Harmon said. “Too large a group becomes a target. Pairs blend. Crowds swallow them.”
Dain and Nyssa went first, smooth and unhurried as if they did this every season. Aurelia and Weslin followed, her hand briefly on his arm. Aldrek needed no sending-off. Neavin muttered something about breakfast and descended. Riven flicked his collar up. Ash went after him like a shadow. Reau paused at the top of the ladder, looked back once at nothing in particular, and went.
At the table, Harmon stood still, watching them vanish into the city one by one. Garr waited at the door.
Only the sound of the wind moved through the loft now. Garr moved to the peepholes with his arms folded across his chest. Morning light slanted through the loft rafters, dust catching golden in its beams. At the center table, Harmon adjusted the thick leather straps across his shoulder and reached for a cane resting against the wall, blackwood, knotted with age, a metal pommel carved into the shape of a closed fist.
He rarely used it. Garr turned from the window. His eyes went to the cane, stayed there a half second, and came back up without a word. Whatever question formed didn't make it out. “Didn’t know you had a limp,” Garr said.
“I don’t,” Harmon replied, testing the cane’s balance in his palm. “But the streets ahead aren’t paved with courtesy. Sometimes, the cane’s not for walking.”
He gave Garr a sidelong glance, eyes steady. “We’re heading for the crater.”
Garr raised an eyebrow. “Crater?”
“There’s one detail all the refugees agreed on, that surfaced again and again in their accounts, even through the shock,” Harmon said, his tone even. “An explosion. Near the heart of the city. It’s the only thing I believe wasn’t a rumor.”
Garr’s mouth tightened. “You think it was magical?”
“I think a lot of things. But I’d rather know.” Harmon stepped to the window beside him, adjusted his cloak. “Too many unknowns. Too many silences where answers should be.”
There was a long pause. Garr asked quietly, “So why us?”
Harmon didn’t answer immediately. He tapped the tip of the cane gently against the floorboards, gazing far away for a breath, then locked eyes with him.
“Because I trust you,” he said. “And I need someone watching my blind side who still knows what it means to believe in something.”
Garr looked down at his hands, calloused from training and battle, then back up. “And what exactly are we believing in today?”
Harmon gave a soft, humorless chuckle. “That the truth still matters.”
That hung between them for a moment. “You think this,” Garr gestured toward the city beyond the walls, “ends with us walking out heroes? With flags and honor and a clean slate?”
“No,” Harmon said. “I think it ends with us bleeding in the dirt, or limping back with ghosts in our pockets. But if we’re lucky, someone else walks out clean because we didn’t.”
He looked at Garr, not as a commander but as a man.
“That’s what legacy means, Garr. Not what you keep… what you give.”
The younger man nodded, quiet for a moment, then offered a lopsided grin. “Sounds like something a mentor would say.”
Harmon smirked. “I’m too tired to be a mentor. Think of me as a very dangerous old man who’s been where you’re going.”
Garr gave a small laugh. “Fair enough. So… to the crater?”
“To the crater,” Harmon echoed, shouldering the cane and stepping toward the stairs. “Keep your eyes open. Ears sharper. And your blades close. The truth never comes quietly.”
Garr followed, slower, still chewing on Harmon’s words. He said nothing more, but the weight in his steps said he carried them with him.
The last team slipped into the winding lanes of Stormhaven, their shadows stretching long across the stone as morning gave way to noon. The safehouse door shut behind them with a final, weighted click.







Stormhaven held its breath. The once-proud capital of Aldoria, carved into the bones of the Blackspine Range, now stood draped in quiet tension. Its slate rooftops shimmered under a gray morning sky, dew still clinging to eaves and cobbled streets as if the city refused to exhale. The wind wound through alleys like a whisper too frightened to speak aloud. The towering walls, once the envy of every kingdom, stood silent, not in defense, but in watchfulness.
Near the city’s heart, jagged rubble and scorched iron marked the ruins of the Governor’s statue in Ironmarch Plaza, the wound no one dared name aloud. Yet, the bells rang. Bakers sold bread. Children played. Laughter echoed too sharply. Nothing had stopped, everything had just… shifted.
Dain and Nyssa walked side by side beneath stone archways and weather-worn sigils, arm in arm like nobles with too much coin and too few worries. His emerald coat gleamed with just the right amount of arrogance, and her silver jewelry caught the morning light like teeth behind a smile.
She tilted her head, watching the crowd watch them. “Half of these people think we're inspecting stables. The other half thinks we're lovers.” An old woman's eyes had not left her since they turned onto the street. Her fingers tightened briefly on his arm.

Dain didn’t miss a beat. “And what, in your estimation, are we?”
“Professionals.” She glanced at him sidelong. “Though you are doing an awful lot of fidgeting for someone who grew up around ballrooms.”
He adjusted his cuffs with mock offense. “I’m not fidgeting. I’m brooding. It’s fashionable.”
“You’re glancing at my neckline,” Nyssa said. 
“I’m keeping watch for knives,” Dain said.
A patrol rounded the corner, too slow, too alert. Every smile on the street froze for half a breath before laughter resumed.
She gave a quiet snort, then reached up and adjusted one of her silver hair combs, an idle touch that, Dain noted, also subtly reset her field of vision.
“You’re sharp today,” he murmured.
“I’m always sharp. You just forget when I’m not throwing things.”
He leaned closer. “So, what is it with you and high society? You sound like someone who’s sat through too many dull dinners.”
Nyssa’s smile flickered, just for a second. “My father hosted auctions, not feasts. But if you want a room full of warhorses and fat merchants to eat from your palm, you learn how to use the right fork, and how to stab with it if the deal sours.”
Dain blinked. Then grinned. “Remind me never to take you to a wedding.”
“Too late,” she said, gesturing to the boutique up ahead. “We’re practically engaged.”
The stone-front shop loomed before them now, all delicate carvings, ornamental lanterns, and windows with thick curtains drawn tightly closed. Two guards in polished black cuirasses stood like statues beside the entrance, eyes sliding over Dain and Nyssa in quiet evaluation.

The smell of lilac oil and scorched metal hung heavy in the air as Dain and Nyssa ascended a marbled avenue flanked by wrought-iron fences and spindled lamps. The cobblestones here were smoother, worn by generations of noble boots and polished carriage wheels. Ornate doors closed silently as they passed. The air was too still. Too watching.
“This district’s too clean,” Nyssa muttered behind a smile as they passed a pair of stone-faced guards in crimson sashes. “Almost like it’s trying to convince itself nothing’s wrong.”
Dain didn’t glance at her. “Which is exactly what people do before a funeral.”
They crossed into a terrace lane overlooking a manicured garden, where a trio of cloaked nobles stood near a fountain, murmuring with cups of steaming leafwater. Dain touched Nyssa’s elbow and veered subtly, guiding them toward a boutique draped in sheer blue curtains and amber glass.
Inside, the scent shifted to lavender, rich cloth, and a hint of something chemical underneath. Gold-threaded tunics and formal gowns hung on suspended rails. A thin woman with ink-black hair and a quill tucked behind one ear looked up from a ledger.
Nyssa leaned in one last time before they crossed the threshold. “You sure you’re ready to play suitor to a third daughter with a dowry of mares and attitude?”
Dain offered his arm like a gentleman. “For you, my lady, I’d brave the entire merchant guild council.”
“Good,” she said, taking his arm. “Because after this, I might need you to carry me. These shoes are an unusual torture.” Just like that, they stepped through the doors, all silk, poise, and perfectly rehearsed lies.

“Welcome to Celairyn Silks,” she said, bowing without warmth. Dain returned the gesture with just enough poise to imply old money without old arrogance. “Lord Theren Vayle, and this is my companion, Lady Liora Quell of Fairmere.”
Nyssa’s curtsy was deep and devastatingly elegant. “A pleasure. I’m here to ensure he doesn’t bankrupt his estate chasing silk.”
“Only chasing quality,” Dain said, letting his eyes travel the boutique before landing on her again. “Though I do tend to overpay for rare finds.”
Madrelis offered a small, sharp smile and gestured for them to come inside. “You’ve come on a good day, my lord. Shipment from Eastern looms arrived this morning. Rich fabrics, resilient dyes, perfect for acquisitions.”
Nyssa touched a bolt of deep burgundy velvet. “We were told this was where the discerning come for more than fashion.”
“Whoever told you that should consider a career in sales,” Madrelis replied smoothly.
“I’ve not seen you before, my lord. What business brings you?” Madrelis asked.
“Horses, I just bought that old stable by the blacksmith shop, looking to train horses here,” Dain replied with an air of pride.
They moved deeper into the shop, where delicate silver bells hung in the corners. Another figure stood examining a rack of ceremonial coats, an older man, lean and balding, with a noble’s polished bearing. He turned slightly at the sound of Dain’s voice, eyes narrowing with interest.
“Lord Vayle?” he said, stepping closer. “I don’t believe we’ve met.”
Dain offered a nod and his hand. “We’ve only just arrived.”

“Just arrived and already found Celairyn? Impressive. Most newcomers take weeks to be seen here.”
Nyssa smiled. “He has me. I find things.”
“She does,” Dain said.
The noble chuckled, offering a hand. “Lord Halvayne. May I ask what brings you to Stormhaven?”
Before Dain could answer, Madrelis stepped in with uncanny timing. “Lord Vayle recently acquired the old training stable. With the treaty signed, there’s talk that the war games may resume. He’s looking to field a new generation of champions.” The detail wasn't for them. Dain noted it the way he noted a blade angled at someone else's throat.
Dain nodded. “I believe there’s no better time to invest in the future. And no better place to start.”
Nyssa added brightly, “And no sharper eye than mine for picking the mares to do it.”
“Indeed, it's been far too long without the games,” Halvayne said, studying her with amused interest. “And your family?”
“My father runs one of the largest horse trading networks east of the Selenmar fields,” Nyssa replied, tone honeyed. “He's hoping this venture becomes more than just trade.” She flashed a rueful smile.
“Oh?” Halvayne’s eyes flicked between them. “A merger of sorts?”
“Something like that,” Dain said with a practiced grin. “I’m evaluating….” He turned and looked at her. “The offer.”
Nyssa gave him a warning smile. “You’ll find I come with few flaws. Yet many assets.”
Madrelis made a quiet sound, something between a cough and a stifled laugh, but her eyes flicked toward the door before she gestured toward the back. “Perhaps you’d be interested in viewing the private collection?”
“Please,” Nyssa said, hooking her arm through Dain’s.
They followed her through beaded curtains into a smaller room of tailored pieces. Madrelis glanced at the other customer over her shoulder and said, low, “There’s a lot of noise these days. People don’t speak plainly anymore. Not unless they know your cut.”
“We’re good listeners,” Dain replied, eyes watching the room.
Madrelis hesitated. “There’s a name. Korr. Just a whisper, really. But people seem to know it… even when they don’t. If you hear it, best to nod and say nothing. It scares me to be honest, but don’t know why.”
Nyssa frowned faintly. “Korr.”
Madrelis nodded, then froze as Halvayne’s voice drifted from the front. “Careful what you share with strangers, Madrelis. Gossip’s dangerous currency.”
She stepped back with a bow. “Of course, my lord.”
Halvayne reappeared in the doorway, smiling. “Still, I have a sense for people. You two strike me as ambitious, the sort who would appreciate a gathering where there are plenty of ears and fewer mouths, with deep pockets. This may be abrupt, but there is a tea later today. Third bell. You should find an ear you could catch.” His glare at Madrelis could have burned the entire shop down.
“Tea sounds delightful,” Dain said.
Halvayne chuckled. “You’ll need this.” He handed them a silk-wrapped token. “Don’t be late.”
Once he’d left, Nyssa whispered, “That was fast.”
“Too fast,” Dain muttered. “Like they wanted us there.”
She adjusted his collar again, then smoothed his sleeve with an overacted fussiness. “Well, Daddy does want me married off. Maybe he’s just trying to help.”
Dain arched a brow. “So now I’m the prize in this little masquerade?”
She leaned close. “You bought a stable, didn’t you? In this city, that makes you noble and rich.”
“Is that all it takes?”
“That and cheekbones sharp enough to mount a saddle on.”
Dain chuckled, but there was tension under it. “They’re watching, Nys.”
“I know,” she said. “And they’ll be watching more at the tea.”
He nodded once. “Then we give them something to see.”
Nyssa smirked. “Let’s go stir the rest of the city before the third bell.”
They were two blocks down, the crowd thinning, when a figure pulled himself out of a doorway that should have been empty. He was short, he was wearing what could be believed to be called clothing, but it was his eyes, they were cloudy, white right over the iris. That is when they noticed he was using a cane to find his way.
This blind man pulled Nyssa aside as she and Dain made their way down the street. “You think you see clearly,” he rasped. “But they’re already gone.”
Dain frowned. “Who?”
“The nobles. Gone… Yet still walk the streets. I know because I hear them. Seen enough faces in my time to know when a voice doesn't match one. And those voices… don't match.”
Nyssa narrowed her eyes. “You expect us to believe that?”
He laughed. “Believe… Yes, that is a funny word, believe in a world of lies and illusion. Believe what you must. But remember this, those who think they can see are the ones who are truly blind, if you don’t wake up soon. You’ll never wake up at all.” He vanished into the alley before they could press further.
“That was strange, yet it doesn’t feel random,” Dain said quietly. His hand brushed his coat where his knife rested, eyes sweeping the nearby doorways.
“From what we have seen so far, that sounds about right. How much stranger can this place get?” Nyssa replied. They started making their way down the street again, arm in arm, both taking turns looking over their shoulders to see if he would return. 
Ash and Riven stepped into the tangled mess of alleys known as Smokeslip, where the taverns had no names, and the doors had more locks on the inside. The smoke here didn’t rise. It clung, fat and gray in the alleyways, curling low to the ground as it knew better than to draw attention. 
Riven adjusted the cuff of his sleeve as they passed a crooked sign etched with a faded flame.
“You sure this fence of yours didn’t skip town with the rest of the rats?” Ash asked, scanning the shadows.
“If he did, he left his tail behind. Same idiot’s been watching us since we turned down Knife Alley.”
Ash didn’t look, but the corner of his mouth curled. “I saw him. Green coat, limp on the right?”
“Patch over the wrong eye, but close.”
They moved with practiced ease, Riven loose and feline, Ash heavy-shouldered with slow, boiling presence.
A door opened as they approached, letting out a waft of stale wine and pipe smoke. Riven didn’t knock; he tapped twice, then paused, then three times fast. The rhythm was old undercity code. Moments later, a slot in the door scraped open, revealing a bloodshot eye behind a rusted grate.
That eye blinked. “Storms and slag... Riven Duskwind?”
Riven grinned. “In the flesh, fully underdressed, and still not dead.”
The door creaked open. Inside, old barrels doubled as tables, and light came from sun-holes bored through stone and painted with glass. Behind the makeshift bar, a wiry man with patchy red hair and too many teeth leaned on the counter. His name was Teck, a former smuggler with debts in every port. He looked Riven up and down. “Thought the Red Cloaks bled you out weeks ago.”
“Only my pride. This is Ash.” He motioned with his chin. “He sets fires and tells the truth about half the time.”
Ash gave a lazy salute. “That’s a generous average.”
Teck poured a cup of something too thin to be wine and pushed it across. “You didn’t come back to settle old debts.”
“No,” Riven said, stepping closer, lowering his voice. “We’re tracking tremors. Word is the tunnels were cleared. You see who cleared them?”
Teck glanced around and lowered his voice. “They came down with branded steel. Red cloaks. Not all Adepts. Some of ‘em wore Morlin cut. Heard ‘em say it was time to ‘cleanse the gutters’.”
Ash leaned in. “And the fences?”
“Rounded up. Some fought. Some… joined them.”
Riven tapped the bar twice, thoughtfully. “And the voices?”
Teck paled. “You heard them too?”
“Just heard about them. Can you fill in the blanks?” Ash asked.
“No one knows. It just starts at night. Some believe it is the voice of those killed the night when the plaza went up. Others say it is just the prison. There are even whispers of demons. But no one knows for sure,” said Teck, leaning towards them all conspiratorially.
“We’ve also seen people act like their strings got cut and retied by someone else,” Ash said.
Teck fidgeted, suddenly sweating. “There’s something under the city, boys. Not just sewers. Older places. There are whispers down there as well. When the Red Cloaks cleared us out, they were not hunting contraband. They were hunting people. They had a list.”
“Whose list?” Ash asked.
“I don’t know. But I heard one name twice: Sythrael Korr. Doesn’t sound like a person. Sounds like a spell someone forgot to end.”
A long silence passed. Even the smoke seemed to quiet.
Then Teck added, almost to himself, “One of the old runners, Tevin, he worked the tunnels near the Breachwell arches.” He laughed to himself. “Working, more like hiding.” His eyes went distant. He shook his head, then continued as if nothing had happened. “He’s been hiding down there for years. Said he’d found something big before the purges started. Been lying low since. If anyone’s got a deeper trail to follow, it’s him.”
Riven stiffened slightly at the name. “Tevin’s alive?”
“Last I heard. But if you’re smart, you’ll pretend he isn’t.”
The door slammed open. A broad-shouldered man stumbled in, swaying like a broken hinge. He blinked at Ash and Riven, squinted, then laughed.
“Foreigners! Lookin’ for heroes in the dirt, are ya?”
Ash tilted his head. “Just the truth.”
“You won’t find it here,” the man slurred. “They already dug it out, bled it, and left its bones in the gutter!”
Riven watched him go with narrowed eyes. “We should go. He’s not drunk, he’s distracted. Someone’s pulling him.”
They nodded their thanks to Teck, who just muttered, “Be careful where you listen down there. Some voices listen back.”
Ash flexed his fingers. “So, we have tunnel cleansings, possessed drunkards, and a name no one understands.”
He adjusted the collar of his coat, eyes scanning the alley mouth like a wolf sniffing the wind.
“And now Tevin’s name is in this mess too.”
“Then we find him,” Riven said. “We have to.”
The alley swallowed them. Shadows on a hunt.
The early afternoon haze settled in the alleys of Stormhaven's merchant quarter like a half-remembered dream. The streets were quieter than expected, muffled in an uneasy hush. Scents of yeast and char and damp stone clung to the air, mingling with the faint acrid hint of old fire. A broken sign above a boarded-up seamstress's shop creaked as Reau and Weslin made their way down the sloping avenue.
Weslin walked with his hands clasped behind his back, chin up, trying very hard to appear as if he belonged. His cloak was too clean. His boots creaked too much. He nodded politely at every third person as if he were rehearsing a nobleman's mannerisms and hadn't yet passed the audition.
Reau, in contrast, strolled beside him with his hood up and shoulders loose, eyes tracking every window and side street. He said little, letting silence fill the space until it begged to be broken.
“You always walk like that?” Reau asked.
Weslin startled. “Like what?”
“Like you're trying to impress a ghost.”
Weslin flushed. “I was taught to walk with purpose.”
Reau grunted. “Good. But maybe not so loud about it next time. You're announcing yourself to half the quarter.”
They passed a closed bakery with soot-streaked windows. Weslin slowed just a little, glancing at the boarded door.
“That reminds you of something?” Reau asked.
Weslin gave a small nod. “My dad owns a bakery in Opindale. A little place near the eastern end of the market road. Nothing fancy, but when it is open, it smells like heaven.”
Reau raised an eyebrow. “Did not know that.”
“You never asked.”
“Fair,” Reau said. “You ever bake, or just eat?”
Weslin gave a small, sheepish grin. “I burn everything.”
Reau chuckled. “You burn bread, and you ended up here?”
“I am not the team’s cook,” Weslin said. “I was a page at the castle. My dad did not want me stuck behind the oven. He said there was something different in me. Something he did not understand. Harmon saw it too. Gave me a chance.”
Reau watched him for a long moment, then looked back toward the quiet shop. “He ever says why he thought you were different?”
“No,” Weslin admitted. “Not really. Just sometimes, he’d look at me like he knew something he couldn’t say. Like he was scared to.”
Reau nodded once, slowly. He didn’t pry.
Weslin shifted, drawing a smooth yellow shard from a small leather pouch at his belt. He turned it over in his hand like a worry stone.
“Still not used to carrying one of these,” he said.
“You tried using it yet?” Reau asked.
Weslin shook his head. “Only listening. However, it’s challenging to determine if it’s effective. Everything goes quiet, as if the world goes underwater. I hear nothing, my own breathing included.”
Reau frowned. “That’s not how it’s supposed to work.”
“I know. Aurelia says to let it flow, not tap it. But I don’t know how to tell the difference yet.”
“Believe me, if you tapped it, you would know. Hell, I would know, the people down the street will know. Just keep at it, it will be fine,” explained Reau.
They stopped outside a small apothecary tucked between two tanneries. The faded signage read: Henrick’s Remedies.
Reau motioned with his chin. “We’ll start here.”
Inside, the air was warm and thick with the scent of herbal dust. Shelves crammed with jars and scrolls lined the walls. A crooked man with a wide moustache and ink-stained fingers glanced up from a bubbling pot.
“Travelers?” he asked, eyeing their boots. “What’re you looking for?”
“Information,” Reau said. “About the plaza. The explosion.”
The man’s eyes darted once to the front door, then back. “Not something you ask out loud.”
Weslin stepped forward, nervous but trying. “We’re just trying to understand what happened. A friend said this used to be the safest place in the quarter.”
The apothecary hesitated, then sighed. “Used to be. Then the banners changed. Soldiers showed up. Red cloaks walking like they own the city. Locals are trying to appear busy and act like they do not notice. Nobles vanishin’.”
“What do you mean vanishin’?” Reau asked.
The man leaned in. “They come, they get escorted once, and they do not come back. Some say it is for safety. Some say it is not. Either way, no one sees them again.”
Weslin lowered his voice. “Anyone mention a name? Someone connected?”
The man hesitated, scratching at his jaw. “I’ve… heard something. Only once or twice. Always whispered.”
Reau straightened slightly. “Go on.”
The man looked between them, then muttered, “Sythrael Korr.”
Weslin blinked. “Who?”

The man shrugged, eyes narrowing in concentration. “Dunno. Just a name. But when I heard it, my stomach turned. And I haven’t slept right since. Like hearing the end of a song you don’t remember starting.”
Reau studied the apothecary carefully. “You don’t know who he is?”
The man shook his head. “No. And what’s worse? I don’t think I’m supposed to.”
Reau walked out without speaking. Outside, he counted back through the day. The boutique. The apothecary. The temple. Three sources. Three separate people who said it without knowing the others had.
 Outside, the wind had picked up, and a red-cloaked figure stood half-shadowed beneath an awning across the square. Weslin swallowed. “That wasn’t there before.”
Reau nodded. “We’re getting close to something. Let’s keep moving.”
Stormhaven’s Temple of the Shining Oath had once stood as a beacon, its marble towers and twin bells known across Aldoria. But now, as Aurelia, Neavin, and Brother Aldrek stepped through its arched entryway, the sanctum had transformed.
Gone were the prayer banners and quiet reverence. The stone iconography had been scrubbed of scripture, replaced by shallow proclamations etched into plaques.
“Unity Through Devotion.
“Harmony Is Obedience.
“Thoughts Aligned, Hearts United.”
Aldrek's face darkened the moment he saw them. “Blasphemy,” he muttered. “They’ve desecrated this place.”

Neavin slowed, his eyes flicking between runes scratched into the pillars and the bizarre symmetry of how the pews had been realigned into rigid squares. “This wasn't just cleared out. Somebody shaped this place like a shaft before a cave-in. Looks solid 'til it ain't.”
Aurelia pressed a hand to one of the stone walls, her eyes fluttering briefly as she opened herself to the echoes. Laughter. Screams. Silence. A voice whispering prayers that did not belong. She drew back, pale. “There were rituals here. Not just prayers… conditioning. Forced compliance. Like trying to overwrite a soul with a false one, and something answered.”
A hunched figure in faded vestments emerged from a side door, an elderly woman with a twisted spine and sharp, birdlike eyes. She carried a basket of dried herbs and eyed them with suspicion. “We don’t take pilgrims anymore,” she said. “The Oath has changed.”
“Changed?” Aldrek stepped forward, his voice low but tight with restrained fury. “Who has the authority to change the Word?”
She stared at him, expression unreadable. “Change comes whether you want it or not. New prayers for a new peace. We follow the Voice now.”
Neavin blinked. “What voice?”
She hesitated. Then, softly: “Sythrael Korr.”
The name rippled through them like a lash. Aurelia’s breath caught, and Neavin visibly stiffened.
“Who is that?” Aldrek asked, voice sharp.
But the old woman just blinked at him. “No one. Everyone. I forget.”
Aurelia stepped closer. “When did this begin? The changes? The new rites?”
The woman scratched her arm. “Since the fire. Since the bells started ringing wrong. Ten days, maybe. It all blurs.”
Aldrek turned and stormed to the altar, now draped in red cloth and rings of polished glass. He tore it away, revealing scorch marks underneath. “This is not worship. This is corruption dressed in piety.”
“Careful,” Neavin muttered. “There are eyes everywhere.”
“Then let them see!” Aldrek snapped. “If they fear truth, then they are ruled by lies.”
The woman began to chant, her voice low and shaking, not in any known tongue. Neavin stepped toward her and watched her collapse into a bench, suddenly weeping. She called out, “Bring my mind peace. Peace, voices no more, bring me peace.”
Aurelia knelt beside her. “Tell me. Do you remember what they did to you?”
The old woman looked at her with broken clarity. “He told us... the heart must open... and the blood must bind. We gave it willingly. That was the rule.”
Neavin drew a slow breath. “They’re using ritual blood binding. It could be connected to how the people have been acting, as if someone else is in control. Blood is potent.”
Aldrek shook his head. “Willing or not, that is dark craft. Only evil requires blood to silence a soul.”
Aurelia reached into her satchel and passed Neavin a small enchanted quill. “Start sketching the rune pattern on the dais. I want to compare it to the northern mind-webs we found in the breach studies.” Neavin nodded and got to work.
Her voice dropped into a low hum, then rose into a tremulous chant. The rhythm was uneven, the words too soft to understand, but they carried a strange weight, like prayer spoken over graves. Neavin tensed beside Aurelia. Aldrek’s hand hovered near the hilt of his mace.
The light from the window dimmed slightly, as if a cloud passed, though the sky outside remained unchanged. Shadows stretched across the floor, dancing like smoke.
Without another word, the woman stopped chanting. Her head dropped forward, chin to chest. Silence. Then she stood, too smoothly, and turned to walk away. She took three steps, then stopped. Her head lifted. Her eyes were no longer glazed. Her posture straightened by degrees, the fog in her eyes burning off unevenly. “Why are you here?” she asked, tone clear and steady.
The three exchanged glances. A beat passed before Neavin offered a carefully measured answer. “We’re travelers. Looking for someone. Following signs.”
She studied him, face unreadable.
Aurelia stepped forward gently. “Can you tell us anything about someone called Korr?”
The old woman blinked. “Who?”
Her hands began to fidget. Then she laughed softly, almost wistfully. “No... but things are better now. So much better. There’s order. Peace. We have food. The streets are quiet.”
As she spoke, her hands drifted to her arms. She scratched idly.
Then her nails dug in, drawing thin red lines across her skin.
Aurelia stepped forward, alarm flickering in her eyes. “Ma'am...”
The woman did not seem to hear her. She gave one last rough scrape, then stopped. She looked up. She smiled. Nothing else came. No words. Just the smile.
Neavin shifted back instinctively. Aldrek lowered his hand but kept his eyes locked on her.
“We need to go,” Aurelia said quietly.
Without another word, they left the sanctum. The adjacent alley felt brighter than it had any right to. As soon as they turned the corner, Aldrek let out a low breath. “That wasn’t possession,” he muttered. “That was something else. Some part of her was still in there.”
Neavin scanned the nearby wall, then paused. “Look,” he said.
A series of strange symbols had been etched into the brick, low, near the foundation, half-scraped away as if someone had tried to erase them in haste. It was the same symbol they’d seen earlier on the side of a burned chapel: a circle with seven lines radiating outward like a sunburst. But here, a second mark had been added, a jagged downward slash through the middle.
“It’s a trail,” Neavin said. “They’re marking something.”
Aldrek nodded. “Let’s find out what.”
Ash and Riven moved deeper into the alleys of Stormhaven’s underbelly, the scent of mildew and burnt tallow thick in the air. Their boots slapped wet stone as they ducked beneath sagging arches and stepped over half-frozen pools of stagnant runoff.
Ash flexed his hand absently, the flicker of heat under his skin a comfort. “This part of town always smells like something died, or is that just today?”
Riven walked ahead, scanning graffiti-covered walls with narrowed eyes. “If it’s dead, it probably still owes someone coin down here.”
They passed a pair of children huddled in a doorway, eyes wide and silent. One held a rusted tin cup. The other clutched a stuffed rabbit with its head torn half off.
“Remind me again what we’re chasing,” Ash muttered, slowing.
“Information,” Riven said, voice tight. “Whatever we can find. But down here, it’s less about what people say and more about what they don’t.”
Ash stopped. He crouched near a brick wall scorched black by fire. Carved into it, faint but deliberate, was a symbol: a circle cleaved by a jagged line. Beneath it, someone had scrawled: “The voices sleep beneath.”
“That means anything to you?” Ash asked.
Riven didn’t answer right away. He stepped forward, traced a gloved finger across the carving. “No. But I don’t like the way it looks.”
Ash stood. “Then we’re getting close.”
They rounded the corner into a wider corridor, a tunnel that dipped slightly downward, half-forgotten by the rest of the city. Cracks in the ceiling let in sharp shafts of light that illuminated torn banners and crushed barrels. The silence was too clean. Even their footsteps seemed muffled.
“This used to be part of the merchant sewers,” Riven said. “Storage tunnels. Smugglers, fences, black market stuff. There used to be a guy here...”
“A guy?” Ash asked.
“Tevin. Self-proclaimed ‘facilitator,’ which means he could get you killed or rich depending on his morning. If he’s still breathing, he’ll know something.”
Ash raised a brow. “And you think he’ll just help us out of charity?”
Riven smiled thinly. “No. But I think he hates the Red Cloaks more than he hates me.”
A distant clang echoed through the tunnels, a metal grate slamming shut. Ash tensed. “That wasn’t the wind.” Riven drew a knife from beneath his coat. “No. It wasn’t.” They pressed forward.
At the base of a split stairwell, they found a heavy iron door with an eye-level slot. Riven knocked twice, then once more, then waited. A moment passed. Then a sound scraped behind the door.
A voice hissed: “You brought fire to my doorstep, Riven.”
Riven’s eyes widened slightly. “Tevin. You’re alive. Still dramatic, I see.”
“Alive because I keep my head down. Unlike you.”
Ash stepped forward. “We’re not here to bring trouble. We’re here for answers.”
The door creaked open. The man behind it was gaunt, wrapped in layers of patchwork leather and soot-streaked scarves. His left eye was milk-white, the other sharp and wary, flicking over them like a blade measuring where to cut. Tevin squinted at Ash, then settled his gaze on Riven. “You come to see the corpse you helped make?”
Riven’s face tightened. He didn’t flinch this time, just held the man’s gaze.
Ash tilted his head. “That's how you welcome an old friend these days, or are you still mad about the fire?”
Tevin’s mouth twitched into something that wasn’t quite a smile. “You always bring the funny one?”
“He brings himself,” Riven muttered, stepping forward. “We’re not here to make amends. We’re here for answers.”
Tevin stood aside with a grunt, letting them pass. Inside, the chamber was thick with smoke and something fouler beneath it, rot, perhaps, or mildew that had grown teeth. Lanterns swayed overhead, their light distorted by greasy glass. Broken crates ringed a low table scratched with knife marks and old ink stains. On the far wall, a map of the undercity was pinned up, frayed, overmarked, a tapestry of desperation.
Tevin gestured for them to sit. “Make yourselves uncomfortable.”
Ash ignored the jab and leaned against the nearest crate. Riven stayed standing, arms crossed, scanning the map. Three sectors had been circled in red, all near the southern spillways.

Tevin moved with a limp, dropping into a stool with the creak of old joints and older grudges. “We lost the Undercircle,” he said without ceremony. “Red Cloaks came with fire and blades. Said nothing. Just cut and burned.”
Riven nodded grimly. “We heard.”
“You heard wrong,” Tevin snapped. “They did not just come to kill. They came to erase. Whole sectors are gone. Contacts gone. Safehouses gone. Like they were never there.”
Ash narrowed his eyes. “Why?”
Tevin’s shoulders rose and fell. “Wish I knew. Some say it is reeducation, others say it is for a ritual. There is a place where they take them. No one comes back from it.”
Ash huffed a humorless breath. “So the choice is chains or kindling. That is encouraging.”
Riven stepped closer. “What kind of ritual?”
Tevin looked up sharply. “You think they let people get close enough to find out? They come masked, shrouded. Chanting things no sane man repeats. Whatever it is, it’s not just for show.”
Ash shifted, voice low. “There’s a name I’ve heard passed around places gentle folk don’t visit. Got some of them scared. You know it?”
Tevin’s good eye flicked to him. “You mean Sythrael Korr.”
Riven straightened. “So you do know it.”
“I’ve heard it,” Tevin said carefully. “That name… people whisper it like it’s cursed. Even the Red Cloaks, I've seen them hesitate at it. But no one knows who or what it is. Just… fear.”
Ash exhaled. “Great. We’re following ghosts now.”
Tevin’s gaze slid past them, toward the door. “Whatever you’re doing, do it fast. The wrong eyes are watching everything down here. Trust me, they don’t all blink.”
“Oh, that day of horror,” Tevin said. “The Red Cloaks came with fire and blades. Said they were clearing rot. They just killed everyone, everyone without something they called a writ.”
“Writ?” Ash asked.
Tevin nodded. “Some new paperwork. You either got it from the new ‘authority,’ or you're dead.”
Riven leaned over the table, resting his hands on the scarred wood. “We need a direction. Somewhere, the trail keeps running.”
Tevin didn’t answer right away. He stared at the map, lips pressed thin. Then he tapped a sector near the southern spillways. “There’s a chemist’s depot. Ruined now. Used to be one of our forward caches. A place called Duskwalk. You’ll find burned ground and silence, but if anyone left clues, it’d be there.”
Ash raised an eyebrow. “That's your best lead?”
“No,” Tevin muttered. Then he stood and limped to the back of the room. He opened a rusted drawer, pulled a folded scrap of parchment, and slipped it into a small leather pouch. Without a word, he returned and pressed it into Riven’s palm.
“For your eyes only,” he said. “And be careful who you trust.”
Riven frowned but nodded. “Appreciate it.”
Riven spotted an open bag on the floor that hadn't been there before. He turned it over. A ragged map slid out, the same sector near the southern spillways Tevin had tapped. One path was labeled with ‘Sewer Valve 13: Rupture Control Node.’
Ash squinted at it. “So that’s what they used to blow the plaza?”
Riven frowned. “Maybe. Or maybe he just wanted us walking into a wall.”
They both nodded, deciding to follow it anyway.
“One last thing. You sure you don’t know anything else about Korr?”
Tevin’s brow furrowed. “Korr?” he echoed, slowly, as if tasting the name for the first time. “Who is that?”
Ash and Riven exchanged a look.
“You just told us about him,” Riven said.
“I did?” Tevin blinked. “Told you about who?”
“Korr,” Ash repeated. “You said even the Red Cloaks fear the name.”
Tevin’s eyes clouded. “That name…” His pupils widened, then lost focus.
He went still for a heartbeat, too still, then his face reset. Calm. Blank.
“I will keep an ear to the ground,” he said suddenly, almost cheerful. “For your friend. If he is worth looking for, maybe I will start looking too.”
His smile was wide and toothy, the first they’d seen from him. Before either could speak again, he stepped forward and gently but firmly closed the door.
Outside, the tunnel seemed colder than before. The lanterns flickered as they stood there in silence for a moment. Then Riven opened the pouch.
Inside was a different address. A name neither recognized.
And a note. ‘Don’t trust what people say. Especially me.’ Ash watched Riven's face while he read it. Whatever Riven felt, he kept it. He folded the note once, pocketed it, and said nothing.






Chapter Thrity-Five
The morning haze was now thinning into shafts of golden light that pierced through broken rooftops and fractured masonry. The square was quieter than they expected, eerily so. Dust hung in the air, catching the light like ash in still water. A metallic clatter echoed somewhere deeper in the ruins, sharp enough to make both men still for half a second. 
Garr and Harmon took the long route to get here, weaving through servant alleys and back walls, sneaking past distracted guards who seemed more like puppets than sentinels. Garr had pointed it out first, how the soldiers didn’t flinch or turn, not even when a barrel crashed behind them. Harmon had made them wait and watch. Only when he was sure no one would follow did they approach the ruins.
The plaza was laid out in a ring of marble and basalt, its outer circle dotted with twelve empty plinths, each formerly bearing a statue of a previous Governor. The center, however, had once been home to the largest, a towering sculpture of the current Governor, now reduced to scorched stone and a warped bronze spine. ‘This wasn’t a collapse,’ Garr muttered under his breath. ‘This was done to them.’ Scattered limbs of shattered stone idols lay in craters, most having been toppled intentionally.
“These statues weren’t taken down randomly,” Garr muttered, crouching beside one of the shattered forms. “Same angle on every break. Like it was coordinated.”
Harmon stood with his arms folded, his cane planted beside him. “Someone knew exactly how to bring this place down. This wasn’t a riot or a mob. This was careful.”
Garr turned a chunk of rubble in his hand. “Always thought this square was ceremonial. You know, pomp and speeches.”
“Could still be,” Harmon said. “But I’ve got a feeling there was more to it.”
They moved deeper into the blast radius, stepping over blackened stone and melted iron. The foundation here was buckled. The cracks didn’t spread outward; they came from beneath. Garr pointed it out, tracing the lines.
“Whatever did this… it pushed up first.”
Harmon's hand found the pommel of his cane and stayed there. “Cities are built on top of their old bones. You layer enough history, and eventually something underneath starts pushing back.”
“Bury your sins deep enough,” Garr muttered, “and the ground forgets how to hold them.”
They worked in silence for a while, sifting through debris, collecting fragments of stone marked with etched lines, faded carvings, and runes too scorched to make out completely. After nearly half an hour, they had laid out a partial circle between them, with lines of runic script forming the remnants of a complex ward array.
Harmon knelt beside the circle, frowning. “Then why destroy every part of it? Why go through this much effort just to tear down a monument?”
“Do you believe it could be symbolic?” Garr asked.
“No, not a complete destruction like this.” Harmon stepped closer to the center, scanning the debris. “If this were symbolic, they’d have left something. This feels like a full removal. Someone wanted every trace gone. Not with the red cloaks occupying the city.”
They split and went to work, sifting through what the blast had left. Garr tapped one of the fragments, brow furrowed. “These look like ward-lines. Or pieces of them.”
“Could be,” Harmon said, looking at what Garr was holding up. “Hard to say with so many pieces missing. But these symbols... this pattern... something was being maintained here.”
“Explains why every plinth was broken the same way,” Garr said.
“Along with whatever it was holding in place,” Harmon finished. “Something the statues were feeding into.”
Garr sat back, wiping grime from his gloves. “You think it was a barrier? A seal?”
“Could be a cage, a shroud, a ward against something crawling up from below.”
“What kind of thing needs a dozen governors' worth of magic just to keep the lid on?”
“Let’s hope we don’t find out the hard way.”
The two stood in silence, staring at the rubble-strewn circle. Garr shifted his stance, as if suddenly aware of the stone beneath him. The air felt heavier now. Beneath their boots, the wind stirred, carrying with it a faint tremor, like distant movement far below the stone.
“That’s the thing about history,” Harmon said. “Too much of it ends up in ashes. And we never ask why the fires start.”
“They broke something,” Garr said, “probably not knowing what it was holding back.”
“Oh, they knew,” Harmon replied grimly. “They broke it. And we need to find out why.”
Just as the thought settled, metal scraped sharply across stone, then voices followed. Two armored soldiers stepped into the plaza from the eastern archway. They wore gray and crimson, a local design that had been warped into something more militaristic. Their eyes didn’t track normally. Their gait was stiff.
One raised a hand. “State your business.”
Garr and Harmon glanced at each other. “We’re from the Reconstruction Oversight Board,” Harmon said smoothly, adopting a noble tone. “Documenting the plaza for restoration records.”
“No orders for civilian presence here,” the lead guard said. “Leave immediately.”
Garr stepped forward, posture casual. “Look, friend, we’re not…”
“You are not cleared,” the second guard cut in, hand already reaching for the blade at his side.
Harmon’s voice dropped low. “Sir, we are just lost, no need to bring steel into this, just show us the way out.”
No reply, the guards locked on them. They cracked their necks in unison. The second guard's hand went for his blade as well. Both of them drew in a synchronized draw, both assuming the same fighting position. The moment froze. Garr reached for his blade. Nothing. “Should’ve known better,” Garr muttered.
Harmon moved first, whipping his cane low and cracking it against one guard’s shin with a hollow thwack. Garr ducked a swing and grabbed a loose chunk of debris from the rubble, hurling it into the other’s face. They dodged and redirected, slipping through the gaps in timing, avoiding each strike by instinct more than planning.
“Don’t try to win,” Harmon hissed. “Just move.”

They dashed for the nearest gap in the collapsed archway, rubble skidding underfoot with every frantic step. They quickly ducked into a narrow street as bootfalls thundered behind them. Garr led, weaving through alleys and broken scaffolds, Harmon close behind.
Only after three turns and a sliding dive into a half-collapsed stable did they finally stop. They crouched behind a broken wall, breaths steady but tight.
“They didn’t even blink,” Garr whispered. “They weren’t acting like men.”
“No,” Harmon said, looking back the way they came. “Someone else is pulling the strings.” He left a space after it, the way a man does when he's not sure the words are safe to say aloud. They looked back toward the plaza ruins, now distant through the cracked alley.
“They destroyed it for a reason,” Garr said. “Now we need to find out what that reason was.”
Aurelia, Neavin, and Aldrek moved in silence, the echoes of their footsteps swallowed by a district that no longer wanted visitors. The Chapel District had once been a place of comfort, broad stone walkways, green courtyards, and sunlit stained glass humming with warmth and prayer. But now the windows were dark, and the breeze through the cloisters carried no song at all.
The trio stepped across the threshold of an abandoned sanctum. Dust swirled in the shafts of light where colored glass had been broken and left unrepaired. The altar had been stripped bare. Scripture pages were torn from books and strewn across the floor, smeared with something dark and dried.
Neavin stepped carefully between the pages, glancing down. “These were burned, then rewritten. Someone wanted the old words gone before replacing them.”
Aurelia knelt, fingers hovering over the jagged script. “They changed the words.”
“Blasphemers,” Aldrek muttered. “This isn’t desecration. It’s indoctrination.”
Neavin scanned the room, gaze pausing on a faint mark burned into the wall behind the altar. “That's not from any chapel I’ve seen.”
The mark was a circle broken by seven slashes, the dried blood still flaking. Below it, one word carved jaggedly into the stone: ‘Open.’
The temperature dropped. A low hum trembled in Aurelia’s skull, a pressure, like thoughts were being pressed outward, not in. “Shield your minds,” she whispered.
A rustling echoed from the side alcove. They turned. An old man in an acolyte’s robes stood there, smiling widely. Too wide. “You’ve come late,” he said brightly, the cheeriness wrong in the ruined chapel. “She’s already given her blood.”
Aurelia took a step forward. “Who gave blood?”
The man blinked. “She did, the priestess. We needed the heart open. The blood binds. We gave it willingly. That was the rule.”
Neavin reached instinctively for a blade he wasn’t carrying, fingers curling on empty air. But Aldrek touched his shoulder. “Steady,” Aldrek murmured. “Not yet.”
The man tilted his head slowly, as if listening to something they couldn’t hear. Then he began to chant, low and garbled, in a language none of them recognized.
Suddenly, the old man’s face slackened, the tension draining away. His eyes cleared into something unsettlingly ordinary.
“Ah, hello,” he said. “Are you lost?”
Aurelia glanced between the others. “You were just talking to us.”
“Was I?” he asked cheerfully, glancing around the ruined sanctum. “I’ve just been dusting candles.”
Neavin stepped forward, testing him. “What can you tell us about Korr?”
The man’s eyes glazed over. “Korr?” His eyes went glassy. “No… that’s not a name anymore. That’s a silence.”
He started scratch his arms. One. Two. Over and over. He was bleeding as he ripped at his skin. He was scratching as if to remove his skin. Before they could get to him to stop him, he just stopped, blood running down his arms. He looked at them, smiled with that same wrong warmth. “The light is cleaner now,” he whispered. He sat down where he stood, crossed his legs, and stared at the wall.
They backed away. In the quiet that followed, “That wasn’t possession,” Aurelia said quietly. “That was conditioning.”
Aldrek’s voice was grim. “Or worship twisted into something far worse.”
“Or punishment?” Aurelia questioned.
Neavin pointed to the far corner of the sanctum where an old ledger had been tossed behind the pulpit. Its pages were blank until the end. Scrawled in different hands, different inks:
“Taken, not lost.”
“Let the name be forgotten.”
“Bled for the gate. Bled for the truth.”
“Sythrael Korr.”
Aurelia traced the page with one trembling finger. “We need to find who they bled for.”
Behind them, the old man began humming. From somewhere in the walls, something that might have been laughter answered.
Far across the district, Reau and Weslin crouched in the shadow of a warped archway, the stone overhead blackened with old soot and laced with ivy, and this quarter had once been filled with masons and sculptors. Now it stood abandoned, like a forgotten limb of the city. Dust motes hung thick in the gold-grey light slanting through broken windows, and the silence pressed in like a held breath.
“Nothing about this place feels right,” Weslin whispered.
“You’re not wrong. Place smells like wet copper and mold,” Reau muttered. “Old buildings like this have too many doors and not nearly enough exits.”
They slipped deeper into the ward, boots crunching on gravel and broken glass. Doors sagged open on splintered hinges. A shattered kiln lay gutted in the corner of a courtyard, and past it, a crumbling fountain with moss-choked mouths frozen mid-song. The streets here seemed to spiral inward—toward what, neither could say.
“I thought you said this area was cleared,” Weslin whispered.
Reau’s eyes flicked to a rooftop, then to a narrow alley. “I said it was supposed to be cleared.”
A door creaked two buildings over. Both froze.
From the shadow, a figure stumbled into the street, a potter’s apron still tied around his waist, but caked in dried black streaks. His face was blank, his eyes glassy, his movements jerky, like his body was following steps it no longer remembered.
Another emerged behind him. And another. Three. Then five. All drifting out of shadow like they’d been waiting.
All wore signs of former artisanship, wood shavings, chalk dust, and stained fingers, but none blinked. None looked at them. Just through.
Reau’s hand hovered over his side, nothing. No blade. “Garr said no steel,” he hissed.
“So… what, we throw rocks?” Weslin whispered.
The first figure twitched, turning. Then the others followed, jerking in uncanny rhythm.
“Run,” Reau said.
They broke left, darting through a shattered fence, over uneven ground. Behind them, the shuffle of footsteps accelerated, more precise now, too precise.
They slipped through a broken artist’s guild, upstairs that turned to dust under their feet, bursting through into a skylit gallery half-collapsed by time. Marble torsos and cracked heads lined the walls like forgotten saints.
Weslin looked back, voice cracking. “They’re still coming!”
“Split!” Reau ordered. “Loop around, draw them wide!”
Weslin obeyed without hesitation, darting through an arch. Reau took the opposite way. The possessed didn’t chase at random. They split with them, perfectly. That was the first thing that chilled Reau. Then two of them leapt, too fast, too coordinated. He dove through a collapsed hall, rolling through dust and broken tile. He turned, ready for the next wave, and then it didn’t come. Just the echo of chasing footsteps growing faint.
Reau doubled back, fast and quiet. He found the boy pinned in a courtyard, breathless, eyes wild. Two of the glass-eyed figures were closing in.
Reau snatched a loose brick, hurled it with deadly aim, and crack! One went down. He sprinted forward and tackled the other, slamming him into a wall. The man groaned but didn’t fight back, just stared at him, lips moving silently.
“Are you alright?” Reau asked, pulling Weslin to his feet.
“I—I don’t know,” Weslin stammered. “What’s wrong with them?”
Reau didn’t answer. His gaze lingered on the man’s vacant stare, the blackened veins around his ears.
“They’re not awake,” Reau muttered. “They’re… something else.”
They dragged themselves to a broken stairwell and collapsed behind it, hearts pounding.
“I thought I could handle this,” Weslin said quietly. “But that wasn’t like the stories. That was…”
“Real,” Reau said gently.
“I tried asking questions. Listening. Watching. None of it lined up. Nothing made sense.”
Reau hesitated. Then spoke more softly than usual. “You don’t have to prove anything to me, Wes.”
“I’m not trying to prove something,” Weslin whispered. “I just don’t want to fail.”
A beat of silence stretched between them. Reau finally said, “Then try again with listening.” Weslin blinked.
Reau reached into Weslin’s coat, pulled out the yellow shard he was wearing around his neck. “You said it goes quiet when you use it, right?” Weslin nodded.
“Maybe quiet is what you need.” Reau said.
Weslin held the shard, let his breath settle, then reached.
Click. The world dropped into total silence. Not hushed, gone. No footsteps, no breath, no wind, only the sensation of floating in cold, thick water.
Weslin drew in a shaky breath, staring at the shard in his palm.
“I need to try… to see their thoughts,” said Weslin.
Reau's brow creased. “You sure you’re ready for that?” he asked, even though Weslin couldn’t hear a word.
He held the shard tight in his hand. He didn’t just reach for the flow. He pushed wide open.
The moment he pushed, the world fell away. But still nothing. So, he pushed harder. A surge of lightless pressure slammed through his chest. The air thickened. Every hair on his arms lifted. Energy roared through the connection like a river too wild to dam, tearing at the edges of his senses.
Reau lurched forward. “Weslin—!”
Weslin’s jaw clenched. His back arched, eyes wide but unseeing, Veins lit faint gold under his skin, pulsing with the shard’s wild pull. The shard in his palm blazed.
Reau crouched beside him, one hand hovering, the other gripping the boy’s shoulder. “Breathe, Wes. You’re drawing too much. You don’t need a flood, just a thread.”
Weslin trembled violently, lips parted, but no sound came. His mind floated in a silence so deep it rang with its own pressure. He was sinking.
“You’ve got to let some go,” Reau said urgently, voice low but sharp. “If you don’t, the shard will burn you out. Right now it’s using you, not the other way around.”
He tightened his grip on Weslin’s shoulder, grounding him. “Wes. Listen to me, not the void.”
Weslin blinked once, just enough to break the spiral.
Then he breathed, a real breath, and the light dimmed, flickering like a dying candle. Then he hit something, like a wall, and with another breath, he pushed until it gave way. And in that breath, he saw…
A chamber, round and vast, buried deep beneath the city. Etched with runes and draped in red fabric. Stone slabs pulsed faintly with a heartbeat rhythm. A figure moved, tall and impossibly still, even in motion, wearing black robes with a featureless mask. Around them, others knelt, hands bloody, mouths moving in silent devotion. One stood too quickly and was struck down. None of the others reacted. The tall figure turned.
There were no eyes behind the mask. Suddenly, the masked figure turned toward him. Weslin jerked back with a choked cry, the shard flying from his hand as his whole body snapped like a cut wire.
Reau caught him mid-collapse, easing him down gently to the floor of the abandoned workshop.
Weslin gasped for air, trembling. “I—I saw… below the city. They’re…it saw me.”
Reau brushed the sweat from the boy’s brow. “Easy. You’re alright. You almost overdrew; you don’t rush a flood through a cracked dam.”
Weslin tried to sit up, still shaking. “Something or someone is blocking us. A spell. A ward, maybe. It’s smothering every listening attempt. It's why I couldn't hear anything before. There’s something wrapped around the whole quarter, like ringing in the air. Maybe the whole city.”
Reau’s eyes darkened. “It’s not you. It’s the city choking everything out.”
“No. It’s like we’re being muted, cut off from sensing thought, unless we force it through,” Weslin said.
Reau picked up the shard from the floor, checked it for damage, and then passed it back. “You could’ve burned out. Or worse. Next time, don’t try to break a boulder with a teacup, alright?”
Weslin let out a short, humorless laugh. “I was scared. Everything hurt.”
“You should be. That’s how you stay alive. But you did it. And now we know there’s something real down there.”
Reau stood and offered a hand. Weslin took it. “I saw a chamber. People kneeling. Blood everywhere. And this thing… no face, just a mask. It knew I was watching.” He hesitated. “But I don't know if it saw me back. Not just noticed me. If it saw what I saw. If it knows.”
Reau shifted uneasily as he listened. “Then we’re not chasing ghosts,” he said, scanning the ruined courtyard again. The two of them moved toward the broken exit of the artisan’s ward, the air colder now, the world quieter, but not silent. “Let’s get you somewhere safe. You are in no condition to be out here if they are looking for us,” said Reau.
Weslin nodded in agreement, then immediately second-guessed the gesture, sending a spike of pain behind his eyes.
The bell above the boutique’s door gave a high, brittle chime as Dain and Nyssa stepped into Lioren’s Elegance. A breath of cool, perfumed air drifted out, too still, too curated, like the room itself was holding its breath.
Muted harp music played from somewhere behind a curtain, and the room smelled of pressed linen, clove oil, and something bitterly sweet—like dried poppies left too long in the sun. Racks of finery stood in military order. Robes, gowns, vests, and capes were arranged not by color or function, but by... intent.
“Clothes with agendas,” Nyssa muttered under her breath, eyeing a floor-length slate-gray robe with razor-slit trim.
A tailor appeared soundlessly, small and silver-haired, dressed all in ivory. She gave a precise nod. “You’ve come from House Vanneth, yes? For the afternoon ceremony? Your measurements were… anticipated.”
Dain tilted his chin. “Indeed.”
“Upstairs, please. The fittings are ready.”
They were guided to a velvet-curtained alcove where outfits were already laid out, tailored to their rough measurements from earlier.
Nyssa raised an eyebrow at a burgundy riding jacket with an embroidered lily across the back. “Bold. But I like the implication of violence in a flower.”
Dain held up a long, dark coat with brass clasps and a deep forest-green interior. “Is this supposed to make me look like a brooding heir to a doomed estate?”
“It's working.” She took the jacket from him and spun it around. “Oh, look at the lining. Gods, you're going to make the widows cry.”
Dain smirked. “What about yours?”
Nyssa held up a silver-and-plum silk gown with one long sleeve and a cinched waistcoat. “This dress was designed by someone who didn’t understand women.”
Dain stepped closer. “You’re sure you can pull that off?”
“Watch me,” Nyssa said, turning toward the mirror, adjusting the dress against her frame. “That name you gave me… at the tailor’s earlier,” she asked.
Dain paused. “Liora?”
She nodded. “It’s beautiful. Sounds like it belongs to someone important.”
“It's my sis…,” he said quietly. “It was my sister’s name.”
Nyssa turned, caught off guard by the sudden gravity in his voice.
“She wasn’t just my sister. She was… everything. My best friend. My first partner in mischief.” He paused, taking a moment to remember. He looked up into Nysaa’s eyes to share. “She used to leave notes in his boot before every mission. Just one line. Something ridiculous. Something that made him laugh before he could stop himself.
