He'd found the last one three months after she died, in a boot he hadn't worn since.” He coughs to clear his throat as he gathers himself.
“We trained together, sparred together. Got each other through things no one else could’ve understood. She believed in me when I didn’t. And then one day…” His voice caught, and he looked away briefly. “A riding accident, they said. But I knew. I knew it was something more. A political move dressed up as tragedy.”
He looked back at her then, and one tear slid silently down his cheek. “When she died, I lost my grip. Started doing things just to feel anything. It cost me everything. My place. My name. My control.”
Nyssa stepped closer, slowly, never breaking eye contact. This was the first time she saw him. He opened the door to her and invited her in. She took the invite. She got close, reached up, and straightened his collar. “Then giving me her name,” she said, voice low and steady, “that wasn’t a game.”
“No,” he said. “It was trust. It was all I had left that mattered.”
She placed a hand over his heart. Leaning in close, their lips inches apart. She never broke eye contact. “Then I’ll wear it like the honor it is. And I’ll never tarnish it.” He took her hand, and they headed off.
The deeper they walked into the noble quarter, the more precise things became. Window boxes were arranged identically, lamps spaced to the inch. Guards stood at mirrored corners, arms folded the same way. Even the shadows had started to fall in orderly angles.
Then they saw it. A tower. It loomed between marble arches, built of blackened stone with veins of something faintly iridescent running through its surface, like an oil slick trapped in granite. Around its base, five citizens walked in a perfect circle, spaced evenly, endlessly looping the structure.
Their steps stuttered, just slightly, like each was resisting the motion even as their bodies obeyed. A woman’s hand twitched at her side. A man clenched and unclenched his jaw in time with the turns. The air around the tower felt charged, humming faintly against Dain’s teeth.
Two guards paced the outer circle, moving slowly and deliberately, like herders keeping livestock from wandering.
They ducked into a walled side garden, pausing just long enough to breathe in the shade of the hedges. Birds chirped overhead, too regularly. Dain's eyes moved across the square, the spacing, the gait, the locked pattern. “They’re not soldiers.”
“Then what are they?” Nyssa asked.
He watched the loop, frowning. “Volunteers who didn’t take. Or prisoners being tested.”
“Same thing these days,” she muttered, as they continued their walk.
Nyssa looked over at him, more serious now. “Let’s line up what we have. You good?”
Dain nodded. “Let’s see…”
She started counting off on her fingers. “Clothing shop, full of mannequins pretending to be people. A tower guarded by meat puppets. A man talking about water like it’s cursed. Strange name whispered like gospel, Korr.”
“Don’t forget the tailor practically shoving us out when that name came up,” Dain added. “That wasn’t nerves. That was programming.”
“Also, the man who stumbled into us near the bathhouse earlier,” Nyssa said. “Kept asking if ‘we’d seen the lights in the drain?’ You remember that?”
Dain grimaced. “I remember him screaming when the guards grabbed him.”
“And yet, this place is supposed to be peaceful,” she said, voice flat. They looked up at the estate gate ahead.
Nyssa reached into her satchel and pulled out the invitation again. “Third daughter of a horse merchant. Courting a rising noble. All smiles. All lies.”
Dain offered his arm. “Then let’s be convincing.”
“Careful,” she said, looping her arm through his. “You’re starting to sound like you enjoy this.”
He smirked. “I’ll tell you after we make it out.”
The gates of House Halvayne opened like the jaws of something old, hinged in black iron, crested with gold trim, and flanked by stone hounds whose fangs caught the light just so. Dain and Nyssa stepped through them arm-in-arm, figures cut from silk and poise. Beneath their feet, the path was ivory tile lined with moss roses, immaculate down to the last petal.
A hush lived here, under the hedgerows. Not silence, never silence, but the cultivated stillness of power pretending at peace.
“I feel like I’m walking into a sermon where they forgot to bring a god,” Nyssa murmured, adjusting her sleeve.
“Just follow my lead,” Dain replied under his breath. “Smile like you belong and never blink first.”
They passed a marble bench where a man sat hunched and rocking. His fine coat was damp, his fingers twitching as they tugged at empty air.
“It’s in the water,” he whispered hoarsely. “Always the water... always... the water.”
Neither said a word. But when they reached the garden archway, Nyssa subtly let go of Dain’s arm.
The rear garden was a maze of ivory trellises, wine-colored vines, and shallow reflecting pools. Beneath a canopy of cloud-white silk, a tea table had been arranged in the center of a circular lawn. Six wrought-iron chairs stood like sentinels around it. Five were already filled.
Lord Halvayne stood as they approached, arms spread like a conductor calling for quiet. “Ah, the last to arrive. Friends, allow me to introduce Lord Theren Vayle, recently arrived from the capital with breeding in his bones and coin on his breath. And this—” he gestured, smile like a blade, “is Lady Liora Quell of Fairmere, whose eye for horses is rivaled only by her taste in conversation.”
Soft laughter rose around the table like mist. Polite. Predatory. Halvayne’s smile never reached his eyes as he gestured to the others. “Baron Rusk of Blackpine, he plays the docks like a harpsichord and knows which strings to pluck.”
“Lady Morenna, voice of the Eastern Faith Circle, sharp of scripture and tongue.”
“Sir Callem Vire, he who turns land into gold, and gold into loyalty.”
“High Notary Vellith, an archivist with memory so perfect she forgets nothing... and forgives less.”
Each bowed slightly, eyes evaluating with every glance.
Dain bowed in return. “A privilege to be among such... finely sharpened company.”
Nyssa curtsied with practiced grace, holding eye contact just a second too long. “I do hope we’ll prove worthy of such discerning company.”
The servants poured tea, amber and sweet-smelling, and placed delicate cakes on plates of frosted porcelain. But Nyssa hesitated the moment the scent reached her.
Dain glanced over. Nyssa leaned in, voice barely a breath. “‘Always the water.’” He didn’t drink. The conversation shifted. Somewhere behind the garden wall, a bird went quiet.
Lady Morenna folded her napkin precisely. “The city breathes a different rhythm now. Not chaos, clarity. The fog has lifted.”
Dain tilted his head. “Clarity can be crueler than chaos. Fog hides things for a reason.”
Baron Rusk chuckled. “Spoken like a man who’s seen a scandal or two.”
“Or outlived them,” Nyssa said smoothly.
Sir Vire gestured lazily. “You’ve arrived at the right time. Once the plaza is restored, morale will shift. Stormhaven was always a jewel; it merely needed a firmer hand to polish it.”
“Was it polishing,” Dain asked, “or excavation of something better left buried?”
Lady Morenna gave a thin smile. “Some stones must be lifted to cleanse the rot beneath.”
Nyssa glanced toward the tower. “And the tower, with those people walking in circles. Is that ceremony… or containment?”
Vellith blinked. “A refinement. The Speaker’s methods are sometimes... elegant.”
“You mean Speaker Albrecht?” Dain pressed.
Vellith nodded too quickly. “He helps people remember who they were meant to be.”
Nyssa raised a brow. “And if they resist that kind of…remembering?”
“Then they become someone useful,” Morenna said.
It was time. Dain leaned back. “We’ve heard a name whispered where names shouldn’t echo.” 
The table paused. “Korr,” Nyssa said, barely above breath, but sharp enough to cut the silence. A spoon clattered. Callem Vire dropped his tea. Lady Morenna stood abruptly. “I should check on the lemoncakes.”

Halvayne didn’t blink. “Names have weight, my lord. Speak carelessly, and they may speak back.”
Nyssa pressed. “There are whispers of a new order. Something beneath the city. Something is being prepared.”
Rusk sneered. “You ought to be careful where you gather your rumors and even more careful where you repeat them.”
Dain let his cup rest on its saucer. “That’s why we came. To sort truth from shadow. But it seems the shadows have excellent memory.”
Morenna snapped, “Then perhaps you belong with them.”
Lord Halvayne stood slowly, brushing nonexistent dust from his sleeve. His smile sharpened like a sickle under moonlight.
“We knew, of course. From the moment you stepped onto the stones with your borrowed silk and farmer’s perfume. You thought you could fool us, thought our eyes were dulled with comfort and tea? No, no. We smelled the desperation in you.”
The other nobles began to chuckle, polite, poisonous, their teacups raised in a mock toast. “You’re not nobility. Not even close. Just rats in silk. And rats, when cornered, make such interesting sounds.”
He took a step closer, voice velvet-slick and cruel. “But worry not. You’ll be put to use. Every traitor has their place. Some serve as warnings. Others as servants. You’ll be cleaned, reshaped, and useful. That’s what the Loyalty Test is for. And you’ll thank us. In time.”
The guards were moving towards the party. Two flanked the exit. Three more emerged from the hedges. Dain offered a half-bow. “Lady Liora, shall we inspect the bloodlines you so graciously outlined?”
“Delighted,” Nyssa said, rising.
The guards moved.
A flick of her wrist. A blade flew, striking a guard in the thigh. He collapsed with a bark of pain. Dain grabbed a silver tray and flung it into another’s path, knocking him off balance. “Move!” he snapped.
“Run, little lord. Run while you still remember your own name.” They ran, not knowing how to get away.
“Just think, by next week, you’ll be serving our tea,” one nobleman jeered, laughter curling sharp as wire.
Through the roses, past the fountain. Another guard gave chase. They dodged his attempt to grab them and turned around to go the other way. “They always run. It just makes the breaking sweeter,” said Baron Rusk.
Nyssa hurled a sugar dish. The glass exploded. Dain vaulted a low bench and pulled Nyssa over a stone wall. They ran past two more guards as they made their way through the garden and back to the main road. “They’re still coming,” Nyssa gasped, glancing back. “They’re not slowing.”
They kept dashing, rounded a corner, and they were yanked into the shadows. A strong hand covered Nyssa’s mouth. Another pulled Dain down.
Garr. Harmon. Both already braced as if they’d been waiting. Harmon raised a finger to his lips. The guards passed. Four hearts pounded. From the garden, laughter echoed, thin and distant.
The sun dipped behind Stormhaven's upper spires, painting the old quarter in copper light as Neavin, Aurelia, and Aldrek passed beneath the crumbling arch of what once might have been a prayer hall. The building was quiet now, but not abandoned. Someone had tried to tidy the debris, and faint incense still clung to the air.
Neavin crouched near the threshold. “The floorboards have been swept. Recently.”
Aurelia nodded, fingers brushing the edge of a wall tapestry. The fabric was freshly hung, depicting a radiant figure wrapped in crimson light. Too clean. Too new. “Someone's trying to resurrect this place. But it doesn’t follow any of the registered orders.”
Brother Aldrek frowned, gripping the hilt of his mace. “The imagery is all wrong. The scripture teaches light by sacrifice, not domination. This... this is distorted.”
They moved deeper. Makeshift pews, irregular and ill-formed, were set in uneven rows before a raised stone dais. Carvings lined the back wall, etched in unfamiliar patterns.
Neavin tilted his head. “That doesn’t match any formal script or liturgy I’ve ever seen. And these lines here, they curve too sharply.”
“It’s not a language,” Aurelia murmured. “It’s mimicry.”
A sudden scrape echoed above. They froze. A boy, thin and pale, descended the narrow stairs from the bell tower. His eyes were wide, unblinking. “You shouldn’t be here,” he said flatly. 
“Neither should you,” Aldrek countered. The boy didn’t flinch. “They said you’d come, that you’d want to see. It’s almost ready.”
Neavin exchanged a glance with Aurelia. “What is?”
The boy pointed to the altar. “The Offering. He feeds on the willing. They say he makes the city clean.” Before more could be asked, the boy turned and fled.
Aurelia stepped to the altar. Carved behind it, almost hidden beneath an overlaid drape, was a symbol, not of any known god or divine branch. It looked like a sun, twisted and spiraled inward, burning from the center out.
Neavin rubbed his thumb across the carving. “Looks like something old trying to be new again.”
“Or something false wearing the skin of the familiar,” Aldrek said.
They searched the rest of the space, finding half-burned ledgers, papers referencing a list of converts and purification dates. All pointed to a ceremony scheduled under the Harvest Moon. A name was signed beneath it: “High Minister Varin of the New Flame.”
Aldrek scoffed. “That title doesn’t exist. It’s a fabrication.”
“Still,” Aurelia said, rolling the parchment, “it’s enough to mislead hundreds. Maybe thousands.”
They gathered the evidence and slipped out into the alley before the dusk bells. None of them noticed the boy watching them from the tower’s shadow.
They should’ve stopped after the false registry. After the woman in the glass shop recited the same too-perfect script, and the child in the alley said he “didn’t remember” his own parents’ names. The whole district stank of something scripted. But Aldrek insisted they press further, and Neavin found a path tucked behind a smithy’s ruined yard, an access shaft hidden by collapsed slagstone and old cart frames.
Aurelia hesitated at the opening. “This isn’t on the city plans.”
“Exactly,” Neavin said.
They went lower. The tunnel narrowed, then bent in a tight spiral that led them down past rusted ladder rungs and old binding stones crumbling with disuse. The air grew thick with dust and heat. Far above, the forge district’s silence lingered like a forgotten echo.
Their boots scraped metal once, then stone again. They didn’t speak. Not until they reached the place where the air changed, the walls opening like lungs into something far older than any of them expected. What they found wasn’t a tunnel. It was a cradle.
The chamber was massive, vaulted stone with ancient supports carved in the old tongue. Stale magic hung in the air like dried blood, too thick to breathe properly. At its center was a platform of obsidian and fused bone. Upon it rested a figure, twenty feet tall, humanoid in shape, but forged of armor too black to reflect light and too intricate to be made by human hands.
Runes burned faintly across its shoulders, like the last embers of a long-dead forge.
Neavin stopped in his tracks. “That’s not a golem.”
“No,” Aurelia whispered. “That’s something older.”
Aldrek made the sign of the Circle. “I’ve read about these in the sealed annals. War-beasts. They are from the Second Magic War. Created using methods we’ve lost, alchemical forging, blood-script binding, soul-fixation. Most were dismantled. Some... vanished. One was said to have razed three keeps in the Eastmere Rebellion.”
The thing on the platform shifted, only slightly. Just enough to show it wasn’t dead.
Neavin took a step back. “That wasn’t sleep. That was waiting.”
Aurelia’s voice turned cold. “They’re waking it.”
Aldrek’s gaze swept the glyphwork circling the room, blood channels, resonance coils, and a broken altar at the far end. “This isn’t just a tomb. It’s a fuse chamber. They’re charging it.”
Neavin turned to the others, face grim. “We have to tell Harmon. This thing, with the Red Cloaks’ Adepts, it’s an army without match.”
None of them moved for a moment. The air in the chamber pressed down like a held breath. The thing on the platform didn't shift again. But none of them looked away from it. He looked back at the construct.
“With this... they could hold the walls against a kingdom. This isn't a deterrent. It’s a declaration.”
They lingered in the shadowed alcove for a long minute after the guards passed, four dark shapes swallowed by the fog-draped alleys. Their boot-steps echoed too rhythmically. Too perfectly.
Garr’s hand dropped from the hilt of the club he’d fashioned from a busted lantern post. He exhaled through his nose, tension bleeding off his shoulders like sweat.
“Not just any guards,” he muttered.
Harmon gave a slight nod, his gaze following the vanishing silhouettes. “No,” he said quietly. “No hesitation. No conversation. Just executioners in uniform.”
Beside them, Nyssa was steadying her breathing. Dain hadn’t said a word since they ducked into the alcove, but the look in his eyes was carved granite, controlled fury. He was still gripping the hilt of his blade-knife with white knuckles, blood from a shallow graze on his arm wetting the cuff of his stolen noble’s sleeve.
“We need to move,” Harmon said at last. “Sun’s dying. The longer we wait, the more eyes will start to see what they shouldn’t.”
Garr, Harmon, Dain, and Nyssa stepped into the alley, careful not to let their boots splash in the puddles of ashwater collecting at the corners. The light was copper-tinged now—dusk rolling in like a tide, casting long bars of shadow through the broken shutters and low eaves of the merchant quarter. A single tower bell rang in the distance, muffled, as if through cloth.
As they moved, Nyssa fell into step beside Garr. “I didn’t think they’d see us so quickly.”
“They didn’t,” Garr said. “They felt us, like wolves in the trees. They weren’t searching. They were hunting.”
Dain looked back once, then forward, saying nothing. “How much longer can this city pretend it’s fine?”
“As long as it takes,” Harmon answered. “Or until someone lights a match.”
They ducked behind a ruined wall that once bore a mural of the Empress’s Accord. Now it was a smear of red dust and faded symbols. Beyond it, the alley veered sharply into the back lanes near the quarter’s edge. Harmon paused there, resting momentarily on his cane.
“Safe house is three turns from here,” he said. “Let’s hope the others found better luck. Or at least fewer knives.”
Dain gave a grim smile. “Luck’s for gamblers.”
Nyssa brushed a fallen blossom from her shoulder and glanced back toward the noble district, where lanterns were starting to flicker on behind barred windows.
“This whole city’s playing cards with a demon,” she said. “And no one’s folded yet.”
The four of them moved as shadows, slipping through the soft skeleton of Stormhaven’s old bones. Whispers echoed from courtyards. A chant rose through the cobbles, low enough that they couldn't be sure they were hearing it, loud enough that it never left them.
Above them, a silver banner caught the last light of the day. It hung limp, torn down the center, and bore no sigil. They didn’t speak again until the safe house door closed behind them.







Chapter Thrity-Six
Snow drifted in lazy coils past the high windows of the old stables. The roof creaked faintly overhead, settling with the cold. In the loft above the main floor, past narrow wooden stairs and between beams thick with dust and hay, Reau and Weslin stepped into the hollow stillness of their temporary safehouse. It was empty.
No voices. No movement. Just the scent of old straw, oil, and worn leather. Crates and hay bales had been pushed to the edges to form barricades, and peepholes cut into the loft walls gave discreet views of the alley, the yard, and the market road beyond. A single cold lamp sat on a crate near the center, giving off a faint yellow glow.
Weslin’s boots scraped softly on the planks. “We’re first.”
Reau glanced at him, noting the boy’s posture, the hunched shoulders, the clenched jaw, the way his hand trembled as it hovered near the yellow shard at his belt.
“That’s not bad,” Reau said evenly. “First means we’re alive.”
Weslin sat on a barrel near the window, head low. “Or it means we did not do enough,” he said. “What if we missed something?”
“You pushed the shard. That’s enough risk for one day.”
“I thought it would help,” Weslin muttered. “But now I feel like I broke something. In me.”
Reau crouched beside him. “You didn’t. You’re rattled, not broken. Let it pass.”
Weslin nodded slowly, but his thoughts still swirled behind his eyes, guilt curling tighter with every breath.
A muffled clatter of wheels and distant boots passed in the street below, then faded. A few minutes later, the door creaked at the far end of the stable. Harmon stepped up into the loft first, snow melting on his shoulders. Dain, Nyssa, and Garr followed, cloaks drawn tight. Harmon scanned the space quickly, old soldier habits never dulled.
“Anyone on our tail?” Harmon asked quietly, then nodded toward the far corner. Nyssa immediately slipped toward the storage room in the corner of the loft, boots clicking lightly. “This dress wasn’t made for rooftop sprints,” she muttered. “And these shoes? My feet are staging a rebellion.”
When she emerged minutes later, she was back in her tight black leathers, practical and familiar, but the noble makeup still framed her face. Dusky rouge, plum lips, and an icy highlight around her eyes.
Dain looked up, mouth twitching. “You forgot to wash the war paint.”
Nyssa tilted her head. “Sometimes a girl just wants to feel pretty.”
Dain didn’t blink. “You don’t need makeup for that.” 
The quiet that followed wasn’t awkward; it was thick. Nyssa deflected with a smirk. “Careful, Theren Vayle. You’re starting to sound sincere.” They both smiled. Real ones.

Then Dain nodded once and turned toward the storage room to change. Nyssa’s gaze lingered on him longer than she intended. Below, hooves kicked against wooden stalls. The horses, restless. More snow hissed against the windows.
Neavin, Aurelia, and Brother Aldrek arrived next. Neavin looked like he hadn’t spoken since they left; Aurelia’s steps were light but cautious, and Aldrek’s eyes swept every rafter as though expecting something to crawl down from the roof.
“Quiet night,” Aldrek said.
“Too quiet,” Neavin replied, brushing snow off his shoulder. “Even the wrong people weren’t talking.”
Aurelia pulled off her cloak, shook snow from her hair, and offered a brief nod to Harmon before scanning the room. Her eyes landed on Weslin.
He sat near the back wall, half in shadow, clutching his knees. His breath came low and ragged, fingers still trembling slightly. He avoided her gaze.
Aurelia approached and knelt beside him. “What happened?”
Weslin didn’t answer at first. His jaw worked, eyes distant.
“I tried to listen,” he said finally. “I did what you told me. I let it flow, tried to hear the passive layer... but there was nothing. Like... like my head was underwater. Nothing but pressure and silence. So, I pushed. Just a little. Then a little more. And then…” He looked at his hands.
“Then I broke through something, a wall. I saw things. Horrible things. I can still see that room when I close my eyes. But to do it, I think I tapped the shard. I think I drew too much. And now... I think I’m broken.”
Aurelia gently placed a hand on his arm. Her face was unreadable, but something behind her eyes flickered, worry... or fear.
“You’re not broken,” she said softly. “But you did something dangerous. And that’s why you need to rest. Don’t carry it alone. We still have work to do before you're ready for that. It's ok, now you know what you pay when you rush.”
Reau’s voice came from just behind them. Calm. Steady.
“He did tap it,” Reau said, stepping closer. “But I was there. I talked him back down before he went too far. He was burning hot, but he came back.”
Weslin jerked away from Aurelia’s hand and stood abruptly, pacing two steps before spinning on his heel. “No. I messed up again. First the ward, now this. I don’t belong out there, I don’t belong here.”
Reau stepped forward and wrapped an arm around him, not as a command, but as an anchor. He pulled Weslin in close, grounding the storm.
“I was just like you,” Reau said, voice low. “Just as young. Just as scared. I didn’t know how to hold it either, not at first. I got thrown in deep and almost drowned. You’re not alone in this.”
He looked over Weslin’s head, nodding toward Aurelia. “She’s here for you. So am I. We’re all on your side.”
Weslin pulled away slightly, tears in his eyes. “But I have to prove I deserve to be here, that I have earned this opportunity. I need to show I’m not just a kid, Harmon felt sorry for.”
Aurelia’s voice, soft and unwavering, cut through the rising storm. “You’re here. That is the proof.”
Weslin shook his head slowly, exhaustion dragging at his limbs. He sank back down to the floor, pulled the blanket around his shoulders like armor, and stared at the dying light outside the stable loft window.
“Maybe I just need to rest,” he said quietly. “Then tomorrow I try again without losing control.”
Reau crouched beside him. “That would be best for now.”
Aurelia gave a gentle nod. “When you wake, you’ll feel better. And we can talk more.”
Snow continued to fall outside the window, a soft hush against the turmoil settling into the corners of the loft. The boy curled inward. And the others, for now, let him.
In the corner, Garr took up watch beside the eastern peephole, still armored, still tense.
“Should’ve been back by now,” he said. “Riven and Ash.”
“They’ve got good instincts,” Harmon said from a crate where he was cleaning the head of his cane. “They’ll come in hot, though. They always do.”
Dain lowered onto a hay bale and began unstrapping his boots. “You’d think we were being hunted.”
Nyssa sat beside him. “We are.”
A slow silence took hold. The kind that gets into the bones. A thump broke the silence. Scuffed boots. The crack of the stable door opening below. Everyone froze. 
Ash burst into the loft first, half-covered in soot and blood. None of it was his. His grin was too wide. “Surprise. I brought a friend.”
Riven followed, limping slightly, one sleeve torn at the shoulder and dark with old fluid. His eyes swept the room like a cat cornered one too many times.
“We were followed,” he said. “But we lost them. Maybe.” Harmon’s eyes narrowed. “How many, how close?”
Garr was already halfway to the stairs before Harmon held up a hand. “Too late to chase shadows. We hold here.” Garr swore under his breath and swung back to the eastern peephole, scanning the yard.
Riven leaned against a post, catching his breath. “They were listening. Every step. I don’t know how, but they were waiting. Feels like the city itself is eavesdropping.”
Ash dropped to the floor beside the others. “We got in trouble. Again. But we brought a mystery.”
No one laughed. Reau stood slowly, and Weslin stood beside him. Outside, snow continued to fall. Inside, every boot that crossed that floor tracked a different story into the dark. The loft had gone quiet, but not still. Breath fogged the air. Cloaks steamed. Muscles twitched with strain. Hunger gnawed from within, and exhaustion sat just behind every eye like a second shadow.
Harmon didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t need to. “Let’s stop spinning around what you saw,” he said. “I want answers. Three of them. What happened to Stormhaven? Who’s behind it? And can we take it back?” He looked across the room, his gaze hard as iron, but steady. “Start.”
Neavin stepped forward, still wearing the dust of the streets. “The shrine we found wasn’t old. It was built to resemble its original appearance. Ritual tiers, red cloth, carved runes, all forged. The doctrine was nonsense. The titles are fake. The scroll was signed by someone calling themselves the High Minister of the New Flame. That position doesn’t exist.”
Aurelia nodded, arms folded tightly. “The people inside believed it. Real chanting. Real sacrifice. They weren’t actors. They’d been rewritten.”
“You think the shrine is the center?” Garr asked.

“No,” Neavin said. “It’s a decoy. They want people chasing symbols while they move underneath.”
“They? Who are they?” Nyssa asked, eyebrow arched.
“Not an army,” Neavin said. “That's what bothers me.”
 “It means they didn't need one,” Nyssa said quietly. 
“You sure it wasn’t?” Dain cut in. “Because what I saw at that tea wasn’t peace. It was an occupation, with lace and a smile.”
Nyssa slid off the barrel she was leaning against. “They dressed it up, made it civil, but we saw the edges, loyalty tests. Families vanishing. The governor’s household? Refused the oath. Gone. Three noble houses followed.”
“And the rest?” Dain said. “Marching in circles. Around the tower. Over and over. They weren’t being watched. They were trained.”
Ash muttered, “Trained for what?”
“To obey,” Aurelia answered.
“They used politeness as a weapon,” Nyssa said. “A smile covers a dagger in that district now.”
“They call it ‘reeducation,’” Dain said. “But I watched a noble flinch when the word ‘Korr’ came up. Nearly spilled his drink.”
“Same name we found,” Aurelia said.
Neavin added, “Always whispered. Never explained.”
Riven, who’d been quiet near the post, stepped forward. “It’s worse than whispered. In the undercity, the name changes people. One man forgot it after he said it. Another froze. Someone else whispered it like a prayer.”
“You think it’s a person?” Garr asked.
“No,” Reau said, stepping forward. “We think it’s a symbol. A trigger.”
He laid down the sketches. The stonework. The runes. The basin. “This is what we found under the forge district. A chamber. Built like a vault, but breathing like a womb. Pressure in the stone. Anchors intact. The runes were old. But active.”
Aldrek crossed the floor and tapped the diagram. “That is a warbeast vault, from the Second Magic War, or older. They were not just storage rooms. They were built to direct constructs. With thought, not voice.” Garr let out a low breath that was almost a whistle.
Reau nodded. “If they activate it, it won’t defend. It’ll lead.”
Ash gave a humorless chuckle. “And we’re worried about nobles with bad posture.”
“You should be,” Nyssa said. “They’re being used too.”
Weslin finally spoke. His voice was soft, but it filled the room. He swallowed once. “I saw it.”
All eyes turned to him.
“When I tapped the shard… I broke through. I know I wasn’t supposed to, but it just happened. When it happened, I saw this chamber. Dozens kneeling. And at the center, a figure. Tall. Masked. It looked at me.”
“Did it see you?” Aurelia asked gently.
Weslin nodded. “It knew I was there. Not sure what it saw, I just saw the mask.”
Neavin’s voice came low. “Did it speak?”
“No. But the others were saying something…Like a chant. Just one name. Korr.”
Ash shifted. “We keep circling that name, and no one has an answer.”
“Because it’s not a man,” Aurelia said, her voice cracking for the first time. “It’s a presence. A doctrine. A lie made powerful by how many people believe it.”
“You’re wrong,” Aldrek said sharply.
Aurelia turned to him. “This isn’t just doctrine,” he growled. “It’s blasphemy. They’ve built a temple over sacred ground. They’ve replaced sacrifice with puppetry. What I saw in those tunnels, those symbols, they weren’t binding anything. They were feeding it.”
Adldrek pointed to the sketch. “You want to know who’s behind it? Look beneath your feet.”
“And the explosion at Ironmarch?” Reau said. “That wasn’t just a rebel strike, was it?”
“No,” Harmon said firmly. “It was destroyed for another reason.”
Garr spoke next. “We saw it. There used to be a protective circle there. Old. Layered through every governor statue. Each one added strength to the seal.”
“They blew it from below,” Reau said. “The crack pattern goes up, not out. Someone knew the seal was there before they moved on to the plaza.”
“And whatever it was holding?” Aurelia said. “Is now awake.”
“Is that what the Red Cloaks came for?” Nyssa asked. “To wake it?”
“They weren’t the first,” Riven said. “We found names. Lists. The people they took weren’t random. They were chosen.”
“For what?” Dain asked.
“To disappear,” Riven said. “Or become something else.”
Weslin hugged his arms. “They’re being hollowed out.”
Garr turned. “Meaning what?”

“I don’t know,” Weslin admitted. “But I saw it. In the way the guards moved. The way the people walked in those loops. They weren’t being ordered. They were being emptied.”
“They were being replaced, either physically or mentally,” Aurelia whispered.
Neavin’s voice cut through: “That old woman we met, do you remember her, Aurelia?”
Aurelia’s brow furrowed. “Yes. I thought she was harmless.”
“You don’t know?” Neavin asked.
Aurelia’s voice dropped. “She quoted from a text that doesn’t exist. She smiled when she said the world was cleaner now. And then, two minutes later, she didn’t remember saying it.”
“Possession?” Riven asked.
“Reprogramming,” Aurelia said. “Piece by piece.”
Reau glanced toward Weslin, then Aurelia. “It’s like someone took what was human and filled it with pattern.” 
Silence.
Neavin broke it. “So that’s what happened. They didn’t take the city by force. They infected it. Corrupted the layers. The nobles. The rituals. The wards. Then, when no one was looking.”
“They created a prison, they don’t know they are in,” Aldrek finished.
Harmon nodded once. “Who’s in charge now?”
“I don’t think there is a ‘who,’” Aurelia said. “There’s a name. There’s a mask. But it’s not worn by one person.”
“Someone’s leading the Red Cloaks,” Garr said.
“Maybe,” Neavin said. “But no one we spoke to has ever seen the governor. Just his orders. His statues. His will.”

“They don’t need a person,” Aurelia said. “They need obedience.”
“They need conversion,” Dain corrected. “That’s what they’re doing. Rewriting Stormhaven.”
Reau folded his arms. “The deeper we dug, the older it felt. As if the city’s foundation was waiting to be rewritten.”
“Stormhaven was not built over ruin,” Aldrek murmured. “It was built over a prison.”
“And that prison,” Aurelia added, “has cracked.”
“And if that warbeast activates,” Aldrek said, “they’ll march under its banner.”
Ash folded his arms. “So, what do we tell the king? That the city possessed?”
“No,” Harmon said. “We tell him the truth.”
“Which is what?” Garr asked.
“That we don’t have one,” Reau said.
“We have pieces,” Neavin said. “No lies, but too many truths. Rituals, tunnels, missing families. But it doesn’t stitch clean.”
“Because it wasn’t meant to,” Aurelia said.
Nyssa stepped forward. “Then let’s start stitching anyway. Everything we saw. Every tunnel, every route, every face that vanished.”
“We map it all,” Reau said.
“Mark the shrine,” Aurelia added. “Even the fake one.”
“Especially the fake one,” Neavin said.
Dain looked at Harmon. “We’ll need more than facts. We’ll need proof. Pictures. Records.”
Harmon nodded. “We build the report. Everything goes to the king tonight. No delay.”
“What do we tell him?” Weslin asked. “What do we call this?”
Harmon’s eyes drifted to the warbeast sketch, then the scattered maps, then to the boy still shivering near the wall. He didn’t hesitate. “We tell him Stormhaven didn’t fall.” He looked up. “It was overwritten.”
Nobody breathed for a moment. The lamp sat untouched. The map lay flat under no one's hands. A pause. Not silence, but reverence. No one moved. Ash shifted his weight as if he wanted to make a joke, then thought better of it. 
Brother Aldrek stepped to the center of the loft. He removed one glove and placed it gently on the floor. Then he knelt. No one stopped him. He bowed his head and began to pray, not loudly, not with the force of his sermons, but with the soft rhythm of someone speaking directly to a god he feared was no longer listening.
“For what was built in stone, you gave shape. What was cast in blood, you gave breath. But now the bones stir with no soul, and the breath speaks lies. We ask not for vengeance, but for clarity. For light enough to see what walks among us. Grant us that, and we will not falter.”
Aurelia sat down beside Weslin. Nyssa leaned into the window frame. Ash stood at the back, arms folded, fire dimmed in his chest for once. Even Riven said nothing.
The wind outside rattled the loft's edge. Inside, a different type of chill took hold, one from a picture that kept forming questions where answers should have been. The room felt as if this night had no end in sight.
Not just in the way Nyssa's hands twitched toward her belt pouch, or in the way Garr stood too still at the window, but in the way they all moved now, slower, stripped of rhythm. The kind of exhaustion that didn’t just sap strength, but bent judgment, stole clarity. Eyes drooped. Shoulders slumped. Muscles ached with cold.
Dain leaned against a support beam, rubbing the bridge of his nose. Weslin, knees drawn to his chest, was still sketching spirals in the margin of an old operations report, charcoal snapping under his fingers every few strokes. Aurelia sat hunched, staring at the same knot in the wooden floorboard for what might have been minutes, lips moving faintly. Reau hadn’t spoken in some time. Aurelia twisted the old woman’s words in her mind like wire. And in the center, Harmon stood upright, composed, unshaken, because he had to be.
“Clean. Direct. What happened here, who’s behind it, and what will it take to get the city back?” He let the words settle into the bones of the room. A few glances passed, but no one moved. One pass to empty the room. Now, a second to find what the first missed. 
The rafters groaned softly above them. “Start with the first,” Harmon said. “Who is behind this? Speak plainly.”
“I believe it’s the Red Cloaks,” Neavin said quietly. “But not just them. They’re the blade, not the hand.”
Riven snorted. “You think they’re acting alone? They’re soldiers. Fanatics. But they’re being led.”
“I agree,” Neavin said. “There’s structure. Timing. And too many psychological tactics to be accidental.”
“Morlin,” Dain offered. “It’s them. Or some that resemble them. We saw their signature,” He made a hand motion between himself and Nyssa, “Rigid social control, symbolic dominance, purging of nobility, restructuring of classes.”
Nyssa nodded slowly. “And deliberate severance from truth. We asked questions that made them twitch.”
“But Morlin wouldn’t need the rituals,” Aurelia said. “They’ve never bothered with that kind of veil. Whoever this is, they’re building a belief system.”
“Maybe they’re copying one,” Ash said. “Spook the locals into compliance.”
“No,” Aldrek said. His voice was sharp. “They’re not mimicking. They’re converting. We found theology, not propaganda. And it’s spreading faster than any force doctrine I’ve ever seen.”
Harmon looked to Aurelia. “Do you believe it’s religious in nature?”
Aurelia hesitated. “Yes. But not in the way most faiths rise. This is deeper. More invasive. It doesn’t ask for your belief. It replaces the need for it. It implants it.”
“And what about this Korr?” Garr asked, arms crossed. “We’ve all heard the name. But no one’s seen the face.”
“That’s the point,” Riven said. “It’s a title, something anyone can wear.”
“Or,” Weslin said softly, “something wearing a person.” Silence followed immediately. The wind slammed against the wall, causing Ash to jump.
Harmon broke the silence. “You saw this.”
Weslin nodded. “In the vision. When I tapped the shard, there was a figure, tall, masked. Everyone around it bowed. It didn’t speak. But it saw me. Not just… noticed. It saw into me.”
“You think that’s Korr?” Nyssa asked.
“I can’t prove it,” Weslin said. “But nothing else fits.”
Dain exhaled, lips thin. “So… a construct? A god? A puppet?”
Reau finally spoke. “An echo. Maybe something left behind and reshaped by what they broke under the city.”
“They didn’t just take Stormhaven,” Aurelia said. “They awoke something in it. Something that was buried.”
“You’re saying it was always here?” Garr asked, voice tightening.
“Buried,” Aldrek said. “Bound. That warbeast chamber wasn’t just a tomb, it was a lock. They broke it open.”
“And the Red Cloaks,” Neavin continued, “took the opportunity. But they weren’t the ones who caused the rupture. They exploited it.”
Riven leaned against a beam, arms crossed. “Then who set the trigger?”
They all looked at each other. No one answered. Until Aurelia’s voice rose again, haunted and quiet: “The people in that shrine didn’t seem coerced. They had nothing left but faith. That means this started long before they got here.”
Harmon nodded once, absorbing it all. “I've seen the Red Cloaks work. This isn't them. Not the whole of it.” He paced once, fingers moving at his beard. Stopped. Turned. “Fine,” he said. “We’ll build from that. Now, what happened to the city?”
Dain pushed off the wall, pacing now, fire returning to his voice. “This wasn’t a siege. It was a surgical replacement. Hit the tower, rewire the upper class, wipe out dissenters.”
“At that tea,” Nyssa said, “there were only four noble families. Four. Out of how many?”
“Sixteen,” Dain confirmed. “And one of those said the loyalty test was mandatory. The rest? Removed. ‘Reeducated.’ Or missing.”
“The nobles are being targeted,” Reau said. “What about the rest?”
“They’ve been turned into watchers,” Aurelia said. “Each class reshaped to control the one beneath. Nobles patrol ritual patterns. Servants recite chant loops. Market folk don’t remember faces. It’s all closed circuit.”
“And the governor?” Riven asked.
“We asked,” Nyssa said. “All we ever got was ‘He is watching.’ Not where. Not when. Just... present.”
“No public appearances,” Dain added. “But new statues. New orders. They use his name, but no one’s seen his face.”
“They don’t need to,” Aurelia said. “The presence is enough. The idea is enough.”
“They're rewriting the city,” Weslin murmured.
“They’re desecrating it,” Aldrek said.
All heads turned. Aldrek stepped forward, unblinking. “I’ve seen what faith looks like when it grows wild. But this… this is deliberate heresy. They’ve buried truth under ritual, turned worship into submission, and they’ve mocked the Creator’s image with a hollow one.”
His fists curled. “The symbols they carve are not divine. They’re parasitic. Feeding on what’s left of the sacred.”
“You saw this?” Harmon asked.
“In the vault. The blood basin. The chanting. It was old magic, but inverted. There was no containment left. Only hunger.”
Reau looked to him. “The warbeast?”
“Still dormant. But twitching. If they finish the rite, that thing will march through stone like air.”
Nyssa gave a sharp laugh. “And what? Lead their army?”
“No,” Aldrek said. “Replace it.”
Garr’s tone turned cold. “So we can’t take the city.”
“No,” Aldrek answered.
“Not directly,” Reau added. “Every citizen could be a relay, or a soldier. Every wall could hear. And if that construct wakes…”
“Then it’s not just us who fall,” Aurelia said. “It’s everything, every kingdom.”
Ash leaned forward, elbows on knees. “So, what, we wait? Watch it spread?”
“No,” Harmon said. “We report. We warn. And we prepare to burn the infection out before it crosses the borders.” He stepped back from the table. “Everyone, bring what we have. We make the report now.”
Reau moved first, gathering his sketches. Neavin and Aurelia passed the ritual documents to him. Weslin slowly handed off his notepad, knuckles white.
Harmon walked into the storage room and closed the door behind him, parchment already unfurled in his hand.
In the main room, the others exhaled. Ash cracked his neck. “Well. That was cheery.”
“I don’t like this,” Garr muttered. “It feels like we’re sitting on a powder keg with a lit fuse.”
“Then sit quiet,” Nyssa said. “We’ll need the energy.”
Riven leaned against a support beam, arms folded, his eyes fixed on Dain like a hawk watching a stray dog.
“You really think it’s Morlin? That neat and clean?”
“I never said that,” Dain replied without looking up.
“You didn’t have to,” Riven muttered. “That smug shrug of yours did it for you.”
Dain stood, slow and deliberate. “You’ve got a talent for hearing things no one said.”
“You’ve got a talent for saying nothing at all,” Riven shot back. “Nobles are good at that, speaking in fog and acting like it’s wisdom.”
“Oh, piss off, Riven.”
“Careful,” Riven said, his voice low but cutting. “You’re not as sharp as you pretend to be.”
“And you’re not half as clever as you think.”
That did it. The tone was too loud. Too pointed. Heads turned.
Dain stepped forward, his posture iron-straight, fists half-curled. “Keep talking. Maybe we’ll see if that clever mouth of yours can still function with a boot in it.”
Riven smirked like a man itching for a reason. “Go ahead. Swing first. You nobles love your formalities. Maybe I’ll even let you draw a circle first.”
Dain didn’t swing. He shoved. The crack of wood and leather snapped through the loft. A crate toppled nearby, dust pluming into the lamplight.
It wasn’t a blow meant to hurt. Just to land. To prove.
Riven’s smile didn’t fade. “You’ve got spirit, noble. I’ll give you that. Like a stray dog who doesn’t know when to back down.”
Before Dain could lunge again, Nyssa shoved between them, shoulder-first and full of fury.
“Enough,” she snapped, eyes flashing. “Gods, you two, grow up.”
They both fell still. The tension didn’t vanish. It just coiled tighter. Nyssa looked between them, disgusted. “You want to fight? Do it after we’re dead. Until then, shut it down.”
She turned on her heel and stalked off, leaving the air jagged behind her.
Ash muttered, “That was productive.” Aurelia sat again, rubbing her eyes.
Riven’s grin faded as Nyssa stormed off. He watched her go, not with regret, but something harder to name. Then he turned, grabbed the coin off the crate behind him, and flicked it once into the air before pocketing it without a word.
He moved back to the shadows near the stairwell and leaned against the post, head lowered. Not sulking. Waiting. Coiled. Whatever storm had stirred in him hadn’t passed. It had just gone quiet.
Dain didn’t follow Nyssa with his eyes. He didn’t move at all at first. He just stood there, breathing slowly through his nose, hands flexing open and closed like he was counting seconds. Then he sat back down, not on the crate he’d been on before, but on the cold floorboards, legs drawn up, arms braced on his knees. Trying to get his anger to leave.
He didn’t look at Riven. He didn’t need to. Whatever passed between them wasn’t over. Just paused. Weslin leaned against Reau’s shoulder, eyelids drooping. The wind howled outside.
Suddenly. A knock. Slow. Hollow. Everyone froze. Garr and Neavin moved fast. Weapons out. No panic in it. There was only quiet. Then a faint creak.
The note was pinned to the inside of the doorframe, ink still bleeding slightly from the cold. Whoever left it hadn’t fled. They’d walked away with calm confidence. 
That detail bothered Harmon more than the note itself. Someone knew where they were. And instead of using that knowledge against them, they'd used it to help. That was either the most dangerous kind of ally or the most dangerous kind of trap. 
Neavin peeled it free and brought it back upstairs. His eyes met Aurelia’s, and without a word, he handed it to her.
She unfolded it carefully, her voice cutting the silence like a drawn blade.

‘The governor’s bloodline has not yet been spilled.
They are held beneath the tower.
Cleansing begins tomorrow evening.
The pattern completes at dusk.’
No one spoke. Reau's breath whistled once through his nose. Nyssa’s hand went to her hip. Garr shifted toward the window.
Aurelia reread the note, aloud, slower this time. Weslin swallowed hard. “They know where we are.”
“And they want us to know,” Reau said grimly.
Neavin stepped toward the side room where Harmon had gone to begin his briefing. “He’s still in there.”
He didn’t knock. He opened the door and walked through, followed by Aurelia, then Nyssa. The others remained behind, the tension crackling in the air behind them.
Inside, the mirror on the far wall shimmered with living light. On its surface stood King Edric, his broad shoulders lit by the high torchlight of his war chamber. And beside him, blurred slightly by the edges of the mirror's range, stood Governor Meridian Drake, fine robes half-unfastened, his eyes hopeful, a sheen of sweat across his brow.
Harmon stood before them, arms braced on a crate-turned-desk, old battlefield posture half-returned. He turned sharply, brow drawn as he saw Neavin enter unbidden.
“Now’s not the time…”
Aurelia stepped past Neavin and raised the parchment. “It is.” She held it up so both men in the mirror could see. The effect was immediate. Governor Drake staggered a half-step closer, pale with disbelief. His voice broke. “My wife. My daughters. My son. My sister… gods.” He turned to the king, half in plea, half in panic. “They’re alive. They are ALIVE! Please.”
King Edric turned sharply toward Harmon. “Is this credible?”
“To my knowledge, yes. This note was nailed to our door,” Harmon said flatly. “They knew where to find us. They knew who we reported to.”
Governor Drake moved until his face dominated the mirror’s field of view.
“If we don’t act,” he said, voice cracking beneath the weight of it, “they die. They are the last of my line. I’m paying for this mission, not just with coins, but with my reputation. I will not pay for it with their lives. There is a high price to failing, as well. Please save them, for all of our sakes.”
The silence held, thick, brittle.
King Edric was the first to move. He turned his attention fully onto Harmon.
“Can your team handle this?” he asked. “You’ve been out there. You’ve seen the city. If I give this order, do they have what it takes to see it through before dusk tomorrow?”
Harmon stared into the mirror, not with defiance, but with certainty.
“That’s why you agreed to this,” he said. “I trust my team.” He allowed a rare smile to flicker. “You should, too.”
The king’s lips pressed into a line, but he nodded once. “Therefore, change of orders then, recover the family and get out, bring back what information you can, and we will go from there.”
King Edric Wyman turned fully toward Harmon, voice sharp with command.
“Then you’ll have every underground map Governor Drake can provide. We’ll transmit them within the hour. Make ready. And may God help you.”
Governor Drake was still in the mirror's frame. His expression was tight, eyes red-rimmed from barely checked desperation. “There’s a vault,” he said, voice low. “Beneath the Capitol’s south wing. The old records chamber, sealed off after the archive fire twenty-one years ago. Most think it collapsed. It didn’t.” He took a breath. “The original plans of Stormhaven are there. Every tunnel, every forgotten route, even the sealed catacombs. And a few maps that were never meant to be drawn.”
Harmon leaned forward slightly. “What about the vault’s protection? Keyed?”
Drake nodded. “There’s a statue of the city's mother in the gardens, high above the city on eastern cliffs. Beneath the dedication plaque at its base is a hidden panel. Press in, then slide left. You’ll feel a catch. Pull it. A lead capsule will drop. Inside is the master key.”
He locked eyes with Harmon across the magical distance.
“If the plaque’s been moved… then they know. And you’ll have to break in.”
He paused for a moment before continuing. “I ask you, please ensure this is done before the end of the feast, so I will have a clear heart when offering to God the Creator in the final ceremony tomorrow.”
King Edric Wyman said nothing for a moment, then nodded. “You have your orders. Move quickly.”
Harmon saluted. “We will.”
He turned sharply from the mirror and crossed the room, already shedding the stiffness of formality.
Without looking back, he said evenly, “Get me Riven and Nyssa.”






Chapter Thirty-Seven
It was near midday when Taerel finally stepped back from his leatherwork, blinking hard as the shapes of the runes bled in and out of focus across his vision. His eyes were dry. His fingers ached. He could still feel the delicate vibration of the scribing blade in his wrist, echoing up through tendons and into his shoulder like a ghost that hadn’t yet let go.
The bands lay in a neat row atop the canvas beside him, unpowered, but intact. Carefully looped, double-stitched, and etched with runes in the pattern he’d memorized from Luca’s bracelet. This method he’d learned from an unconscious memory, not from teaching.
The leather he used had come from the stolen merchant horse saddle bags, which he had liberated from the bandits a day before, and it was clean, well-tanned, with the fresh smell of oil and dye still lingering in the grain. It wasn’t ideal, but it was better than scraps. He’d reinforced each band by doubling it up and finding scraps of metal around the cavern to work as fasteners. 
That was the thing with scribing. You didn’t write from diagrams. You wrote from the pulse in your blood. The deeper the magic, the older the lineage, the louder the pulse.
He touched the final band with two fingers. The runes were crisp, precise… and inert.
They wouldn’t activate until he enchanted them. And for that, he needed a shard.
He exhaled through his nose, leaned forward, and held his forehead in his hand.
The camp was moving around him. That was the only word for it, moving. Not thriving, not struggling. Just… moving. People hauled crates from the far stores, checked rope stockpiles, and relit lamps in deeper corridors. They were scavenging all they could find around them. There were children here, hiding, mostly, but he saw one pass by with a piece of bread, mouth already working on the crust before her feet stopped.
Luca walked up from the lower corridor, wiping a stained cloth across his wrists. His sleeves were rolled, his hair tied back, and the acrid scent of boiled roots and rot clung to him like smoke.
“How’s it going?” he asked.
Taerel gestured to the bracers. “Ready. Structurally. Not enchanted.”
“Still no shard.”
“Nope.” He glanced at the runes. “They’ll hold the enchantment once I can transfer power from a shard to the runes. I built a slow-feed into the binding loops, won’t take much power to keep them running.”
“How many?” Luca asked. 
“Three bands. One spare.” 
“Wish we had one for Lysana and Aymir.”
Taerel nodded. “Would’ve made things easier.”
Luca’s gaze flicked toward the entrance. “When are they due back?”
“No clue,” Taerel said. “Depends on whether the trail was clean. Depends on how far the caravan made it. Depends on whether they’re improvising. I guess it just depends.”
Luca said nothing. Then: “Yes. It does.” 
Aymir stepped into the alcove, voice low. “Do you think he was right to ask us to find where they’re going?”
“Not my place to answer that, but I would like to know if there is a back door through the mountains. Also nice to know who is at my back when the killing starts.”
Aymir nodded once. Didn't look convinced. A distant whistle echoed down the corridor. Taerel and Luca stiffened at once.
Another shout followed, closer this time, from one of the outer scouts. “Recent movement!” a voice called. “Wheels. Cart-size.”
Taerel shot Luca a look. “We didn’t send a cart.” 
“No,” Luca said. “We didn’t.”
They reached the upper ridge just as the narrow switchback path trembled with clattering wheels. Dust plumed in the cave’s filtered light, and two figures rode alongside a loaded cart pulled by the same horses that had left with the soldiers three days ago.
Luca’s eyes narrowed. “Well, I’ll be damned.”
The soldiers waved. The cart creaked in. Ropes bound the top like a makeshift lid, and inside were barrels, bundled food, nails, hinges, tools, even a sack of worn linens tied off with a civic seal.
Taerel raised his voice. “Where the hell did all this come from?”
One soldier hopped down, breath short but grinning. “Ridge outpost. East of the old tree line. It was being used as a merchant drop. We knocked. Someone knocked back.”
The second soldier added, “Local farmers had stashed supplies there, scared, mostly. But they offered. Said better us than the Orcs.”
Luca pulled aside the tarp and saw rows of coiled chain, sealed water skins, and a satchel packed with tools that still smelled of the forge.
He blinked. “And they just gave this to you?”
“They’re sending more tonight,” the soldier added. “Few of them want to join when we hit the camp. They’re arming up now, leaving a skeleton crew behind to hold the outpost, just in case.”
Taerel opened a side crate. “No trouble?”
“None,” the soldier said. “Quiet all the way back.”
“No ogres?”
“No.”
Luca nodded slowly. “Good, that means you were followed, too.”
They hauled the supplies into the deeper alcove, where the cavern-turned-command post had been hidden from the world. Some of the people they’d rescued from the city helped unload, thin and quiet but willing. One woman cried when she saw the bread sacks. A child kept staring at a spool of thread like it might vanish if he blinked.
“I’ll take these to the runners,” Luca said, lifting a box of gears.
The soldiers followed, bringing what they could to the narrow crawlspace that connected their cavern to the inner fort. They’d widened it just enough to pass food, tools, and scrawled instructions to the engineers inside the broken gatehouse.
The fort’s eastern wall had jammed. The counterweight was split. Until it moved again, they couldn’t send anyone through. But now they had the parts. Now they had a chance.
Later, after the crates were stacked and the people fed, Taerel found himself pacing the upper ridge. The stone felt familiar now. He walked it daily. Watched the camp beyond.
It was always the same. Orcs moved in loops. Repeated actions. Fetch wood. Load catapult. Fire. Wait. Not once had they advanced. Not once had they approached the gate itself. They weren’t trying to breach the fort. They were trying to… maintain something.
Taerel narrowed his eyes. He watched the rhythm. The pattern. The calculated sameness of it all. He’d fought orcs before, feral ones, tribal ones, warbands from the far east. This wasn’t like them.
Then the thought struck him. This was staging. A performance, not an assault. But to what end? That was the question biting at the edge of his mind. He left the orcs to their pattern and went to find Luca.
Lysana and Aymir had been tracking the cart since before the sun had fully crested the horizon, its first glow bleeding slowly into the canyon like the embers of a dying forge. Early light stretched long and golden through the sparse clouds, tinting the distant stone a reddish hue, like old blood dried into granite. Wind whispered low through the ridges, tugging at cloaks and scattering sand like tiny scraping voices.
Aymir rode ahead, his rifle tied across his back, reins in one hand and a half-eaten apple in the other. The crispness of the morning had long since deepened into a biting chill, the kind that sank into their gloves and stiffened joints with every passing hour of the ride. Below them, the orc supply cart moved slowly along the basin trail, a worn path carved more by repetition than purpose. Dust kicked up around the mules' hooves, lingering in the air like smoke. The orc driver didn’t look back once.
They had kept to the high ground most of the way, pausing at ridges, crossing crests under cover of thin rock spires, staying low whenever the trail bent wide or narrowed too much for concealment. They hadn’t spoken much since they set out, relying instead on hand signals and shared glances. It was work, quiet, methodical, precise. Neither of them trusted easy words when hunting.
Now, hours in, they stopped again beneath the shadow of a slanted crag, both crouched and silent. The cart had disappeared.
Lysana knelt beside a boulder, fingertips brushing the trail’s edge. “Tracks go straight through,” she murmured, eyes narrowing, “and then… nothing.”
Aymir leaned beside her, scanning the terrain. “No wheel grooves. No dust trail. No fresh turns. Just stops.”
He shifted to his feet, squinting at the jagged ridgeline ahead. A narrow split in the stone yawned open like a half-closed mouth.
“Could be a sinkhole,” he said.
She shook her head. “Too clean. No collapse, no drag marks. The rock’s undisturbed, just… gone.”
They stared at the cleft.
Aymir’s fingers gripped the pommel of his blade. “Well. That’s unsettling.”
They led their horses down into the narrow gulch, tying them beneath a low overhang half-covered in bramble. The animals snorted and pawed the ground but didn’t resist.
“Stay,” Lysana whispered, patting her mare’s flank.
Then, as one, they turned to face the split in the rock.
The air spilling from the crack was cold and stale, like a tomb that hadn’t been opened in years. It carried a strange, almost metallic scent, a mix of iron and dust with something sour and earthy. The stone bore no tool marks. The edges were oddly smooth, but not from erosion. The shape was too... intentional.
“Looks more like something tunneled out,” Aymir muttered.
Lysana nodded. “Recently?”
He knelt, brushing at the ground. “No. The tracks are layered over dust. This tunnel’s old. Whatever dug it, it was here long before the Orcs started using it.”
He stood and drew a thin-bladed dagger. “Let’s find out where it goes.”
They moved slowly inside, boots soft on layered dust. The air grew colder the deeper they walked, and the walls changed, no longer simple rock, but shot through with veins of dark crystal and strange, hardened streaks that looked almost like fused bone. The tunnel widened unexpectedly, and a gust of wind whistled through from somewhere deeper, carrying a faint sound like whispering voices.
“Lovely,” Aymir muttered.
Lysana gave a tight grin. “Don’t worry. If it’s a ghost, I’ll let you run first.”
“Chivalry,” he said. “Dead and buried.”
They stopped to listen. Nothing ahead. Just the wind.
After a moment of quiet, Aymir broke the silence again. “So… what did you say to him?”
“To whom?” Lysana asked, puzzled.
“Luca.”
She raised an eyebrow.
He gave a small shrug. “You know, we have noticed. So what did you say to melt the assassin’s heart? Word is, he once cut off a man’s tongue just for finishing a job too loudly.”
She laughed softly. “You believe all the old stories?”
“I believe Adin, and he told me that one. Said Luca left a mark on the table afterward. A reminder to speak softly and don’t gloat.”
“Well,” she said, brushing dust from her sleeve, “maybe I didn’t melt anything. Maybe I just didn’t flinch.”
Aymir smirked. “You think that’s the trick? Not flinching?”
“Worked on you, didn’t it?”
He barked a laugh, quiet but genuine. “Yeah. But don’t tell Luca. I’ve got a reputation.”
They kept walking, the banter easing the tension between them as the tunnel curved again. The light from their torches danced wildly now, long shadows leaping ahead of them on walls shaped like ribs. The deeper they went, the more the stone resembled something biological. Not carved, not even dug. It felt… grown.
“Don’t say it,” Lysana whispered.
“I wasn’t going to,” Aymir replied.
“You were thinking it.”
“I was thinking,” he said slowly, “that I really don’t want to meet whatever creature called this home.”
She didn’t laugh this time.
Then, movement. A scraping sound. Shuffling claws on stone.
Both froze. A glimmer of something pale skittered into view, then ducked back into the dark.
Lysana dropped into a crouch, arrow already nocked.
Aymir scanned the shadows and listened. “Three… maybe four of them. Not orcs. Not human. Too small.”
They waited.
From the dark came a snarl and a chittering hiss.
A shape lunged, jagged limbs and glinting eyes. Lysana’s arrow thudded into its chest mid-leap, and it dropped with a screech. The others came fast, lean, feral things with sinewy torsos and insectile jaws. The air exploded into motion.
Aymir met the next with steel, blade slashing upward in a blur that caught it across the throat. Blood, not red, but black and smoking, splattered the wall. Lysana spun behind him, dropping two more with precise, fluid shots.
The last creature fled into the shadows, howling.
They panted, standing still, backs nearly touching.
“You good?” Aymir asked.
“It got my shoulder. Just a graze,” she muttered, wincing as she rubbed the welt.
“Not poisoned?”
“Wouldn’t be the first time.”
He glanced at her. “We should talk about that later. Sounds like a good story.”
Further in, the air thickened. The ceiling opened into a wide, hollow space, and below them stretched a vast under-chamber, lit faintly by glowing green fungus and streaks of mineral light. Dozens of Joblins moved about in rhythm, hauling crates, directing carts along wooden paths. The scale of the operation was stunning.
“They’ve turned this place into a damned supply hub,” Lysana breathed.
“They’ve been using this passage to funnel goods straight through the mountain,” Aymir said. “This isn’t just a supply line,” he muttered. “It’s a damn artery.”
As they backed away, movement near the far mouth caught their attention.
Another cart emerged, drawn by fresh mules.
“Another one?” Lysana whispered.
He cut his eyes toward her. “Is it coming our way?”
She was already moving. “Yes.”
They slipped out quickly, rising into the fading daylight just as the tunnel receded behind them.
They were halfway back to their horses when Lysana slowed, hand rising instinctively. Aymir followed her line of sight across the open terrain toward a bend in the lower ridgeline.
Dust. A plume rising against the horizon. He shaded his eyes. “Riders?”
“Eight,” she murmured, narrowing her gaze. “With a cart between them.”
They moved to the slope’s edge, hidden from above, but still with a clean view downhill. The cart and its escort weren’t approaching the tunnel; they were further off, traveling southward, hugging a trail that eventually curved toward the river-cut valley far below.
Lysana crouched low, scanning the riders one by one.
All wore armor, half-plate by the cut, each set matched and polished to a dull gleam. Not military regulation, but not bandit scrap either. Custom. Expensive. Purpose-built. Their horses were well-groomed, laden with rations and water skins. This wasn’t a raiding party. It looked more like an insertion team.
“What do you think?” Aymir asked.
“They’re not from Aldoria military, I can tell you that. Too polished. Too clean. And no insignias.”
“No supplies in the cart,” Aymir noted. “Which means either they’re bringing it in empty to pick something up, or… they already dropped it off.”
They both watched as the group rode steadily toward the distant haze that marked the riverlands.
Lysana frowned. “If they’re smugglers, they’re rich ones.”
“If they’re mercs, they’re far too comfortable.”
Aymir exhaled through his nose. “Whatever they are, they’re not part of any kingdom I’ve seen. You don’t ride like that unless you’re answering to someone powerful… or dangerous.”
Lysana hesitated, then nodded, making marks on a folded map. “We’ll mark the trail. It might be worth tracking later if Luca wants to know where they came from. But for now…”
“Let’s get back,” Aymir agreed, already turning toward the ridge.
They mounted swiftly, leaving the strange convoy behind as the sound of distant wheels and hoofbeats faded into the canyon wind.
Aymir rode for a while without speaking. Deep in thought over what they say, 'Eight riders. No marks. No banners. Heading south.' He turned it over in his mind. What was happening beyond this area? Was someone moving pieces quietly? And they were doing it from more than one direction. 
They knew they were getting closer when the air started to smell of food again. Smoke drifted upward in smooth ribbons from the controlled cook fires. Somewhere beneath the canopy of hanging tarps, children laughed for the first time in nine days. It was not joyous, not yet, but it was something close to safe. Safe was a miracle.
Civilians rotated in from the town, moving carefully along the hidden route. Many bore splints, wraps, or crutches; others carried bundles wrapped in cloth, dry bread, scavenged herbs, and the odd strip of jerky. Every time someone returned from the ruined city, a quiet tension gripped the camp. And every time they made it back, that grip lessened. It was like the cave itself was breathing again. Those who couldn't make the trip weighed on everyone, and every returning face got stopped for news. 
Taerel sat by the low ledge of the eastern drop, watching the orc camp through his rifle glass. Behind him, the hum of distant voices echoed softly, conversations floating in and out of earshot.
He didn’t glance up when Luca approached. He simply shifted slightly, giving the assassin space to crouch beside him.
“They move like machines,” Taerel said. “Every hour, the same rotations. The same pattern. Even their bombardments hit the same points. Like they don’t care if they break the wall… or maybe they’re not trying to.”
Luca narrowed his eyes, tracking the distant movement. “A diversion?”
Taerel shrugged with one shoulder, his bandaged arm stiff. “Could be. Or something worse. Something patient.”
“They’ve got a foothold on this side of the mountains,” Luca said. “They should be pushing, not sitting.”
“Unless they already have what they came for,” Taerel said.
“What do you think that could be?” Luca asked.
“It reads like patience. And something patient is waiting for a specific moment,” Taerel said, eyes still on the camp below.
“Agreed, then we keep watching until we see why,” Luca said. 
The words hung for a moment. A quiet passed between them. Then Luca exhaled, slow and steady.
Behind them, soldiers finished offloading the last of the supplies from the arriving team; the five from the outpost had finally joined the fight. They brought what they could carry on foot after hiding the cart below the second ridge: crates of field rations, spare arrows, coils of climbing rope, and a wrapped bundle containing four more sledge hammers. 
Luca and Taerel followed them into the cavern. A young boy darted past with a wooden spoon in one hand and a half-split heel of bread in the other. A woman called after him, laughing through the tightness in her voice.
“You see that?” Taerel muttered. “That’s the first time anyone’s run in days.”
“They’ve earned it,” Luca said.
“So have you.”
He didn’t reply.
Coming down almost on their heels were Lysana and Aymir returning.
Their cloaks were streaked with dust and wetness, hair wind-tossed, expressions sharpened by the hours on the trail. Their horses stood near the ramp, tied off and drinking from a shared pail. As they stepped closer, the chatter around the fire thinned.
For several minutes, they relayed their findings in clipped, low tones, each moment shared not as a report, but as a memory still raw on their boots. Their voices lowered slightly when they spoke of the tunnel’s shape, not natural, not carved, but something in between. Something made... by a creature long gone, or perhaps something that had simply left for now. The discovery that there wasn’t just one cart supplying the Orcs, but several. And a small mention of the strange company of eight mounted men, riding with discipline but no sigils, no banners. Not Aldorian military. Not marked at all.
When they finished, Luca nodded and turned away for a moment. He stepped into the shadows along the edge of the cavern and whispered across the bond, sending the information to Weslin. His voice carried only across the link.
When he returned, he didn’t speak at once.
Instead, he walked to the crate at the fire’s edge, pulled free four vials, each sealed, each distinct, and set them on the crate.
“Here’s what we’re doing.”
Everyone leaned in.
“The first,” he said, holding up a dull green glob about the size of a walnut, “is for the stew. It dissolves clean. No smell. Wait until the pot starts bubbling and drop it in fast. It’ll blend and start poisoning the broth in under a minute. Fast-acting. Ugly death.”
He tapped the second, a pale blue powder sealed in a paper twist. “This goes in the spice satchel. I will switch their mix for tonight’s meat, so when it gets seasoned, it gets this.”
Lysana raised a brow. “And they won’t notice?”
He grinned faintly. “It’s orc cuisine. I doubt they’ll notice anything short of a flaming arrow.”
Lysana rolled her eyes. A grunt of amusement came from Brehn. Someone muttered, “Charming.”
“And the third?” Aymir asked.
Luca picked up a dark vial filled with swirling red-gold liquid.
“Their ale,” he said. “They store it in a single keg, west side of the camp. Lightly guarded. I spike it, they drink, and they die in time for the main course.”
“And if something goes wrong?” Lysana asked quietly.
He picked up the fourth vial. “This is for arrows. The new men have bows. If any survive the first three, that handles it.” His eyes found Lysana. “And if the whole thing goes sideways, you ride. Everybody out. Burn the plan.”
She nodded once. “Fair.”
Aymir and Taerel exchanged glances. “We’ll cover him from the ridge,” Aymir said.
“Already picked my favorite angle,” Taerel added. “Straight through their firelight. If he goes down, they’ll lose three before they blink.”
One of the new soldiers, a dark-haired man named Brehn, stepped forward. “We’ll hold the fallback line leading down to their camp. Just say the word, and we’ll push or pull.”
Luca looked around at the team, the assassins, the scouts, the soldiers, and the civilians who’d somehow held a sliver of ground amid the ruins of a kingdom.
“Then let’s move.”
They ascended back to the overlook ridge. As they climbed, shadows lengthened, and the sky turned the color of dried blood and bruised slate.
From their vantage, the camp sprawled like a nest of embers. Fires stoked, shadows grew long. The Orcs were settling into their routine, the pattern they’d never once broken.
Luca adjusted his gloves, stepped out from behind the ridge, and melted into the darkness.
Taerel watched him go, rifle steady on the rock. “Hope he dances better than he flirts.”
“Barely,” Lysana muttered. She stepped up beside Aymir and smiled slightly. “But he means it.”
Below, the orc camp stirred. Fires roared higher. Sentries rotated. A stew pot boiled in the center of it all.
Chow time was coming. And death… came with it.






Chapter Thirty-Eight
Governor Meridian Drake stood at the window of his guest chambers and watched the feast burn below him.
Torchlight blurred against the frost-glazed glass, glinting across the golden gowns and deep violet banners. Every courtyard glowed with lanterns strung high in curling threads of firelight. Minstrels played. Nobles laughed, a thousand lives carried on in choreographed joy.
And he hated them for it.
This was supposed to be a triumph. The summit reaffirmed the Accord. A celebration of peace, prosperity, and shared strength. Ten days of culture, song, and open tables, a living reminder that the fractured kingdoms of man could still come together.
Instead, for him, it had become a funeral stretched over nights.
He hadn’t eaten since yesterday morning and hadn’t spoken more than a handful of words aloud. Even the simplest acts, such as shaving, buttoning his tunic, walking down the hall to retrieve wine, had become hollow routines, performed like a ghost replaying its death.
The cold helped. It kept his hands from shaking too visibly. He pressed his fingertips to the window’s edge, feeling the pane’s bite. From this vantage, Opindale’s southern towers stretched like cathedral pillars into the dark. The city looked invincible. Ancient. Eternal.
But he knew better now. He knew how fragile it all truly was. He knew what they wanted him to break. The dagger sat behind him, in a violet-lined box on his writing table. He hadn’t touched it tonight. He didn’t need to. Its presence saturated the air.
He could still feel it, like a second heartbeat, off-tempo, intrusive, marking the seconds he had left. He still didn’t know what it truly was. He only knew what it meant. He had opened the box two nights ago. It had arrived sometime after the fifth day of the feast, after the warning. There had been no crest, no markings, just a note tucked beneath the silk.
‘To aid you in your task.’
At first, he thought it a mistake. A cruel jest. But then Colton came. No guards. No bluster. Just a folded slip of parchment in one gloved hand… and a lock of his daughter’s hair in the other. The precise honey-brown she braided every morning.
That had been four nights ago. Colton hadn’t needed to say the rest. The steward’s voice had been calm, pleasant, almost warm as he detailed the terms.
“If the king still draws breath when the final bell tolls on the tenth night… the family will be processed. Efficiently. Irreversibly.”
Not exile. Not imprisonment. Not even reeducation. Elimination. All of them. His bloodline, cut at the root. Drake turned from the window and looked at himself in the tall mirror near the chamber’s hearth.
He looked like a man carved from fatigue. The silk robe hung loose on one shoulder. His jaw had stubble. His eyes were hollow. There was blood at the corner of one fingernail, torn earlier from a reflexive clench. He didn’t remember doing it.
He didn’t remember sitting down, either. But there he was, lowered onto the edge of the settee, hands folded in his lap like a child awaiting punishment.
“This was supposed to be a celebration,” he whispered to the room.
His voice didn’t echo. He blinked slowly and looked again at the box on the desk. The dagger lay on violet silk. Thin. Almost delicate. The hilt was plain except for the shimmer, a faint pulse of color that moved like something alive and slow. Nothing about it looked like a weapon. That was the worst part. 
The dagger didn’t glow. It didn’t whisper. It didn’t move. And yet, it demanded more from him than any throne, any enemy, any oath he had ever made. He had once withstood a siege without flinching. Had argued down two belligerent kings in the Accord’s founding summit. But now? Now he could barely draw breath.
A knock. Soft. Polite. Final. The door creaked open before he could rise. Colton entered. Impeccable. Unhurried. Not a crease out of place. The Head Steward of the palace in Opindale closed the door with silent precision and moved across the room with the easy grace of a man walking into a library rather than a battlefield.
“Governor Drake,” he said smoothly. “Forgive the hour.”
Drake didn’t answer.
Colton smiled, as if that was expected. He stopped before the desk and looked down at the open box. The dagger rested inside, untouched.
“I see it’s still there.”
Drake’s voice, when it came, was hoarse. “I wanted to know what it does.”
Colton gave a soft, approving nod. “Curiosity is a noble instinct. Most would fear to ask.”
“Does it kill?” Drake asked. “Or… does it do something worse?” 
Colton didn’t blink. “It does not kill, Governor. It replaces.”
Drake’s breath caught.
Colton continued, tone gentle as snowfall.
“It swaps the soul of the one it pierces with a prepared vessel. Crafted, tuned, and aligned to the exact magical signature of the target. The bloodline does not notice. The wards do not notice. The magic itself accepts the new occupant as the rightful king.”
Drake felt his stomach turn.
“Edric would die,” he whispered.
“And the world would never know,” Colton said softly. “To the Accord, to the realm, to the gods themselves, he would still reign. But every word from his mouth… would be ours.”
The fire hissed low in the hearth.
“And if I don’t?” Drake asked, not looking at him.
Colton’s voice didn’t change. “You already know the answer, Governor. Do you really want me to say it aloud?”
Silence.
“You don’t need to decide now,” Colton said, turning toward the door. “Only before the tenth flame dies.”
He opened the door partway, pausing in the threshold.
“For what it’s worth,” he added, with a faint smile, “this is history, Governor. You should feel honored to be at its fulcrum.”
