Drake flinched as the door latched shut, not from fear, but from how quiet it was. He remained seated, staring at nothing. The dagger waited behind him. And in the dark glass of the window, his reflection no longer looked like a governor. It looked like a ghost, one that hadn’t yet decided who to haunt.
Drake soon left his quarters. He closed the door behind him and paused just outside it. The click of the latch echoed like a warning. The halls of Opindale’s upper palace were quiet this time of night. The kind of stillness that gnawed at the corners of a man’s thoughts.
He stood there for a breath, then another, adjusting the cuffs of his formal coat with a precision that masked the tremble beneath his fingers. The weight of the dagger, Whisperfang, rested inside the lining, light as a whisper, heavier than guilt.
The walk to the ballroom stretched before him like a corridor through his conscience.
Torches flickered along the polished stone walls, casting long, distorted shadows that followed him whether he walked toward the light or away from it. The opulence of the corridor, with its ornate columns and marble reliefs of past Accord victories, only pressed harder on the part of him that still remembered what he was supposed to be. He had walked this path a dozen times before, sometimes beside the King, a few times ahead of honored guests, never like this.
Never with the world teetering just behind his ribs.
He passed the statue of Veydras the Peacemaker and slowed, not in tribute, but in dread. His legs didn’t want to go any further. His knees ached beneath his state robes. His heart refused to beat. Even his breath was careful now, as if any misstep might trigger something final.
Once, he might have paused to admire the view from the open gallery, the garden spires lit with enchantment, the bridge of nations draped with silks bearing the sigils of three proud kingdoms. But now it all looked hollow. A stage for dancers who didn't know the play was ending.
He descended the final staircase slowly, boots measured on the velvet runner.
Then, with a final breath, he stepped into the light.
The ballroom shimmered with warmth and polished grandeur, a jewel of light and pageantry set against the cold political games of the day. Candlelight flickered through crystal fixtures, and laughter curled like smoke between gilded balconies. Nobles from three nations mingled in sweeping arcs, like stars in a slow, deadly constellation.
But Drake saw none of it.
He moved like a man walking through a painting, part of it, yet somehow not. Murmurs greeted him. Bowed heads. Raised glasses. But every gesture, every voice, passed through him.
Ten nights of peace. Once, that would have meant something. A promise to future generations, forged by sacrifice and held through blood and diplomacy alike. It should have been a joyful occasion. Instead, it was a funeral in slow motion.
He was late, as most of the lords had already found their places among the colonnades and crystal fountains. He made his way to the high table and took his seat.
Music swirled from the dais. Gowned nobles glided through courtly waltzes beneath chandeliers strung with lightglass orbs. Diplomats from across the continent laughed with small glasses in hand, each gesture precise, rehearsed, sharpened by years of performance.
And there, at the heart of it all, stood King Edric Wyman and Queen Mirelle.
Drake’s breath caught before he could stop it. They weren’t just regal, they were… alive. Their hands found each other easily, naturally, as the gravity of affection pulled them together. His thumb brushed over hers mid-step. Her eyes softened with the touch. Not a performance. A marriage of equals. The sight burned. If he went through with it, he wouldn’t be ending a symbol. He’d be extinguishing a man and destroying the woman beside him.
What a celebration! What a renewal! Ten days of torture. They saw it as a time to gather allies, settle rivalries, remember the long wars, and raise a glass to their absence. He thought, 'Once I would have raised a glass with them. That man is dead.’ The weight on Drake’s shoulders dragged him further with every breath.
He took in his surroundings, looking for a way out. He saw Lord Ferric of Varendor, jaw locked in fury as he debated an Opindale port official about grain routing agreements through Aldoria. Ferric's voice cut through the noise. “You gave them favorable rates. You starved our southern lines.” Then it blended in with the music, the chatter, all the different sounds pounded in his head.
He moved, needing to escape. Not far from them, three Moradaer spellwrights stood under a silver-braided banner, dressed in robes the color of extinguished coal. They moved like a single organism. One, Lady Veysa, tapped a finger to her temple and muttered, “If you let them into the Accord, you dilute it. It becomes a market, not a pact.”
Drake passed through them like a ghost. Mouths moved around him. He stopped hearing the words. Too many titles. Too many smiles. Too many handshakes meant knives.
Their whispers followed him. As he made his way to the balcony to take in a deep breath, that was when the tears started to fall. He stood there until he was empty and then until he was decided. A long breath. The cold air on his face. He turned, wearing a smile that didn't belong to him. Whatever it took. Whatever it cost. He would not let them die. 
As he made his way back to his table, a voice caught him. “The Northern Pass resurfaced, with whispers of reopening it and lifting travel restrictions for those with the means or a cause. Imagine the profit.” Lord Carven of Velmor was saying. He was a silver-bearded and loud-lunged businessman who offered expedition shares to anyone who would “clear the first ridge.” Most dismissed it as suicide, but too many leaned in, already counting what they'd make if the numbers held.
‘If they only knew.’ He slowed at the fountain terrace. He caught the end of a conversation between an Opindale trade minister and a merchant from Dornmere. “Stormglass,” the Dornman said, “is the future of locomotion and lighting both. If you want a share, speak now.” The minister smiled, but his eyes flicked to the King’s dais, as if weighing how long Edric might still be king.
Even among allies, the air bristled.
Everyone played their game. Everyone reached. Drake used to admire it. Now he only saw a table set with poisoned fruit.
He pressed a hand to one of the marble columns, steadying himself. A servant passed, and Drake waved him away before he could speak. He didn’t need wine. He needed silence.
He found it in the reflection of the window.
His face looked pale, the dark shadows beneath his eyes now permanent. His posture was still stately, but it was only maintained by years of training and the last remnant of discipline. He ran a gloved hand down his jaw.
Five days since the message. One left.
And still… no answer.
The knife was there beneath his coat. A thin, impossible thing with a violet shimmer at the hilt. Whisperfang. They had told him that if he used it on the king before the tenth day’s end, then his family would be spared and not reeducated. Not executed. Spared. Moved to safety. Respected for their station.
He wanted to believe it.
He couldn’t.
Above him, on the roofline of the eastern tower, a shadow perched motionless among the gargoyle spires.
The figure said nothing at first. Then, very softly, he spoke.
“Two done.”
He tilted his head toward the ballroom below.
“One to go.”
He watched the Queen from above, Mirelle’s silhouette radiant in the light. She smiled easily, unaware that a gaze held her with the weight of obsession. The shadow’s fingers hovered over his hip, twitching slightly, like they ached to touch her, or end her.
“No one can see it coming.”
He chuckled to himself, then whispered again, though no one answered.
Looking back on the floor, he saw Drake’s steps slow as he caught a moment at the high table.
The King had leaned toward Mirelle again, brushing a stray curl behind her ear. She caught his hand before it could fall away. Their fingers wove together.
This brought a smile to the figure's face. “She does have a lovely smile.”
He continued to watch them. Not with envy. Not with admiration. Just watched. That intimacy… was real, he thought. He turned away.
On the floor below, Drake recoiled from the smell of stormfruit glaze on a passing servant's tray. 
He moved through the crowd like he was the only one who could see the cage. He saw them all as wild animals in a menagerie. In this crowd, an assassin waited. Somewhere in this theatre of power and opulence, the third victim's breath still filled their lungs.
The applause in the ballroom thundered yet fell on the deaf ears of Meridian Drake. He stood apart, his back to a marble pillar beneath the high banners of Aldoria, watching a sea of light and silk blur around the king and queen. Laughter chimed from clustered nobles. Toasts rang out in a dozen dialects. Plates gleamed. Wine spilled like ritual blood.
He was inside the heart of the Accord, surrounded by celebration, and he had never felt more alone.
A steward passed close, murmuring something in polite tones. Drake did not respond. He hadn’t heard the words. His hand was inside his coat again, fingers closed around the lacquered hilt of the dagger. Whisperfang. The blade that promised peace by way of betrayal.
He had counted the days. Nine since the warning. Eight since the second note arrived. Two since his knees buckled in the dark of his chamber, alone with the weight of their lives on his shoulders. And now, the ninth night.
His wife. His son. His daughter. His sister-in-law. All still alive, for now. He had received no message. No proof of life since the lock of his daughter’s hair was delivered in silence. No assurance, only threat.
‘Kill the king before the tenth night ends. Or we’ll cleanse what remains.’
The blade felt warmer now. Was that its nature, or just the heat of his guilt, trapped under layers of fine cloth?
He watched Queen Mirelle touch King Edric’s arm, and the gesture, so simple, slashed at him harder than any blade.
They looked at each other like they still remembered who they were before power. Not puppets. Not icons. Just people. A shared smile. A private joke. She leaned into him as he whispered something. They were lovers still.
Gods, forgive him. He couldn’t even remember the last time Karethiel looked at him that way.
His stomach clenched. ‘If I do it, I become the butcher of kings. If I don’t, I become the executioner of my own children.’
Drake pressed his palm flat against the wall beside him. The stone was cool. Anchoring. He swallowed hard and tried to push the noise away.
Someone bumped into him, a young noble, drunk on power or wine. The man gave a lazy apology and moved on.
He didn’t even recognize Drake for who he was.
Good.
The music changed, a softer melody. A slow-dance lull meant to evoke a sentimental mood in the room.
King Edric offered his hand to Queen Mirelle. She took it with a graceful smile, and together they stepped onto the center floor. The new song was the beat of a slow waltz, one meant for dancing with a partner. Their movements were quiet, precise, unrehearsed, but deeply familiar.
They danced not for performance, but for each other.
A page stepped up near the musicians and called out, his voice clear and youthful. “By His Majesty’s kindness, those who wish to join the king and queen on the floor, you are most welcome.”
That single invitation brought warmth to many faces. To be invited, by the Crown, into their dance, it was more than an honor. It was a memory made real. Dozens of couples moved forward. Old soldiers with stiff knees. Young nobles with eager steps. Foreign delegates were curious to participate. For a moment, the hall truly felt like a dream given breath.
But not for Drake.
He looked up toward the balcony overlooking the courtyard. Torches shimmered against the stained-glass windows. Past that, the tower spire rose like a blade in moonlight.
Harmon’s team had to be out there. Somewhere. Moving in silence. He prayed they were cutting toward the chamber… Perhaps they’ll find the cell. Maybe they’ll stop this before I…
He couldn’t finish the thought.
Drake shifted his weight and leaned harder into the pillar. His vision blurred. ‘Let them save her. Let them save them all. Please, God. If you're watching, free me from this burden. I don't want to wear this crown of blood. But I will. If that is what it takes, I will.’ The thought died as a hush swept the upper tier.
A presence moved above him, silent and cold. A glass clinked behind him, but it wasn’t that. It was something colder. Something watching. He didn’t look. He already knew.
Eyes like knives. A weight that didn’t belong. He moved toward the edge of the ballroom, every motion controlled, practiced. He nodded to a few dignitaries as he passed, smiling without meaning it, just another governor making his rounds.
The shadows near the arch were empty when he glanced back.
The dagger felt heavier now, pulling at him like a chain. He needed space. Distance. Anything but another step in that hall.
One more night. That’s all, just one more.
If Harmon’s team succeeded, none of this would matter. The blade would be returned in the box. His hands would be clean. His children would still have a father. He would still be a husband.
He knew they would not hold up their promise, or everyone would have seen his actions. No, he was already dead, whether by their blade or his own guilt. All that remained was which ghost he’d become.
His head shook in resolve. He would trade his soul for theirs. He would die in silence, hated, scorned, and they would live. That would be enough. But not tonight.
Tonight, he was still a man walking the line. Governor Meridian Drake slipped through the archway and disappeared into the dark. Behind him, laughter bloomed like flowers across the ballroom, and no one noticed the world held its breath.






Chapter Thrity-Nine
The wind held its breath as Luca crouched just below the ridgeline, his cloak wrapped tight, eyes narrowed on the Orc war camp nestled in the hollow below. The camp boiled with motion, guttural barks, clanging iron, and the methodical tramp of boots. Spiked tents rose in haphazard rows, thick with soot and blood. Black-smoked cookfires blazed from stone pits, and a massive cauldron already steamed near the center of the camp like a bloated toad, waiting to be fed.
Everything about the camp was wrong.
The Orcs moved too cleanly. Their timing was too sharp. Even the war thralls, half-broken Goblins in tattered bone necklaces, worked in silence, stacking crates and prepping meat like men who’d been drilled, not born into chaos. It was discipline wrapped in flesh, and Luca hated it.
He reached for the pouch at his hip. Four poison types. All handcrafted. Each one was built for a different kill, slow, fast, hidden, or loud. The camp churned beneath him while he worked, the contrast making his hands steadier than they had any right to be.
He had a black onyx shard around his neck, cracked, old, but still charged, pressed heavily against his skin. Not warm. Not alive. Just… waiting. If he overdrew, it would die. And so would he.
Behind him, Taerel exhaled and whispered, “Almost thirty of us. Over a hundred of them.”
Luca glanced back. The archers crouched along the ridge, dipping arrowheads into the poison vials he’d distributed. The other soldiers were checking straps and blades, each man deathly quiet.
“That’s not that bad of odds,” Aymir muttered, scanning the camp. “That’s a sermon waiting to be preached over a hundred graves.”
“Remind me to play Kingspit with you,” Lysana said from the next rock over, not looking at him. “You clearly think this is an easy hand.”
A few of the younger archers chuckled, thin laughter, cracked by fear.
Luca stood and, without a word, he dropped over the edge.
He descended the ridge like mist, slipping from shadow to shadow, boots silent on loose rock, yet still sure-footed, breath held between strides. The air was sharp with smoke and charred meat. He moved through it like a man dissolving into the night.
Two Orc warriors marched past him, less than five paces away. Their armor clinked, their gazes empty. One had red paint smeared across his lips, some war mark or ritual, maybe both. Neither noticed him.
He crept past tents, behind crates, past a stack of flayed bones still wet from the butcher. His path to the cauldron was blocked by a Red Thrall cook, crouched and tossing fat chunks of meat into the bubbling pot.
Luca crouched low. Waited.
The cook stepped away, muttering something, and he moved.
He reached the cauldron, pulled the stew orbs from his pouch. One, two, three. No splash. But the fourth slipped from his fingers mid-throw.
It landed on the rim. Wobbled.
A voice barked behind him.
He twisted fast, crouched behind the cauldron’s smoke, and froze. An Orc was yelling at one of the Goblin thralls for burning the meat. Not at him. Not yet.
Still crouched, Luca stretched his dagger out, hooked the wobbling poison orb, and flicked it clean into the stew.
As he slid back from the edge of the fire, a bellowing argument broke out between two Orcs over a ladle. One shoved the other, who swung wildly, nearly dumping the pot in retaliation. Neither killed the other, just a snarl, a punch, then back to line.
Luca narrowed his eyes. For all their strange discipline, it wasn’t perfect. There was still chaos beneath the surface, mistakes, tempers, and ego.
Good. He moved. There was still chaos in them. He could use that.
He stayed low, belly to the dirt, and moved.
He quickly crawled to the meat station. The slabs were hanging from a crossbar beside a prepping table. Orc blood soaked the ground below it, forming a sticky puddle. As he reached the first leg, footsteps closed in from behind.
He ducked, rolled under the prep table, and held his breath.
An Orc cook, a massive brute, slammed a cleaver into the board above him, humming a low tune. Luca could hear the slap of flesh on wood, the grind of bone under steel. He was close enough to smell the rot in the Orc’s breath.
Then, behind them, a flare of shouting, two Orcs in an argument over a ration crate. The cook grunted, spat, and stormed off to investigate.
Luca didn’t hesitate. He slashed a shallow line across three pieces of hanging meat, shoved the rub in fast, and slipped back into the alley between tents.
The ale barrels were stacked near the east wall. He was almost there when he froze. A patrol of three Orcs rounded the corner. He ducked back, no cover.
Nowhere to run.
They came closer.
Luca drew from the shard. He stepped into the shadow of the tent wall and vanished.
He reappeared on the far side, gasping, heart pounding in his chest like a war drum. His legs buckled. Too much pull. Too close.
But he was through.
He reached the barrel. Drew the final glass spheres. Popped the casing. Dropped them into the half-tapped cask. They fell without a sound.
He turned and found himself face to face with a Goblin thrall carrying a tray of stacked cups.
They stared at each other. The Goblin didn’t blink. He just sniffed. Luca didn’t move. Then the Goblin relieved himself mid-stare. Luca blinked once, then shoved the distraction out of his mind as the camp’s noise sharpened back into focus.
He melted back into the dark.
He crested the ridge fifteen minutes later, sweat matting his collar, legs aching, shard buzzing under his skin.
He stumbled into view.
Lysana was the first to reach him.
“You’re late,” she said, brushing hair from her eyes. Her voice was light, but her eyes searched his face.
“I got held up,” he rasped. “And pissed on. Not in that order.”
Taerel winced. “Details we did not need.”
Aymir just handed him a waterskin.
Luca took it. Drank deep. But Lysana didn’t let him walk away.
She stepped close, hand lightly on his wrist. “Luca.”
He looked up.
The noise of the ridge, the soldiers, the wind, it all fell away.
He saw the concern in her eyes. The way she looked at him was like he wasn’t just a killer. Like maybe she saw something left.
He opened his mouth. Closed it.
Then, finally, quietly, “It’s been a long time since I thought I’d come back from anything at all.”
Her hand tightened slightly.
“You will,” she said. “And when you do…”
He smiled. “Then we’ll talk.”
Lysana smiled back.
And for a second, the war vanished.
A distant clatter rose from the camp, metal on stone, snapping the moment back into the cold. She turned, fingers lingering a moment too long, and made her way to join the archers. Her bow was already strung. Her arrowheads dipped in poison.
Luca crouched beside Aymir and Taerel, staring down into the camp below.
Luca looked between them, voice low. “They’re not all gone.”
Both brothers turned. “Who?” In unison, like they'd practiced it. 
“The Orcs, their bloodlust. It’s still in there. Whatever’s guiding them hasn’t erased everything. I saw two nearly throw each other into the stew over a spoon.”
Aymir gave a half-smile. “Would’ve saved us a poison ball.”
“Means there’s still cracks in whatever’s steering them,” Taerel muttered. “Cracks we can use.”
The Orcs started gathering. A hundred or so strong. Lining up at the cauldron, which was steaming and ready. 
And those on top of the ridge, they waited.
The wind slipped cold across the ridge.
Nearly thirty souls watched the Orc camp below with the tense stillness of hunters holding their breath. Shadows stretched longer now, dusk turning the snow-lined stones a bruised violet. The smoke from the campfires drifted thick and low, stirred only by the occasional grunt or barked command.
Luca sat back on his heels, watching the movements with narrowed eyes. He ran the mission back in his head one more time and caught it. “I never used the fourth poison,” he muttered.
Taerel glanced over. “What?”
“The fourth one. Meant for the bread,” Luca said. “They stack it in crates by the far tent. I just... things were moving too fast. I didn’t want to risk it.”
“Let’s hope they’re not craving toast,” Aymir said.
Lysana added dryly, stringing her next arrow, “And pray the moldy bread wasn’t the main course. I hear Orcs like their loaves aged with a hint of battlefield mud.”
That got a few chuckles from the nearby archers, who crouched just inside the ridgeline brush.
They were good soldiers. Luca didn’t know all their stories, but names had been passed down like a roll call of grit. The waiting gnawed at them, so Luca let his attention drift across the faces he’d be trusting his life with.
Dorn was crouched nearby, the beard on his chest practically resting on his knees, quietly describing to Fenrick the correct way to brine wild boar. Fenrick, who looked barely seventeen, was only half listening. He was still fiddling with his arrowheads, turning them over like worry stones. Mira didn't look at either of them. 
She just sat with her shaved head down, adjusting a fletching with the focus of someone who preferred not to think too far ahead. Beside her, Halden was already doing his rounds, checking a man's wrapped ankle and murmuring something low and steady, the way a priest talks to someone who already knows the verdict. The fifth was Brant. Older, lean, carrying a limp like a souvenir. His eyes moved the way a marksman's do, always measuring distance.
They were joined by Sergeant Rockwen and his seventeen other soldiers, all armored and silent, veterans from the northern pass and defenders of the fort. They crouched in staggered lines along the slope, bows and blades ready.
Only a few civilians were with them now, two older men and a sharp-eyed woman acting as field medics. The rest had remained back in the cavern refuge, watching over the wounded and children and managing supplies.
Luca sat beside Lysana, his pulse still erratic from the earlier infiltration.
“You good?” she asked softly, handing him her waterskin again.
He took it and sipped. “Mostly. Still trying to believe I didn’t get my head lopped off.”
Lysana smiled. “It’s weird.” She paused, looking into his eyes. “A week ago, I didn't know you. Now losing you would mean something. That's the weird part. “
Luca glanced at her, caught off guard by the blunt honesty. “Yeah,” he said quietly. “Same.”
They both looked away, awkward for half a breath.
Then, without thinking, he reached for her hand, just a light brush of fingers across hers. She didn’t pull away. Instead, she turned her palm over and laced their fingers together, warm even in the chill wind.
“I was always better on my own,” Luca said. “But... this week.”
“Don’t ruin it with words,” she murmured. “Just hold on.”
Taerel coughed behind them, clearly watching.
Aymir grinned. “Well then. Shadow finally found himself a candle.”
“Careful,” Taerel added. “He’s getting soft. Next thing you know, he’ll write poetry.”
Luca didn’t let go of her hand. Instead, he raised the other and gave them a sharp two-finger salute, like an old court insult. “Eat snow.”
“Classic,” Aymir said, grinning.
“You know,” he said, quieter, “for years I thought the talent was reading a room. Turns out I was just looking for exits.”  
Taerel snorted. “That was before you kept company with people who bleed for a living.”
“Maybe,” Luca said. “But watching you three, the way you move together, cover for each other, throw insults like it’s strategy... It’s different. Feels like it works. Even if I’m not sure what the hell I’m doing half the time.”
Aymir grinned. “That’s the trick, Luca. No one ever does. We just bluff better than the next bastard.”
“Still,” Luca said, quieter now, “if this thing falls apart tonight, I want you to know, I’ve never trusted a crew like this one. Not since... not ever, really.”
Lysana bumped her shoulder lightly against his. “Then stop thinking about how it ends. Start thinking about how it begins.”
Dorn told a story quietly to Fenrick about his time guarding the eastern border. Mira sharpened a knife, humming under her breath.
Halden knelt beside an older civilian, checking his wrapped ankle and adjusting the cloth.
The tension was there, tight, coiled, but for now, it was laced with quiet purpose. Everyone moved like they belonged.
Still, every few minutes, all eyes would shift back to the camp below.
An hour passed. Nothing.
Then movement, one of the Orcs at the outer ring, wobbled and staggered. Halden straightened, arrow notched.
But the Orc simply bent over and vomited violently before righting himself with a growl and stalking away.
“Too early,” Luca said. “Could be something else. None of mine should cause vomiting.”
Another twenty minutes.
A Goblin fell off the back of a wagon, rolling into the mud. Two others laughed and pelted him with scraps.
“Also nothing,” Taerel muttered. “That one tripped on a rope.”
They waited.
A cold gust swept the ridge, carrying silence with it, then conversation slowly bubbled up again as nerves tried to fill the void. Dorn talked about spices with Mira. Sil Brant made a bet with Aymir over who’d notch the first Orc’s eye. Fenrick asked Luca if it was true that he once killed a man with a spoon.
“No,” Luca replied, deadpan. “It was a fork.”
“Seriously?”
Luca shrugged. “No. But I did throw a spoon into someone's eye once.” 
“Wait, you’re serious?”
Luca just smiled.
Lysana leaned close, lips brushing his ear. “You’re awful.”
“I know. I love it,” he whispered back, eyes still on the camp. 
Taerel, adjusting his rifle, winced. He had to brace it differently now, resting it against the support rocks rather than pulling it tight to his shoulder. The wound still ached. But he didn’t complain.
“See anything new?” Luca asked.
“Pattern’s still the same,” Taerel said. “Except... something’s off.”
“Off how?”
“It's like someone’s giving direction, without fully leashing them.”
“Guided chaos,” Aymir said.
“Exactly.”
“Then someone’s holding that leash,” Luca murmured.
Another silence fell.
A single Orc, near the stew line, buckled to one knee. Another behind him growled and pushed past him, not noticing.
Then a third Orc lurched sideways, hitting a post.
Taerel exhaled slowly. “Here we go.”
Everyone stood a little straighter.
“Poison’s taking,” Luca said. “Took long enough.”
They all readied weapons, quiet now. Arrows dipped. Blades loosened in sheaths. The brothers took their final positions, rifles steadied against rocks, scopes aligned.
Lysana stood beside Luca, her hand brushing his again, just once.
“You sure about this?” she asked.
He nodded once. “No. But I want it anyway.”
She smiled. “Let’s go kill some monsters.”
And the wind rose.
The order came with the wind.
“Archers, loose three volleys, center mass!” Luca’s voice cracked sharply over the ridge.
The command sliced through the dusk, and Mira was the first to move. Her bow sang once, then twice more, followed by the entire line, five archers rising in sync, loosing poisoned shafts that cut through the evening air. The hiss of strings and the twang of release filled the hillside like a violent chorus.
Below, the first volley struck with blunt inevitability. Orcs stumbled mid-step. Two collapsed before they could lift weapons. The second volley thudded in among those moving to react. The third punched through a tightly packed group near the main fire.
“Keep firing until you’re empty!” Luca shouted. “Taerel, Aymir, start picking targets!”
The rifles began barking moments later. One crisp shot, then another. Taerel grunted, adjusting the brace under his elbow, wincing through the pain. Aymir fired again, faster, more fluid. One Orc took a round to the throat and dropped. Another keeled over near the stew.
From above, it looked almost surgical.
But the poison was doing its own work too. Dozens had already dropped, some shaking, others simply slumping where they stood. It was working, gods, it was actually working.
They were going down.
Luca spotted three Orcs collapse before Mira’s next arrow was even nocked. “Save your arrows!” he called out, raising his hand. “They're already falling. No sense wasting steel.”
The archers lowered their bows one by one, Mira exhaling slowly as she reached for a cloth to wipe her fingers. Dorn clapped Fenrick on the shoulder, the young soldier looking stunned at the ease of the takedown. Even the veterans, hardened, weather-worn, allowed the tension to slip from their shoulders for a breath.
Luca turned, face set. “Brant, Halden, Dorn, you’re with me. Everyone with a blade, move. Aymir, Taerel, you stay and cover us. Lysana, with me.”
She was already beside him, sliding her bow across her back and drawing her twin daggers in a single, fluid motion.
“We do this clean,” Luca said, voice low as they descended the ridge. “Check the bodies. Finish what the poison started.”
They moved in a loose wave, boots crunching the frost-lined slope. As they reached the lower slope of the valley, the true scale of what they’d done began to register. There were bodies everywhere. Orcs, Goblins, even the monstrous cooks, all crumpled in heaps of slack limbs and spilled weapons. Steam rose from collapsed tents. The stew still boiled.
Luca crouched, checked a still-breathing Orc, and drove his dagger clean into its throat. No flinch. Just muscle memory.
A few of the others moved through the camp like ghosts. It wasn’t a fight. It was an execution.
Until the ground moved.
Silence dropped through the smoke first. Then the vibration began, faint but rising. He paused, frowning, then looked to Lysana. She was already glancing back toward the ridge.
“What was that?” she asked.
“I don’t—” he began, before the ground heaved hard enough to stagger them both.
The sound that followed was not like the ground moving. It was like it was opening.
One of the largest tents at the camp’s far edge tore open from below, its wooden supports splintering as the ground erupted with a spray of mud and frost. And from the gaping hole poured shapes, scores of them. Twisted, long-limbed, hunched things with wide mouths and bulging black eyes. The Joblins.
They came like a wave.
Hundreds, at least. Scampering and bounding over one another with shrieks and chatter and hoots like iron dragged across bone. They wore scraps of fur, bits of armor, jagged tools, and crude weapons. Many were unarmed, yet each one moved with purpose, as if flung by instinct.
Luca’s heart hitched.
“The tunnel...” he muttered. “They’ve been digging. This whole time.”
Lysana’s breath hitched. “The bombardment… it wasn't random. It was a cover. They were hiding this.”
Luca heard it land even through the noise. If that was true, the fort team had been fighting the wrong battle the entire time. He filed it. Dealt with it later. Right now, there was only the next thing trying to kill him. 
“Form up!” Luca shouted. “Everyone, form up! Hold your line!”
The archers scrambled to the edge of the camp, Mira shouting orders, Fenrick fumbling with his next arrow. Taerel and Aymir on the ridge opened fire again, shots cracking down into the charging swarm. Joblins fell, but the horde didn’t slow.
Lysana had her bow out again, arrows flying with terrifying rhythm. “One,” she muttered. “Two. Three.”
She didn’t miss.
Luca saw a Joblin coming at her from the side and lunged. His dagger struck the base of its neck, and the creature collapsed into a gurgle. Another was already in motion behind it. This time, his offhand blade sank into its gut.
The magic of his belt flared, and both blades vanished from his grip, reappearing at his side in twin sheaths moments later.
He didn’t pause, but the flare stung sharper this time, a reminder that the belt wasn’t endless. At his chest, the cracked shard pulsed once and went quiet. Not dead. But closer.
More Joblins swarmed from tents, from the pit, from under half-collapsed shelters.
The rest of the soldiers were now in the fight. Brant drew a heavy saber. Halden pulled civilians back while still notching arrows. Dorn carved a path through a knot of bodies with a war axe. 
The ridgeline thundered with more rifle fire.
And through it all, Luca caught sight of Lysana, her face set, eyes hard, cutting through the chaos with precision. He moved to her side again.
“Watch your flank!” she called.
“I’ve got it,” he said, spinning to drive a blade through a leaping Joblin’s throat.
They locked eyes in the chaos, panting, smeared with blood and frost. “Let’s survive this,” Luca said, voice low and certain. And then they turned and fought.






Chapter Forty
The Joblins were already on them. A tide of snarling, gray-skinned bodies poured from the breach, dozens, then hundreds, spilling over one another in a mad, slathering rush. Their screeches split the night, some guttural, others sharp and yipping. Teeth bared. Eyes wild. Clawed hands grasped at blades and flesh. Behind them, a handful of Goblins wove through the swarm, more coordinated, less reckless, but no less bloodthirsty.
“Hold the line!” Luca shouted.
Steel rang out as the first wave hit.
Luca’s dagger buried itself in a Joblin’s neck. He spun, the other blade catching another in the gut. Blood sprayed, black and greasy, with a smell like burnt oil and decay. His belt pulsed with heat as the blades vanished and reappeared at his sides, already ready for the next kill.
To his left, Dorn bellowed as he swung his axe in wide, brutal arcs. Each blow cleaved a path through the swarming bodies. The man looked like a blood-drenched windmill.
Halden had his back against a crate, one hand keeping a civilian medic safe behind him while the other fired arrow after arrow into the horde, each shot clean and quick.
Sil Brant fought as a man possessed, his saber flashing in tight, vicious cuts. He’d already taken a slice across the thigh but hadn’t slowed down.
The air stank of blood, bile, and unwashed bodies. It filled Luca’s nostrils with every breath. The Joblins didn’t fight like soldiers. They didn’t parry. They didn’t flank. They just charged. Reckless. Feral. Biting. One leapt at Mira, scrambling up a corpse to get height, teeth snapping for her face. She drove her blade into its throat and shoved it away, gasping.
Luca ducked under another, slashing it open from hip to chin. His eyes burned from the smoke and stink. His arms ached. They were still coming. Everywhere, climbing over their own dead, clawing for anything warm, something to kill.
“Shields!” he barked, pushing one of the soldiers back as a Goblin with twin knives ducked low and struck high. Luca intercepted with a rising slash that snapped bone and dropped the thing cold.
A scream tore through the noise. Fenrick.
Luca turned just in time to see the youngest archer go down, tackled by two Joblins who bit and clawed through his armor. He vanished beneath the writhing mass. Mira screamed, breaking formation, but Dorn caught her by the arm and yanked her back.
“There are too many!” someone shouted.
“Keep fighting!” Luca growled.
Above them, the ridge flared.
CRACK.
Aymir’s rifle boomed. One Goblin spun in midair as the bullet punched through its head.
CRACK.
CRACK.
Taerel fired next, slower, more measured, but no less deadly. His shoulder was trembling now. He’d switched to a supported firing position, resting the rifle on a stacked brace of rock. It slowed him, but it gave him steadiness.
“Too many,” Taerel muttered. “They really couldn't coordinate a faster death, could they? This is dragging terribly.”
Aymir reloaded fast, jaw set. “If we keep this up, we’ll run dry before they stop coming.”
Taerel looked down at the valley. “You thinking what I’m thinking?”
Aymir gave a grim nod. “Time to join the fun.”
A gust of freezing wind dragged more screams up the ridge, close enough to rattle their boots. The brothers stood, slinging rifles over their shoulders. Taerel winced, the strain pulling across his healing wound, but he said nothing. Before he turned, he reached into his bag and pulled free two black, fist-sized orbs. Then they descended fast, blades drawn, boots kicking up frost and blood-drenched soil.
Below, the formation was barely holding. Joblins were crawling over corpses, friend and foe alike, biting, ripping, shrieking. One had its jaw locked around a soldier’s thigh. Luca stabbed it twice before it let go.
He was covered in blood now, some was his, most not. Sweat stung his eyes. His breath came ragged. But still, he moved.
The Joblins didn’t care about numbers. They didn’t care about death. They just came. One lunged for his face, too close to dodge.
Thunk.
An arrow drove through its temple.
Luca glanced to the left. Lysana was there, face grim, the scarf at her collar snapping in the wind, bow already drawn again.
He exhaled. “Good shot.”
“Get your damn head down,” she snapped, nocking another arrow.
Luca grinned despite himself and dove back into the fray.
The battle roared.
Steel met flesh. Teeth met bone. Soldiers yelled, stumbled, and shoved each other upright. The civilians were retreating into the far tents, dragging the wounded with them. Halden limped after them, blood trailing from his calf.
Dorn dropped to one knee beside Fenrick’s body. “Gone,” he growled. “Little fool didn’t even scream long.”
Luca felt the pang, deep and hard. The boy hadn’t belonged here. None of them did. But now it was too late for regret.
Another screech cut across the field.
A Goblin this time, lean, armored, and fast, ducked through the clash and drove a blade at Brant. Brant twisted, barely dodged, and caught the Goblin with a thrust under the chin.
But they were tiring. All of them.
Luca’s vision pulsed at the edges, a dull throbbing haze every time he blinked. Even his hearing warped, screams stretching like they were underwater. He wasn’t the only one. Even the strongest of them, Dorn, was beginning to grunt with each movement.
The tide hadn’t stopped.
Then came the roar. Not from the enemy. From Taerel.
“DOWN! BLACKFIRE OUT!”
Luca hit the ground, yelling the same command to those around him.
Everyone ducked.
Taerel, standing ten paces from the front line, hurled a metal orb the size of a clenched fist into the advancing swarm. It gleamed with runes, pitched black, threaded with red.
It landed.
BOOM.
The explosion was thunder. Fire. Shrapnel. Dirt. Blood. A pulse of death.
Dozens of Joblins disappeared in the blast, torn apart mid-scream. The concussion knocked several back into their allies. Even the Goblins hesitated, but only for a breath.
They regrouped and came again. The humans surged. “We’ve got momentum! Push the advantage.” Aymir bellowed, slamming his blade into a stunned Goblin.
Luca pushed forward again, daggers flashing. This time, the tide felt different, but the numbers still pressed in.
Bodies fell faster now. Arrows sang overhead. Dorn rallied the line with a brutal roar. Even Mira, face streaked with tears, found her rhythm again, every shot fired with surgical rage.
Taerel hurled the second orb. This one landed at the edge of the mouth of the tunnel wear the Joblins immerged from.  
Another BOOM. This time muffled coming from deep in the tunnel. A roaring detonation punched through the earth like a buried thunderclap. Stone collapsed. Tents buckled. A cascade of rubble buried the tunnel, sealing it with finality. Dust billowed outward.
Luca turned, panting, blood dripping from a dozen shallow cuts. His shoulders ached. His hands shook. But for the first time that night, they had the momentum.
“Great shot! Tell me you’ve got one left or we’re all screwed!”
“Last one,” answered Taerel.
“Then now is the time to push forward!” Luca bellowed.
The swarm was thinning, but not breaking. Goblins fought with savage precision, parrying and lunging. The Joblins never fled. They kept coming. Bruised. Bleeding. Dying and yet still coming.
And then… A groan. One of the Orcs went from motionless to beginning to rise. Then another. And another. Twelve total were now standing.
Luca’s stomach turned to stone. The poison hadn’t just failed, it betrayed them. 
But these hadn’t just survived. They were moving. Slow. Twitching. But alive. Massive. Hulking. Still deadly.
Aymir stood beside him now, panting, sword bloodied. “That’s... not good.”
“No,” Luca said. “It’s not.”
Taerel chimed in, “If they want to die fighting, who are we to stop them? Let's give them what they want, death.”
The three of them nodded their heads and got back to work, just as the Orcs charged. Even poisoned and unbalanced, the twelve brutes that had risen from the wreckage held ground like stone towers in a river. Their poisoned minds twitched, their bodies buckled, but their violence hadn’t dulled. Not enough. They bought time. And blood.
Goblins and Joblins regrouped. The swarm surged again from every shadow, climbing the wreckage, crawling over each other, shrieking war cries in a hundred ragged voices. The humans’ momentum cracked, then buckled. Screams tore through the ranks. Blades flashed. Bones shattered. The snow turned black. It should have been a rout. But the tide turned again, and this time, toward death.
Luca ducked under a rusted cleaver, swept the legs out from a charging Goblin, and drove his short sword through the skull of a crawling Joblin trying to bite his boot. Blood hissed against the snow, steaming. His lungs were raw. His eyes burned. His muscles screamed for reprieve.
A soldier went down, a clean slice across the thigh, then a dozen Joblins on him in a blink. They tore and bit and slashed. The man didn’t scream for long.
“Hold the line!” Brant roared, trying to push the soldiers tighter.
Sound folded in on itself, metal grinding, boots skidding, someone choking on smoke. And still the tide poured in.
A massive Orc, one of the twelve, barreled straight for Luca’s exposed back, broad, snarling, axe raised high.
Taerel caught the movement and tried to raise his rifle. Pain lanced through his shoulder, white-hot. The stock wouldn't seat right. He fired anyway. Missed. Swore. Adjusted and tried again. 
Another miss, snow kicked up beside the Orc’s foot, but the beast never slowed. “Luca!” Taerel bellowed.
Too late. Luca turned just in time to see the axe begin its arc. Instinct took over.
He pivoted, parried high with his short sword, but the Orc’s weight overwhelmed him. He twisted, dragging the brute’s momentum to the side, and hurled the Orc forward into a tangle of Goblins. They collapsed in a mess of limbs and curses.
CRACK, CRACK rang out, and Taerel found his mark this time as the Orc lay still.
Yet, more were closing and closing fast.
Two shapes flanked him, a Joblin and a Goblin, blades drawn, mouths open with madness, one from the side, the other from behind.
Arrows whistled.
One struck the Joblin in the chest.
The other pierced the Goblin’s eye. It fell without a sound.
Luca turned, breath ragged, heart pounding.
Lysana, still standing. Still calm. Still with him.
Their eyes locked. She smiled, and for half a breath, that was enough. He saw there was something more behind it.
He mouthed ‘thank you’ for saving him again. Something caught his eye. A shadow above.
A Joblin descending, dagger raised.
Luca saw it. He reacted, daggers flung from his belt, whistling through the air with lethal purpose.
He watched as time slowed down around the whole battle. He knew. He knew, even in the frozen stretch of that heartbeat, the dagger would be too late.
The creature landed on her shoulders, driving his blade into the side of her neck.
Lysana gasped. Blood blossomed, bright against her leathers. Her knees buckled.
The Joblin never got another breath. Luca’s blades found it instantly, one through the back, one through the throat. It twitched. Then died.
But she was down.
Luca didn’t scream. He moved. Spinning. Cutting. Breaking. His body was on fire. His blade was death. He didn’t pause. Didn’t falter.
He left a trail of death behind him. A Goblin rushed, he ducked, rolled, came up behind it, and opened its spine with one slice. A Joblin leapt, he impaled it in mid-air, yanked the blade free, and let it drop twitching.
Fifteen paces. 
Ten.
Another Orc reared up, weapon high, and Luca’s dagger slammed into its eye, dropping it like a tower.
Five paces.
He was there. Lysana’s body lay in the snow, eyes still open. He dropped beside her. Cradled her. Blood on his hands, on his neck, his chest.
The battlefield fell away. She blinked.
Once. Tried to speak. Couldn’t.
But she smiled, a final gift. Her fingers slipped from his, a moment later. She was gone. Her hand went limp in his.
Something inside him stopped. Not broke, stopped. Like a spring gone still.
Blood pooled beneath her. He took her hand anyway.
All sound dulled except the wheezing in his chest. The pulse in his ears. The weight of her hand in his.
He whispered her name. Once. Twice.
Aymir reached them first, sliding on his knees, hands shaking. “No—no no no—”
He gathered her up, sobbing openly. Her scarf bunched in his fists.
“She was right here. She was right…”
Taerel came slower, favoring his arm. He didn’t cry. Didn’t breathe.
Just stared. He had never seen death up close. Not like this. Not to someone who’d laughed beside him. It was the first time someone he knew had died, and died in front of him. 
Luca was still.
Then he rose. A new look on his face. Lysana's body lay back in the snow.
He looked at the battlefield, the writhing masses, the beasts that had taken her, the nightmare not yet over.
He reached for the shard and pulled. Every ounce. All of it.
And the world went dark.
At first, there was only confusion, a collective gasp as sight snapped away. The Darkness fell over everyone and everything. It wasn’t the absence of light. It was the presence that filled this grove. It filled the lungs. It pressed behind the eyes. It smothered everything like a wet cloth over a flame.
Sight vanished. Sound dulled.Complete deprivation of the sense. Then the screams began. Not human.
Not normal.
Screams like metal folding into itself. Like something clawing its way out of a stone throat. Screams from things that didn’t speak, just fed.
There were gurgles. Snaps. Wet, sucking gasps. Cracks like bone being chewed. A hiss, long and low, that slithered into the eardrums and coiled there like smoke.
Someone tried to shout a warning, but only a strangled rasp came out. A soldier whispered, “Gods…”
Something brushed Mira’s face. She screamed. Dorn drew his axe and swung blindly, hitting nothing. One of the younger Archers collapsed, sobbing, hands over his ears. Halden chanted prayers, faster and faster, the words blurring.
Somewhere, something let out a bubbling howl that rose until it fractured into three distinct voices, all shrieking together. The screams would curdle fresh milk. It was nothing any of them had heard before. Aymir thought the scream in the inferno plate would sound like laughter beside these gut-wrenching shrieks.
And still the darkness held. Long enough that time stopped meaning anything. No one moved. The snow stopped falling. Even the wind forgot how to breathe. The battlefield was a sealed tomb of screams and slaughter.
Then…
A single sound.
Crack.
The sound of a goblet hitting a stone floor. Loud enough to sound like something breaking open the sky.
As fast as the darkness engulfed them, the darkness vanished.
Light returned. The moon shone. The snow returned, and most importantly, they all could see, but what was around them scared them more than the darkness.
Around them was nothing but death.
Joblins looked gnawed apart. Goblins lay folded like snapped traps. Orcs slumped where they stood, as if the life had been poured out of them.
Three human soldiers who had fallen during the battle were now visible. There were two more on the ground, barely breathing, blood painting the frost.
The rest stood silent. Frozen. At the center of it all, Luca knelt beside Lysana again.
The onyx shard was gone. Only black dust remained.
Taerel limped forward. Aymir followed. They stopped beside him, staring at the ruin.
“Luca,” Aymir whispered. “What… happened?”
No answer.
Taerel swallowed. “Luca.” One word. Nothing more.
Luca released her hand, looking to the heavens, and slowly rose. The wind tugged at his cloak. He turned, gaze empty.
Aymir stepped forward. “Luca.” He took another step closer. “Please. Say something.” Aymir tried to speak again, but the words collapsed in his throat. His voice, dry as dust, cracked.
“I did.”






Chapter Forty-One
The climb was cold, steep, and miserable, but Riven liked it that way. Misery, at least, was predictable. The wind screamed across the face of the mountain, pulling at his coat and whistling past his ears like some banshee laughing at the climb. Below them, Stormhaven lay in darkness, save for flickers of torchlight and the thin silhouettes of patrolling guards. The city was full of monsters and liars. Up here, the only lie was the next handhold.
Nyssa was already ahead of him, her body moving with the same sharp efficiency he remembered from years of near-death misadventures, her boots bit into the stone, her braid swinging like a metronome, unbothered by the cold.
He'd chased her like this for a decade.
“Tell me again why we don’t take the road like normal people?” she called back over her shoulder, breath fogging in the air.
“Because normal people aren’t trying to save a governor’s family from being butchered in the next sixteen hours,” he muttered. Then louder: “You said you wanted to beat the sunrise. I’m just giving you the chance.”
Nyssa snorted. “You always give me just enough rope to hang myself.”
“And you never take it. That’s the worst part.”
They crested the first rise, crawling up onto a narrow ledge. Riven leaned against the rock wall, flexing his fingers. They ached from the cold and the climb.
Nyssa was already scanning the city below, wind brushing strands of hair across her face. He watched her a moment longer than he meant to.
“You’ve been different,” he said.
She blinked. “What do you mean?”
“I mean you, you’re more focused. Is it the new crew? Is it Dain?” he asked with a slightly childish tone in his voice.
Her shoulders stiffened. “You’re not going to let that go, are you? What is your problem with him?”
Riven shrugged, still catching his breath. “Why would I? And nothing.”
She gave him a sideways look. “It was harmless flirting at first. We all do it. You do it.”
“Sure,” he said. “But now you actually like him. Admit it.”
She looked away.
Riven pressed on. “I knew it. I’ve watched you roll your eyes every time someone mentioned Dain back in Dunlow. You couldn’t stand him.”
“I didn’t know him then.”
“Exactly.”
She hesitated, then sat down beside him on the ledge. The wind pushed her coat against her frame. “He surprised me. He’s not what I thought. Not some pampered relic of a crumbling house. He listens. He fights smart. He’s good with Weslin.”
Riven nodded slowly. “He is. Doesn’t mean it doesn’t sting.”
She flinched. “Riv...”
“Just once,” Riven said, turning to face her, eyes sharp. “Just once, I want to know why it’s never me. Why is it always some brooding fool with a blade and a history he won't shut up about?”
Her jaw worked, but no words came.
He wasn’t done. “I’ve been falling for you since we were barely old enough to swing a dagger. Every stupid, dangerous year after that just made it worse.”
“I know,” she whispered.
“Then why not me?”
She looked up at him, eyes glassy with unshed tears. “Because I can’t lose you.”
That hit like a hammer.
“If we tried,” she said, voice tight, “and it broke... if it didn’t work... I wouldn’t just lose a lover. I’d lose the only constant I’ve ever had. You’re my anchor, Riven. You’re the part of me that doesn’t shake, no matter what hell we’re in.”
Riven stared at her.
She kept going. “All those other guys? They were warm bodies. Distractions. Even Dain. At first. But something’s changed. Not just with him. With this whole damn team. I didn’t know what to expect when we began this mission, but I enjoy being part of it. I like fighting for something bigger.”
She glanced at him, tentative. “Both Harmon and Dain talked about family. A new home, after. Maybe a life, a future, a real future of not stealing for my next meal. And for once, that didn’t sound awful.”
Riven exhaled slowly. The ache in his chest was worse than the one in his fingers.
“Dain’s not a bad man,” he said at last. “He fights like hell. Cares more than he lets on. But I don’t envy him. Not if he ends up with you.”
Her eyes flared. “Excuse me?”
“You’re a lot, Nyssa. All fire and knives and secrets. You tear through people like they’re cobwebs. You don’t mean to, but you do.”
“I never wanted to hurt anyone.”
“I know. That’s the problem. You hurt people without even realizing it. I can't blame you for it.” Riven paused, held her gaze. “I think he'd be good for you. If you let him.” 
“That almost sounds like approval.”
“No,” Riven said. “But I don’t disapprove either. And if he’s serious, really serious, then maybe for once, you should give him a chance. I mean a real chance. Let yourself be happy.”
She looked down at her hands, eyes glassy but dry. “And what about you?”
“I’ll survive,” he said. “Always have.”
She was quiet for a long time.
Then she said, “Do you hate me?”
He barked a bitter laugh. “I could never. Even when I should. Even when it hurts. Gods, Nyssa, I want to hate you sometimes, just so it’d be easier.”
Her hand found his. Cold fingers laced together.
“I do love you, Riven,” she said. “Maybe not the way you want. But I do. And maybe one day I’ll be brave enough to risk it. But until then, I need you. I need us.”
He looked down at their hands. Then out over the ledge.
“Then don’t run,” he said. “Not from me. Not from him. Not from yourself.”
She gave him a look. “You trying to be wise now?”
“Trying,” he said, “but wisdom keeps dodging.”
They both laughed.
Then Nyssa said, “Remember when we stole that baron’s carriage and sold it for gambling chips in Ashvale?” 
“You mean the one with the stuffed bear head inside?”
“Still creeps me out.”
“I still have the poker set.”
They sat together for a while longer, the wind carrying the silence between them.
Then Riven stood. “Come on. We’ve got a statue to rob.”
Nyssa stood too, brushing frost from her legs. “With traps. And a possible ambush.”
“Wouldn’t be us if it wasn’t.”
And side by side, they climbed into the night.
The climb leveled out into a narrow plateau nestled among the trees after a while. Snow dusted the ground in a soft layer. The world was so quiet it felt like they were the only two souls in it. Pines swayed gently above, and in the clearing stood the statue.
She wasn’t grand, not in the way kings built statues to themselves. No crown, no pedestal etched in gold. Just a woman in weathered armor, hands on a broadsword, the edges of her face softened by time and frost.
“Lady Veyra,” Riven muttered, breathing hard from the climb. “Builder of the old bastion. First architect of the northern defenses. Died before the city was ever finished. They say she mapped every stone of this mountain in her head before she laid the first brick.”
Nyssa blinked snow from her lashes. “Romantic.”
“She was the only one who ever built something here that lasted. Until now.”
They walked toward it slowly, their boots crunching over frozen soil. Riven crouched at the base first, brushing snow away from the hidden latch.
Only it wasn't hidden anymore.
The small recessed compartment beneath the statue's base had been forced open, splintered at the seams. A broken hinge hung loose. Bits of brass and steel lay in the snow like shattered teeth.
Nyssa crouched beside him. “Someone beat us to it.”
“Looks fresh. Within the day, maybe.”
She looked around, instantly alert. But the forest was still. No tracks, no waiting blades. Whoever had come and gone hadn’t stayed.
Riven sighed and leaned back on his heels. “So much for easy.”
“Since when have we done easy?”
“Easy would’ve been suspicious anyway.”
She offered him a hand and pulled him to his feet. They stood there for a beat, silence spinning between them again. They scanned the area.
Nyssa broke it first. “We should look around to see if we can find where they went.”
“Agreed.”
“Riven, we haven’t had the time to talk like we normally do. I am sorry for that.”
“I understand, we have been in a go-go-go pace. Don’t apologize. We’ve barely had room to breathe,” replied Riven.
“Details, details. Never let them get in the way before, why start now?” Nyssa paused as something cleared in her mind. “I have something I want to ask you. I haven’t really stopped thinking about it since you said it.”
“Get it out, doesn't need such a build-up,” Riven said. 
“Fine. Back when we were climbing, you said something back there... about me giving this a real chance. What did you mean?”
Riven nodded. “I did. And I mean you should give him a real chance, and I meant it. If this situation with Dain is different, as you said, then treat it accordingly. Don’t use the same excuses. Don’t keep one foot out the door while pretending you’re ready to open it.”
Nyssa folded her arms. Her gaze drifted past him, out over the edge of the ridge to the city below, lights flickering beneath a veil of early snow.
“I didn’t even know him,” she said. “Not really. Before this mission, that is. Just stories. Rumors about the loud-mouthed noble with a sword bigger than his sense of subtlety. We were always up for the same contracts. He stole two of mine without even realizing it. So I made sure to even the score.”
Riven smiled faintly. “Naturally.”
“Then we both answered Harmon’s call. And I met him for real. Not the job-stealer. Not the myth. Just this... weird, brash, grieving bastard who acts like he has all the answers.”
She shrugged. “I hated him all over again.” Riven laughed.
She kept going. “But I kept watching. And underneath the bluster, the cocky grin, the 'I-always-have-a-plan' routine... he was just this guy. Hurting. Lost. The worst part is that he is unsure of himself and uses anger as a means to mask his insecurities. Sounds like anyone you know? Like when you and I split. I saw myself in him. Or who I used to be.”
Riven tilted his head, voice softer now. “Mask his insecurities? Those are some big concepts coming from you.” A beat. “Maybe he deserves better than being your next distraction.”
She looked at him sharply. But not angry. “Maybe we both deserve better than the messes we used to choose.”
Riven exhaled slowly. His breath fogged the air between them.
“If you think it’s real,” he said, “then give it a real shot. Don’t treat him like the others. We know how it ends when you do. One of you leaves first, the other pretends they weren’t surprised.”
Nyssa winced. “You make it sound so simple.”
“It’s not. But it is a choice.”
She was quiet for a moment.
“What about you?” she asked. “What’s next for Riven, master of the backup plan?”
He grinned, “Hmm… A warm bed. Decent food. A city where I'm just some man with a pint and no history. Teach a few orphans the trade. Pretend I've never heard of a heist. Acting all respectable.”
She rolled her eyes. “Be serious.”
“I am. The next Mr. Hogan, remember him?”
“Yeah, that could work for you, but I know you are not serious. Maybe you should stay as well.”
He tilted his head, his smile fading a bit. “Maybe I can find a place like Dain wants to build. Quiet. Honest work. If you stay, maybe I will stay too.”
Nyssa looked at him, eyes softening.
“You still mean that? After everything?”
Riven nodded. “Always did. But we will see.”
She walked over to him and hugged him. “You’re coming with me.”
He just shrugged.
They turned together, moving past the broken statue and toward the narrow path beyond it. Trees closed in overhead, the scent of pine and damp moss rich in the air. Their boots crunched softly on packed snow.
After a moment, Nyssa spoke again.
“Harmon ever say what happens after this?”
Riven shook his head. “But I think he knows this is more than a mission. For him, as well as the other. The fresh start is nice as well.”
Nyssa nodded. “Then let’s not waste it.”
Riven looked at her the way he always had when the words ran out. “Let’s not.”
“Well,” Nyssa muttered, still looking around for any sign of where the keys might have gone. “They’re definitely not here now.”
Riven walked up beside her, “So what do you think, someone on our trail, or did we just get outpaced by some unlucky bastard on a scav hunt?”
“Wouldn’t be the first time this city handed us a coincidence with a knife behind its back.”
He frowned, tapping the empty compartment. “This was done fast. Sloppy. Whoever took them didn’t care about hiding their tracks.”
“Or didn’t have time.”
“Or both,” he added, sitting back on his heels. “Still. We know where the map room is. Can’t exactly go back and tell Harmon we failed the mission because the keys were gone.”
Nyssa sighed, standing and stretching her arms overhead. “So what? You gonna pick the lock?”
“Not exactly. I’ve got something better,” he said, brushing his palms together. “But I’ll need my tool kit.”
She raised a brow. “We didn’t exactly bring a lot when we busted out of that prison. And unless you’ve been keeping a satchel in your teeth, I don’t remember you carrying anything.”
Riven smirked. “I’ve got a stash.”
Nyssa cocked a brow. “A stash?”
“Yeah. A little bolt-hole. Hideaway. Cache of goodies.”
“A ‘stashy-stash’?”
“Don’t mock the sacred.”
She smirked. “How come I don’t know about this?”
Riven shrugged. “We were apart for over a year. And a boy’s gotta eat.”
Nyssa rolled her eyes. “So you took some jobs.”
“A few.”
“Anything exciting?”
“You know the kind. Dangerous, poorly paid, morally questionable.”
“Ah. So your usual.”
He gave her a wink and dusted his gloves. “C’mon. It’s not far. We rappel down, hook around the cliff face. I’ll take you there.”
She blinked. “Wait. Your little secret hideout is right near this cliff?”
“Hey, you never know when you’ll need a quick exit.”
Nyssa chuckled as they unhooked the climbing rope. “This feels like old times.”
Riven grinned and clipped his harness. “Race you to the bottom?”
“You’re gonna regret that.”
They dropped over the edge in near-unison, rappelling face-first down the stone face like ghosts sprinting down a wall. The cold wind bit at their cheeks as they moved, boots kicking snow from narrow ledges, ropes humming with strain.
Riven touched down first, barely, and raised both arms in triumph. “Still got it.”
Nyssa landed beside him, unclipping with a huff. “You cheated.”
“Define cheating.”
“You started before me.”
“There are those details again.”
They moved quickly through the broken shale, around the narrow cliff base where the snow drifted thick and undisturbed. Riven crouched behind a moss-covered outcrop and felt for a flat stone.
Nyssa tilted her head. “Don’t tell me this is another one of your trick walls.”
Riven didn’t reply. He twisted the stone hard, and the rock groaned inward. A gap opened beneath the brush, revealing a dark crevice that descended into the stone.
Nyssa peered in. “How long has this been here?”
“Three years. Maybe four. Found it on a job running messages through the old tunnel routes.”
She followed him inside, ducking under low arches of stone until they emerged into a chamber carved from the natural rock. It wasn’t large, maybe the size of a small cottage, but it was dry and layered with soft sand and old furs. A lantern hung from an iron hook on the wall, still functional, still full.
Nyssa lifted it and lit it with a match. Warm light filled the room.
The space wasn’t luxurious, but it was homey in a haphazard way. Two battered lockers stood against the far wall, both sealed with old Dwarven latches. A cot. A dented kettle. A pile of black and gray gear neatly folded beside a small field desk.
“Not bad,” she said, arms crossed. “A little less than impressive, though. Where’s the butler?”
Riven walked past her to the lockers. “He quit. Something about my charming personality.”
He popped one open. Inside: weapons, rolls of tools, and a black leather satchel lined with iron picks and magical thread.
Nyssa poked at the cot. “So you’ve been playing house while I’ve been doing actual jobs?”
“Someone had to live comfortably.”
“Comfortable? Riven, this place looks like a goblin’s pantry.”
He ignored her and grabbed a folded tunic from the bottom shelf, then the gloves, belt, and cloak. In minutes, he’d stripped out of his travel-stained garb and stepped out in sleek gray and black. The new gear hugged his form like a second skin, tight leather, reinforced shoulders, and a hood he pulled low.
He turned. “Well?”
She blinked. “Damn.”
“Told you I cleaned up,” Riven said. 
“You had this while we were walking around in rags?”
“No, only in the last two years. I still travel light. Rags work.”
She threw a glove at him. “You’re the worst.”
He caught it midair and tossed it back.
The teasing faded after a breath, replaced by quiet.
Nyssa sat on the cot, staring at the flame in the lantern. “You know, this team... It’s different. I didn’t expect to like them.”
Riven said nothing.
She looked up. “I figured they’d be another crew we’d forget by next season. But... Dain’s not who I thought. And Harmon... he’s like a war priest without the prayers. Ash’s hilarious. Weslin’s, well, he’s a kid, but he’s trying.”
Riven leaned against the stone arch, listening.
“I think,” she said, softer, “If this is something more, I might want to stay. If Harmon would have me. This team, I mean. Maybe we could find something that actually... lasts.”
She looked at him. “Not just you and me running the next scam or stealing from the next noble. A place. A life.”
His voice was low. “You really do want me to stay, too?”
“I don’t want to build a life without you in it. Look, I’m sorry for the hard sell,” she said suddenly.
Riven looked over, brows lifting. “Didn’t know you were selling.”
“Please.” She huffed. “That whole ‘maybe we stay after this job’ bit earlier on the mountain, then this little part? That was me playing at subtlety.”
“Subtle as a brick through glass.”
“I know.” Her smile didn’t quite reach her eyes. “Time’s catching up. Feels like the world’s moving on without me. And I’ll blink, and we’ll still be running, still surviving, nothing more.”
He nodded slowly, saying nothing.
She glanced at him, then looked away. “And I want you in it. Whatever comes next, I want you there. So... sorry for the pitch. I just…” She stopped, inhaled. “Harmon asked me to say something to you. I think he wants you to stay. He thought maybe you’d listen to me.”
Riven leaned against the stone wall, arms crossed. “You’re the only one I do listen to.”
“Then listen now,” she said, turning toward him. “I don’t know what happens when this mission’s done. But I want it to be something more than just another night we survive.”
Her voice lowered. “I’m tired of counting victories by the number of wounds we didn’t take.”
He studied her, quiet, unreadable.
Then finally, he said, “That’s not a hard sell, Nyss. That’s just you saying you’re ready.”
She gave him a tired smile. “Maybe I am.”
For a moment, nothing passed between them but the sound of the flame flickering.
Riven held the moment, then let it go. “All right.” He shook his head. “You still owe me seventy silver from Ironvale.” 
“I’ll put it on your tab,” Nyssa said. 
They smiled at each other, faint and genuine. “Then let’s go steal a map.”
They reemerged into the cold, locking the hideout behind them, and started the trek back toward the hidden entrance to the Sixth Tier.
Whatever waited in the vault beneath Stormhaven, it wasn’t guarded by just a broken lock.
And they were running out of time.
The city was a sleeping giant by the time Nyssa and Riven moved again.
Midnight had long passed, but the streets still twitched with life in narrow alleys and forgotten courtyards. Lamplight flickered on the fog-slick stone. A bottle broke in the distance, followed by a man’s slurred curse. The only people out this late were the desperate, the drunk, or the dangerous.
They stuck to the shadows.
Ducking low behind broken carts and slipping between awnings, they moved in silence, fluid, practiced. This was the kind of night they'd trained for. Cold air carried the scent of piss and rain-soaked ash. A cat hissed and vanished into a cellar door.
Riven tapped Nyssa's shoulder and nodded up ahead. A squat building hugged the base of a crumbled watchtower, more decorative than defensible now, one of the old city’s leftover bones. “That’s it.”
“A king’s vault without a king,” she murmured.
“Fitting, right?”
It didn’t look like much. A cracked dome, an ivy-choked lintel, and a faded sigil long since worn to memory. But this was the site, beneath it, the Builder’s Cache. A six-tiered archive, sealed and forgotten, where the original blueprints and fail-safes of the city had been buried under royal order.
And guarded.
Two figures paced the outer courtyard.
“Who are they?” Riven whispered. “They look like the same ones we saw back in the alley near the north gates.”
Nyssa crouched beside him. “Why here?”
“They’re looking for something. Maybe the same thing we are.”
“Two isn’t bad.” She loosened her daggers. “Want to see who’s rustier?”
Riven smirked. “Loser buys the next round.”
She nodded. “Hope you brought coin. I’m thirsty.”
They split.
Riven ghosted through the overgrown hedges, low to the ground, blade drawn. Nyssa moved to the left, dancing over loose bricks and crunching moss. The first merc heard something, turned, and caught a knee to the throat. Nyssa spun him around, jabbed her dagger into his side, then caught the falling crossbow before it hit the ground.
Riven went wide and fast, launching a stone past his target’s head. The man flinched, just long enough for Riven to close the distance and smash his elbow into the back of his skull. The merc crumpled.
Nyssa looked over, raising a brow.
“Still got it,” Riven mouthed.
They dragged the bodies into the vines, then circled toward the main door.
A handprint panel, old tech. Riven pressed his palm flat. Nothing.
“I thought you said you had something.”
“I said I might.”
Nyssa rolled her eyes. “You’re such a liar.”
He pulled a flat, rune-etched key from inside his boot. “Let’s call it flexible truth.”
The door groaned open. He looked at her with a big, toothy cheese-eating grin. She smirked, and they walked in together. 
Inside, the Builder’s Cache was a tomb of forgotten knowledge. Rows of stone shelves, built deep into the mountain’s edge, stretched into shadow. Dust coated everything. Lanterns sparked into life as they entered, reacting to movement.
“Looks like no one’s been here in decades,” Nyssa said.
“Except for the four armored assholes heading toward us,” Riven said, pointing at the advancing danger.
Two had already crossed the second tier, weapons raised. The others flanked low, moving with trained discipline. Crossbows first.
Riven ducked behind a stone lectern as a bolt cracked overhead.
Nyssa dove into a roll, kicking over a rusted support beam. It collapsed with a clang, drawing fire. She came up slicing, catching one merc’s leg and twisting him down into the stairwell.
Riven charged the flanker, trading steel. His blade scraped off the half-plate, but he feinted left, then swept the man’s legs and drove his dagger between the plates under the arm.
The last two regrouped.
“Trade?” Nyssa shouted.
“Switch!”
They crossed paths. Nyssa tackled the one coming at Riven, grappling with him between the shelves. She jammed his helmet sideways, blinded him, then cracked him over the head with a steel-capped scroll tube repeatedly until he stopped fighting.
Riven faked a stumble, baiting the final merc close, then yanked the merc forward by his collar and smashed his head into the railing.
Silence fell again.
Nyssa wiped blood from her lip. “Four beats two. You're buying.”
“We’ll call it a draw,” Riven said, breathing hard.
They moved quickly, checking corners. No more enemies.
Now came the real work.
They tore through drawers, map cases, and scroll racks. Dust choked the air, ancient vellum cracking under careful fingers. Riven found city plans, hundreds of them. Sewer systems, postern gates, maintenance tunnels, old codebooks, and ledgers.
It took time. The archive wasn’t organized by any clear system, just tiers and categories in an old script, some crumbling with age, others sealed in old iron boxes. They split up, calling out anything relevant. Lanterns flickered over their shoulders. A soft whir echoed as another torch came to life.
“There!” Nyssa pointed to a silver-sealed case tucked behind a false panel. They pried it open.
Blueprints. Diagrams of the tower. Not just the structure, but the protections. Wards. Locks. Triggers.
“Jackpot.”
Riven tucked the bundle into his bag. “Time to go.”
But as they exited the room, Nyssa froze.
“Five more. Coming fast.”
Five men wearing the same half plate flashed beneath the lanterns, crossbows leveled, footsteps hammering stone.
“We’ve got seconds,” Nyssa hissed, eyes cutting toward the corridor’s far end. “Options?”
Riven scanned the hall, no cover, no retreat. “No window. Just a one-way drop to the city’s bones.”
Nyssa grinned. “That’s why we're not taking the hall.”
She grabbed his arm and pulled hard left, toward a narrow recess in the wall half-hidden behind a stack of sealed crates. An old brass hinge barely glinted in the dim lanternlight.
Riven blinked. “Wait, is that—?”
“Builder supply shaft,” she said, already kicking the latch. “Used to drop gear down to the bottom level, below ground. We have done this before, remember?”
“I thought I was drunk that night.”
“You were. Still a good tip.”
The hatch groaned open, revealing a tight vertical chute just wide enough for one. Rusted rails lined the inside. Riven didn’t hesitate. He threw himself feet-first, boots skidding against the metal guide. The sharp scent of oil and mildew hit him halfway down.
Above, Nyssa grabbed the rope, flipped, and launched herself after him, headfirst. Wind whipped her cloak as she angled her descent, twisting at the last second to avoid colliding.
They dropped into darkness, boots slamming onto damp stone as they landed side by side in the old reliquary shaft, narrow, slick, and dripping with age.
This part of the secret archive was in worse condition than the rest of the place. 
Nyssa staggered upright first, shaking damp from her hands. “We’re not out yet.”
“Not even close.” Riven spun, listening. Above, muffled voices echoed down the shaft, angry, urgent. A crossbow bolt clattered off the stone lip and sparked beside them.
“Lovely. They’ve got angles.”
Nyssa snatched a lantern off the wall and shattered it on the floor behind them. The oil hissed across the stone. Riven lit it with a striker. Flames leapt up, snarling a wall between them and the shaft.
“Won’t stop them for long,” he said, turning.
“Doesn’t have to.”
They sprinted down the corridor, books and crates stacked haphazardly along the walls, ancient maps left to curl and rot. Water dripped from the ceiling in fat, steady drops. A heavy gate loomed ahead.
Riven cursed. “Storage lock. External.”
He dropped to one knee, pulled a blade from his belt, not for fighting, but for prying open the casing on the wall. “Keep an eye back,” he muttered, hands working fast. “This is a Builder lock. Needs a pattern pulse, but I can brute-force the timing pins.”
Nyssa took cover beside a stone column, eyes flicking between the fire behind and the hallway ahead. Shadows danced on the walls, in the firelight. Bootsteps pounded closer, sharp, angry, too many to count. The men were descending.
“I’d rather not get skewered while you do math.”
Riven didn’t look up. “Then buy me ten seconds.”
A bolt struck the archway overhead, shattering stone. Another zipped past her shoulder and pinged against metal. She ducked and threw one of her knives blind, heard a surprised grunt, then Riven’s voice: “Got it!”
The gate hissed open.
They ducked through and slammed it behind them. Riven jammed the locking bar into place and twisted until it groaned. The mechanism clicked shut.
Nyssa let out a breath. “Now what?”
Riven scanned the final chamber. It was small, no more than ten by twenty feet, lined with shelves of scrolls and dusty crates, and across from them: a stone wall slick with water and moss. He pressed his palm to the far corner.
“The runoff drains to the outer service trench,” he said. “There should be a fault seam.”
He shoved. Stone shifted, barely. Just enough to show a hairline crack.
“Help me.”
They both leaned into it, gritting teeth, groaning in effort. Metal buckled under their combined weight, and footsteps hammered the gate behind them. The seam gave way, opening a hidden vent barely wide enough for a person to crawl through.
“Builder engineering. Always a tight fit,” Riven muttered.
“Ladies first?” Nyssa asked with a grin, breath ragged.
“You’re taller.”
She slipped through, boots scraping metal. Riven followed, dragging the cover back into place behind them just as the sound of metal slamming against the last gate echoed down the corridor.
They crawled for a hundred feet through slime and pitch-black air thick with stone mold and dust. 
A grate gave way, and they tumbled out behind a drainage canal near the western barracks wall, hidden beneath the old smeltery that hadn’t burned coal in a decade.
They lay there a moment, chests heaving. The cold air had never tasted better.
Nyssa finally sat up. “Let’s not do that again.”
Riven grinned, bruised and grimed. “We made it.”
“Barely,” Nyssa said. 
“But we’ve got what we came for,” Riven said, while he patted the satchel beneath his cloak, the stolen blueprints wrapped in waxed cloth.
Footsteps echoed in the alley ahead. They both froze. But it was just a dog… emaciated, sniffing a pile of old bones, uninterested.
Riven stood. “Come on. Time to disappear.”






Chapter Forty-Two
