The first light of dawn had yet to crack the horizon. The sky hung low and bruised, shivering with mist as the team crouched together in a tight circle near the edge of a broken canal path, stone-lined and half-choked with weeds and shadow.
They hadn't dared return to the safehouse after splitting up. Too risky. Eyes were everywhere now, and the city was no longer asleep.
Their breath clouded in the chill. The only sound was the whisper of their gear shifting and the scrape of Harmon’s blade as he used its tip to draw in the dirt between them.
“We’ll be fast. Precise,” he said, not looking up. “In, out, no mistakes. You all know what’s at stake.”
Dain crouched on one knee beside him, brows drawn. “We have less than thirteen hours to get them out alive. We’re not waiting for sundown.”
Ash exhaled slowly, rotating one shoulder beneath his fire-scarred coat. “Not how I thought this job would go. But it's more fun this way. We hold our ground, and we don’t break. Never thought I’d be crashing a tower under blue skies.”
“Better sky than a funeral pyre,” Garr muttered.
Harmon finished the sketch. Three entrances. Two patrol rotations. Distances he'd already walked twice in his head. In the dirt, it looked small. He knew it wasn't. “The goal is to move before the city finishes waking up. Chaos favors speed. 
Reau shifted slightly behind the others. The movement was small, but the stillness around them made it loud.
“I'm not going with either team,” he said. No one moved. Even Ash, who moved constantly, stopped. Harmon looked up sharply. “What?” 
Reau stood straight, voice quiet but solid. “I need to retrieve my sword.”
Harmon pushed himself upright. “We’ve been over this. We don’t have time for….”
“It’s not a luxury,” Reau interrupted. “It’s a necessity.”
Ash tilted his head, eyeing the other man curiously.
Dain crossed his arms. “We don’t have time to start new missions, Reau. We’re barely going to make it as it is.”
“I understand that,” Reau said. “But if this city tips into open war, I’m dead weight without that blade. I can’t defend you. I can’t defend anyone.”
Ash tilted his head, eyes narrowing slightly. “You think it’s more than just steel?”
“I know it is.”
Harmon’s brow furrowed. “Even if you knew where it was, which you don’t, how would you get in?”
“I do know,” Riven said, stepping forward from the edge of the circle. “Merrick’s manor, east ridge of Ember Hill. Big stone estate with a slate-colored spire. I remember the dog statues at the gate. The inside's changed over the years, but the outside? Still the same.”
“How?” Nyssa asked.
Riven smirked faintly. “Thieving days. I used to run messages for someone who worked the manor.”
Harmon’s expression hardened. “That place is probably a fortress.”
“Most likely,” Reau agreed. “But if there’s even a chance my sword’s there, I have to take it. If everything starts unraveling, and it might, I need to be ready. That sword’s part of me. Without it, even if you take off this collar, I’ll still be crippled.”
Silence stretched again.
“We can’t split like that,” Harmon said. “We need every hand for the rescue—”
Riven raised a hand. “We’ll link back up. You’ll need a fallback point, right?”
Harmon hesitated only a heartbeat.
Riven dropped to one knee, cleared a patch of dirt next to Harmon’s, and began drawing a second layout. “Here. Blackcap Alley. The smuggler’s route I used years ago. It connects to the river path and two open-air grain silos, flat ground for wagons, and is enclosed enough for cover. You can get there with carts.”
“Speaking of,” Harmon said, glancing at Weslin. “You’ll need to buy those. Two carts. Doesn’t have to be pretty. Just fast, quiet, and big enough for wounded and supplies. Bring them to Blackcap Alley.”
Weslin paled but nodded once, already calculating routes and coin.
Dain looked around. “All right, so we’re splitting three ways now? Merrick’s house, the tower, and the wagon run.”
Garr grunted. “It's what's got to happen. We're past choosing and past waiting.”
Aurelia stepped forward, pressing her fingers gently to her temple. Her face was pale, drawn, the brightness behind her eyes dimmed to something quieter. “Let me try to link us again. If I can just….” She stopped. Winced. Tried again. A quiet grunt escaped her lips, and her shoulders sagged.
“It’s no good,” she whispered. “It feels like a smooth wall. Nothing to get a grip on. I can’t break through either. Something powerful is blocking it.”
Silence rippled again through the group.
Harmon’s jaw flexed. “No communication, then. All we have are verbal and hand signs. Stay visual when possible.”
“Anything else?” Harmon asked, scanning them.
He looked over. “Reau, Riven. You’re on the sword. No detours.”
Riven gave a lazy two-finger salute. “We’ll be ghosts.”
Reau tightened the wrappings around his collar, voice low. “We will go now, then.”
Riven gave Nyssa a wink. “Try not to bring the tower down until we’re done.”
Nyssa rolled her eyes. “Try not to die.”
Harmon began gesturing to his sketched map. “Here’s how we divide, Garr, Ash, Dain, Brother Aldrek, and Nyssa. You’ll breach the tower. Use the building layouts we pulled to slip in. Be sure to do a quick check to make sure no changes have been made, and improve the plan. Then improvise the rest. We’ll adjust on the ground.”
Ash rolled his shoulder and offered a toothy grin. “ So, the fallback is Blackcap Alley if everything goes to hell?”
“We meet at Blackcap Alley,” Harmon said. “No matter what.”
“And if we don’t make it?” Nyssa asked, her voice light but her eyes serious.
Harmon looked at her. Then at all of them.
“Then the rest of us finish the job anyway. I never said this would be easy or promised safety.”
A weight settled over the group. Not fear. Not yet. But gravity.
“This is the big one,” Dain said softly. “No do-overs. No backup. We pull them out today, or we fail.”
Brother Aldrek traced a slow circle over the hammer etched into the edge of his armor. “May the Light make a path.”
“And may we be fast enough to follow it,” Aurelia added, eyes closed.
The group stood in near-silence. The air smelled of cold ash and rising bread from some unseen oven. A dog barked faintly in the distance.
Then Harmon clapped him hands once.
“Weslin, go get those carts and loop wide around Ember Hill. The rest of us move as soon as the streets are light enough to see our feet. That tower doesn’t wait.”
He gave them all a once-over. “You start this, you'd better finish it. Once we step out… we’ve kicked the beehive.”
Dain snorted. “More like a hornet’s nest.”
Ash cracked his knuckles. “Let’s burn the bastards down.”
The group split without a word, slipping into alleys and shadowed streets.
And somewhere in the city’s sleeping bones…
The streets near the upper ward stank of burnt oil and damp stone.
Even after more than a full day inside the city walls, the absence of life still gnawed at them. Not empty, just curated. People moved through the avenues like figures in a puppet show, too quiet, too rehearsed. Merchants wiped counters that didn’t need cleaning. Children walked in perfect lines. Lamplighters ignored cloaked strangers at odd hours.
It scraped the edges of normal. 
Riven tugged his hood lower. “Still wrong. Creeps me out.”
Reau said nothing, his eyes fixed forward, but his posture had changed, taut, flexed, ready. His fingers twitched near the small of his back, as if muscle memory was reaching for a sword that wasn’t there.
They passed a butcher hauling empty crates. He didn't look up. Didn't blink. Just turned the corner and vanished like a dropped coin.
A woman at an open window was combing her hair. The comb moved in exactly the same pass, exactly the same arc, again and again, like a clock mechanism. She was looking at something outside the window that wasn't there.
The silence behind them pressed in heavier than footfalls.
They reached the mouth of Merrick’s district and paused under a crooked overhang of old timber and rusted gutter teeth.
Across the street, the estate loomed.
It wasn't elegant. It was defensive. A hulking merchant's fortress dressed in failing nobility, tall stone walls, crooked spire, and mismatched balconies. Someone had added iron shutters to the second-floor windows at some point, thick ones, the kind that bolted from the inside. Not for weather. For people. Ivy crawled over the surfaces like old scars. A rust-colored banner sagged in still air. No guards were visible, but that somehow made it worse.
“That’s Merrick’s house?” Reau asked, incredulous.
Riven chuckled, low. “You expected marble? The man was gutter-born. Spends like he’s still afraid someone’s going to take it all back.”
Reau tilted his head. “I thought it would try harder to pretend.”
“Refined is for show. This is a barricade with better furniture.”
They waited. While looking around, casing the place, they found cover beneath an old wagon carcass, half-sunk in the overgrowth. Riven used the flat end of his dagger to sketch a rough layout in the dirt beside them.
“North wing’s guest quarters. The east wing is his study. The west side is the servant access. Stables are off the courtyard. If the sword’s displayed, as you believe, it’ll be in the study, not the vault.” He tapped the hilt against a crooked X. “Patrols hit this lane every ten. There’s a drainage grate back here, tucked behind overgrowth. Gets us into the cellar.”
Reau nodded. “And after that?”
“We improvise.”
He arched a brow. “So the plan is ‘no plan’?”
“The plan is simple,” Riven said. “Adapt fast, keep your head down, and don’t invite attention.”
Before Reau could answer, a soft click echoed from the alley behind them.
They froze.
A figure leaned against the brick arch, hooded, cloaked, angular. She stepped into view like she’d been waiting for applause.
“Thieves in daylight,” she said, eyes glinting under the cowl. “Bold.”
Riven’s hand went to his belt. Reau didn’t move.
She stepped forward, fluid and unhurried. Her cloak clasp bore a sigil they both recognized, red-and-black thorns.
“Relax,” she said. “If I were going to raise the alarm, I’d have done it before you played cartographer in the dirt. Been tracking you two, during your not-so-subtle casing of my house.”
“You live here?” Riven asked.
She shrugged. “Define ‘live.’”
“You always greet trespassers?” he said, smiling faintly.
“Only the interesting ones.”
He studied her face as she dropped the hood. Violet eyes. Scar along her inner forearm, just visible beneath her sleeve. She was young, but moved like she’d grown up watching every step.
“You don’t seem worried,” Reau said.
She tilted her head. “You’re not here to burn the place down. And you’re not stupid enough to be amateurs.”
“What makes you say that?” Riven asked.
“You’re scouting at the right time, not the busy time. You didn’t try the front gate. And you're carrying more silence than armor.” She smiled tightly. “That narrows it down.”
“You’re his daughter,” Riven said at last, snapping his fingers.
Her expression flattened. “Unfortunately.”
He leaned slightly toward Reau and murmured, “She’s no older than Weslin’s age.”
Keryn didn’t blink. “Who’s Weslin?”
“Doesn’t matter,” Reau said, just a touch too fast.
She watched him, but didn’t press. “You’re here for something.”
“A sword,” Reau said. Riven backhanded him hard on the shoulder.
She smiled faintly. “Tidebreaker’s his favorite. Curved grip, gold accents. He claims he won it from a southern warlord in a duel. It’s mounted in his study.”
Reau shook his head. “That’s not mine.”
Her eyes narrowed slightly, thinking. “Silver and black? Script along the blade?”
Reau nodded. “That’s it.”
She straightened. “He displayed that one, too. Said it meant the gods chose him again. Hung it about two weeks ago.”
“Two weeks ago?”
Her expression sharpened. “Exactly.”
“That’s when he took it and me,” Reau said.
She paused. “I’ll help you get it. But I want something.”
Riven folded his arms. “Let me guess. Family heirloom?”
“A dagger. Silver guard, red gem. It was my mother’s. He keeps it in his desk. Locked drawer.”
Riven raised a brow. “Sentimental?”
“Stolen.”
Reau’s voice was even. “We’ll get it.”
She nodded. “The study’s east wing, second floor. South-facing. The vault’s a trap—he keeps it for show. The real stuff’s displayed, where he can gloat.”
Riven stepped forward. “Why help us?”
She looked at him. “Because I want to see the cracks start. And because I think you might be the blade that makes him bleed.”
And just like that, she vanished. One step into the shadow, and gone.
Reau blinked. “She’s good.”
“She’s better than good,” Riven muttered. “Come on.”
The garden was silent. Damp ivy curled along the stone like green smoke. They found the grate easily enough, just as she’d said. It gave with a soft sigh and opened into the wine cellar. The air inside was thick with cork rot, ash, and the heavy hush of wealth.
They crept up the stairwell and into the manor proper.
“Smells like ink and money,” Riven whispered.
“Smells like lies varnished with perfume,” Reau muttered.
No guards.
They reached the study door in silence. Riven cracked it open and nodded.
Inside was a collector’s dream and a soldier’s insult. Trophies lined the walls. A curved blade sat on one plaque, and another, smaller frame held ribbons from a campaign Merrick had never fought in.
And there, centered in a glass case atop a pedestal of polished duskwood, Reau's sword. Stark, elegant, veined with silver and shadow. Real.
He stopped breathing for a second. Not from relief. From something older than that.
“There,” Reau said, voice rough.
“Let’s see if we can find a key for it,” Riven said, already moving to the desk. “And maybe one for that,” He nodded toward Reau’s collar. “But we can’t be here all day.”
Without another moment of hesitation, they got to work.
Riven casually stole things as he went, small coins, a cufflink, a seal stamp, and as his fingers brushed a dull, heavy medallion on a cracked leather cord, it vibrated faintly in his grip.
“That’s odd,” he muttered, and dropped it into his pouch without a second thought.
“Are you stealing everything?” Reau asked.
“It's a habit,” Riven said. He stopped, both hands lifted in a gesture of mock surrender. 
Then they found the bottom drawer, locked, no keyhole, etched with strange geometric carvings. “It's not a standard lock, more like a puzzle or pattern,” Reau said.
Riven smirked. “Figures.”
They worked at it together, fingers pressing indentations, rotating small plates hidden under a false lining until finally, with a muted click, it opened. Inside, they found a dagger. Silver hilt. Red gem at the pommel. Polished, sharp, intimate.
Riven took it carefully. “Got it.”
Beneath the dagger’s drawer sat a narrow shelf. Reau pulled it open, expecting more ledgers — instead, he froze.
A single book lay inside. Ancient. Its leather warped and cracked, its binding stitched by hand rather than by press. The ink on its spine had faded into nothing.
He lifted it carefully. The pages were filled with dense, slanted handwriting, a style he hadn't seen since he was a boy. His breath caught. His father had kept books like this, not many, just two, locked in his private study. He remembered the smell of them, old parchment and something sharper underneath, like struck flint. He remembered tracing the symbols in the air when no one was watching, and the sound of his father's boots on the floor as the study door shut hard. Reau blinked, the memory dissolving.
“This isn’t Merrick’s,” he muttered.
Riven glanced over. “Then whose?”
Reau didn’t answer. He slid the book into his cloak. “Later.”
In the next drawer, buried beneath old ledgers, they found a folded map. Locations marked in red ink. The heading read: Artifact Dig Sites.
“Looks like Merrick’s digging where others are digging too,” Reau murmured.
Another paper slipped free, different handwriting, darker ink, thinner parchment. Only one word: Irothis.
Riven frowned, but didn’t speak this time. Something about the ink felt wrong. Old. Heavy.
A chill rippled through him, sharp as a pinched nerve.
He glanced around, suddenly aware of a wrongness, a feeling like they were being watched.
“What is it?” Reau asked.
“Just… odd sensation is all,” Riven muttered, tucking the page into his coat.
They turned back to the case.
“No latch. No runes. No lock,” Riven said. “You ready?”
Reau nodded.
He drove his elbow into the glass.
A pulse of magic exploded outward, silent but heavy, throwing them both against the bookshelves. Blue light crackled through the room like distant lightning.
“Alarm,” Reau coughed.
Riven shot him a look. “Brilliant deduction.”
Reau seized the sword, sheathing it smoothly.
They ran, boots thudding over rugs and polished wood, weaving between bookshelves and trophy cases as guards converged from opposite halls.
And just as they were about to be cornered, Keryn’s voice cut from the far corner. “Knew you’d trip something.” She stood half-shadowed beside a marble bust, one hand pressing an iron switch embedded in the paneling. “Through here!” she barked.
A concealed door ground open. They dove inside as bolts shattered against the stone behind them. “This way, he keeps a private exit,” Keryn said, running now, cloak sweeping the narrow tunnel’s walls.
They followed, breath loud in their ears, sweat sharp on their skin. Their nerves buzzed, every step too loud in the narrow dark.
The passage angled steeply down, cool air rising from cracks in the stone. The distant roar of the river below guided their path.
Finally, the tunnel ended in a narrow archway covered by thick ivy.
“Cuts under the wall,” Keryn said, pulling the vines aside. “You’ll come out near the riverbank.”
Riven handed her the dagger.
Her fingers closed around it, and her mouth twitched, almost a smile.
“Thank you,” she said softly.
Reau met her gaze. “You'll be alright?”
She laughed quietly. “I've been alright for a long time.” She paused, just for a moment, her fingers still closed around the dagger. “Just go finish what you started.”
And then she stepped backward into the shadow, disappearing again, gone as quickly as she came.
Riven looked at the space where she'd been. “She's going to be trouble,” he said quietly. He didn't sound displeased.
They didn’t stop moving until the manor was far behind them, until Merrick’s house was swallowed by silence and night air and the sound of their breathing.
Reau kept his sword tight against his spine.
Riven went through what he'd stolen. Nothing stood out. Until the medallion, still vibrating against his palm, steady and faint, like something breathing. He held it. He didn't know why. Not yet. 
The tunnel spat them out near a bend in the river where snow fell in slow, lazy flakes. The air carried that damp, raw cold that seeped into joints and sat there. The world felt muffled, footsteps quieter, voices distant, as if the city itself had retreated under a blanket of frost.
Riven pulled his collar up higher as they made their way along narrow alleys toward Blackcap Alley, boots crunching lightly on snow-dusted stone. Even midday felt like twilight beneath the low gray clouds, and everything smelled of damp stone and distant woodsmoke.
There was no change to the people playing their parts, and with these new conditions, it was getting harder to tell who was truly controlled and who was just pretending to survive.
At the mouth of Blackcap Alley, they finally saw him.
Weslin sat atop one of two carts, reins bundled in gloved hands, cloak too large around narrow shoulders. The horses, their horses, eleven in all, stood tethered and restless, nostrils puffing mist into the cold air. Four were already hitched to the two wagons, the others tied nearby.
The boy’s face was pale, drawn, but his eyes widened as soon as he spotted them.
“I thought you weren’t coming,” he called, voice cutting through the quiet.
“That’s because we nearly weren’t,” Riven replied with a crooked grin.
Reau was already checking tack and straps, fingers moving expertly even as he scanned the alley’s entrance. “You did well,” he said. “Horses look good.”
Weslin gave a quick, proud nod, though his fingers twitched nervously on the reins.
“Can’t be here all day,” Reau added, eyes still sweeping the street.
Riven climbed into the back of the nearest cart, settling among a stack of folded blankets and burlap sacks. “Feels like half the city’s watching without watching.”
Weslin gave a thin smile but said nothing.
Riven tilted his head toward Reau, who was staring off in the distance, back from where they came. Worry was written on his face. “You thinking about that dagger?”
Reau rested an elbow on the rail, exhaling slowly. “Something in it felt… wrong. Not the metal. Something deeper.”
Riven nodded. “You think it was a mistake, leaving it with her?”
Reau’s lips pressed into a thin line. “I don’t know. Maybe. Maybe it’s worse in her hands.”
“Could be,” Riven agreed. “But… problem for another day?”
Reau’s gaze lingered down the alley and nodded. “Another day.”
A merchant passed at the far end, an old man, gray-bearded, wrapped in a heavy wool coat, leading a small pony-drawn cart of his own. As he passed, he muttered loud enough for them to hear:
“They’re watching us all… every breath, every step… I keep my head down, but it doesn’t help… none of it helps…”
Then, as if realizing he’d spoken aloud, he straightened abruptly and whistled tunelessly, guiding his cart forward, his steps too rigid.
Riven watched him go, a chill that had nothing to do with the weather running down his spine.
Weslin cleared his throat, shifting in the seat. “We're waiting here then?”
“Yeah,” Reau said. “No one moves until the rest return. That’s the plan.”
The snow continued to drift. Horses stamped occasionally, steam curling from their nostrils. A long moment stretched in silence before Riven broke it, leaning forward on the cart rail.
“You ever play Havern Ball, Weslin?”
Weslin blinked, startled. “Havern Ball?”
“I did. A street league back in Ashgate,” Riven said, grin returning. “Leather ball, two net poles at each end, no hands allowed. And that midfield stone, if you bounced it right and scored within five seconds, it counted double.”
Weslin snorted faintly. “I’ve seen it. Looks ridiculous.”
“Sounds brilliant,” Reau countered, folding his arms. “And brutal.”
“Brutal’s the point,” Riven said. “You didn’t grow up playing?”
Weslin shook his head, relaxing just a little. “No… I watched once. Some older boys tried to rope me in. Looked like they were all out for blood.”
“Exactly. It teaches you how to get hit without losing your teeth,” Riven said.
Reau arched a brow. “I played once. Lost a tooth. Worth it.”
“I bet you were terrible,” Riven teased.
Reau smirked faintly. “Not as terrible as it sounds.”
Weslin grinned despite himself. “If you two played now, I’d put my silver on Reau.”
“Betrayal!” Riven declared, throwing up his hands. “The boy’s picking favorites already.”
The banter was light, but the tension never truly left their shoulders. Every clatter of hooves beyond the alley’s mouth made them glance up. Every voice made them shift their weight and turn heads.
Then Riven stood suddenly, dusting snow from his sleeves. His expression changed, less playful, more focused.
“I’m going,” he said.
Reau frowned. “Where?”
“To find the others. See if they need help.”
“That’s not the plan,” Reau said flatly.
Riven shrugged. “I know. But I have a feeling I’m going to be needed.”
Reau moved as if to rise, too, but Riven shot him a look. “Stay. Someone needs to keep an eye on Weslin and these horses.”
Weslin straightened then, clearing his throat. “Actually… Harmon left me orders. After an hour of you two returning, I’m going to meet him at the old safehouse. Help recover anything left behind.”
Both men blinked. “Well,” Riven said slowly, “Damn.”
Reau sighed. “That sounds like Harmon.”
Weslin was already gathering his cloak more tightly around himself. “I’ll wait until the hour’s up… then I’m gone.”
Riven clapped him gently on the shoulder as he stepped down from the cart. “Good man.”
Riven adjusted his collar and started for the alley's mouth. He got four paces before he stopped, tilting his head, the way he did when something he couldn't name told him to wait. 
Reau settled back onto the cart’s bench, eyes still scanning, but his fingers brushed the hilt of the sword at his back, as if reassuring himself it was still there.
And Weslin sat tall, determined but pale, as the snow drifted softly over their quiet waiting place, and the market beyond continued its too-perfect hum.
The snow kept falling, soft and steady, cloaking the sound of hooves and voices alike. The cold crept into seams and cuffs, threading itself through wool and leather.
Reau sat quietly on the cart’s bench, eyes ever-watchful, while Weslin adjusted a strap, fingers stiff with cold but determined. They’d settled into a waiting stillness, but Riven’s gaze kept drifting.
Something felt off, more off than usual.
He shifted in place, leaning forward on one knee. Then he caught a flicker of movement high above the opposite rooftop. A figure, too far to make out clearly, was moving slowly along the edge. Not rushing, not hiding. Just… there.
“Someone’s up there,” Riven murmured, nodding his chin toward the slanted rooftop beyond the far stall rows. “Look. No cloak. Moving smoothly. Not even pretending to care.”
Neither Weslin nor Reau answered right away.
Riven frowned and kept watching, squinting as the figure stepped gingerly along the icy edge, pausing now and then as though surveying something unseen.
Then Reau’s fingers gripped Riven’s shoulder, hard.
“Riven…” Reau’s voice was low, urgent. “Look down.”
Weslin was already standing beside the cart, face pale, eyes wide. His breath smoked sharply in the cold.
Riven reluctantly dragged his gaze away from the rooftop.
And froze.
The marketplace had gone completely still.
Vendors, pedestrians, workers, stable-hands, every last person. All perfectly still. All perfectly silent.
Every single one of them had turned to face the cart. Their faces were slack, but their eyes were sharp, bright with unnatural clarity. And then one of them, a man in a vendor's apron, his hands still resting on an empty crate, tilted his head just slightly, as if listening to something Riven couldn't hear.
Weslin's hands had gone white on the reins.
Riven felt his stomach drop. All staring directly at them. No sound. No motion.
The only thing that moved was the falling snow.






Chapter Forty-Three
The snow kept falling, thin and constant now, a cold veil draped over Stormhaven’s streets as midday deepened toward afternoon. It collected in the cracks between stones, softened the edges of rooftops, and muted even the sound of boots moving fast and quietly through slush.
This was Garr’s team. Not a squad. Not a formation. Just a collection of professionals used to working without needing to fill the silence with chatter. After the last span of days that passed, he wouldn’t want anyone else for this job. This was the strike team, the sharp edge of Harmon’s operation.
Garr led, sword sheathed, one hand resting near the hilt but fingers loose. He didn't need it yet, and until he did, it was dead weight. Dain moved close to him, loose-limbed in the cold, head shifting constantly to catch every alley corner and shopfront shadow. Nyssa ghosted one pace off Garr's left shoulder, eyes cataloging cover and approach angles like a second instinct. Behind them, Ash kept his pace even and quiet, a faint tension in his hands that never quite turned into fire, and Aldrek moved broad and slow beside him, mace at his hip, measuring every narrow choke point. Neavin and Aurelia held the rear as they always did, marked in both their minds as the last line if everything went wrong. 
Even now, Aurelia’s face was pale, her dark eyes distant, lips pressed thin. Whatever power she once carried felt… disconnected. Neavin kept close to her, his spirit sharp as ever, but worry was etched behind his eyes.
At last, they reached a cut in the alley, just shy of a small market square where carts sat half-abandoned, and snow was already swallowing the outlines of footprints.
And looming over it all, the Bastion of Steel.
It wasn’t a building, it was a message. Black stone, cold iron bands crossing its walls in jagged lines, murder holes high overhead that allowed no banners or beauty, no softness at all. This was a fortress first, a tower second.
Harmon caught up as they paused under a leaning stone wall, their breath steaming, their boots crunching softly in the deepening snow. He stood a long moment, taking in the sight, before turning to Garr.
“I’m not going with you,” he said quietly.
There was weight in that. No hesitation, just the hard acceptance of what needed to be done.
“I have to secure the withdrawal route,” Harmon continued. “Last time I stayed on mission like this…” He let that sentence hang for half a breath before Dain filled the space for him.
“Last time,” Dain said flatly, “you had to kill four men, and you nearly died yourself. We carried you unconscious for eighteen hours.” Dain’s words hit hard, but no one argued.
Harmon nodded slowly, that brief, tired smile cutting across his face again. “Exactly. I know the signs, I have learned.”
“Just be careful, that's all I am saying,” Dain said. 
Harmon simply said. “Thank you.”
He then turned to Neavin and Aurelia. “You two hold here. You’re the rear security. If this goes sideways, you’re our last eyes and last line.”
Neavin gave a short nod, already focusing inward. His falcon spirit, a sleek gray bird, circled tight over his head before perching on his gloved wrist, feathers flickering faintly as it waited.
Aurelia met Harmon’s gaze, her face pale but steady. She understood exactly what was being asked: they would not follow inside. They would stay, watch, and die if need be to hold the way clear.
Harmon clasped Garr’s shoulder, not needing to say more.
Then he stepped away, boots soft in the snow, disappearing into the narrowest gap between buildings with the quiet grace of a man who no longer needed words to say farewell.
For a moment, Garr just watched the gap in the wall. He'd been handed the sharp end of the knife, same as he always was. He was fine with that. “Eyes up,” he said. “Weapons ready, but not drawn until needed.” 
Nyssa gave a sharp nod. Dain smirked faintly but said nothing.
They approached the tower deliberately, using the broken line of market stalls for cover. The smell of damp wood and rust rose around them, but there was no sound except their boots crunching snow and the distant clatter of a loose shutter high above.
No matter what they already knew, Stormhaven itself still felt wrong. It wasn’t empty. People moved here and there, but beneath their steps, a stillness lingered, a strange, eerie hush that kept everything on edge.
The Bastion itself felt impenetrable. Its walls bore no obvious weakness. That was because the Bastion of Steel wasn’t simply a tower. It was a fortress compound, built for endurance and intimidation. An outer curtain wall surrounded it, rising nearly three stories high, reinforced with layered black stone and heavy iron bands. The wall had been designed to repel siege, every inch of its surface marked by craftsmanship meant for war, not beauty. Arrow slits pierced its face at perfect intervals, and walkways behind its crenellations gave defenders commanding fields of fire over every approach.
At the heart of the compound, the tower itself rose from the inner courtyard like a hammerhead spike driven into the sky, square-cut for much of its height, but narrowing slightly near the top where its open carousel sat like a watchful eye. Thirty-five floors climbed above the ground, and beneath it, the team knew from Harmon’s stolen plans that four full sub-basements were descending deep below street level, a labyrinthine depth carved into the bedrock of Stormhaven itself. Garr turned what he knew over in his mind. The plans had given them routes. Routes weren't the same as a way in. 
They took their time circling the tower. Each of them had their eyes scanning for cracks, some forgotten entrances. The diagrams retrieved gave them routes inside, nothing more. No hidden passages, no forgotten doors. 
Nyssa slipped forward to check a side passage, a drain channel too small for more than a child. She shook her head once. Garr tapped a finger on the nearest wall, iron-cold beneath his glove. There would be no easy way in. At the far western edge of the outer wall, Dain was looking around. He was with Nyssa. He then saw it. “Puzzle door ahead,” Dain said quietly, gesturing toward a heavy stone entrance recessed into the wall, its face covered in strange geometric patterns.
Nyssa was already moving and quickly crouched before a recessed iron panel almost invisible from even a few paces away. The dwarven lock was built flush into the stone, lacking a handle or visible keyhole, its surface etched with layered geometric patterns designed to conceal rather than invite. Its position was perfect: hidden beneath a shadowed buttress, partially obscured by weathering and snow, a detail most would overlook entirely.
This was not a door meant for attackers or visitors. It was an old supply entrance, a maintenance tunnel built by dwarven engineers long ago, a forgotten path Harmon had found only through recovered architectural plans. If solved, it would bypass the open courtyard entirely, leading directly into the lowest cellars, beneath guard posts and patrol routes.
Nyssa brushed her fingers over the cold iron face, eyes narrowing slightly as she traced one pattern after another. This wasn’t a brute-force puzzle; it was a craft puzzle, meant to test patience and precision, not strength. The grooves were tight, half-hidden under frost and grit, nested in a way that required memory and instinct both.
She brushed a gloved thumb over one groove. “Old dwarven work. This isn’t something we force; it’s something we solve. See here,” she said, pointing to a spot on the lock. “It is a Tri-key sequence. Partially stuck from rust, too.”
Dain knelt beside her, not crowding, watching her fingers move.
He leaned just slightly closer, voice pitched low. “Can you do this?”
Nyssa didn’t look at him right away. Her fingers continued tracing the cold metal, her mind working fast and focused.
Her reply came without emotion, steady as stone. “I believe I can. Just need to think and work.”
Dain nodded once. “Okay. I’ll give you time. I have your back while you work it.”
At that, Nyssa finally turned toward him. Her smile came broad, warm, and real.
Their eyes met for a beat longer than necessary.
“Thank you,” she said simply, and meant it.
Nothing else needed saying.
Ash paced nearby, fire at his fingertips but hidden still beneath a clenched fist.
Aldrek stood guard near the tower’s corner, watching the street. People were watching them now, casually, but too many. Heads turned when they passed, too coordinated, too quiet. Minutes slipped past.
Nyssa worked the latches, sweat already slick on her temple despite the cold. A soft click. One down. She exhaled slowly, shaking out her fingers.
Garr watched the exchange; he watched them all. And then, without a word, he gestured for Neavin to come over.
Neavin moved quickly to Garr's position. “What do you need?”
“Let's get a bird's eye view. Everything from the Tower to us. Approaches, the street we’re coming in on. I want to know what's moving before it reaches us. “
Neavin nodded, then closed his eyes, head tilting back as the falcon spirit surged upward in a burst of shadow and wind, wings flashing as it climbed fast into the frozen gray sky.
Neavin’s body stiffened slightly, one hand raised as if balancing an unseen weight. His eyes fluttered, but did not quite close. He was “gone” now, his sight turned upward, watching through the falcon’s sharp eyes as it swept across the tower’s flanks.
He didn’t speak for long seconds. His breathing slowed, barely perceptible in the freezing air, and then his voice came low and even.
“Patrols are on rotations. About five minutes out. Tight. Disciplined.”
He turned his head slightly, adjusting for the falcon’s perspective.
“No gaps. Guard stacks at every main entrance, quad-stacked at the south and east gates.”
Another pause, longer this time. “North face. Three Red Cloaks. One Adept. He’s scanning the streets, slow and methodical. He hasn’t made us yet… but he’s close.”
Garr gave a single nod. “What about near us?” he asked. 
Neavin’s falcon circled once more, high and tight.
“Coming back around, now,” Neavin paused, then panic covered his face. “We have two… No, make that three coming right at us now from the west.” 
His breath hitched faintly as it spiraled back down, landing silently on his wrist and vanishing into shadow as it returned. He blinked, rubbing his eyes as if returning from somewhere far away.
Nyssa kept working on the puzzle lock, her breath came steadier now, fingers sliding from groove to groove with almost unconscious precision. She was at work. The tension of their situation didn’t disappear, but her mind knew exactly what to do.
The rest of the team prepared for the unwelcome visitors. They stood ready, and they waited. Then waited some more, and just when they thought the danger might have passed them. Garr then spotted movement at the far end of the alley. Two figures. Red cloaks peeling off from their pattern, walking casually but angling toward their position.
They weren’t alarmed yet. They didn’t know what they were seeing. But soon, they would. 
Nyssa worked faster, her fingers finding tiny latches hidden in the grooves, her breath clouding in front of her face. Dain shifted subtly, sliding one foot behind the other, casual but prepared. Ash stepped just slightly to the side, adjusting his coat, one hand brushing over his belt but keeping the flame hidden. Garr angled himself toward the wall, half-shadowed. The first Red Cloak’s gaze swept toward their corner. Their gazes locked on Garr, then flicked quickly to the team as a whole.
They didn’t hesitate. The first shouted a warning, raising a curved sword high, and sprinted forward. The second followed, boots hammering stone, face tight with fury.
“Contact,” Garr snapped.
Before his eyes could narrow, Nyssa was already moving, smooth, precise, silent.
A knife drawn from beneath her cloak slipped under his ribs as she closed the distance fast, her free hand bracing the back of his neck to ease him down as he died without a sound.
Dain stepped smoothly into the second’s path, one hand rising in what almost looked like a greeting, but the other swept low, rapier flashing out in a tight arc, catching the man just beneath the sternum.
A wet choke, a gasp, and then nothing.
The third Red Cloak hesitated. Almost too late.
Ash was already beside him, a step from shadow, a palm landing flat against his chest, not fire, not yet, but a twist of balance, a brutal shove that sent him staggering sideways right into Aldrek’s waiting arm.
Aldrek’s gloved hand clamped around the back of his neck, wrenching, quick, and efficient.
The third man dropped.
Three bodies down. No alarm raised. No shouts. No blood spilled on stone beyond what they could cover.
Nyssa went back to working on the lock, her fingers moving faster now, heart hammering in her chest. Another click. Almost there.
The snow whispered against stone, falling steadily as it coated the narrow streets. Even now, midday light was dim and watery, caught behind thick clouds that pressed low over Stormhaven. The air smelled of wet iron and old smoke.
Garr watched the people moving through the district, a scene that should have seemed alive but felt anything but. Everything Garr looked at told the same wrong story. Bread for sale, yet it had gone completely moldy, still arranged with care. Merchants fussing over goods nobody browsed in days. Cleaners sweeping stone that was already clean. The show must go on, Garr thought grimly. It was all performance. The only thing that ever broke the pattern was the Red Cloaks and the guards, whose patrols cut the false calm like blades.
His eyes narrowed as he scanned the Bastion of Steel’s shadowed base. No cracks. No gaps. Every surface was hard and cold. He turned toward Aurelia, where she stood near Neavin, her face pale, her brow furrowed.
“Aurelia,” Garr said, keeping his voice low but firm. “Can you reach out? Quietly. Not just a count, I want to know what’s inside. How many Red Cloaks, guards… what we’re walking into.”
Aurelia hesitated only a moment before nodding. “I can try,” she murmured.
She lowered her head and closed her eyes, two fingers brushing her temple. Her breathing slowed. The snow settled gently on her hood and shoulders.
Nothing happened. Then it did. She seized, hands flying to her head, knees hitting stone hard enough to crack the silence, and the sound that came from her was sudden. She gasped, sharp and ragged, and then she screamed.
She choked, wrenching sound tore from her throat as her hands clawed at her head, shaking violently.
The team spun toward her instantly. Neavin’s eyes went wide as he stepped in, instinctively reaching for her shoulder.
Aurelia’s mouth worked, but no words formed, only desperate, broken fragments.
She babbled nonsense at first: “The veils... the old stones... shadows beneath the stars... blood of the First... cracks in the firmament...” words that had no meaning, but chilled the air around them.
Her fingers dug into her scalp, and her face twisted in agony. She let out a scream that would haunt the dead.
Dain moved to Garr’s side. “Garr, what do we do?”
Before Garr could answer, Aurelia’s body locked. Her back straightened unnaturally, her head tilting up as if jerked by an invisible cord.
And then it stopped. All the screaming vanished as if cut by a blade.
She rose smoothly, too smoothly, until she stood upright, arms limp at her sides, her face blank.
When she opened her eyes, they were different, pupils blown wide, irises pale and clouded. And when she spoke, her voice was guttural, ancient, with an accent that didn’t quite belong. The words came slowly. Like they had all the time in the world.
“I let you flies pretend long enough. I let you scurry and scheme. You believed yourselves clever. You believed yourselves free. You were neither. Every step that brought you here was a step I permitted.”
Her eyes were open, but she wasn't behind them. 
It continued. You were seen before you arrived. You were marked before you chose your path. And now… now it is time to stop. Step forward, and you do not merely trespass. You volunteer. You offer yourselves for His design. I serve the Great Lord to come, and in His sight, you are not warriors or saviors… You are insects. Chaff to be gathered, broken, and remade. Leave now… or join the chorus that sings only His name, forever.”
Her head tilted slightly, birdlike, eerie. A silence heavier than stone fell across the street. It was broken not by sound, but by stillness. Every single person in the district froze where they stood.
A merchant was setting his wares. A woman folding linen on a windowsill. The boy kicked snow along the curb. Every head turned toward Garr’s team in eerie unison, slow, synchronized, unnatural. Dozens of eyes locked onto them.
The puppet show had paused. But it was still watching. Aurelia’s body shuddered once, and the pain returned. She gasped and staggered backward, nearly collapsing into Neavin’s arms before she bolted, running a few paces down the alley, breath ragged, hands still clutching her temples.
Neavin’s falcon, perched nearby, let out a shrill cry, its wings flaring.
Then Neavin himself swayed, closing his eyes as his connection to the falcon faltered for a heartbeat, unbalancing him. He recovered quickly, but his eyes found Aurelia first, before anything else, before the tower, before the team. 
Ash’s voice broke the heavy silence first, sharp and tense. “We should leave. Now. We’ve seen enough. The whole damned city is watching.”
He glanced toward Garr. “This isn’t just a tower anymore. This is a trap.”
The only sound was Nyssa's fingers on the lock.
Even Nyssa’s fingers froze at the puzzle-lock as doubt bled into her expression.
Brother Aldrek stepped forward beside Dain, one hand resting lightly on Dain’s shoulder. His voice was low, almost gentle, but steady.
“I know how it looks,” Aldrek said. “I know the fear. But duty doesn’t wait for comfort.”
“Duty!?!” Ash said flatly. “I'm here for coin and mischief. Not duty. But I'm not stupid either, and that thing just told us it's been watching since before we arrived.” 
Aldrek's gaze swept the group. “We came here knowing this wouldn’t be easy, that it might cost us everything. And we come this far, only to walk away now?”
Dain nodded once, voice tight but clear. “If this were my family… I would want you to finish what you started. This isn’t about gold anymore. Or promises. There are innocent lives on the other side of that wall. Children’s lives. We volunteered for this, we finish it.”
Ash didn’t fold immediately. His jaw clenched, but he shook his head, voice sharp, coming from a place more of fear than defiance. “How do we even know what the hell that was?” he snapped. “That voice, maybe it’s just bait. A trap to pull us in.”
His breath came faster now, and his eyes darted to the civilians who still stood watching them, unmoving. “What if there’s something worse waiting inside? Something none of us are ready for?”
Somewhere behind them, one of the watching civilians took a slow step closer. Not running. Not threatening. Just closing the distance by one careful pace. 
Brother Aldrek stepped forward, and he placed a hand on Ash’s shoulder.  His voice came low and steady, but with a weight that came from a lifetime of service.
“I have stood before darker thresholds than this,” he said, meeting Ash’s gaze without hesitation. “Fear is no reason to turn back, not when there are lives that depend on us walking forward. Whatever waits inside, we face it. That’s what we should do. It is what is right.”
Ash hesitated, eyes flicking from Aldrek to Dain, then to Nyssa, who hadn’t stopped working at the lock despite the rising tension. Ash exhaled slowly, nodded once. “Alright,” he said, his voice low but resolved. “Alright.”
Nyssa finally spoke, her voice soft but resolute. “What about Aurelia?”
Neavin straightened fully now, nodding quickly. “I’ll stay with her. I’ll put the falcon on her. She won’t be lost.”
Garr’s nod came fast, without hesitation. “Good. Then you two hold here. Rear security.”
His gaze swept over Ash, Nyssa, Dain, and Aldrek.
“You four, forward. We finish what we came for.”
Garr’s voice was low but carried an authority that cut through the tension. He looked at each of them in turn, his breath misting in the cold air.
“We’re not just getting in, we’re going to have to get out. With no means to communicate. We will have no way to know what is happening outside this tower while we’re inside it… so anyone who goes through that door is responsible for finding the way back out.”
His gaze settled briefly on Nyssa as she worked the dwarven lock, then on Ash, Dain, and Aldrek.
“I need all of you thinking about the exit, every step of the way. If this is our path in, this might not be the path out. We are very likely to have to improvise the exit. “
He let the words settle. “Once we breach, we move as one. Quiet, careful. If we get separated… we don’t stop. We keep going. We keep pushing until we reach that family.” He met each of their eyes again. “No mistakes.”
Nyssa returned to the lock, chewing her lip. Her thoughts flicked like sparks: It’s all on you. The mission. The family. No pressure, right? 
Nyssa’s gloved fingers trembled, not from fear, but from the biting cold that was seeping deeper as she worked the dwarven puzzle lock. She could feel the pressure of the team behind her: waiting, watching, every second stretching longer than the one before.
Her breath clouded the metal face of the lock, a sheen of condensation leaving dark smudges where she leaned close. The grooves and nested slots were complex, more intricate than even she had anticipated, layers buried under layers, meant not just to guard but to frustrate.
She’d almost solved it twice already. Almost.
But the last catch eluded her.
Ash leaned close behind her, his breath tight. “What’s the hold-up?”
Nyssa didn’t answer immediately. She squinted, brushing a line of frost from the lowest groove. And then she saw it, not what she’d missed but how she’d misunderstood it.
A false groove, a decoy etched into the pattern, drawing the solver’s eye away from the true sequence.
She exhaled slowly, muttering to herself, “Crafty old bastards…”
Her fingers moved fast now, resetting the sequence carefully. This time it felt right, a subtle click as she twisted the final node into alignment.
The lock shifted under her palm with a muted thud.
A seam appeared.
A deep grinding noise rumbled from behind the wall, old gears turning, dust falling from stone.
The door eased inward.
Cold, stale air rushed out, thicker and damper than the street air, carrying the smell of deep earth, iron, and ancient stone.
Ash gave a sharp nod. “Finally.”
But Nyssa didn’t rise right away. Her eyes narrowed.
“Wait,” she said. “Something’s wrong.”
The team stepped closer and looked past her shoulder.
Inside was a narrow stone passage, but after only ten feet, it ended abruptly in a wall of collapsed stone and twisted metal supports. Damp earth spilled through the cracks. Blackened timbers jutted at odd angles, some scorched, the ceiling beyond long since given way. 
“Damn it,” Dain muttered, pulling back. “It’s dead.”
Nyssa pressed a hand to the edge of the opening, leaning in for a better look. “This should have gone under the courtyard straight to the cellars… but it’s gone. Fully collapsed.”
Ash swore under his breath, his face tight with frustration. For a moment, no one spoke. Aldrek crouched beside the entrance, peering into the rubble. He ran gloved fingers along one side, brushing aside dust. “This collapse isn’t new,” he said quietly. “Years old.” The realization sank in. The plans had been accurate at the time they were drawn. But this path had been cut off long before their mission.
Nyssa leaned back, breath sharp in her throat. “We’re back to square one,” she said. But then she stopped, fingers brushing an uneven line in the stone just inside the doorway, a small indentation worn smooth with age.” 
Something tucked into the alcove, a heavy iron key, looped through a corroded ring, hidden where no one would casually find it.
She pulled it free, holding it up.
“What’s this?” Ash asked, leaning forward.
“Old,” Nyssa said. “Dwarven make.”
Ash spoke first, voice tense. “Could be a backup. A key for something inside.”
Nyssa nodded. “It’s worth holding onto.”
Nyssa held up the ancient dwarven key, its weight reassuring in her hand, but something about the architecture felt incomplete. She stepped back, scanning the wall carefully.
She walked back in with a feeling that she had missed something. She began examining the walls with perception, running her eyes over every inch. Something near the base of the wall caught her eye. She crouched low again, running her gloved fingers along the wall just inside the ruined threshold. There, a faint seam in the stone, almost invisible, but precise.
“Aldrek,” she called quietly. “Look at this.”
Aldrek knelt beside her, breath misting. “There’s something behind this. Old stonework, almost ceremonial. But sealed.”
Nyssa tested the key in her hand. Its teeth didn’t match any visible keyhole until she angled it sideways and noticed a shallow socket hidden at the base of the seam.
She slid the key in, turned.
A soft metallic click sounded deep within the wall.
The seam split open, a narrow compartment sliding aside to reveal a recessed chamber no larger than a cabinet.
Inside lay another key, but this one shorter, thicker, clearly meant for a different lock.
And beside it, etched into the stone back panel, a dwarven sign:
“Where stone falls and steel rises, trust four hands to hold weight.”
Nyssa frowned, translating aloud for the others.
“What does it mean?” Dain asked, stepping forward.
Ash pointed toward the floor. “Look at this.”
A ring of faint, circular grooves radiated out from a section of stone at the center of the chamber floor, hidden by dust until now.
This wasn’t a dead-end.
Nyssa stepped back slowly, her gaze sweeping the chamber again. The rubble that blocked the tunnel wasn’t random, and this small room, this apparent dead end, felt far too deliberate.
Her eyes narrowed as she ran her palm along the nearest wall, fingers brushing over fine seams and subtle chisel marks almost lost to time.
“Here,” she whispered. “This space… It’s hiding something.”
As she pressed gently at a faint depression, the wall groaned inward, a section sliding aside with a low grind.
Beyond was a narrow chamber, no larger than a storage closet, and inside it: four squat stone columns arranged in a perfect square, each rising from the floor and disappearing into the ceiling. Carved dwarven runes spiraled down each column.
Above them, etched into the stone lintel, a single line in dwarven script. “When one stands alone, skill serves; when many stand together, trust prevails.” Ash read it and said nothing, which was unusual enough that Garr noticed. 
Aldrek stepped forward, eyes narrowing as he read. “It’s a counterweight system,” he said quietly. “Each column controls part of the locking mechanism for the door.”
Dain ran a hand along one column’s base. “They rotate,” he noted.
Nyssa tested another, feeling how it gave slightly under careful pressure. “But they’re interlinked,” she said. “When you adjust one, it changes the others… Look, watch this.”
She gave her column a careful turn, a soft metallic groan followed, but then one of the other columns shifted slightly back in response.
Ash grimaced. “So this is a balance puzzle.”
Aldrek nodded. “It’s meant to challenge a lone dwarf. One person could do this, but it would take patience and finesse.”
He ran a finger along the edge of a groove at the base of his column. “But with four? We can feel the adjustments together. Make it faster.”
Dain straightened, flicking a bit of dust from his coat. “Alright, let’s get moving, we’re burning daylight.”
He stepped forward first, brushing his fingers over the nearest column’s edge, feeling the grooves worn smooth by centuries. He tested a careful turn, just a fraction.
The column shifted beneath his hand, a low metallic groan echoing from deep within the walls. But as he moved, Ash’s column shifted in response, drifting just out of alignment.
Ash grunted. “That moved mine.”
Aldrek tested his own, adjusting carefully, feeling how it resisted at first and then yielded, but as he did, Dain’s column tipped the other way.
Nyssa drew back slightly. “They’re all connected.”
“Of course they are,” Dain muttered, crouching low to peer at the base of his column. “Trust the dwarves to turn a door into a test of patience.”
Ash shook his head, rolling his shoulders. “Alright. Let’s try again. Slowly.”
They worked together, coordinating their movements.
Nyssa guided first, adjusting her column gently.
Ash followed her lead, but too quickly this time. His column slipped, and a sharp metallic snap rang out. The mechanism reset with a loud clunk.
Ash swore under his breath, hands tightening into fists. “Damn it… Sorry.”
Aldrek placed a steadying hand on his shoulder. “It’s not about speed. Feel it. Let the stone tell you.”
Ash exhaled slowly. “Yeah. Okay.”
They began to move in smaller increments, each one calling out their adjustments.
“Quarter turn here,” Nyssa murmured.
“Hold,” Aldrek said, pausing to feel the counterweight shift.
“Little more on mine,” Dain added, turning carefully, his gloved hands precise.
Ash braced himself, easing his column deliberately.
But again, the mechanism resisted. Somewhere inside the wall, the weights pulled against each other. A metallic groan filled the chamber, but not the right kind.
Then, a jarring clack as it locked once more. They froze. A moment of shared frustration passed between them, cold sweat running down Nyssa’s temple despite the freezing air.
Ash raked a hand through his hair, muttering, “This thing’s rigged.”
Dain crouched again, this time pressing an ear against the stone near his column. “It’s not cursed, it’s built to break your patience.”
Aldrek allowed himself the faintest smile at that. “It’s dwarven work. It wants us to think together.”
They stood for a moment, hands off the columns, not speaking. The cold pressed in. Somewhere outside, boots passed on stone, unhurried. Then, without a word, they returned to their positions. 
This time, no one rushed. They felt for every shift, every vibration in the stone. Nyssa made the smallest adjustment yet, a whisper of movement.
Ash steadied himself, waiting for Nyssa’s next cue before adjusting in turn. Aldrek watched both of them carefully before applying pressure to his column, slow and even. Dain handled his with exquisite balance, moving fractionally to offset the others.
They began to breathe together now, falling into an unspoken rhythm. The columns moved, this time with a deeper, smoother groan, the sound more harmonious.
Nyssa glanced around. “We’re holding it… Keep going.”
Ash smiled tightly. “This feels better.”
Aldrek nodded slowly, face set with focus. Dain called out gently, “A hair more here… just a hair…”
And then... A deep thud reverberated through the stone floor. The columns locked into place. A hidden section of the floor beneath them shuddered. From somewhere deeper in the stone, Nyssa thought she heard a note, like a deep chime, resonating. As if the old dwarven hall had been waiting.
The wall rumbled beneath their feet. Dust cascaded down from seams overhead as a hidden section of stone slid aside, revealing a descending stairwell. Narrow. Dark. Cold.
Nothing came from below. No light. No sound. Just cold air pressing upward like a hand against the chest. Ash exhaled sharply. “Damn. That felt earned.”
Dain smiled faintly, wiping sweat from his brow despite the cold. “Let's hope it's not the first of many.”






Chapter Forty-Four
The stone stairwell descended into a darkness that felt older than the city above it. The chill deepened with every step, not just cold, but ancient. It bit through their cloaks and wrapped their spines in a pressure that didn’t feel like air. Damp stone underfoot, the sharp tang of rust and mildew in the air, and the steady drip of unseen water amplified the silence. The flames of their torches seemed too small for the weight of the dark around them.
They emerged into a broad chamber at the base of the stairs, a vaulted cellar, wide and cold. Empty racks leaned against the walls, their wood rotted and bowed. Barrels lay split and scattered, their contents long gone or reduced to black rot. Mold climbed the walls, and thin white roots snaked through cracks in the stone.
Nyssa’s eyes scanned every surface, sharp and deliberate. She crouched low near a dust-draped crate, fingers brushing a faint scuff across the floor. It wasn’t old; it was purposeful.
“Someone’s been here,” she murmured, her voice low.
Aldrek stepped to her side, crouching carefully, his gloved hand hovering over a half-filled bootprint. “Not careless either,” he added quietly. “And not long ago.”
Ash slowed behind them, closing his eyes briefly. His breath fogged. “It’s not just cold. It’s wrong.”
It was true, it was not just mildew and damp, there was a deeper cold, a hollow chill, as if something below the stone drained heat from the space itself.
Dain’s fingers brushed the hilt of his rapier as he scanned the rows of crumbling racks. “Quiet doesn’t feel right,” he muttered. “Like the walls are holding their breath.”
They advanced slowly, every step deliberate. The shuffle of boots on stone seemed louder here, more intrusive. And then, movement.
Two figures emerged from a side passage at the far end of the chamber. Red Cloaks. Not the hollow, mindless shells they’d feared, but disciplined, controlled, careful. Swords already half-drawn, eyes sharp and alert. Soldiers.
Aldrek didn’t hesitate. His hand shot up, a signal.
The team froze.
And then it broke all at once.
Ash moved first, fast, slashing across the nearer guard’s sword arm. Steel rang on steel, a bright spray of sparks in the gloom.
Dain surged forward, ducking low beneath the second guard’s swing. He caught the man’s wrist, twisted, and drove a shoulder into his chest, slamming him back into the damp stone wall.
Aldrek advanced with brutal efficiency. His mace swept low, catching the first guard behind the knee with a wet crack. The man buckled with a sharp gasp before Aldrek followed through, rising fast and driving the mace head into the man’s ribs. The sound was sickening, bone and flesh yielding all at once.
Nyssa struck with precision, darting in as the first guard dropped to one knee. Her dagger found the exposed throat, clean and final. The man collapsed soundlessly.
The second Red Cloak wasn’t done. He surged forward, blade high, teeth bared, but Dain was already moving, rapier sweeping across in a tight arc. The edge caught the guard’s temple with enough force to draw blood and stagger him.
Aldrek stepped in, mace raised high, and brought it down in a single, decisive blow.
The fight was over almost before it began.
Ash wiped his blade clean on the Red Cloak’s tunic, face tight, taking labored breaths. “They weren’t… empty,” he muttered.
“No,” Dain agreed quietly, glancing at the bodies. “But they were careful. Trained. Whoever’s running this place isn’t just relying on those mindless puppets.”
They gathered quickly, stripping the fallen Red Cloaks of anything useful, pouches, blades, keys, and left the bodies where they fell. Silence settled again, heavier than before, as if the cellar itself disapproved of the interruption.
At the far wall, Nyssa paused before an iron door set low in the stone. Its surface was rusted, the handle worn, but it was too obvious. A door like this, in a place like this, was a lie.
She knelt, studying the seams around the frame. No hinge, no lock to pick.
Aldrek stepped beside her, brushing at the stone near the base, and there, nearly hidden, was a small recessed lever.
“Decoy,” Nyssa murmured. “Figures.”
She pressed it slowly.
The iron door didn’t budge, but behind them, a section of wall groaned, stone sliding on stone. A hidden panel swung outward, revealing a narrow passage cut into the rock, almost invisible until now.
A grim smile crossed Ash’s face. “Always something with dwarves.”
They slipped through into the hidden passage, torchlight casting long, wavering shadows across the stone. Here, the air changed again: no longer simply cold and damp, but carrying a faint, unsettling hum.
Ash slowed, his fingers brushing one of the stone blocks. Thin metallic rods were embedded here and there, set flush with the surface. They hummed faintly, a vibration felt more than heard.
Ash rubbed his temple absently. “Headache,” he muttered, quieter this time. “Behind the eyes. Started when we came through.”
The others didn’t answer.
Dain felt it too, not the ache, but the discomfort of the architecture itself. The symmetry was wrong. Angles were slightly off. Proportions unsettling, lines curving where they should have been straight. His instincts as a fighter, honed on awareness of geometry and movement, screamed at him that this place was designed to confuse. They advanced carefully.
Ahead, a stone stairwell rose into darkness. They began the climb. Ash paused first, torch raised high. The same moss patch. The same faint crack in the stone. The same iron nail juts from the wall.
Nyssa frowned. “We’re doubling back.”
Dain’s eyes narrowed. “It’s looping. Damn clever.”
Aldrek rested a gloved hand on the nearest wall. “A dwarf wouldn’t waste stone without reason.”
Nyssa dragged a bloody finger across the wall, then swore softly as they circled again to find her mark already there.
Then she spotted it: a nearly invisible depression in the stone near the bend. A catch. A switch. She pressed it.
The stairwell shuddered softly. Another seam appeared, and a second, narrower stair opened alongside the first, hidden in the thickness of the wall itself.
Colder still. Narrower. Real.
Ash rubbed his temple again, blinking against a sudden wave of pressure behind his eyes. “It’s… heavier,” he muttered.
Dain touched his shoulder lightly as they climbed. “Next chamber,” he said. “We’ll take stock there.”
Ash nodded, silent now.
They climbed carefully, the darkness around them deepening, but so too did the sense of being watched.
The climb continued, every footstep measured, every breath felt, the air thicker now with something none of them could name.
The narrow stairwell leveled out into a long, low corridor. Stone walls pressed close, the ceilings just high enough for Aldrek to pass without stooping. The air was no longer simply cold; it had weight. A dampness clung to their cloaks, but there was something else: a faint hum, like iron vibrating somewhere deep behind the walls.
Ash winced and pressed his palm to his temple again. The sensation behind his eyes was sharper now, not a headache, not pain exactly, but a pressure, as though something unseen was curling into the edges of his thoughts. He didn’t say anything yet.
Nyssa slowed, her sharp gaze catching the floor’s subtle scuff marks, fresh, deliberate, but not careless. “Someone’s passed through here,” she whispered. “Recently.”
Aldrek studied the stone, running a gloved hand along the wall. His fingers brushed one of the thin metallic rods embedded at intervals, silent and inert but humming faintly if you touched them directly. “The stone is speaking, but not to us,” he murmured.
Their torches barely pushed the darkness aside now. Every shadow felt heavier, every echo sharper.
As they moved deeper into the passage, they passed the first one, a man in a butcher’s apron standing behind a cracked, empty workbench. He was sharpening a cleaver, back and forth, back and forth, the blade glinting in the dim torchlight. His eyes never moved. He didn’t look at them as they passed, but his face was slack, expressionless.
A few paces later, a child sat on the floor, mending a fishing net with delicate fingers that never faltered, never slowed.
No voices. No reaction. Just the eerie precision of lives hollowed out.
Ash’s hand drifted to the hilt of his blade as he walked by, heart thudding louder than the footfalls around him. The pressure behind his eyes pulsed in time with it.
Then Nyssa stopped suddenly, holding up a hand.
Ahead, the corridor branched into two perfect, mirror-image hallways. Both identical: same cracked tiles, same faint marks on the walls, same dim, flickering torch brackets, but one wasn’t real.
Dain frowned and crouched, tracing his fingers along the seam where the right-side corridor met the floor. “Hollow,” he said quietly.
Aldrek moved to the left-side passage, where a heavy dwarf-forged metal door stood half-shrouded in shadow. Its face was smooth, seamless, marked only by a relief of a forge hammer and an anvil.
“It has no hinges,” Nyssa whispered.
“No lock,” Aldrek added.
Ash’s headache sharpened again as he stared at the metallic rods set into the walls nearby. Something about their hum seemed stronger here, more insistent, like a breath brushing the inside of his mind. He grimaced and looked away quickly.
Nyssa stepped closer to the dwarf door, tracing her gloved fingertips around the anvil relief. A groove, almost invisible, circled it.
“This is no ordinary door,” she murmured. “It’s a puzzle.”
Dain nodded, his instincts sharp. “They built it to slow anyone who wasn’t invited.”
Ash muttered under his breath as he watched them work, “Dwarves do love their damn puzzles.”
Ash reached out but pulled back when he felt the hum of unseen energy prickling his fingers. “Careful,” he said softly.
Aldrek moved forward with Nyssa, crouching beside her.
“The forge and anvil mean something,” Aldrek murmured. “Strength and craft. Together.”
Nyssa braced her hands on the carved plate, feeling the faint give as it began to rotate, but it resisted in strange ways: uneven, as if weighted incorrectly on purpose.
“Help me,” she said.
Aldrek joined her, adding steady force, letting the stone tell him when to press and when to ease back.
They turned the plate clockwise. It caught. Locked.
Nyssa swore under her breath. “Reset.”
She took the second attempt, slower and more deliberate.
“Hold tension,” Aldrek whispered. “Feel the shift…”
They adjusted their grip. They shifted together, turning the mechanism bit by bit. Each moment of pressure mattered, too much, it resisted; too little, it froze.
Ash turned to watch the corridor behind them, his palm lit faintly with controlled flame. He went still. 
There, back in the gloom, another civilian, a woman this time, stood perfectly still, broom in hand, facing the team but making no move, her blank face illuminated faintly by the flickering torchlight.
She stared without seeing, yet the atmosphere tightened nonetheless. The hum behind the walls deepened. Dain shifted uncomfortably, casting another glance back. “Hurry…”
Nyssa nodded, sweat dripping down her temple despite the cold. She twisted carefully, felt the shift, and with a final breathless effort, a deep metallic thud echoed through the stone.
The heavy dwarf-forged door slid inward with a slow groan, revealing a stairwell beyond, steep and narrow, cut perfectly into the mountain itself.
They stepped through quickly, but the pressure didn’t lift.
Instead, as they climbed, it worsened: a slow tightening inside their heads, a heaviness behind the eyes that made thoughts feel sticky and slow.
The pressure had changed. It wasn't behind his eyes anymore. It was inside them. The pain was keeping him from speaking, in fear of making it worse. 
They passed another mindless civilian, an old man kneeling on the stairwell, polishing an iron pot over and over again with a rag that was already threadbare.
No one spoke.
The stairwell twisted tighter, darker. At the next landing, a single Red Cloak stepped into view. This one moved differently. No wasted motion, sword already drawn, eyes locked on theirs from the first step. And this time it was ready. 
The Red Cloak at the landing moved with precision, not hesitation, his blade already raised before Dain’s foot struck the stone. His gaze locked on them, sharp and alive.
Dain surged forward without waiting for an order. His rapier flashed in the torchlight, angled low to catch the Red Cloak’s weapon, twisting it wide, forcing the man back. But the guard was trained; he dropped his shoulder, recovered balance, and countered in a smooth, disciplined motion.
Aldrek stepped into the fight, mace held low. He didn’t hesitate either. His first swing was a feint, but the second landed, a brutal, arcing strike that caught the guard’s sword arm mid-swing. Bone cracked audibly, and the blade fell from the man’s fingers.
Before he could cry out, Ash was there, fast, vicious, striking a deep cut across the guard’s upper chest. Blood splattered the stone.
But even as he staggered, the guard didn’t give up; he lunged with his bare hands, face pale, eyes fierce.
Nyssa moved next, low and swift. Her knife found the side of his neck with a clean thrust. The Red Cloak finally collapsed, his last breath wet and ragged.
The fight was fast, brutal, and ugly. No one said anything afterwards. That was new. 
Ash wiped his blade clean on the dead man’s tunic and didn’t speak.
They advanced quickly into Basement level four.
Here, the air smelled different: dry rot, dust, cracked leather. The old furniture level.
Rows of decaying chairs and overturned tables lined the stone walls. The ceiling hung lower here, the arching supports carved with dwarven motifs but softened by years of neglect.
Chairs stacked atop tables. Cabinets missing their doors. Dust inches thick in some corners. No footprints. No sounds but their boots.
Nyssa led the search, darting down one aisle and back, eyes sharp for any hidden threat, but this place was dead.
The tension still tightened with every step.
Ash slowed near a sagging armchair, brushing one gloved hand over the faded upholstery. His fingers froze as the subtle vibration in the walls pulsed again, crawling into his skull like a whisper.
He winced and kept walking.
Aldrek fell back slightly, his eyes scanning the carved beams overhead. He muttered something, a quiet prayer for the dead, but it felt thin here, as though even the Light itself didn’t want to linger.
The team crossed the length of the floor in silence.
Nothing. No ambush. No guards. Just dust and decay.
At the far stairwell, they ascended quickly into Basement Level three, where everything changed again. The rooms here were active, crates stacked neatly along the walls, tools laid out on benches, every surface in use.
And people.
Mindless civilians moved with eerie precision: stacking crates, sorting rusted tools, sweeping floors that did not need sweeping.
Their faces were slack. Their eyes were empty. They worked in perfect silence.
A blacksmith at a cold forge lifted his hammer, let it fall, lifted it again, a hollow ritual, never striking true.
An old woman folded cloths and placed them neatly in a chest, then unfolded them and folded them again.
Ash watched them as they passed, his lips pressed into a tight line. 
Aldrek slowed again, falling behind the others for a breath, watching intently.
“This isn’t obedience,” he murmured, voice heavy with something deeper. “It’s judgment, penance, and punishment.”
Dain glanced back at him, brows drawn tight. “How do you mean?”
Aldrek’s gaze stayed on a man polishing a table endlessly. “Look at them. Each is doing some mundane task… but it isn’t work. It’s a sentence. Like a purgatory where their souls are trapped, and forced to repeat their most hated labor, forever, until debts they can never pay are forgiven.”
His voice was grim, steady. “This isn’t control, it’s condemnation.” Aldrek was quiet for a long moment after that, eyes still on the folding woman. Then he turned and walked. The team said nothing in reply.
They pressed on, wary of every movement but never interrupted. The civilians didn’t block their way, didn’t speak, didn’t seem to notice them at all.
Until one man, a dockworker judging by his clothes, rag in hand, lifted his head as they passed.
He didn’t speak, didn’t move. But he began to follow. Step for step. Slow. Silent. Inevitable.
No sign of the family here. They made the climb to basement level two. So did the dockworker, following close behind.
This floor, the walls pressed closer, the oppressive pressure heavier again.
The metallic rods embedded in the stone were more frequent now, their faint hum an almost constant background note. Ash rubbed his temple again, his breath tight in his chest. The pulse behind his eyes was worse, a low, insistent throb that made thoughts feel sluggish.
Nyssa kept leading, swift and precise. They moved fast, hugging shadows and avoiding every civilian’s blank gaze, skirting crates and benches.
Finally, at the far wall, a heavy door, which gave the hint of a prison.
The gate was exactly where the plans had said it would be, massive, dwarf-forged, barred, and guarded. Red Cloaks stood beyond it, weapons ready, watching the hallway carefully.
But they never needed to test that door.
As Nyssa approached, she caught the telltale signs of something hidden. There was dust undisturbed at the threshold, hinges frozen by age. This entrance hadn’t been used in years.
She signaled them around.
A narrow service archway lay partly hidden behind old crates, just wide enough for them to slip through. It was cramped on the other side. There was a lock on the inner hatch, brittle with rust, but Nyssa made quick work of it. They didn’t speak as they passed through.
Inside was dead silent.
The prison was empty. Not empty as in “recently cleared,” empty as in forgotten.
Dust-covered floors. Cells standing open, their doors rusted and crooked. Chains trailing from walls.
A few bowls were scattered across the stone, dry, empty, cold.
The warden’s office stood at the far end, its interior bare save for a single stone table.
At its center, they found a polished silver dinner plate, perfectly clean, resting atop a folded napkin.
Dain squatted down beside it. “Someone was here… not that long ago.” He examined the plate and found no dust and no disturbance around it either. It felt wrong.
“Perfect,” Nyssa muttered.
Dain let out a bitter, humorless laugh. “Of course.”
Ash grimaced. “Creepy as hell.”
Aldrek stepped forward, touching the plate, rocking it gently until it clinked faintly on the stone surface.
“No one’s been here for a long time,” he murmured.
“Then what about the plate?” asked Dain.
“No idea,” Aldrek said, shaking his head in disbelief.
Before they could debate it further, from the shadows of the office doorway, a figure appeared.
The man in dockworker’s clothes, the silent follower from the lower level, had somehow made it in after them.
He stood just beyond the threshold, his eyes vacant and glassy.
And then he screamed, a sound without words, raw and jagged and endless. The noise shattered the stillness, echoing through every stone corridor of the prison floor.
Ash swore aloud. “We’re blown.”
From beyond the main corridor, where the guarded door had been, came the clatter of boots on stone, armor shifting, weapons drawn.
Ash’s curse was still hanging in the air as Nyssa and Dain threw their weight against the heavy dwarven door, slamming it shut just as boots crashed into it from the far side. The iron rang like a cracked bell, hinges groaning as it held.
“Find something to bar it!” Dain snapped.
Aldrek swept through the nearest pile and came up with a rusted iron rod. Dain and Aldrek wedged it through the door brackets just as another thundering blow landed. The team fell into place, weapons ready. Breath harsh, nerves tight.
And still… silence inside the prison.
“Back through the tunnel!” Dain snapped.
But Nyssa was already sprinting toward the service archway. She reached it, skidded to a stop, and cursed.
The opening they’d come through was sealed now. A heavy, dwarven-grade siege door, smooth and cold, no visible lock, no handle, just a single round impression in the metal, pulsing with a faint, steady hum.
She pressed her palm to it and felt it vibrate. A low, harmonic thrum, almost familiar.
Nyssa’s eyes widened. “It’s the same pattern… Reau’s collar. It’s a vibration lock, and we don’t have a key.”
Ash joined her, shoulder to shoulder. “Can you bypass it?”
“Not from this side,” she muttered. “It’s not meant to open inward, most likely. That’s the point.”
She stepped back, heart hammering, mind already hunting for alternatives.
“They secured it from the inside. So no one could escape that way.”
“Which means we’re sealed in,” Dain said grimly.
Nyssa and Dain turned together, just as the heavy dwarven door behind them shook from the first pounding impact of armored boots.
They all looked around. “That screamer didn't walk through the door we came through,” Ash said. “So there's another way. Let's find it.” The others agreed.
Nyssa paused quickly and whispered, “That cell wasn’t open before…”
Her gaze fixed on an iron-barred door cracked open, dark inside. A second across the room, also ajar. Foul, musky air crept from both.
Something moved.
The stench grew worse: old blood, rot, iron, a wet animal smell that clung to their throats.
Then came the voice—low, guttural, heavy in their skulls, as if spoken through a vast loudspeaker but with no direction, no echo, just there inside them all at once:
