“Ahhh… finally you arrive. And yet so slow. So tired already… I wonder… will you even amuse me?”
Two creatures crawled out of the cells, horrors, crawling horrors.
Insectoid yet somehow humanoid, long-limbed and jointed wrong, torsos emaciated, faces pale and eyeless. Their mouths were jagged circles of needle teeth. Their limbs ended in claws sharp enough to gouge stone, dripping black ichor that hissed as it struck the floor.
The team froze for a heartbeat, and the voice laughed again, curling coldly inside their skulls:
“Ah… my hounds stir, little mortals. Their hunger is endless… and your fear will season their feast.”
The first creature lunged, faster than any Red Cloak they’d fought. Ash met it halfway, shouting as he drew flame into his palm. A searing arc of fire lashed outward, lighting the room orange, but the creature twisted aside, the flame merely scoring its chitin.
It crashed into him with a sickening crunch. Ash staggered, wind-driven from his lungs, the stink of it overwhelming, wet rot and bile.
The second creature moved faster than thought.
Its limbs didn’t walk, they spidered, long, jointless things pulling its body across the stone with unnatural precision. It reached the dockworker before anyone could react. One moment, he stood there, mouth still open from the scream, and the next, he was lifted into the air like a puppet yanked by invisible strings.
The man showed no fear. He didn’t even resist. His mind was already gone. He just kept screaming… until he didn’t.
The creature’s face split open, revealing not teeth but writhing tendrils, slick with something that steamed in the cold. They burrowed into his skull, through ears, nostrils, and eyes. He didn’t even flinch. He just shuddered once, violently, then froze. A flicker of light left his eyes as his body went limp, limbs twitching with one last spasm.
Then the creature dropped him, lifeless and boneless, like a discarded rag soaked in blood and bile. Nobody moved for half a second. Long enough to know they'd all seen it. Short enough that none of them could afford to think about it yet. 
Aldrek stepped to the one near Ash, his white robes flaring as he swung his mace with two hands. The iron head smashed into the creature’s flank with a meaty crack, but the beast didn’t fall. Its claw lashed out, raking across Aldrek’s thigh. Cloth and leather tore; blood flowed warm down his leg.
The priest grunted, pain flashing bright, but stood fast.
Dain circled right, rapier flashing. His blade darted in, piercing a soft gap between armor plates. Black ichor sprayed his sleeve, hot, sticky, foul.
But the second creature was already on Nyssa. She ducked low, feeling air split where its claws slashed, then stabbed upward with both daggers. Metal struck flesh, but shallow. The thing shrieked in fury, its jaws snapping close enough to tug at her hair.
“So exquisitely breakable… your flesh slows, your minds stumble. You were never meant to endure me.”
Ash recovered, flames licking up his arms. He thrust one palm outward, fire lancing from his fingers. This time, the flame caught the first creature full in the chest. It screeched, an unholy noise that split their ears, and fell back, smoke rising from cracked chitin.
But not dead. It lunged again.
Aldrek swung low, aiming for its legs. The mace collided with a knee joint, splintering it, and the creature staggered. Aldrek raised the weapon again, pain in his leg sharp but ignorable, his breath ragged.
Nyssa rolled beneath the second creature’s outstretched limbs, slicing at its underbelly. Her blade tore a long gash, black ichor gushing, sizzling on the stone. The stench was unbearable.
“Yes… bleed… not for death, but for revelation. Your suffering will peel your minds open… and I will feast on what spills out.”
The first creature darted sideways, unexpectedly fast despite its injury, and slammed into Dain, claws raking his armored shoulder. He fell back, breath driven from him, but kept his rapier up, deflecting a killing strike.
Ash’s flames flared again. Sweat poured down his face as he drew deep on his Adept strength, fingers trembling from strain. Fire shot forth, catching the creature’s side, curling flames around its limbs.
Aldrek followed immediately, mace smashing down into its back. Bone cracked loud enough to echo in the chamber.
The first creature finally collapsed, smoke rising from its twitching limbs.
But the second was still alive.
It darted toward Aldrek as he turned and slashed across his arm. The priest cried out, blood streaking his robe’s white sleeve.
“Ahh… your healer bleeds,” the voice crooned. “You will fall… all of you…”
Ash turned, fire ready, but Nyssa was faster.
She leapt atop the creature’s back, driving both daggers deep into its exposed neck joint. The thing screamed, a noise that made the air feel thin, and writhed beneath her, claws scraping stone. It bucked violently.
Dain was there, stabbing low, driving steel through its abdomen.
Ash added flame, his hands alight as he poured burning heat into the wound.
The creature’s final shriek tore at their ears, and then it slumped, smoking, ichor pooling beneath it.
The voice faded with it, not gone, not defeated, but withdrawing.
“Bask in your small triumph… the mind is patient. I will unmake your thoughts slowly… piece by trembling piece… until even your screams serve my will.”
Aldrek staggered, bracing himself against the stone. Blood dripped from his arm and leg, but his eyes were steady. “I’ll manage,” he said, breath ragged, one eye squinting against the pain.
Ash wiped sweat from his brow, his limbs trembling with exertion. They gathered around Aldrek. The three standing took a knee to take a breath.
They had barely caught their breath when the door behind them shuddered, splintered, and crashed inward.
Red Cloaks poured into the room.
Six of them, disciplined, coordinated, fast.
And at their center, an Adept, robed in deep crimson, his fingers already tracing glowing runes into the air, magic building fast.
Ash looked at Nyssa. She looked back. The Adept's runes cast red light across the floor, reaching toward them like fingers. They had nowhere left to go but forward.






Chapter Forty-Five
The barricade gave way with a deafening crack, iron rods and splintered wood clattering to the stone floor as dust billowed into the ruined prison chamber.
Through that dust stepped six Red Cloaks, disciplined, armored, precise, their crimson cloaks hanging heavy, their helms catching the flickering torchlight. At their center moved the Adept, lean and dark-robed, his lips moving soundlessly, blue glyphs already forming and pulsing in the air around his hands. Two of the Red Cloaks raised crossbows, aiming straight for Ash and Nyssa. 
Lethal purpose burned in the eyes of both sides.
Dain, panting, his blade dripping with black ichor from the dead beast-like creatures, took a half-step forward, trying to summon one of his trademark quips, but his throat was raw, his mind scattered and exhausted. Nothing clever came.
Nyssa glanced toward him, lips parting as if to speak herself, but closed them just as quickly, her gaze narrowing with sharp resolve.
Without a command, the Red Cloaks fired. Two crossbows snapped, bolts screaming across the short distance, aimed straight for Ash and Nyssa’s hearts. The Adept unleashed his spell a heartbeat later, a molten orb of arcane magic twisting through the air, a blast meant to obliterate whatever it touched. In that instant, Dain and Nyssa had the same thought. They saw it in each other's eyes. Then Ash moved. 
Ash tapped his shard, drawing everything the fragment had left. His fingers burned with crimson flame as he hurled both arms up. The fire shield roared to life, an arcing sphere of flame and force that swallowed the crossbow bolts in a puff of ash and smothered the Adept’s blast in a crackling explosion of light and heat.
The shockwave buckled the stone beneath their feet. Heat washed over their faces. Then nothing. They were still alive. 
Inside the sphere of protection, Ash gritted his teeth, sweat pouring down his temples. His hands trembled as he forced the wall to stay up, knowing the cost. His breath came in ragged bursts. His knees almost buckled.
Dain turned toward Ash, breathless, eyes wide with disbelief and fierce respect.
“By the gods’ beard, Ash… you didn’t just save us. You held back death itself.”
Nyssa said nothing. Her daggers were already in her hands. 
He could feel the shard fraying now, threads of power unspooling too fast, beyond his ability to rein them in. “Aldrek,” he gasped, “now…!”
The priest stepped up beside him, robes torn and blood-streaked but eyes clear. He placed one palm gently on Ash’s shoulder, and a soft golden glow flowed from his fingertips. The pain in Ash’s hands eased slightly, the trembling slowed, but Aldrek’s power was finite too.
“I can’t hold this forever,” Ash whispered, teeth clenched.
“I know,” Aldrek murmured, “but I can buy you moments.”
And with that, Aldrek raised his other hand, tracing a swift circle of white light in the air before him. A shimmering second shield snapped into place, paler than Ash’s, thinner, but reinforcing it.
The two walls pulsed together now, fire and light woven into a fragile sanctuary.
Dain moved to Nyssa’s side, his voice low but sharp. “We need a plan, now. The moment he drops that shield, we’ll have a breath, maybe two.”
Nyssa nodded, sliding a dagger into each hand, eyes flicking over their foes. The Red Cloaks didn’t rush. They waited, disciplined, as the Adept continued weaving his next spell, preparing another assault the moment Ash’s protection failed.
Dain swallowed hard, sweat burning his eyes. He felt every bruise, every ache, every breath scraping raw in his lungs. But he raised his blade. Dain's mouth felt dry as sand, his throat raw, but he spoke. “They're not going to stop.” 
“No,” Nyssa replied, her daggers loose in her hands, knuckles white. “And Ash already has had it up for a long time.”
Ash was already shaking, sweat pouring down his face, jaw clenched so tightly his teeth ached. His shard’s warmth inside his chest had faded from a steady flame to a sickly flicker. He could feel it. He was bleeding it dry.
Aldrek stood beside him, his white robes streaked with soot and blood, his free hand pressed gently to Ash’s shoulder, maintaining a thread of healing light, just enough to hold him upright. His mace was gripped tight in the other, ready.
The Red Cloaks were positioning for the next strike, and Ash knew if he let this shield drop, their blades and spells would be inside them in seconds.
But the shield wouldn’t last. His power was slipping. He felt it slipping.
Dain’s gaze flicked to Nyssa and then to Aldrek, quiet resolve behind his exhaustion. “We move the second it drops,” he said.
Nyssa gave a tight nod. “No hesitation.”
Ash finally spoke, his voice hoarse but steady. “Get ready.”
He took a single breath, steadying his stance, flames swirling erratically now, his hands trembling violently.
Dain turned his head slightly, just enough to meet Nyssa’s gaze. For a heartbeat, they both knew. “On my mark,” he whispered. Ash grunted. “Tell me when… because when I drop this, they’ll come fast.”
“Now,” was all Ash heard before he let go.
The shield flickered once. Then again. Then shattered.
A rush of hot air and crackling flame whooshed outward as Ash let it fall. He staggered back, chest heaving, vision blurring, but the others were already moving.
“Cut them down!” barked one of the Red Cloaks, a voice from behind the Adept, sharp and commanding.
Aldrek set himself. He raised his free hand, and the second wall went up to replace the first. White light instead of red flame. 
The blast from his shield boomed out, pushing everyone outside of it back. The blast still hummed through the stones. And yet… the Red Cloaks didn’t break. They regrouped quickly, then spread out, disciplined, methodical, helmets gleaming, short swords drawn, eyes sharp behind steel visors. The Adept’s fingers traced more glowing runes into the air, building toward a second, deadlier spell.
“Rorek, flank left!” another shouted. Their discipline was clear, tight, and drilled, no wasted motion. But the team met them head-on.
Nyssa was first. She darted sideways, evading a lunging sword stroke from one of the crossbowmen who had dropped his bow for a short sword now. Her daggers slashed low, she felt the satisfying catch of steel on flesh as she hamstrung him, blood splattering across her boots.
His scream cut through the chaos, brief and sharp, but Nyssa didn’t linger. She rolled past him as another Red Cloak swung for her head, his blade hissing through empty air.
Dain parried a Red Cloak’s strike, steel ringing against steel. His arm ached, heavy and slow, but he pushed forward, catching his opponent’s wrist on the next swing and driving his rapier into the man’s side. The blade bit deep, ribs cracking, but Dain barely registered it, his body moving from reflex and desperation, getting away from his grapple. 
“By the gods’ beard,” he muttered under his breath, “just fall…”
Ash lashed out next, too weak for a wide flame burst now. His fingers sparked as he directed a thin lance of fire toward the Adept’s face. The Red Cloak Adept twisted aside, his own magic completing at last.
A sphere of blue fire formed in his palm, a searing, deadly thing, and he hurled it straight for Ash.
But Aldrek was already moving. He stepped in front of the blast, raising his palm in a smooth, practiced motion. A radiant sigil flared into being before him, ancient, precise, and the blue spell struck it dead-on.
The bolt vanished with a thunderclap of light and pressure, the energy swallowed entirely by Aldrek’s ward.
The White Adept didn’t flinch. His voice rang out in cold defiance, echoing off the stone. “Not today.”
Aldrek moved in immediately. His mace swept upward, catching a Red Cloak in the ribs with a brutal crunch. Blood spattered Aldrek’s white robes. He pivoted on his heel, his injured leg almost giving out, but he stayed standing, running on instinct and pure adrenaline.
A second Red Cloak rushed him from behind.
Aldrek raised his free hand, and a searing flash of pale light burst from his palm. The Red Cloak screamed as the light seared into his face, temporarily blinding him. Aldrek turned, brought the mace around, and struck the man’s knee, sending him sprawling.
Nyssa intercepted the staggered Red Cloak, daggers flashing. She buried one deep into his neck, twisting hard.
“Lorn, down!” one of them yelled. Another raised his sword mid-order: “Circle left! Shut them do…” Aldrek’s mace caught him in the side of the skull mid-command. The man’s voice cut off with a wet crack as he collapsed sideways, armor ringing like a dropped bell. “Enough of that,” Aldrek muttered, eyes hard. Their discipline frayed as their numbers thinned. 
Dain fought two at once now. He could barely lift his arm, but he ducked and spun, parrying one strike while narrowly dodging another.
He tried to speak, to offer one of his usual barbed jabs, but no words came. His lungs burned, his mind blank with exhaustion. Ash drew steel at last, his short sword rasping from its scabbard as he stepped into a Red Cloak’s guard.
His fire was gone, his shard almost spent. This was blade work now. He caught a strike on the flat of his sword and countered, driving the point into the man’s thigh. Blood flowed hot across his hand as the Red Cloak fell, screaming.
“Kael! Kael’s hit!” another shouted, a panicked voice now. Only the Adept and one sword-wielding Red Cloak. The Adept snarled, gathering magic for a final burst, but Aldrek was faster this time. He stepped forward, blood trailing down his leg, pain etched on his face. His hand raised, glowing again, not healing now but radiant force.
“Enough,” he said, voice hard, and released it.
A brilliant blast of white light shot from his palm, striking the Adept square in the chest. The Red Cloak Adept’s spell collapsed in a flare of blue sparks as he fell backward, slamming into the wall and slumping, stunned. Dain stepped forward immediately, driving his rapier through the man’s throat. 
One Red Cloak left, cornered, bleeding, desperate. He raised his sword but froze as Nyssa’s dagger found his throat. Her voice was cold. “Drop it.” His weapon clattered to the floor. She then brought an elbow across his jaw, laying him out. 
They stood together at last, battered, bloodied, drenched in sweat, but alive. Ash went to one knee, breath ragged, blood slicking his side from where a blade had caught him earlier. Nyssa leaned on her knees, panting. Dain wiped sweat and blood across his face with a shaking hand. Aldrek limped but stood, mace still in hand, white robes streaked red. The last Red Cloak was alive, but only just.
The air hung heavy with heat and soot, thick as wet cloth in their lungs. The last crackle of magic had faded. No more fire, no more bolts. Just the low hiss of cooling stone and the quiet sounds of pain.
No one spoke at first. Ash sagged against a wall, breath stuttering, his knees still trembling. Across the room, Aldrek was binding a torn muscle in his thigh with a strip of cloth, face pale but focused. The Red Cloak prisoner lay facedown, one arm twisted behind his back, still alive but unconscious. 
Dain looked around the scorched room. “Secure the door. Then rest.” They gave themselves one minute, maybe two.
Nyssa nodded and moved to drag a broken chair into place, wedging it beneath the ruined handle. Aldrek joined her, checking their makeshift barricade with a tired grunt.
Ash moved first, slow and quiet. He crouched beside one of the fallen archers, sifting through the man’s gear with practiced hands. Bolts, three still in the leather quiver. He took the whole quiver. Another body nearby, another fallen Red Cloak. Another two bolts.
He pulled the light crossbow from beneath the corpse’s arm, tested the draw mechanism with two tired cranks, and heard a satisfying click. A Dwarven self-load, well-crafted, well-balanced. “Still works,” he muttered, half to himself.
He kept moving through the bodies in silence. 
From a third corpse, he pulled a satchel with dried rations and a length of waxed cord. “This one died mad,” Ash muttered. “His dagger’s clean.” He tossed the satchel aside. Then he moved to the adept, the one who’d thrown the blue fireball.
Ash flipped the man over and carefully pried open the chest plate.
Inside, nestled in a copper cradle beneath the ribbed gorget, pulsed a dull violet shard. Arcane. Still warm. Ash stared at it. Not his affinity. Not fire. But usable. He twisted it free and rolled it between his fingers. “Arcane shard,” he muttered to the others. “Won’t hit as hard as a red one… but it’ll carry me through.”
He slid it into the binding socket at his collar and exhaled. The warmth that pulsed into him was thin, sharp-edged. But it was something.
Behind him, Nyssa’s voice broke the silence. “Find anything else?”
“Making a pile,” Ash replied, motioning toward a crate. “Dagger, darts, one rope with enough length for binding, and,” he picked up a small pouch and gave it a shake, “steel ball bearings.”
He tossed them onto the pile.
“This yours?” He held up a slim throwing knife.
Nyssa snatched it from his fingers without a word.
Ash nodded toward another pouch and opened it. “Dain, you use firestones?”
“I prefer not to burn my eyebrows off,” Dain muttered. “But I’ll take one.”
Ash tossed him two. “You’ve got pretty eyebrows. Would be a shame.”
Nyssa gave a little laugh while looking at Dain, picturing him with no eyebrows.
Aldrek glanced toward a flask on one of the fallen’s belts.
Ash held it up. “Water. Nothing else.”
Aldrek shook his head. “Keep it. You’ll need it more.”
Ash took a swig, then passed it on.
Dain, meanwhile, crouched beside the prisoner. The man’s breath was shallow, his jaw bloodied. Aldrek knelt beside him, resting his hand on the man’s chest and sending a thread of white light into his ribs, just enough to wake him without truly healing. The Red Cloak groaned and stirred. “Don’t fix him too much,” Nyssa said. Aldrek didn’t look up. “Just enough to talk.” Dain rose slowly, wiped grime from his hands, and turned to the others. “How far do we want to push him?”
Ash leaned on his crossbow. “As far as it takes.”
Nyssa didn’t speak, just checked the edge of her dagger.
Aldrek’s voice was level. “I’ll keep him alive. That’s all I’ll promise. I don't kill someone who is out of the fight.”
Dain nodded once, then crouched and slapped the man lightly across the face.
The Red Cloak’s eyes fluttered open. His gaze was unfocused at first, then narrowed as he saw them surrounding him.
“Welcome back,” Dain said. “Now talk.”
A dry, broken laugh rasped from the man’s throat. “No.”
Dain didn’t move. “That wasn’t a request.”
“What’re you going to do if I don’t?” the prisoner muttered, voice gravel-thick with exhaustion. “Kill me? Leave me here to rot?”
“We’ve got options,” Nyssa said, crouching beside him, the point of her knife resting casually near his ribs. “Neither of them is pleasant.”
Talron's gaze darted to her, then to the others, Ash leaning on his crossbow, Aldrek looming quiet as a tombstone, the scent of soot and iron still thick in the air.
“I’m already a dead man,” he said flatly. “Whether it’s you or what waits upstairs… makes no difference.”
“That's just a matter of perspective,” Dain said, settling into a crouch. “If we like what we hear... arrangements can be made.”
Talron’s mouth twisted. “Tell you what? The secrets I had are cooling on that floor. Whatever's left won't matter by morning.” 
He coughed hard, blood spraying his chin.
“You want names? Plans? Secrets? No,” he said.
“You’ve got one minute, until…” Nyssa said coldly. “Make it count.”
For a long moment, Talron didn’t speak. Just watched them.
Nyssa studied him, truly studied him. The bruising, the blood, the lines of exhaustion etched deeper than any wound. She let out a deep sigh.
“It’s like you said,” she murmured. “You’re a dead man either way. Why not cooperate? You look like someone who stopped wanting to fight a long time ago.”
Talron didn’t respond, not with words. But his jaw shifted slightly, the first crack.
Dain’s voice followed, low but steady.
“I’ve stood where you are. Surrounded. Wounded. Thinking the only way left is down.”
He knelt beside the prisoner, meeting his gaze without threat, just weight. Truth.
“The only reason I’m breathing is that someone gave me a way out I didn’t believe in… not at first. So here’s your chance. Take it, or don’t. But I’m telling you… It’s real.”
Then he whispered, “My name’s Talron. It always has been.”
Nyssa raised a brow. “Why the second part?” 
“Because everything else in this city has changed.” He closed his eyes, jaw clenching. “I just wanted something left that didn’t.”
Dain tilted his head. “What changed?”
Talron opened his eyes again, dull, gray-blue, ringed with red. “We weren’t meant to take Stormhaven. Not like this. We were told to cause unrest. Strike key points. Pull the lion’s tail while the governor was off playing diplomat. It was supposed to be loud and fast.”
“How many of you?” Aldrek asked.
“Two hundred.” He swallowed. “And fifty of us were Adepts.”
He glanced toward the body Ash had stripped, the one lying twisted near the broken pillar.
“Forty-nine now.”
Ash’s eyes narrowed, but he said nothing.
Talron looked away, voice rough. “We came to sow chaos. But when we arrived… something changed. We weren’t met with blades. We were invited in. The Garrison commander opened the gates. Said we were expected.”
“Expected by whom?” Nyssa asked.
Talron gave a bitter laugh. “That’s the question, isn’t it?”
Ash stepped closer, arms folded. “What then?”
“Then more came. Reinforcements. Not Red Cloaks. Not Brotherhood. Men in strange armor, faces I’d never seen. They set up control posts. Whispered to our commanders. Then we were told to hold, not just strike. Hold the city.”
“And you listened?” Dain asked.
“We follow orders, don’t you?” Talron said simply. “And Stormhaven fell without a drop of blood spilled. The gates, the watchposts, the towers. All ours. It was beyond what anyone on my team could dream of.” 
Talron hesitated, his voice low and almost reverent. “They told us to take this tower. Secure the highest point.”
He glanced toward the ceiling, as if the weight of the stone above meant something more.
“There’s an old tale,” he said. “Older than the war. Older than the Red Cloaks. Says the tower isn’t just the crown of the city, it’s its spine. Break it, and Stormhaven breaks with it. And if Stormhaven falls, Aldoria won’t be far behind.”
He looked at each of them in turn. “Maybe it’s just a story. But the ones giving the orders believe it. That’s why the orders changed, well, that is why I believe they changed. We were told to place something on its crown.”
“What kind of something?” asked Dain. 
Talron shook his head. “A box. Tall. Sealed. No hinges, no latch. Blacker than pitch. Not the sort of thing you open, just something you carry like it’s breathing.”
The team exchanged uneasy glances. Dain said nothing. Nyssa said nothing. Ash looked at the ceiling, like he could see through thirty floors of stone to whatever was sitting up there. He couldn't. But the trying said enough. 
Aldrek took a turn to ask a question, “So Red Cloak leadership wants to take Aldoria? That doesn’t make much sense. Not from a rabble group, that's not what Red Cloaks do.” He paused. “Someone told them to become something different. Who?” 
“I never said it came from our leadership; it came from someone. Someone with the power to control us, Veydrassil. They really don’t include me much in the planning councils.” 
Nyssa leaned forward. “Fine, what do you know about the excavation?”
Talron’s face twitched. “It was already underway before we got here. Deep below the old Unity Square. Something buried… old magic. Older than any of us. Some kind of arch or gate, or whatever. From what I gathered, it was sealed by the square and its statues, so they sent us to take care of it, well, the adepts.”
“So you destroyed them,” Ash muttered.
Talron nodded slowly. “Smashed everyone to dust. The most fun we had around here. “
Dain’s voice went taut. “Tell us more about this gate.”
“Stone. Spiraled with runes. Cold even in torchlight. We were told to activate it, the adepts, I mean. It was always the adepts. When it flared to life, he stepped through.”
Nyssa’s voice was barely audible. “Who?”
Talron’s voice dropped into reverence. “He was our commander. Until then.”
“What’s his name?” Dain asked.
Talron’s eyes flicked to him. “His name doesn't matter now. When he walked back through the gate, he called himself something new.” He paused before saying, “Sythrael Korr.” He said it and looked immediately toward the door, as if speaking it aloud might bring something. 
“Sythrael Korr.” The name landed heavy, like a dropped blade. None of them spoke.
Talron went on, voice quieter now. “He was… changed. Taller. Paler. His voice echoed wrong, like stone underwater. He looked at us, and we knelt. We couldn’t not. Since then… we’ve followed. Everywhere we went we could hear that voice, sounds like it was coming from every wall.”
“Through walls,” Ash repeated, like he was checking whether he'd heard it right. Ash’s knuckles whitened as he was squeezing his fist tight, not realizing he was doing it. 
Talron nodded, something haunted in his eyes. “Not aloud. Not always. He speaks like a whisper behind your thoughts. And sometimes… the stones listen too. He sees. He knows. He commands.”
“And you obey?” Aldrek asked.
Talron’s lips twitched. “He doesn’t ask twice.”
Dain stepped forward. “Was he the voice we heard? In the Tower, during the fight?”
Talron froze.
“You heard him, too?” he whispered. “Then I’m not mad. I’m not alone. Never knew for sure if it was just me.”
“What is he?” Nyssa asked.
Talron’s voice turned strange, half fear, half reverence. “He’s become something more. A vessel. A herald. He said the crown is broken, and we are to pave the road for the Uncrowned King.”
“The what?” Ash muttered.
“He is coming,” Talron whispered. “Korr rules in his name. Builds his army. Calls his beast.”
“What beast?” Dain asked.
“I'd guess it's what they dug up down there. Bound like stone. The Warbeast from before the Divide era. From what I was told, they are waking one. Soon it will stand guard over Stormhaven.”
“And who commands them?” Aldrek pressed.
Talron’s lips cracked into a broken smile. “The one named in shadow. The general you don’t see. The voice that waits. He watches. Waits for the final bell.”
“Why stay with them?” Ash asked. “You’ve got a brain. Could’ve walked.”
Talron’s gaze flicked again to the dead Adept.
“That was my brother,” he said. “I followed him into the fire. Watched him pledge to the Adept Lords. Swore I’d protect him. I did. Until the end.”
Ash said nothing. Ash looked at the body. Then at Talron. Then away. Some things didn't need commentary. 
Talron looked down, breath catching. “I bled trying to raise him when he fell. That’s when I knew… whatever’s left of me… It’s not enough.”
A silence settled.
Aldrek stepped forward at last, voice firm but kind. “Then maybe it’s time to remember who you were. Not what they made you be.”
He laid his hand gently on Talron’s head. “You are still a man. The choices are yours.”
Talron blinked at him. Then… he laughed. Not the dry, tired wheeze from before. This was broken. Hollow.
“A man?” he said, shoulders trembling. “I’m no man. I’m a puppet… a ruin… something that remembers being whole.”
His voice dipped low. “Since the day he walked through that gate, I haven’t had a real thought of my own. And now I’ve spoken. I’ve failed him.”
He looked at the ceiling as if it might split open. “I’m surprised he hasn’t killed me already.”
Nyssa took a step back.
“He doesn’t need to be here,” Talron whispered. “He never does.”
Aldrek crouched beside him, resting a hand on the side of his head. “Maybe I can help break that hold. Maybe you’ve already started.”
Talron didn’t flinch. But his eyes fluttered.
Aldrek focused, his fingers glowing faintly white as he probed with care, finding something wrapped tight like chains around the man’s mind. Solid. Slick.
But fractured.
“There are cracks,” Aldrek said softly. “There’s still hope for you.”
Talron turned his gaze toward the dead Adept, his brother.
“I just wish there was hope for both of us.”
He looked back at the group. “I need to go home. I need to tell our mother. I need to make this right. It was meant to be a strike. Noise and symbols. But now…”
He shuddered. “Now it’s something else. Something worse.”
And in that quiet, none of them disagreed.
Dain crouched again, voice low but direct. “We’re here for the governor’s family. Where are they?”
Talron blinked slowly, like it took effort just to focus. “They moved them. Said the cells weren’t... suitable. Too damp. Too dark. So they put them in the south wing on the thirty-second floor. Diplomatic suites. More comfortable. More public.”
Nyssa’s breath hitched. “And when are they set to hang them?”
“Seventh bell. Grand courtyard. Red banners. Gallows already built.” A cold silence followed.
Dain stood and paced a few steps. “We can’t fight our way up thirty-two floors.”
Ash muttered, “Not in the shape we’re in.”
Talron’s head tipped back against the stone. “I can help you,” he said hoarsely. “I know a way up… but you’ve got to do something for me.”
Dain narrowed his eyes. “What?”
“You let me go. Help me get out of here. I’ve given you this much already. I’m dead either way, but I’d rather not die in this damned tower.” A long pause passed between them. Then Dain nodded once. “Talk.”
Talron coughed, steadied himself against the floor. “Service stairs. Old dwarven cut. Hidden behind the kitchens, down at the lowest level. It was for the Thane who ruled this place before. Private access to the twenty-eighth floor. Doesn’t reach the suites, but… close enough.”
Aldrek gave Dain a quiet nod.
Dain nodded back. “Heal him enough to move.”
Aldrek returned to Talron and laid a hand on his chest, sending a controlled wave of white light through his ribs and spine. The man winced, but the worst of his tremors eased.
Nyssa stood, voice sharp now. “Even if we make it up... how do we get out again?”
Dain rubbed his jaw, thinking. “We improvise.” 
He turned to Talron. “Supplies. Anywhere nearby?” 
Talron gave a slight nod. “Fifteenth floor, south corridor. Second door on the left. They used it as a storage annex for the old barracks. Should still have weapons, rope, maybe some other thing. I've only been there once before.”
Dain looked to the others. “We’ll check it.”
Then he straightened, glancing down at Talron. “And there's still the matter of you.”
Ash continued, “He said if he didn’t report back, they’d send someone. Probably come through that door we’ve got barricaded. We should move soon; it's been quiet for too long.”
Nyssa’s expression darkened. “Then we need a way out that doesn’t walk straight into the company.”
She looked around the blackened chamber, then toward the far corridor. “The way we came in is sealed. So unless one of you can bore through stone…”
She let the silence linger.
Ash turned, eyes narrowing. “What about the screamer? That bastard had to come from somewhere.”
Nyssa paused, considering. “You’re right. He got in here somehow. Maybe there’s another passage we haven’t seen.”
Ash’s gaze slid toward the hallway. “We saw him come from the warden’s office.”
They all looked toward the shattered remains of the man’s body, twisted and broken, half-crushed beneath a splintered support beam near the eastern archway.
Ash stepped past without flinching.
“Let’s check it out,” he said. “If there’s another way in, then there's a way out.”
And without another word, they moved as one, toward the warden’s office, and whatever secrets it might hold.
They shut the warden’s door behind them with a heavy clunk. The door had three locks on it. Ash slid home the top bolt, then the middle, then the bottom, thick steel bars that locked the door flush into its stone frame.
“That’ll hold longer than the barricade,” Nyssa muttered, pressing her palm flat to the wood. “Not forever. But long enough.”
They all knew the front barricade wouldn’t last. 
Dain turned and scanned the office. “Everyone, spread out. Look for anything out of place, book, lamp, tile. Something triggered that hidden door.”
Ash gave a tired grunt and started near the desk, fingers brushing past ledgers and a cracked inkwell. Aldrek took the shelves by the wall, scanning spine after spine of old ward records. Nyssa crouched beside a locked cabinet, testing its hinges with a dagger tip.
Talron was lowered into a wide-backed chair near the corner, still bound, still bruised, his expression unreadable. They’d kept the bindings tight, for his sake as much as theirs. Anyone who saw them needed to believe he was a prisoner.
Ten minutes passed. Then fifteen.
It was Ash who found it, a raised groove beneath the edge of the desk. He pressed it, and with a low click, a seam appeared in the stone wall behind the bookcase. A panel slid aside to reveal a cramped passage just wide enough for a man to squeeze through.
Dain stepped forward and eyed the opening. “That’s our path.”
They slipped into the passage one by one. The panel shut behind them with a final thunk. Ash went last and broke the release mechanism with the butt of his dagger, sealing off the way. Ensuring that no one could follow.
The passage slanted upward, dusty and narrow, eventually opening into a forgotten storeroom, Basement Level One. Crates and sacks lined the walls in musty rows. A door ahead led into the main corridor.
They moved quietly now. Talron took point.
“I used to ditch assignments all the time,” he murmured. “This way’s always been quiet. Too far from the officer’s quarters for them to care. That’s how I knew.”
“You weren’t a true believer,” Nyssa said.
“No,” Talron admitted. “I joined for my brother. That was the only cause I cared about.”
They crossed the main floor without incident, ducking through unused side halls and cold storage alcoves. Talron led them up to the Grand Floor and slipped them through a side entrance into the vast, echoing kitchen.
The smell of long-spoiled meat lingered. “There,” he said, pointing to a crack in the tiles near the hearth. He stepped down hard. A faint grind echoed through the stone, and a seam split open near the larder, revealing a spiral stairwell descending into darkness and climbing steeply upward. “It goes both ways.” 
Dain gave a nod. “Stay here. Just out of sight.”
Talron nodded. “About halfway up. I’ll tuck into the shadows.”
He started up, then paused and looked back. “Wait.” They turned. “You asked before if there’s another way out. I don’t know for sure. I’ll check below.”
Dain narrowed his eyes. “You sure?”
Talron shrugged. “I’ll be careful. Just… give me a minute. I’ll see what I find.”
He began to descend into the lower levels.
“Oh,” he called over his shoulder, “remember the supply room? Should be on the 15th. Halfway down the corridor, left-hand side.”
He disappeared into the dark.
Dain turned to the others. “All right. We climb.”
And with that, they climbed. Nyssa's fingers found the hilt of her longest blade before she'd taken the first step.






Chapter Forty-Six
The loft above the stable was still and quiet. It was dimly lit by slanted sunlight through the warped wooden slats of the shutters. The air was stale with the scent of hay, sweat, and dust. Harmon stood over the war map still spread across the crate in the center of the room, fingers pressed against the parchment as if trying to will the plan into permanence. His jaw clenched. One more run. One more clean withdrawal. He could do that. He had to.
The sound of bootsteps behind him stirred him from thought.
“You’re late,” Harmon said without turning.
“I’m not late,” Weslin replied, breath just a touch quick as he pushed the door closed behind him. “You told me to wait an hour after Reau and Riven got back. I left on the dot.”
Harmon exhaled through his nose and nodded once. “And they’re safe?”
“Yeah. No injuries. Sword’s back. Manor didn’t burn down. As promised.” Weslin tightened a strap on his bag and crossed to the satchel he’d left behind. He knelt, rummaged, then froze. “Forgot my dagger today,” he muttered, drawing a dagger from its sheath at the bottom. “I’m not used to carrying it.”
Harmon turned, brow furrowing as he looked the boy over. “Weslin…”
He let the name hang there for a moment, then softened his voice, not angry, just firm. “You can’t keep rushing in with your head down. I know you want to prove yourself, but every mission, every life we try to save, depends on us thinking two steps ahead. Not one. Two.”
He stepped closer, the steel in his voice gentled by experience. “I know there's a clock running. So does every man in that tower. That's exactly why we cannot afford to add our own carelessness to the pile. Next time, check your kit before you leave. That's not training anymore. That's survival. Forgetting your dagger might not seem like much until the moment you need it. That could mean life or death, and not just for you.”
Weslin’s eyes dropped, ashamed, reflective.
But Harmon rested a hand on his shoulder. “This isn’t blame. It’s training. You’re still learning, and you’re learning fast. But we have to work on this. Because next time, there might not be a chance to come back for what you forgot. There's no shame in stopping to think before you move. Take it.”
Weslin gave a small nod, strapping the dagger at his side.
The two moved quickly through the loft, gathering the remaining packs and saddlebags, everything that hadn’t been taken during the mission prep. The space was nearly clear now. Below them in the stable, the remaining horses shifted softly, one letting out a snort and a low stamp of hooves. Somewhere outside, a wheel scraped stone and then stopped. Harmon moved to the stairwell door and unlatched it.
It slammed open with a thunderous crack, and a boot struck Harmon square in the chest, sending him sprawling back across the floorboards. He landed hard with a grunt, air driven from his lungs.
Weslin's eyes snapped to the doorway. “Torn?”
Framed in the light, armored in a mail shirt and dark leather trousers, stood the man they’d rescued from the prison. Just that familiar face, twisted now by something meaner. A slow, malevolent grin peeled across it.
Torn stepped forward and kicked Harmon in the ribs, hard.
“I’ve waited a long time for this. I have been following you since I saw you at your camp, thinking of all the things I would do to you. First time I have smiled in years.”
Weslin took a step forward, voice rising. “Torn, what are you doing? We rescued you!”
Torn didn’t even look at him.
He dropped down, driving a mailed fist into Harmon’s face with the pommel of his sword. Blood welled at the edge of Harmon’s mouth.
“I used to look up to you,” Torn hissed. “Back in the Academy. Back when I was your student. Now I get to look down on you.”
Harmon pushed himself up to his elbows, blinking blood from his eye.
Torn stepped back, sabers raised. “Say my name.”
Harmon’s breath rasped as he wiped his chin. “Teralon Odris. Shieldbearer to the Eighth Blade. Commander-in-training of the Skyguard.”
A flash of teeth. “So you do remember.”
His voice dropped, venomous. “I was Shieldbearer to the Eighth Blade. A rising commander of the Skyguard. All gone now. Burned away by your blind obsession with victory and your loyalty to the crown, no matter the cost.”
Torn’s eyes narrowed. “You remember the screams? The betrayal? Or do you block that out, too?”
Harmon grunted. “What betrayal? We were on a mission.”
“That’s all you ever cared about, the mission,” Torn snarled. “Not the men. Not the ones who died because of you. You climbed the ranks on the backs of their ashes. I didn’t forget. I hear them every night.”
He raised the sword again. “They tell me what to do. How to make you pay.” The word was still forming when Weslin lunged. Torn spun and backhanded him with brutal precision, sending the boy sprawling against a stack of gear.
“You were never the man you were supposed to be,” Harmon muttered, rising slowly. “There was always something in you. I saw it even then. I should’ve trusted my gut.”
As he was saying this, Torn, with incredible speed, moved to where Weslin was getting up and landed a solid kick to Weslin’s midsection, to a loud thud and a crack echoed throughout the loft. Weslin fell to his side, doubled over in pain. As fast as he was there, he was gone back to confront Harmon. 
He didn’t spare a glance back. Instead, he stalked toward Harmon, sabers dragging faint grooves in the wood.
“Look at you now,” he sneered. “Still wearing that cursed ring. Still pretending you stand for something.”
Harmon rose, breath low and steady, his jaw set beneath the shadows of his hood. The glow of the Ring pulsed faintly, no burst, no fanfare, just a low, harmonic hum like the promise of thunder.
Shadow-forged steel formed in his hand, edge first, the sword trailing wisps of black heat as it solidified. Enchanted armor rippled across his frame, piece by piece, locking into place with quiet finality.
The man he’d been, the commander, the knight, the protector, stepped forward in silence.
Teralon’s grin widened. A thin, wolfish thing stretched tight across blood-stained teeth. “Finally.” He raised both blades and dropped into a stance that spoke of years of repetition, of perfect form. The same stance Harmon had drilled into him back at the academy. Only now, it carried intent twisted by bitterness.
Harmon said nothing as he prepared. He knew what was coming.
Torn’s nostrils flared. “I used to imagine what I'd say when I got here.” He looked at Harmon for a moment, something moving across his face that was not triumph. “I can't remember any of it now.” Torn moved to attack. 
Harmon met Torn’s charge with a sweeping arc of his greatsword, testing for overreach, for that old mistake Teralon never corrected. Torn twisted beneath it, a blur of chain and leather, and his sabers flared in reply, crossing once to deflect the blow, then separating to strike. One carved across Harmon’s vambrace, the other clanged off his cuirass, leaving a spray of sparks and a gouge of metal.
Harmon grunted, footing staggered. “Still leads with the left. Still overcommits on the backstep.” He adjusted, pivoted hard off his rear leg, slashing his blade down like a hammer. The impact split an overhead beam behind Torn, dust and splinters raining down.
Torn laughed. “You fight the same way you commanded. Like if you hit hard enough, it stops being your fault.” 
Their swords locked, grinding metal on metal, close enough to smell each other’s sweat. Harmon breathed through his nose once. “You call this justice?”
“No,” Torn sneered. “I call it repayment.”
He drove his knee into Harmon’s thigh, then disengaged with a flick of both sabers, slicing the strap of a pauldron. The armor piece hit the ground with a dull thud.
Across the room, Weslin stirred, groaning. One hand braced on a beam, the other gingerly at his ribs. Blood ran from his lip. He blinked through the haze, watching, helpless, for now.
Torn pressed forward, sabers dancing. Harmon caught the first with his blade, deflected the second with a gauntleted forearm, but the third stroke cut deep across his side, and Torn followed with a spinning backfist that sent Harmon stumbling into a stack of gear. Leather and cloth burst into the air.
“You remember what you said?” Torn spat. “Orders first. Feelings later. Sacrifices are just the cost of command.”
Harmon surged upright, parried two strikes in quick succession, then shoved Torn back with the flat of his blade. “I said that… to keep boys like you alive!”
Torn didn’t hesitate. He leapt back in, sabers spinning in tight arcs, then feinted low and came high. Harmon turned, caught part of the blow, but the rest tore his helm free. It clanged against the stone wall and rolled away.
Weslin’s breath caught.
Harmon’s voice came low, sharp as broken glass. “You want truth, Teralon? Fine. The men you mourn, those righteous brothers-in-arms? They died because they ignored direct orders. They disobeyed the fallback command and held the line long after we pulled out.”
Teralon’s face twisted in disbelief.
“We had to move on or we all would’ve died,” Harmon said. “I didn’t choose to leave them. They chose to stay. They made themselves martyrs. And it was their pride that buried them.”
“You’re lying!”
“I didn’t even know what they’d done until after you vanished. I read the full report weeks later, after you ran. After you abandoned the debrief. You were too much of a coward to face the truth of what happened.”
Teralon faltered for just a heartbeat. Harmon pressed. “You want to know what else I learned? After they stayed behind, they torched a village. Claimed it was a rebel safehouse. But there were no weapons, no threats. Just families. Children.”
Teralon’s hand trembled.
“They took everything I taught them and twisted it. And you, who were supposed to lead them, you vanished, before the truth ever reached you.”
“Shut up,” Torn whispered, voice cracking. “Shut your mouth.” With a scream of rage, Teralon charged, sabers flaring, footwork reckless. But Harmon was ready.
He caught the first strike, rolled his shoulder to deflect the second, then smashed the flat of his blade into Teralon’s side. A sharp elbow to the jaw followed, then a rising cut across the ribs that split chain and leather.
Teralon staggered, stunned. But not for long. “You don’t get to rewrite their memory!” Torn howled, surging forward, sabers spinning like teeth. “I know what I know. I lived it. You think I’d let you poison it now? You’re just trying to trick me. Twist it. Disarm me with guilt.”
He drove Harmon back with each word, every strike a punctuation. He took a breath. “No. I know what I know. I was there.” 
Harmon barely kept his footing. One blade scraped his shoulder, another clipped his thigh. Blood ran freely.
“You ruined everything!” Torn screamed, eyes wild. “You took my loyalty, our purpose, and turned it to ash. You ruined the Skyguard. You ruined me.”
And then his voice dropped, low and venomous.
“You want to know how deep this runs? It was me, Harmon. From the beginning.”
“I was the one who warned the nobles about Dain’s true name. I was the one who left the note that drew the others away, so you’d be alone, and they are heading into a trap.”
Something shifted behind his eyes. He kept his feet. 
“Every setback since the prison? That was me. The missteps, the near-misses, you weren’t cursed, Harmon. You were hunted.”
He struck. Harmon couldn’t stop it. A saber cracked against his ribs, armor buckling. The second swept his legs. He fell hard, his sword skidding away. The ring-forged armor shimmered, fractured, and vanished in a whisper of smoke. Only his travel-worn plate remained, dented, split, bloodstained.
Torn stood over him.
Harmon’s face was bloodied. A cut across the brow, sweat in his eyes. 
“Look at you,” Torn hissed. “The mighty knight. The ringbearer. Reduced to groveling.”
Harmon rose again, slow but steady, letting the ring hum at his side, its pulse barely perceptible, power contained. “You wanted a monster. I tried not to be one.”
“You failed,” Torn growled. “You failed me. You failed them,” Motioning to the place where he last saw Weslin, “You failed all of us.”
Torn went for another blow, and Harmon summoned his blade again.
Their swords met again. This time, Harmon drove forward with force, his back foot skidding across the loft as he shoved Torn across the space. Dust billowed beneath them. Torn reversed, dropping low to kick Harmon’s knee and slash at his exposed flank. His side told him he'd taken a cut. He noted it and kept his feet. 
Weslin, unnoticed, had drawn his dagger. He kept to the shadows, each motion slow, purposeful, his breathing ragged.
Torn pivoted, sabers whirling. “You knew we weren’t ready for that raid. You knew we didn’t have the support. But the mission mattered more than the men, right?”
“It wasn’t that simple. Your hate has twisted what happened back then,” Harmon muttered.
Torn struck, one blade high, the other low. Harmon blocked one, took the second on his side with a grimace. Torn was not even listening to any of it. He pressed forward. “You ordered the push anyway,” Torn shouted, pressing the attack. “Six dead! My twin among them!”
Harmon staggered, barely keeping upright.
“I carried his body back myself,” Torn snarled, voice raw. “I buried him alone.”
“I…” Harmon faltered, then found his voice again, low and firm. “I lived with those choices. Every damned day.”
The sabers dropped an inch. Just an inch. And for a beat, Torn was not a man with weapons and a plan. He was a man on his knees in the dirt with his hands full of his brother and no one else around, and that look had lived in him for years without a single person to aim it at until this moment. “Not enough,” he said. Not a shout. A verdict on everything that had come before it. Then he charged. Because grief has nowhere to go, and anger at least has a direction. 
The charge had no finesse. Just weight and velocity and years of accumulated damage aimed at one man. Harmon tucked and caught it on the blade, the impact driving him to one knee. 
Torn circled once, eyes flicking over Harmon’s battered form, then added, “You forget, old man. I was by your side longer than most of them. I know your stance, your timing, every counter, every feint. You made me... and now I’ll unmake you.”
He disarmed Harmon again with a twin strike, blades shearing against the greatsword and flinging it across the loft in a crash. Harmon fell back, dazed, armor cracked, blood running freely now.
Torn loomed, sabers crossed at Harmon’s neck. “Now you kneel,” he breathed. “Good. Stay that way.”
Across the room, Weslin stood. Silent. Focused. A shimmer of light rippled across the floor. Torn didn’t see it. His gaze narrowed to Harmon alone. Torn raised his blade for the final stroke.
Then paused. Head turning.
A creak. Torn looked to where he had left Weslin, but he was not there. He looked around, but Weslin was nowhere to be seen. “And you called me a coward, as your squire ran away. Smarter than I gave him credit for. I’m looking forward to killing him next.”
Torn looked back at Harmon, but what he saw was Harmon still on his knees, head bowed in a silent prayer.
“Pray all you want,” Torn sneered, lowering his sword. “Your gods won't save you.”
He swung. The blade sliced through smoke. An illusion. Torn stumbled forward, eyes wide, suddenly exposed, and behind him, Weslin moved. One step. Two.
The dagger was in his hand. His whole body shook. But his grip was firm. Two steps ahead, Weslin thought. With determination driving him, he plunged the dagger forward. Steel punched through flesh, easily going from the back of the neck through the front, ripping open his throat.
The illusion collapsed the moment the dagger found its mark. Weslin barely noticed. There was a ringing behind his eyes from holding it, and something worse in front of them from letting go. 
Torn stiffened. His swords fell. He saw Harmon lying flat on the ground behind where the illusion was. Blood ran down the blade. Harmon rose quickly. Torn’s eyes widened. Blood burst from his mouth. His legs buckled. He collapsed forward into Harmon’s arms, dying on the man he hated most.
Silence followed. Thick. Absolute.
Weslin stood frozen, dagger still in his grip, the blade still in Torn's neck. The boy's chest rose and fell too fast, too shallow, eyes wide, face drained of all color. He stared not at Torn’s body, but through it. Through the blood on his knuckles. Through the ringing in his ears.
Harmon reached up slowly from where he knelt and curled his fingers around the hilt of the dagger. “It’s done,” he said gently.
Weslin didn’t move.
“Wes.”
At last, Weslin blinked. His grip loosened, and Harmon guided his hand away. The dagger came free with a sickening wet sound. Harmon set it aside, then eased Torn’s body down and let it rest. Once a student. Now a body on a loft floor. Harmon had made peace with worse things, but this one would sit differently. 
Harmon turned. Weslin hadn't moved. He was standing in the same spot, both hands loose at his sides now, but his face had gone somewhere the room couldn't reach.
“I didn’t…” Weslin’s voice cracked. “I didn’t know it would feel like that.”
“There’s no glory in it,” Harmon said. “And there’s no taking it back.”
Weslin’s jaw tightened. He shook his head, just slightly. “I thought I was ready. I thought… with the training, with everything… I thought I understood.”
“No one does. Not until the first one.” Harmon stood, slowly, painfully. Blood trickled down his side. “But you did what had to be done.”
“I didn’t even think,” Weslin whispered. “I just saw you kneeling, and I…”
“You acted. You saved my life.” Harmon rested a hand on the boy’s shoulder, firm but not heavy. “There's no clean version of this. None of us got one.” He kept his hand on Weslin's shoulder. “The weight you're feeling right now is what separates you from what we just put in the ground. Don't try to get rid of it. It's going to tell you things. Listen to it.” 
The silence that followed was thick with breath and blood and things neither of them could say. Then, quietly, Weslin dropped to one knee.
He looked at his hands first. The blood on his knuckles had dried to rust at the edges, and he stared at it until the room settled. Then he looked up at Harmon, and the words came. Not from anything he had planned. Not from training, not from anything his father had taught him, not from a book or a ceremony he had witnessed. From somewhere older than any of that, somewhere he could not point to. He heard himself beginning and kept going because stopping felt like the wrong thing to do, like breaking something that was being passed through him rather than something he was saying himself. 
Weslin’s voice was steady. “You are my knight. And I am your squire. I will carry your orders, guard your back, and rise when you fall. I serve not just you, but the mission and the team we are. I take this oath freely, without reservation, without regret. And if you’ll have me… then from this day forward, we face what comes together.”
He stopped speaking, surprised by the silence. He had heard himself saying the words and known each one was true even as he was surprised by them. He looked at his hands again. They were still shaking. But not from the same thing as before. 
Harmon’s jaw worked. He reached out, hand cupping the back of Weslin’s neck, and bowed his forehead to the boy’s. He summoned his sword and touched both shoulders of Weslin, “I accept.” He held the boy for a moment, one hand at the back of his neck. When he stepped back, something in his face was different. “Those words have been waiting a long time for someone who meant them. You did.” 
The loft, thick with the weight of what had transpired, seemed to exhale. Harmon blinked, then turned toward the open door. Down below, hooves pounded stone. Cart wheels clattered into the alley. Then voices, familiar, urgent. “Move!” Reau’s voice rang like a bell. “Now!”
Harmon moved first, his breathing shallow but steady. Torn’s body lay where it had fallen, blood staining the wooden floorboards beneath. No parting words. No rites. Just the echo of unfinished vengeance fading in the corners of the loft.
He and Weslin shouldered the last of their gear, bedrolls, satchels, and half-spent supplies. They descended the narrow stairs with haste, Weslin favoring one side, a hand pressed lightly to his ribs. 
The dagger was back in its sheath. His hand kept finding it the way a tongue finds a loose tooth, not to do anything, just to confirm it was there, and that the weight of it was now different from what it had been an hour ago. 
The world outside the loft had no mark on it. No record of what had happened above it. The slush, the shadows, the distant sound of a cart wheel, all of it exactly as they had left it. Weslin felt the gap between that and what his hands still remembered like something physical, like a second weight he was now carrying that had no shape yet. 
The air had a weight to it that the loft hadn't. Not weather. Something the city had been gathering while they were occupied elsewhere. The buildings hunched closer, shadows running deeper. Eyes followed them from windows and balconies, faces slack but eyes too bright, watching with a precision that had nothing to do with curiosity. The city was awake. And it knew them.
There were no children. Harmon had not noticed until now. Every occupied city he had ever moved through had children in the streets, regardless, they found ways in and out of anything. This one had none. Whatever the occupation had done to the residents, it had done it thoroughly enough that the children were gone from the street completely, and he did not want to think too carefully about where. 
Riven sat perched on the front of the cart, twin blades at his back and fury in his eyes. Reau was already off the bench, surveying Harmon’s battered armor and the state of his face.
“What the hell happened in there?” Reau asked, jerking a thumb toward the loft. He didn’t wait for the full answer. “Never mind. We’ve got a problem.”
Harmon reached into his coat, pulled the folded map from its oilskin pouch, and handed it to Weslin. “Take the rest of the horses to this point here, see it?” He tapped once. “Use the northern alleys. Stick to the shadow line and avoid the plazas.”
Weslin nodded, face still pale but determined. He tossed what he was carrying into the back of the nearest cart, then sprinted for the stable’s main door. 
Harmon watched him go, then hauled himself into the second cart with a wince, settling against the sideboards just as Reau climbed up front and took the reins. A moment later, Riven cracked the whip on the lead cart, and they rolled out.
The streets narrowed quickly, pressing shadows in on either side as the wheels rattled over cobbles slick with melt. Harmon stayed quiet for a while, letting the rhythm of motion dull the edge of his wounds.
Finally, he spoke. “Anything we need to worry about from that manor?”
Reau didn’t glance back. “There was a ledger in the study. Looked like it hadn’t been touched in months. We flipped through, marked deliveries, coordinates, artifact references.”
Riven called over his shoulder, “And one name. One we’ve never heard before.”
Harmon leaned forward slightly. “What name?”
Reau reached into his coat and pulled out a folded slip of parchment, offering it back without turning. “Written on its own page, different ink. Just one word.”
Harmon took it. A single name, scrawled in looping script, ‘Irothis’. The moment he read it, something pulled at his gut. A hollowness. Like breath drawn too deep in a cold room. The word landed the way old wounds do when the weather turns. Familiar. Wrong. Already making plans for how long it intended to stay. 
Riven’s voice was quieter now. “When I said it aloud, it felt like something… shifted. Like the walls leaned in.”
Reau nodded. “Didn’t feel right. Didn’t feel normal. Almost like someone was watching.”
Harmon folded the note again, slower this time. He tucked it into his belt pouch. The bolt of violet came from the tower's crown while they were still moving. Riven pulled on the reins. Reau's head came around. Harmon was already watching the tower. He did not flinch. He looked like a man confirming something he had not wanted confirmed, and when both of them looked at him, he said nothing, and that said enough. 
They rode in silence for another minute, wheels bumping over uneven stone. Somewhere behind them, a bell tolled from a distant tower, three slow chimes swallowed by the chill. Riven broke the quiet. “Weslin was covered in blood. He okay?”
Harmon didn’t look up. “He’ll live.”
Reau glanced over his shoulder. “That wasn’t just a scrap, was it?”
Harmon sat back, breaking his eye contact with the tower. “It wasn’t his, it was Torn’s.”
That landed hard. Riven exhaled slowly. “Last time I saw him was when he took that horse and rode off from the Forgehallow camp. Didn’t say a word. Just disappeared.”
Reau nodded. “He didn’t trust anyone. Anyone, he always stood a little apart. Quiet. Guarded. But he pulled his weight.”
“Yeah,” Riven said. “You knew he had demons, but he worked. Never saw this coming.”
Harmon’s voice dropped. “You didn’t see it because I wasn’t around yet.”
Neither of them responded at first. Then Riven asked, quieter now, “Is this gonna come back on us?”
Harmon didn’t look up. “No. He’s not anyone’s problem anymore.” No other words had to be said.
At the end of the street, Garr stood waiting beneath the jut of an overhang, one hand resting on the hilt of his blade. Neavin crouched nearby atop a flat section of rubble, falcon-eyes distant, tracking something overhead. Both were still as statues, save for Garr’s fingers drumming a slow, deliberate rhythm on his belt.
As the carts creaked to a halt, Garr stepped forward.
He raised a brow. “Didn’t expect backup.”
Harmon gave a grim nod, eyes scanning rooftops and windows. “Plans shifted.” He glanced toward the tower, where the tower cut the sky above the roofline. “No contact since they entered?”
Garr shook his head. “Nothing. They made entry a few hours ago, got in clean. We’ve seen no movement, no signals. Not a sound since. And the longer it's quiet, the louder it feels.” Garr's eyes went to the tower and did not come back. Both Riven and Reau nodded. 
Harmon folded his arms. “Where’s Aurelia?”
Garr's fingers stopped drumming on his belt. He took a breath before he spoke.
“A few hours ago, she tried a mental sweep. Light probe, nothing she hadn't done a dozen times. Something pushed back, and she went down screaming. Then she stood up.” He paused. “Wrong. She stood up wrong. Back too straight, chin up, hands flat at her sides like she'd been arranged. Then she opened her mouth, and it wasn't her.”
He said the last part plainly, the way a man says something he has been trying to find a better explanation for and given up on.
“Cold. Not angry. Not afraid. The way something speaks when it doesn't have to feel anything about you to deal with you. Said to leave. Said there was nothing here worth what we were risking. Said it, looking directly at me, like it was waiting to see if I'd comply.” He shook his head. “When I didn't move, it turned her head and looked at Neavin.”
The silence that followed that was brief and not comfortable.
“She tore free a few seconds later. Clutched her skull and ran. Neavin tracked her to the pond off Eastveil Lane.”
Harmon looked at Neavin.
Neavin hadn't moved from his piece of rubble. His eyes came back slowly, the way a man pulls his attention from somewhere both distant and close at the same time.
“Still there,” he said. “Feet in the water up to the ankle. Been rockin' since I found her, same rhythm, ain't changed once. Lips movin' but I can't make out what.” He paused. “Eyes are open. She's lookin' at somethin' in the water. Ain't sure it's the water she's seein'.”
Something shifted in Harmon's face.
Not an alarm. Not the focused quiet of a commander triaging a problem. Something older than either of those things, something that moved through his expression the way a current moves beneath ice, there and then controlled, but Garr had spent enough time around Harmon to know what the normal register looked like, and for three full seconds it had not looked like that.
“What exactly did it say?” Harmon asked. The word “exactly” came out weighted in a way that had nothing to do with tactics.
Garr repeated it word for word.
Harmon was still for the duration of it.
“Did she fight it,” he said, “or did it release her?”
“She tore free,” Garr said again, slower this time, because the question itself had not been casual. “Neavin thinks she pulled herself out.”
“Good.” He said it the way a man says it when he is identifying the category of problem in front of him, not celebrating anything. His hand had found the cane pommel. He made himself let go.
The specific quality of what Garr described was not new to him. The voice was cold because it had no reason to be otherwise. The patience behind the words. The way it turned her head to check whether Neavin would comply. These were signatures. He had encountered them before, in a different city, under a different name, in a war whose records no longer existed anywhere except in the memory of the people who had survived it.
He had thought, in the years since, about what he would do if he came across it again.
“We retrieve her on the way out,” he said. “We leave no one.” He let that sit for a moment. “And if it is still using her when we find her, if she has not come back yet, you let me speak to it first.”
Garr looked at him. “What?”
“If it is wearing her when we arrive. You let me speak to it before anyone else does.” He met Garr's eyes and held them. “I will know the difference. And so will it.”
Neavin said nothing. His head turned back toward whatever he had been watching in the middle distance, the place where Aurelia was sitting in the cold with her feet in a pond and her lips moving and her eyes on something below the surface that was not the water.
He turned to the carts and pointed to a new position deeper in the alley, away from the tower’s sightlines. “Shift the carts here. We’ll stage for recovery. If they’re being chased, this is where we break contact.”
Reau and Riven exchanged a glance as they paced in the slush-rutted alley beside the cart. Riven’s fingers were twitching against the hilt of his dagger. Reau leaned on the front rail, arms crossed, scanning the tower’s upper windows as if daring someone to show their face. They had the look of men who had been told to stay and were burning through the word “stay” one second at a time. “We need to help them out,” Reau said. 
Riven nodded. “A few well-placed blades, maybe a distraction or two. We’ll clear a path.”
Harmon, seated in the cart bed, shook his head. “If you go in without a way to communicate, then we will have two teams flying blind. If they come out and we don’t know where you are, then we are still in the same position. What if they have people on their tails? No, it's not good tactics for this.”
Reau frowned. “So we just wait?”
“No,” Harmon said. “If you want something to do, start scouting exit paths. Low-profile. Look for any signs they might be carving a new way out. If you hear anything or see anything that looks like an escape in progress, move to help. If they’ve got civilians with them, your priority is getting them out safe.”
Riven gave a sharp nod. “Stay low, move quietly. Eyes out, ears sharp.”
“Exactly,” Harmon said. “Be smoke until you need to be steel.”
Reau cracked a grin. “Now that sounds like the Harmon I remember.”
The tension eased, but only slightly. Reau vaulted down from the cart, Riven following. The two of them slid into the deeper shadow of the adjoining street, footsteps vanishing into the city’s noise.
Garr snorted faintly. “Better to aim their fire at something useful than let it burn a hole in their nerves.”
Harmon stayed seated, watching the tower. He didn't move. He was still enough that Garr stopped watching him after a while, which was the point. 
“Whatever came next, we’ll have to be ready for it.” His gaze stayed fixed on the skyline beyond, where the tower loomed like a half-buried spear in the ribs of the city. 
Wind tugged at the edges of his cloak. Somewhere below, a shutter creaked. The tower was dark except where it wasn't. That bothered him more than the noise would have. 
“Let’s be ready,” Harmon said, voice low, iron beneath it. “Whatever breaks loose next, we meet it standing.”
Then he turned to the carts. A sudden flash brightened the sky, then another.
Everyone looked up, from the crown of the tower, violet lightning, wrong in its color and wronger in its silence, lashing twice from the tower's crown and leaving nothing behind but the smell of scorched stone. 
Garr and Harmon asked in unison, “What the abyss was that?”






Chapter Forty-Seven
The stairwell to the twenty-eighth floor was narrow and sweltering, carved into the side of the tower like a last-minute afterthought by architects who clearly never intended for anyone to use it during a siege. The stone steps were slick with condensation, the air thick with the sharp bite of burned oil, old blood, and the bitter aftertaste of wards that had long since discharged. Shadows clawed the walls from their torch crystals, all flickering blue and orange as the group ascended.
Ash was the first to collapse at the landing.
“Two hundred and thirty-eight,” he groaned, flopping back against the curved wall, one hand bracing his side. “I counted. Twice. That’s more stairs than I’ve climbed in my entire life.”
Dain slumped beside him, panting, his tunic damp with sweat. “You only counted twice because you lost track halfway.”
“Still counts,” Ash muttered. “My lungs are writing their last rites.”
Brother Aldrek stood near the stairwell door, upright and silent, his mace resting against his shoulder. Though his breath was steady, a thin gash still leaked down the side of his face, dried blood painting a dark streak beneath one eye. His robes were torn along one arm, scorched near the hem. He made no complaint.
Nyssa hadn’t sat. She stood near the stairwell door, eyes narrowed, adjusting the strap on her vambrace in small, precise motions. She hadn’t spoken in the last fifty steps, but the tension in her shoulders said plenty.
A distant groan rolled through the stone.
Not a creak. Not settling. A low, drawn-out moan from deep within the tower’s bones, like the echo of something ancient shifting in its sleep. The sound rattled behind the eyes, deep in the skull.
Ash looked up slowly. “What in the gods’ hollow teeth was that?”
“The tower,” Aldrek said. “It hurts.”
Dain ran a hand down his face. “Let’s get it over with.”
Ash pushed off the wall with a grunt. Aldrek pulled the door open.
The twenty-eighth floor opened like a preserved memory. Twin doors loomed ahead, tall enough to shame giants, each slab engraved with deep-relief carvings that glinted softly beneath the amber light. Long-bearded kings stood locked in eternal vigil across their surface, hands clasped over rune-etched axes, while stylized beasts curled and twisted around their feet, basilisks, thunder wolves, deep wyrms, all icons of dwarven legend. Every figure had been carved by hand, worn smooth in places by reverent touch or the slow march of centuries.
Dain pressed his shoulder against the left door. The hinges resisted with a groan like slumbering stone, then gave way. A rush of colder air whispered past them as the door yawned open.
They stepped into silence.
The throne room was cavernous, more a sanctum than a room, carved from reverence and memory. Its vaulted ceiling soared above, ribbed in dark granite and inset with crystal panels that caught and fractured the low light into a thousand shimmering fragments. The effect was like standing beneath a sky of slow-turning stars.
Pillars marched down the chamber’s sides, each massive and ornately cut, bearing the etched names of clans long vanished or exiled. Most were unreadable now, their lines dulled with time, but here and there a sigil still caught the light: crossed pickaxes, rising anvils, the coiled rune-drake of the Hollow Spine.
Heavy banners hung between the columns, some moth-eaten and torn, others miraculously intact. Deep crimsons, faded indigos, the colors of old dwarven bloodlines. Threads of gold still clung to a few, defiant in the face of dust and disuse.
“It’s not just abandoned,” Nyssa murmured, voice low. “It’s preserved.”
Aldrek nodded once. “This place wasn’t forgotten. It was kept, still used, sparingly. The governors hold ceremonies. The chair still matters.”
And there it was.
At the far end of the hall, under the tallest arch, the throne waited. A slab of blackstone, unadorned except for the intricate mithril veins that wrapped its base like living silver. Crimson velvet lined the seat, not newly sewn but clearly maintained, as if someone still came here from time to time just to clean, just to remember.
It was not the throne of a king born to rule. It was the seat of one who had taken power and held it against all things. Solid. Unyielding. Rooted.
Ash tilted his head as he took it in. “Big chair. Bet the view was great.”
“Depends on what you were willing to ignore,” Aldrek muttered, stepping forward.
They moved slowly, drawn deeper into the hush. Even their breaths seemed subdued now, caught under the weight of a thousand oaths and accusations that still clung to the stone.
Dain let his fingers brush one of the banners as they passed, and the fabric crumbled slightly at the edge. He pulled back quickly, muttering an apology, though no one answered.
Dain didn't move immediately. His eyes went to the pillar inscriptions, the clan names in stone, the crossed tools and coiled drakes of houses that no longer existed except in this room. There was a kind of dignity in being remembered in stone even when you were gone. He wondered what his own house would leave behind. Whether the name Dain had spent his whole life protecting would merit anything as permanent as a sigil carved into good granite.
He caught Ash watching him. “We're moving,” he said and walked on.
Beyond the throne, side corridors led into the Thane’s private quarters. Alcoves stood behind thick velvet curtains, dusty now, their gold trim dulled. Ash peeked into one and found an old war map still mounted on the wall, its pins rusted, the lines drawn in faded ink. Another held a bedframe of solid ironwood, stripped bare but unbroken. A ceremonial forge sat cold in the corner, its bellows sealed with wax.
“These rooms... so well preserved,” Nyssa observed. “They were left. Like a tomb someone still visits.”
“Because they do,” Aldrek said. “In times of great need, the governor retreats here. The last three used this floor during major crises. One even signed the Stormhaven Armistice from that throne.”
“And now?” Dain asked, stepping out of a bedchamber whose walls were lined with ancient dwarven poetry. “It is empty.”
“Yes, mostly memories,” Aldrek said.
They fell into silence again. Not one of dread, but of respect. Even Ash didn’t break it.
It took time to find the stairwell. Unlike the narrow shaft they'd climbed to reach the floor below, this one was tucked behind a slatted bronze gate in the southeast wing, half-obscured by a collapsed tapestry. It was smaller, almost hidden by design, meant for dignitaries or nobles wishing to pass unseen between the royal and servant levels.
Dain reached for the latch. “Let’s hope the next floor’s quieter.”
Ash smirked. “You just jinxed it.”
The latch clanged open, and they moved into darkness once more.
The stairs to the next floor wound tightly, but had room to walk two by two. They climbed in silence. Gone were the marble panels and golden sconces.
The twenty-ninth floor bore none of the majesty of the Thane’s hall below. Here, the tower narrowed into function, shaped by calloused hands and sleepless necessity. Stone replaced luxury, bareness, grayness, and utilitarianism. The walls closed in. The ceiling hung lower. Iron sconces jutted from support beams, many of their lamps long extinguished. The few still lit cast a wan, cold-blue shimmer that flickered like breath on the edge of dying coals.
It was warmer here, but not comfortably so, stifling, thick with the scent of old oil and sealed dust. As they stepped from the stairwell landing, the air shifted again. Beneath the stale heat clung something else: dried herbs, faint soapstone, lavender, a ghost of domesticity.
“Something’s wrong,” Aldrek muttered, low.
He was right.
The corridor stretched ahead, uneven in pitch, floorboards creaking in sections where stone gave way to patched slats. Doorways lined both sides, rows of servant quarters, most left open like mouths mid-sentence. Each room was small, just large enough for a narrow bedframe, a basin, and a wall shelf. Most shelves were bare. Some beds remained made, others half-unraveled, blankets turned down as if someone had only stepped away for a moment.
But no one was here.
No bodies. No blood. No clear signs of struggle. Just… stillness. Like the occupants had vanished between one breath and the next.
Ash stepped into a room with a small pair of boots neatly aligned at the threshold. He bent slowly, staring at them.
“Someone left in a hurry, but not in panic,” he murmured. “These aren’t tossed. They’re… placed.” He touched the heel lightly, showing no dust. “Too clean. Like someone wanted us to see them.”
Nyssa swept a slow arc with her gaze, moving past the ajar doors, her voice low. “It feels like they were taken all at once. Like the whole floor exhaled and everyone went with it.”
“Or turned to vapor,” Ash said, forcing a smirk. It didn’t land.
They moved deeper. The silence clung heavily here. Not like a quiet room, but like the air was pressing against them, listening.
The corridor opened into a wider chamber halfway down the hall. Not a throne room, not a gathering space, just a storage concourse ringed with benches and half-empty racks. And in the center, crates. Three of them.
Ash slowed as they stepped forward. The crates were unmissable, each the size of a hay wagon, dark-wood slats reinforced with black-iron banding, bolted directly to the floor. A canvas tarp half-pulled away revealed cushioned compartments within, nestled recesses shaped for cargo they could only guess at.
Nyssa’s brow creased. “Why store something like that here?”
