Aldrek’s hand brushed the side of one crate. “Not stored. Secured.”
“They’re recent,” Dain said, crouching near the base. “No dust buildup along the latches. No signs of rot.”
Ash circled one slowly, laying his palm along the wood. “They’re too big to have come up the stairs. Even if you broke them down, there’s no way they fit through that last hall.”
“No pulley rigs either,” Nyssa added, scanning the walls. “No recessed platforms. No loading slots. Just stone and pipe.”
“Then they were brought here another way,” Aldrek said, finally. “A different lift. Hidden. Something meant for the tower’s upper floors.”
Ash looked to the ceiling, then back toward the wall, eyes narrowing. “That, or they came from above?”
Nyssa glanced at the nearest door. “We don’t have time to solve this.”
“Still,” Ash said, reluctant. “Feels like we just walked through someone’s secret.” He'd touched the arcane shard briefly when they were close to the crates, half expecting something, a heat signature, a residual ward, anything a trained hand could read. What he got was the sensation of reaching into water and finding the water had been replaced with something that only looked like water.
“Someone's secret,” he said again. He kept moving. He kept the part about the shard to himself.
A bell reached them through the stone. After hearing that first bell, Dain started to count them. By the count of the third one, he walked faster. The count ended at five.
They pressed on, boots tapping lightly on the stone as they moved past the crates. The corridor narrowed again, turning at a slanted angle where the masonry changed. It took them longer than expected to find the next stairwell, tucked behind a false alcove door.
Nyssa found the latch first. It opened with a reluctant click, revealing another narrow flight spiraling upward into more shadow.
“Guard house, should be above,” Dain said, glancing up the stairwell. “Everyone ready?”
Ash cracked his knuckles and rolled his shoulder. “No. But we go anyway.”
They continued up the stairwell toward the Thirtieth floor. Behind them, the crates loomed in the shadows, silent, massive, unexplained. Ash cast one last glance back as the turn of the stairwell swallowed them.
The passage narrowed again, walls pressing in like the throat of something ancient and slow to wake. The air thickened, hot and metallic, the scent of scorched iron and dry stone rising with every step. Their boots echoed with a strange hollowness, as if the space ahead had already been emptied of sound.
Dain reached the landing first, pausing at the door. He tilted his head, listening.
Nothing.
He pushed it open.
The heavy door groaned like a wounded thing, revealing a chamber cloaked in stillness. The barracks level. But there were no voices. No movement. No breath.
Instead, there were piles.
Piles of gear. Not scattered or discarded, but arranged. Each one exactly where a man might’ve stood. Boots paired neatly. Greaves aligned over leggings. Chestplates stacked, weapons leaned gently against them. Even helmets rested atop, their visors shut as if watching the door.
Aldrek stepped through and halted. “Saints preserve…”
It looked like fifty men had simply vanished mid-march. As if they’d melted straight out of their armor, their equipment falling to the ground in perfect order.
Nyssa moved low and slow, blade drawn. “What the hell is this?”
Ash crouched beside one of the sets. He didn’t touch it. “These aren’t damaged. No signs of a fight. No scorch marks. No blood.”
“There’s no dust,” Dain added. “This didn’t happen days ago. This is recent.”
Brother Aldrek moved between the piles like a man in a graveyard. His voice dropped to a rasp. “Their gear’s warm. Not hours old. Minutes.”
Nyssa stiffened. “Warm?”
Aldrek nodded, jaw set. “Like it was just worn.” One boot in the nearest pile was still tied. A double knot, the kind a man who had learned the hard way tied every morning without thinking about it. The kind you did not stop to undo in a hurry, the kind you never expected to be the last time.
Aldrek looked at it for a moment. Then he moved on.
Ash exhaled, low and shaking. “I’m really hating this place.”
The Thirtieth floor had no guards. No bodies. Just the armor. Rows of empty armor.
They advanced carefully, past the first line, then the second. Every pile was identical. Every piece was precisely arranged. It wasn’t tossed, nor looted, nor aligned. As if the men had evaporated and something had set their gear down in their place. Ash muttered something under his breath that no one caught.
The far end of the barracks opened into a broad assembly hall, once meant for morning briefings. Here too, rows of armor. And in the center of the room, directly opposite the next stairwell…. A trail.
Small, wet footprints. Child-sized. Not smudged or scattered, centered. As if the child walked with purpose, undisturbed. Leading into one of the side rooms.
None of them spoke. None of them followed. “Why aren’t we following that?” asked Dain while pointing out the tracks. 
Aldrek answered, “Because some paths are meant to be walked only once.”
Dain held on to Aldrek's words for one beat, “Stairs. Go.”
The exit was across the chamber, an open stone archway with another door waiting beyond. Nyssa took point, stepping lightly through the eerie silence. Ash followed, his eyes everywhere but his feet. Aldrek gripped his mace tighter, eyes flitting to the rafters. Dain brought up the rear.
The stairwell swallowed them one by one, it curving tighter as the walls shifted from bare stone to the soft gold hues of noble stonework, leaning to the Thirty-First Floor. Velvet-lined sconces gave off a warm, amber glow, casting rich shadows that danced with returning grace. The scent changed as they got closer to the Thirty-First floor, no longer stone and sweat, but polished cedar, lilac oil, and the faintest whiff of ink and parchment.
Dain reached the landing and paused, eyes sweeping across the hall. It was pristine.
“Feels like stepping into someone else’s life,” Ash murmured.
“Someone very rich,” Nyssa added, eyes flitting to the gilded trim and marble busts.
Carpets padded the floors, thick and embroidered with Aldorian royal weave. Arched ceilings gave way to grand chandeliers of crystal and brass, dimmed but clean. Doors stood evenly spaced along the corridor, each etched with silver calligraphy and inlaid with house crests.
Ash exhaled slowly, eyes roving. “And not a damn speck of dust. Either ghosts clean in their spare time or someone’s been keeping this up.”
Aldrek stepped in behind him, expression unreadable. “The king’s family used these chambers during their stays. You can feel the legacy in the walls. The Governor uses it for the same as well as special guests. This tower is still active, not only as a widow to the past but as a fort for the city in times of war. People are here every day to maintain these floors. But, I can see why you would think this would just be an old house.”
Nyssa's fist went up, and the room stopped. One beat. Then two fingers forward, a command in a language older than words. She was already past them before they'd fully processed it. 
They moved in silence, blades drawn, shadows to shadows. Down the main corridor, they passed four rooms, empty but immaculate. The fifth, a lounge of sorts, had light leaking through the seams of the closed door.
Nyssa peered in.
Two guards.
Not Red Cloaks. Regular palace men, young, tired-looking, their leather armor worn smooth from years of use rather than battle. They stood at the edge of the corridor, guarding the passage that led to the prisoners, those scheduled for execution within the hour.
One sat slumped against the wall, lazily eating from a tin bowl, steam curling into the still air. The other leaned near a shuttered window, stretching his arms and rotating his neck with the sluggishness of a man who hadn’t seen real combat in months.
Nyssa watched them from the shadows, her breath low and even.
She gave the signal.
Dain veered left, silent as dusk. Aldrek ghosted behind Nyssa, mace in hand. Ash melted to the far wall, eyes sharp.
It was over in less than ten seconds.
Dain took the first without a sound, hand over mouth, blade finding the place between the ribs that ends things quickly. Aldrek took the second the way a man drives a nail, one motion, no hesitation, the mace landing where it needed to and not where it looked impressive. 
Dain wiped his blade on the man’s tunic. “They weren’t ready. Just men doing a job.”
“Wrong job,” Nyssa said under her breath. “Let’s move.”
At the corridor’s end, a heavy arch framed another stairwell, this one wider and far older, its stone steps worn smooth by centuries of use.
Nyssa ascended first, slow and silent. The wood-and-iron banister creaked beneath her glove, a rhythm like a taut bowstring. She reached the top, crouched low, and peeked just enough to see the floor beyond.
The Thirty-Second Floor was long; at the end of the hall, it opened into a ceremonial chamber.
Grand. Circular. Vaulted high with marble ribs that caught the light like skeletal wings. Once-beautiful wall hangings were gone, only dust outlines and empty brackets remained. Sconces burned low. No sound. No motion.
And yet, at the room’s heart, stood a long, stone table, carved from dark granite and chained to the ground by all four legs. Thick links. Tarnished iron. Built to anchor decisions, or prisoners. Spaced out around the room were doors, used by diplomats upon their visit to their quarters for their stay.
Three throne-like chairs stood along the far end.
And seated in the center…
A woman.
She wore layered robes of deep burgundy and gold, woven with heavy silk and trimmed in pale white fur. Her sash bore the emblem of the Governor’s line, two mirrored stags beneath a radiant sunburst. Her collar stood tall behind her head, a symbol of courtly station. Her fingers rested delicately in her lap, her chin lifted just slightly, her posture poised in perfect dignity.
Still. Unmoving. Regal. But something in her stillness was wrong. Nyssa didn’t blink. Didn’t breathe. Then she slipped back down the stairs.
“She’s there,” she said softly. “The governor’s sister-in-law. I saw her once, “About a year back. Riven and I were running a ring-swap con. She was playing hostess for some charity banquet. She looks the same now as she did then. Same formal robes. The dress is right. Governor's seal, fur collar, the whole presentation. She looks like she belongs here.” 
Ash’s fingers twitched, the faint glow already building beneath his skin.
Dain looked at Aldrek, who simply nodded once, face hard.
Aldrek’s voice was quiet, but resolute. “Then we go. One floor left.”
They went up without discussion.
The stairs curved tighter near the top, and the air changed before the floor did, cedar and old parchment and the specific stillness of a space that had been waiting. Dain registered it as he climbed. Not the absence of people. The presence of quiet. Those were different things, and this was the second one.
The 32nd floor was wide. Amber-lit. The kind of space built to make people feel the weight of what happened inside it. Marble columns lined the corridor, sconces burning at intervals, warm light falling across stonework that generations of ceremony had polished smooth.
Ash took in the ceiling first, the columns second, the shadows third. His eyes were doing the inventory his hands did in a fight: what was where, what could move, what already had.
Aldrek came up last and stopped at the landing for a half-second longer than the others. Something moved across his face that was not readable. Then he followed.
The corridor curved ahead. At its end, through a carved stone archway, candlelight warmed a wider space. They could see the edge of a chair. The edge of a woman's robe. Burgundy caught the light along its hem.
No one spoke. Nyssa had already done that work.
They moved forward in the particular silence of people who had agreed without saying so to be ready for whatever the next thirty seconds held. Dain's hand was at his blade. Ash's skin held a faint warmth at the palm that he was not fully releasing. Aldrek's lips moved once, private and brief.
The archway opened. They stepped through.
She was exactly where Nyssa had said. Seated. Still. The governor's seal at her breast. Her hands folded with the practiced dignity of a woman who had spent her life being looked at in rooms like this one. Her chin held the precise angle of composure under pressure.
The wrongness came a half-second later. Not from her. From the room itself, from the specific quality of the silence around her, the way the candlelight moved and nothing else did, the sense of a space that had been configured rather than inhabited.
Ash felt it in the shard before he named it.
Nobody moved for a count of three. Then Nyssa pulled back from the archway and led them down the corridor, past two more closed doors, into a chamber wider than the rest. The ceiling arched overhead, ribbed with white-painted beams and set with hanging crystal orbs. A long ceremonial table sat in the center, fixed directly to the floor with iron pins and bolted legs, made to hold peace treaties and royal guests, not to be moved.
But Nyssa barely glanced at the table. Her eyes were on the far alcove. “She was over there,” she said, pointing.
A small receiving room adjoined the larger space, oval-shaped, draped in emerald green curtains. Candlelight glowed behind the silk folds. The team fanned out again, clearing the corners, checking each side room. Empty beds. Sitting nooks. Folded towels and clean water basins, untouched.
Aldrek tested one of the doors. “Still warm. This place was used recently.”
They returned to the main chamber and crept forward toward the room Nyssa had marked.
And there they were.
Five figures sat in silence behind a lattice divider. It shielded them partially, more for ceremony than security, but through the open space between panels, the team could make them out.
The woman in the center wore layered silks of burgundy and soft gray, cinched with a golden sash and high fur collar. Her shoulders were square, posture precise. A clasp bearing the seal of the governor’s house gleamed at her breast. Her hair was braided in the old noble style, dignified, formal.
Nyssa nodded. “That’s her. The Governor’s sister-in-law.”
Two children sat to her right. A boy and a girl, maybe eight and ten. Wide-eyed, still, clinging to each other but saying nothing.
Also with them was a woman in a fine dress, plainer than the others but still regal. The governor’s wife.
The fifth figure was a man. Silent. Broad. Wrapped in a servant’s cloak with his face turned away, crouched slightly in the corner. He didn’t speak. Didn’t move.
Aldrek lowered his mace. “We’ll clear the rest of the rooms. Quietly. Then we get them out.”
They spread out again, Dain and Nyssa sweeping left, Ash and Aldrek right. Nothing. No other guards. No Red Cloaks. Just stillness.
When they regrouped, Dain nodded. “Clear.”
Ash approached the family slowly. “It’s safe. We’re here to get you out.”
They moved quickly but with care, blades flashing only long enough to cut the bindings. Ash kept his head low as Nyssa led the way to the prisoners, her dagger working cleanly through each rope.
The children were first. They didn’t cry, didn’t speak. The boy looked down at his wrists as though unsure they were still his. The girl clutched the front of Nyssa’s coat without a word. The governor’s wife sat upright with perfect posture, trembling only in her fingertips. Beside her, the sister-in-law didn’t move at all, just stared into nothing with an expression caught between grace and terror. And then there was the fifth figure.
He was slumped against a pillar, face hooded beneath a thick cloak, posture oddly still. Broad across the shoulders. Easily mistaken for a guard or a man in shock.
Ash glanced at him, but Nyssa cut in front of him.
“Start on the others,” she whispered. “I’ve got this one.”
Ash moved without answering, crouching beside the governor's wife first, working the rope at her wrists while Nyssa moved to the fifth figure. Steel whispered through rope as bindings fell away. Ash felt sweat prick under his collar, not from effort, but unease. The silence in the room wasn’t normal. The walls seemed to breathe around them, stone holding its breath.
The girl clung to Nyssa’s leg as she rose. “It’s okay now,” Nyssa whispered. “We’re getting you out.”
Ash stepped back to the fifth figure. The others had been lifted. Guided to their feet. He remained motionless.
Too motionless. Ash crouched beside him. “Hey,” he whispered. “You alright?” 
No response.
Ash stepped forward slowly, his breath shallow. The hooded figure sat at the edge of the group, slumped, heavy, oddly still. Something about the way it breathed, or didn’t, unsettled him. It was too still. Too deliberate.
He reached out, hesitant, fingers brushing the edge of the thick cloak.
It slipped off without resistance.
And what waited beneath wasn’t human.
The skin was stretched wrong. Pale, bloated, veined with purple threadwork and black suture lines. Its torso was too wide, patchwork muscles bound with strips of discolored flesh and old uniform cloth. One eye was stitched shut. The other stared, lidless and milky. Its chest heaved with no breath. Its arms, those were the worst. Thick as tree trunks, ending in hands the size of hammers, fingers swollen and twitching. It smelled like copper and rotted marrow.
Ash stumbled back, heat flaring in his palms. “Flesh golem.”
His voice was barely above a whisper, but it was enough.
The thing stood.
Nyssa turned toward the mother, already reaching for her shoulder when the woman began to weep, softly at first. Then her sobs turned into choking gasps. Black ichor streamed down from her eyes like ink bleeding through porcelain. She looked at Nyssa with terrible clarity.
The terrible part was that nothing in her face was wrong. Not her eyes. Not the set of her jaw. Not the exact quality of dignity that Nyssa had seen at the banquet a year ago and recognized on the stairs an hour ago. All of it exactly right. All of it empty.  
“I’m sorry,” she whispered. “But you shouldn’t have come.” She was out of the chair before the sentence finished, closing the distance in a way that did not account for how far the chair was from Nyssa. 
The child beside her moved in the same instant, her tiny mouth distending with impossible width, strands of viscous goo stretching between jagged, uneven teeth. Her eyes turned obsidian. The boy followed, grinning, mouth tearing wider as his jaw unhinged.
Dain shouted, blade already up. “It was a trap!”
The mimics came at them together, which meant there had never been a family here at all. The laughter came from the walls. Low. Unhurried. The kind of sound a thing makes when it has arranged something carefully and is watching the arrangement fulfill its purpose. None of the creatures in the room was making it. That was the worst part. 
Steel clashed against shrieking claws.
Nyssa didn't hesitate. That was what she told herself in the instant it took her hands to move. She didn't hesitate. The thing in front of her was not a child. It had been dressed as one. That was different. Her hands disagreed by about a quarter-second.
Then her dagger moved. Nyssa ducked, twisted, and drove a dagger into the side of the mimic-child’s neck. It shrieked, gurgled, and collapsed into black tar. “They’re not human!” she snapped. “These are some kind of mimic, nothing I have ever seen.”
Ash threw fire, but it sputtered; his shard burned the wrong hue. Weak. Mismatched.
“Dain! On the big one!” he yelled.
The flesh golem barreled forward, swinging an arm like a siege club. It smashed into a wooden table, turning it into wood chips and shrapnel. Aldrek raised his mace, the warding prayer on his lips, but the thing didn’t stop. It barely slowed.
Ash ducked behind a pillar and flung a narrow arc of fire. The golem’s shoulder caught flame, but it didn’t scream. It didn’t even notice.
“Too stupid to feel pain!” Ash growled. “Too strong to ignore!”
Dain charged the side, slashing deep across its ribs, but the golem backhanded him, sending him skidding across the floor. Nyssa leapt over a mimic, rolled, and slashed the leg of another, turning it to goo. She stabbed downward again and again until it stopped moving.
Aldrek moved to intercept, his mace glowing with holy fire. “In the Light’s name. Back! Beast!”
He struck the creature’s knee with a prayer-enhanced blow. The golem stumbled, dropped to one knee, then roared and slammed both fists into the floor. The impact cracked the stone beneath them.
Ash gritted his teeth and circled, looking for an opening. “Dain!”
“Still breathing!” Dain snarled, wiping blood from his lip. “We need to drop this thing fast!”
They rotated, Aldrek holding its attention with pulsing white light, Ash flanking, Nyssa clearing the last mimic off the wife, and Dain closing in with a flurry of rapid slashes that tore through the golem’s back. Still, it fought.
Ash finally planted both feet and shouted, “Move!”
The others scattered.
A column of fire erupted from his hands, washing over the golem’s upper half. Its flesh boiled and blistered, but even then, it stood.
Dain sprinted in, leapt onto its back, and drove his blade deep into the neck seam where several corpses had been stitched together.
The golem thrashed once, its head was severed halfway, then it hit the ground like a felled boulder. Ash went to one knee beside it, panting. “Dead. Tell me it’s dead.” Aldrek crouched over the creature briefly. “As dead as something like this gets.”
The room held its breath for two full seconds. Then the door they had come through buckled and buckled again. Then something hit it from the other side with enough force to crack the frame, and the sound it made was not human at all. Nobody moved. Nobody spoke. Dain's eyes went to the door, then to the stairwell above them, then to the door again. Two options. One of them led up toward what they had come for. One of them was currently deciding whether to come through the frame or through the wall.
Dain looked at the others. “Up,” he said.






Chapter Forty-Eight
Every window on the eastern wall exploded inward in a roar of glass and screaming wind. Lightning crackled across the ceiling, casting shadows that twisted in all directions like broken limbs. The air turned thick, sulfur, sharp, and choking, riding on the back of something unnatural.
From the sundered frame of the largest arch, a figure stepped forward, not climbing, not flying, but coalescing. He emerged from a cyclone of violet flame and smoke, his form solidifying with each step. He was tall. He wasn’t monstrous. But he was wrong.
Each footfall landed heavier than the one before, echoing louder than stone should permit. His cloak billowed in still air. His eyes glowed with that same violet pulse, the kind of light that didn’t reflect, but swallowed. His face… almost human. Almost.
The presence around him pressed against their skin like humidity before a storm. Aldrek’s lips moved before his mind caught up. “Sythrael Korr.” He said with dread thick in his voice.
Nyssa stepped back. Ash froze. “That’s not…. No,” Aldrek whispered. “That’s an astral projection.”
“It can still kill us,” Ash replied. “And I think it plans to.”
Korr’s voice rang across the chamber, bouncing from marble to ceiling to soul. “Before kings carved lines through the land and called it theirs… it was mine. You may have taken my tower, but you will never hold my dominion.” He raised one hand, and a pulse of violet energy tore through the air.
Aldrek reacted first by shoving Ash out of the way, taking the full blast in his chest. His body launched through the wall, crashing into stone and steel with a crack that shook the frame of the room.
Outside, lightning struck the tower’s top, searing purple across the sky. The sulfur thickened.
“Aldrek!” Dain shouted, running.
“Go!” Ash yelled, already dragging Nyssa with him. “We can’t take him like this!”
“Scatter!” Nyssa barked. “He can’t maintain that form forever!”
Korr stepped slowly, unhurried. His eyes flickered for a moment. His chest dimmed, just slightly. Ash saw it.
“He’s drawing power from somewhere,” Ash muttered. “He’s draining. Every blast is costing him.”
Another bolt cracked down outside, purple light strobing across the cracked marble. With it came another wave of sulfur.
Korr smiled at them like a predator watching deer panic.
Dain reached Aldrek, blood down his face, arm limp, but alive.
“I’m here,” Aldrek rasped. “Still breathing.”
Ash glanced toward the side wall. “We need the family. Now. If they’re here, we’re out of time.”
Nyssa vanished into a side corridor lined with treaty murals. Ash tore through a ceremonial lounge, columns half-collapsed. Aldrek limped through a darkened chamber reeking of incense and blood.
Nothing.
Then the floor cracked behind them. Korr advanced again, his projection rippling with flame and rage. His form stuttered briefly, only a flicker, but real. His power strained the bond holding him in place.
“I told you,” his voice echoed, almost casual. “Run where you like. Every path leads to me.”
Aldrek managed to get upright. He looked at the others the way a man looks when he needs them to understand something, while he is still deciding if he is injured. “Astral projection. Not his physical form. Every use of power here costs him twice over.” A pause. “We can survive this. We cannot fight it.” 
His eyes locked onto Nyssa. He lifted a hand. A lance of energy screamed forward.
Dain was already moving.
Steel rang out. His blade caught the strike, glowing white-hot. He stumbled back two steps, but didn’t fall.
“I’ll hold him off the best I can,” Dain growled, sweat dripping. “I’ll buy you some time!”
Korr didn’t speak, only watched with growing amusement.
Nyssa was frozen, her mouth open, eyes locked on Dain.
Dain gave her a confident smile, then a wink, sweat running down his face as he held back the blast.
Ash yanked her away. “Move. Now.” 
They sprinted. They passed shattered stone, torn murals. They passed a door, carved with the mark of the governor’s house. A door that was not there before.
They heard it, a Bang. Bang. Bang. Muffled at first, like a fist striking the inside of a casket.
Then louder. That was when the screams started. “This is it!” Nyssa shouted.
She skidded to the door, heart hammering. It wasn’t barred. It wasn’t locked.
It was sealed.
An unnatural shimmer ran across the wood, glyphwork etched deep, woven with ill intent.
“They’ve been screaming this whole time,” Aldrek muttered. “We just couldn’t hear it.”
Ash stepped forward and placed his palm on the seal. Firelight flickered from his hand into the runes. They hissed and sparked, resisting. “We don’t have time to disarm it. I can burn it, but we know what could happen.” A pause. “It could blow.”
“Do it,” Nyssa said.
Fire danced across his fingers, then surged into the seal. It was harder than usual, but he managed to force the energy flow with concentrated focus. 
The glyphs fought back. Yet after only a few seconds, they started to buckle. Then crack, and with a final snap. The seal exploded outward. Ash positioned himself to send the burst of energy towards Korr. This outpour of energy engulfed him. He didn’t slow down. It was as if it didn’t even faze him. 
Ash yanked his hands back. The heat that came with them was significant. He turned his palms over once, checking the damage the way a man checks for a hole in a boat, quickly, practically, hoping for less than he finds. Ten fingers. He filed it under acceptable and turned back to the door. 
Smoke rolled back. Inside the room was dim and cramped, lit only by a half-burned-out luminaire-rock in the ceiling. Crates lined one wall. In the center, four figures huddled, bound at wrists and ankles. They weren’t moving much. Yet, it was enough to tell that they were alive.
The one believed to be the governor’s wife looked up, lips parted in disbelief. The next oldest clutched the youngest child. The eldest girl trembled, still shielding them with her body.
Ash went in first. He scanned the room. He exhaled through his nose. “Clear,” he said. And the word had never meant more. The others followed on Ash’s heels.
Nyssa rushed over to the group and dropped to her knees, blade flashing, cutting the restraints.
Dain ducked under a backhanded sweep of Korr’s projection, the force of it sending spiderweb cracks through the wall behind him. His sword rang against the arcane steel of Korr’s conjured blade, sparks scattering across the floor like embers from a forge.
Another strike. Dain caught it, barely. Sweat streamed down his temple. His footing was slipping. One more hit, and he'd lose his stance. “I’m losing ground!” he yelled.
“Two minutes,” Nyssa said without looking up. “Hold.” 
Aldrek stepped forward, his good hand locked around the shard at his chest, the other arm held against his side. His lips moved in fervent prayer, words spilling in the Old Tongue, ritual, command, plea.
“By light unbroken, by flame unyielding…” The crystal at his chest blazed white-gold. “Send me your guardian. Not to strike in wrath, but to shield those who still carry hope. Let your light walk beside us.”
Out of that brilliance stepped a figure, tall, faceless, armored in mirrored light. A divine sentinel, spear and shield in hand, born of faith and old covenants.
It took position between Dain and Korr. Korr's attention shifted to the new threat. He swung to strike the newcomer. The guardian met his blow with his shield. The impact shook the walls. The force rippled outward like a thunderclap. Korr’s projection reeled back half a step, expression unreadable.
A third bolt cracked from the tower. Sulfur bloomed again.
Dain stumbled clear, panting. Sweat and blood were running down his head. Aldrek, his voice barely above a rasp, said as loudly as he could muster, “That's your two minutes.” 
Nyssa looked up from the last binding. “Then let's not waste them.” 
“Eyes open,” Dain warned, stepping between the bodies. “We just fought things wearing their faces. No more mistakes.”
Aldrek checked for marks. “No psychic sigils. No shadow burns.” He looked up. “Saints above… I think this is them.”
Ash knelt beside the boy. “You’re safe.”
Nyssa looked into the governor’s wife’s eyes. “Lady Karethiel, we’re here for you. Your husband sent us. We’re going to bring you to safety.”
The woman sobbed. Just sobs, nothing else. Real.
Dain leaned in. “What do you remember?”
“Dreams,” she whispered. “Then being dragged… A windowless place. Then… silence. I told them nothing, I swear on God’s mercy I didn’t.”
“You held,” Nyssa said softly. “Stronger than most.”
Lady Karethiel nodded, face tight. Then looked down at her children, huddled and shaking, but breathing. “Please… get us out of here.”
Behind them, heavy boots slammed against stone in the distance, growing louder.
Ash stood. “That’s our cue, we need to move,” he said, already helping the youngest child stand. “Eyes open for an exit.”
They moved as one, silent, swift, weapons raised, shields of fatigue and adrenaline welded tight. The stairwell reeked of scorched dust and old oil. They moved fast, but carefully, carrying the weak and guiding the stunned. The sounds of the duel between the heavenly being and Korr were coming to a end, as a burst of light shone, bright as a sun on the rise on that floor. 
“He will continue his pursuit of us, soon,” said Aldrek.
On the thirtieth floor, a shadow moved.
“Wait!” Dain snapped.
The figure froze, hands raised.
“Talron?” Dain asked. 
“Yeah, it's me. So I did find a tunnel, but a dead end,” he rasped. “Whatever’s coming is behind me.”
Nyssa stepped past him. “It’s behind us, too. Stay close.”
“Where the hell are we going?” he asked.
Ash said, “Down. Until we find something that doesn’t want us dead.”
They all reached the twenty-ninth floor. Dain saw the crates again, “They got these up here somehow, maybe that could help us,” Dain muttered, his eyes scanning the stacked crates, all tightly banded and perfectly aligned.
“There’s something more,” Nyssa said, glancing down the corridor. “You don’t bring a shipment like this up thirty floors without help.”
Briala moved forward next to one of the crates, brushing dust from her sleeve. “These are mine,” she said softly, fingertips trailing the edge of one polished crate. “Summit gifts. Formalwear. Tools for display. I was meant to have rooms on this level… I liked it here.”
She pressed a hand to a faint seam in the side.
Click.
The crate shifted on hidden wheels, then slid back to reveal a vertical shaft hidden beneath its false base, wide, rune-etched, and humming faintly with residual magic. A column of dim glyphs spiraled downward into darkness, each one carved into a metal rail embedded in the stone.
Ash crouched low, peering into the drop. “Wind-catch descent system,” he murmured. “Dwarven design. Old, but… gods, it still breathes.”
Briala pointed to a recessed panel on the side wall. “That’s the catch control. Base-level station sets direction. Up can be modulated at any level. But down?” 
“Down only ends one place,” Ash said, finishing her thought. “All the way to the base.”
Dain’s hand hovered near the edge, testing for a breeze. “How does it work?”
Ash tapped the glyph plate. “Set it down, you jump. The catch runes read your weight near the bottom and slow the fall. You land lightly. Mostly.”
“And for people?” Nyssa asked.
“Doesn’t matter what it is,” Ash said, a grin tugging at his lips. “If it falls, it lands softly. Dwarves build for permanence, not precision.”
The boy, four, maybe five, clutched his mother’s coat, eyes wide. “I don’t want to fall.”
Ash knelt beside him, eye-level. His voice softened, steady like coals banked beneath snow. “Hey, listen. I know it’s scary. But I’ll be right there with you. You’re not falling, you’re flying like a stone hawk. These runes? They’ve caught things ten times your size. Armor. Wagons. War steeds.”
The boy’s lip trembled. “What if it breaks?”
“It won’t,” Ash said. “You know why?”
He reached into his coat and opened his palm towards the boy, letting him see the faint ember-glow of his shard. “Because I’m going to jump with you. And I don’t break easily.”
The boy looked at him, then nodded, not quite believing, but willing to follow.
Ash ruffled his hair. “Good lad.”
Dain’s eyes flicked upward. “No more time. We go in pairs.”
Ash stepped forward, one arm steadying the boy. “We lead.”
He gripped the panel, thumb pressed firmly. The glyphs flared amber, downward, ready.
Ash and the boy leapt together.
Wind roared.
For a heartbeat, they plummeted, just enough to seize the stomach.
Then the glyphs caught them.
Light flared. Their descent slowed. They floated the last fifty feet like leaves carried on still air. Then vanished below.
Briala cradled the younger girl and whispered something soft into her ear before stepping to the edge. “Hold tight,” she murmured and jumped.
Nyssa turned to Lady Karethiel. “Ready?” The governor’s wife hesitated, trembling. “What if…?”
“Don’t,” Nyssa said gently. “You’re stronger than you think. I’ve seen how you held on.”
The woman met her gaze. She nodded, and together, they jumped.
One by one, bodies vanished into the chute, caught and carried by dwarven craft.
Talron needed no direction. He jumped next, with no prompting. 
Dain turned to Aldrek. “It's time, we go now.” 
But before they could leap, the air at the top shimmered. A figure stepped into view, Korr. Fully formed now, radiating violet wrath. His voice slithered down the shaft. “You think the fall saves you?” He raised his hand. 
Both Dain and Aldrek jumped into the shaft.
A bolt of jagged purple fire screamed down the tunnel. It struck Aldrek mid-jump, his form spiraling. He quickly vanished into the darkness of the shaft. A stone cracked somewhere deep below. A cry of pain rang off the walls.
Dain vanished after him.
Glyphs caught them both, but Aldrek still hit hard.
Above, Korr’s voice followed like a curse. “The deeper you run… the closer you come.”
Dain hit the stone and rolled to his feet, breath ragged. The air at the bottom of the shaft was thick with old dust, the scent of stone oil, and the lingering scorch of magic. Above, the shaft stretched into shadow, empty now. Silent. 
Aldrek lay crumpled at the base of a splintered support beam, half-buried in fallen chain links. His legs were twisted beneath him, one arm limp at an unnatural angle. The other still clutched the haft of his mace, knuckles white despite the unconsciousness.
Dain dropped to one knee beside him. “Aldrek.”
No response.
He leaned closer, listening.
A breath. Shallow, but real.
Still alive.
But his face was slack, jaw slackened to the side. His shard glowed weakly at his chest, flickering as if trying to pulse, trying to reach out for something.
Dain pressed a steadying hand over the priest’s sternum. “Still with us,” he muttered. “But barely.”
Behind him, Nyssa knelt near Lady Karethiel, checking her for injury. The governor’s wife was pale, lips pressed into a thin line, but she gripped Nyssa’s hand like it was the only solid thing in the world.
The children were huddled together against a crate, wide-eyed and silent. Ash knelt in front of the boy, his voice low and steady.
“You held it together better than most grown men I’ve met,” he murmured. “But from here on, I’ve got you. Just keep holding on.”
The boy didn’t answer, just nodded and tucked his face into Ash’s shoulder. Ash hugged him back. After he stood up, the boy stayed close to him. 
Nyssa placed a hand on the governor’s wife's shoulder. “We’re below it now. Whatever’s coming, we’ve bought space.”
Lady Karethiel nodded, jaw clenched. “Thank you… all of you.”
Dain stood, scanning the chamber.
The room they were in was round, wide, with ceilings that rose just high enough to hold old lifting chains and rusted pulley tracks. Every wall bore the faded stamp of freight marks and dwarven construction, reinforced stone lattices built to carry weight that could crush a lesser tower.
Ash stepped up beside him. “How’s Aldrek?”
“Breathing,” Dain replied. “That’s all I can say.”
“We need to keep moving. Get him and the rest of us out of here.”
Dain gave a grim nod, eyes already scanning for the next threat.
The shaft above was silent. A thread of violet smoke curled where the lightning had been and then came apart. Dain watched it go. Whatever Korr had spent to follow them down here, he had spent it. That was the only comfort available. 
Ash caught the movement and grimaced. “He can’t come down here. Not directly.”
“No,” Dain said. “But he knows where we’re going.”
“Then let’s not be standing still when he does,” said Ash.
The girl leaned into her aunt’s side, trembling but silent, eyes locked on the shaft above. The boy clung to Ash’s coat with one fist, rubbing his eyes with the other. Neither cried, but the fear was written in their every movement.
They found a stash of discarded cloaks and servant garb near a stack of sealed crates. With swift, urgent hands, they disguised the governor’s family, shrouding the boy in an oversized hood, giving the girl a baker’s apron, and smearing soot over Karethiel’s face to dull her noble features. Briala tucked her hair into a shawl and dirtied her sleeves.
Dain crouched beside Aldrek again. The priest’s breathing was shallow, eyes fluttering but unfocused. He was alive, and Dain wanted to keep it that way.
With effort, he hoisted Aldrek across his shoulders, bearing him like a fallen brother through battlefield smoke. Aldrek’s arms dangled limp across Dain’s front. Ash came over and took Aldrek’s mace and strapped it to Aldrek’s hip.
Dain grunted under the weight and turned to the rest. “Let’s move. We’re not safe yet.”
Ash adjusted the boy in his arms and gave a sharp nod. “Right behind you.”
They climbed the ramp as a group, pressed close. At the top, Nyssa reached the iron latches and threw her weight into them. The doors groaned but opened wide, and the false dusk poured in.
They emerged into one of the tower’s ceremonial courtyards. It was a massive open space framed by the circular bulk of the tower and four low wings radiating outward like spokes. The stone underfoot was patterned with old emblems of the kingdom, sigils now defaced or half-painted over in crimson. 
They moved along the inner wall, slipping past a broken arch. Just beyond that, a raised platform was visible in the square, ropes hanging slack; that was where the gallows were assembled. Ash muttered, “We were minutes from being guests of honor.” Nyssa didn’t reply, but her knuckles had gone white on her blade.
Dain grunted. “One wrong step and we’re still the finale.” Footsteps sounded on stone. Everyone tensed as two figures approached at a steady walk. Not running, not rushing.
Nyssa’s hand went to her knife. “Easy,” Ash said, eyes narrowing. “Look closer.”
Riven and Reau stepped into view. Riven stopped a dozen paces away and smiled as if they'd just returned from a stroll through the market. “Took your time.” Nyssa crossed the space and hugged him hard, chest tight with relief. 
“You made it,” Riven said softly, arms briefly around her. “I was starting to worry.” Dain walked over and shook his hand as they all greeted each other.
“We shouldn’t be standing still,” Reau said, scanning the area. “Harmon and Garr are waiting with two carts over the rise,” he pointed without stopping to look. 
“Let's not keep them waiting,” Riven said. “I am done with this place, and I’m sure the rest of you want out of here, as well.”
They fell in beside the group, helping with the wounded and glancing warily at every corner. Dain adjusted Aldrek’s weight again before moving.
They made their way across the courtyard’s far end. Watchers were beginning to notice. Movement on balconies. Windows. A door creaked open and then slammed again.
Briala whispered, “They’re watching us…”
Ash nodded grimly. “Let them look.”
But then came the voices.
“Traitors!”
“They’re hiding nobles!”
A glass bottle crashed near their feet. Someone threw a rotten root. Then another.
Riven stepped closer to the front, hand already on his belt. “They’re drawing too close.”
Nyssa hissed, “Keep moving, don't give them an excuse.” 
The crowd picked up in volume and in the number of objects hurled their way. But that was a long part of their walk, and then came the real threat.
A figure burst forward from the crowd, shoulders wide, eyes wild, something jagged gleaming in his hand.
“Back!” Reau shouted.
This man was running right at them, at what looked like his full speed. 
But Riven moved faster. His hand flicked, and a throwing knife buried itself in the attacker’s eye. He collapsed mid-stride, crumpling like a dropped canvas.
No words. No apology. The crowd screamed and surged back, but the damage was done.
“Weapons out,” Nyssa snapped. “Stay tight!”
Briala scooped up the girl and ran. Ash grabbed the boy and pulled him to his chest, covering him with his coat.
The group of them moved as fast as they could, but doubt started to sink into them. But Reau pointed out, “There on the hill.”
They looked up. The two carts waited on the rise, exactly where Harmon had said they would be. Nobody said anything. They just ran harder.
On one of the cars, Garr was standing tall atop the driver’s bench, longbow drawn. He loosed an arrow, then another and another. Each finding their mark. Guards dropping. Aggressors stumbling. He didn’t stop, loosing arrows with mechanical precision. Every shot dropped another hostile, worker, guard, or someone bold enough to lunge. It didn’t matter. Garr never missed.
From the other cart, Harmon stood, cloaked, one boot braced on the rail as he watched the courtyard unfold below. His expression didn’t change, just that cold, calculating stare, measuring each angle of retreat, each threat. 
Beside Harmon on the driver's bench, Neavin sat motionless, his eyes cloudy and unfocused as he channeled his bonded spirit outward. His hands rested in his lap, jaw clenched in quiet focus. He wasn’t seeing this street, not with those eyes. He was watching from somewhere else, somewhere far above.
Nyssa shouted orders as she pulled her blade, breaking the crowd with sharp elbows and shoves. Briala lifted the girl higher on her shoulder. Ash surged forward with the boy gripped tight to his chest, his coat shielding the child from debris and flame. Dain still carried Aldrek across his shoulders, face soaked in sweat and grit as he fought to keep pace under the weight.
Behind them, the mob swelled again. Another bottle arced. Someone screamed for the guard. A chorus of boots thundered from alleyways as pursuit spilled into the courtyard.
Garr didn’t flinch. He dropped two more figures and pivoted to cover the right flank.
Riven pointed. “There! North wall, just past the blacksmith’s alcove!”
An archway barely wide enough for a wagon stood open ahead, part of the old outer maintenance ring. The way out.
“Go!” Dain barked, muscles straining as he shifted Aldrek’s weight.
Reau sprinted ahead, clearing crates and barrels in his path with his forearm. Nyssa and the others fell in behind him, flanking the family as best they could. The girl whimpered once but kept her grip. The boy buried his face against Ash’s chest, shaking but silent.
The archway yawned wider with every step.
And behind them, somewhere deeper in the bones of the tower, Korr’s voice found them again. Not loud. Not screaming. Just a whisper, carried on memory and smoke. “Run, little ones... The end waits where you began.”
They didn’t look back. They ran harder. Straight for Harmon. Straight for the wall.
The breach in the outer wall loomed ahead, half-collapsed, overgrown, forgotten by most but not by Riven and Reau. They’d scouted this path hours ago, just in case. Now it was their only chance.
“Through there,” Riven barked, drawing a short blade from beneath his cloak. “Go!”
The wind hit them hard as they cleared the final slope from the courtyard. Stone and moss, slick with evening dew, gave way underfoot. Reau moved smoothly, slashing down a man who got too close while keeping pace with the retreating group. Behind them, feet slapped cobbled ground, pursuers, angry now. Some in guard uniforms, others in civilian rags, but armed all the same.
Another bottle arced through the air, shattering near the lead cart with a hiss of flame. Garr didn’t flinch. Standing atop the driver’s bench, he loosed arrow after arrow with calm precision, each one dropping another would-be captor. The longbow thrummed like a drumbeat of death. 
The group surged through the breach. Riven dropped one last pursuer with a clean strike to the throat, then turned and followed. The wagons waited just beyond, nestled in the shadows of a forgotten grain passage lined with cracked stone and dead ivy. The horses snorted, anxious but trained, shifting beneath the tension in the air.
Harmon sat on the front bench of the second cart, reins already in hand, his cold gaze fixed ahead. Beside him, Neavin remained in silence, eyes distant, still tracking his bonded spirit through unseen air.
Dain moved swiftly, hauling Aldrek’s limp body up and into the cart. He laid him gently across the wooden slats behind Harmon, ensuring the wounded knight wouldn’t jostle during the ride.
“We split,” Harmon said without turning. “Garr, take the rest to Weslin. Get the horses ready. Get moving.”
Garr gave a sharp nod and called over his shoulder, “Everyone in!”
Ash passed the boy into Briala’s waiting arms as she climbed into Garr’s cart. The child whimpered but clung to his mother without protest. Nyssa helped the girl up beside them and threw a tarp over the family for added cover. Briala wrapped her arms protectively around both children, her jaw tight, eyes alert.
Dain gave a final look toward the regrouping team, then vaulted up into Harmon’s cart.
Garr cracked his reins, and his cart lunged forward, wheels groaning as it bounded into motion.
Harmon’s cart turned east, peeling away toward the broken towers near the far edge of the city. Neavin didn’t speak. 
Harmon's face had no expression at all, like it was carved from stone, eyes already searching the road ahead. He was going to bring Aurelia back. No one left behind. It didn’t take them long, Harmon, following Neavin’s directions.
She was right where Neavin had seen her, through his falcon eyes. She was by the edge of a dry pond, knees drawn to her chest, fingers half-buried in the mud. Her eyes tracked nothing. Her lips moved, but no sound escaped.
Harmon approached slowly, dismounting with a grunt. “Aurelia.”
She flinched, not from fear, but from something deeper, as if his voice tore her from a dream that didn’t want to let go.
“They’re gone,” she whispered. “All of them. One by one, they burned out. I heard them go. I heard the silence.”
He knelt beside her. “You’re not making sense. We need to go.”
She looked up, eyes wild. “It’s him. The old one. The silent crown. I felt it.”
Her words trembled with a weight he didn’t yet understand.
“Aurelia…”
“We’re not ready for this. You know that, don’t you?” She reached for him with trembling hands. “The thing that’s coming… It’s already inside,” She said, and lifted one trembling finger to her temple. “I tried to look. I shouldn’t have looked.”
She laughed, sudden and sharp, then pressed both palms to her eyes. “I let them down. I wasn’t strong enough.”
“You’re coming with me,” Harmon said gently, but firmly. “We’ve made it this far. Don’t quit now.”
A long pause.
Then, something in her gaze shifted. Clarity returned, just enough.
She nodded slowly, as tears carved fresh paths down her dust-streaked cheeks. “I’m sorry.”
“I know,” Harmon said. He helped her to her feet, steadying her as she swayed. He led her to the back of the cart while Dain fished through the gear to find a blanket. When he was up in the back, Dain wrapped her in the blanket. She just sat and rocked back and forth. 
By the time they reached Weslin’s rendezvous point, Garr’s cart was already there, hidden beneath an overgrown stable awning. Weslin was crouched beside a ring of saddled horses, checking each cinch, eyes flicking up only when he saw Aurelia.
His breath caught. “Is she?”
“She’s with us,” Harmon answered.
Aurelia gave a small nod to the boy. Weslin looked ready to cry.
They were all moved like the aftermath of a storm, jagged, breathless, and barely holding shape. Every step forward was a silent agreement not to look back.
The governor’s family clung together at the center of the group, their once-fine clothes dirtied and torn, faces hollowed by the sheer force of what they'd seen. The boy had stopped crying hours ago, his small hands twisted in the fabric of Lady Karethiel’s cloak, eyes blank and staring, as if whatever spark had been in him had been traded for silence. Lady Karethiel herself, regal by habit and duty, now walked with her head low, lips pressed to the boy’s crown, whispering a litany of promises she didn’t know if she could keep.
The girl didn’t speak either. She held her aunt’s hand with an iron grip, refusing to let go, the way a drowning swimmer might clutch to a drifting plank. Briala, though scratched and bloodied, kept her shoulders squared and her steps even, murmuring directions to no one and everyone at once, her voice the only thing tethering the children to motion.
The rest of the group wore the hardened expressions of survivors, but even they carried the haunted weight of what they had narrowly escaped. Ash’s jaw clenched so tight it trembled. Nyssa scanned every shadow with a blade already drawn. Dain hadn’t spoken since lifting Aldrek into Harmon’s cart; blood still painted the back of his collar.
No one shouted. No one gave orders. They simply moved. The shape of the group rearranged itself around the family, the way water moves around stone, each person finding the place they were needed without being told. Ash had the boy. Nyssa had the perimeter. Dain had Aldrek. Briala had the girl.
They split when Harmon said, “Split.” That was all the plan there was.
His voice was low but commanding. “Follow your path. I’ll see you all at the rendezvous point.” All headed in their assigned direction. The shadows of the events of the day were painted on each of their faces as they rode away. 
Shadows stretched over the battered streets as they slipped through the city’s hushed skeleton, two carts and a ring of riders weaving their way toward separate exits. Just the rhythm of hooves and wheels grinding over cracked stone, and the weight of silence pressing against every breath.
In Garr’s cart, Lady Karethiel sat bundled between her children, arms locked around them, as if afraid they might vanish the moment she let go. Her once-commanding voice had thinned to a whisper, repeating names and prayers and promises that didn’t quite make sense. The girl clung to her with wide, dry eyes, not a word spoken since the courtyard. Beside them, Briala sat ramrod straight, not from pride but from duty, guarding the family with her presence alone. Talron rode in the front corner of the cart, silent and stiff, his hands kept where everyone could see them.
Aurelia was wrapped in a heavy blanket near the rear, her knees pulled to her chest, staring at something no one else could see. Occasionally, she muttered to herself, half-nonsense, half-warnings, her voice soft as unraveling thread. Neavin sat close, not touching her, but watching as if willing her to come back from wherever she had gone.
In the second cart, Harmon drove. Aldrek’s unconscious form lay cradled against the back rail, still breathing but unmoving, his armor scuffed and stained. Harmon’s gaze never left the road ahead, his jaw locked, his ring faintly glowing, prepared for anything. He said nothing, but his presence kept the group’s forward momentum from collapsing entirely.
The rest rode on horseback, grouped by instinct more than design.
They split at the old statue roundabout, just before the broken rail district, three teams, three gates, three slim chances to escape the city alive.
Ash and Nyssa rode on either side, guarding the family cart, with Garr still on the reins. Their route hugged the old warehouse quarter, weaving past fire-scarred walls and crumbled archways.
As they passed near the gutted barracks yard. A deep, wet groan echoed through the broken gate.
Nyssa looked around for the source of the noise. When she saw it, her mouth dropped open. Her eyes locked on what was walking down the street towards the main gate, “What in the name of all that is holy is that?” she said.
Garr turned and looked, voice flat. “That’s the Warbeast. That is the kind of problem that outlives the people who made it.” His eyes locked on it. “They are dealing with stuff better left alone. They will learn that some secrets are better left burned,” Garr said, unaware that he was talking out loud.
A cold chill of fear ran up all their spines at the mere presence of that thing. Chains dangled from its massive limbs as it lumbered toward the main gate road. The sigils were lit, all up and down its back. 
The chains weren't binding it. They were remnants. Whatever had once held this thing had broken, and these were what was left of the apparatus. The sigils on its back were not controlling it either. They were lit because it was awake. Those were different things.
Ash kept his mouth shut and kept moving. So did everyone else. The group veered off fast, covering the cart with urgency now sharpened by dread.
Riven and Reau led the westernmost team, looping through the merchant quarter and toward the riverbend stables.
There, they slowed. The townsfolk had changed.
Not just in posture, but in purpose. Men and women who had seen haggling over onions days ago now stood in silent formation, shoulder to shoulder in purple sashes, spears in hand, eyes vacant and shining.
Riven didn't slow the horse. “They didn't need soldiers,” he said. “They already had a city full of them.” 
“Stormhaven is lost,” Reau said. Nothing else needed saying. They rode by in silence, just watching as these people in the distance were gathering their weapons of war. Just... watched and rode on.
Dain rode with Weslin, flanking Harmon’s cart with quiet vigilance as they cut east through the broken fountain plaza.
There, the air shimmered. A ring of a dozen or more Red Cloaks stood in a ring, arms raised in silent unison. They weren’t attacking. They were chanting. Energy arced between them like veins of molten glass, tethering their bodies to an ancient artifact half-buried in the cobbles. As the artifact pulsed, a dome of violet shimmer rose above the city’s heart, stretching wide, wide, wider, until the group realized what they were watching was no attack.
Harmon had not seen adepts channel in concert in his lifetime. Not this lifetime. The frequencies didn't align. They couldn't. And yet the evidence was in front of him, and it came down to whatever was buried in the cobbles. The adepts were not the source. They were the conduit. Something else was the source. He had known that distinction once, a very long time ago, in a different context, under a different sky. He did not enjoy being reminded of it. 
Light surged outward like breath held too long, and then exhaled.
“A ward?” Said Harmon in complete surprise.
A dome, invisible until it flickered, stretched wide over the center of the city. Harmon looked at Dain and asked, “Do you think it is a protection ward?”
Dain muttered a curse under his breath. “No,” he said. “I believe it is a prison.” Harmon said nothing, but his stare at it was as if to burn a hole in it.
Lightning lit the figure on the palace balcony. Cloaked in violet. The hint of a crown on its brow. Alone on the highest point of a city that had bent its knee without a war.
Harmon stopped breathing for two seconds. He was not aware of it. Then he exhaled. And the discipline came back, the armor he had been wearing since he was someone else, in a different era, under a sky that no longer existed. He put it on.
He had not seen that crown in a very long time. He had hoped, with the specific and private hope of a man who knew what the word meant over centuries, that he never would again. 
Not Korr. Korr was a herald. This was the thing that sent heralds.
He did not look away. He did not speak. 
Dain, riding beside him, tracked his gaze and saw the figure. “Harmon.”
“I see him,” Harmon said. Two words. Steady as stone. Giving nothing.
But his ring pulsed once, faint and cold, and that was the only thing in thirty years that had made it do that without being asked. 
Not a usurper. Stormhaven had not been taken by ambition. It had been taken by something patient enough to wait for exactly the right moment and old enough to recognize when that moment arrived. He shook his head. Get clear first. That call comes after, he thought.
He pulled his eyes from the balcony. Ahead. Road. Now. He clicked the horses. “We go,” he said. His voice was even. It was always even.
Then the bell struck, seventh bell, first chime, deep and sonorous, rolling through the bones of the city.
Nyssa turned her head toward the sound, wind tugging at the hood around her face. She rode just ahead of Garr’s cart, one hand on the saddle horn, the other resting near the hilt of her dagger. She didn’t look back at the tower. She couldn’t. In the cart behind her, the family huddled, Lady Briala murmuring to the children, her voice barely audible. Talron hadn't spoken in miles.
Nyssa chewed her lip. They’d saved them, for now. But Stormhaven was gone, and whatever lay ahead, whatever they’d stirred, was watching.
The bell struck again, the second chime. Ash squinted through the mist as he guided his horse along the southern trail. He rode alone, save for the whisper of fire in the back of his mind. The path ahead split into brush and shallow forest. No one followed yet, but the feeling hadn’t left his spine, the burn of being hunted.
They’d done it. Pulled the thread. Broke the spell. Now came the unraveling, and it wouldn’t stop here. Ash rubbed his thumb along his scar. This city won’t be the last, he thought grimly.
And in his mind, the voice of the flame whispered. They’re waking up.
Third chime. Weslin gripped the reins tighter. His horse moved with a steady rhythm, but his thoughts scattered like leaves. They hadn’t told him what happened. Only that they were heading east. That Aurelia was safe. That Aldrek still breathed. That they’d done what needed doing.
But as the tower receded behind him, a shadow clung to the corners of his vision.
He heard the whisper again.
Not from the shard. Not from Aurelia. From something older, something buried, and watching.
And it knew his name.
Fourth chime. In Harmon’s cart, the wind snapped at the corners of the tarp. Aldrek stirred, groaning faintly. Neavin sat cross-legged beside him, eyes closed, reaching for the last echo of his spirit hawk’s sight.
Harmon didn’t speak.
Didn’t blink.
He watched the road stretch ahead, hands steady on the reins.
The crown he’d seen in the shimmer of the ward burned into his memory.
Not Korr. Not yet.
But something worse.
He would need to send word. They all would.
But not tonight.
Tonight, they ran.
Fifth chime.
The river bend came into view. One group peeled westward, hooves muffled in soft loam. Another veered south, weaving between broken hedges and orchard fields. The third angled northeast, cutting past a line of watchtowers gone cold. Above them, the ward glowed faint violet against the sky. Silent. Watching.
Dain kept pace with Harmon's cart, one eye on the road and one on the bundle of robes and armor in the back. Aldrek saved them by summoning a divine sentinel with a limp arm and then taking a bolt down a shaft for the privilege. Whatever came next, Dain was going to make sure the man lived long enough to have opinions about it.
It was the only thought he had for the next few miles, and he was committing to it.
Sixth chime.
Riven kept his eyes forward, the tower’s glow a faint smear in the distance. “We tell them everything?”
Reau’s answer came without hesitation. “Only what they can carry.”
The rest could wait. 
The rest would keep them up at night.
Seventh chime.
They did not speak.
They did not stop.
They rode beneath the sound of a fallen city still echoing through the hills, each heart heavy with what they’d seen. And what was still to come.






Chapter Forty-Nine
The rain whispered against the stained-glass windows of the war chamber, streaking the colored panes like tears. Logs hissed in the fireplace, dimming now to amber pulses of heat. A thick silence draped the stone room, broken only by the occasional pop of a coal giving up its life.
At the long obsidian table, King Edric Wyman sat forward in his chair, staring down at the mirror.
It hadn’t lit up again, not since dawn.
The polished oval sat still on its iron base, its surface dark and smooth. Given to him by Harmon before the teams departed, the mirror had been used several times throughout the past ten days, once to show him a map, once to transmit a coded report, twice just to confirm a location. It reflected the image of whoever held its twin, linking the two like a private door between minds.
Now, it remained dormant. Across the room, near a marble pillar, Governor Meridian Drake stood in the half-light, shoulders squared, hands clenched at his sides.
They hadn’t spoken in nearly an hour. Edric’s eyes flicked up. “Still nothing,” he said quietly.
Drake didn’t move. His voice, when it came, was tight. “We’re past dusk.”
“The final fire hasn’t even gone out yet,” Edric said. “And the seventh bell hasn’t rung.”
That wasn’t comfort. It was math. A grim reminder that the window hadn’t closed, yet. The Governor shifted, and Edric turned back to the mirror. The room felt colder than it should.
Drake’s fingertips twitched near his belt, then stilled. Sweat beaded on his brow, though the hearth hadn’t lost all its warmth. He tried to focus on the room, the dark banners of the Accord hanging high, the old map of the Northern Territories behind the King’s chair, the wine decanter that hadn’t been touched.
He didn’t look at the King. He couldn’t. He looked, instead, at the dagger pressing against the small of his back beneath his coat, the hilt bruising his spine like a secret he couldn’t confess.
A soft hum broke the silence. The mirror pulsed. Both men turned.
Light shimmered along its edge, flared once, then went dark again. Nothing followed. No voice. No image. No words.
Drake was the first to speak. “Did you make anything out?”
Edric stared at the mirror for another heartbeat before answering. “No. I don’t know. They could still be moving,” Edric said.
Drake ran through the rest faster than he could stop himself. “Or they had to break contact. Or the route changed. Or the signal failed.” He stopped. “Or it didn't fail.” He stopped again. 
“Yes,” Edric said quietly. “All of that's possible.”
Drake’s voice thinned. “Or the mission failed entirely. Or…” His voice cracked. “Or they’re dead, and the mirror’s just….”
Edric didn’t answer immediately. “It could also mean,” he said carefully, “that they succeeded and decided not to risk another transmission until they were clear.”
Drake nodded once, but his eyes stayed locked on the mirror.
Edric tilted his head, studying it. “Or Harmon pressed the wrong sigil and activated the wrong side. Wouldn’t be the first time he’s misunderstood instructions.”
Drake didn’t smile. Didn’t move.
Edric sighed, then stepped closer and placed a steady hand on Drake’s shoulder.
“Meridian,” he said. “I could mean a hundred different things. We will know when we know. You’ve done everything you can. Whatever this means, it doesn’t mean it’s over. Harmon is relentless. If there’s a path out, he’ll find it.”
Drake swallowed, but said nothing.
His gaze drifted inward, thoughts folding in on themselves, spiraling deeper as the silence closed back around them.
Then the bell rang.
Clank.
The first bell rang, deep and heavy from the courtyard.
A chill ran down his back, a memory, a field soaked with ash and ice. Horses screaming. Swords crossing. The moment he’d turned to find a young prince, Edric, standing over him, back-to-back, their blades red with firelight. They hadn’t spoken then, just fought. That night, they held the line together against the New Morlin army, and neither of them had forgotten it since.
Clank.
His eyes closed. A hallway. Candlelight. The smell of lilac and ink. Karethiel laughed as she read him a letter aloud, teasing him for mispronouncing a noble’s name. Her voice always calmed him. He had not heard it in ten days. He had written her a poem once, terrible and off-rhythm, and she’d framed it anyway.
Clank.
His heart squeezed as two little faces entered his vision. Camryn, cheeks sticky with honey, chasing butterflies in the garden. Lysa perched on his shoulders, asking if all kings wore hats that shiny. He remembered her hand in his, asking if he'd be back before the moon was full. He told her yes.
He lied.
Clank.
He flinched. A hallway again. This time, darker. Colton’s gloved hand reached into a velvet pouch and pulled out a lock of blood-matted hair. “Do what is required of you,” the Steward had whispered. “If you don’t… it will be a work of art.” Then he was gone.
Clank.
The blade’s name was Whisperfang. He hadn’t known it at first. The Steward told him only after he'd accepted it. A dagger that didn’t just kill. A dagger that hollowed. The soul of the target, gone. The body, left standing… for someone else.
Clank.
His fingers slid beneath the back of his belt. The dagger was there. Cold. Waiting. This was the moment. No more delays. One clean strike, and maybe they would live. His breath caught. He looked at Edric one last time. The King hadn’t moved. Still watching the mirror.
Still trusting him. Still.
Clank.
He drew the blade and lunged. It struck iron. The blade skidded sideways, and Drake's wrist wrenched with it. Edric had taken precautions. Drake hadn't planned for that. He should have.
Edric spun.
The chainmail glinted as the dagger deflected off his ribs. Without a word, the King struck him, hard, backhanded, and Drake staggered into the stone, pain blooming along his face. Blood dripped from his lip, hot and bitter.
The chamber erupted in motion. The door slammed open. Sergeant Josiah burst in, followed by two guards, steel drawn. But Edric didn’t yell, just raised a hand, and they all stopped mid-step.
He reached into his coat and pulled free a parchment. He held it aloft. On it, one line:
Don’t trust your closest friends.
Drake didn’t move.
He was on his knees, breath heaving, hands open. Tears streaked his face. He looked not at the King, but at the floor. Just one word came from the King’s mouth. “Why?”
“I’m sorry,” he whispered. Drake’s lips trembled. “I didn’t want to. I swear it. But they had them, Karethiel… Camryn… Lysa. They said if I didn’t, if I didn’t.” His voice broke. “Steward Colton. He gave me the blade. He gave me the hair.”
“Where?” Edric said.
“My room. He’s been here the whole feast. Ten days. Watching. Waiting.”
“And you were waiting for a signal?”
Drake shook his head. “No. Not a signal. Just… confirmation. Anything from Harmon. Something to tell me my family was safe. But it never came.”
He wept openly now. “I thought…” he gasped. “If I didn’t… they’d be gone. And I couldn’t. I couldn’t lose them. I waited as long as I could, but…I’m sorry.”
Edric looked at the dagger lying on the stone. He bent, picked it up, and studied the blade. “What is this?”
“Whisperfang,” Drake whispered. “It wouldn’t have killed you. Not really. But your soul…” He broke again. “They said you’d keep ruling. Just not as you.”
The room was silent. Then Edric straightened. “I understand,” he said softly. “If it had been Mirelle or a son or daughter of mine, I would’ve broken too.” He turned to Josiah. “Take him to his chambers. Post guards. Ensure he doesn’t leave, and no one reaches him.”
Josiah saluted. “Yes, Your Grace.”
Drake didn’t resist as the Guards helped him up.
It had been silent through the bells. Silent through the kneeling. Silent through the words that had come out of Drake in pieces. Then it flared. The mirror, still sitting at the obsidian table, alight now with Harmon's hue.
Harmon’s voice crackled through, “Governor’s family secured. Karethiel, Camryn, and Lysa are safe. They’re with me now. Tell him his wife never doubted him. Not once. We are making haste home.”
Drake stopped cold. He turned. His knees buckled. One of the guards caught him as he sobbed again, this time from relief.
Edric stared at him for a long moment, then looked back at the blade. “Lock it away,” he told Josiah.
“Yes, Sire,” answered Josiah. The guards led Drake from the room.
As the door closed, another opened. Queen Mirelle swept in, the hem of her gown still damp from the rain. She crossed the floor without a word and wrapped her arms around her husband’s waist. He didn’t flinch. She said nothing. Her hands found his face for one moment, checking, then dropped. She stepped back and let him be the king.
Josiah stepped forward. “What are your orders, Sire?”
Edric’s voice was steel. “Find the Steward. I want him in chains before the dawn.”
Josiah nodded and vanished.
Queen Mirelle entered her private chambers in silence. The wine poured first. Deep red, slow swirl, steady hand. She didn’t sip. Not yet.
The echo of voices from the war room still lingered like fog behind her eyes. Drake’s betrayal. The dagger. The note. The confession. All of it, a performance that was now behind closed doors.
She crossed the room without pause and stopped at the open balcony. The chill kissed her skin.
He was there. A shadow draped in silk and smoke, perched near the stone railing, unmoving. She didn’t look at him when she said, “You’re early.” A grin stretched beneath his hood. “I’m eager.”
“And?” she asked with a half-raised smile.
“Three. Gone.” He stepped forward, breath quickening. “It’s done.”
He held out a small pouch. She took it, opened it, and found bloodied cloth, torn insignias, and the stench of copper inside. She smiled softly. “Proof. Well done.”
He inhaled as he stepped closer, nose almost brushing her hair, fingers twitching at his sides. He moved close. His eyes stayed too long. The kind of looking that forgot it was looking. 
“Now… my payment.”
She turned to face him, eyes unreadable. Her hand rose slowly, a single finger pressing to his lips before he could lean in. She let her fingers rest against his chest for just a moment, light enough to be accidental, deliberate enough not to be. “You think I have forgotten?” she said, and something in her voice was genuine enough to be dangerous. “I haven't.” She let that land. Let him wonder which part she meant. Then the smile came, slow and private. “I keep my promises. Every one of them. And when this is finished, I intend to enjoy keeping that one.” She stepped back just far enough. “Good things are worth finishing for.”
He kissed her anyway, desperate and gasping at it. She returned the effort, letting it last long enough to tether his hunger tighter.
His hand slid down her body to her hips, and he moved to pull her closer. For half a second, she held her face slightly away, restoring the expression before he could read the restoration. Then she stepped back. “Not yet.” 
“But… I thought…” he said.
From her sleeve, she pulled a folded note. “This time, no names. Only instructions,” she said.
He took it, trembling fingers betraying the illusion of control. “After this… you’ll be mine?”
She smiled again. Let him dream. That was the leash. “After this, you’ll get everything you deserve.”
He leaned forward again. “One more kiss?”
She obliged. Deeper. Longer. She let her lips linger just enough.
“Now go,” she murmured. “My husband is coming.”
The balcony emptied in a blink. She stayed facing the door, hand on the stone rail. The scent of him still clung to her dress. She wondered briefly if Edric would smell it. Then decided she did not care. There was nothing in this room she would not tell him if he asked.
Footsteps. Warm arms wrapped around her waist from behind. A kiss to her neck. Then his voice, low in her ear, “Is it done?”
Her reply was a whisper: “Oh yes. Men are so easy to manipulate. For most… it is one thing.”
Edric didn’t move. “What has it cost?” His breath caught slightly. “Did you…?”
She turned in his arms and pressed a hand to his chest. “No. That is only for you. You’re the only one who’s ever been man enough to keep up with me.”
He smiled, then kissed her. This time, deeply. No politics. No games. Just him and her.
“It is rare in these royal marriages to find someone you love and someone who can rule beside you. I was told the two rarely came together. God the Creator made a liar of everyone who told me that.”
She smiled back. “He smiled at us both.”
They stood there for a moment. Then she spoke again, voice like silk-wrapped steel, “He’s ours now, Drake. He will never rise again. He owes you everything.”
Edric didn’t smile. But he didn’t disagree. “And after I ride into Aldoria with my forces to help secure their border, with the people watching me lead and him follow…” He exhaled through his nose, dark satisfaction in his voice. “He will bend the knee. And I will have control of them.”
Mirelle’s lips curved with approval. “Now it’s accelerated,” she said, brushing her fingers over the mirror’s base. “Thanks to Aldoria’s chaos, we can take advantage of that and move everything up. Once my part is finished.”
Then she looked up at him, eyes gleaming.
“…your father’s dream, your bloodline’s right, will be fulfilled.”
Edric pulled her into one final kiss, slower this time, but no less intense.
When they parted, he looked down at her with a faint smirk. “When that assassin returns,” he said, “he won’t get the reward he thinks he will.”
She let out a quiet laugh. “As I said, he will get the surprise he deserves.”
The warmth in his eyes did not match his smile. He pulled her close. “I want you tonight. Come to my chambers,” he said, and the command in his voice was the same one he used when reviewing maps.
She raised an eyebrow, playful. “How many others have you invited to your chambers since we wed?”
“None,” he said, brushing her cheek. “You’re the only one who’s seen them after dark.” He kissed her. She let it be what it was. She had known before she asked, she always knew. Some questions were worth asking for the way he answered them, like he had never once considered saying anything else. 
They separated, and he turned to go. Her smile widened. “I was already planning to.” She let him take one step, his head half turned away, before she added, “I will be waiting for you in your chambers. Wearing only a smile.”
He turned back in a flash.
“It is time we gave the people an heir,” she said. “For me to give you a son.”
His smile changed. Quieter than the political one. Truer. “A daughter works as well,” he said. He could see it without trying. A younger version of her, with her mind, her nerve. Her specific ruthlessness applied to problems that mattered. Whatever name the child carried, this kingdom would not want for leadership. 
She moved close to him again, their lips meeting once more. Then he pulled away, reluctantly. “I must go. Need to say goodnight to our guests.”
“Go,” she said softly, watching him go.
“Tonight,” he said as the door closed behind him.
She stood alone, picked up the glass of wine, and took a long drink, eyes still on the rainy sky beyond her balcony. Holding the glass by her face, deep in thought, she whispered to herself, “Soon.”
King Edric stepped out of his wife’s private chambers, adjusting his collar as he moved down the corridor.
Outside the great hall, nobles milled about in small clusters, their voices low with fatigue and wine. Servants extinguished lanterns as the final night of the feast wound down.
“Lord Merrin, safe travels in the morning,” Edric said with a nod to the aging noble and his wife, who bowed and began ascending the eastern staircase.
“Lady Sereva,” he added with a polite smile. “I trust the musicians didn’t offend.”
“Only their tempo,” she quipped, earning a chuckle from the king.
He turned toward the eastern archway and slowed. A compact woman in a deep indigo sash stepped forward with the deliberateness of someone who had been waiting for precisely this moment. Merchant-Admiral Sola Drey of Varek. Three island chains south of Opindale, ten port towns on the Merchant Island alone. She was the kind of woman who made other negotiators feel they were behind on their paperwork.
“Article Seven,” she said without preamble. “I want to confirm my fleet reads the harbor access language the same way your trade minister does.”
“I imagine it reads the same to both of you,” Edric said, “which is why both of you left the table satisfied.”
She studied him. Then something like respect crossed her face, quick as a weather change. “Good evening, Majesty.”
He moved on.
Near the base of the main stair, a man stood alone. Factor Jeld of Ashmark, the one surviving city on the Mirror Sea's northern coast. He wore good formal wool, but the cut was heavier than the room called for, the collar higher than fashion required. A man who had learned to dress for indoors and outdoors at the same time because in Ashmark, the difference was sometimes academic. He had no country colors. Ashmark had none. Only the coin and the long memory of a city that had survived the burning of everything around it, then thrived from it.
