“Things are moving in the north, Majesty,” he said when Edric reached him. Not a greeting. Not quite a warning. “Not our business to say what. But Ashmark thought you should know the passes are opening earlier than they should.”
Edric kept his face still. “I appreciate the observation.”
“No charge,” Jeld said. “Tonight.”
He stepped back into the crowd without looking away. That was Ashmark's manner. They always watched while retreating.
A young lord fell into step beside Edric for half a corridor before seeming to realize that required nerve. Lord Colven of Serath, the small coastal nation west of the peninsula, here representing his father, who was too old for the crossing. He smelled faintly of salt air even indoors.
“The timber clause,” he said quickly. “My father wanted me to say thank you. The timber clause was the thing.”
“Your father negotiated it well,” Edric said.
“He'll be pleased to hear that.”
“He should be. He didn't give any ground he didn't have to.”
Colven smiled and dropped back. That was Serath done.
A voice interrupted before the king could respond further. “Majesty,” called a man from across the hall, lifting a hand in greeting, one of the foreign dignitaries, his formal sash trailing. “Might I have a word before…”
Another voice cut in. Quieter. Older. Deeper. “Forgive the intrusion,” came a voice. “But I believe I’ve earned the next word.”
The dignitary blinked, faltered, and stepped back as a robed figure moved between them with unsettling ease, white-haired, weathered, and short in stature, but cloaked in a presence that stole attention. His garments were formal, but two generations out of fashion. Rings lined his fingers. His eyes held centuries. He walked without effort, like the air itself made room for him.
Edric turned, the warmth still on his face from Mirelle’s parting smile. It faded. The old man noted it before anything else. He had seen that particular warmth before, on a face this one would never have recognized. The same pull at the corner of the eyes. The same breath before someone said a name they trusted. He held it for one beat, then put it somewhere quiet. His expression didn't change. It never changed. But his hands were very still at his sides, the way a man's hands went still when he was holding something carefully that no one else could see. 
“I don’t recognize you,” the King said carefully. “Are you with one of the attending nations?”
The man gave a soft smile, neither kind nor mocking. Just… knowing. “No. Just a guest tonight. A friend.”
Edric raised a brow. “Of whom?”
The man’s head tilted. “Of the realm.”
The words found something in him that was already waiting for them. 
Edric stepped closer, lowering his voice. “And what does this friend want?”
The man’s gaze swept the crowd and then returned to the king’s with quiet weight. “To tell you something you need to hear, though you already feel it, don’t you?”
Something in Edric's posture shifted. “Feel what?” 
“That a door is opening,” the man said. “One that was closed at great cost, not long enough ago. That beneath the lights and the laughter, something long denied has begun to move again. Something that remembers power, not age.” 
Edric’s breath caught, just for a moment. “What do you know,” he asked, “that I don’t?”
The man didn’t answer at first. Looking at the king, he said calmly, “What I know would take more nights than this feast has left. Tonight, one piece is enough.” He took another step forward, his voice lowering like dusk falling. “The Uncrowned King is returning.”
Edric stiffened. 
“He just made his first play,” the man continued. “Stormhaven was the first jewel in his unclaimed crown. It will not be the last.”
The king swallowed. “You’re certain of this.”
“I am,” the man said. “And I come with more than certainty.”
His fingers tapped against the side of a silver ring. “My ears are many. They gather whispers. Warnings.”
He leaned in just enough for only the king to hear.
“Here is the one you must remember. The Time of Man is over.”
Silence stretched between them like a held breath.
Edric’s voice came low. “Who are you?”
But the man was already turning. Before he moved, his gaze swept the hall once. Unhurried. The practiced arc of a man who had been reading rooms longer than most rooms had been standing.
The crowd moved the way crowds moved. Glasses lifted. Heads turned. Laughter came and went.
One figure near the north stair column did not move with it.
He watched for ten seconds. Not the stillness. The eyes. A real person blinked when something moved nearby, when a laugh broke across the room, when a tray clattered two tables over. The eyes responded because the mind responded. This one's eyes blinked on their own rhythm, steady and private, like a pulse that had nothing to do with the room around it.
He had seen that tell before. He knew what it meant.
He kept walking. Natural. Unhurried. The path took him close enough to the column that the servant's gaze crossed his for half a second before moving on.
The chill he felt had nothing to do with the breeze from the open window.
The cold behind those eyes was different. It was not just a lack of feeling. It was a lack of everything. As if whatever stood behind that face had never once needed the things that made a person human. The servant looked at the people around him the way a man looks at graves he has not yet dug.
He had felt that before. Once. A feeling a person did not forget because it did not allow itself to be forgotten. A feeling that had reshaped the world the last time he had stood close enough to it. One he had believed was buried. Gone. Dealt with the way things got dealt with when enough people paid enough of a price.
He couldn't shake it. And then it clicked. Some things were more useful in motion than stopped. He kept walking. Fought the urge to look back, careful not to draw those eyes to him. He didn't truly vanish. He simply stepped into the current of the crowd and was gone, swept back into the motion of the chamber as though he’d never been there at all.
Edric glanced back toward the place the man had stood. Nothing. No cloak. No trace. Just an empty patch of floor and the particular silence a person leaves when they were there and then were not. He stood still for a moment longer than he meant to. Had he spoken with someone? The voice was real. He was certain of the voice. He was less certain of everything else.
Then he felt it. Eyes from above. The upper gallery, somewhere in the shadow of the second-floor railing. He did not look up directly. He had learned long ago not to look directly at things that watched from the dark. He let his gaze drift upward the way a man's gaze drifts when he is only thinking.
Nothing he could name. Nothing he could point to.
He relaxed his posture and looked back at the crowd. The delegates. The wine. The last of the lanterns were burning down. Someone had been watching him talk to the old man, that was all. One of a dozen people waiting for their moment with the king, held back by the stranger who had stepped in ahead of them. That was all it was. He moved on.
Across the hall, unnoticed by most, a servant watched the whole chamber from the edge of a tall support beam. His lips had moved with every word. He smiled faintly. Then turned.
As he passed a darkened side alcove, he stepped lightly over a crumpled body, the true servant, pale and lifeless, beneath the folds of linen.
With a soft roll of his shoulders, he shifted. Bones cracked. Skin rippled. His form bent and blurred. The changeling walked on in silence.
The weight of the words lingered, each syllable etched like fresh script across the back of his mind. Return.
Edric had nearly reached the great hall again when something pulled him back. A voice. Hesitant and edged with worry. Three foreign delegates stood near the stairwell, cloaked in their lesser kingdom’s colors. One bowed, another sipped nervously from a goblet. The third was Countess Avren Talisse of Drenthal, her forest-green sash the only still thing about her. Sharp-eyed, composed, with the posture of someone who had been deciding whether to approach for the last hour and had finally decided. 
“Majesty,” she said, “forgive the hour.”
Edric nodded. “You’re far from home. I make time for those who honored my feast.”
“We’re grateful,” she replied. “But… some among our parties have gone missing.”
Edric tilted his head. “Missing?”
“Our king,” she said. “And two of his advisors. We’ve not seen them since the fourth night. No word. No sight. They left their rooms, but never returned. We thought at first they’d left early, but their horses are still here, and their cloaks are still in their chambers.”
Edric’s fingers curled inward, the gesture small, but not unnoticed.
They weren’t on the list. No one else was supposed to die. Only the heads of state.
And yet, some eggs must break before the feast can begin, his wife’s voice whispered through memory.
There is no unity without sacrifice. We were never made to be small. He had heard it so many times that it no longer sounded like a voice. It sounded like his own thought. 
Edric closed his eyes for half a breath, then forced the thoughts away.
He met the delegate's gaze. “Our city opens itself fully during the Accord,” he said carefully. “It can be disorienting. I can promise you, some guests... wander.”
“Yes,” she said. “But the king rarely wanders far without his crown.”
A long pause. “I’ll have some of our best look into it,” Edric replied at last. He smiled, she returned the gesture, as he turned away.
But his chest clenched, tight and urgent, as if the whole dream might crack if he didn’t hold himself steady. If he wavered now, the kingdom they wanted would crumble before it rose. He let it pass through him and kept moving. There was still a feast out there that needed its king.






Chapter Fifty
Snow drifted over the body at Aymir’s knees, catching in her hair, settling in the blood that still glistened dark against the frost. Lysana lay as she had fallen, her bow at her side, one hand still curled as if reaching for an arrow that would never be loosed.
Aymir didn’t move. Didn’t blink. The wind cut at his face, but he barely felt it. His rifle rested across his lap, his fingers loose on the grip, every part of him fixed on the ground before him.
Taerel stood a few paces away, his left arm hanging low at his side, shoulder turned slightly where the ache had settled deep. The air between them was silent but heavy, the kind of silence that only follows the worst kind of noise.
The other survivors moved with quiet purpose. Five soldiers, still on their feet and able to fight, kept a loose perimeter, their eyes fixed on the tree line and the broken ridges beyond. Three more knelt in the churned snow, tending to the wounded with what supplies they had left, bandages torn from cloaks, water from dented flasks. The rest… were gone. Their bodies were being gathered in a single line just inside the kill zone, armor dented, blades still in hand.
No one spoke above a murmur.
The massive gate that barred the pass loomed above, iron-banded timbers scarred by claw and steel. It had been sealed since the attack began, its great chains still. Now, with a groan that rolled through the cliff walls, the lock pins began to drop. Metal slammed against metal, each blow echoing like a hammer on a coffin lid.
Neither brother turned toward the sound. The locks gave with a heavy, reluctant thud, and the massive timbers began to lower.
When the gate thudded into place, a column of soldiers poured out from the fort, armor dulled, helms shadowing their faces. They slowed as they crossed into the killing ground, the smell of it rolling over them. None spoke.
At their head strode Captain Vance, flanked by two of his guards. His gaze moved over the carnage, over the huddled survivors, before finding a familiar face. “Sergeant Rockwen,” he called.
The sergeant straightened from where he’d been crouched beside a wounded man, his helm under one arm, his armor streaked with soot and blood. He stepped forward with a limp and saluted.
“Report,” Vance said quietly.
“Sir, Sergeant Rockwen, Ford City platoon.” His voice carried a gravel edge, the words worn by exhaustion. “Twenty-five in. Eight standing. Forty-five civilians were held in the chapel until these two and their team came through and led us out into the mountains. Without them, we wouldn’t have held.” He let his gaze go to the figure at Aymir's feet. “Those are the only two left of their team. The field was chaos. The enemy pressed hard and didn’t stop. We won, sir… but it doesn’t feel like it.” He looked back at the rows of still forms. “Too many won’t be going home.”
Vance said nothing for a moment, his eyes on the still forms beyond Rockwen's shoulder. “You did what you could.”
Rockwen shook his head faintly. “We all did. These men fought well.” He hesitated. “They shouldn’t be left in the snow.”
“Your first real combat?” Vance asked.
The sergeant hesitated, then gave a single, deliberate nod. “Yes, sir.”
“You did well,” Vance said, voice low but firm. “You kept as many alive as you could. That’s more than most can claim. But in war, you can’t keep them all. See to your remainder, water, food, and rest. You’re relieved for now. We have fresh troops moving up from the fort.”
Rockwen saluted again, slower this time, then turned back toward his men.
Vance exhaled, the frost curling in the air. Beyond him, carts began to roll from the fort, drivers hunched against the wind, healers bundled in heavy cloaks. They skirted the bodies without comment, heading for the wounded.
The brothers didn’t move. The captain’s gaze lingered on the shrouded figure between them before he gave a short nod. “We’ll leave her be.”
Aymir straightened, voice low but clear. “Thank you. We’ll take care of her body and belongings when we return from getting our things. It’s time we go.”
More soldiers were filtering out now, fresh-faced and unbloodied, their armor gleaming in the cold light. The tide of movement was steady, purposeful. This fight was in the clean-up stage, and it was no longer theirs to shoulder.
“It seems,” Aymir said, “you’ll have everything in hand soon enough.”
The captain’s mouth thinned. “Is there anything I can do for you?”
“Food for the road,” Aymir said without hesitation. “Nothing fancy, something that’ll keep.” He paused, then lifted a gloved hand toward the west. “There’s something else. About three hours that way, in the shadow of the ridge, we found tunnels that pass under the mountains entirely. They were used. They bypass the pass altogether. That’s where the orcs and goblins came through. You’ll want men there. We saw enough to know it’s not the only time they’ll try it.”
The captain’s eyes sharpened. “We’ll see it secured. And… thank you.”
Aymir gave a short nod, then turned to his brother. Without another word, they left the gate and began the long walk back to the cavern.
The path narrowed quickly, winding between frost-slick rock faces. Their boots crunched on gravel and thin ice. The silence between them wasn’t empty. It was thick with unspoken things.
“I should’ve done more,” Aymir said at last, his voice carrying low in the cold air.
Taerel glanced over. “You did enough to be standing here. That’s more than most can say.”
Aymir's hand tightened on the rifle. “Not enough for her.” 
Taerel looked back at the path ahead. “Then it’s my fault, too. I wasn’t at my best. You saw how slow I was. How I couldn’t keep the rifle steady?”
“Don’t.” Aymir’s tone was gentle but firm. “You were there. You fought until you couldn’t.”
Taerel huffed out a breath that might’ve been a laugh, but there was no humor in it. “Then maybe we both failed her.”
The words hung between them until the cavern mouth came into view, a dark slash in the rock.
Inside, the air was still and cold. Their makeshift camp felt hollow now, the echoes of its life already fading. They went about their work with quiet efficiency, rolling blankets, bundling supplies, packing, and checking saddles.
When they reached Luca’s sleeping area, it was empty save for a single bracelet lying in the dust. Taerel crouched, turning it over in his hand. It was his communication bracelet to talk to Weslin. The leather was scorched, the metal warped. Broken. He didn’t need to say it out loud. He slipped it into his pack with the others he’d constructed, the leather strap joining his growing tangle of salvaged gear.
Lysana’s things were next. Each piece was folded or wrapped with care, as if the neatness could grant some measure of respect to the loss. Neither spoke as they worked, tucking it all with care into her pack.
Before they headed for the horses, a healer approached Taerel. “Let me see that arm.”
“It’s fine,” he muttered, but the man was already unwrapping the blood-stained bandages. Taerel went rigid as the healer applied an ointment and fresh linen to his wound, wrapping it tightly. Before he would let him go, he fitted him a sling for that arm.
When Taerel finally got away, he met up with his brother, where they tied up the horses. They checked saddles and saddlebags, taking their time to make sure they were ready to ride out.
Mounting up was clumsy for Taerel with the sling; pain made his balance awkward, but he got there. Luca’s horse still stood tethered nearby, saddled and ready, but empty.
“He must’ve kept walking after he packed up,” Aymir said quietly. “If he’s heading south, maybe we’ll catch him on the road.”
“Maybe.” Taerel didn’t sound convinced.
They rode out, their third horse carrying the bundles of Lysana’s gear. Back at the gate, they returned to her body. Together, they wrapped her in a sheet, then a blanket, tying the layers snug with rope. She was lifted gently onto her horse and secured for the road ahead. Her weapons were packed away with her.
Before they left, they paused. The siege camp outside the fort was being dismantled in grim silence, tents pulled down, barricades toppled, the bodies of orcs, goblins, and joblins heaped and set to the torch. Smoke curled upward, carrying with it the stench of blood and burnt flesh. Soldiers moved through the ruins with practiced detachment, but the hollow in their eyes told the truth.
Neither brother spoke.
Aymir shifted in his saddle, the leather creaking under his weight. The wrapped form of Lysana lay draped across her horse between them, secured with rope and blanket, swaying faintly with each restless shift of its hooves. He glanced at her once, then fixed his eyes on the road ahead.
The weight in his chest wasn’t just grief; it was the words of the dying men still echoing in his head, heavy as stone. That shattered face Corren had described, the sickly-sweet stench of blood and smoke… Aymir doubted those would ever leave him.
They started forward, guiding their mounts past the wreckage of the field. The cold wind funneled through the pass, biting at exposed skin, carrying with it the smell of burned timber from the ruined siege camp they’d passed. Ahead, Sergeant Rockwen and the five soldiers still on their feet worked in silence, hauling the bodies of their fallen from the trampled earth. Frost clung to armor, the bodies stiff with cold.
When the brothers drew near, the sergeant spotted them and gave a firm salute, hand in fist over his heart. The others followed, their movements weary but precise, the gesture heavy with meaning.
Aymir reined in, returning the salute without hesitation. Taerel brought his horse in closer, holding out his good hand. “Names,” he said simply.
One by one, they clasped forearms, the cold biting through the leather of their gloves. Names were exchanged, hard, short syllables that carried the grit of men who had survived when most hadn’t. No speeches, no promises, just the quiet acknowledgment of shared ground and spilled blood.
Taerel gave a single nod, and Aymir added, “We’ll carry your part of this with us.”
They turned their mounts again. “The captain said he would like to see you before you leave,” said Sergeant Rockwen.
“Where is he then?” asked Aymir.
“He took a group of soldiers to that tunnel you told him about, starting to secure it from my understanding,” Rockwen replied.
Aymir drew a slow breath and glanced at his brother. “Guess we're headin' that way then.”
“What do you think waits for us out that way?”
“It could be anything, but no sense in making it wait. Let's go.” The two of them headed off towards the captain and whatever was waiting for them.
The ground covered more quickly on the return. Neither of them spoke. The valley gave them that much, at least, the bare ridges and the pale sky and the frost-still air, before the clang of hammers and the bark of orders found them and pulled them the rest of the way back. Soldiers moved in purposeful lines along the ridge, setting stakes, stacking stone, and stringing rope, turning the mouth of the tunnel into something that might hold if the enemy returned.
Aymir and Taerel reined in just short of the work, eyes moving over the activity. The beginnings of a fortified post were taking shape, a narrow palisade already stretching across the slope, dirt piled behind it in a low wall, sentries posted with bows in hand.
Aymir studied it for a long moment. “They’ll hold it. It feels good that they took our warning to heart.”
“They didn't wait,” Taerel murmured. There was approval in it.
Aymir gave a short nod. “Good. This needs to be sealed for good.”
They had barely shifted in their saddles when a figure broke from the organized chaos. The captain they’d spoken with earlier, his dark hair damp with sweat, jaw shadowed with stubble, strode toward them. His boots crunched over frost-hardened dirt, the lines of fatigue drawn deep into his face.
Aymir straightened in his saddle. “It’s looking good here. You’ll have this sealed and defended before long.”
“We will,” the captain said, glancing back toward the rising fortifications.
Taerel added, “We’ll pass along what we’ve seen when we make it back. The Crown needs to know about this passage.”
The captain’s gaze held theirs a moment, the weight of shared battle still in it. “See that you do. Every hour counts. But, before you go,” he said, voice low but urgent, “there’s someone who says he must speak with you. Says it can’t wait.” His gaze lingered, weighing them. “He insists it has to be someone from the Crown. I’m guessing that’s you?”
The brothers exchanged a glance. There was hesitation in the shared look, neither truly sure they counted as anything close to official, but Aymir inclined his head. “Yes,” he said after a beat. “That’s us.”
The captain’s hand lifted, signaling to the rear. Two soldiers stepped out from the shadows of the palisade, half-guiding, half-supporting a man between them. His sergeant’s coat hung in tatters, the once-crisp lines scorched and blackened, the crest on his shoulder charred and curling at the edges. A broad bandage wrapped his ribs beneath the coat, dark in places where blood had seeped through, and another strip of linen crossed his neck.
He walked under his own power, but each step was a stiff, measured thing, like he was bracing against a jolt of pain that might unseat him. His skin had the pallor of wax beneath the grime, and his lips were cracked from heat and thirst. Every so often, his breath caught, not quite a cough, but the kind of sharp inhale that betrayed broken ribs.
Even from a few paces away, they caught the copper tang of blood mixed with the bitter reek of scorched cloth and poultices. His eyes, though shadowed by fatigue, burned with stubborn focus, the look of a man who’d already been told to rest and refused. Whatever it had cost him to stand here, he’d decided it was worth it.
As they got closer, the sergeant’s eyes were cloudy with pain. His voice came raw, a whisper edged with desperation. “Messengers of the Crown?”
“We’re here,” Aymir said, standing beside him, taking the place of the soldier who helped him out here.
Taerel stood on the other side. “What’s your name?”
“Sergeant Corren Vey,” the man rasped, breath hitching. “Fort Dreknor garrison… Forgotten Lands side.” His fingers twitched weakly.
Aymir leaned in, the cold air biting at his cheeks. “Go on.”
“I was… Sergeant of the guard,” Corren began, eyes drifting toward the gray sky. “One of the men, quiet, kept to himself, looked me dead in the eye… and his face changed.” His breath shuddered, showing how each word was a challenge. “Not like shifting shadows. It was… like glass shattering. Pieces falling away until there was someone else looking at me. Someone… wrong.”
Taerel's breath slowed. He filed the word “wrong” somewhere cold and didn't take it back out.
Corren’s hand tightened into a trembling fist. “He smiled. I’ll never forget the smell, gods, I’ll smell it in my grave. Sweet, like overripe fruit left to rot in the sun… and underneath it, oil. Lantern oil, thick and sharp. It clung to him. Like he’d bathed in it.” He swallowed hard, eyes unfocused. “Then he was on me. Knife in the gut before I could draw breath.”
Aymir glanced at Taerel. His brother had gone still.
“While I was on the ground… I heard the horns.” Corren’s voice dropped, as if speaking too loudly might summon it all back in full. “Orcs. And a few Red Cloaks with them. Their leader, tall, broad, with scars down his jaw, wore the old Brotherhood coat. The crest was torn, frayed, but it was there. He moved like he knew every step before it happened.”
Something moved through Corren's face. Not fear. Recognition. Like a man who has not yet stopped living it. He breathed once, deliberately, and kept going. “On his left hand, three fingers were gone to the knuckle. He didn't seem to notice. He gave orders like a man reading from memory, his voice low and even, and the orcs listened. That was the part that stayed with me. Orcs listening. They hit us hard and fast… burned the stables, cut down anyone who stood, and left the rest screaming.”
He coughed, a wet sound, and one of the stretcher-bearers shifted uneasily.
“They weren’t here to take the fort,” Corren pressed on. “It was a raid. In and out. They knew exactly where to hurt us. Stores, barracks, command. And the changeling, he didn’t run. He moved with purpose. He went to the other gate to get to its mechanism. Jammed it, broke the gearing… whatever he did, it won’t open without a full rebuild.” His eyes locked on Aymir with sudden intensity. “They’ll be back. And next time… they won’t stop at the gate.”
For a moment, only the wind moved, carrying the faint bite of woodsmoke and the sound of hammers striking home.
“How do you know what he went to do?” asked Aymir.
“Because… He told me. They were going to cripple the Fort and make us pay, make us watch. He said I was to be spared the story, so they knew it was true and what was coming.” Corren took a moment to catch his breath before continuing, “There is one last thing he said before he left, ‘The time of man is over.’” Taerel filed it quietly. Seven words. Clean. The kind of thing that gets said the same way every time because someone decided it was the message. Not the changeling's words. Someone else's words, coming from the changeling's mouth, in a burning fort.
Corren’s head turned as he went into a coughing fit, trying to catch his breath between coughs. “Had to tell someone… before…” He lowered his head. His legs went uncertain beneath him, and one of the soldiers caught his arm. He didn't resist. They walked him away slowly, and he kept his eyes on the ground, like a man who had already spent everything he had.
“Is he going to be alright?” asked Taerel.
“He may never be the same. What he saw will stay with him,” answered the soldier to Corren's left. “But he insisted. Said he had to do something.” Taerel watched Corren being helped back to the fort, then made a decision. “Get him to Opindale. He needs a real healer, not a field kit.” The soldiers hesitated. Taerel met their eyes. “I speak with the authority of Harmon Deim.” The name landed. Both men came to attention. “Yes, sir.” They moved before he'd finished. Taerel didn't move for a beat. He had borrowed that authority the way you borrowed a coat that wasn't yours, hoping it fit well enough to pass. It had. He filed that away for later.
“I hope I don't get in trouble for that,” Taerel said. Aymir said nothing, the weight of Corren's words still settling in his gut like lead. He was already moving toward his horse, his hands finding the reins out of habit more than intention. Taerel mounted a moment later, working around the sling with the careful effort of a man who had learned what hurt and what didn't. Neither of them spoke again.
The captain’s men moved around them in brisk, purposeful lines, shouts carrying over the hammering of stakes and the scrape of shovels biting into frozen ground. Somewhere, an order was barked to double the watch. Taerel met the captain’s eye.
“We’ll pass this on when we link up with the other half of our company,” he said, his voice low but certain. “They’ll want to hear this.”
The captain gave a short nod, his jaw set. “Then ride safe. Words like that can change the shape of a whole campaign, or start one.”
They didn't need to discuss it. Their part here was done, and the burden they carried south would not be lighter for the distance. They turned their mounts south, the road to the port stretching ahead in the pale winter light. Somewhere out there, Luca walked alone, and the brothers carried what you carry when someone walks away instead of falling.
Snow thickened into a slow, relentless fall, softening the world until hills and road and sky blurred into a single color. The horses’ breath smoked in steady pulses. Leather creaked. Rope rasped where it was tied around the blanketed form draped over the third horse. Every few strides, the animal flicked an ear, adjusting to the unfamiliar weight.
They rode a long while without words. For the brothers, silence was unusual, unnatural even, but it fit the shape of the day. Grief had a way of swallowing cleverness.
Between them, the third horse carried its silent burden, Lysana wrapped and secured, the weight of her absence heavier than any gear they’d hauled before. Now and then, Aymir's gaze would drift toward her form. He always looked away before it cost him too much. Taerel kept his eyes forward, but in the corner of his vision, the shape was always there, a reminder that felt carved into him.
Memories pressed in with the silence. Aymir thought of home with the particular ache of someone who knows it is still there. Their father at his bench. Their mother calling them in. The smell of the sweet cakes she just made. The life that had not changed because they had.
Taerel thought of the old jobs, how they’d lift ledgers from lockboxes without a sound, or deliver a sealed parcel to a man who didn’t dare admit he’d paid for it. He remembered the long nights in smoke-hazed gambling halls, Aymir leaning back in his chair, eyes narrow and amused, as another mark overplayed a hand. And the other side of it, the quick bolt over rooftops when a deal soured, the hard laughter when they made it to a safehouse with the goods in hand.
And there were newer memories now, too. Taerel remembered Lysana laughing under her breath the night they sat up, telling stories. How her eyes had glinted when the flames caught them from the fire. Aymir remembered the way she’d stood her ground in the fight, quick and fierce and utterly without fear. The ache in his chest was the price of having known her.
Taerel cleared his throat at last, a small, human sound in the muffled white. “When we reach the port,” he said, voice rough, “then what?”
Aymir didn’t look over. “There’s ‘what,’ and there’s ‘after,’” he answered. “You mean after.”
Taerel nodded once.
Aymir watched the road unspool beneath the horses’ hooves. “Home is west,” he said. “Mother’s garden, Father’s workbench. The smell of oil and hot iron from the foundries. The clockmakers’ street with all those little brass hearts ticking in the windows.” A corner of his mouth twitched. “Ly used to say the West was loud because it was alive. She liked that.”
“She liked the pastry carts by the shipyards,” Taerel said. “Almond braids. She’d pretend she didn’t, and then steal half of mine.” His breath fogged and drifted. “We could go back. See them. See everyone. Let the workshop dust settle on our coats again and pretend we’re the kind of men who stand still.”
Aymir let the thought sit there, warming his chest and cutting it at the same time. “Or we sign on with a captain. There’s coin in keeping a deck honest. The West builds ships faster than it names them. Steel ribs, reinforced keels. I can shoot off a listing gunwale as easily as on a ridge.”
Taerel’s sling creaked as he shifted. “And I can reload one-handed now,” he said dryly. “A useful talent for impressing drunk sailors and getting myself killed in a storm.”
“Still,” Aymir said, and that one word carried storms and coin and far horizons.
They fell quiet again. Snow gathered at the brim of Aymir’s hood until he shook it free with a small, irritated motion.
“Or,” Taerel said after a time, “we lean back into what we were good at before anyone handed us a righteous errand.” His tone didn’t boast; it remembered. “Acquisitions. Doors that needed opening. Papers that needed walking. Rare things changing hands for the right price and the right client. Dice, cards, the long hustle when the purse was fat and the mark was mean.” He exhaled. “We were good, Aym. Better than most.”
Aymir didn’t answer at once.
“Or,” Taerel added, softer still, “we find Harmon again. If there’s even a ‘crew’ to go back to. This was told to us as a one-time thing.” He glanced at his brother. “Maybe it was. Maybe it should be.”
Aymir’s jaw worked as he chose his words. “This,” he gestured at the snow, the road, the blanketed shape between them, “was the worst of it. But it was also… the clearest. Every footstep meant something. I’ve stolen gold because it was gold and lied because lies are tools, and I’ve never lost sleep over either. But this… I knew which way was forward. I knew why.” He paused. “I didn’t like all of who I was in it. But I liked not guessing who I should be.”
Taerel’s eyes stayed on the line where white sky met white road. “Whatever we choose next, home, ship work, or finding another job like this, it could end the same way.” His glance flicked toward the third horse. “Maybe not tomorrow. Maybe not for years. But it’s always waiting somewhere.”
Aymir’s breath plumed in the cold. “It’s the cost, one way or another. You take the work, you take the risk. Doesn’t matter if the pay is coin, or cause, or both.” He nodded toward the wrapped form. “She knew it. We know it. Pretending we don’t is just lying to ourselves.”
Taerel nodded. “So maybe the choice isn’t about safety. Maybe it’s about what’s worth carrying the risk for.”
Aymir’s gaze shifted to the space where a fourth rider should have been. “Some people decide it’s not worth it anymore. They lay it down and keep walking.”
Taerel understood without needing the name. “And sometimes that hurts worse than the fight itself.”
“Sometimes people break, and he broke,” Aymir said simply. “We all did. He just… did it first. And loudest.” The snow made a soft hiss across the plain as the wind shifted. “Maybe he needed to not be near us to keep breathing. I don’t have to like it to understand it.”
Taerel kept his eyes on the road. “You're more generous than I am,” he said, and it wasn't a compliment or a criticism. Just an accounting.
They rode through a stand of winter-bare birches, the white trunks like bones. The sea’s cold breath was faint on the wind now and then, a far-off promise that the world still moved even when they felt fixed in place.
“Home means faces we love and a table that’s ours,” Taerel said at last, more to himself than to Aymir. “It also means laying all this down and letting it rust. I don’t know if I can do that. I don’t know if I should.”
“Work on a ship,” Aymir answered, “means never sleeping in the same bed twice and letting the weather decide your days. We could do it. We’d be good at it. It would feel like movement.”
“And going back to acquisitions,” Taerel said, “means we choose the weight we carry and set it down when the coin changes hands. It means using the worst parts of us like tools. Those tools fit our hands. They always have.” He glanced over. “This… whatever Harmon started… asks for the best parts. I didn’t know I had so many to spend until someone asked me to spend them.”
A long silence. The kind brothers could share without it feeling like a wall.
“Maybe the West has room for both,” Aymir said eventually. “For people who fix broken locks and people who stand when the wind tries to blow a city down. Maybe the next thing we do tells us who we are.”
Taerel huffed, a small cloud. “You’re getting philosophical in your old age.”
“I’m only two years older than you,” Aymir said.
“And I’ll remind you of it until you’re dust.” Taerel’s mouth moved, almost a smile, and then didn’t. He looked at the wrapped shape again. “We bring her home first. Whatever ‘home’ can mean, this is far from where she wanted to be.”
Neither of them spoke after that. The honest answer was that they didn't know where home was for her. She had never said, not directly. What she'd offered were glimpses, the name of a city she sometimes pronounced differently when she thought no one noticed, the way her jaw had set when someone mentioned the eastern sea. They'd ask when they reached the port. Someone would know.
They rode until the early light began to thin from gray to slate. The world inhaled cold. Snow beaded along the horses’ manes and stuck to the brothers’ lashes. A raven paced them for a time, beating black wings against the pale sky, then veered off toward the coast.
“Parents will be glad to see us,” Aymir said quietly. “Mother will pretend she isn’t counting the days. Father will try not to ask what we did, then ask anyway and apologize in the same breath.”
“We’ll eat too much,” Taerel said. “Sleep too long. Wake up and realize staying put doesn’t fix anything here.” He tapped his chest with the knuckles of his good hand. “Too much to decide now.”
Aymir nodded. “In the city.”
“In the city,” Taerel echoed.
They let the words settle like a marker driven into frost. No oath. No promise. A place to stand when they reached it.
Snow thickened, falling in slow veils that softened the edges of the world until the road wound like a pale ribbon between the shadows of winter trees. The third horse plodded between them, burden swaying in a rhythm that seemed to beat in time with their thoughts.
They rode in silence, not the kind that feels like absence, but the kind that comes when two minds are busy turning over the same unspoken thing. The talk was done for now. What awaited would soon enough ask its questions.
Taerel shifted in the saddle, digging into the pocket of his coat. When his hand came out, it held a small, dulled coin on a twist of worn twine. He turned it between his fingers, rubbing at the edge with his thumb until a faint gleam caught the low light. “Made this in Father’s shop,” he murmured, half to himself. “Scrap brass from a clock gear. Said it was lucky.”
Aymir glanced over. “It’s still round,” he said dryly. “That’s luck enough for something made in our hands.”
Taerel smiled faintly, holding the coin up so it caught the pale gold of the rising sun. “Almost the same shine. Makes you think the sun's just a bigger coin, and every morning it decides to land the same way. Heads. We get another day.”
Ahead, the road bent west, and the light came stronger, amber cutting through the gray, throwing long shadows across the snow. The glow spilled between the bare trees, tracing the frost on every branch. It carried the faint tang of salt from the unseen coast, and with it, the first warmth they’d felt in days.
The woods thickened, and the smell of pine and damp bark stirred memories: their father bent over his bench, the air sharp with sawdust and oil; the two of them hauling cut boards through the shop door while he grumbled about “apprentices with more muscle than sense”; long walks home after deliveries, boots caked with snow, stopping to skip stones over the frozen edge of the river.
For a long while, they didn’t speak. Hooves crunched in the ruts, breath plumed from the horses. Somewhere in the quiet, Taerel found himself turning the coin more slowly. The time of man is over. He didn't say it aloud. No point in giving it more air than it had already taken. But it had hitched a ride south with them, the same as everything else, and he suspected it would still be there when they arrived.
Finally, Aymir’s eyes slid toward his brother. “You know,” he said slowly, “this might not be the moment we decide what’s next. But…”
“We should schedule time to go see Dad,” Taerel said at the same time.
They both stopped, blinked at each other, and then, just for a heartbeat, laughed. Not loud, not long, but enough to warm the cold between them.
“Guess that’s settled, then,” Aymir said.
“Guess so,” Taerel answered, tucking the coin away.
The road ahead glowed in the morning light, the trees thinning to show the sky opening wide. Neither of them knew what the city held. They'd figure that out when they got there. Together.
The horses kept their steady pace toward the horizon, three shadows stretching long across the snow until the bend in the road swallowed them.






Chapter Fifty-One
The clearing sat like a held breath in the woods. Nothing had touched it in a long time. No footprints broke the snow’s thin crust. The old fire pit was nothing but a shallow depression rimmed with frost, its stones half-swallowed by moss and years of fallen needles. Wind hissed through the bare crowns of nearby maples, carrying the scent of old pine and the faint metallic tang of frozen earth.
Riven reined in first, his horse’s hooves crunching in the stillness. He didn’t dismount right away. The place had the wrong kind of quiet, not peaceful, but the watchful kind, like the forest itself was deciding whether to keep its presence a secret.
Reau rode in a slow half-circle behind him, scanning the edges where shadow pooled deep under the trees. “Looks dead,” he said, though his voice was pitched low, as if speaking too loud might stir something best left sleeping.
“Dead doesn’t mean empty,” Riven answered.
They moved through the clearing with the deliberate patience of men who’d lived this routine too many times, checking where the tree line dipped, where a half-rotted log might hide the curve of a crossbow limb. Riven knelt by the pit, scraping away a layer of frost with the edge of his glove. The black ash beneath was powder-dry, brittle between his fingers.
“Months,” he said. “Maybe longer.”
Reau eyed the tree line again before swinging down from his saddle. “No one here, then. Or no one who wanted to be found.”
“Same difference.”
Only then did Reau pull a twist of pine-scented kindling from his saddlebag. The flint strike cracked sharply in the cold air, and a few sparks caught in the resin-rich wood. The first curl of smoke rose thin and pale, then thickened into a gray ribbon that wound up through the branches, a signal meant for distant eyes.
“Fire’s our flag,” Riven muttered. “If anyone’s watching, we just told them where to look.”
“Then we’ll deal with it,” Reau said, though the words carried the weight of a man already making contingencies.
They kept their saddles on the horses, loosening the girths but leaving everything else ready to move. Neither spoke much. The clearing, for all its emptiness, still felt like a place with a memory, and neither of them trusted memories they couldn’t read.

It was Harmon’s group that broke the quiet an hour later, the crunch of wheels in frozen ruts, the steady beat of hooves. Harmon drove the lead cart, Neavin beside him. In the back, Aldrek lay unconscious under a thick blanket, his face pale, lips parted in the slow rhythm of deep, spent sleep. Aurelia sat near his feet, hood drawn, one hand pressed against her temple as if the cold itself had teeth. Weslin rode a short distance behind, scanning the tree line like the shadows might follow them.
Harmon reined in near the fire and took in the camp with a quick, measuring look. “Clear?”
“For now,” Riven said. “We walked the perimeter. No tracks in the snow but ours.”
Neavin helped Aurelia down, steadying her as her boots hit the snow. She leaned on him a moment longer than she meant to, jaw tight. The further from Stormhaven they’d come, the lighter the pressure in her skull had grown, but it still pulsed, sharp, sudden flashes of noise and heat bleeding through her thoughts: the roar of the crowd, the burn of fear in the air, the hollow tolling of the bell.
Harmon climbed into the back of the cart, kneeling beside Aldrek. He placed his ringed hand against the unconscious man’s chest; the firelight caught the band’s engraved edges, and a low vibration seemed to pass into the air. A faint glow sank into Aldrek’s armor, subtle as warmth bleeding into frozen metal.
“That’s all I can give him,” Harmon said when he climbed down. “Any more, I’ll be joining him in the back.”
They set to work without being told. Neavin dug through supplies, passing a small pot to Reau to fill with snow for melting. The first hiss of water over the fire joined the snapping wood. Harmon moved among the group, checking small injuries, a split knuckle here, a shallow slice there, cleaning and binding with salve that stung sharply but was clean.
Riven prowled the perimeter again, the tip of his boot breaking frozen moss as he passed, while Reau scraped ice from the stones around the fire pit. The smell of pine resin thickened as more wood caught, and the clearing began to feel less like a waiting place and more like a temporary home.
The second cart announced itself with voices, Nyssa’s low and wry, Garr’s deeper rumble answering. She rode in first, her horse’s breath ghosting in the cold. Ash followed a few paces behind, the lines of fatigue carved deep into his face. Garr drove the cart, and the governor’s family huddled under blankets in the back with Tarlon. Tarlon had one hand on the cart rail and his eyes on the woods. He hadn't stopped watching since they left the city. All their eyes widened at the sight of the smoke curling above the trees.
Dain rose from where he’d been crouched near the fire. He stepped toward her without thinking, catching himself halfway and shifting his weight as he’d only meant to check her tack.
“You made good time,” he said.
Nyssa arched a brow. “Were you worried?”
“Who would I be if I didn’t?” he said with a half-smile. “But the place looks better with you in it.”
Her smirk softened into something warmer, eyes catching his like a hook. “Careful. Keep talking like that and people will think you actually missed me.”
Dain didn’t step aside right away. He let the words hang, a flicker of challenge in his gaze. “What if I did?”
That one landed. She blinked, just once, but it was enough for him to see the shift. “Then you’d be admitting more than you mean to,” she said, voice quieter now.
“Maybe I mean to,” he countered, lips curving into a slow grin.
For the first time in days, she didn’t deflect. Instead, she closed the distance, her shoulder brushing his as she passed. Then, just as he started to turn, her voice came low, close enough for the warmth of her breath to touch his ear. “Then maybe I’ll stop making you work so hard for it.”
It froze him for half a beat, long enough for her to be three steps past before his smile returned, sharper this time, the kind a man wears when he’s just been given something worth chasing.
From where he stood, Riven’s glance toward them was short, but with a smile.
Someone got the pot on the fire. Snow in first, then the meat and onions, hitting the water with a hiss that the clearing hadn't heard in months. The smell was rich with fat and spice, cutting through the cold. Bread was torn into rough halves and passed around. The rescued family ate quietly, murmuring thanks.
Aurelia sat a little apart, blanket pulled tight around her shoulders. Each pulse of her headache seemed to match the flicker of the fire, dragging with it another sliver of Stormhaven, a street she hadn’t walked in years, the echo of shouted orders, the faintest brush of another’s thoughts like fingers against glass. Neavin crouched beside her, speaking low until the tension in her jaw eased.
Somewhere beneath the noise and the faces and the heat, there was an architecture to it. A shape. Something had been built over Stormhaven, and it was still standing, and she could still feel the edges of it from here.
The fire popped, throwing an ember into the snow, where it hissed and vanished. Around them, the clearing had settled into a quiet that wasn’t quite peace, more the brittle pause between storms. Garr knelt beside the family’s youngest, showing the boy how to hold a strip of bread over the fire without burning it. Ash sat a little apart, polishing soot from the metal buckles on his coat, his gaze slipping now and then to the tree line, the way a man watches when he's already decided something is out there.
Weslin hunched over near the horses, rubbing them down with slow, methodical strokes, his breath fogging in the cold. He moved down the line with a patience that had nothing of exhaustion in it, even though he hadn't slept any more than the rest of them. The horses were calmer when he was near them than they were at any other time. No one had mentioned it.
Dain and Nyssa were close enough to share the same patch of firelight, though not quite close enough to touch. She was sharpening a dagger, the rhythmic scrape of steel on stone oddly soothing in the stillness; he was pretending to watch the flames, though his eyes kept drifting her way. Riven prowled the perimeter again, a shadow among shadows, his boots whispering over the crusted snow.
The smell of stew thickened as the last of the onions and dried meat surrendered to the heat, steam carrying it into every breath. Bellies rumbled, a sound almost comical against the hush, and when Garr finally ladled the meal into rough wooden bowls, no one needed telling twice.
They ate in small clusters, conversation low and scattered. The family kept to themselves, their murmured thanks barely above whispers. Those not on watch claimed whatever warmth they could.
It was the kind of rest that comes between things rather than after them. And when the bowls were scraped clean and the pot set aside, the camp began its slow shift into the long watch of the day.
After they’d eaten, Riven sat cross-legged near the fire, pulling a worn leather pouch from his belt. He loosened the drawstring and poured its contents into his palm, a scatter of items that caught the light in dull glints: a brass-capped quill, a small glass vial stoppered with wax, two signet rings, and, last, a dull, heavy medallion on a cracked leather cord, its surface marked with curling, unfamiliar sigils.
Nyssa passed behind him, eyeing the collection. “You always loot with such… variety?”
Riven smirked faintly. “Took what looked worth the space… and a few things I just liked.” He turned the medallion between his fingers, the firelight sliding over the engravings. “This one? No idea. But I didn’t feel like leaving it behind for Merrick.”
She stopped, crouched beside him. “Mind if I…?”
He tossed it over without ceremony, and she caught it in one hand. It was cold against her palm. A faint, steady vibration hummed through her fingers.
Nyssa’s brow furrowed. “It’s… vibrating. Did you feel that?”
Riven nodded. “Yeah. Didn’t think anything of it. Figured it was a ward or some old charm.”
She turned the medallion over, eyes narrowing at the etched sigils. “No… this feels familiar. Back in the tower, we ran into a frequency lock, the vault doors. It felt just like this.” Her gaze cut to Reau. “Like your collar.”
“Did you try it on it?” she asked. Reau’s head came up.
“No,” Riven said. “It doesn’t look like a key.”
“It could be,” Nyssa countered. “If the frequencies match, that’s all it needs. Every lock’s different.”
They exchanged a brief look, the kind that carried risk and possibility in equal measure, and then moved to try it.
“You think that thing’s going to work on this?” Reau asked, fingers brushing the iron band at his throat. Frost had gathered along the seam where metal met skin.
“Only one way to know,” Nyssa replied.
He hesitated, then shifted to one knee, lowering his head to give her access. She pressed the medallion's edge to the collar's seam. The vibration deepened instantly, running through all three of them the same way, at the same instant, like a lock recognizing a key. The sigils on the medallion flared, not blinding, but a molten, ember-glow that sank into the metal.
A muted click broke the stillness. The collar loosened, slid down over his shoulders, and fell into the snow with a solid, ugly clink.
Reau’s first breath was almost a sigh, his shoulders easing as though a weight had been peeled away from his bones. His eyes half-closed, lips parting slightly, the magic sliding back into him like the handclasp of an old friend, warm, familiar, welcome.
But welcome turned to invasion.
The warmth swelled to heat; the steady seep became a river, then a torrent. It hit him like a dam breaking, shoving past every barrier his body had grown to protect itself. His breath caught. Muscles twitched. His fingers curled hard against his knees.
“Too fast,” he ground out, voice tightening to a rasp. “Gods—”
The next surge drove through him like hammer-blows, filling every nerve, crowding every thought. His spine arched. A blue light bloomed behind his eyes. The sound dropped to a muffled roar like rushing water under ice. The air around him almost seemed to shiver.
Color drained from his face. Sweat slicked his skin despite the cold. Then his stomach revolted. He doubled over, retching hard into the snow, the steam curling upward in thin, ghostly threads.
From the cart, the family watched. The mother pressed her youngest against her side. None of them spoke. They had learned in Stormhaven not to ask questions about things they didn't understand.
Nyssa was already bracing his shoulder. “Easy.”
“It’s…” His voice broke; he swallowed against another wave. “It’s like drowning… in my own blood.”
“Breathe,” she said sharply, steadying him with one hand and the medallion still clutched in the other.
Riven moved in without a word, catching Reau under the other arm. Between them, they got him to the cart, his boots dragging ruts in the snow. By the time they eased him into the bed of it, his breathing had slowed, but his gaze was unfocused, glassy, every muscle slack as if the magic still churned inside him, refusing to settle.
Without opening his eyes, Reau’s mouth twitched faintly. “Might not want to… for the next few hours,” he murmured, “but I’ll live.”
From the fire’s edge, Harmon had been watching. He didn’t move to interfere, but his jaw was set, his expression caught between disapproval and calculation. Merrick’s men had been the ones to clamp that iron on Reau’s neck, but it was what Reau had done to himself before that, the lines he’d crossed and the risks he’d taken, that put the weight in Harmon’s stare. Such choices carried a shadow. Some called it taboo. Others simply called it reckless. He didn't like it. He'd had this argument with himself before, and it never ended differently.
His gaze lingered on the boy longer than it should have. A faint tightening at the corner of his eyes. The smallest shift in his mouth, almost a smile. For a heartbeat, it was the same look he used to give during those early training days, when Reau was still raw and eager, before ambition and desperation had carved sharper edges into him.
The affection was still there, stubborn and immovable beneath the years and the mistakes.
Reau had been seventeen the first time he'd burned himself reaching past his limit. Harmon had been the one who'd found him and said nothing, just wrapped his hand and waited for the questions to start. They always started. He'd answered what he could and lied about the rest, which was the same thing every teacher did with a student worth keeping.
Harmon's eyes narrowed again, the softness shuttered away. He shook his head once, a quick, private motion, and settled apart from the rest, journal balanced on one knee, quill back in hand. Every few lines, his gaze lifted toward the tree line, long enough to weigh the shadows between the trunks, then back down to the page.
The sharp crack of a branch split the quiet. Not a twig’s casual snap, but the brittle, splintering sound of something heavier underfoot. Harmon’s head came up, pen stilled mid-word.
“That’s close,” Riven said from his post, eyes narrowing toward the sound.
Harmon closed the journal without a sound, tucking the quill into its spine. “We’ve rested enough,” he said, voice low but carrying. “Pack it up.”
Movement rippled through the camp, blankets shaken and rolled, buckets upended, the pot lifted from the fire with a hiss of steam. Boots thudded against the frozen ground. The clearing pressed in around them.
Another sound came then, a faint shift of snow, like something moving parallel to the camp but not yet pressing in. Garr crossed the distance to Harmon in a few long strides, Neavin following. The mental haze of his spirit-sight wasn’t in his eyes now, but his expression held the same watchful focus.
Garr kept his voice just above a whisper. “Sir, half our people are in the back of those carts, and the family's scared enough to bolt. A stand-up fight right now is a way to lose what we kept.”
Harmon’s gaze swept the camp, Aldrek still limp in the cart, Aurelia with her head lowered against a blanket, Reau pale under another. He took the measure in silence, then gave a sharp nod.
He raised a hand and caught Dain’s eye, curling two fingers to bring him over. Dain stepped in quickly, already reading the set of Harmon’s jaw.
“Pick two,” Harmon told him, voice pitched low. “You ride out now, find the other team. They started their part from the port city, heading there first.” Harmon handed him a map of the area with the city circled. “You have two days. If nothing, get on a boat and head home.”
Dain’s brow furrowed. “And you?”
“The rest of us go south,” Harmon said. “We’ll keep to the back roads, away from the river and towns unless we need supplies. Three, maybe four days if the weather holds. Right now, we don’t know who’s who, or whose side they’re on.” He fixed Dain with a steady look. “I don’t care how long it takes you to find them. Don’t come looking for us. I won’t have another team lost chasing ghosts. You get to a boat, get home.” He held Dain’s gaze until the meaning was clear. “We’ll all meet back at the stable.”
Dain's answer was immediate. “Clear.” Riven, who had closed the distance without anyone noticing, echoed it. Nyssa had edged in as well, listening.
Dain turned, all business now. “Nyssa, you’re with me.”
Neither of them acknowledged what had passed between them by the fire. That was its own kind of acknowledgment. Riven’s voice cut in before she could reply. “Let me go with you.”
Dain measured him for half a breath, then nodded. “Good. We ride in five. Grab what you need.”
The camp moved with purpose. Saddles tightened. Bedrolls cinched. Reau’s horse was led forward, its tack shifted to Garr’s cart. Weslin unhitched his mount and fastened it to Harmon’s wagon, climbing up into the driver’s seat so Garr could ride bow-ready.
Harmon took one last glance toward the tree line, listening. The forest’s sounds had changed. The wind was still there, whispering in the high branches, but beneath it came a layered murmur, the faint crunch of snow that wasn’t theirs, the slow drag of weight through frost-stiff grass. Whoever was out there knew enough not to charge, but not enough to stay silent.
A cold draft curled through the clearing, lifting the last smoke from the fire pit. The smell of pine and damp ash hung heavy. Neavin’s head tilted slightly toward the dark line of the woods. “They’re moving with the wind,” he murmured.
Harmon looked at the carts. The wounded. All of them. Ash was pale, the hollows around his eyes deep with it. Aurelia had her head in her hands, crying. She had been since the city. She didn't know what was real anymore and what was bleeding in from Stormhaven. Aldrek hadn’t stirred since they left the city. The rescued family huddled together in Garr’s cart, their eyes darting toward every shadow.
Somewhere in the distance, a bird cried, a sharp, abrupt sound that cut off too cleanly, like it had been interrupted.
Harmon didn’t hesitate. “Ride! Now.”
The group split without another word, snow crunching under hooves and cart wheels as they pulled away from the clearing. In moments, the fire was a dark patch of trampled ash, and the trees closed in behind them.
The woods seemed to lean closer as they rolled forward, the tree trunks swallowing what was left of the clearing. For a moment, Harmon thought he caught a flicker of movement. Two dark shapes, not enough to identify, but enough to know they’d been right to leave.
Dain didn’t look back. The road northwest was little more than a frost-hardened track, winding between the dark flanks of the pines. He kept his mount, an iron-gray gelding, just ahead of the others, the cold air burning his lungs as he breathed deep. Behind him, Nyssa rode with her hood up, amber eyes scanning the brush with that restless thief’s gaze, and Riven followed close, one gloved hand resting on the pommel of his saddle dagger.
They’d left Harmon’s carts less than an hour ago. Dain hadn't looked back, but the distance was there. South was safe for the wounded and the family. Safety didn’t find lost comrades. This northwest route was a gamble, and he felt it with every crunch of hooves on frozen dirt.
A jay screeched somewhere to their left, the sound sharp enough to turn all three heads. Nyssa’s gaze narrowed.
“Company,” Nyssa murmured. They slowed to a cautious trot, the forest closing in until the track dipped into a shallow hollow. That was when they saw them. The forest here felt older, heavier, the kind of place where sound went to die.
For a time, it seemed they’d slipped the danger trailing them.
Suddenly, just ahead of them, four shapes broke from the tree line, scaled, long-limbed, eyes like burnished copper. Lizardmen. Broad shoulders hunched under mismatched bits of scavenged armor. Each of them was armed with something mean. Their weapons ranged from a rust-pocked cleaver to a short, brutal sword. Long tails lashed behind them, shifting snow in slow arcs.
“They’re blocking the trail,” Riven said, voice tightening.
Dain’s hand went to his hilt. “Then we clear it.”
They dismounted in unison, boots sinking deep into the cold powder. The Lizardmen spread to match them, tongues flicking the air in slow, tasting movements.
The spear came first, lunging for Dain’s chest. Steel clashed as he swept it aside, stepping into the counter. The axe-wielder was already charging Riven.
Riven sidestepped, blade flashing low, too slow. The axe smashed against his guard, jolting up his arm, and a tail whipped around with bone-snapping force. It took his legs out from under him, throwing him flat into the snow.
The cleaver was already rising above him.
Riven’s eyes locked on the descending blade, and then Dain was there, sliding in like the strike belonged to him. His sword came up under the cleaver’s guard, wrenching the lizardman’s wrist wide. In the same breath, Dain’s boot drove into its midsection, shoving it back just enough for Riven to roll clear.
They came up together. No words. Just the kind of look men give each other when they’ve both seen the same edge.
Then they ended it. Dain’s sword took the creature through the side of the neck in a vicious cross-cut while Riven drove his dagger up under its chin, the point bursting through the top of its skull. The lizardman sagged between them before they shoved it to the ground.
“On your left!” Nyssa’s voice cut across the clearing.
They spun. She was already a whirlwind, one knife embedded in the axe-wielder’s ribs, another flashing toward the short-sword fighter’s exposed side. It struck true, staggering him, and she closed the gap in three strides. Her blade flashed again, low and decisive, and the creature dropped with a wet hiss.
The spear-carrier came for her next, thrusting high, but she ducked under it, sliding across the snow. Her dagger punched into the soft flesh under its jaw, and when she wrenched it free, blood steamed in the cold air.
The last lizardman, wounded but furious, swung wildly at Dain. He caught the blow on his guard, dragging it low, and Riven stepped in to finish it, blade biting deep under its ribs.
Silence fell in jagged gasps. The snow was trampled and stained dark red, steam curling from fresh blood. Nyssa moved among the bodies, plucking her knives free one by one, wiping them clean before sliding them home.
Riven let out a long breath, meeting Dain’s eye again. “Owe you one.”
Dain only grunted. “You’ll pay it back.”
Then Riven’s gaze snapped to the tree line. Movement, dozens of shapes, weaving between the trunks. “There's more.”
“We shouldn't just hang around then,” said Dain. They mounted fast, spurring their horses into a gallop. Wind burned their faces as they drove the animals hard, snow spraying up behind. From the tree line, a tide of scaled bodies and glinting steel filled the trail behind them. They veered northwest, pushing hard, the pursuit loud behind them. The three of them leaned into it, the cold burning in their lungs, the port city somewhere ahead in the trees. Behind them, the shapes kept coming. They didn't slow down to count.






Chapter Fifty-Two
The frost-laced wind had lost the stench of the lizardmen by morning, replaced by the cleaner bite of pine and distant salt. Dain let his mount stretch into a steady lope, not quite a gallop but enough to put more miles behind them before midday. The fight still sat in his muscles like cold iron, a dull ache where adrenaline had burned through and left him hollow.
Riven rode to his right, back straight despite the shallow cut along his ribs. He kept scanning the ridgelines as if expecting another patrol to crest them at any moment. Nyssa was just ahead, her cloak snapping in the breeze, braid pulled tight against the wind. Every so often, she glanced over her shoulder, not to check the trail behind them, but to make sure the two men were still keeping pace.
The land here sloped down toward a narrow valley, the trees thinning enough to give them a view of the town tucked along the bend of a wide, steel-gray river. Chimney smoke smeared the pale sky; masts swayed in the harbor like thin black spears.
They slowed at the crest of a rise, allowing the horses to catch their breath. “There it is,” Dain said, lowering the map.
“Big enough to get lost in,” Riven muttered, eyeing the maze of streets visible even from here. “And big enough to have eyes we don’t want on us.”
“That’s why we split,” Dain said. He pointed with two fingers toward the dockside sprawl. “Two go into town, keep it casual. One rides north for an hour, sees if we cross paths with anyone moving inland.”
Nyssa adjusted her gloves, expression unreadable. “So who’s getting the cold ride?”
“You like cold rides?” Dain asked.
“Only if they end with something worth the trouble,” she shot back, and he thought, just for a heartbeat, she wasn’t talking about travel.
Riven cut in before Dain could answer. “I’ll take the city's main road. If there’s trouble, I will have backup.”
Dain nodded. “Nyssa, you take the docks. I will head north. Remember, we have two days, after that we cut, and hopefully they will be ok.”
They sat there a moment longer, letting the wind speak in the dry grass and the faint hammering of some unseen dockyard drift up from below. Then, wordless, they nudged their mounts apart, Nyssa angling downslope toward the docks, Riven toward the town, and Dain easing his horse into the track that skirted the town’s western edge, heading north.
Dain had been riding long enough for the cold to creep into his boots when he spotted movement on the road ahead, two riders, their silhouettes framed against the pale sweep of winter sky. Aymir and Taerel.
He slowed his gelding to a trot, letting the wind mask the sound of hooves while he studied them. The road was straight here, visibility wide, and a direct approach would have them spotting him half a mile off. Where was the fun in that?
A narrow deer track curved off into the scrub to his right, running parallel to the road for a short stretch before rejoining it. He took it, ducking low under the bare arms of an overhanging oak, and brought his horse out at an angle that would put him just behind their blind side.
When he was close enough to hear the jingle of tack and the creak of leather, he kicked forward. “Road tax,” he called in a sharp bark. “Pay up or turn back!”
Aymir jerked around, hand flying to the hilt at his belt. Taerel spun his mount halfway before his eyes registered who it was.
Dain grinned widely, reining in beside them. “By the Creator’s good humor, I must be the luckiest man alive. Barely half an hour’s ride from the port city, and I stumble right into you.”
Taerel exhaled hard through his nose, the corner of his mouth twitching. “That was reckless.”
“That,” Dain corrected, “was inspired. And it means we’re in no rush. I’ve got Nyssa and her brother Riven searching the city itself. We’re to meet at a point outside the walls in about an hour and a half.”
Aymir frowned. “Riven?”
“Nyssa’s brother,” Dain said, matter-of-fact.
Dain’s eyes swept the road ahead, taking in the two riders, then flicking past them, searching for the rest. “Where’s everyone else?” he asked.
Neither brother answered right away. That was when he saw it, the third horse trailing behind, riderless but burdened. The shape slumped over the saddle horn was still, wrapped in a makeshift shroud.
Dain’s stomach tightened. “Who? What happened?”
“Lysana,” Aymir said, the name alone weighted enough to dull the edge in his voice.
Taerel kept his gaze ahead. “She put an arrow through a joblin about to reach Luca. Another dropped from above, out of the beams, gods know how, straight down. Blade to the throat. Quick. We couldn’t get to her in time.”
Aymir said nothing after that. He didn't look at the covered shape behind them. He'd been doing that since the pass, Dain realized. Not looking at it directly. Like if he looked at it straight on, it became something he'd have to carry differently. 
Dain’s jaw worked. “And Luca?”
Aymir’s expression was grim. “Went dark. Killed every one of them. I mean, every living enemy that was still drawing breath. Slaughtered. Scariest thing I almost saw.”
Dain looked at him sharply. “Almost saw? You were there, right?”
“Oh, I was there,” Aymir said. “But this… darkness rolled in over the whole field. Couldn’t see the hand in front of my face. Just the sounds. Screams. Things breaking. It was over fast.”
“True,” Taerel added quietly. “And when it cleared, nothing moved but us.”
Dain let out a slow breath. “Luca… where is he now?”
“Gone,” Taerel said. “After he killed everything still standing. He walked away. Didn’t speak to us, didn’t stop. We’ve been moving without him since.”
Dain let that sit. He'd known there was more to Luca than the job. Standing next to him, you could feel it sometimes, like standing near something that had been still for too long and might not be anymore. He filed it without comment. Some things required a quieter moment than this. 
The cold wind carried a long stretch of silence between them before Dain finally asked, “What else?”
Aymir gave the bare bones of their last few days. No embellishment, no lingering on details.
When they finished, Taerel glanced over. “And you?”
“Where to begin?” said Dain, then he cleared his throat and just started. “The king changed our orders after what we saw had happened to Stormhaven,” Dain said. “We went from recon and information gathering to a straight rescue mission. We got a threat that they would be executed at the seventh bell yesterday. So we had to pull the governor’s family out before they could make good on said threat.”
Aymir gave a low whistle, his breath steaming in the cold. “And you made it clean?”
“Clean?” Dain’s tone carried the weight behind the words. “It cost us.” The silence that followed said the rest.
Taerel glanced over. “Who is Riven, exactly? You have mentioned him twice now.”
Dain exhaled through his nose, almost a laugh but not quite. “Riven’s a Silver Cloak. We needed one after Nyssa was recognized; half the country wants her head, so she couldn’t wear the hood anymore. We had to find another. The only answer was Riven.”
He glanced at the brothers, expression caught between wry and weary. “Getting him wasn’t simple. He was rotting in a Forge Hollow cell, and we had to break him out. But he’s worth it. Not just some cutpurse with a silver clasp, he’s Nyssa’s brother. Grew up alongside her in the same orphanage. Not blood, but he calls her sister, and she calls him the same. Closest thing to family either of them’s got.”
They let the horses carry them a while, the sound of hooves muffled in the hard-packed dirt. The conversation slid into safer waters, stray observations about the frost creeping over the roadside grasses, complaints about the worn state of their saddles, and an argument over which tavern in Opindale poured the strongest ale.
The meeting place came up faster than expected. Dain had been watching Taerel's riding since the last valley. The way he held himself was too still, the arm tucked slightly wrong. He filed it. First order of business when they stopped. 
The group reined in at the edge of the meeting ground, a shallow rise overlooking the faint sprawl of the port city. The air smelled faintly of salt, carried inland with the steady wind off the sea. Dain swung down first, boots crunching on gravel, and motioned the others to follow.
“Let’s stretch a bit,” he said, loosening the straps on his horse. “We’ll need the rest before the ride in.”
Taerel dismounted stiffly, holding his bad arm tight against his side. The bandage beneath his tunic was dark at the edges, the cloth clinging. Dain crouched beside him, pulling free the satchel of supplies Harmon had pressed into his hands before their split. The smell of poultice hit the air as he uncorked a jar, sharp and herbal, cutting against the tang of sweat and leather.
“This’ll sting,” Dain muttered.
Taerel grimaced but didn’t flinch as the ointment touched raw skin. A thin sheen of sweat broke across his forehead anyway. Dain’s hands were steady as he worked, unwrapping and rewrapping, tugging the fresh bandage snug before easing the arm back into the sling.
“There. Good as it’ll get until we’re somewhere with a proper healer.”
Taerel huffed out a breath, flexing his fingers once. “Feels better already.”
“Don’t lie to me,” Dain said, half a smile tugging at the corner of his mouth.
They shared a small laugh, the kind that loosened something in the chest without quite clearing it. Then they all settled in the grass, the weight of silence hanging for a moment before light talk filled it.
Aymir tipped his head toward the city below. “Hard to believe that place once looked bigger than the whole world. First time Father brought me here, I thought every house was a fortress.”
“Not me,” Taerel said, his tone dry. “I thought every tavern was a fortress.”
That drew a laugh from Dain, unexpected and grounding. They went back and forth for a while, 
childhood tales, half-serious arguments about which trade fair had the best food stalls, even a few barbs about Dain’s terrible sense of direction. The sort of talk meant to push the heavier things back for a while. 
The laughing had settled back into quiet, and the quiet had settled into waiting by the time Nyssa crested the road. Wind tugged at her cropped auburn hair, her eyes sharp as they swept the group. A heartbeat later, another rider emerged, darker clothes, lighter build, with an easy posture that made him look like he belonged nowhere and everywhere at once.
“Well,” Dain said, rising to his feet, “look what I found.” He pointed at the brothers beside him.
Nyssa slid from her saddle before the horse even stopped, her gaze locking on Aymir and Taerel. They rose, greeting her with clasped forearms before turning toward the second rider.
“You must be Riven,” Taerel said.
The man swung down and offered his hand without hesitation. “That’d be me. Good to finally meet you two.” His grin flashed quickly. “She tells me you’re part of the original crew. I got drafted in when things went sideways.”
“Drafted,” Dain snorted. “That’s one way to put a prison break.”
“Details,” Riven said, shrugging easily.
Introductions passed quickly and cordially. After everyone was acquainted and updated, Dain clapped his hands once. “All right. Let’s get this moving. I’ve got the coin, let’s get a boat,” said Dain.
The city closed around them in a crush of stone and timber, narrow streets spilling down toward the docks. The scents hit first, brine and fish guts, woodsmoke, pitch, and the faint sweetness of spilled ale. Dockhands shouted over one another, gulls wheeled and screamed above, and the steady thud of cargo hitting planks rang through the air. Horses stamped and shifted at the strange sounds, but the group pressed through, weaving between carts and barrels until the open piers came into sight.
They didn’t linger. The boat was chartered quickly. Dain returned to the others after speaking with him, adjusting the strap across his shoulder.
“Half an hour, maybe less,” he said. “They’ll prep the vessel, and they will load the mounts in a moment. Leave your reins with the deckhands, they’ll get them stowed.”
The brothers exchanged a glance, then Taerel spoke. “Leave the personal cargo to us. We will find something to eat before the boat is ready. Preferences?”
“Fruit,” Dain said without hesitation. “Something to keep the edge off.”
“Same,” Nyssa added. “Whatever you find is fine.”
Riven lifted a hand in a lazy wave. “Bread. Don’t care what kind.”
“Waters for all of us, too,” Dain said, passing over a few coins. “Make it enough to last the trip.”
The brothers nodded, their weapons still slung at their sides, and slipped away from the group. 
Aymir stopped one of the dockhands with two fingers on the man's arm. Quiet. Firm. The horse doesn't move. What's on it doesn't get touched. They'll be back. The man nodded once and found somewhere else to be. The brothers left together, walking toward the town without a word between them.
The brothers came back before anyone expected them, bread, fruit, and water, set on the dock rail with no ceremony. Then Aymir drifted to the far end of the pier, settling between two stacked crates where the torchlight didn't reach. Taerel took the walkway above the gangway, arm in the sling, rifle across his good shoulder. They didn't look at anyone. They just waited, quiet as men who have already decided what they will do when the time comes. 
The three who remained drifted to the edge of the pier. The river stretched out before them, iron-gray under the sinking sun. Salt stung the air, and the sound of waves slapping wood carried a strange steadiness, like a drumbeat waiting for something to march to.
Small talk picked up again, softer this time, threading between them as the bustle of the docks went on around. Riven told a half-serious story about his first botched pickpocket in Forge Hollow.
