Nyssa leaned against a piling, smirking and tossing back barbs. Dain listened more than he spoke, his eyes half on the water, half on the crowd. For the first time in days, the moment almost felt like peace.
Riven was telling the story with his hands by now, Nyssa making a face that was equal parts disbelief and delight. Dain leaned on the rail and let them have it. He'd been watching Riven since the prison break, the way he moved with Nyssa, easy and warm and utterly unguarded in a way that most people who'd survived what they'd survived never managed again. Some people came out of the dark intact. He filed that thought somewhere quiet and let the story play out. 
It didn’t last. A pair of dockhands, half-drunk and carrying coils of rope, stumbled past and clipped shoulders with Aymir. He muttered something sharp under his breath, but the men just laughed and kept walking, their boots clattering down the planks. The air smelled of brine, pitch, and sweat, gulls wheeling overhead with hungry cries.
Thirty minutes would come quickly enough, and with it the boat, the food, and the next step of their journey. For now, they had a thin hour of borrowed quiet to breathe, though even that seemed fragile.
The horses were nearly secured, the creak of rope and splash of water filling the air around the empty berth. Nyssa had slipped off, saying she’d find supplies before the boat was ready. That left Dain and Riven together, shoulders bent beneath the labor of hauling gear across planks slick with river mist.
Riven broke the silence, voice pitched low. “You care for her, don’t you?”
Dain’s hand stilled on the strap of a saddlebag. He glanced up, wary, but Riven’s expression was calm, serious, almost brotherly.
“She’s been through more than most know. I’ve spent my life watching her keep everyone at arm’s length. You’re the first she’s let that wall slip for.” He tilted his head, sharp eyes narrowing. “What are your intentions?”
Dain let out a rough laugh, rubbing at the back of his neck. “Intentions? I don’t know if I’m foolish enough to put it into words. I just… don’t want her carrying it all alone anymore.”
Riven studied him for a long moment, then nodded. “Fair. If this thing of yours is more than a one-time fire, maybe I’ll stick around. If there’s room for me in whatever you’re building.”
For once, Dain had the right answer. He knew exactly what he wanted to say. He felt it. A snap cut the air, crossbow string.
Riven jerked, a bolt driving into his shoulder, spinning him down onto the planks. Dain cursed, lunging toward him, only for pain to sear through his leg as another quarrel slammed into his thigh. His knee buckled, blood soaking fast through the cloth. His face met the planks. He tasted blood before he felt the pain.
Bootsteps. Heavy. Measured.
Out of the drifting fog, three figures advanced. Gray half-plate dulled by grime, no crest, no color. Helmets hid faces, except the man at their head. Bare-headed, hair cropped short and iron-gray, eyes flat as slate. His gait was steady, predatory. They looked like death itself walking the dock.
Captain Thane Rouric’s mouth curved in a humorless smile, the kind that promised nothing good.
“Lord Merrick keeps a list,” he said, his voice carrying like iron across the water. “And every name on it is his to collect. Property, gold, blood, it doesn’t matter. He always gets paid.” His blade lifted, the steel gleaming cold in the torchlight as he leveled it at Dain. “And lords with loud mouths? He likes them silenced. So ending you, Lord Alric Rendsdale, will be my pleasure.”
The name hit like a blow. Dain spat blood, forcing himself upright on his good leg, defiance flaring behind the pain.
Movement stirred at the edge of the dock. Rouric’s head tilted slightly, that grin widening, as though he’d been waiting. “Come out, little fox,” he called, voice cutting like a lash. “No sense hiding. I can smell fear better than smoke.”
Nyssa stepped into the open, boots dragging on the wet boards, her hands empty at her sides. Her daggers hung forgotten. Her face was pale, her eyes locked on the two men she couldn’t lose.
Rouric’s laughter was low and without warmth. “Ah. Just as I thought. Three names from Merrick’s list, all lined up for me. Fortune’s kind tonight.” He let the silence stretch, savoring it. “But me? I like to play with fortune.”
From the shadows, two more crossbowmen emerged, weapons trained on Dain and Riven. Four in total. No mistake. No escape.
Rouric’s voice dropped to a near-whisper, more terrible than a shout. “Let’s make it a game. You’ll pay Merrick back by choosing.” His eyes never left Nyssa as he raised his hand, fingers spread wide. “One of them lives. One dies. You decide.”
The two crossbows shifted, steady as executioners’ axes.
The river slapped against the pilings. The torches hissed and guttered. Nyssa’s stomach turned to water, the world narrowing to the dark holes of the crossbows aimed at the men who meant the world to her.
Rouric’s smile thinned, cruel and patient. “Choose.” His hand began to close, one finger folding down at a time, the count steady, inevitable.
“Five.”
“Don’t listen to him,” Riven snarled, forcing himself upright though blood seeped black into his tunic. His teeth were red, his face ashen, but his eyes burned. “He wants you broken, Nyssa. Don’t give him that.”
Nyssa’s head shook violently, tears already blinding her. “I—I can’t…”
“Four.”
Dain shifted, bracing on his good leg. His jaw tightened, but when his gaze found hers, his voice steadied. “Nyssa. Look at me.”
She did, and through the pain, he gave her a crooked half-smile. “If it has to be one of us, make it me. Let him live.”
Her breath hitched, breaking. “No…”
“Three.”
“You’re not listening.” Riven shoved off the berth post, his hand trembling but his voice fierce. He jabbed a finger at Dain. “He’s the one she needs, not me. He’ll fight for her. Die for her.”
His words split her like a blade. “No! Don’t you…don’t you dare, please, please.” Both hands found her skull, fingers digging in like she could hold herself together. “Don't make me choose between them” 
“Two.”
Rouric’s grin widened, wolfish. “Tick tock, little fox.”
Dain braced on his good leg and made his voice do what his body couldn't. “Nyssa.” Just her name. Then: “Let him live. I mean it.” 
Riven’s eyes never left hers. The trickster mask was gone. No bravado, no lies, only raw truth. His voice dropped to a whisper, steady as the river’s pull.
“Don’t lose him.”
Rouric’s hand froze, fingers curled tight. His voice cracked the air like a whip. “Enough. Choose now.” Both crossbowmen held. Fingers tight on triggers. Waiting for one word.
Nyssa’s breath caught, her chest caving. Her mouth opened, but no sound came. He found her eyes one last time. Steady. Decided. No mask, no joke, and nothing left to hide. Then Rouric’s hand moved, swiping down. The crossbow came to life, the quarrel loosed with a vicious snap, releasing its bolt towards its target.
Riven moved. With a surge of strength no one expected, he shoved Dain sideways, stepping square into the crossbow’s line.
It struck him high, punching through his chest with brutal force. The impact rocked him backward, boots skidding on the slick planks. He staggered, arms flailing once, and for a heartbeat his gaze found hers, no mask, no trick, only raw apology and fierce love.
Then he toppled over the rail. The river swallowed him whole, black water folding shut without a splash. One moment, he was there, Riven, stubborn and smirking even through blood and pain, and the next, nothing but ripples catching torchlight.
Nyssa’s scream tore free, raw and jagged, scraping her throat until it bled. Her knees buckled, crashing to the wet dock. Palms spread wide, she pressed to the wood as if she could anchor him, drag him back with nothing but will. Her vision blurred, her body shaking, the taste of rust and river water thick in her lungs.
But the current gave nothing back.
Nothing but silence.
Her mind became her enemy as well. A hundred flickers of him at once: a grubby boy pressing half a stolen apple into her hand; a wiry shadow teaching her how to run rooftops faster than any city guard; a laugh, bright and reckless, echoing through the alleys of their youth. The weight of his arm around her when nights were too cold, whispering, We’ll make it, fox. We always do.
But the river didn’t care. It kept it all. She could smell the river. Brine and rot and cold wood. She would smell it for years.
“No…” The word cracked, small and helpless, leaking past lips that could barely shape sound. Her fingers dug splinters from the dock as if she might claw her way through to him. “No, no, no…”
Behind her, Dain groaned, struggling to push himself up off the ground. His voice reached for her, strained, aching. “Nyssa.”
She couldn’t answer. Her chest felt hollow, scooped clean. The crossbows still glared from the shadows, but all she could see was the black water rushing away with her brother.
Her throat seized, the scream twisting down into a broken sob. Tears blurred her vision, but the ripples never sharpened back into him.
And beneath it all, a new sound rose: laughter.
Rouric’s. Low, guttural, pleased.
“See?” Rouric drawled, boots grinding the planks as he advanced, the torchlight catching hard on his grin. “Lord Merrick doesn’t forgive. He doesn’t forget. What’s taken from him is his again, one way or another.” His blade dipped toward Dain, his eyes narrowing with contempt.
Her chest clenched around the thought and wouldn't let it go. He can't be gone. He can't be gone. But the river's black churn gave nothing back, only ripples fading to flat water, and the torchlight moving across the surface like nothing had happened there at all. 
Rouric’s gaze slid back to her, pitiless. “Riven spoiled my game. Stole the choice from your hands. Now I’ll take my frustration out on him.” His chin jerked toward Dain. “Your… friend. And thanks to your little stunt, girl, Merrick collects his due twice over.”
The flat of his blade smacked across Dain’s jaw. Blood spattered the planks.
Nyssa's body moved before she could hold it still, one short step back, involuntary, and she hated herself for it. 
Rouric’s eyes glittered. “Ah. He matters to you.” His blade pricked into Dain’s side, dragging along the bolt already buried deep. Dain arched, a guttural cry tearing from his throat. His grin widened as Nyssa’s face twisted, horror and fury bleeding raw. “Lover, then.” He leaned close enough for her to smell the rot on his breath. “Which makes this sweeter.”
Rouric’s voice sharpened. “Does he even know?” He jerked Dain’s head back by the hair, making the noble grit his teeth against the pain. Rouric released him and drove his boot into Dain's ribs. Another crack split the air. 
“Does he know?” he asked again. “Does he think this is the price of his own mouth? His own pride? “ Rouric’s grin widened, sharp as a blade. “No. He would already be dead. Simple. Done. No, he must know what it means to touch Lord Merrick’s,” he gave Nyssa a look up and down, “Property. Then they have to pay the cost. This one has a high price.” He drove his fist into Dain’s face. 
He grabbed and twisted Dain’s head to force his ear next to his mouth. His voice dropped, venom slow and deliberate.
“This,” he reached down and ground the bolt deeper into Dain’s thigh, tearing a scream from him. “This is all because of you. Every broken rib, every scream. Every drop of blood. It's you. This is the price of your betrayal.” He looked at her. Held it. Let her carry the weight of every sound.
He let go. Dain hit the dock and got his arms under him. Blood slick on his palms. Still trying to fight. 
He drove his boot down again and again until he stopped trying to get up. More rib cracks were audible. Dain coughed blood, teeth bared in a grimace.
Nyssa gasped, her body wrenching against the men holding her.
“Hold him,” Rouric ordered.
The armored thug beside him obeyed, lifting him, so the other could press a gauntlet hard against the quarrel buried in Dain’s thigh. He wrenched it sideways, then back again. Dain’s cry ripped raw and unrestrained, his body seizing against the wood. His fingers clawed splinters from the planks.
“Look at him!” Rouric barked, seizing Nyssa by the hair, twisting her head until her eyes locked on Dain’s suffering. Her body bucked against the men restraining her, but she couldn’t look away, her vision swimming with tears.
The soldier slammed his fist into Dain’s ribs, once, twice, each blow a dull, wet sound. Another twisted the bolt again. Dain’s roar turned guttural, shredded, a sound that clawed Nyssa’s soul raw.
“Look,” Rouric snarled, seizing Nyssa’s hair and wrenching her gaze forward. “Watch what your choices cost. Do you see?” Rouric leaned close to her ear, voice a poisonous whisper. “Every scream. Every drop of blood. It’s you, little fox. This is the price of your theft, your betrayal. This is what you bought him.”
Her chest convulsed. “Stop! Please—”
But they weren’t finished.
The captain crouched beside Dain, his blade’s flat edge tracing over the man’s ribs, then down lower, deliberate. “What good is a lover when he’s useless as a man?” He pressed the steel flat across Dain’s groin, the cruel smile widening as Nyssa convulsed against the hands that held her.
Her voice cracked, wild and desperate. “Take me! I’ll go, I’ll do anything you want, just leave him!”
Rouric chuckled, rising to his full height. “Oh, you’ll go. You’ll go on Merrick’s leash. You’ll be his jewel, his plaything, his shadow. You’ll pour his wine, warm his bed, and dance when he pulls the string. And when you think you’re free?” His teeth showed, wolfish. “That’s when you’ll beg him for more. Because you’ll know nothing else but him.”
“Finish it,” he said to the men.
The gauntleted fist cracked across Dain’s jaw, the sound sharp as breaking bone. Blood sprayed the dock in a crimson arc. Dain sagged, body crumpling when they dropped him, collapsing hard to the planks, gasping shallow breaths.
Nyssa’s shriek ripped her throat raw. Her knees buckled, but the men wrenched her up by her hair again, forcing her to see him broken.
Rouric leaned close, his breath hot with rot and iron. “Remember this, little fox. Tonight’s only the beginning. Merrick doesn’t just collect debts. He owns you. You’ll never stop owing him.”
He crouched down to her level. Patient. Eye to eye. “Your brother died fast,” he said. “He doesn't deserve credit for that. The bolt made that choice, not him. But fast is what it was.” Something moved behind his eyes. Not anger. Closer to grief, if grief belonged to men like him. “I had built something for him. Something I have been refining for years. The kind of work that outlives the man who does it. Stories do not start with the ones who swing the blade. They start with the ones who understood what the blade could be made to say.” He looked at the river once more, then back at her. “He took that from me.” A pause. Long enough to breathe in. “So I am starting over. New subject. New canvas.” His eyes didn't move from hers. “You should know that what I do to you will be remembered long after your name is forgotten, long after mine is. That is what I built. That is what I leave behind.” He rose from his crouch, unhurried. Straightened his coat. “Welcome to being a work of art.”
A crack split the air. Sharp, clean. One of the crossbowmen at the far end of the dock dropped without a sound, a hole in his helm.
Before Rouric could bark an order, another shot echoed. The second crossbowman staggered, fell into the river with a splash. The two gray-armored around Dain whipped their heads around, panic flashing in their eyes. Rouric snarled, dragging his sword free. “Archers!”
Another crack. Too close. He cut himself off as one of his men fell beside him. The brothers had come.
Rouric cursed, fury flashing hot before freezing into something colder, sharper. He ground Dain’s head into the planks with his boot, leaning close enough that only he and Nyssa could hear the rasp of his words.
“This isn’t over. Merrick doesn’t forget.”
He shoved off, motioning his men to fall back. Boots thundered across the dock as they scattered into the shadows, but Rouric didn’t turn. He retreated slowly, deliberately, his gaze never leaving Nyssa’s.
At the edge of torchlight, he paused, blade lowering just enough to gleam like a promise. His voice carried, low and certain, wrapping around her like a noose.
“Every time you close your eyes, remember, he screamed because of you,” he said, tone mocking the word like a curse. Then his lips curled, cruel and deliberate. “Run if you like. You’ll only run in circles. Back to him. Back to us. And you’ll remember tonight. Every time you close your eyes.”
The river lapped behind them, black and merciless, swallowing the last echo of retreating boots. Rouric’s shadow dissolved into the dark, leaving only silence and the stink of blood and river rot.
Nyssa’s body collapsed forward as though the strings had been cut. Her arms shook beneath her, scraping raw against the planks as she dragged herself toward him. Every inch closed between them felt like a mile. Her chest heaved, lungs burning, but she forced herself on, palms slipping in blood that was spreading wider with every heartbeat he spent on that dock.
Dain lay where they had dropped him like a broken doll, his face battered until he was barely recognizable. One eye swollen shut. His lip split to the bone. His jaw was slack and red with blood. His chest rose shallow, but every breath was wet, ragged, rattling with a sickening gargle that made her stomach turn to stone. He was drowning. Drowning in his blood.
“Dain…” The word tore from her, jagged, more sob than voice. She pressed her hands hard against the wound in his side, desperate, useless, the warmth of him spilling hot and steady through her fingers no matter how tightly she pressed.
His good eye blinked, searching, dragging open against swelling. Somehow, it found her. It clung to her with stubborn force, tethering her even as his body failed him.
“No. No, don’t you dare.” Tears blurred her vision, dripping onto his chest. She bent close, forehead pressed to his as if sheer will could chain him to the world. “You’ll live, Dain. You hear me? You’ll live. I won’t lose you, too.”
He tried to speak, but it came out broken, bubbling, just a rasp tangled with the gurgle of his blood. His lips shaped a word that never made it past his throat. A sound that should have been strength, defiance, but was only pain.
Her whole body trembled as she cupped his face with one slick hand, forcing him to see her even if his eye drifted shut. “Stay with me. Please. You’re all I have left. Don’t leave me, not you.”
She held him like that, knelt in blood and splinters, as the world tilted and the horror pressed down. His breath rattled, shallow, wet. Her sobs wracked her, but she whispered the words again and again like a prayer that the river, or the gods, or anything might hear:
“You’ll live.”
The brothers moved around them, Aymir tearing strips of cloth, Taerel scanning the shadowed docks for any sign of pursuit. But to Nyssa, their voices were muffled, drowned by the weight of her heartbeat and the river’s slow, relentless churn.
Her lips moved before her thoughts caught up. A prayer, raw and unpracticed, spilled out.
“Creator, if You see me now… if You hear me, then let justice fall upon them. On Merrick. On Rouric. On every soul who raised their hand tonight. Don’t let them walk free. Not after this. Not after him. Take whatever you require… just let justice be done.”
The air shifted, and it wasn't silence that followed. It was presence. The river’s roar dimmed, the ache in her chest stilled. A warmth pressed against her heart like sunlight breaking through storm clouds, steady and sure.
And then, clear as a bell, a voice touched her mind. ‘Contract granted.’
Nyssa froze, eyes wide. She looked up, but the brothers hadn’t stirred. The voice had been for her alone. But it hadn’t been cruel. It hadn’t been cold. It had been radiant, vast, and merciful, terrible in its certainty, but shining with the weight of something higher, something just.
Her fear tangled with awe, her grief edged with fire. She bowed her head again, and a tear slid down her cheek, not of despair, but of resolve. Justice had answered her. And justice was already moving.
The brothers were the first to move, breaking free of the shock that had frozen them all. Aymir shouldered beneath Dain’s arm, taking his weight, while Taerel steadied his wounded side. Between them, they half-lifted, half-dragged him from the dock, his boots leaving smears of blood across the planks.
Nyssa stayed close, blades still clenched, though her eyes never left the river. Every ripple, every swirl of foam was another chance, another hope, that Riven might break the surface. But the current rolled on indifferently, carrying him away.
Dockhands scrambled under shouted orders, hurrying the horses aboard. The boat rocked as ropes were loosed, the river’s pull already tugging at its hull. Amid the chaos, Taerel swung back to the last of the animals. The riderless mare that carried Lysana’s body shifted nervously at the gangway, the slumped form threatening to slip. Together, he and Aymir steadied her, then bound her carefully in place before leading the horse aboard. 
Only once she was secure did they step back, both men pausing, heads bowed, before following the others aboard.
Dain was lying on a narrow bunk below deck, blood and sweat shining on his face. Nyssa brushed his hair back with shaking hands before pulling away, unable to stay still. She rose to the rail again, searching the water even as the shoreline began to slip by.
The brothers lingered there too, silent, eyes fixed on the dark ribbon of river. None of them spoke the truth aloud, that Riven was gone, and Dain was holding on by a thread, but it hung between them heavier than a chain.
As the sun sank low, bleeding red across the current, the boat turned downstream. The city’s spires fell away behind them, swallowed by dusk. And still Nyssa stared into the water, lips moving in a prayer only she could finish.
The river carried them on.






Chapter Fifty-Three
The streets of Opindale were quieter in the pale warmth of morning, the kind of warmth that came off the sea breeze rather than the sun. Gulls cried faint and sharp overhead, their voices carrying down the narrow lanes. Harmon's boots struck steadily against the cobbles, Weslin keeping close but a half-step behind, his head bent in thought.
Ahead, Breckenstall Stable crouched at the lane's end, its timbers gray with age, its loft windows blank with dust. In lamplight, it had once seemed a den for ghosts. Now, in daylight, it only looked smaller. The years showed plain in sagging beams and weathered stone, yet a weight clung to it still.
“It doesn't look the same,” Weslin said at last, breaking the long silence between them. “Smaller than I remember. Dirtier too.”
Harmon glanced at him, then back at the building. “The place hasn't changed. You have. That's why it looks different.”
Weslin considered it, mouth set in thought. He shifted, fingers brushing the hilt of his short blade. “What does it really take?”
“To do what?” Harmon asked.
“To be a good squire. Good enough that you'd let me be a knight someday.”
Harmon slowed a fraction. “An arcane knight,” he corrected. “You're an adept, Weslin. Whatever you become, you carry that into it. Don't let anyone hand you a smaller word for what you are.”
Weslin's brow lifted slightly, then settled. “An arcane knight, then. What does it take?”
“Learning to see. To listen. Knowing when to speak and when silence does more than words can. Knowing yourself plainly, what you can carry and what you can't, before you ever try to carry someone else.” Harmon tapped his temple once. “Sword drills will build your arms. Yet you will have to build your mind just as much. This is what makes a knight, arcane or otherwise.”
Weslin nodded slowly, chewing on it. “So, the blade comes last.”
“The blade comes last, always. Everything that matters comes before it.” Harmon said.
For a time, only their footsteps filled the lane. Then Weslin asked, quieter, “The ring. How does it work?” His eyes flicked toward Harmon's hand, then away. “When I was small, I heard a story that a Ringbearer could walk through an iron door like it wasn't there.”
Harmon was quiet for a moment, then shook his head. “There are a lot of stories. Most of them wrong. A few of them are less wrong than I'd like.” He flexed his hand once, the dull metal catching the light. “What it does in truth is give me power. Strength when I call for it, speed when I need it, reach past what my body alone could manage. But it wasn't a thing I bought or earned in any market. It was a gift from God, and gifts of that kind carry a weight to them.”
“What kind of weight?”
“This morning kind,” Harmon said. “Every time I draw deep on it, there's a morning after where the body wants to stay on the floor. The more I take, the longer that morning lasts.” He looked ahead. “And no, it doesn't walk me through iron doors. That part you can let go of.”
Weslin studied him sidelong, catching the things Harmon had chosen not to say. He didn't push. He opened his mouth, closed it again, and nodded once.
They reached the stable doors. Sunlight pooled across the yard, warming the wood without lifting the smell of long neglect. The boards groaned as Harmon shoved them wide, and the stink met them both, stale straw, old hay gone sour, a rot that had settled into the rafters years ago and never left.
“Smells the same,” Weslin muttered, wrinkling his nose.
“Some things don't age well,” Harmon said. “Leave filth long enough, and it becomes part of the structure.”
They walked the long aisle, boots whispering over brittle straw. Light fell in narrow shafts from the loft windows, catching dust that drifted slowly in the still air. Weslin remembered the last time he had walked this hall, shadow pressing every corner, his pulse loud in his ears. Now, with the sun at their backs, he noticed things he'd missed before. The narrowness of the passage. The thinness of the rafters. The way the table in the back room had seemed massive once, and now only looked worn.
He paused where the hall pinched in, just before the feed room. Last time he had kept close to the wall here, made himself small. His feet didn't do that now.
“It felt bigger before,” he said quietly.
“You were smaller,” Harmon answered. “And you carried less.”
At the hall's end the warped feed-room door sagged on its hinges as it always had. Harmon pressed it open and crossed to the back wall where the boards met unevenly. The ring brushed the wood. A faint click answered from somewhere inside the frame, and the hidden seam opened.
“Still standing,” Weslin murmured.
“Still keeping what it was built to keep.”
Harmon glanced back once before stepping through. “When we're done here, you go home for a while. See your family. Enjoy your time with them, there might not be much moving forward. It is ok to tell them what you've done and what it's made of you, all of it. They've earned the truth, and they love you enough to carry it with you.” Something showed in his voice that rarely reached his face. “We've learned too well how short that window can be.”
Weslin swallowed hard. “I will.”
“Good. When you're ready, there's more to learn. Blade, shield, oath, what it costs to hold another person's life in your hands. All of it.” He turned and stepped through.
Old air moved past them, stale leather, old ink, the musk of years pressed into the wood and the stone beneath it. Voices stirred in the shadows beyond. Harmon set his shoulders and went in. Weslin followed closely.
The room was smaller than memory had kept it. After Stormhaven, after the pass, most things were. It wasn't the place that had changed. It was them.
Several had already gathered. Aldrek stood near the table, broad and steady on the surface, though the way he held himself told the truth to anyone paying attention. Every movement measured, nothing spent that didn't have to be, a man whose reserves had been drained to the floor and had crawled back to just enough. Garran leaned against the far wall, arms crossed, shoulders set like a load-bearing beam. Ash sat hunched on a bench, scarred hands laced, eyes on the floorboards as if something still burned there just under the surface.
At the back, Taerel had settled into his chair with the particular ease of a man who has decided a room will accommodate him rather than the reverse. Aymir leaned forward on his elbows beside him, both brothers watchful but each in his own manner. Reau sat off to one side, coiled and quiet, present in body and somewhere else entirely in mind, his eyes fixed on a stretch of wall that had nothing on it.
The scrape of Harmon's boots drew attention without demanding it. Voices fell. Postures shifted. Every one of them was marked, some plainly in skin and sinew, some in the way they held their faces when they thought no one was watching. They were here. All of them. That alone was something.
Weslin's eyes moved around the room with a different kind of attention than he'd carried the last time he stood in it. He caught the scratches gouged into the chair legs, the ink stains on the corner desk where someone's pen had gone wrong years back, the grooves worn into the floor by chairs dragged forward and back over time. His voice came out hushed. “Feels different this time.”
Harmon allowed himself the smallest smile. “That's because you're not the boy in the corner anymore. Once you sit at the table, nothing looks the same again.”
“Sir, it also feels like I found a place where I belong. I am one of them, not just someone watching. Thank you, sir,” Weslin said.
“No thanks needed, you were destain for this path son. We can discuss this more in the coming days.” Harmon replied
Across from the door, Nyssa sat alone, her chair turned just slightly from the rest. Her eyes were fixed on the two empty seats in front of her and hadn't lifted when Harmon entered. She stared at those chairs with the deliberate attention of someone who has decided that looking away would be a mercy she didn't deserve. Two chairs. Two names pressing on her chest with a weight that felt physical. Guilt had settled into her the way cold settles into stone, all the way through, into everything.
Harmon's gaze moved there and away. He didn't press it.
He crossed to the head of the table, set both palms on the scarred wood, and let the silence thicken until it had weight of its own.
“You're all here, well the majority of you.” he said at last, voice even and heavy together. “By blood and steel and the kind of sacrifice coin doesn't repay. I count it no small thing to stand in a room with every one of you still breathing.”
He drew a flat leather case from inside his cloak, set it on the table, and opened the clasps. Inside lay neat rolls of parchment, each sealed with the personal wax of King Edric himself, the mark pressed deep enough to leave no argument about where it came from. Beside them, purses with enough weight to announce themselves.
“Your pay.” He nodded to Weslin, who stepped forward and moved the length of the table, setting each scroll and purse down with both hands. “And more than pay. These are pardons, signed by King Edric. Whatever you carried into this, it's gone. Every charge. Every warrant. Every name on a list in some magistrate's drawer. Clean. You walk free.”
The words went into the room and didn't come back.
Garran's hand shook as he broke his seal. He didn't open it. He pressed it, still rolled, to his chest and held it there with both fists. Ash made a short, dry sound too tired to be a laugh, muttered something no one caught, and tucked his away inside his coat. Taerel accepted his with a flicker of a smirk that didn't quite hide the weight of it, trading a look with Aymir that held what neither chose to say aloud. Aymir's nod was brief and real.
Aldrek took his scroll in both hands and bowed his head over it. The motion was small and cost him visible effort. He said nothing.
Reau's lay in front of him, untouched. His eyes came up to Harmon.
“Yours is a different matter,” Harmon said. “We talk after.”
Reau held the look and gave one short nod.
Nyssa's scroll sat in front of the empty space where her attention had gone. She hadn't reached for it. She hadn't reached for anything.
Harmon let the room settle, let the sound of seals cracking and purse strings being tested fill the quiet for a moment, then drew a breath and brought them back.
“Before I ask anything of you, you're owed something first. The whole picture. Not the piece of it you stood in.” He looked around the table. “We fought this in two places. Most of you only know one of them. I won't be the only voice in this room laying it out, because most of you lived parts of it, I only heard about secondhand. So, we tell it together, and when we're done, everyone in this room knows what everyone else paid.”
No one moved for a beat. Then Harmon began.
"Stormhaven. We went in blind. Find out what happened to a city that went dark without a sound. Scout it, get the governor's family out if they were still alive. No messenger had come out. No flares. Just refugees stumbling south with whatever they'd kept in their heads."
He turned it over to the floor.
"Riven got us in," Ash said, picking it up, the dockside push in his voice. "Old fencing runs under the city. Thieves' road. The kind you can't buy a map for, because the men who knew it would sooner take a knife than sell it. Without him we're standing outside a wall the whole trip." He scratched a thumb along his scarred jaw. "City was scrubbed clean by the time we got down there. The Veydrassil had swept the streets till nothing was left moving. People didn't lose a fight. They got caged, and most never knew by what."
"There was a presence over the city," Aldrek said, the grave weight in it the priest gave anything that mattered. "The Red Cloaks raised it from inside the walls, anchored to something old buried beneath the streets. A ward, broken by the time we found it. Built to keep something in, and to hide what it was." He paused, the words deliberate. "When it failed, we glimpsed a part of what it had been hiding. A Warbeast."
The room had gone very still.
Harmon took it back. "What met us above was bad enough on its own. I'll give you the name, because it's the name it is." He said it plainly. "Sythrael Korr."
The effect moved through the room at once. Taerel's ease left him. Aymir's elbows came off the table. Garran's arms uncrossed. Even Reau turned from the wall.
"Korr is a knight of the Nine," Harmon said.
The shift that followed was hard to name. Not panic. The stillness of people who've just heard something old and large enough that it had stayed in stories rather than memory. Ash sat back slow. Garran's shoulders pressed flat to the wall behind him, as though the wall had become necessary.
Ash leaned forward. "The Nine. All of them, then. Loose."
"No." Flat and immediate. "The Nine are where they have always been, and by everything I know they stay there. This was one of their knights. Korr, and Korr alone. He found a crack the rest never have, and what came through wasn't whole. Not yet." He let that sit. "If the Nine themselves were loose, we would not be sitting here drinking the same air. I'd have you scattered to the four corners of the realm, and I'd be somewhere else entirely."
That settled some of them. Not all.
"There was something else," Harmon said, and his voice dropped, which was more than most things made it do. "Something I can't name yet with the certainty it deserves. Korr was a herald. This was the thing that sends heralds. I saw enough of it to know what I was looking at, and I have hoped a long time that I never would. Until I'm sure, it does not leave this room. Not a word of it. We don't even speculate where others might hear."
No one pushed him.
"The family came out alive," Aldrek said into the quiet, the court polish sharpening rather than softening as he held something hard. "Korr's projection cost him across that distance. Every blast he threw, he paid for twice. Threw me through a stone wall, and I got up anyway, which is the only reason some of us are sitting here.”
Harmon then finished it up, “They got them out. Then I split us up at the clearing and sent a group northwest to find the other team. Now, what happened at the pass?” Harmon said to hand it off, then looked to the brothers. 
Aymir sat forward. There was nothing ornamental in his voice, military-clean, structured, but not without warmth even now. He spoke it the way a man speaks something he's run through too many times in the dark to keep any illusions about.
“Luca's team moved on an Orc war camp holding the pass. The plan was Luca's. He went in alone the night before and salted their stores, the stew, the meat, the ale, four poisons, each built for a different job. Come dusk they gathered to feed like they did every night, and we hit them from the ridge with poisoned shafts while they dropped.” He stopped. “It worked. For a while it worked too well. We came down to finish it and that was when the ground opened.”
His thumb moved once against the table and went still.
“They'd been digging the whole siege. Every bombardment we counted, every volley we logged, all of it was cover for the sound of it. A tunnel under the far tents. When it broke open the Joblins came out of it in the hundreds, Goblins running them from behind. We'd been watching the wrong battle the entire time and none of us knew it until the dirt came up.” He let that sit. 
“We held the line as long as men can hold against something that doesn't care how many of itself it loses. Then the poisoned Orcs started standing back up. The stuff hadn't finished them. Twelve of them rose out of the dead and came at our backs. Complete chaos.”
Ash made a sound that wasn't a word and pressed a fist against the table's edge. Garran's head had gone down, one hand flat on the wood.
"Lysana was covering Luca." Aymir got the name out and something in his face moved that he couldn't stop. He pressed the back of one hand hard against his mouth, held it there, breathed through it. "She saved him three times over that night. The last time she dropped two that had him flanked, and they just looked at each other across it. Half a breath." He stopped again. This time it didn't pass. He gave a short shake of his head and looked down at the grain, and his shoulders told the rest of it while his voice wouldn't.
Taerel took it up quietly, not looking at his brother, giving him the room. "A Joblin came from above her. Luca saw it coming and threw and knew he'd be short. He was. It put the blade in her neck before his ever landed." His thumb pressed slow against the wood. "He killed it in the same breath. It didn't matter. She was already going."
“After that,” Aymir said picking the brief backup. “Luca went dark. Not cover. Dark in a way none of us has a name for. The whole grove went black around him, and it wasn't the absence of light. It was a presence, the kind that presses on the lungs. When it lifted, nothing on that field was moving but us. He walked off after. No word. No stop. We've had nothing from him since.”
The silence held that. The ones who had been in the tower were hearing the pass for the first time. The ones who had been at the pass were hearing the tower. All of it in the same room now, the same shared weight, nobody carrying their piece alone anymore.
Harmon let it work, then let it go.
“While we were gone, the war reached home, too.” Harmon's tone shifted, the briefing cadence giving way to something he was carrying straight off the road. “I've just come from the king. There was an attempt on Edric's life during the Feast. Governor Drake was the hand meant to do it.”
Harmon then recounted what happen at the palace, he then went on, “Edric was already wearing mail under his coat. The blade turned on steel. Drake broke and confessed all of it, the steward behind it, the whole arrangement. His family was reached in time. They're alive.”
“How'd the king know to wear the mail?” Garran asked.
“Because the warning reached him,” Harmon said, “through a channel most of the court doesn't know exists.” He turned slightly toward the corner where a man had been sitting quietly since before any of them arrived. “Which brings me to the one some of you have been wondering about.”
The man stood, easy, with the manner of someone who has never once needed to fill a room with noise to own it. “Adin,” he said. “Collector of rare things, keeper of other people's secrets, and the reason a fair number of you still have heads on your shoulders.” The grin was real, the sharpness behind it sharper. “The note that put the mail under the king's coat that night. The whisper dropped in the right ear to move a caravan that was need, that was me.”
He raised his right hand. The ring on it was the twin of Harmon's. The company drew breath as one. Even the brothers went still.
"Adin is a Ringbearer," Harmon said, and gave that a moment to land. "There are fewer of us than fingers on my hand, and I trust him further than I trust most things in this world. Everything he just laid claim to, he did. All of it his." He let it carry. "Every one of you owes a piece of still breathing to a man you never knew was there. I wanted you to know it before I ask you anything else."
Adin dipped his head at that and said nothing yet.
Harmon brought their eyes back to him. "Which is why I asked you here. Not to pay you and pardon you and send you off, though you've earned both and both are done." He set his palms flat on the wood. "I have believed one thing my whole life, through every rank I ever wore. A handful of the right people, aimed right, does what an army never could. You proved it. Four of you at that pass limited what the enemy took out of it. You didn't stop the war. Nothing stops a war. But there are soldiers marching on Aldoria right now who will live because of tunnels you mapped and patterns you learned with your own blood. Fewer graves get dug because you were there. That is not a small thing. That is the whole thing."
He looked around the table.
"And there are things coming that no soldier and no column will ever be a match for. You saw one under Stormhaven. A man doesn't line up against that and win by counting heads. It takes people who can find the one blade in a field of blades and pull it before anyone knows a hand moved. People who can act and leave no name behind, so a strike inside one kingdom never becomes a war between two." He paused. "That is what I mean to build. Not soldiers. Something quieter, and a great deal worse to be on the wrong end of."
He drew a breath, and the set of him changed, the weight of a thing already done rather than one still being decided.
"This morning, I stood before Edric Wymark and I resigned my commission. I am no longer of the crown's staff." He paused before he closed it. "He let me go with his blessing. More than that. He gave me leave to carry this work forward on my own, answering to no throne and no court. We serve the good of the realm. We do not take our orders from whoever happens to sit above it. When a king is worth standing behind, we'll stand there gladly. When he isn't, we owe him nothing, and no one will ever know we were in the room."
Adin spoke into that, dry and easy. "Which raises the question a room like this always gets around to. Who pays for it." The grin came back, thinner. "Not a treasury. Not some lord with a ledger who can call the debt due the moment we turn inconvenient. The men we go after are rarely poor. They hoard. Coin, land, goods that don't survive a close question about where they came from. We take it off them, and it funds the next one. Every bastard we put in the ground pays for the bastard after him." He spread his hands. "No paymaster. No leash. The work feeds itself."
"And here is where he sits in it," Harmon said. "Adin doesn't ride out with you, except under a need none of us want to see arrive. His ground is the work behind the work. The eyes and the ears. The map of a place set down before your boots ever touch it. He gets you what a mission needs and he sees what you can't from inside it." His voice went flat and final. "In the field you answer to him the way you'd answer to me, because when he asks a thing of you, I am the one asking. And if Adin is the one asking, the situation is already past the point where anything else will do."
Adin eased back where he stood, unhurried. "My reach runs wide, and runs at every level. Tavern cellars in port towns. Correspondence rooms in kingdoms that would not open their gates to us. I have people in places our enemies are certain are safe, and they tell me what those people would much rather keep quiet. Targets. Routes. Names. What's planned, and when, and by whose hand." The grin dropped into something cleaner. "What I don't have is anyone who can act on it. That's you. I hand you the picture and the means to move inside it. You do the work. You never walk into a room I haven't already mapped."
"There's a war ahead of us no matter what any of you chooses tonight," Harmon said. "The alliance army is already moving to take Aldoria back and free the people still under the heel of what did this. They'll manage it. It'll cost, and it'll be slow, the way armies are slow, because a column has to be seen to move, and everything that can see it gets a say." He let it sit. "A team like the one I'm putting in front of you changes that math. We go where the column can't. We cut the throat the army would lose a hundred men reaching. Aldoria comes free faster because we're doing the one thing an army was never built to do. That isn't a boast. That's just what you are, used the way you were meant to be."
He set his hand flat on the wood.
"And it won't end with the enemies who wear the name. There are men who sleep safe inside this alliance, who carry its banner and prey on the very people they were set over to protect. Men who believe a title and a treasury and a high wall put them past anyone's reach. We will teach them otherwise. In their coffers. In their names. And when it comes to it, in their blood. No throne will send us to do it, because no throne can be seen to. That is exactly why it falls to us."
The room held it without moving. “What I will tell you is this. The ones who aren't in this room paid the real price for what we're about to start. What we are building here was bought with what they gave. I mean to make it worth that. I need to know if you do too.”
Garran's eyes had come fully up. The storm-dark steadiness in them said he'd heard that part clearly.
"I know what you're carrying," Harmon went on, quieter now. "I know the ghosts that followed you off that ridge and out of that city. Lysana. Riven. Luca, wherever he's walked to. Aurelia is still fighting her way back at my manor, and Neavin hasn't left her side, which is the only reason the two of them aren't in this room tonight. But I've spoken with Neavin, and he's already given me his answer. He's in. Whenever Aurelia is strong enough to speak for herself, I expect she'll have her own." He let it rest. "Every one of you came into this with something and is leaving with more than you came in with. That's the real cost, and I won't stand here and call it clean or fair."
The room was filled with silence, nothing moved. Before the silence could close around them all, Reau pushed his chair back. The sound of it cut sharply through the quiet. He stood without looking at anyone, hands flexing at his sides, eyes on the door.
“You've been family to me, Harmon,” he said, voice low and direct, few words and no flourish. “What you gave me when I had nothing doesn't get forgotten. You know that.” He stopped, something tightening behind his face. “But I have a hunt that isn't finished. My father was betrayed and murdered by the same people who turned on this realm, and the ones who did it are still breathing. I won't sit at any table, this one included, while that's true. None of you would sleep right knowing I was out there with it undone, and I won't ask you to.” He looked at Harmon. “I'm sorry.”
He turned for the door.
“Reau.” Adin's voice was quiet, but it stopped him. The shadow man pushed off the wall and crossed the room without hurry, drawing a folded scroll from inside his coat as he went. Harmon moved to meet them, and the three of them stood close by the door, heads low, the scroll open between Adin's hands.
The rest of the room caught nothing but fragments. Adin's voice, pitched low. “Path's already cut.” Harmon's, lower still. “Closer than you think.” And then, from Adin, almost gentle: “Your hunt ends here, if you let it. We've been building toward the same thing from different ends. You just didn't know whose hand was on the other end of it.”
Whatever was written on that scroll, Reau read it twice. His jaw worked. His eyes moved over it a third time as though the words might rearrange themselves into something he could refuse.
Then his voice was loud enough to carry. “All right. I'll hear it out. I'll stay for that much.”
He came back to his chair and sat, the scroll folded small in his fist. His shoulders were still tight, and the set of his face said the decision was costing him even as he made it. He'd made it anyway. That was enough. Whatever the rest of that scroll said, he kept it to himself, and no one asked.
Before Harmon could bring the floor back, Nyssa stood, sharp and sudden, and heads turned. She stood with her hands at her sides and her eyes moving around the table without settling, without finding the one face she couldn't trust herself to find yet. When she spoke, the words came fast, the way words come when the fear is that slowing down means they stop.
“I want to say yes,” she said. “I do. But I can't. Not yet. There's something I owe first, and until that's done, I'm not in a position to give what being here would ask of me.” She stopped, steadied herself. “When it's done, I'll be back. That's not hope. That's what's going to happen.”
Harmon's nod was slow. “Then the door is open when you're ready.”
“Thank you.”
She reached out and picked up her pardon. Left the coin where it sat.
And then, because she had spent the whole of this gathering refusing to look, refusing to let herself confirm what she was afraid to confirm, and because some part of her had known since she sat down that she could not walk out of this room without doing it once, she looked up and around the room.
Dain was there.
He had been there the whole time, seated beside Aldrek, still enough and shadowed enough behind that broad frame that when she'd come in with her eyes already going to the empty chairs, she built her guilt around them both. She did move her eyes for a long moment seeing him there. Sitting with the particular stillness of a man who has come through something and knows it and isn't ready to call it over yet. His face was the face she knew, unscarred, because Aldrek had spent what was left of himself making certain of that, but his eyes were older. Not in years. In what they had kept.
He was looking at her.
No accusation. No demand. Nothing that asked her to be other than what she was. Just the same thing he'd been telling her since the dock, the same thing he'd been trying to tell her for longer than either of them had admitted, quiet and patient and entirely certain.
I'm still here.
Her breath caught. She held his eyes for as long as she could, which was not long, and then she looked away and walked to the door. The latch clicked. She was gone.
Nobody rushed to fill the silence. Dain's hand had moved to his cane without him noticing it there. Nobody said anything about it.
The lantern shifted in a draft. The stable groaned once above them.
Harmon let it breathe, then set his hand flat on the scarred wood, the ring catching the lantern light, and looked at each of them in turn.
“Who stands with me?”
Aldrek rose first, slow and deliberate, his mace-hand flexing once as if testing what remained in it and finding enough. “I do. For faith. By the will of God the Creator. And for those who gave more than we can pay back.”
Dain followed. His leg took its moment, nothing broken, nothing Aldrek hadn't mended, but a body doesn't forget what was done to it on a dock in the dark no matter how clean a healer leaves the bone. He came upright carefully. When he spoke, it was quiet, the polish steady over the ache underneath. “I'm in. Because walking away would mean it broke me.” A pause, short and certain. “It didn't.”
Aymir and Taerel exchanged one of their wordless conversations, the kind that had run between them their whole lives, fluent in everything that didn't need saying. Aymir's half-smile settled it. Taerel drew a slow breath out through his nose and let one brow rise.
“I find,” he said, with the unhurried precision of a man who has weighed exactly how much a moment is worth before he speaks into it, “that the company is poor, the pay irregular, and the lodging a stable.” He let it hang. “And yet I cannot think of anywhere I would rather suffer all three. We shall remain.”
Aymir put out his hand. Taerel looked at it a beat in the way he looked at most things before he accepted them, then clasped it firmly, and the two shook once. That was the whole of it, and from the brothers it was a great deal.
Ash leaned back, smirk sharp under eyes that hadn't slept right in four days. “You're all insane, you know that. But hell, I like insane. Count me in, long as nobody objects to the occasional fire.”
The laugh that came was not clean or comfortable. It was the kind that escapes when grief and exhaustion have run long enough that something absurd finally catches them off guard, the seal cracking just a little. It moved around the table in pieces, a sound from Aymir, a breath from Aldrek, the slow release from Taerel. Even Dain's face came loose for a moment.
Then Garr.
He stood slowly, the kind of slowly that says this matters, and the silence gathered around him the way it gathers around a man who has carried something long enough that the room can feel its weight.
“If I do this,” he said, his voice rough with something he wasn't going to name, “there's one condition. No more half-name. Not Garr.” He stopped. Said the rest plainly. “Lysana gave me that name. It was hers to give, and it stays with her.” His eyes were dry. The weight in them was not. “If I stand here, I stand as Garran Thornebrook.”
The name landed the way names land when they've been held in silence too long and are finally set down in a room able to hold them. Heavy. Permanent. Real.
Harmon inclined his head, and when he gave the name back, it carried the weight of a recognition. “So be it. Garran Thornebrook.”
One by one the rest gave their answer. No vow spoken in unison. No recited oath. Just a circle of people who had bled together choosing to do it again, each in their own way, each in their own time, the ones not in the room present in every word and in the silences between them.
Harmon watched every face. The circle was smaller than when this began. He didn't look away from it. He let himself see it plainly. The empty chairs. The coin was still sitting on the table where Nyssa had left it. The absences pressed down heavier than furniture. What Lysana gave at that camp. What Riven gave on a dock in the dark. What Luca carried off that field alone, walking away from a fight he'd just won without once looking back. What Aurelia was still climbing out of, four days on, at his manor. What Aldrek had spent of himself to keep one more of them breathing, to include himself.
“Go to your families,” he said at last. “The ones who love you and the ones you love. Time is a cruel thief. Every one of us has watched it cut a life short without warning or courtesy. Don't waste the days that are yours.”
He let a breath move through him.
“My manor is open to those who'd rather stay close and when you return. When Weslin comes back from his family, he'll need a hand with the blade. I expect more than one of you to be there for it.”
That pulled something from the room. A dry, wry stir. Taerel elbowed his brother, the two of them sharing the private grin of men who had just signed onto something larger than themselves and weren't above enjoying it. Ash muttered something about fire being a more useful trade than sword work. Garran's shoulders squared like a man who'd already decided.
	
Harmon's gaze moved last to the empty spaces. Not the chairs alone. The shape of what was gone, the absences with more weight than anything in the room that still had a body attached to it. His voice softened, but the thing beneath it didn't.
“We buried friends. We bled past what any accounting could hold. But what we've built here, out of ruin, out of broken pieces, out of people who had every reason in the world to walk the other way, it will hold. And if we carry it honestly, it will be worth what it cost.”
He stepped back from the table and stood straight in the lantern glow.
The weight in the room was not silence. It was something built of grief and purpose together, the kind of resolve that doesn't come from the absence of loss but from the decision to carry it forward anyway. Garran bowed his head, fists at his sides. Aldrek murmured a prayer too low for the rest to hear. The brothers shared a nod slower and more serious than their usual. Ash, for once, kept his quiet.
Dain used the table to push himself upright, the phantom weight dragging at a leg that had been healed whole. His eyes going not to the floor but to the others, one by one.
And Weslin, still at Harmon's shoulder, stood straighter than he had walking through the stable doors that morning. The boy gone from his face. The beginnings of something harder and more deliberate settling in its place.
Harmon nodded once to them all.
“Go.”
The scrape of chairs. The rustle of cloaks and the low murmur of words already moving on to the next thing. Footsteps out through the stable and into the morning. One by one they filed past, each carrying what they'd come in with and something more that hadn't been there before.
On the table, in the space where Nyssa had been, her coin lay untouched.
Harmon looked at it once.
Then he walked out and left it there.






Epilogue
The chamber was silent, save for the drip of unseen water and the faint rasp of cloth against stone. It might have been underground, or in the hollow belly of a fortress long abandoned. It didn't matter. The air was damp, heavy with a salt-bitter tang that clung to the walls, and the only light came from the thing in the center, a mirror framed in iron so black it drank the torchlight. Its surface did not reflect. It rippled faintly, as if its silver skin were water disturbed by a breath too shallow to hear.
Before it stood Zhaelor, his long fingers clasped before him. The ridges of his head gleamed with a dull sheen, his eyes entirely without surface, the kind of eyes that took everything in and gave nothing back. Even in stillness, he was not still. The thing that moved was not his hands or his posture but something behind his face, measuring.
"My lord," he said at last, his voice low, resonant, devotion held at arm's length from something older and colder underneath. The mirror's surface shivered, and with it came a voice, calm, distant, yet filling the chamber as though it seeped into the stone itself.
"Speak."
Zhaelor bowed his head. "The first foothold is secure. Stormhaven reels, its wards shattered. Sythrael Korr commands in our name. Your knight returned to you. The city's council stumbles like blind men, ripe for plucking. The populace is already under our hand."
A pause. The mirror's surface trembled with a flicker of heatless light.
"But," Zhaelor admitted, his mouth tightening, "there was a complication. The governor's family was not killed. They were recovered. A small fracture in the plan, nothing more. The governor yet breathes."
The voice in the mirror did not rise, but its stillness made the air itself heavier. "And the king?"
"King Wymark remains himself." Zhaelor's tentacled mouth pressed flat. "Drake broke before the final bell. When he moved, the King was already wearing steel beneath his coat. A whisper reached him ahead of the blade, not one of ours. The changeling was in the hall and could only watch."
For a long moment, the mirror gave nothing back. Then, at last, it spoke. "Do not gnaw on scraps, Zhaelor. The governor's kin were never more than a distraction. As for the king…" The voice grew smoother, almost indulgent. "I will dispatch another hand. A different servant will see to him. Do not trouble yourself with Wymark. His kingdom is already ash in the making."
Zhaelor's eyes narrowed. "Another hand? Another lieutenant?"
"Yes," said the voice. "Hidden from even you, as you were hidden from her. My reasons are my own."
Zhaelor's lips thinned, though he bowed once more. "As you command."
"And my sons?"
Zhaelor answered without pause. He had expected the question. "The first delivered what is left of the Brotherhood to your cause, and in doing so, destroyed what remained of their order from within. The traitor Arthur was slain in doing so, as you desired. The changeling nearly broke the king's line, but the window closed before he could move. Both still serve. Both are weapons loosed."
"Good." The mirror pulsed faintly, and something pleased moved under the calm. "Let them be storms without tether. The kingdoms cannot fight a thousand tempests at once. Spread them thin. Break them piece by piece, until even their stories are dust."
Zhaelor inclined his head. "The Morlin legions wait. They are ready to march at your word."
The mirror's surface flared once, a dull heartbeat of pale fire, before it stilled again. "Then march they shall. And you, Zhaelor…" The voice softened, and the softening was the threat. "Prince of my new kingdom. Steward of what I claim. Do not fail me again."
The iron frame groaned as though something pressed against it from the other side, and then the mirror fell still. The chamber darkened, and the cold settled back in.
Zhaelor stood alone, the torch guttering at his side. For a long time, he did not move. His long fingers flexed once, then curled back into his robes. In the silence, he spoke words not meant for any ear but his own.
"In the end, my lord… we shall see whose chains hold whom."
The mirror gave no answer. Only the steady, dripping silence remained.
***
The river town had no name worth remembering, a clutch of warehouses and weather-worn inns where barges stopped only long enough to trade, drink, and leave again. Locals called it Darrowmere, after the black stretch of water that bent around its edge. To Nyssa, it felt less like a town and more like a shadow someone had forgotten to sweep away.
The warehouse she sought leaned half-sunken into the mud near the riverbank, its roof sagging, its shutters nailed tight. Lantern light flickered faintly from cracks in the boards, though no footsteps stirred. The air inside stank of damp wood and rat musk.
Nyssa slipped through a side door, boots whispering over warped planks. The silence was thick, the kind that pressed against the ribs. She gripped the hilts of her daggers, though her fingers trembled.
A hand settled on her shoulder.
She spun, blade half-drawn, only to freeze.
Luca stood in the gloom as though carved from it. His storm-gray eyes glinted with a light that belonged to something older than him. His coat, torn and dark from battle, pulled the shadows toward him.
He led her deeper into the dark. The only light came in thin ribbons leaking through cracks in the boards. A small fire burned in one of the corners. 
"I heard your cry," he said. His voice was low, and it had weight to it, the kind that bypassed the ears and landed somewhere behind the sternum. "We will have our justice."
Something went still in her chest, then kicked hard. "Justice?" she whispered. "Or vengeance?"
He tilted his head, almost smiling. "Both. Always both."
Her grip on the dagger slackened. Her unease did not. "What do you have planned?"
"What I always do." Something underneath his voice moved when he said it, and the shadows in the room shifted with it.
She swallowed. "And what is that?"
He paused. "Did the brothers never tell you who I am? What I am?"
Nyssa shook her head. "No."
For a heartbeat, something flickered across his face. Surprise, regret, distance. His gaze dropped, and he exhaled through his teeth, muttering as though to himself. "I stayed too close. Too long." Then the distance closed back over him. "It doesn't matter. Not now."
He lifted his hand. Between his fingers gleamed a shard of black stone, polished smooth as glass. Power hummed faintly from it, a sound that felt more in the bones than in the ears.
"I've accepted your contract," he said. "As I hold this." He turned the shard once in the light. "This once was in Adin’s hand, as it has been through thousands of others. Now it is mine. It came to me at the pass. Now I decide where justice is owed. I hear the prayers of those whom others have failed." He closed his fist around it. "I am finally trusted and ready to hold it. For you, I offer a choice. I can see to this myself, or I can give you the means to take that justice with your own hands. I offer you a different stone. At a different price."
"If I walk this path with you," she asked, her voice small, "what does it mean?"
He stepped closer, the shadows coming with him the way shadows do around a man who has stopped casting one of his own. "It means severance. No ties. No connections. If you become what I am, you will no longer be Nyssa Quill. You will be a shadow, a whisper, a story mothers tell to keep their children in bed. A glance caught from the corner of the eye, and then nothing.” 
He moved around her as he said it, slow, unhurried, a man who had delivered terms that would not be offered again.
"And Dain?" The name slipped out before she could stop it.
Luca turned his back on her, speaking toward the flame. "I see your heart, and I will not pretend otherwise. If you want this power, he cannot be part of you. Not in love. Not in bond. Stand beside him if you must, fight beside him if fate wills it. But he cannot be yours. This is the price. My price."
Nyssa's hands shook. She looked down, and her gaze caught on the gloves she wore, the same ones from that night on the dock. She had never washed them, not truly. A faint stain lingered still, a smear of Dain's blood from when she had pressed her hands to his wounds, holding his life in while the river tried to take it. In her pocket, folded deep, she carried something else. A lock of his hair she had cut that night, when she thought he might not live. A piece of him, hidden.
Nyssa's fingers tightened unconsciously on the small token she'd carried with her from the docks. She shut her eyes, and for a heartbeat, the darkness gave her something softer than blood and grief. Dain's crooked grin when he'd teased her at the tailor's, the way his eyes had flicked nervously after the words left his mouth, as though he hadn't expected her to answer back. The brush of his shoulder against hers when they walked too close, neither giving ground. The night by the fire when she'd caught him watching her hands as she sharpened her daggers, and she'd asked if he wanted a lesson, half mocking, half invitation.
Flirtation had been their armor at first, a game they both knew the rules to. But somewhere between the danger and the silences, it had stopped being only a game. His voice had gentled when he spoke her name. She had found herself holding her breath, waiting for his laugh, his glance, his steadying presence. And when she thought she might lose him on that dock, when she saw him broken beneath those armored boots, it had torn something in her she hadn't been ready to name.
Her breath caught. She wanted to speak, to deny, to cling, but another memory came instead, sharp and unbidden. Riven's face. His grin, his lies, his loyalty. His sacrifice. The river swallowed him whole.
Her eyes burned. Her chest ached. She pressed her gloved hand over her mouth. Held it. Breathed.
When she lowered it, her eyes were dry. Her jaw set. She met Luca's gaze.
"I want it all."
Something shifted in his face. He reached inside his coat and drew out a pure black shard, larger and darker than the one he wore, an onyx the lantern refused. He had kept this one a long time. “It is a seed,” he said. 
He stepped in close and lifted his hand, pressing the shard of onyx against her chest. His other hand cupped the back of her head, steadying her as if she were prey about to be drowned.
He whispered words in a tongue she did not know. The sound was wrong, older than the river outside, older than the stone walls that held them. The shadows in the warehouse stirred, slithering across the floor toward them. They gathered, circling, tightening. They crawled up her boots, over her legs, winding up her arms, pouring into her mouth, her lungs, her veins.
Nyssa gasped. Her eyes flared blue, brighter, colder, unnatural. She staggered, then straightened, cloak now black as midnight, her old clothes burned away into something woven of shadow itself. Her hair blazed red in contrast, almost aflame in the gloom. Around her neck, where the shard had pressed, a necklace now hung, black onyx set in silver, pulsing faintly with power.
Everything she had worn, everything she was, burned away. It was all gone. She was remade into shadow. Everything but one thing. Deep in the dark of her new cloak, her fingers closed on the lock of hair, still folded, still his. The change had burned away the rest and left her that. She closed her hand around it and said nothing.
She looked at her hands, no longer trembling. She breathed, and the shadows breathed with her.
Her voice, when it came, was steady. "There's nowhere Merrick can hide now."
Luca smiled. "Good." He let his hand fall away, his shadow merging with hers until they were one. "Then let us begin."
The lanterns guttered out. Darkness took over the whole warehouse.
